Space Epic Untitled is a very simple space sim that would right at home on mobile if it was reworked but the way it is right now I couldn't recommend it to anyone. The fact that this game makes it hard for a person to actually play solo is already bad enough but to lock features that are behind a phone app makes no sense.
Don't expect any type of story here, there isn’t any to care about, and don't attempt to find a semblance of one in the "characters" (That's non-existent too) as the voice acting sound like the actors are friends of the devs who were bribed with a free meal if they said the lines. The game as it is right now is basically dead, its extremely rare to see other people playing and this game kinda requires other people playing otherwise your flying around dead space with nothing to do since matchmaking is incorporated in each chapter.
Gameplay for chapter 1 is basically: you the base hanger, go shoot some space rocks, collect ore, return to the base hanger to deposit the ore, upgrade weapons, rinse & repeat until match is over. which to your very dread is still 10mins+. Chapter 2 is the same but this time you are attacking an enemy star-ship/destroyer type, without other players to help take it down, so be prepared to die a lot. Whats worse is every time you die you are forced to watch cringey short videos, made by the actors or by other players...yup you can make short videos for other players to see with the mobile app...for some reason. The gameplay is very generic but would work far better for a mobile game.
The Graphics are what you would see from an mobile game on PC. The maps for chapter 1 & 2 are the same so be prepared for that sight to get stale very fast.
The Controls are pretty wonky, especially the mouse sensitivity. It was hard to control my ship at first but after a while you get kinda used to it. One of the big things they seem to be pushing with this game is their mobile app controller. It allows you to have 2 other friend playing besides yourself via a phone/tablet. They take up positions as either the engineer (video communication with other ships and can control you boost ability) or the gunner (more firepower via turrets and repairs shields). Sounds cool...its not as the fact there is hardly any one online to play with, what would your friends be left doing, and to make things worse you dont have access to these things in solo play, they limit the player on purpose.
The Sound/Music is generic, every chapter has its own specific song that plays and it plays over and over constantly. while not to annoying to me its still not forgivable.
There are better space sims to dive into and for free, just like this game here but don't be fooled but that free price tag, as this game does have a cost, and that is your dignity and sanity.

I almost abandoned this game shortly after starting it but I persevered through most of the game and now think it would have been better if I had given up right at the start. The main problem with the game is the combat. You start off as a melee fighter and the combat mostly relies on using combos. These require slowly pressing different combinations of the mouse buttons which feels unnatural as you expect the combat to be fast paced, they are easily interrupted too. After a while you unlock a ranged character which has a standard FPS style in combat and is quite fun to begin with. As the game progresses the fights get more drawn out and tedious, you end up just running round avoiding enemies, hitting them to remove tiny amounts of health until you finally wear them down. The game also keeps splitting up the party with most the boss fights being one on one, so once you find the character who suits you best you will still be forced to use the ones you hate.
Another thing that aggravated me was the amount of retracing your steps you have to do if you want to complete the side missions. For example in the first village you arrive at the villagers talk about a ship wreck and it must have been the Amazon delivery ship because half the village was expecting something on the ship. So this seemed like an easy bunch of side missions, just head down to the beach collect all the flotsam and return. However it doesn't let you collect all the items at once you have to go back and forth to the beach 3 times and of course all the enemies respawn. There is a fast travel system but that is only unlocked so late into the game I had already lost all interest in doing anything that might prolong the game.
The bit that finally got me to give up on the game was near the end you have to escort a character to safety and I had saved my game when this NPC had low health without realising that I could not use any of the many healing potions I had on her This meant that no matter what I did she immediately got killed in the next section of combat and I really couldn't be bothered to go back and try again from my last save point so I just looked up the ending on youTube.
Other minor annoyances were as follows. The camera controls, moving the mouse up and down does not rotate the camera up and down as you would expect, this is really disconcerting at the start but I got used to it. The voice acting is terrible, it is like they thought it would give the characters more life if they had a wide range of voices but they just ended up with a bunch of terrible stereotype accents. There is no mouse cursor in the menus, this creates the weird control scheme of being able to select items with a mouse click but having to use the keyboard to navigate the menu. The pre-rendered videos are terrible quality, much worse than the gameplay.
Credit where credit is due apart from the lack of cursor in the menus the PC port is actually decent. The visuals were pretty good, a little dated but still good. The story was entertaining too but not enough to make the game worth playing in my opinion.

This is a pretty good point and click adventure with really good pixel art, the few space landscapes it provides being the pinacle of that - including one that seems a mild 2001 refrence, one among plenty of other references, like Cowboy Bebop (which I really didn't expect at all here).
It has decent enough voice acting, but you can turn it off, if for some reason it bothers you, or if you're really retro..
The gameplay is quite something. Unlike a lot of other recent point and clicks where you mostly handle an inventory with combine features, and just click on an object to interact with it (whatever it is: looking, touch, take, etc), this game has a few extra options like: look, touch/take, walk.
Unfortunately this isn't to the game's advantage, if I can understand making look and interact different behaviours, I can't quite get the point of having anything more than that. Particularly in Gemini Rue a lot of the actions are just plain awkward to do with so many controls, and a mere interact would just make everything simpler, for instance: There's a point where you have to climb to a ladder, but you must first get on top of a box to reach it - how do you do this apparently simple action? Well, first you must "touch" the box, move it (A or D) then press W to go on top of it, and then press touch on the ladder. So now you're on top of a balcony, but wait - how do you come down? Well in that case you have to "walk" into the ladder, you can't "touch" it you have to "walk", and then S once on top of the box. Fairly non-sensical if you ask me. Even with these awkward moments because they're somewhat occasional they're not much of an hassle.
But then there's gunplay, yes, you read that, gun play in a retro p&c adventure. How does it work? Well, if you built a time maching and got a gun, whent back in time, and pointed said gun at the head of the developers of-- I don't know-- Beneath a Steel Sky-- and forced them to have gunplay in their game, I'm pretty sure they'd come up with something very similar to this. To answer the question: you use WASD + ctrl + R (+ whatever) to do things like: take cover, aim through the left, aim through the right, turn on a little bar that if you skillshot it right your character hits an headshot, change target, reload. Let's just say I appreciate the attempt, but it doesn't work all that well, better yet, it "works", and I'll leave it at that.
Most of this game's puzzles are fairly intuitive and I did most of this game by myself, but it couldn't be a p&c without a couple of off the wall puzzles. The first one comes up when delta-6 has to take a gun away from the testing room, I'd have never, ever in a million years figured it out. I'm not saying it doesn't make sense, it does, but it takes something like 20 steps, including taking an unsuspicous prop (that's not even clear that you can even take it) from an apparently unrelated room to solve it. Fortunately most of the game isn't like this.
Finally the story. It's decent, memorable even, or at least has memorable moments, and even interesting themes and undertones. Yet the twist is forseeable from 20 miles away, and isn't that worth it, I'll argue a better story could have come out of not having it at all. And the climax is nicely built up, but loses itself. And the final remark said by one particular characters doesn't help either. But considering what you usually get off of these games, this one is worth some praise.

The dual-pronged storyline features a former assassin trying to rescue his imprisoned brother, and Delta Six, an inmate in a detention centre, with severe amnesia. Eventually, these two stories mesh in a remarkably well-written plot.
Gameplay is simple enough, with regular point & click features with a dash of combat thrown in for good measure. It's not quite long - clocking up at about eight hours or so (without achievement hunting) but it's also under ten quid, so the trade-off is not unfair.

You are Azriel (!) Odin (!!) -- a trench-coated P.I. (!!!), former assassin (!!!!), and intergalactic-war veteran (!!!!!) -- who, with the help of his partner Kane (!!!!!!), must brave the always-raining planet Barracus (!!!!!!!) and its ruling cyberpunk (!!!!!!!!) Yakuza (!!!!!!!!!) before orchestrating the breakout of Delta Six (!!!!!!!!!!), a prisoner in an experimental brain-wiping facility (!!!!!!!!!!) run by a nameless "director" (!!!!!!!!!!!) that lies hidden inside a nebula (!!!!!!!!!!!!).  With ludonarrative consonance, Gemini Rue's gameplay is built around a "kick" command taken from Full Throttle, action gunplay sequences from Rise of the Dragon, Playstation-era box-pushing puzzles, and a simulation of cafeteria cliques. In short, the game is nothing less than the Trapper Keeper doodle fantasy of every dorky middleschooler hopped up on Cowboy Bebop, Blade Runner, and Max Payne. Its sheer exuberance stands naked before the player with prelapsarian shamelessness, and any past or present dork (myself included!) will share in that delight.
Gemini Rue is the game that built Wadjet Eye Games, and for that reason alone is worth your attention. Before its release, WEG had developed a few Blackwell titles and The Shivah, niche products that, despite well-earned fandom in the Adventure Game Studio community, could not support full-time development. After Joshua Nuernberger developed Gemini Rue and won acclaim for it at the Independent Games Festival, WEG savvily picked up the game as its publisher. Gemini Rue proved a runaway success in its own right, selling hundreds of thousands of copies and receiving numerous critical accolades. It was also a watershed: WEG went on to publish XII Games' Resonance, our own Primordia, and Technocrat Games' Technobabylon. These third-party titles financed WEG's shift to full-time game development, yielding fantastic titles like A Golden Wake, Blackwell Epiphany, Shardlight, and the upcoming Unavowed, all made by salaried staff.
Yet while every WEG title *after* Gemini Rue is a fairly sober-minded affair, Gemini Rue itself is all coltish enthusiasm. Primordia, Epiphany, Shardlight, Resonance, and Technobabylon all hope to be *digested,* while Gemini Rue just chants, "Chug, chug, chug." Little wonder so many people have loved it! By Odin, you should get drunk on it too!
[Disclaimers: I received this game for free from a Primordia fan who thought I should try it. Primordia was published by WEG, which also published Gemini Rue. Primordia and Gemini Rue were both made in Adventure Game Studio, and I'm a big supporter of adventure games, indie games, and especially indie adventure games made in AGS. So season this review with ample salt.]

I believe that at its core, this is a good game with an interesting story, but some of the basic elements I find mandatory for a good RPG game were just not present.
I found that the world was well crafted, it looked nice for a game of this time period. This is where the game really shines, I really enjoyed the diverse and creative map design that this game features. The character design was also very nice, featuring unique and well crafted characters.
The voice acting was a bonus for sure, but the dialogue overall did not feel at all natural, as if the dialogue was there only to quickly give you information relevant to the the story, delivering it in a way that felt forced.  It had no enjoyable feel to it. Although this did not affect the story in a large way, the player must 'translate' what came out of the dialogue and piece together the story which makes almost no sense at all until mid-game.
I'm not sure if I was missing something, but the battles were not fun at all. There are areas in the world that spawn enemies, locking you in the battlefield until all the enemies are defeated. This was frustrating because there is no opportunity to escape from a battle, there is no way around battle zones and you must replay the battle even when passing through a battle zone you have previously defeated. The battle system itself was not bad, but battles seemed to take a very long time, especially once enemies started regaining health. As the game progressed, the battles got only slightly more difficult, while the length got unbearably long as you deal minuscule amounts of damage.
The keyboard controls were terrible, making movement and battle very difficult. It is much, much better with a controller.
Overall, even for the $6 this game costs, I cannot recommend it.

If I have to compare this game to other titles, I'd say - Another World, Brothers, Ico, Shadow of the Colossus, Limbo. Action-adventures in which you care about someone else, and there's some form of drama.
Exploration and drama. That's what this game is all about. To some extent, it is inspired by the interactive hopelessness in the face of your impending doom, a theme explored by games like Shadow of the Colossus and Journey. But Submerged does something new with it. It is an emotional experience and goes in a direction that most games would never take.
It's quite shocking that the game is almost completely devoid of challenge. There's no violence even though there are scary things in the world. There are no puzzles, and you can't die. I usually hate games that don't offer challenge... but this game successfully challenged my obsession with challenge.
Because of the inability to die and make real mistakes, some people tagged this "a walking simulator", but the gameplay does way more than that. Just exploring the city, recovering its story, climbing buildings with the cute teen protagonist, searching for secrets, and being paranoid about things that may cause potential infection, and also, who's friend and who's foe, provided me with enough choice and thrill to keep playing.
Also, it's the first game I've played that does environmental storytelling so well - the first game that made me really enjoy piecing together the story of the city, of the world, of its inhabitants, of my own origin, all of that without any words being used, or explanations handed to me. You can even decipher the glyphs in the game in a very intuitive way.
The lack of violence allows for a unique way to relate to the other... lifeforms that you meet - your doubts, your fears, your hopes when you meet them wouldn't have been the same if you had a weapon you could wield whenever you felt insecure.
Finally, the way you're moving towards your inevitable doom just to help someone you love is done better than any other game I've played. Come to think of it, all 3 things mentioned in this paragraph (uncovering the story through the environment, dubious creatures that are maybe friends, maybe foes, and doom and self-sacrifice) are present in some form in Shadow of the Collosus, but I'd dare to say that this here is done better and affected me more (if it weren't for the ruined ending). It reminded me why playing and making games is worth it, something that all the noise around me makes me forget.
P.S. Unfortunately, the ending sucks.
Still, I usually care more about a game's idea than about its execution. I can't recommend this game enough.

I played the first Mass Effect on a console several years ago, and I loved it.
...before I rip this game to shreds...
There are a few good things that are worth mentioning...
First and foremost...
All the Mass Effect lore is there... and it is fantastic.
Lots of characters make reappearances, and this game provides a great nostalgia trip if you ever played the first game.
Although some things are a stretch... the game's creators did a great job of setting the stage for a Mass Effect sequel.
The choices/dialogue are probably one of the better aspects of this game, coupled with the Paragon/Renegate system which is cool.
...but I feel like none of it actually matters.  You can perform Paragon or Renegade interactions regardless of your demeanor.  (Its not like you are locked out of doing the good guy stuff for being a bad guy or vice versa)
This only compounds the already linnear and watered down feel this game has when compared to other games of this style.
Some other things that are bad are:
Tedious, forced minigames that aren't fun to open containers/get loot.
The over simplified weapon/loot system... You almost always find one of three things... ammo... credits... or lore.
every now and then you interact with something that automatically upgrades your equipment is some aspect... but you never even equip anything really besides choosing your equipment loadout... which is beyond boring.
The cover/aim/jump over system is terrible.
Running is awkward, and conflicts with the cover system... so you are fighting the game's controls more than you are fighting the actualy enemies sometimes.
overall the gameplay is just bad.
Not to mention this game is a port from a console game which comes with its own shortcomings.
The UI simply isn't optimized for PC, but it did not come with controller support...
For example:  Holding shift allows you to stop combat to make "precise" movements.... but the ♥♥♥♥ing mouse cursor is not in the same place as the crosshair where your character is aiming.
who the ♥♥♥♥ designed this garbage?
Overall this is a bad port of a mediocre game.

This game will hate you. It will leap up and slap you in the face. And as a result, you will never want to leave its side.
As a wise man once said: Life has no Ctrl 'Z'.
A great many things are beyond your control, unusual in a strategy game but far more true to reality.
Perhaps you will pause in your travels at a tavern, nurse a cool ale, and the tavern will explode, killing you instantly.
Son of a... Is nothing sacred?
Or maybe your favourite son will take over as regent when you grow old and decrepit, only to steal all your titles and imprison you.
Bet you're regreting your refusal to aid your brother in killing the little sod now, aren't you?
Perhaps you become just another in a long line to die from Medieval Europe's most dangerous plague - 'Suspicious circumstances'?
It's never entirely clear how suspicious they are, or what you're supposed to do about it, but you know what they say - Life's a female dog.
Or maybe, at the ripe old age of 84 you'll die from syphillis.
Irritating it might be, but you'll be unable to fight the surge of pride that you were still getting it on at an age when most men's fading eyesight ensures they can't even see the appropriate body parts any more.
And the list goes on: vassals tearing your Empires apart, mobs killing your tax collectors, rioting zealots, crusades, becoming blinded, castrated, imprisoned, diseased, incapable, having your son born the anti-christ, or, god forbid, losing your favourite hunting hound (why, why, oh cruel, wretched world?).
CK2 will punish you, and you will love every second of it, because when you do manage to pull everything together, nothing in life will bring you more joy.
Not since Firefly has anything been more deserving of the tagline 'Someone ever tries to kill you, you try to kill 'em right back.'

It´s not World of Tanks - but it doesn´t want to be.
It claims to be an arcade tank shooter.
In this perspective it´s a surprisingly good game. Take into account that it is still in dev and f2p.
Talking about f2p - it is NOT a pay to win. You can buy skins for real money, but that´s it.
Some skins are even purchasable via earnable game credits. In my book that´s a very fair thing, no cut-throats.
You earn credits quite fast, so there is no trouble with upgrading or buying new equipment.
From close to long ranged combat there is a weapon for everyone(no weapon is op, just better in a certain situation). You just have to find the tank/turret setup that works best for your playstyle.
The only things that annoy a bit are:
1. The lack of crating own games or joining as a group of friends(who knows, maybe this will be added).
2. The aiming system(for ranged weapons). When there a more than 1 enemy close to each other you might have troubles hitting the one you are aiming for. You can not lock onto a target. That means it can happen that you lower an enemy but fail to deliver the killing blow because your target switches unintentionally.
All things considered:
If you want a nice arcade shooter to pass some time - try it.

All indications so far are that the developers of PINBALL have spent about as much time on this game (especially since its release) as they did on the name. They failed to provide portrait mode (itself not actually all that uncommon among indie pinball developers) but they included controller input ONLY (and poorly at that, according to player response.) That means that without the option for rebinding keyboard keys, many players can’t play at all, or only with varying degrees of limitation.
Perhaps Pinball’s more serious transgression is to release on a Friday, assuming that numerous copies will be sold before the overused excuse of “Who works on a weekend?” expires on Monday. In other words, there has been ZERO developer response to issues brought forth in Pinball discussion forums. One presumes that developer baKno Games  will offer players their in-game online Support as reason to ignore Steam discussions, but most of what’s online is in the form of FAQ or player forums. And after 15 games, bakNo surely knows what Steam players expect, and that is to have all player issues available to them in one place, not to hide them (or themselves) online.
I said above that the developers of Pinball spent minimal time on “their” game. Well, not only have they ignored their customers thus far, but the entire premise of this game is that the players are supposed to be the ones doing most of the work, by means of a table editor included with the game. (What is offered on the Store Page is 10 baKno tables and “unlimited” player tables, a claim impossible to either measure or validate.) Perhaps this whole concept of “The Invisible Developers” was the entire strategy behind Pinball in order to emphasize the editor (and a strategy with some merit perhaps), but it’s sort of hard to place a lot of faith in a company that has released 14 of 15 Steam games for the same price….exactly $4.99. As in, “Hey! Let’s put a selling price of EXACTLY $4.99 worth of resources into a pinball game!” (Perhaps this "profit wall" is the reason for the lifeless “Custom” settings button.) Or perhaps this entire game serves no other purpose than to gain legal control of the name “Pinball”.
In full honesty, I haven't played any Pinball, but not for lack of desire. I'm one of many players that doesn't CHOOSE to rebind keyboard keys, but instead NEEDs to rebind keyboard keys to be able to play with my one good hand. (In literally thousands of hours of Steam pinball, rebinding to be able to play has never been an issue before.) I’ll wait to refund, but mainly in the event I need to have ownership to continue reviewing. And despite all I’ve said, the reason I purchased on Day One is that I really wanted more pinball. But only if it’s actual pinball, and so far, Pinball isn’t pinball.

Sudeki is a real time action rpg with a little bit of everything.
Set in a fantasy medieval era where two nations are at war, you play as a protagonist named Tal who assembles a party of somewhat unique characters that must learn to trust each other to meet their individual goals.
Of the four main playable characters, two are melee and two are ranged. Melee characters perform combos to attack, ranged characters have a FPS POV. Every character has their own skills that are almost identical to the others such as line, arc, and AOE, but also have unique powerful skills of their own.
Combat is clunky but is not hard to get used to. Once the player understands how to coordinate attacks and abilities between multiple characters combat becomes easy. Very easy unfortunately. However it is still very fun because the game throws multiple different types of enemies and enemy compositions at you that successfully winning with little to no damage taken feels rewarding. The player must learn to adapt to situations where they do not have a full party, are playing as a single character in some encounters, and during dreaded escort missions
One great aspect of combat is the ability to actively switch between different weapons. This allows you to use weapons that have increased damage at times when you need to burst, or when you need to steal life or mana, or dispel magic from enemies. Overall, combat in Sudeki is good and unique but has some balancing problems. For me the game shines in it's exploration.
The world is small but offers a lot of variety. Landscapes are cool, bursting with treasure to find, npc's to talk to that occasionally offer quests or information about the world. Dungeons are very much labyrinths that can be confusing to navigate along with some puzzles that range from ridiculously easy to one in particular that took me a solid 20 minutes to figure out.
For $6.00 I recommend this game to anyone at least willing to try it for 2 hours before deciding on finishing the game. A playthrough is short, clocking in between 15-20 hours.
As with all old games you have to play knowing the era. For 2005 everything is decent but lags behind. Compared to Fable which was released a year prior, the graphics and voice acting are a little dull.

Lots of people are talking about pros so I'ma share some cons.
This game will waste your time away, and by waste I mean WASTE. For starters you have to be save scum to the max. There are elements in the game that are insta-kill, and it will destroy you as simply as opening an unmarked door. Some battles will made you replay over and over and over and over again. Also if you don't invest in teleportation, you'll literally be dropped in a fiery pit with no means of getting out. Who knew? Or perhaps you'll enter a new area, be locked in a dialogue with no hope talking your way out, then being pulled into a fight and wiped out in the first turn (of course the enemy goes first...).
Long battles. Some people love the strategy in them. But as deep as the mechanics go, it gets pretty stale by your 100th tangle. What also gets stale is how long it takes for moves and attacks to animate out. If there are 10+ characters and an uneasy terrain, a fight can take well over 5 minutes, 10 minutes, and if you lose you'll have to redo it! (Unless you saved -midbattle).
Levelling system means in order to stay well equiped for adventure you'll need to spend about HALF OF YOUR TIME managing your inventory and buying/selling with merchants. You grow no attachment to your items, there is not a smug of aesthetic customization as most items both look the same and you can't see them until you put them on. Plus this isn't Skyrim so you can't just loot whatever exists in the game. Its more old school and loot is either randomly generated or placed.
A lack of seriousness. Sure there's a bounty of comedy in the game. But as far as I can tell you don't really get attached to any characters or their interests along the way. Sure there isn't a forceful light or dark path for you to take, rather its usually a I-Don't-Even-Care kind of path you end up on.
Level design is nothing new. Dragon Age has more memorable places and more interesting map corners.
Psychic enemies knowing your weaknesses. You'll literally need a mod in the workshop to make it a little more realistic and not computerized. Also you'll begin to realize that some battles have pre-programed movesets for the enemies, such as a marksman immediately teleporting to some far-reaching platform right away. This both makes fights really repetitive and also very procedural. PROCEDURAL.
Quests that don't Close. There's about a dozen or so quests that just won't Close properly. If you have OCD this game might just kill you. Plus the instructions are stylishly like a journal - in other words - often do not provide direct instructions. Think this makes it more immersive? NOT WHEN YOU HAVE NO IDEA WHAT YOUR CHARACTER EVEN MEANS IN HIS/HER OWN JOURNAL.
Soul-less characters. Revenge is a common option in the game. Most of the time its meaningless if the characters are described to be stoic and unhinged til oblivion.
90% of enemies know magic. 90% of enemies have ranged attacks. Even 'swordsman'. FYI.
Hotkeys that shift around even after you 'locked' them.
Confusing exterior-transitions. Usually to enter a building you have to click move into a space that isn't revealed yet (until you enter). How many times have I accidently 'stole' something as I'm trying to enter a building....
If you can overlook these gripes (and some others), then I'll recommend this game...

Wadget Eye Games has been releasing indie video games for a bit over than 10 years. They specialise in point-and-click adventure games - the games intentionally have pixelated graphics to remind us of the good old days when it comes to this genre. Gemini Rue is not the first in their library of software, but the first I picked up years ago and completed just recently.
What I like is that after a while in the story we are given the option to control 2 characters. We can switch between them whenever we want. Of course, once the individual story is completed for one we can only control the other for a while. Azriel is an agent of some sort who is looking for his brother on a planet called Barracus. Delta-Six, on the other hand, is a patient trapped in a facility far away who's desperate to find out more of his personality as well as to escape.
First and foremost this game has excellent storytelling. I thought Delta-Six is the actual brother Azriel is looking for but the revelation is more surprising once we get there in 6-7 hours. I have already mentioned the pixelated graphics the game has to offer - yes, this is a bit old-fashioned but the great voice acting, music and sound effects all help with the immersion. Remember the dialogues in the old LucasArts games? Here they do not appear right over the characters' heads but on top of the screen next to their portraits as their faces are not very detailed due to the pixels.
Beside interacting with our environment, solving puzzles and conversing with characters we'll do our share of combat, too. The game uses minimalistic mechanics for this purpose and these shooting sequences are the ones we can fail - rest assured the game does an autosave just before every encounter. Achievement hunters will like the idea of completing every sequence without losing any health so this is definitely a challenge for them.
As for achievements: there are a couple related to collectibles and my favourite was looking up words in the terminal you find on Barracus' streets. You have to search for some key words to make the story progress - you can look up other words to get more info on the world of the 23rd century and, most importantly, on what the Gemini War really was.
Gemini Rue is a great adventure game that offers a great story as well as the option to do additional walkthroughs in case of missed achievements and a developer commentary mode is available to hear some making-of monologues along with the bloopers of the voice actors. I highly recommend that you play this game if you like the genre.

Also, the animals! Some of the whales are so big, and don't get me started about those weird plant humans.
Nighttime and daytime are gorgeous in this game. The graphics aren't stunning, but that didn't mean I didn't love the way the water reflected the sky, sunrises/sunsets, and the rain for example.

I guess there's such a thing as too-early access, especially when a game is so similar to others which have had a lot more dev time. While I enjoy what actually works in Conan Exiles, this game has been out for over a month now and is still borderline unplayable. If you can get it to launch or connect at all, you probably won't go half an hour without running into crippling bugs and poorly designed systems. Patch progress seems to have slowed drastically, and each patch seems to break more than it fixes. Patches are released with known issues which will be fixed "as soon as possible" but still exist more than a week later after the next patch. Features are removed entirely because apparently exploits which revolve around them are too difficult to fix. Thralls, items, and buildings seem to disappear or become corrupted even on private servers when they're restarted or patched. I had hoped this would be a nice alternative to Ark because I really don't like how mount-focused Ark is, from gathering to combat. Conan has no mounts currently, and using this as a baseline for the design appeals to me a lot more. But in its current state and especially with the current pace of development progress, I can't recommend this game. So consider this an "early access review"... maybe I'll check back in 3 to 6 months to see if it's improved, and "patch" this review if it is.

This game has really great atmosphere.  That is because most of the content is ripped straight from the Wasteland/Fallout universe. I'm torn about this game because, quite frankly, the community is just awful.  Instead of Zone chat like in most mmo's, there's a Help chat.  It's filled with players that have been there for a while, but most of them have that whole "elite" attitude.  Help chat is supposed to be used for people with questions, thus the name.  These "Elitists" will use Help chat for anything they want, berate and accuse new players of trolling, then turn around and lecture everyone on the "proper way" to use Help chat.  The GM's are even worse.  They constantly hand out mutes/bans, but ignore any complaints towards the preffered players that have been there for a long time or spent probably $500 in the cash shop.
Also, the GM's are crazy about censoring peoples' screen names.  I had a name that wasn't even offensive, I played for a bit and when I came back, my name was Cupcake1244.  Yes, if they deem your name offensive, you get to roam the Wastelands as Cupcake____.  And you only get 1 character slot as a F2P player.  I contacted a GM about changing my name and guess what?  Oh, you can BUY a name change in the cash shop.  $10 because you got offended for no reason?  Hah!
Unfortunately, I'm the type of person that's going to argue right back with you when you're acting douchey.  So I told everyone off in Help chat and am uninstalling  :)
To sum it up, if you enjoy the crafting side of mmo's with a Fallout/Wasteland atmosphere, go for it.  But if you're not going to spend money on it, I'd suggest that you keep the chat window closed and just chat with people locally.  You're going to want to avoid these Basement-Dwellers.

Overall this is worth the time and money to play. I can't recommend it without qualification though.
PROS
-The story and writing are strong for a video game. Some interesting philosophical themes are raised and handled in an intelligent way, as befitting the sci-fi and cyberpunk genres. There are several twists that are well-executed and genuinely interesting instead of cheap.
-Puzzles are usually logical and well-integrated into the story and context. There were several occasions where I did what I would have if I faced the situation at hand in real life, and was able to smoothly solve the sequences without feeling like they were too simple.
-Voiceover work is good.
-At 5-6 hours of gameplay (I had the game minimized for a bit so my time is misleading), the length is good. It feels meaty enough to justify the price, without being long enough to overstay its welcome.
CONS
-The combat system involving shootouts is repeatetive, frustrating and tacked on. It's adds absolutely nothing to the experience except mild annoyance.
-Autosaves are relatively infrequent, but there are times when autosaves are automatically loaded upon death, even if you manually saved more recently...then you can't immediately load the manual save without going through a bunch of dialogue and scenes that happen immediately after the save point. This is very frustrating.
-Characters walk at a slow, casual pace even when this is completely inappropriate for the circumstances. The most infuriating example is one point where there are cylinders that drop from the ceiling and crush your character if they are standing under it, and you must walk across the room and avoid this. The cylinders drop slowly and could be easily avoided by jogging, and yet your characters casually stroll along and will be killed if you don't execute the sequence perfectly (to make things even more annoying, this is immediately followed by the aforementioned automatic loading of an autosave).
-As with every single point and click adventure/puzzle game I've ever played, there are a few puzzles that are illogical and/or immensely frustrating. I did need to consult a walkthrough on a few occasions, and without exception I was left feeling that the puzzle design and not my own incompetence was at fault.
-There were a few occasions where the way of interacting with certain objects was counter-intuitive, contradicting existing ways of doing things established within the game, and were just frustrating.

Overgrowth is a third person action game where you get to play as giant rabbits, rats, wolves and more fighting against other rabbits, rats, wolves and more. The game's main selling point is it's brutal combat which is best witnessed in the arena where you are automatically pitted against enemies either with your bare hands or with one of the game's few weapons. If you don't want to play the arena you can wander around one of the game's other maps and if you wish you can even spawn in enemies to take on. Despite all of these features the game has one glaring issue which completely changes whether or not you should buy this game.
+Great graphics
+Brutal and enjoyable combat
+You can slow down time
+Good controls
+Maps are quite nice and reasonably large
+If you play on the arena you are automatically put in to teams (or not) to fight other enemies and you are equipped with weapons automatically
+A number of different species you can play as
+There are different challenges for you to complete
+Good physics
+Decent modding community
+Good platforming mechanics
-This game has been in Alpha since 2008 and it's currently on build 209, updates are few and far between and offer nothing more than bug fixes, they do not add any more ways to keep you playing and more importantly they still haven't added the campaign modes which were promised
-Gets very repetitive very quickly
-Horribly overpriced considering what you get
-The game's platforming mechanics are wasted on the maps that are currently available, i.e. they're very flat maps or easy to get around
-Frequent crashes
-Long loading times
Verdict:
Do not buy this game.
It's a wonderful concept but I don't think the execution could be much worse and with it's current price tag and considering it's effectively just a tech demo with little to do you'd be wasting your money on a project that has been in Alpha for 7 years and is likely to remain in Alpha for the next 7 years.

But soon you'll realize that half the story (that of the city) is told through random collectibles that are a bit of a chore to get. This was my first disappointment with the game. If that's your thing, well, great. But narrative and superfluous collection don't go well together. The good thing is it doesn't take /that/ long to get them, you'll just have to backtrack occasionally.
My second disappointment was that barely any of the buildings are explorable. You've got the 10 buildings in which you fetch medical supplies, the 1 building you occupy, and a bunch of generic, copy and paste, smaller, hollow structures littered around the city that all have one collectible story piece in them. They're like those frustrating islands and beaches in Black Flag you land at to find one chest, or one song sheet. The rest of the buildings are filler. The 10 main buildings have a little variation between them, but not much. Earlier in my playthrough I found myself circling a lot of the non-enterable buildings checking for a docking station.
Why am I recommending this game if I only have bad things to say about it? Well, the good thing is that the game is short, so the repetition doesn't last long until the game is over, so you can focus on the beautiful music and the stunning views while playing, and trying to save your brother is enough to motivate you through the few hours.
In summary, this is a short, fairly shallow but pretty game that I would recommend just for a quick distraction.

In the first few minutes of the game, you are presented with Miku and her younger brother climbing out of a boat. Her younger brother is hurt very badly, and it is up to you to explore the world to find supplies to help take care of him. Already the story feels heartwarming and heart wrenching and it is up to you to interpret. The game does not contain any written storyline, and tells the story through pictures you unlock as the game progresses.You will learn not only about Miku and her brother, but about how the world came to be Submerged.
A vast city awaits your exploration, but it's one that is a maze of skyscrapers and ruined technology. Nature has reclaimed practically everything, and you'll learn more about that as you discover the secrets hidden throughout. Initially the world might seem dead, but that is not the case. Various creatures roam the world, and some will even interact with you. Many times throughout the course of game play you'll have a pack of dolphins following your boat, or even a whale trying to get by on his hunt for food. You never feel alone playing Submerged, but that doesn't make the eerie feeling of desolation and destruction go away.
The soundtrack is beautiful and atmospheric and really helps absorb you in the story and your quest.You cannot lose the game, there is no combat, and there are no time limits.Everything is so visceral and relaxing. Each building is small challenge to navigate and the stunning visuals always provide you with a unique and exemplary view on the world with each wall you climb.
The beautiful visuals of this game, the immersive and ethereal soundtrack and the way the game leaves you to figure out and interpret the story yourself makes this game certainly one that you will never forget.

Absolutely nonviolent, Submerged presents no real enemies, no combat systems, no quick-time events, and not a single way to die. The worst consequence you could expect for miscalculating was having to double track a longer route. Having that in mind, and with game’s easy-going atmosphere I was able to immerse myself completely in Submerged’s remnant world.
Despite the lack of combat and „bad guys“ you are not alone in this crumbled world, as many sea-dwelling animals accompany you along the way, as you progress with your trusty motor-boat in search of medicine, and other optional collectibles. And it really is a joy to ride in your boat, and explore the seemingly bland world around you learning its secrets and backstory along the way. Almost everything you collect is depicted in unique and easy to understand pictograms, as there is virtually no voice or text in Submerged.
The sense of mystery is ever present, you can really feel it as days go by, weather changes and some strange looking, almost rotten-looking, folks start to show up. The world looks good, actually amazing sometimes like in sunny dawn for example. Water textures especially. One thing I really did not enjoy when it comes to world design is that sometimes streets feel familiar even though you never been there before, and you feel that very early in the game. But, I guess it is just a try to make the game as immersive as possible, and I appreciate that.
Story-wise Submerged offers a lot of emotion and you feel conected to Miku and her sick brother really early in the game. Heart-warming and mystic is a rare storytelling combination in modern video games and maybe thats the reason why you’ll never lose your interest in it. Gameplay boils down to a lot of climbing and even more boat-riding, actually that’s all there is to gameplay, in absence of combat.
Climbing itself is a linear and straightforward affair, sometimes with few surprises along the way. Some puzzles or alternative routes would be great to have, and that the other important thing Submerged is lacking. It would surely get some extra hours of gametime if puzzles were included, if nothing else, cause game is a short adventure altogether.

Pros:
The game is beautiful and hauntingly serene.  The graphics are medium to top notch.  The way this game plays leaves room for all ages, although it does expose human suffering regularly through interactions with the injured boy.  I found the controls to be simple and straitforward.  Plays perfectly on my Xbox 360 controller as well as my mouse and keyboard.  If you are looking for a slightly saddened, but colorful exploration game this could be perfect for you.  Atmosphere reminds me of the movie waterworld from back in the 90's but with a bit more color.  Colorful patterns swirl on the water surface like oil and I can see nothing under the water.  Strangely familiar creatures leap from the water surface as they are drawn to my engine noise.  Two blocks away I can hear something very large splashing between the buildings, and off in the distance an abandoned bridge stands guard over what used to be a mighty river, but is now an underwater trench.  This game pulls of atmosphere perfectly.
Cons:
No underwater exploration.  Not really a con, but people should know.  No depth of field adjustment:  Makes game unplayable on my Nvidia 3d Surround setup.  If anyone knows of a functional mod, or file adjustment I can perform to enable this I would love to know.  Game isn't about combat, and is set in a region of abandoned city so repetition is par for the course here.  Buildings start looking the same and climbing all feels the same.  This is what makes the game relaxing and ambient, but can also make it very boring.
Conclusion.
10/10 If it had a FOV slider.
5/10 Because it doesnt.  I have way too many exploration games that look beautiful spread accross my 6018x1080 Nvidia 3d Surround display.  Forcing me to fill my view with the shoulders of my character breaks this game for me, and killing two of my monitors to play on 1/3 of my display size is foolish at best when I have other options for entertainment.

This game will hate you. It will leap up and slap you in the face. And as a result, you will never want to leave its side.
As a wise man once said: Life has no Ctrl 'Z'.
A great many things are beyond your control, unusual in a strategy game but far more true to reality.
Perhaps you will pause in your travels at a tavern, nurse a cool ale, and the tavern will explode, killing you instantly.
Son of a... Is nothing sacred?
Or maybe your favourite son will take over as regent when you grow old and decrepit, only to steal all your titles and imprison you.
Bet you're regreting your refusal to aid your brother in killing the little sod now, aren't you?
Perhaps you become just another in a long line to die from Medieval Europe's most dangerous plague - 'Suspicious circumstances'?
It's never entirely clear how suspicious they are, or what you're supposed to do about it, but you know what they say - Life's a female dog.
Or maybe, at the ripe old age of 84 you'll die from syphillis.
Irritating it might be, but you'll be unable to fight the surge of pride that you were still getting it on at an age when most men's fading eyesight ensures they can't even see the appropriate body parts any more.
And the list goes on: vassals tearing your Empires apart, mobs killing your tax collectors, rioting zealots, crusades, becoming blinded, castrated, imprisoned, diseased, incapable, having your son born the anti-christ, or, god forbid, losing your favourite hunting hound (why, why, oh cruel, wretched world?).
CK2 will punish you, and you will love every second of it, because when you do manage to pull everything together, nothing in life will bring you more joy.
Not since Firefly has anything been more deserving of the tagline 'Someone ever tries to kill you, you try to kill 'em right back.'

Two words: it is amazing! Okay, that's three words, but it's seriously a good game as opposed to its prior Morrowind, which I've only ever played for about an hour or so. I've played more hours on here with mates than I care to bother counting and, admittedly, I still haven't completed it.
The main quest is interesting, with yourself being tasked to find a new ruler as well as stop the return of a daedric lord (I shan't give any more away, as this is only a review); the side-quests are interesting, with there being numerous Guilds to join and side-quests, which in fact do retain some mearning as they can affect your character background (vampirism, wealth, and just general improving skills); and finally, there are a great number of NPCs that differ from one another and whom you must either help or ignore, which makes it so that you've an actual choice in the gameplay. There are also so many mods avaliable for this game to enhance your experience, so that you can continue even when you've completed it a bunch of times.
My only faults with the game is that there are still some glitches with it. I can recall that, not even two months ago, I was attempting to fulfill the side-quest of the White Lodge and couldn't find the NPC that you and the Knight-orc are required to kill. Eventually, after searching the web, I found a solution and completed the quest, but having to search for ages killed the entertainment of completing that quest for me.
Also, another fault is that, although the game world is large and diverse, it still remains a tad linear, with the main quest requiring you to aid the Prince against the dadric. Although you've a choice in how to kill (bow, magic, etc) and whether you allow your comrades to die or restart and attempt to make them live, the actual quest still remains with you helping. Seriously, no becoming a vampire or dadric ruler above all for you.
So, all in all, it is a brilliant game. It kept me intrigued for hours, from rumaging through caves killing vampires and mages to visiting the Prince of Madness (a quest that I adore completing). If you're looking to waste hours on a fun game, with differing races to meet and Guilds to become involved in, then all I can say is: prepare to be amazed ;)

Gemini Rue is a story heavy point and click adventure game that takes place in a Scifi Gritty and somewhat bleak setting.
If you want to play a short story heavy game that might trigger an internal debate in your mind on various topics that might be a reality in the future. Play this game.
+ The voice acting was pretty good.
+ The setting in the game is represented very uniformly and I was quite immersed in the world throughout.
+ Although the hints in the latter half were a little too apparent and gave away the plot twist quite readily, the conversations after the twist is what I will remember years after having finished the game.
The game brings up quite a heavy discussion and the Main antagonist's take on it was enough to give me a pause and make me really think about what he did and can it be easily classified as right or wrong.
+ From a game designer's standpoint this game makes really good use of limited resources.I can see all the places they've cut corners but they seem to have ticked all the major boxes that matter.
+ Most of the puzzles weren't too outlandish (4Lbs really?) and I didn't have to wade through walkthroughs to progress.
- Some of the NPC decisions make them seem flat and two dimensional.
- Even though the game was well paced, a lot of the gameplay felt like busy work. I didn't feel like the creator(s) used the medium to its full potential.
- I'm not convinced that really low detail pixel art is a good choice for a game that relies on the visual perception of the player to pick out objects on a screen.
- There are some areas in the game that look so similar (same asset), I was confused if I was backtracking accidentally. Just changing the color of the walls can completely alleviate that problem.
- The minimal UI helps in immersion but I wish the icons were better to help distinguish the objects.

Definitely a nice game. Decent story and top tier visuals for it's time. You see MMOs with worse visuals than this in current modern day so these haven't aged THAT much. The style is semi cartoonish as well so there's no real need to go so intricate with graphics anyway. For those who have played this on XBox and are afraid of the ultra long load times this game had in that console, I'm glad to say those days are gone. The game has near no loading now. Also this game now has HD visuals so everything just looks prettier than you remembered. As sounds and voice go, the acting is average. Does the job but some characters sound less lively than others. My only gripe is that some cut scenes remained in low resolution. Mainly the very first intro to the game world, which would make players think the game is not HD. They used the in game engine to render them but they are still FMVs. An upgrade to these could have been nice, if possible. But it's minor in the end as many cut scenes are made non FMV.
As for gameplay. This game is an action RPG with some first person shooter elements. See, you play (eventually) as four characters. Two use melee weapons, one uses staves that can shoot magic and the last one uses magic infused guns. In combat, you switch through these characters at will, switching from third to first person depending on the character. Your spells are done in bullet time, as the game slows down to almost a full stop. Your enemies are fast and relentless so you need to strategize with all four characters if you want to survive. Combat itself is medium paced for melee users. Reminds me a bit of Phantasy Star Online and it's three attack combos for melee characters. First person is pretty much as you'd expect. You aim and shoot and that feels good and evenly paced.
The world is rather big for it's time and you have to run in the early levels to places that are rather far, yet there's no real loading times between most doors so the experience feels very open world. There's stuff laying about the world for you to check and interact with, and places with hidden treasure or screenshot worthy vistas. All in all running around the game world is an interesting experience.
In the end, yes, I recommend this game. It's good, solid and you can sink a few hours in it. A great job of a game indeed.

Pros:
The game is beautiful and hauntingly serene.  The graphics are medium to top notch.  The way this game plays leaves room for all ages, although it does expose human suffering regularly through interactions with the injured boy.  I found the controls to be simple and straitforward.  Plays perfectly on my Xbox 360 controller as well as my mouse and keyboard.  If you are looking for a slightly saddened, but colorful exploration game this could be perfect for you.  Atmosphere reminds me of the movie waterworld from back in the 90's but with a bit more color.  Colorful patterns swirl on the water surface like oil and I can see nothing under the water.  Strangely familiar creatures leap from the water surface as they are drawn to my engine noise.  Two blocks away I can hear something very large splashing between the buildings, and off in the distance an abandoned bridge stands guard over what used to be a mighty river, but is now an underwater trench.  This game pulls of atmosphere perfectly.
Cons:
No underwater exploration.  Not really a con, but people should know.  No depth of field adjustment:  Makes game unplayable on my Nvidia 3d Surround setup.  If anyone knows of a functional mod, or file adjustment I can perform to enable this I would love to know.  Game isn't about combat, and is set in a region of abandoned city so repetition is par for the course here.  Buildings start looking the same and climbing all feels the same.  This is what makes the game relaxing and ambient, but can also make it very boring.
Conclusion.
10/10 If it had a FOV slider.
5/10 Because it doesnt.  I have way too many exploration games that look beautiful spread accross my 6018x1080 Nvidia 3d Surround display.  Forcing me to fill my view with the shoulders of my character breaks this game for me, and killing two of my monitors to play on 1/3 of my display size is foolish at best when I have other options for entertainment.

I feel like the dev team is taking this game seriously, which is a breath of fresh air in a land slide of abused and abandoned early access games.
ALSO since I don't see this being made into a big deal... People host their own servers alongside official servers, what does this mean? It means that each server owner has their own tailored SETTINGS to the server which gives you a unique gaming experience on each server. Feel like the game is too slow? Go to a x5 harvest/exp server. Feel like the game is too easy? Go to a PvP server where you drop all of your items when you die. Want to build stuff and be left alone? Go to a 10x harvest PvE server and chill out.  Seriously... I love it.

- Early Access Review -
This is a fantastic, game with adult themes.
Prepare to pick the size of your sexual parts.
Prepare to enslave natives and fellow exiles.
Find any of this offensive?
Consider spending money somewhere else.
Yes, there are some bugs.
Yes, there are some server issues.
Despite this, I've sunk almost 100 hours in already, and I expect to sink 100s more.
My recommendation to enjoy this game at this stage of development is to get started on a x5 server.
Anything less than x5 is going to be kind of a slog until more content is added.
Here are my recommended server settings, whether you are playing alone, or creating a server:
Player XP Rate Multiplier 5.0 (IMPORTANT)
Player XP Time Multiplier 5.0 (IMPORTANT)
Player XP Kill Multiplier 5.0 (IMPORTANT)
Player XP Harvest Multiplier 5.0 (IMPORTANT)
Player XP Craft Multiplier 5.0 (IMPORTANT)
Day Cycle Speed 0.5
Day Time Speed 1.0
Night Time Speed 10.0 (IMPORTANT)
Dusk/Dawn Time Speed 5.0
Catch Up Time 10.0 (no idea what this does - maybe catches up players to be in sync with the server day/night cycle if they fall out of sync?)
Stamina Cost Multiplier 0.5 (IMPORTANT)
Player Active Thirst Multiplier 0.5
Player Active Hunger Multiplier 0.5
NPC Respawn Multiplier 1.0
Thrall Wakeup Time 600 (maybe how many seconds they get knocked out by the truncheon?)
Avatar Lifetime 120 (I think this gives you 2 minutes to be a god if you summon one)
Disable Avatars leave unchecked (don't you want to be a god?)
Item Spoil Rate Scale 0.5
Harvest Amount Multiplier 5.0 (IMPORTANT)
Resource Respawn Speed Multiplier 1.5 (remember that any resources, thralls, mob spawns near where you build all de-spawn permanently - so don't build too close to stuff you care about!)
Land Claim Radius Multiplier 1.0
Crafting Speed Multiplier 0.1 (IMPORTANT)
Anything else can be left at defaults for single player.
For anyone building a server, a good way to allow your community to clean up after itself is to keep buildings destructable. This allows the server community to clean up after noobs who put down foundations near important spawns (which despawns them in the process). Nothing is more demoralizing to a server community than being unable to access certain important spawns. No admin can possibly police everything in an effective manner, so let the players handle it!
TL;DR
GOOD SETTINGS = GOOD ENJOYMENT

Have to say I have no idea how i missed this game. While the initial learning curve is relatively steep and some controls initially feel clunky it progresses nicely to become second nature and not what you initially thought.
The community is simply fantastic, i have never seen such an active Help channel with old timers, GMs, mentors and new players all chipping in to assist with any questions. On that note I have also never encountered a game so well moderated, trollers/spammers etc will actively be muted and banned if it becomes excessive and the GMs do not hide, they actively PM responses to  Help channel queries or respond direct to the channel.
The game itself is essentially Fallout 3 turned MMO mostly, 95% of in game items are craftable. You start only being allowed one character and one crafting queue slot plus a limit on chip (in game money) amount but a very small real money purchase on the store unlocks additional characters, crafting slots and removes the credit limit. You can earn store cash through surveys so no real money is even necessary. 5G1C is needed to buy a "Return to home" device and that can be earned six times over from one survey.
So the gameplay, its a crafters dream and nightmare as you will spend a ton of time just trying to hoard resources :) Combat is targetted in that you actually need to swing for the head or arms or shoot for the location and if your cursor is off, well you miss. On that note you get six, YES SIX, weapon slots on your character which all show in the game. You can have a primary meleee two hander on your back, a primary ranged two hander on your back, two pistols on your hips and two one hander melee on your hips. Its choicetastic ;)
Seriously recommend that as its F2P you check it out and just give it a few hours after running the tutorial as you learn a ton through the inital and subsequent missions. Well worth checking out, so much so i subbed after only 20 hours of playtime.

Get your own dynasty and♥♥♥♥♥♥around in medieval Europe until the borders are so messy they make your eyes bleed and your family tree is so huge that you lag when you open too many branches.
Pretty much a Paradox Game through and through:
-Good strategy game. The base game by itself is good, it goes somewhat deep, it has a bunch of things to do and playstyles to explore along with hidden mechanics you'll be finding out years later if you don't read the wikis. Paradox Interactive has been doing grand strategy games for many years, they know the formula, they have the budget (from those diehard loyal fans) and they take their time. They might be bad distributors (just read about East and West: a Hearts of Iron game somewhere), but they're decent enough developers.
-Damn expensive (and barebones) DLC. Each update's more or less the same thing: add a mechanic or two to each religion/government type, slap a 20$/€ tag on the ability to play it and release it to the wild. People buy it because there's no competitor to go to. The updates are fun gimmicks, but it's in no way worth paying the money for it.
-Amazing modding scene. Now this is simply what makes the paradox games turn from okayish to great, they're so damn moddable! The modding scene in PI games have been around since (I believe) the second Hearts of Iron and Europa Universalis games. Some of these modders have been meddling with paradox games for more than ten years, some of them even got hired as employees by paradox. What this means is that the mods for CK2 are diverse. From gameplay tweaks to reduce that OP seduction focus to total overhauls. What's more, PI knows that this is their games' strong point, so they made organized, up to date and heavily moderated forums to gather the entire modding community into one hotspot of creativity.
I'd say three fourths of the charm of CK2 is the mods. So many mods, so many total overhauls that cover most of the most famous fantasy universes: A song of ice and fire, the elder scrolls, warhammer fantasy, middle earth. Of course, there's also the big mods that set out to give you the best experience in medieval europe (Like Historical Inmersion Project, Lux Invicta and CK2 Plus).
Some people tell you the game is worth it just because of the modding scene it has, they're right. These modders do their work for free yet they don't skip on the quality because of that, they put their hearts and souls into it (along with hours of their lives they could spend doing something else). And we should all be damn grateful that they do.
tl;dr: buy it, get a mod, have fun for a hundred hours; get another mod, have fun for another hundred hours. Also ♥♥♥♥ overpriced DLC.

: Warframe is essentially Space Genji Sim.
Warframe is a futuristic game set in the solar system (I'm not suer if it's in our timeline or alternate) which was controlled by 3 major factions. The Grineer, Corpus and The Infested. You play as a Tenno, a relic of a long lost history where The Orokin
once controlled the system. After you were woken up from a long cryosleep, You gear up and join others in the fight for the people of the system. The Tenno use Warframes (basically Power Armors) and variety of weapons in thier fights, from sci-fi looking laser rifle to basic guns and swords.
Each weapon you can choose feels different. No 2 guns are the same. Such as the AK-looking Soma to the cannon like Zarr. Weapons in this game depend solely on Mods. These Mods let you increase the damage output, firerate, accuracy, critical chance and MUCH more. And there a a LOT of Mods to be obtained. The Devs keep adding new one in and there are basically endless combinations!
The movement and overall gameplay is fast, really fast. You can Bulletjump and glide through the air very quickly and there's no cooldown for it! Your weapons gradually hit harder, fire faster and getting better the more mods you have. By the time you've unlocked the starchart (The Map) all the way through, you'll be stomping low level enemies very easily.
When you reach the mid game you'll eventually meet someone with shining white and gold warframe. When ypu take a look at their names you'll see that it's the same warframe you've got but it ends with Prime. These Prime warframe and weapons are basically better versions of their normal counterpart. It's DE's way of keeping things fresh for end-game players. You can farm them from relics (randomly dropped rewards) and craft them like other items. Or alternately, you can purchase them from other players using Platinums (premiun currency). This create the in-game economy where players fram and sell Prime parts and blueprints.
Warframe is still going strong in 2017 after years of improvments. It has deep lore and stroy which currently isn't finished yet, great gameplay and mechanics and at last, great community, nice devs that update the game's progress often and regular updates. For me, It's 8.5 out of 10.

Chivalry is a hugely intriguing game for anyone with an interest in a competitive and highly skill-based multiplayer game.
The good:
The bad:
It's hard to describe just how much fun Chivalry's combat really is. Concepts from sport fencing such as distance control, initiative and tempo translate appropriately into the combat, but it's so much more than just that. You can manipulate your weapon in real time to speed up or slow down your attack, which means you can keep your opponent guessing with each blow. Land a couple fast attacks then quickly shift gears and slow down then watch the other guy struggle to keep up.
You can also do things like contort your avatar's posture to force your opponent's attack to miss. He's trying to stab you in the face? You won't always need to parry. Lean back hard at the waist and watch his blade fly right over you. Load up an overhand while you're at it then chop into his head while you straighten back up.
Like a lot of good games, you're given a set of capable tools then granted the freedom to learn how they work and apply them in action. It might sound like cheesy marketing lingo but there's so much expression in the way you play this game that each kill is profoundly satisfying.
The best time to get into Chivalry was probably a couple years ago but you can still have a fun time online. Buy a copy with a friend during a sale and join the mayhem, just understand that it'll take some effort before you become competitive.

You do get to control all members of your party during combat. Combat also is more than button mashing. For the melee fighters, there is a combo system. Three hits in a row and you execute a combo. Ranged fighters are in first person view. For the most part the AI for the other party members is decent. I heard it is way better than the original XBox version.
There is a skill system. Each of the party members have both defensive and offensive skills. I did find that they seemed very unbalanced. And then there are the skill strikes. Bestowed upon the characters by the Gods themselves these are extremely powerful attacks that you must defeat enemies in order to charge the skill strike meter.
I did have some crashes near the end. Also, the arena fights of the boss monsters sometimes left crazy camera angles and not much time to correct them. This was distracting more than anything, but getting walloped due to poor camera angle plain sucks. I also didn't care for the fan service. The female characters, as is seen in much fantasy, barely had any armor on.
Not a bad game, but not necessarily one that I can recommend.

About an hour into the game, Gemini Rue makes a massive misstep in the fusion of game mechanics and narrative which wrenched me out of this initially immersive little world.
I do admire the creators for introducing gun fights into a point and click adventure. Gun fights where you can actually lose your life, and for a moment they introduced some tangible excitement and danger into the story.
The game drills into you the idea of conserving your ammo, putting yourself at risk in order to get a more accurate, deadlier shot and therefore save a few bullets.
And then it happens.
You're in a corridor, you have 8 bullets, with enemies on your tail. Your character gets behind cover and a shootout ensues. An enemy is leaning out and firing wildly, but you're patient, calculating the timing of your enemy's shots. When you spot a window you lean out, and you focus your attention on just this one shot, not a bullet to waste. Of course you're exposed as you do this; it's a risky action. But you can't fire with wild abandon like them. You have to save ammo.
Your pursuer leans out. Bang. A bullet in his head.
It feels good, you've bought yourself some time. You and your partner run down to the end of the corridor to make your escape. And then you - YOU - your virtual persona. The character you have been inhabiting, controlling and roleplaying for the last hour forcibly stops at the foot of those stairs which lead to safety. He turns back towards the corridor. The computer has taken control of you. The story kicks in.
Your avatar: "I've got to hold them off!"
bang
bang
bang
bang
bang
bang
bang
Exactly 7 shots. You counted them. Every last bullet, fired pointlessly into the ether by the computer. Your character then turns up the stairs and thus begins a dumb timed puzzle where you have to break down a door before a bad guy bursts in and shoots your stupid, defenseless, magazine-emptying idiot of an avatar. If only you could have just kept running up those stairs and saved those bullets for when the bad guys followed you up there.
I died a few times and had to replay this scene. Each time I performed a bit differently during that first shootout (where I had control) and I used up a different amount of bullets.
The real kick in the balls here is that the game programmatically counts how many bullets you used up, and then once the computer takes over control it fires the exact amount of rounds that you had remaining. They actually did that. They coded that. This is something worse than terrible game design. It actually feels like being trolled by the developers.

I can't believe I finally get to review this game now that it's out of early access!
Overgrowth is a game about a ninja rabbit who fights other ninja animals (in a nutshell). Taking place after the story of Lugaru (to which this game is a sequel), Turner is traveling in an attempt to find a calm life, only to (of course) be met with great resistence by enemy forces. I must disclose that I bought this game maybe 5-6 years ago when it was in alpha (this thing was "Early Access" before that was a widely used term!). Knowing that, I might be biased in this review.
Gameplay is easily the best thing about this game, and the aspect that the devs worked on the most. The context sensetive fighting is pretty easy to learn, but insanely difficult to master, and after 70+ hours I still haven't completely mastered it (although I'd say I'm pretty damn good). The engine is well crafted and very mod-able, which is incredibly impressive given the small development team of only a few people! Speaking of the engine, the tech it uses is impressive. Some aspects of it weren't even used in AAA games before not too long ago. Phenominal blood physics (with dynamic blood streams stemming from wounds and dynamic dripping as well) and procedural animation are always impressive to feast your eyes on. The devs have also given anyone who buys the game the ability to use the powerful level editor to create your own levels or change existing ones (neat!).
However, that's mostly where the fun stops. Other aspects seem to suffer as a result of most of the development time going to the engine and the combat system (which, again, I must praise to the highest level!). Level design, characters and character development, dialogue, and plot all take hits due to not enough time invested into creating them, resulting in their mediocre nature (but it is an excellent exuse to FIGHT SH*T). The game also ends VERY aprubtly. The story doesn't seem like it should end there, but it does indeed.
But don't let that stuff stop you from considering to buy this game! The arena mode has allowed me to milk many hours out of the game; you're dropped in with or without a weapon (random chance) against foes, either in a team, or in a free-for-all (or one-on-one). The more foes you defeat, the more difficult the next foes become, and whenever you are defeated, the enemies get easier. You respawn in this cycle forever, until you quit, obviously.
Did I mention that the previous game, Lugaru, has been entirely remade in Overgrowth's engine? Yep.
The engine has been developed with mods in mind, and there are already many to choose from at the moment. Fan made stories (like "Therium-2" which is actually better than the main story mode IMO), levels, skins, arena maps with enemy/weapon spawn points already set up, etc. etc. are there already, and the amount of mods will no doubt increase with time, but supporting this game will allow more attention to be directed towards it, and with that comes MORE and BETTER mods, which makes everyone happy.
