1st/3rd person open world, adventure-survival, fantasy game with RPG elements based in Conan universe.
I will start off by saying that Arnold Schwarzenegger is my all time favorite actor, and I absolutely loved the Conan movies back in the day with him. There was something primal about them, where there was fantasy world filled with evil and a buff hero with sword on his way of revenge and saving beautiful women. I know parts of the movie were funny and not amazing but it was enjoyable part of me growing up. Anyways.
I used to play the MMO that Funcom launched back in the day, I think it was one of the few actual adult MMO's on the market. And with Conan actually being in the game it was fun experience to go through even though not many people were playing it as new MMO's were coming out. Non the less it was fun game and I had my time with it.
After that there were no real Conan based games around until Conan Exiles. Even though it starts off as an Early Access game (further as EA), it rolled out with quite good number of features and content for an AE game. I'm not a beginner with EA games, bought quite the number of different genre titles and was burned only once (TheStompingLand). I know many have been burned way more than me, thus people tend to stear clear of EA titles.
I believe that a AAA game can be as bad as an EA game, and an EA game can be as good as a AAA game. It also depends how interested you are in the games lore and if you are willing to help the developer.
Anyways how about we continue to the actual review, if anyone is still even reading this. :)
At current state, Conan Exiles has decently sized, open world, sandbox map. It is hand crafted map with small to medium sized NPC camps and cities. Map is also filled with many hostile and non hostile beasts, animals, critters and monsters. As well as basic and rare resources you can obtain from the land and beasts.
Main aspect of the game is to survive, build a shelter, armor and weapons and protect yourself from the dangers. Then expand your camp, craft better equipment, capture and break enemies (NPC's) to be your allies and group up on larger and more powerful enemies on the map. If you play online, you either protect yourself and your clan from other players or the environment.
Main aspect of survival is to hunt, get meat, cook meat, then eat it and drink it down with some fresh river water. Pretty much more fed you are, more healthy you are overall and more health you will regenerate if injured. Thirst only affects the stamina regeneration, so it's good to be full on not only food but water if you plan to journey across the land. As of yet there is no weather influence on the body, I'm sure they add something that affects your body if you are in a desert or maybe caught in the sandstorm. Also make sure to remember that similar to real life, food will spoil and eating such food is dangerous.
My favorite aspect of the game is building and crafting. There are currently 3 tiers of building block structure elements and I'm sure they will add more at some point. Those are basic Sandstone, pretty much stones held together by sand based mixture and wood. Very primitive and cheap to build, yet not as durable as other tiers. Stonebrick is the 2nd tier, and like you would guess, you make bricks from stone that you use instead of the simple stones in the Sandstone building, that you also hold together with sand based mixture and wood. Last (for now) and the most durable and fortified building tier is the third, the Reinforced Stonebrick. Which is your tier 2 Stonebrick but reinforced with iron reinforcements, pretty much instead of pure wood and sand mixture it is held together with iron bolts and iron frame with reinforced wood which is much more durable than the standard one.
All three tiers look different and the higher tier you go, the more rewarding the feeling is that you made something that will better protect the folks you play with. That said my personal favorite (visually) is the Stonebrick tier but mostly I tend to build tier one houses as they are much more cheaper.
There are different building elements for every tier, from basic foundation, walls, walls with doors, windows to fences, ceilings, stairs, pillar supports for taller ceilings and much more. Many decorative elements that are not just for looks but also can be used as storage, lighting, crafting or just simply sitting, like a chair. Countless clutter items like pots, metal dishes, candles, banners, trophy mounts, shelves and much more.
Crafting in this game is done either directly through the inventory or on armor benches, in forges, campfires, blacksmiths anvil, tannery, carpenters bench and/or by other means.
From harvested materials you can make pretty much everything, if you have learned the right recipe. You learn those by spending points you get through leveling up. You also get attribute points you can spend to increase your health, stamina, carry weight, damage with melee or ranged weapons, your agility to mitigate more damage from enemy attacks, your basic survival instincts so you receive more from food and water sources around you and more.
If you play in group, I advise to split the roles in the clan, for example if someone likes to gather resources, they can invest more points into carry weight to carry more goods with each gathering run. If someone likes to fight, or be a tanky character, you can focus on health and agility, or if you want to be a heavy hitter up close, invest into large amounts of pure strength. You can be an eagle eye with high accuracy shooting down enemies in few arrows, bolts or throw some axes and spears. Of course you can just spend the points how you like and be a hero you want.
Now to my second most favorite element, the characters and the world you are in. Funcom did a really good job on the character models, even with the limited character creation, you can make a somewhat unique looking hero. Male or female, many different races for RP purposes (for now, maybe they will add some cool passives), religions with different perks depending on which one you choose to go with, as well as character customization options. Starting with some facial features like nose, cheeks, chin, etc. Skin color, hair styles and color, eyebrows, height slider, breast slider and of course nudity options (mature game, remember kids?).
Playable character animations are great, with good textures not only on characters but also on the world around you. Animations on NPC's and beasts need a bit more polish though, most of them look static and not as refined as could be.
Game runs decently on recommended PC's considering there's little to no optimization for low-medium systems. And I'm sure as time goes game will run better. The only issue I've had with the game was intense use of the GPU, that wasn't an issue in other games. Temperatures were so high, nearly to the point of overheating, but I managed to fix the issue with MSI Afterburner's Power/Temp control with fixed maximum temperature.

This game has A LOT of potential, and I will say right off the bat that this review is for the current build for the game.
+Pros+
+The combat is fun, when you get the hang of it.
+The character creation is similar to RPG titles. You can pick race, appearance, body shape, and even the size of your sexual characteristics if that's your thing.
+There is a lot promised that could be immensely fun, including possibly sorcery and use of religion to help you through your survival.
-Cons-
-The combat, while fun, is IMMENSELY imbalanced! Enemies have more range than you, and don't be surprised if a human, an imp, and a crocodile decide you're enemy #1 and team up to chase you for several miles.
-Survival is as equally unbalanced as combat, but you can shift that to your liking when making the server.
-There's no real stat system for items, and the current weapons make no sense. A pike and sword have the same range, the pike is slower, and yet weaker than the sword of equal quality?
-The mining and crafting system has a slight essence of runescape. I am not kidding, expect to find a grouping of rocks that are black, or slightly more grey in color to find the materials you need. While not inherently bad, this definitely ruins the immersion for me. There are better ways to work in mineral veins!
-No tracking. Don't expect to have an easy time cooperating with people, as you will never know where they are if you're not in direct contact. This can be considered immersive, as we don't track people on a compass IRL, but with how badly balanced the game is against you, a little break couldn't help.
-Last, but not least, no progression! You have literally zero reason, aside from curiosity, to go out and explore this world they put before you. I am not suggesting rails, but a good survival game makes you WANT to go out. So much looked essentially the same to me, and why bother going out into the world when you have all the food, water, and materials you need right where you are or close by? There was no real reward to step up and out, only more difficulty.
In short, for those who don't wish to read, while the game has a lot of potential, I cannot recommend it until some of that potential begins to show itself!
Save your money , Buy something that is finished or has more than one developer.

The TL;DR is that War for the Overworld is a good game, but with some boring levels. Campaign is a good tutorial. Multiplayer is where the real challenge and fun is. My Pet Dungeon and Crucible offer vastly different ways of enjoying the same mechanics (and feel like different games), but a lot of the game isn't designed for those modes and doesn't interact too well with them, so expect some frustration or unused elements.
If you are unfamiliar with Dungeon Keeper 2, skip to the next paragraph. For those familiar with Dungeon Keeper 2, this is a faithful and solid followup with several welcome changes. It's faster-paced and more challenging, and doesn't seem as atmospheric as that game as there's more emphasis on constant management and combat (as well as fewer truly dramatic moments, such as summoning the Horned Reaper or saving up enough mana to instantly wipe out an enemy). In general, this game is more focused on balance, competition, and challenge; if you've beaten DK2, this should be a welcome change of pace and step up.
For those unfamiliar with DK2, this game sees you managing a dungeon with minions you can't directly control (though close enough, generally). It splits the difference between domestic management of elements of your dungeon (such as food supply, sleeping quarters, training rooms, etc.,) and military strategy, though neither element has much individual depth.
Instead, the depth of the game largely derives from how the two intermingle. Your minions constantly need to eat, sleep, and get paid; how do you construct a dungeon where they can do so easily while still being sent far afield on raids? Each map has a significantly different geometry, forcing you to adapt your designs and consider what you really need. That having been said, many maps can still devolve into hour-long force-build phases, followed by huge (but dull) battles at the climax as you overrun the enemy; many scenarios and campaign maps aren't designed to keep the pressure up or keep changing things around as you progress, but simply put higher and higher walls in front of you, requiring larger and larger battering rams to breach, in effect.
When the game has a cleverly-designed scenario, however, that changes entirely. One campaign level strips you of a dungeon altogether, for instance, forcing you to manage a group of necromancers and keep them alive as you build up your army of undead by sneaking around the champions of a crypt and raise the dead. It's not all samey, and the final few levels of the campaign step up the pressure by pitting you directly against enemies that expand and build forces as you do, meaning you are pressed to apply everything you know quickly and efficiently, and alter your tactics on-the-fly. This is where the game is most satisfying.
Notably, the game has several modes designed to challenge the player in different ways. Due to its emphasis on fast-paced building and combat (especially compared to its spiritual predecessor), and the more satisfying and visceral experience to be had opposing a foe that builds up as you do, the multiplayer in the game is excellent, and seems to be where the game shines most. Between the multiplayer-style levels at the end of the campaign, and the many multiplayer maps (which can be played with bots of varying difficulty), there's a lot of variety to be had just in that aspect of the game, even if you don't have anyone else to play it with. Perhaps the best term is that it is best played 'competitively', against a foe that follows the same rules that you do.
This isn't the only place where the game manages to be compelling, however. Altogether, War for the Overworld has the following modes: Campaign, My Pet Dungeon, Crucible, Multiplayer (called 'Skirmish'), and Scenario/Sandbox. Scenario/Sandbox gives you two open sandboxes to mess in (one which largely featureless, and another which is set in a quirky, hard-to-build-in environment, forcing you to get creative and practice your adaptation), which are ideal for practicing the basic mechanics. The Scenarios offer three additional levels, similar to the Campaign mode but without any real story or sense of progression to them (I found the first of these to be fairly dull after the first few minutes).
The Campaign has both a special sandbox (where you can spawn enemies/collect gold freely and otherwise mess around, but are limited strictly to the items you have already unlocked in the campaign mode, meaning you're expected to go there in between missions to test features), and a variety of scenarios. While most of these have the same gameplay progression (Defend, build up, invade), they do slowly introduce more and more unit types/room types to the player, with each level being designed to really highlight the purpose those tools serve. For new players, it can be a satisfying (if overly drawn-out) tutorial with a climactic finish, but don't expect truly memorable experiences.
Crucible is a high-intensity survival mode, where the attacks come fast and furious and there's barely any time to build forces or organize defenses. Furthermore, you get attacked from multiple angles at once, forcing you to spread your forces thing to cover all of the approaches. This mode excellently tests your dungeon-adaptation skills, as the Crucible levels are very difficult to build on properly, and can help a player see the game in an entirely different light; that having been said, the mode isn't balanced to mesh too well with the game's existing balance (which is more designed for periodic fighting rather than sustained), and deliberately bars the player from taking many of the most useful upgrades (called 'Aspects'). While it takes an existing game and gives it a fresh look, it's not what the game was designed for, and it shows at times; it's fun, challenging, but sometimes weird or aggravating as well.
My Pet Dungeon is virtually the opposite of Crucible in intensity; each My Pet Dungeon has a few objectives to complete, but they are very much unlike the scenario/campaign levels in that the objectives require little-to-no soldier buildup to complete. Typically, the only enemies you will find on a My Pet Dungeon map are the ones you choose to spawn for yourself; it goes entirely at your pace, and your goal is to get a high score by building and managing your dungeon. This can be challenging, as the maps are sometimes difficult to build on and require adaptation, but there is no risk of failure; eventually, you will win on a My Pet Dungeon map simply by managing your dungeon over time. It's much more engaging than a regular sandbox mode, but without pressure. Note that those who own the default game can play two My Pet Dungeon levels (beating the first unlocks the second); the "My Pet Dungeon" DLC adds seven more on top of that.
With all of that taken together, it seems War for the Overworld really lets the player toy around with virtually every way in which the core gameplay can be challenging or engaging. Unfortunately, along the way, the player will stumble across many aspects that are less engaging as well; not all levels/scenarios are made equal, and the game can drag on at times. This problem is badly compounded by a common engine issue, where the game lags and stutters noticeably (to the point that clicking on something reliably can be difficult) if the game has been running for too long. The devs believe this problem is linked to the game engine (Unity) and will be fixed in the next patch, but it should only affect systems with 16GB or more of RAM in that instance; my system has 8GB, and the issue crops up in precisely the way others describe on mine as well, so the issue may take even more time to fix (as of the time of this writing, it has been ongoing for over a year). While not an issue on shorter-lived maps, it can interfere heavily with Crucible and drawn-out Scenario/Campaign levels.

I wasn't sure about getting this game at first because of all the negative reviews, but I got it when it was on sale and I was pleasently surprised how much I enjoyed it. Though I can see why there would be quite a few thumbs down on this game, especially at it's full price.
Pros:
- The art and backgrounds are nicely done, and appealing to look at through the whole game.
(The Chibis of the characters are freakin' adorable!!!)
- Nicole herself is not a blank slate character. She has some personality, which seems to be a rarity in otome protagonists.
- Buying your guy gifts.... <3 (Though you might want to save the game if you don't want accidently give a $100 gift to the wrong guy.... like me.)
- I LIKED EVERY GUY!!! I can't stress this enough. Usually in otomes you have a favorite guy, but with this one it's hard for me to pick one!
every guy had their sweet moments with Nicole that I loved.
Cons:
- One of the biggest drawbacks the game suffers from is it's execution of it's premise. While the premise of Nicole has the opportunity to make a compelling story for the protagonist, it just ends up falling flat. And by the end if you choose to ' solve ' the mystery, it just makes Nicole look kinda dumb by running headfirst into danger without a second thought.
- While the stat raising wasn't a problem for me, it can start to
feel like grinding. Especially if you want to see both endings, which causes you to raise two stats all the way to full.
- Nicole does have a personality, but sometimes she can seem pushy and a bit unlikable at times.
- There aren't many CG's. The only ones you get are in the endings, and the only way to access them in the menu once you're done is to play the ending over.
- That Price. While I did enjoy this game, I'm sure my mood would sour if by the end of the game I realized I paid $20 for the stuff in the game that really irritated me. I got it on sale for around $12, and that was the main reason I bought it in the first place.
So in conclusion would I recomend this game,.... yes, on sale.
I got this game for around $12, and the amount of stuff I liked seemed to balance out with what I paid. There are some things in this game that just irritated me. The mystery aspects didn't really play that much into what I truly enjoyed about this game. The best part of this game really is the guys, which, to me at least, were all well done.
So, go get this game on sale if you're looking for another otome game.

This game was one of those guilty pleasures I enjoyed during my teenage years with the original xbox. It was as corny as hell, but it had its charms-none of which had anything at all to do with Buki's outfits...... >_>
If you like your fantasy RPG's to be fanciful and colourful, Sudeki's got plenty of it. And with full HD support at 60 fps, there are few pre-DLC games of its type that can stand with it on steam. You've got unique gameplay elements, mixing hack n slash, and first person shooting with your RPG-all in real time!
...that being said, it's a 10 year old game. And it shows. Though the artstyle holds the graphics up well, you can see its age through all those blurry textures. It's nothing a mod couldn't fix, but given that this is such a niche title, it's unlikely anyone would take an interest in it.
And while the gameplay as a whole works, its individual elements fall short on their own. Melee combat feels sluggish. The timing of combination attacks is too slow, and too often you'll end up taking a pounding while waiting for the next button prompt. And that goes without mentioning the lack of a free dodge system which we all take for granted in today's games. Meanwhile first person shooting is hampered by your movement speed. The gameplay only seems to show its strength when you've got a full party of 4. Anyone goes missing(this will happen often), and you'll start to see the holes, resulting in difficulty sparks abroad.
Finally, we gotta talk about that voice acting. It's not Chaos wars bad, but jesus christ guys. Let's look at our protagonists here. Tal sounds like he's trying too hard at being generic, Elco sounds like every European guy ever, Buki sounds much older than she looks, and then there's Ailish........ No words man. No words.
Do I recommend it? Only to existing owners who appreciate its charm, and want that cheap trip down nostalgia lane.

Disclaimer: This is the first game from GameHouse that I have played, but I've seen many more of them on Twitch (Delicious, Fabulous, Dr. Cares, Heart's Medicine, etc.).
This is yet another fabulous game from GameHouse. It's their same formula: a dash of drama, lovable characters, and a familiar time management style. The system for each level is easy to pick up. It's based entirely on clicking your mouse and paying attention. As a note, though, the variety in this particular installment surprised me. Unlike previous incarnations between the series, you aren't limited to one genre. You will serve food, sell school supplies, make dresses, and so on in 'Angela's High School Reunion'. It's not nearly as strict as its predecessors, which can be a nice relief here and there.
(If you want a time management game limited to fashion, I would recommend 'Angela's Fashion Fever' over this one.)
Oh! A tip: if you can't find the mouse right away, hit the pause button. The menu will slide out and cover part of the screen. This allows you to scan the area thoroughly. If the mouse isn't to be seen in the greater part of the level left uncovered, then it's probably behind where the menu is. It's an easy way to either locate the mouse or narrow down where it is.
Achievement Advice: you will get almost all of them through playing naturally. 1. As far as Carl's achievement is concerned, you only need to find him on all 60 levels. Challenges don't count. 2. Endless mode doesn't apply to any achievements. It's only useful for farming stars / money (which, truthfully, is easier and faster on regular levels).
Good luck and have fun !

This game has been out for a while, and, compared to other currently active MMOs, Fallen Earth does fairly well.
If you like the post-apocalpytic theme, crafting a variety of items, shooter action-rpgs, and playing with others, you should enjoy this one.
The aesthetics are pretty good, the equip-able armor and weapons are all visible on your character. The music and sounds are decent.
The controls are easy to familiarize yourself and, like most MMOs, the beginning tutorial is extremely helpful in establishing your bearings in the game world. The learning curve is moderate to challenging, depending on how familiar you are with MMORPGs and their mechanics.
Crafting is a very fun part of this game if you are into that - you can craft almost anything you see in the game world (which beats having to spend your resources on merchants. Within the first 2 hours I already was driving around in my own ATV. The gameplay is pretty good, however, it still remains fairly buggy in many areas. The AI has godlike sensors, able to detect and chase you across the map once you have aggro'd (hostile interaction) them.
Grinding in this game is actually pretty fun considering that the rewards are very reasonable and the variety in missions is very, very good - they aren't 90% fetch or find quests typical of many MMORPGs. Combat can be weird and clunky at times, and hopefully this will be improved, however, it has been a long time and these problems still remain.
If you can look past these bugs, and enjoy grinding and crafting in the post-apocalyptic setting, then give this game a try.
Recommend.

Having played many adventure games (closest comparison in setting to this probably Beneath A Steel Sky or Dreamweb), I unfortunately feel this is quite a bit below average.
The story was... middle of the road. Slightly engaging in part, tedious and slow in part, not very long (my time spent is mostly idling). The main issue is that what your time is spent on is very tedious, niggling clicks to get from place to place. If you are using a touchpad, this is unbearable.
Leftclick on a door to go through it. It's closed. Rightclick to open tiny action box. Leftclick on tiny hand icon to open door. Leftclick on doorway to enter. EVERY door requires rightclick-leftclick-leftclick. The screen area is quite small, so walking across a single area needs several clicks. You will often be lost and spend time backtracking, so it's basically an endless clickfest to do mundane actions whilst going through a very slow and not very engaging story.
Dialogue is stilted and unnatural, voiceovers medium minus, classic immersion-damaging techniques (puzzle requires an item, the item does the task but breaks), very cliche plot devices, artificial constraints (you have lockpicks, and there's endless locked doors you cannot use them on). I feel there are much better ways to spend $10. Only for really hardcore adventure completionists desperate for the setting.

I really enjoyed playing this game, but it is not without it's flaws.
The game is your standard dating sim. Your protagonist is an attractive, somewhat ditzy youngwoman at college. You meet 4 cute boys. You raise the state
of the skill that most appeals to the boy you want to date. You say the right things and give the right gifts, and a relationship begins.
Also one of them is totally an evil abductor. The mystery was way less mysterious than it could have been. I guessed the culprit the moment I met him,
before I knew anything about him besides what his major was. For a while I entertained the idea he was a red herring, or that the culprit changes depending on your choices.
Nope, it's always the same guy, though to the game's credit, things play out differently depending on which boy you cosy up to.
Of course the mystery is entirely optional. If you don't investigate it, nothing happens. You just date a guy. (Who might be an evil abductor).
I did find it frustrating that Nicole stubornly decides to tell NO ONE (including the police) about events she REALLY should have.
The game has what I've come to see as standard for games of this type, an utter lack of compatibility with ANY of the romance options.
You're capable of getting a happy ending with any of these utterly differnt guys, despite there always being some quite serious personality flaws (on both sides), that do not mesh well.
One poor romance option is painfully shy and introverted. How does our lovely protagonist handle this? By dragging him kicking and screamign out of his comfort zone, then being confused when he gets upset.
Also the stats, aside from morale and energy, are only useful for one specific guy. Upping any stat will increase the rate at which you find clues, and how much money you make at the assocciated job. But there really is no reason to develop unrelated stats. Which means if Nicole isnt' dating the relevant guy, she will never bother doing her homework or taking extra classes.
All in all I loved the game, but I fully admit parts of it make very little sense.

Alright, I finally got around to fully completing Nicole (otome version).  Although I’m sure many have already pointed out the pros and cons of this game I feel like I should also point out how I feel about this game. Before I begin I want to let you know two things. I played this game on ‘hard’, so some factors affecting my critiques may differ to others who have played the game on other difficulty modes. Any “examples” I use in my explanation are not actually in the game itself, they are merely a way to show what I am talking about.
+This game meets the basic requirements of what it’s set up to be which is a mystery, dating, choice simulator and visual novel.
+The music and sound effects all add to the atmosphere of the game.
+The game has a basic system of ‘skill building’ and time management.
+The characters all have basic differing personalities.
+The backgrounds are very well drawn and colored.
+The chibi characters are adorable. (However the guy’s chibi characters are only ever seen when you want to give gifts)
- (This one’s more of a personal preference) While having characters have different outfits is nice, there is no correlation to when a character wears a particular outfit. For example Nicole can wear the exact same outfit for consecutive events happening in the same week one day after another and no character happens to comments that she’s been wearing the same exact thing for more than once. (I’d like to point out that there is no option available for the player to choose what Nicole wears at any point in the game).
-Some of the character’s clothing doesn’t look as polished as others and some of the guy’s outfits are basically the same thing except for a change in the coloring.
- (Personal preference alert) some of the guys clothing doesn’t quite fit their personality in my opinion.
-The text window often increases in size to accommodate for more text which can become slightly distracting.
-When images are transitioning or fading out it often is either abrupt or results in a fuzzy pixelated look which degrades the art style and distracts the eye until the frames refocus.
-After going through route after route the dialogue tends to get very repetitive.
-There is a big lack of CG’s (meaning images that tend to show a particular interaction between characters and scenery or characters and other characters, often these images/drawings tend to be of very high quality and are used to emphasis something or show emotion) within this game and it disappoints me since there are a lot of scenes in which CG’s could’ve been used to really express what was being described.
-The game lacks explanation or introduction to uses tools such as the manual skip button “Ctrl” or the somewhat ‘automatic’ skip button “Tab” to fast forward ‘seen text’ instead of just spamming the left mouse button.
-After the first route the system of skill building can become somewhat robotic and tiresome from its lack of any ‘special events’ tailored specifically for each route. Everything follows a basic pattern, for example: on day ‘X’ event ‘Z’ will occur regardless of the route you are pursuing; This in itself is fine however it would be nice if there were occasionally ‘random events’ that occurred to prevent the droning and mashing of my left mouse button during ‘skill building’ while I slowly counting down the remaining days until a said event will occur.
-Many of the ending scenes contain chunks of the same dialogue regardless of the route the player chose.
-Sometimes there is no music or background noise for such a long time that it breaks the player’s immersion in the game.
-There is no possible way to ‘win’ the game without fully romancing one of the characters.
-Sometime the dialogue will mention information regarding the scenery; however the background shown will not match that description.
-Some of the dialogue is poorly written often seeming ‘unsophisticated’ for a novel (meaning that it lacked purposeful word choice, detailed explanation/description, etc). I also noticed a few grammatical errors.
-After solving the mystery once and playing again the game mostly follows the same exact process and ends with basically the exact same result regardless of the route. Meaning that basically once you have uncovered the mystery there remains very little content in the game that you don’t already know.
-I often had to redo routes because the game tends to be picky about the ‘date’ that your skills have to be maxed out by in order for you to get a ‘good’ ending. So even though I maxed out the required skills days before the ‘deadline’ the game wouldn’t register it. (This led to me to have to redo many past weeks for some of the routes which was slightly annoying and repetitive to say the least).
- The character sprites do not always reflect what the text is saying. Example: “Guy Character looks at me (the guy character sprite’s face looks neutral). But when our eyes meet he frowns… (the guy character’s face remains neutral)”. Beyond that often times the text will talk about a character being out of breath, or an action that they are preforming and that character’s sprite does nothing but stand still on the screen(this is where CG’s or more sprite drawings could be added to show the movement described within the text).
-No choices made negatively impacted a character’s relationship. (At least as far as I could tell)
-The game is kind of pricey for the content within this game.
=This game contains no voiced characters
=Some character’s fall into typical stereotypes, for example: The flirtatious jock.
=There are no hidden ‘Easter Eggs’ (at least as far as I could tell)
=The structure or anatomy of some of the character’s bodies isn’t quite ‘right’ looking, however those features do not stick out so badly that it negatively impacts the immersion.
=I would’ve liked it if there were choices available to choose that would help to shape Nicole as a character, because often times it seemed like the game gave us choices that would possibly shape who Nichole was but then later it would become apparent that she was still the exact same character/personality regardless of the choices you made.
Overall, I believe that this game has potential, but ultimately it falls short of my expectations. I give it a score of 6 out of 10. The game was fun at first but become repetitive fast. The ‘reward’ players get for their relentless efforts of button mashing, in my opinion, don’t outweigh the time and effort spent to receive that reward. The characters seem to bond slowly at first and then before you know it they are best buds and possible romantic partners with little to no build of emotional attachment between Nicole and the characters to explain why. The story itself is simple enough, but for a mystery visual novel it falls flat after ‘winning’ the game since most if not all of the suspense and mystery are gone now that the player has already solved the mystery once. Honestly I ended up skipping most of the dialogue when I replayed the game because I had already seen it; this made the game seem kind of shallow for a lack of diversity in routes or dialogue options when replaying the game. However, the game itself can be enjoyable at times (especially some of the character’s dialogue). I highly suggest that if you are deciding or considering buying this game that you buy it on sale and understand this game has its faults.

So I recieved a key for this game a few days ago and played through it, it's a really short game which is great because it matches my attention span. Don't let that drive you away from this game though, just sit back and let me spin you a review.
Submerged was developed and published by Uppercut Games and it revolves around a young girl Miku and her near death Brother Taku in a world that seems to have been drastically changed by the effects of global warming. We play as Miku throughout our adventure and we have to explore a large flooded city desperately looking for suppiess to help our Brother. Our goal is to find these supplies by climbing our way up tall skyscrapers in an assassins creed style way of parkour and getting to them by using our squrrelly as ♥♥♥♥ boat.
Heres a question, where did she get these crazy climbing skills? She lives in a flooded world with basically no way of climbing anything and she's a pro at this stuff, I still have trouble rock climbing with a pully system and yes, I lift.
Anyway, in order to find these supply crates we have to use our telescope to keep a look out for flags on certain buildings, and after every crate we get treated to a four slides revealing a bit more of our characters story.
But Justin? What else is there to duu?
That's the main story, Ten crates, 40 slides (I can maff) and about an hour and a half of in game time. There are a few side quests you can do such as finding a bunch of journal entries that give us the story of what happened to the city, finding all of landmarks across the ocean or finding the 8 different types of animals hanging about. Just 8, the rest are dead, Just like my dreams. I'm sure if you did everything there is to do in this game you'd top out at maybe 4 hours for a slow run or 2 and a half to 3 for a more focused run.
Over all this game is beautiful, the ambient sounds are great and the controls are responsive and easy, easy enough to let my four year old take a crack at the game, and while the story is neat it's not worth what the publisher is asking, I really did enjoy the game, but there isn't enough content here for a $19.99 price tag. Rocket league is $19.99...
Take the $20 you were going to spend on this and grab something with a bit more depth, but pick this game up when its 90% off on the next steam sale because it's a good way for us to actually finish a game for once and make us think we're making progress on our steam libraries.

First of all, Nicole was an overall good experience. I wouldn't call it the best vn I've ever played but it was good enough to play through all of the endings from the romanceable characters (I've postponed playing the bad ending for the time being but I will... sometime).
While I must say that I was enjoying the characters, the story itself and the art, the vn was lacking serious depth. I mean the case was actually quite good but I've felt that I - the player - could have gotten more out of playing and reading the story, whereas the romance parts where quite good. They weren't great but really cute.
The character profiles were quite profound. Jeff, for example, was the most intriguing one. I've begun with his path and thought the others would pale in comparison. I was mistaken. The romanceable scenes were always nicely written as I've already mentioned.
The only thing that was really bugging me, is the gameplay. The idea itself seems to be good but unpolished. You can choose a variety of actions every day but you could almost go on choosing the same option over and over and - to be completely honest here - it's gotten on my nerves. That was the only thing that would keep me from playing. IF there would have been an option like skipping that part completely or make it shorter, this would have been nice.
It's just a little sad that it doesn't really matter where you "level up" your skills. I would spend my days in-game just clicking the same option over and over again until I've reached the special ending.

Pretty much a Paradox Game through and through:
-Good strategy game. The base game by itself is good, it goes somewhat deep, it has a bunch of things to do and playstyles to explore along with hidden mechanics you'll be finding out years later if you don't read the wikis. Paradox Interactive has been doing grand strategy games for many years, they know the formula, they have the budget (from those diehard loyal fans) and they take their time. They might be bad distributors (just read about East and West: a Hearts of Iron game somewhere), but they're decent enough developers.
-Damn expensive (and barebones) DLC. Each update's more or less the same thing: add a mechanic or two to each religion/government type, slap a 20$/€ tag on the ability to play it and release it to the wild. People buy it because there's no competitor to go to. The updates are fun gimmicks, but it's in no way worth paying the money for it.
-Amazing modding scene. Now this is simply what makes the paradox games turn from okayish to great, they're so damn moddable! The modding scene in PI games have been around since (I believe) the second Hearts of Iron and Europa Universalis games. Some of these modders have been meddling with paradox games for more than ten years, some of them even got hired as employees by paradox. What this means is that the mods for CK2 are diverse. From gameplay tweaks to reduce that OP seduction focus to total overhauls. What's more, PI knows that this is their games' strong point, so they made organized, up to date and heavily moderated forums to gather the entire modding community into one hotspot of creativity.
I'd say three fourths of the charm of CK2 is the mods. So many mods, so many total overhauls that cover most of the most famous fantasy universes: A song of ice and fire, the elder scrolls, warhammer fantasy, middle earth. Of course, there's also the big mods that set out to give you the best experience in medieval europe (Like Historical Inmersion Project, Lux Invicta and CK2 Plus).
Some people tell you the game is worth it just because of the modding scene it has, they're right. These modders do their work for free yet they don't skip on the quality because of that, they put their hearts and souls into it (along with hours of their lives they could spend doing something else). And we should all be damn grateful that they do.
tl;dr: buy it, get a mod, have fun for a hundred hours; get another mod, have fun for another hundred hours. Also ♥♥♥♥ overpriced DLC.

Main flaw about most Winterwolves games, is the stat building to get to the route you want, and the time schedule. Basically, you'd have to know which stats you need to get what route, and where to go on which day exactly, to get a scene with the person whose route you want in order to build up points with them. It's the same in 'Always Remember Me', and in 'Roommates' as well.
For me this really draws away from the story, which is a shame because the stories in these games aren't half bad. I got almost all Winterwolves visual novels in several bundles once (Except the flower shop ones, which aren't any different apparently), and I know most of them are aimed towards a female audience, but that doesn't really matter to me if a story is good in a game, I enjoy it, such as 'Amnesia'. But this game, just like the others I've mentioned, is too focused on stat building, and it causes me to not be able to really get into it. The game becomes more of a chore.
Now if you look at a game such as 'Gakao Love 100 days', that one does it right when it comes down to managing stats. It doesn't draw away from the immersion. Naturally, you CAN get a bad ending, and if you wanted to get to every route you'd have to most likely resort to guides, but point is, in all the other non WinterWolves novels I've played, in those even a bad ending doesn't leave you empty handed and unsatisfied.. A bad ending in those, is still a route. But it's not, in WinterWolves games. it leaves you with a sense of not having achieved anything at all, and just having wasted a whole lot of time.
Also, I can play those other games, without a guide, going with personal choices, that appeal the most to me (That's always how I do a first playthrough of visual novels) and see where that gets me. It's the most fun, but I feel that in a game such as this one, I really can't. I can't go meet up with a character by choice, whose route I want to play, I have to run into them by going to the right place, at the right time.. That's just.. Not cool.
If you're into visual novels that you have to play with basically a guide to get anywhere, then I'd say this game isn't too bad, but I personally find it a flaw that really doesn't make this worth playing. I quit almost all of their games halfway through due to this. The only one that I can truly recommend from WinterWolves is: Loren, the Amazon Princess. That one's pretty awesome. I really think WinterWolves isn't bad at the stories they present in their games, I just wish they executed it differently.

This is a complex game and it's very different. Your family (a.k.a Dynasty) and spreading it is a big part of the game and warfare is generally secondary. So as a grand strategy game, while you can start as a noble with a family where you constantly war, this isn't at all necessary. So it's very different in this way.
CK2 is very detailed in lots of mechanics to manage your noble and your family as well as others who control lands and are your subjects. You can have people trying to assassinate you, rebel against you and much more. You can end up with a heir that you will be playing who has a hunchback, is a dwarf and is slow witted yet marry a genius wife who makes up for all of your characters drawbacks (Heaven help the children, one of which you'll likely play next).
There are multiple government types and cultures, though you will need paid DLC for some, such as merchant republics. The game itself spans about 800 years all told, so you'll take a long time to exhaust the possiblities for all the nations in the game over the game's timeframe, if that's even possible. So the replayability is pretty high, imo.
One downside which I don't think most people will actually see as a downside, is that with certain countries/nobles starting out, it's not considered hard to conquer the world by veteran players. On the other hand, not everything in a game is redesigning it so that doing just one thing, like a World Conquest, is harder or easier. The game as a whole is immersive and quite fun as you never know who you might want to assassinate or sleep with next :D
The other thing about CK2 is that while PI does put Pay Walls in this game as they've done with very direct and brutal reworks in another game (EU4 and Common Sense), CK2 thus far has mostly had paid additions that make the game better without taking away things that are present in the base game.
So CK2 seems to be cleaner and more ethical in how its free patches versus paid DLCs are developed. out. While this could, of course, change, so far it hasn't and that's quite refreshing given Paradox's history elsewhere.

This is a great RPG and I highly recommend it. It has pretty decent graphics (it is an almost 10 year old game) and the gameplay is engaging and fun. You go through a quest that gets bigger and more complicated as you continue. You pick up sidequests as you go along. The combat is fun, too. It is an action RPG and as you get more playable characters and skills, things become more challenging.
Incredibly, the game reminded me a lot of Landstalker for the sega genesis. The reason is because the game world is so beautiful and well put together. Each town has a destinctive look and feel and even seems alive. Also, the pacing is just right with a progression that feels natural and is interesting.
Overall, I was suprised at how deep the game is. It has virtually everything you could want from an RPG.
One other note: the game is amazingly optimized for PC. The loadtimes which I assume existed on the console are eliminated on PC. The game worked great with keyboard and mouse, but I prefer playing with the gamepad. Also, the graphics options are easily accessible and modifiable.

Gemini Rue is a nice little throwback to point-and-click PC gaming of the 90s. It looks like it came right out of 1994 with its low-res pixelated graphics but that doesn't mean that the game doesn't have a unique atmosphere. Set in an off-world colony in the future it reminded me a lot of Cowboy Bebop, then, whaddya know, Spike, Ed, and the rest of the gang show up. Fine inspiration indeed.
It plays out as a gloomy noir mystery as you struggle to find your missing brother amid a plot gangsters and conspiracies. It's simple enough and fairly easy-going entertainment with a decent soundtrack. I doubt it will be a classic, though it may well have been had it actually come out in the mid-90s.
After playing through it once I can say that I enjoyed the game but I won't be going back for seconds. The plot twist seemed a lot like Second Sight and I predicted it about an hour in advance. A fine effort nonetheless.
There are 15 trophies/achievements and some trading cards included.

I got this game on sale and was very satisfied with it.
Pros:
- If you're into the whole sci-fi existential thing, this is your storyline
- Retro feel and pixel art is spot-on (I appreciated the various nods to point-and-click games of old)
- Immersive atmosphere with great soundtrack
- Gameplay is not that long
Cons (mostly technical):
- I played on a Mac, and to right-click you have to use option+left click instead; it was a pain
- Walking from place to place repeatedly can be a chore, more so than most other point-and-clicks I've played (though there is a function to skip the walking with the esc key)
- Clunky combat system
- Voice acting a bit choppy at parts
- Some players found the twist shocking, but I guessed it halfway through so the big reveal wasn't as impactful as I'd hoped
This game isn't for everyone, but bottom line is if you like a good sci-fi storyline with secrets to be uncovered and you appreciate the retro point-and-click vibes, you'll probably enjoy Gemini Rue.

Sudeki was a game that I started out thinking was ok, was impressed with for a bit, then disappointed.
It is a game that had incredible potential, that was wasted on simplistic puzzles, shallow story and pidgeon holed game play in which certain characters were not available during certain sections of the story. In some cases, that made sense, but in other cases, like the final boss - (in which you think you'd have access to whatever character you wanted to play, you were limited to one), it was distressing.
It's a game that idea-wise was great, but in execution left me cursing at the stupidity of the story at times.
Don't get me wrong, it does have it good points. And it was fun for as long as I did play it, but at some points there was simply confusion as to what to do next, how to progress the story, etc...
I just wish that more time were devoted to the concept and an engrossing story, because it did have potential to be a great game, but missed the mark in my opinion.

Great story, music, and overall world design bogged down by the inherent tedium of point and click gameplay (in a game that, at times, requires both timing and precision) made worse by a horrible, "whack-a-mole" style combat mechanic. Check it out if you're desparate for a well-written cyperpunk noir accompanied by a solid soundtrack (and only if it's on sale), but probably not worth the trouble for the casual gamer (just setting it up on Windows 10 requires trial and error with compatibility settings and, even then, there's the issue of save file locations) - even in the case of the former (which is where I was when I bought it), the rough edges of this gem made it pretty hard to enjoy.

Character customization is decent.  Concept is good.  Default keybinds are not intuitive, and make switching weapons clunky - especially since there's no way to draw two one-handed weapons at once.  Skill/AP system looks shiny enough, but there is no apparent in-game info on what's most beneficial/what should be focused on - ask on the help channel, and you get pointed to the wiki site.  I'd rather be able to play the game than spend all day doing research on a wiki.  Combat is awkward, with targeting being off to one side of the character rather than in front, and the hitboxes seem off sometimes.  Running away/kiting doesn't seem to be a viable option, as melee enemies are able to hit you from several feet away - you'll just die tired.
Found the game on a top 20 MMO list, decided to give it a try.  Was excited to find there might be an RP element, but never saw any of that in-game - might be difficult as a F2P player to RP anyway, since there's no access to public channels?  Must be at least a "Freemium" player for that.

If you have not yet played a TES game, I definitely recommend starting at Oblivion, GOTY or no. I made the mistake of playing Skyrim prior to Oblivion, and I was spoiled because of the graphics and features Skyrim provided. But, this will not be a comparison between Skyrim and Oblivion.
Disregard graphics altogether. Oblivion came out in 2006. Besides, there is a plethora of ways to improve upon Oblivion's 'primitive' graphics if you are playing it on the pc (which you probably will be if you're reading this): OBGE, primarily.
The gameplay of Oblivion is fabulously open-ended. There never seems to be an end to the quests, and if you manage to complete all of them, you are a whole different kind of person.
The class system and leveling is highly rewarding, the stat boosts given by leveling are extremely useful. The only downside is, you need to know exactly what type of character you are going to be and what path your character is going to take in the beginning. If you don't know that your character is going to be, let's say, a ranger vs. a full-fledged destruction mage, then you are already behind.
The art style of Oblivion seems to be rather bright and colourful, which I admire. It really seems to complement the environment of Cyrodiil.
If anything else, I recommend buying the game for the soundtrack, though. It's that good. The one thing Bethesda seems to get right every single time in their video games are the soundtracks. The music and ambience fit in perfectly with every given scenario within the game, whether you are strolling along in the Imperial City or fighting Daedra in the planes of Oblivion.
Overall, Oblivion gets an exceptional 9.5/10

Okay first of all, this game isn't bad and I'm not trying to say it is. It's a fine game, but I just can't recommend it for several reasons.
First of all, it's very very hard. Yes yes, I know, people are going to say crap like "get gud" or whatever, but sometimes the issue goes beyond that, like in my case. I have memory and attention impairment issues which do not pair well with these kinds of games. However, I like basebuilding and I usually like the general flow of these games so I like to play them, but on easy difficulty to counteract my impairments. This is not possible in this game, it has one extremely hard difficulty and that's it. It cannot even be modded, so there are no difficulty mods available. This is simply not fair for those of us who paid for this game but cannot access the content we paid for because of disabilities that cannot be helped.
Second, the cut scenes can only be hurried but not skipped. It's fine generally, but if you've got to play the same level over and over then you'll be mashing space bar while the camera interrupts you and takes you over to whatever it's talking about. I couldn't find a way to shut this off, but perhaps I just missed it.
The voice over is great, and I was enjoying the silly over-the-top evil story for as far as I could reasonably get., but sometimes it gets SO ANNOYING. I know my stupid minion is unhappy, but I literally just started a fight and I can't let the thing go and I would really appreciate if you would SHUT UP ABOUT IT. I've had many occasions were minions get stuck staring at whatever they're supposed to do to make themselves happy but never actually do it. I've had them stand in the middle of a full treasure vault and not pick anything up while the VO keeps reminding me that this minion is unhappy because it hasn't been paid. I've had minions walk out of empty sleeping quarters even though they are tired and the VO keeps saying that minion is unhappy because it's tired. I even have built NEW rooms to try and give more space for those needs and even then the minions ignore them. The whole happiness system is a mess really, I think it should be scrapped.
Then I have a lot of little complaints. I don't like mouse scrolling for instance, but there is no option to toggle it. You'd think that would be a given. Why can't I make a guard room? I can only make traps, and traps are pretty weak compared to minions. I think they tried to make up for that part with warbands, but warbands are trash. You can't tell what minions you have in them, if you rally it to a point then minions get unhappy because they are stuck there and can't go satisfy their needs. You can't just assign them to patrol that area like you could with a guard room in the Dungeon Keeper games. These are broken systems that work against you, making an already difficult game much harder and not on the basis of anything good.
I do like how it looks, I love how the different rooms have their own looks for reinforced walls, I love how the rooms look in general. I like the graphics and I like the general feel. Everything is just brought tumbling down with an insane difficulty level and broken systems.
In the end, I really wish I hadn't wasted my money on a game I can't even play. I'd rather just play the old Dungeon Keeper games, I can actually get through those and enjoy myself. In fact, I think I'll go do just that.

Submerged is a beautiful game with a great soundtrack and environment. It feels a little like a cross between A Tale of Two Brothers & Lili: Child of Geos in terms of the worldly feel & gameplay. The game is essentially exploration and you start off boating your injured brother Taku to a submerged city. From there you boat place to place, trying to find "crates" that contain survival stufffs. The story is pieced together literally via little pictures that you either find throughout your travels or receive after finding each crate (there are sections for animals, the city, the protagonists, landmarks...). You also have the option to search for capsized boats for upgrades, which is essentially a nice speed boost (very useful later on from getting between points A and B). The platform like levels are clever and quaint. The environment does change from day to night depending on how long you explore and admittedly, while beautiful, it does get unsettling at night in abandoned submerged buildings.
This is certainly not an "exciting" or "fast-paced" game, it's about the slow and beautiful exploration of the world and its environment, so if you're looking for that kind of excitement, this may not be the game suitable for you.
My computer is about 3 years old so the game runs decently enough though the loading screen is unusually long for me, so it's just a heads up for people with older graphics cards and things. If you save & quit in the middle of nowhere at night, for example, when you load up, you will start at homebase in the day but all your exploration progress is kept. Also, definitely use your Telescope since it locks on to points of interests and records it in the map for later use. For people who'd like to save time instead of boating to the same place since they missed something: crates prompt an immediate return to home, therefore I'd recommend searching the area and interacting with the crate last since it would be a bit annoying to have to come back if you accidentally grabbed the crate first instead of the collectible book.
There does appear, however, to be a bug of some sort at a landmark site called "The Net Tower" which essentially looks like a tall communication tower with a squarish base. Unfortunately, getting close to it prompts the mini aesthetic cutscene and crashes the game. I would recommend steering clear of that area for the time being. There is the occasionally problem of the girl jumping from ledges (typically, if possible, she would drop down the ledge to climb) but this is remedied by the game loading up your progress from a few paces back. For the ledges I'd recommend walking up the edges and then climbing down, since it's wonky.
TLDR; it's a beautiful game and I definitely recommend it!

: If you're up for a simulation game with a bit of romance and mystery, give it a try. This is definitely the best Winter Wolves offering I've played.
---
: It's meant to be a mystery-romance story, and while those elements are
, I wouldn't pick it up for that experience. The romance elements seem heavier than many of the Winter Wolves games I've picked up, but you don't really get a lot of "mystery" at all. There are certainly some thriller elements, but the character's exploration of the mystery of the title is done entirely in simulation. Like most Winter Wolves games, the simulation part of the title is the majority of the gameplay and can really quite interfere with the story flow. That said, I did enjoy the title, but I want people to know what they're actually getting when they buy this one.
: Overall, if you're okay with the premise of "girl in danger", you ought be okay. Honestly, I think if you can watch a PG-13 movie, you're more than qualified to handle the story's content.
: N/A - as far as I know, English is their first language.
: There were no errors in the text itself that I noticed. (I did notice two elsewhere, but I really doubt many would notice either.)
: Overall, quite lovely. The style is super cute. My only issue is really that there were very few CGs and they didn't really match the sprites - often being dressed in something entirely different. (Also, the background for one area did not at all match what the text said.) I love that the sprites had multiple outfits - it really helped a lot. I just wish that there were a few more expressions since sometimes the expression didn't quite match the text.
: I loved Nicole's sprites. Her outfits were always great. Overall, the designs for the love interests were pretty good too. (Didn't always match their personalities, but...)
: I hate that the simulation overtook the story. I hate that the kidnapper was who I knee-jerk thought it was the moment I talked to them. I hate that they never outright stated why Nicole was a target of the kidnapper, given the reasons for the other kidnappings. I hate that the endings more than 60%, word-for-word the same as every other ending and you can't even skip through the bits that are the same.
I hate these things because otherwise, I really enjoyed it.
It really bothers me that gathering the 999 clues necessary to "win" does literally nothing (as far as I can tell) except trigger the difference between the good or bad ending. Nicole spends all semester gathering Clues and only is able to find anything out at the end of the game. It's a disconnect that probably wouldn't bother most people, but certainly makes me think "Ludonarrative dissonance". It would have been better to me if a certain number of Clues gathered triggered different scenes where she gathered information, so it really felt as if all that work she'd done reading old news articles, observing people, and talking to people amounted to anything.
: Certainly a woman of her own! I didn't like her much at the beginning of the story, but she grew on me. She is, however, an extrovert who doesn't "get" introverts in the slightest, so if you're a fellow introvert, her "playful" bullying of the introverts might annoy you.
: As with many of my otome reviews, I seem to have more complaints than compliments. Please don't take that as a suggestion not to read/play the game, though! Nicole has a lot to offer to those where the concerns I brought up aren't deal breakers. Hoping Winter Wolves continues to improve.

Submerged is a game that is solely about exploration.  It's vast yet empty world creates a haunted landscape filled with secrets and collectibles for you to acquire.  The graphics in this game are stunning, and more then that, the world itself is imaginatively  put together.  The sunken city seems to combine elements from a variety of cultures leaving you wondering both where and what was this city.  What happened here?  What happened to the world?  And the answers can be found through a few hours of thorough combing through the cities buildings and many landmarks.  As day turns to night and night to day you will constantly find yourself stopping to take a moment to appreciate how the light is hitting the water, how the animals seem to move keeping the world alive, yet still barren.  The music creates a perfect ambiance to back this journey of exploration.
The only area where this game really seems to lag is in the gameplay.  The actual gameplay elements are all perfectly functional, but far too simplistic.  I found myself growing tired of the climbing within the first few buildings because there was just no challenge.  There's two parts to gamplay, riding in your boat and climbing.  The climbing is just pointing the direction you want to go and nothing else.  And the gameplay never evolves.  The only thing that changes throughout the 2 hours it will take you to complete the basic storyline is the boost on your boat increases as you collect other fallen boats.  I would have loved a more challenging climbing system, or possibly some obstacles to overcome/puzzles to solve, something to add a bit difficulty.  Without is the game can seem to start dragging at times.
Overall through I would say in all elements except for gameplay this game was a 10/10 for me.  Gameplay is a 6/10 -perfectly functional but lacks engagement or escalation.  I would absolutely recommend this to anyone who might be looking for a game a bit more cathartic, or relaxing, or who just really wants to see what a strong imaginative team of developers can come up with when they really try to create something beautiful.

+ Art is very nice, especially the sprite art
+ Music is pretty atmospheric and pleasant
+ Well written. The choice setup has nice variations. I wound up saving beforehand to see each choice's reaction. Ted is my favorite for having his accent reflected in his dialogue.
+ The in-game tips were very helpful. I had no difficulties in figuring out the stats system and getting all the endings.
+ Each of the characters had different outfits for different scenes. This small attention to detail was a plus for me.
+ Characters have believable flaws. The romance felt really natural. Nicole's personality worked dynamically well for each guy. The three pair scenes were really fun as well. Otome games usually don't include 3P scenes unless it's a love triangle, so it was refreshing. Only one route was kind of questionable.
+ The pacing of character scenes is good. They are well padded throughout the game. They give a good amount of time to catch up on stats without having to save and reload if you are efficient.
- The mystery endings all led to the same conclusion, so they ended up being a little repetitive.
- UI is a little wonky when taking screenshots and seeing the sprites bleed out of the game window. I would have liked a proper CG gallery with the full uncut CGs.
Being the same developer, I was wary going into the game, but left feeling impressed. Nicole was much more enjoyable and pleasant to play through than Always Remember Me.
I think getting this during one of Winter Wolves' 50% off sales would be best.

This is a fun and breezy otome game. In it, you play as Nicole, a college freshman, who is investigating the abductions of three girls at her university. The goal is to collect clues throughout the semester in order to solve the mystery by winter break. Since this is an otome game, you also need to build up your relationship with one of four guy characters.
Without giving too much away, the romanceable characters are essentially:
-Kurt - a flirty jock on the football team
-Ted - an obsessive workaholic
-Darren - a painfully shy classmate
-Jeff - an intelligent upper classman
My only complaint is that even if you collect enough clues by the end of the semester, the bad end seems to trigger if you don't have a relationship with one of the guys. I would have liked to have seen an alternate ending where, if you gather enough clues, Nicole effectively handles the mystery by herself without needing to also be in a relationship.
All in all, this was a fun otome game that I would recommend to fans of the genre. Also, if you're going to play this one, I would recommend romancing Jeff first.

I am a little mixed about this game but like it enough to give a positive recommendation. I give it a recommendation because I like the art and 2 characters and there is something likable in a “home grown” visual novel which targets an English speaking audience (leaning toward American as they are in Florida)
The art is really made me buy this game. I think it's geared more to a English speaking audience but doesn't cross into the line of silly cartoon style of the West. Also the character designs are cute and the clothes are defiantly something that you would see an American college student wear rather than a Japanese/Korean. I think this makes the characters more likable because I felt like I was back in my own college days and these could be my own friends, where as characters targeted at a Japanese/Korean market always make me feel a little alienated, even though I did study in Japan for half a semester.
The writing isn't bad, but has an overly simple plot. I'm really not huge on raising sims, I just want to read the story, so my view would probably more skewed toward the quality of the story. I felt quite a bit let down after solving the “big mystery” of the game, there is much potential for a much more in depth story. There is a bit of surprise on one path that I did enjoy, but I don't want to spoil the game in a review.
However after playing so many VN/Otome games made from the Japanese market, it felt really refreshing to play a game that was actually targeting English speakers. Culture references, ways of speaking, quirks that make characters more interesting (accents, etc), characters that were designed to target English speakers all make this game more unique.  Also stereotypical characters can even be interesting when you feel like there are so many rehashed characters in the Japanese market (more seen in mobile games).
The game play isn't bad, but I'm not huge on stat raising games. It took me  a bit of time to find the best way to raise the stats but after that it got a tad bit boring. I like games that at least try to add a bit of dialogue for every time a stat is raised, makes it feel a bit more exciting than just simply dry game play of stat raising games.
TLDR- Buy this game if you are looking for something different than the standard otome game

This is a decent Action RPG. I'd recommend it for anyone out there looking for a simple ARPG if you're not afraid of a few ugly 3D models. It's not my place to criticize the character design but they're a bit over-the-top and heavily influenced by anime, not that it matters but this game is not japanese.
This game was one of the handful of RPGs that Microsoft made with interest of slipping the Xbox console into the Japanese market. While the game was not a commercial success, what we ended up having was easily a fantastic RPG on Xbox and even though it's been out for PC for quite a while, it's such an obscure game that nobody really noticed it much and now we have it on Steam and I couldn't be happier.
The story, as well as the characters are somewhat forgetable, but it's got amazing scenery, the style of the world is similar to Fable and Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning. Very colorful, full of fantastic devices and monuments and very green with lots of vegetation too.
The gameplay is the most important element in this game: it's fluid and it gives you a few choices, you can play an action hack-and-slash type of character or a First Person Shooter type.
You get 4 characters to play with, all play together in the battlefield but you take control of one while AI takes over the others. 2 of them use Melee (Hack-and-Slash) and the other 2 use long range attacks (FPS).
Each of them has different skills and combos and you can enter a slow-motion mode when you go through the skills and pick one to use, so the game never truly feels like it comes to a halt. This makes things stay interesting for a while.
I could go on and on about who's who and what each character does but honestly, it's not that important, just know they're all very different in their style even if their gameplay is similar. Combos are different, they use different weapons, skills are definitely very very different so you'll have favorites. Also, all their one-liners are SUPER CHEESY so you can't escape those either way.
The voice acting is not very good, you can see it's not a big budget game but these fantasy RPG type of games are TEXT-HEAVY so the voice acting is basically cutscenes and one-liners.
On the technical aspect of the port: I am playing with an official Xbox 360 Gamepad and it's playing really GOOD, no complaints on the controller scheme, it's basically the same as back on the Xbox (although it's been almost 8 years so...don't quote me on that). The only problem I see is how the game text uses  "Button1" and "Button2" instead of labeling it "X" and "A", but that's not a big deal.
I'm not on the high-end of PC gaming but I can run this game fine and so far I've seen no issues with widescreen or sudden crashes (from a bit of play-testing) and the frames per second seem fine too, I do see some issues with vertical sync but it doesn't take away from the experience. I do wish there were some mods for this though, some 2D art and 3D models are ugly (my opinion) and I'd love to change them.
Although it is not some sort of hidden underrated gem, it's definitely a good game that didn't get enough attention and I'm sure most sales for this will be nostalgia-induced, and that's not necesarily a bad thing. It's based on something real good, enough to stay in your mind and make you want to play it again.

When i originally bought this game in early 2013 i was enjoying it a lot. Unique first person fighting with pretty good graphics, awesome sound and especially voice design on top of a good old directional combat system akin to Mount and Blade.
However i could no longer enjoy this game or recommend it to others :gloomy:
I was trying to get back into this game for last two years, but i wasn't able to get any pleasant experience :steamsalty:
I'll explain why.
1.  No matchmaking, no skill rating, no balance. Noobs start in paddling pool for little kids and then get thrown straight into adult life to get destroyed by pros.
2. Annoying shaking on getting hit - disorients you, disrupts your concentration, destroys your aimed attacks.
3. Hard to judge the distance and reach of your weapon(either 1st p. or 3rd p.) => miss attacks, and get unexpected hits due to bad distance estimate. (it gets better with experience, but still feels odd compared to some other games and i dont know why)
4. Combat mechanics are too simple and prone to abuse("balerina-knights", reverse overheads, combat sprinting and other questionable "techniques")
: Either get it on sale and enjoy till rank 15, or play M&B:Warband and wait for Mordhau.

First off let me comment on the most popular reason in steam reviews - playing above 15 rank.
Basically to find a match you go to a Server Browser, pick any server you like and jump in. However, teams in the match are only balanced by size and anyone can join any team as long as teams stay equal in number of players.
The only thing to allow decent experience to new players are low rank servers, avaiable only to players below 15 rank.
Ranks are gained by earning points in games - for kills, objectives and such, so your ranks is just amount of kills and other stuff you did in game over all your career. Shows nothing but your game time.
But as soon as you get above 15 rank you are thrown in combat against players of all levels.
Which together with lack of any team balance mechanic or skill rating system means matches are often poorly balanced and overall experience is not enjoyable.

Camera shake - every time you get hit in Chivalry your camera shakes(violently).
It is very irritating and anticlimactic. It ruins the rhythm and pace of the game, it disorients the player. essentially kicks your eyes off the screen for split second destroying your contentration. Also because it takes fixed amount of time before you get back full control over camera - it also often makes it very hard to protect yourself after getting hit.
Not only that, but it also affects your weapon too! Which means perfectly aimed strike can suddenly turn away in the last moment if you take a hit.
I can't remember right now, but i am pretty sure that they added camera shaking about half a year after the initial release.
There is no option to turn it off or reduce intensity.
(In case anyone wonders about motion sickness/simulation sickness - i've never had it, the camera shake just irritates the crap out of me, it is simply anti-fun)

Doesn't matter if you play first person or third person - it is very hard to judge how long is the reach of your weapon and how far away your target is. It gets worse when you use higher FoV(which you need here).
There are no tools to help a player with this. You can only rely on your camera perspective, and somehow it feels a bit off compared to other games, even at similar FoV values. In fact overall camera responsiveness feels odd, i don't seem to be able to aim any attack or shot... (mouse smoothing is off)
It gets better with experience, though.
(I dont have any suggestion how to fix this, other than by adding some markers or a radar)
I also want to comment about combat and how boring it can be, but i'm sure many people will disagree with this, especially new players and veteran fans.
In short combat is centered around directional attacks and blocking. There are four directional attacks plus thrust, but only one
type of protection - blocking. One particular class also can dodge, but the it feels clunky and unresponsive.
There is no weapon collision, no chambering, nothing like that.
In an overly simplified view combat is just repeated attacking and parrying until one person makes a mistake (a mistake of any kind - bad footwork, missing an attack or a parry, missing a feint(cancelled attack)).
Of course there are also advanced techniques - footwork and combat sprinting, crouching and looking down(camera also controls your torso), but they are not as clear and streamlined as i think true game features should be.
Please comment and let me know if you agree, disagree or think i am wrong!
Thanks for reading!
