I Started playing this game when it first got greenlight, here on steam. And I was really excited and had high hopes of re-living  the amazing memories I had with Dungeon Keeper series. I told to myself " This is it, this game will be the successor of Dungeon Keeper. It was really promising, the feel, the mechanics, everything smelled like nostalgia except the polished up graphics. However, my opinions changed overtime.
Most people enjoyed dungeon keeper so much because that game was more of a dungeon simulator than of a RTS. Building your own dungeon, managing your diverse creatures, carefully planning rooms, taking your time to train your creatures and beginning the action at your own leisure. I remember spending 3-4 hours before having any fights with the enemy. I could chose when I want to open my doors to the enemy, and take my time, enjoying my little dungeon get build. However War for the Overworld is much more fast paced compared to it. The maps are quite open ended. There is literally no way or point to plan a dungeon to your liking because most of the time you dig a wall, your dungeon will be wide open almost to %70 of the map. This takes away the simulation and dungeon building aspects of the game, making you play fast and act fast. This also renders traps and doors quite useless because its hard to build a decent sized dungeon with choke points. You can clearly see that this game focuses on Multiplayer elements rather than single player.
Also the creatures lookdiverse at the beginning but they lack characteristics. I remember having to build different lairs for different creatures in dungeon keeper, because some of them couldn't get along with each other. You had to seperate flies and spiders, because, well they are natural enemies, or vampires and warlocks etc. And their lairs would grow bigger as they leveled up. And they would also get bigger in size. Between 50 creatures you could easily spot that dragon or bile demon that you trained so much. Those small details made every creature unique in dungeon keeper. However in War for the Overworld every creature feels the same, even though they have different appearances and spells. They just feel like numbers, that's all. Some of them stronger, some of them weaker.
There are many other things I dislike about this game. Giving you high hopes of resurrecting a legend but failing to do so. Still worth the price on sale, and if you were a dungeon keeper fan you should have it in your library. But don't get any hopes of reliving Dungeon Keeper otherwise you will be disappointed like me. Just try to enjoy it as a brand new game, not inspired by DK.

So this is my first time reviewing a game on Steam. I first picked up Dungeon Keeper 2 in 1999 and played it on and off (keeping a dedicated Windows 98 computer kicking just for it until around 2007). Needless to say, I’m a huge fan. I followed this WFTO through its Kickstarter, and was playing it release day.
It’s beating a dead horse now but the initial release product wasn’t great. It was bad enough that I couldn’t play it between slowdowns, crashes, and bugs. I put it down and forgot about it till this year. After picking it up this summer I’ve just beaten my way through the main campaign and the Heart of Gold expansion, as well as the My Pet Dungeon expansion. I’m around 200 hours logged.
PRO'S
If you didn’t know any better you would assume this was an authorized third game. The sounds, creatures, and enemies all really feel like they would belong in the original games.
I loved the new constructs, like construct earth to fix dungeon walls and the gold portals. Both were highly appreciated additions.
The peaceband and custom rally flags were also incredibly helpful (although I didn’t discover it till about a 100 hours in). I immediately went back and restarted the main campaign and heart of gold after I discovered these features.
CON'S
I guess one of the best complaints about a video game, it’s too short. I want more. The main campaign was only 13 missions which flew by way to quick for me.
Halfway through the main campaign there is a Necromancer mission. It drag. The level takes way too long and it isn’t very interesting. During the level there isn’t much to do for the player except drop rally flags and wait. I get what they are trying to do and it’s very similar to the facility levels in Starcraft, but it’s just not very fun.
Finally, that ending… I had to go check the forums to make sure my computer didn’t bump me out of an ending video. I get what they were implying but it was so short and anticlimactic that it feels like the developers ran out of time. I’d love to see a more developed ending eventually patched in or have it directly expanded upon in an expansion.
OVERALL
If you are looking for something to scratch that DKII fix, this is it. The dev's have worked hard to fix the product since launch and it is a fantastic spirtual sequel.

I highly recommend this game. Its fast, skillful, satisfying, challenging, gorgeous, well animated, smooth, gruesome, runs very nicely on even some lower-middle end computers, highly customizable in that the editor is outstanding and intuitive which allows for a large community to express itself, and it is extremely detailed and accurate in both it's combat and animation.
It would be very cool to see this have a vast open world compaign with a script written with help from the community. As of now it is only closed levels but they are quite large, customizable and beautiful.
With all this being said, there is still one major issue I have with this game: So you've got a game, a very well sculpted game, that has a vast amount of code and attention to detail, but its almost as if you've built a mansion on wobbily stilts. Its like a one legged chair, the leg is rounded on the bottom yet you have a masterpiece of a throne on top. The game crashes a lot. It needs a stronger foundation in order to keep itself upright, if you want to think of it that way. Thankfully the crashes usually come during intense combat and not level editing from what I've seen, it could be different for others
So would I recommend this game? Whole-heartedly, yes. There are plenty of fixes for the crashes and you can send the crash files to the developer. The game has been in development for a long time and has only gotten more and more popular.
As a side note to the developer, I and probably a large portion of the community, wouldn't mind a period of time (however long it takes) where the only updates were crash fixes and foundation builds. The game is very much so a sandbox and doesn't need menu updates or any of that for a bit in my opinion. I would just like to see a stronger base. Thank you.
And to whoever is reading this, I would pick this game up ASAP or at least keep it in the top 3 of your wishlist. Its a great game and I don't think I will ever get sick of it (that means a lot coming from the person who can't stay on other games for more than 5 minutes).

This game is a successor to the All-Great Dungeon Keeper Series that I played since my childhood. I think it is developed by parts of the team from the old Bullfrog, which means, it is not a cheap clone or some but indeed sort of Dungeon Keeper 3. Since EA holds the copyright they cannot use this name.
The game feels instantly right. It carries on the spirit of the old Dungeon Keepers but with some very nice improvements and innovations. In the old games, you only had Rooms, Creatures, Spells and Defenses. Now, they added new content in the form of some new mechanics namely Rituals, Potions, Constructs and Shrines.
Many things are made clearer e.g. the efficiency of rooms is now directly related to the number of "Props" and for each prop the number of surrounding fortified walls. Life points and the description of skills of the creatures are also much clearer.
One of the best innovations is the number of possibilities that you have with your prisoners. But that you may discover yourself.
There are some issues that make this game seem unpolished i.e. sometimes laggy input and UI, too exaggerated possession-POV-effects and some others.
But I am very glad, that I finally got this game in a nice sale and very happy with it.

Submerged is a game that is solely about exploration.  It's vast yet empty world creates a haunted landscape filled with secrets and collectibles for you to acquire.  The graphics in this game are stunning, and more then that, the world itself is imaginatively  put together.  The sunken city seems to combine elements from a variety of cultures leaving you wondering both where and what was this city.  What happened here?  What happened to the world?  And the answers can be found through a few hours of thorough combing through the cities buildings and many landmarks.  As day turns to night and night to day you will constantly find yourself stopping to take a moment to appreciate how the light is hitting the water, how the animals seem to move keeping the world alive, yet still barren.  The music creates a perfect ambiance to back this journey of exploration.
The only area where this game really seems to lag is in the gameplay.  The actual gameplay elements are all perfectly functional, but far too simplistic.  I found myself growing tired of the climbing within the first few buildings because there was just no challenge.  There's two parts to gamplay, riding in your boat and climbing.  The climbing is just pointing the direction you want to go and nothing else.  And the gameplay never evolves.  The only thing that changes throughout the 2 hours it will take you to complete the basic storyline is the boost on your boat increases as you collect other fallen boats.  I would have loved a more challenging climbing system, or possibly some obstacles to overcome/puzzles to solve, something to add a bit difficulty.  Without is the game can seem to start dragging at times.
Overall through I would say in all elements except for gameplay this game was a 10/10 for me.  Gameplay is a 6/10 -perfectly functional but lacks engagement or escalation.  I would absolutely recommend this to anyone who might be looking for a game a bit more cathartic, or relaxing, or who just really wants to see what a strong imaginative team of developers can come up with when they really try to create something beautiful.

As you can see, I generally recommend this game, but it's not that simple. Thi is still an alpha title and you should take this into account should you consider to spend money here. I have posted the following text on the forum a few times and I think it is still accurate. But before I start, let me give you the tl;dr version: do some research first to find out if you can justify spending money on this title right now. Watch gameplay videos and tutorials. Try to get an idea of what there is right now and what you can expect in the future. Then make a decision.
The game has two major gameplay selling points. The movement and the combat.
The game lets you move around very quickly. You can jump up very high and you can run along walls and jump off of them and grab ledges to reach higher platforms. All these features are very easy to control and feel very fluent. The game lets you move around at high speeds and jumping around like that is very satisfying for some people.
If you just want to have some stupid fun you can use the debug keys to slit your character's throat and enjoy the way blood is handled in the game or making enter one of the ragdoll modes and watch him tumble down a cliff.
[/u]Combat:[/u] The combat is absolutely outstanding. Every move is triggered by your own movement and the character will perform the most appropriate move for his position in relation to the opponent. This may sound as if it was automatic, but the way the fights are handled in the game actually gives you complete control over what you are doing. After some training you will be able to position yourself just right to do exactly what you want to do.
For me, the hand to hand combat is just about perfect. It's probably the best combat I have ever seen in an action game. Every move has its purpose and you can really use tactics to fight certain opponents. The weapons still need some more balancing in my opinion, but they are fun as well.
You have to keep in mind that there may be a bunch of maps and even an arena that puts in one fight after the other and makes the opponents tougher or weaker depending on your performance, but none of that is tied together by any sort of story yet. If you get your fun in games from progressing through a story and moving from one map to the next one, you should probably wait until the campaign is there. If you enjoy combat and like to play around in a sandbox style game, you can already get it and will have fun with it.
The game has a map editor. It is still pretty bare bones, but you can create simple maps fairly easily by editing an existing map, putting models into it, modifying them and then saving it. If you invest some more time you can create more elaborate maps, for example by putting cutscenes in that trigger when the character reaches a certain point. There are many tutorials available for more complicated things (e.g. creating your own terrain so that you don't have to edit an existing map, or for creating caves), but creating your first map is pretty easy.
Some more experienced users have created custom characters and models to give the community more stuff to play with. Maybe you have some experience with modelling and would like to do that too.
If you like creating stuff the game has plenty to offer, even if you are not a very technical person. The map editor is easy to use and you can create your first map in a very short time. If you have some experience, you can create your own models, characters and complete maps. There are tutorials on the Wolfire Forums that can get you started.
The community has created tons of stuff that you can add to your game. There is even a tool, the SUMLauncher, that will help you to install maps, objects and characters with just a few clicks. It cannot handle script mods, but that feature will probably be added at some point.
There are very many maps, ranging from very simple attempts, to parkour maps and massive structures for you to explore, all the way elaborate maps that tell little stories. Some maps are also used to present custom assets.
This content comes in the forms of new characters (a few examples: we have a few human characters, a bird creature and a zombified version of the main character), new weapons, objects for building structures (e.g. assets to create a modern city with streets and skyscrapers, or a Viking scene), objects tied to scripts (e.g. a landmine, a homing missile, rain, snow, water), new moves and probably some stuff I am forgetting. It's a lot.
There are also a few mods out there. Some change little things about the game, some add features and some change the gameplay. My Favourites are Last's Blood Mod and Korban's First Person Mod. The first person mod is pretty self explanatory. The Blood Mod started as a mod that gave a you a few options to make the game more or less bloody, but has since become a collection of a few mods. A few of the features that can be activated individually: there's a flying mod. It lets you flap your arms to gain height and glide. The controls a very fluent and you can get some serious speed while gliding. There is a feature that makes your character enter ragdoll mode if you run into a wall or another character at high speed. This can effectively be used as tackle. It adds a few debug keys, for example to make you invincible. There are also some experimental features.
These mods have to be installed manually and are often not compatible with one another, since they edit the same files, but installing them is usually just done via drag and drop.
The community has created so much stuff for users to play with. If you preorder it you should definitely check it out, especially if you want to make maps yourself or get into modding the game.
I hope this helps you to come to a decision. Please take your time. This game probably is not for everyone and 30$ may not be very expensive for a game, but since it is still an alpha some features simply are not there yet and you will have to put some trust into the developers. If you cannot do that right now, you should probably wait.
Please also keep in mind that there are many videos online that can show you the game in action. I especially recommend the videos over at Overgrowth Weekly.
He has some of the best tutorials especially for parkour and combat. But he also tells you how to get the game in the first place and how to use the editor. He also hosts regular Q&A sessions with the team, where they tackle questions by the community.
Parkour tutorial:
Hand to hand combat tutorial:
The uploads by Wolfire themselves also feature a lot of gameplay and editor footage and always tell you the latest additions to the game.
One last thing. If you eventually decide to preorder the game, compare the prices on Steam and the Humble Store. Both will give you the same thing (i.e. Overgrowth, plus Receiver and Low Light Combat), but depending on your region, Steam might be more expensive. Both websites also have it on sale from time to time.
Getting access to the Secret Preorder Forum on Wolfire is also a lot easier if you preorder from the Humble Store. I have read many complaints from people who had trouble getting access after preordering from Steam. If you preorder from the Humble Store you will be able to get your Wolfire account the way people have done it ever since the game was announced and you can get it on Steam with two or three clicks from your Humble Store page.

Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is a good idea that, over the course of years, has been slowly been turned into a worst one. Granted, the game offers a more approachable gameplay than "War of the Roses" but also feels much more basic.
The gameplay was originally very interesting and even enticing but slowly turned into a rather unpleasant mess that carries little to no weight other than making impacts feel artifically heavy.
As stated before, the game was once an approachable, easy to learn and difficult to master kind of experience. Fights felt fair and while there were instance of people giving up melee combat for ranged combat entirely, you rarely ended up with rage-quitting situations unless you fought very sour players.
Nowadays however, the 'fun' has been thrown out of the window entirely with players able to experience a shadow of what the game felt like from rank 0 to 15 servers and even then, that is a very deceptive expectation given the amount of experienced players making alt-accounts only to be able to beat down on new players.
Post rank 15, the game becomes a very glitch-abuse heavy experience where actual reflexes and skill have no more meaning. People will abuse the game to the point of making fights completely unmanageable and unless you are willing to partake in such abuse yourself, then you will be at a severe disadvantage.
It seems the balance has also been heavily modified and some of the map designs have very obvious flaws, often giving objective maps a very obvious advantage to the defending team (and while that is a logical advantage to any defense worth its salt, it goes to the level of attackers getting ganked the moment they step out of their spawn with disgusting frequency).
There are still bugs that remains that makes some matches completely unplayable, one in particular that affects me at times is that it is impossible to join the action even after choosing a team and a class, being stuck in spectator mode even though there are open slots in the server.
I know it is a rather strange bug to have though it seems to persist after installing the game from my old computer to the new one which leads me to believe it might be Steamworks related.
Post release and a few months after, the game had potential; it was fun, people fought for the fun of fighting with swords. If you are now considering the game, I would advise against buying it simply because the experience has devolved into an unpleasant mess that favors the exploitation of glitches that aren't being fixed and is certainly no longer worth the retail price of 27 CAD$.
A shame that a game once loved has only gotten this worst with time.

First Impressions: At first, this appears to be a chaotic mess of a game, with armored men charging at each other's flanks and hacking eachother to death with giant swords. It felt very loose, and senselessly challenging.
My Three Hours: I spent my three hours with the game playing multiplayer on public servers with strangers. I also spent a lot of that time very sweaty from moving, and increasingly tipsy from cheap wine. With that said, my opinion of the game rose considerably during my time with it.
Most of the game consists of team or free for all multiplayer melees, using Medieval arms and armor. This is a challenging game to master, as there are many different ways to attack and parry based on movement and a number of alternate attacks.
However, in spite of the possibility of complex, dance-like melees of feints, parries and counter attacks, the most effective strategy is often to flank an opponent and hit them a bunch with a sword. (This was what I tended to do).
Reach and weapon speed also matter quite a bit, so my alternate favorite strategy became running in very close, then engaging with a dagger at a range where my opponents had trouble hitting me with a sword or spear.
My highlight: Playing at 1 or 2 am, running around with a spear, listening to Hamilton and playing as a mean spirited opportunist, but imagining myself to be a dashing and brave knight while I stabbed people in the side with a spear.
The verdict: This is a fairly dumb, fun game with a deep and well thought out approach to melee combat, which typically falls away in the face of armored men cutting eachother in half with claymores from behind or the flanks.
It's a great silly use of time, and worth purchasing if you see it deeply discounted on a steam sale.

Submerged certainly has good taste in influences; you can see more than a dash of many critically acclaimed games in its DNA, games like Journey, Ico, Windwaker, Shadow of the Colossus, Dear Esther, and The Vanishing of Ethan Carter.
Whilst these games clearly have been very influential, it’s a shame that Submerged feels like it simply borrows elements from them relatively ineffectively, and never carves a strong identity of its own.
The game is exploration-focused, with no combat. This gives the title an eerie calm, a gentle post-apocalypse. You sail a small motorboat looking for supplies for your brother, spotting landmarks and finding story pages along the way. Whilst the plot and gameplay are minimal there is definitely a certain joy and beauty to be found in sailing about and watching some of the wildlife, even if just for a few minutes. The soundtrack is also very effective, at times moving, stirring up similarities to Jessica Curry’s ‘Dear Esther’ soundtrack at points. I felt the soundtrack did a lot of the heavy lifting in creating the atmosphere in the game.
The plot of finding supplies for your brother is initially quite motivating, however it quickly loses any sense of urgency. You must collect ten supplies (bandages, medicine, water, food… all located atop ruined buildings), although eventually the story gives up the pretence of narratively engaging supplies and simply has you searching for ‘more medicines’ towards the end. These supplies exist in a kind of meta-state, whichever large building you find that is climbable will have the correct supply at the top, satisfying the next stage of your ‘quest’. This isn’t much of a problem, meta-thinking aside, as it allows you to tackle the buildings in any order, but it certainly drains from the narrative focus and tension. Your brother lies in wait, unmoving, and the collection of each supply has an almost identical animation of returning to the tower, administering the supply, sleeping, and waking before you set out for the next supply.
As you complete the main quest and gather collectables the game unlocks story images; simple pictographic slides that collectively tell a story. This element is clearly inspired by the images used in Journey to wordlessly provide context to the world, but here it falls flat. Journey’s story worked because the aesthetic and the theme were designed to be beautifully minimalistic and almost ‘culture-neutral’, with the pictographs carefully timed to provide deeper context for the world you travel through… But here the design feels lazy. There’s little extra context provided, and the cave-painting aesthetic of the pictographs didn’t feel genuine against the setting of the New York-esque city (even considering the post-apocalypse setting). It simply felt like a hollow execution of a fairly lazy idea, wrapped in a collect-a-thon sidequest just to provide something else to do.
The lack of combat or challenge weren’t a problem for me, in fact many of the games I list as clear inspirations don’t have much challenge or any combat. However, those other games succeed where Submerged falls short due to strong narrative themes or visual aesthetics providing potent artistic experiences. Submerged lacks severely in this area, sadly, and also lacks polish, leaving it feeling like a hollow game that is less than the sum of its parts. All too often it simply feels like a rushed and unfinished game. Buildings are blocky and ‘gamey’, wreckage feels lazy and repeated, and the majority of the textures are flat and lifeless. Whilst certain moments can be particularly beautiful visually, these are more often surrounded by ugly textures, poorly placed foliage, clumsy repeating objects, uninteresting story, and clumsy animations that pull the artistry back down.
I admire what Submerged wanted to be, but it lacks a strong aesthetic and any meaningful central theme, along with virtually no plot development or polish, instead feeling like a rushed and unfinished homage to a half dozen greater games.
If you’re happy to play a slow-paced, short but relatively relaxing game with a lot of rough edges, give it a try and you might get some fun out of this. But if you’re looking for story or a meaningful, artistic experience, Submerged sadly falls below the line.

Standing on the top of a long abandoned crane, rusty beams creaking out a song of defiance against the forces of gravity struggling to pull them apart, I was filled with a crushing sense of melancholy for what could have been. The sun had already set, and from my position I could just make out the outlines of the tallest buildings in the silent moonlight, the last remaining testament of a sunken city through which I was now scavenging for anything useful that may have been left behind. It was at this moment more than ever that I wanted desperately to be taken in by Submerged and its dilapidated beauty, to be swept up in the wondrous world it had conjured and the ambitions which seemed to drip out of the moss covered walls as they struggled to find a place for themselves.
It is a cruel irony then that Submerged’s ruin is its own overbearing grip on the player. Developer Uppercut Games has gone to such enormous lengths to direct the player and ensure they’re never at a loss as to where to go or what to do, that I felt alienated by my own needless presence. My attempts at exploration became less and less adventurous as I quickly discovered how limited my ability to explore actually was. Immediately I was trapped in my tiny motorboat, able to drift through the gaps of the structures still towering above the murky ocean but unable to so much as reach out and touch them and prove they were more than props in a dystopian tour.
Occasionally I’d be presented with a red vine signaling my chance to make port and clamber up the side of a building to see what was on top, but by then it was already clear that the world of Submerged was not one to be discovered but consumed. Every landmark, collectible, and handhold had been designed with the sole purpose of giving me something to do and observe. Aggressive camera angles directed me toward every significant structure I passed, forced my view toward a collectible I might have missed or a path I needed to take, all the while removing me of the ability to do anything but tell my character what direction to go as they did the rest.
Submerged traps itself under an omnipresent need to control and focus the player’s attention, and in doing so brings the entirety of its artificial existence to the surface. There was nothing more it could do to make me care about its characters or the history of the underwater city I was only glimpsing the top of; I was stuck behind the layers of antagonistic design allowing me no room to breathe as I performed Submerged’s song and dance wishing all the while that it would soon be over.
Once you strip Submerged of its fabricated openness and shell of a narrative there’s very nearly nothing left. What remains are your character’s clumsy movements as you guide them through monotonous platforming routines. It’s not the clumsiness you’d expect from a child attempting to scale a skyscraper with her bare hands, but a robotic awkwardness that creates an agonizing amount of disorder between what you do and how the game responds. I cringed every time I had to make my way up a long wall or choose between continuing the main path or grabbing a collectible, as I knew it meant a long struggle with a climbing system that all but plays itself but still needs you to tell it where to go.
I would be lying if I said that there were not times I found Submerged staggeringly beautiful and affecting. Rocketing my watercraft over waves as dolphins swam beside me or watching the sunset from the top of a building overlooking what remained of a bridge, I felt what Submerged had been trying so hard to create. Quiet, beautiful moments followed me throughout Submerged, springing up at random moments as I saw something astonishing out of the corner of my eye, but it was always during a time when I had managed to momentarily remove myself from the pressing control of a game that believed it could force me to feel and appreciate something. And then just like that they would disappear and I would be left alone again with the cold mechanical systems urging me forward.
By the end of Submerged I had stopped trying. I’d given up finding something that was being intentionally withheld from me, allowing the game to point me where to go and sooner allow me to leave. This was not a voyage but an entrapment; a siren’s call to a dead end and a meandering crawl back out. The game Submerged could have, and by all accounts wanted to be is still hidden here somewhere, but that hardly matters when it so fervently refuses to let you see it.

So I have no idea how this ended up in my library. I must have bought it, or had it given to me, but I really don't know where I got it. I vaguely remember a game by that name for (I think) the Xbox, which I didnt own. Having gamed since 1984, I can tolerate old games better than some, so I fired it up.
I noticed it has many positive reviews, mostly it seems from people who remember it back on Xbox. I didnt play it back then, so theres no nostalga factor involved. But I will do my best to review the game for ots own era, and only point out things by today's standards if they are so glaringly dated that it ruins immersion.
Its a 3rd person JRPG-art style action RPG. You know, button mashing so your guy swings his (ridiculously long) sword around and stringing together combos, theres an inventory where you can get better gear, a monster compendium, map, stats you can improve. Standard action RPG fare.
The graphics are nice for the era, and are brightly colored. Of course they look a bit dated, but not terribly or distractingly so.
So far everyone, including random NPCs in town seems fully voice acted. Now, I am not a fan of full voice acting in RPGs. (Long story short - you can get a MUCH more in depth story hiring one programmer to write many lines of text for NPCs to "say" vs. having to hire people to voice different NPCs. Voice acting is expensive, and having full voice acting for everything, not just main cutscenes/characters, makes the story detail shallower. Case in point Morrowind VS Oblivion) But I digress...
Anyway. By today's standards the voice acting is terrible. And even by the standards of the time (which I am trying to review this game by), the voice acting is laughable at best. Comparing the voice acting in this to say, Persona 3 (PS2 game) or even Baldur's Gate 2, there's just no contest. This sounds like it came out of the era when the first put badly voiced scenes in games circa 1992. Take the worst dubbed-anime voices and timing you can imagine. Yeah. It sounds like that.
Again, a case where it would have been better to only have a couple main characters voiced fully and save my ears. There are a few decent voices though. The main character Tal is listenable at least, as well as a couple other NPCs who's names escape me at the moment.
The script is ok. Not great. Its kinda...overblown and really seems translated from a different language. Not as bad as the voice acting though, just not great. I actually don't think it owuld have come off as bad if the voices were better.
One great thing is that its fully Xbox controller compatible (or Xinput for us Logitechers), as playing an action RPG like thos without a controller isnt advised. The controls are smooth on my Logitech, easy to understand and intuitive. Its fiun to go around bashing the crap out of enemies and learning new skills and making combos. THAT is where this game really shines
Overall, its not terrible, but at least for what Ive seen of it (I will update it if it blows my mind through awesome plot development later on - but as of right now I doubt it), the nostalgia factor seems to weight heavily in on whether people like it or not. If you are a fan of this type of game and are way more into the combat and character levelling then by all means, grab it.

This has a few bad reviews but reading the description (and video!) none of them had me very convinced.  There weren't many so I decided to give it a go myself.  And after playing it for a bit, I think it's been given an unjustly bad rep so far.
Yes it's a cheap and cheerful game, but what it does it does pretty well.  The sub is fun to control, the different height of your dives and their impact on the game make it diverse and interesting.  It's a fun little action game to play.
To address some of the criticisms:
- That they call going fast a "sprint" and that boats don't sprint.  Technically I agree that sprint probably refers to a human running strictly speaking , but coloquially it's often used as a general term to refer to short bursts of maximum speed (usually at the expense of being able to perform any other function at the same time).  And that's what holding the shift key in gives you - it gives you a short burst of maximum speed during which you can't fire, turn well, etc.  So get over it (the terminology), it's not that bad.  If you want to use the correct nautical terms, play a sailing sim.  "Sprint" very accurately represents its function in this game.
- That a sub can outgun a ship using only its deck gun.  Yeah well in CoD you can take 50 bullets over the course of half an hour, and still walk without a limp.  In Skyrim you eat an apple to recover from an axe to the head.  The day we start judging games by their parrels to real life is the day we call all games♥♥♥♥♥♥
- That you can't use the mouse.  Yes but you don't need to, it's not a point and click game.  The menus aren't difficult to navigate without.  Game pad support would be welcome, but you can use a mapper such as joycur or antimicro (I tried the latter and it plays really well!).
- That the map isn't high res.  I don't think it's supposed to be.  The idea being you're given only basic direction so that navigation is a bit of a challenge (similar to being on a real boat!) and part of the game.  For example there are plenty of shortcuts not shown on the map that you have to work out yourself.
- That the sub doesn't control well.  It doesn't control like a car, which is what they seem to be making comparables to.  To be fair it doesn't control like a boat either, but again it's an arcade game not a sim!  I actually like the way it controls.  It feels very fun to play.
- Someone mentioned getting annoyed by the sonar beep.  Didn't bother me, it's not very loud.
- That the graphics aren't great.  I personally quite like them, I think the whole environment's done pretty well.  If I'd paid £30 I'd be more critical, it's not the best, but it does the job quite well.  I like the water effects and the sub looks cool, so do the ships.
Don't get me wrong, this isn't an epic.  It is a cheap, fun game.  £4 is probably about right.
One reviewer said you'd be better off buying Sid Meier's Pirates.  That may be true, but that's a very old game that has been played to death.  It didn't cost £4 when it first came out.  It's also a story/quest/RPG/strategy type game, whereas this is just action and tactics.  Not a fair comparison.
Some indie games have huge ambitions, and make early access games with massively complex ideas, and none of them end up working very well, and they end up with a shambles of a game that they never actualyl finish.  This on the other hand has done it right IMO.  They've kept it simple, and what they've done they've done well.
It also has some nice touches like how ships can target you at dive level 1, but planes can't (however if you've recently finished diving the existing fire will still hit you); how the sonar works properly eg it's not a real time display of where the enemies are, it only updates as the scan goes round; you can only dive to level 2 in the deap sea, and can't dive at all when it's really shallow; snow effect when you go to the north east, damage effects when ships/sub is low on health; the instruments on your HUD getting damaged; you unlock new subs all with different characteristics, of which there is plenty of variety (fuel, oxygen, hull strength, seperate damage speed and ammo count for torpedos, AA, and deck gun).
I also think they deserve a lot of credit for originality.  While top-down naval shooters have been done before, I'm not aware of any putting a spin on it like this, so the whole controls and fighting is not like any game I've played before.  there are some similar, but the whole sprint, dive 1&2, deck gun, torps, aa mix gives it much more depth to traditional top down shooters.
I think a star rating on your success on each level (similar to the one in Orcs Must Die and CastleStorm for example), and a difficulty setting would go a long way to increasing its appeal to the more hadcore gamers.
At the end of the day indie devs are on a budget, they can't throw the resources at it like big company's can.  Whoever's written this has focused on the important things i.e. gameplay; rather than spending there limited resources on in-game music and various refinities it'd benefit from.  I'd like to see more features and more refinement in future, but it's not an early access game, it's fully functional and entertaining as it is now.
If you have a few hours to kill and a few quid (UK) to spare, you could do a lot worse than this.  I enjoyed it.

Technicals:
Options- Virtually none. there is no options menu in the game and the only place you will be able to find an option to use is while you are in a mission and that is the option to disable sound.
Performance: The thing runs at 1000fps according to my computer which it better considering the low graphics but even then the main menu still manages to produce screen tear when you are scrolling through the mission thumbnails.
Graphics/appearance:
A mixed bag of bad. The game runs in 4:3 inside of a square frame hud thing which doesn't even properly fit the screen, The map is ridiculously low resolution (Imagine if you were playing an early 2000s videogame and zoomed in all the way to stare at the ground) and isn't even well designed it looks as if land masses were just shoved all over to make it look fuller but it just looks horrendous.
The units have a completely different aesthetic to them, the map (despite the low res) is a kind of "realistic" texture meanwhile the units have a mixed bag of drawn textures or just flat colours and some of the models just look terrible like the boat you start in.
The one cool thing I will say is that when your boat takes enough damage the hud gets damaged and your fuel guage falls right off which is pretty amusing.
Sound: You start off with some rather satisfying music at the main menu but the instant you enter a mission the music stops...there is no in-game music. The only audio you will hear for 90% of the time is the sound of the submarine's engine (which sounds more like a muffled jetski than anything) with a bit of sounds from combat.
Gameplay: The submarines control horribly and unrealistically. Turning while moving is the most sluggish thing ever but when I stop holding the forward key I can turn do a 180 almost instantly. When you aren't submerged you can hold shift to spring...yes sprint, because that's a thing boats do.
Anyway, holding shift makes your boat move at a ridiculous pace, you are just speeding across the map like no tomorrow despite even your normal movement speed being more than twice as fast as battleships.
Units make no sense, I can go up to a battleship and stare it down for 10 seconds while my single deck gun autofires at it and I will win despite not using any torpedoes and the battleship being twice my size and having twice as many guns which should be stronger as well. Speedrunners is a brilliant, 2d, sidescrolling, racing game where you race against up to 3 players, locally or online in a battle of speed and wits. I used to dislike this game, until very recently when it was much less buggy and I got to understand the mechanics of the game. It is early-access, but a very good one at that. Continue reading, to learn more.
Your goal in speedunners, is essentially to win the race. However, there aren't any laps, nor are there any special objectives. Instead, all of you have to do is be so far ahead of the rest of the racers, that they vanish off the screen. The race screen follows the leader, so it is key to stay close to the leader in order to stay alive. Once the opposing racers have hit the bounds of the screen, you as the leader win a round. Winning 3 rounds makes you the overall winner of the race. Sounds fairly easy? Well it would be, if this game didn't have items or grappling hooks.
The grappling hook is one of the most useful and essential items in this game. It allows you to traverse terrain rapidly, or continue your momentum, which is key for this type of game. Any roof-like area with a white patch can be grappled at any time once your hook can hit it.
Items complete this game, turning it from Need for Speed, to Mario Kart. A well timed shockwave can block enemy yellow grappling hooks, while an Invinci-Drill can bring a player from last place to the lead in a matter of seconds. The items give this game an important element of skill and timing. Wasting a valuable item can leave you open to attack from your opponents, and many times, it could be the last mistake you ever make as your opponent speeds his ways past you with a well timed grapple, into boost.
There are also unique stage elements which make the gameplay vary. There are usually multiple paths to get to a destination, Each with their own strengths and weaknesses. Some paths may have a boost charger, but may trigger a lever that opens a path with item pickups. If you're careful enough you can dodge these levers, but it's not always possible.
Momentum is a key mechanic in this game, which seperates newbies from pros. Learning the levels, as well as timing your grapples, boosts and jumps are essential to going through an area at top speed and leaving all the competition behind.
There are many unlockables in the form of characters and outfits, as well as a rewarding levelling system. Fancy a more serious challenge? Head to ranked where the bravest challengers make their names known.
The visual style of this game is simplistic, yet effective. I especially love the visuals for super speed. The game really emphasizes the sense of speed you get after well timed jumps, grapples and boosts. However it's nothing mind-blowing, it's just neatly done.
I like the sounds in the game. The music is always upbeat and gives you a proper adrenaline rush especially in those clutch moments where you're neck and neck with your opponent.
Speedrunners is turning out to be quite the impressive game. I normally don't recommend early-access games to people very quickly, however I must make an exception here, as right now this game has a lot already, and feels pretty well polished in all aspects.
For a highly competitive, super fun, racing and parkour game, Speedrunners is defintely worth playing.
8/10 Worth buying
9/10 With friends

Before I get into this review of the Nicole Otome game, I’ll admit that I have a small piece of history with the game. I was a writer for the Yuri version of Nicole until my health dropped out. I think I was the third writer before I passed the baton to a friend. I wrote a good chunk of Bethany’s path, though I am unsure how much of my work will make it to the final game. That being said, while I had a good experience working with the creators, my review will not be softened by said experience. Still, I am excited to see the second game, as I have high hopes for it.
The plot is okay at best, mostly due to glaring plot holes involving the mystery. As a fan of the mystery genre I was really disappointed when my gut instinct told me who the culprit was the second time I saw him and I ended up being right. There was no twist or great challenge.
While there are potentially great characters, the delivery falls flat, especially when some of the characters show violent tendencies towards women. But we’ll go over that soon enough.
The dialogue isn’t too special, though it is stylistically consistent and has it’s funny moments. It provided just enough amusement to keep me interested through the first playthrough. However, once you read the same scene for the second, third, and fourth times to get a different ending, it gets a bit boorish, so I recommend using the skip text function. You can customize that in the options menu.
The moral of the story could be that it’s okay to be an overconfident young lady, because even when that bites you in the♥♥♥♥♥and you are cornered in a dangerous situation, it doesn’t bite too hard because you’ll be saved by another man or be too lovestruck to care that your boyfriend just trapped you and is most likely a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Not a great moral, but I’m pretty sure that wasn’t the intent.
I’m always happy to see games directed at a female audience. However, some of the morals I mentioned above let me down as a female player. Also, I didn’t see very many scenes with the other girls, and when I did they seemed to be short and kind of meaningless.
I was also really thrilled to see a character in the first scene who wasn’t white! Her name is Chandra and she is Nicole’s soft-spoken roommate. My excitement, however, was almost instantly cockblocked by the main character wishing she could be tan like Chandra. This made me uncomfortable. While Kurt is tan, Chandra is not. Let’s not whitewash everything, folks.

Pros and Cons
Tanki X has decent graphics which are not extremely taxing on most computers, which leads to my next point:
This game can run on nearly any computer with low-medium graphics settings; most lag, if any, is caused by the server.
Most importantly, Tanki X has fun and arcade-like gameplay that keeps you playing multiple rounds before leaving.
In addition to the satisfying progression through 101 ranks, there is also a mastery system that allows you to upgrade turrets or hulls by using them in battle.
You have the ability to select which gamemode and map you want to play, and there is always a server with a map you want to play that hasn't started yet.
Maps load almost instantly and matches are relatively quick (around 10 minutes if you join a match at its start)
There are a good amount of cosmetics that you can pay for, but these do not affect gameplay in any way, shape, or form. You can purchase X-crystals to buy regular crystals to use for upgrades, but you still need to upgrade your mastery for your turret or hull to upgrade it. Crystals are pretty easy to get, anyway.
Finally, there is satisfactory turret, hull, and module (mines, invisiblity, health regeneration, etc.) customization with more promised to come.
The in-game tutorial isn't the greatest (it only provides basic controls), but you can find any information you need on the Tanki X forum.
There are some balancing issues regarding a few weapons, especially when you are using the starter tank against opponents with better tanks with upgrades. On the plus-side, these have been promised to be fixed by the developers.
You can't change most controls at the moment.
Depending on the map and gamemode you are playing and your spawn position, it is quite possible to get destroyed a few seconds after spawning by an enemy.
This game shows a lot of promise, with not nearly as many problems as some other games had when they were released in early-access. All the issues I had with Tanki-X have already been promised to be addressed, showing that the developers are definitely dedicated to improving the game. I suggest you just download it and give it a try, because after all, it's free.

The MAIN reason this is a NO is the price, It's more than double what I would pay for the amount of game I got (£13.49 with 10% off is a little much for 2 hours of game), but even then it may be a little overpriced.  Maybe wait for a £5 sale to make the most of this one.
The game itself is VERY basic in what it does.  You scootch around a dead and flooded city in a little boat using a telecscope to look for care packages to heal your sick brother.
This boils down to...
Look through telescope and 'see' certain objects and care packages in the world.
Hop in boat and go to the building said object is on.
Hop out of the boat onto a ledge of the building and climb it.
Find care package and press A.
Get teleported back home to start again on the hunt for the next care package.
The boat controls are a little sluggish, even with the boost function that you get from collecting parts that you tag using your trusty telescope.
The walking and climbing controls are basic, VERY basic.  up, down, left, right.  That's it, The main character does everything you need her to do by pushing in one of the cardinal directions and nothing else.  You can't even jump.
The sound isn't all that great either, just the basic plinks and plops, splashes and whale/dolphin noises you'd expect.
The music however, is fantastic, if a little short-lived and scarce.
There are plenty of collectibles to discover in the world, from animal pictures to the history of the city and what befel it, and the size of the open world isn't too bad, it takes quite a few minutes to get from one side to the other.
It may not sound like it but I rather enjoyed the change of pace with this game, although the high price was always nagging at the back of my mind.

Sudeki is open world but not to the point that you'll ever find yourself lost - Much like Ocarina of Time. The world is large enough to backtrack through and mess around with secret areas you could not previously but it definitely doesn't have the scope of an Elder Scrolls game - More puzzles and personality than walking.
The combat is fair - It takes a step back for every one that it takes forward and so therefor I can not judge it positively or negatively but at least you're not left-clicking your way through the game so Sudeki's combat is definitely a salvation for those with boxes filled to brim with broken  Diablo mice. The battles can often times grow challening and control schemes are sophisticated enough to offer a sense of interactivity but you're definitely not going to find the action you would in a game like Devil May Cry. Interestingly enough, ranged characters are forced into First Person perspective when selecting over to them.
Right off the bat Sudeki does alot of things right that recent developers have forgotten all together like skipable cut scenes and skipable dialogue. Oh! But if you do like dialogue everyone you come by has something to say and it's all been vocally acted.
If there's only one complaint it's that this game was almost kid-safe but alas bloody & messy corpses litter the land.
I have no preference to kid-safe games, of course, however when you're so close to clean it's a shame that they stepped off that trail a tad and clipped the game just short of being appropriate for eveyone.

You can switch between members on the fly and they change how you'll play the game. A melee character can combo their way to victory while a certain caster enters a first person style shooter mode. There isn't much outside of the core game however, you can do enchants but it's basic and you're free to determine your characters growth (for better and worse!) so it lets you meta-game to an extent.
Graphically, the game runs and looks better than the CGI cutscenes, which is pretty funny. Luckily they aren't used as much as other turn based RPGs.
Just be aware, apparently others are having problems getting the game to run. I haven't had such an issue but just be wary about it when you get the game, which at $5 USD I completely recommend.

I've wasted ~569 hours on the Mass Effect series (200 on Mass Effect 1, 206 on Mass Effect 2, 113 on Mass Effect 3 and ~50 on Andromeda) and it was definitely worth it. Be warned, none of the DLC is on Steam, so you'll have to buy it on Origin.
+Characters and how they develop
+Greatly expanded amount of romance options from the first game, with each one feeling unique
+Combat, which is VASTLY improved from the first game
+Individual missions (I'll explain below)
+Some of the best DLC from any game that I've played
-I'm bitter that I can't romance Garrus as a male Shepard
-Overarching story (I'll explain below)
-Jacob and the fact that he exists in my general direction
-
Allow me to explain Mass Effect 2's story and its structure. If one is to really look at the overarching main story, it's actually the weakest of the entire series, and if one was just to play the main missions, then the story would be rather boring. Basically, the main story is just "Cerberus resurrects Commander Shepard to destroy the Collectors and he/she destroys the Collectors." However, the story is told less like a straightforward story and more like a collection of stories that can be played in any order. The individual stories of each mission are either hit or miss. The vast majority of side missions are extremely weak and some don't really have a story at all. However, every other mission in the game (recruitment missions, loyalty missions, main story missions) have amazing plots, and this game has some of the most memorable individual missions in the entire series.
Anyway, I enjoyed this game, and I hope you do too.

Very nice game which is obviously trying very hard to draw parallels with both "Beneath a Steel Sky" and "Blade Runner". Storywise it's up there with the very best of sci-fi gaming, with plenty of mystery, intrigue and plot twists where you least expect them. It's very beautiful to look at, in a VGA sort of way....and the sound design is top notch too. I know some people didn't care for the voice acting but it seemed fine to me. Even if the "grizzled hardboiled" protagonist sounds like Harvey Fierstein imitating Marlon Brando :D
Unfortunately the interface is needlessly cumbersome. Rather than, say, left-click to look and right-click to use like the aforementioned Sky which they so liberally borrow from, you have to right-click, choose which part of your body you want to use to interact with an item and then click on it. It gets even more complicated when you gain a sidekick and have to drag them around in the same way. If you come across a ladder, do you use your foot or your hand on it? Actually, either works, but why give us the choice? "Use" really should be context-appropriate nowadays as most of the choices the player is given are either stupid (You're not going to use your mouth on the ladder) or don't matter (hand or foot works)....
Oh, points also deducted for introducing a needless real-time combat system. Adventure games don't need real-time combat. I thought we learned this with Harvester, Blade Runner, Maddog Williams....at least Full Throttle let you skip the arcade sections if you didn't want to do them....

In conclusion, Mass Effect 2 is the best game in the franchise, buy it instead of Andromeda, which killed the franchise.

I wanted to like this game soo badly since I love all the Wadjet Eye games I've played so far - but I just couldn't bear to finish it. The user interface in this game is absolutely terrible and everything feels clunky/buggy. The story and graphics are great, but that's about it. The story, which I finished by watching a walkthrough video, was absolutely amazing and almost made me wish that I stuck with it despite the annoyances..
Annoyances:
- Terrible / non-existant game menus
- Restoring a saved game from a rainy area has a bug where the graphics get all messed up for half the screen
- Cover positions for shooting feel like they have weird keystroke/timing delays
- Constant issues with path finding - always getting stuck on things on way to a door/exit for a scene
- Some doors/exits have unusually small click areas toward very edges of the screen which is annoying to target
- Every action is in a small pop-up menu that only comes up when right-clicking an object or person. There's no default actions for the most basic things such as having a left-click on a person start to talk or left-click on a door try to open it. You have to constantly right-click for everything which gets tedious.
- Some of the hidden objects seem like they're two pixels in width so you can only find by mouse scanning versus being attentive to each scene
- Puzzles are more difficult to solve due to user interface confusion. I aquired two objects, one which is needed to fix the other, and couldn't figure out how to use them on each other. Due to having to right-click an object to get that pop-up menu (also the only area to see your inventory), how do I combine two items that are both in my inventory? Well I have to right-click on a completely unrelated object to get the pop-up menu, at which point (according to a walkthrough video I saw) I should only need to click the object in my inventory that does the repairing. This games is a little hard to describe without saying the phrases "Fallout 3", "New Vegas", "MMORPG", or "Son of a ♥♥♥♥♥ I can holster HOW many weapons!?"
It certainly wasn't the game I was expecting, but it is the game I've been looking for, in a way. It's a perfectly/near-perfectly executed post-apocalypse MMORPG, and that's a rarity. My only complaints are that I found it looking for something else entirely, and that the story at the beginning reminds me of the early 90's Apoc D&D settings. Otherwise, it gives you a horse two minutes in, something most MMORPGs take you days to get, and then they're usually expensive and just sort of bleh. In this case, I was just given a free horse, and it felt like it actually made sense. You're in a desert wasteland. Here, the one thing you need the most, in a desert wasteland.
And you can holster six weapons at once. I have a fireaxe, a rifle, two knives, and two pistols. I look like some sort of crazy gunslinger, and I'm not even an hour into the game!
Overall, as first impressions go, unless this game just suddenly becomes awful, this is probably the best MMORPG I've seen in years.

I was really unsure if I should buy the game, since there were so many bad reviews about it, but in the end, my inner fangirl won out, and I bought it. And I didn't regret it. I really like it, but there are a few points, that might be the reason why it's not for everyone.
First, it's a stat-raising dating Game - so the story is told in a few cutscenes - and the rest of the game, you choose what you do in your free time so that you can raise your stats or search for clue-points (which you need if you want the real ending of the game)or  work to earn money and buy your sweety a present. I really liked the Characters (Jeff) - that's the most important aspect of a game for me - so, even though I don't like stat-raising Otomes, I still liked the game. Altough the time between the cutscenes, was sometimes a bit tedious. Especially at the Ending (when I already had maxed everything I'd need for my Ending out) it was really boring. Still, that's not new with stat-raising Sims.
But what really came short, for me, was the mystery aspect. All the relevant scenes came at the ending at of game, and I didn't feel like my collected clue-points mattered at all. I just knew, that I had to max them out to get the real Ending. And the mystery - well, I just might have watched to many crime shows, but it just wasn't enough for me. Not scary - not suspensful enough. But I really liked the rest of the game. I liked Nicole - in most routes - and I really liked Jeff (me, the fangirl), and the dialouge was funny/witty (most of the time). And I absolutely love the art.
I'm not sure I can recommend the game to everybody, but I had fun with it.

Nicole is one of those games that I have a hard time understanding exactly why I like it as much as I do. With tedious gameplay that is neither engaging or interesting and a predictable storyline riddled with clichés and unbelievable situations, you'd think I'd have played an hour or two and tossed it in the "File and Forget" bin of my library. On the contrary, I found myself plugging 15+ hours into the game, playing through all four character routes, and falling in love with each of the guys along the way (well, 3/4 of them anyway). Perhaps this review is my way of figuring out just what makes Nicole so appealing to me despite so many flaws.
Our story begins with the title character arriving for her freshman year at college. She's a plucky, perky 18 year old girl who has spent most of those 18 years loving fashion, getting straight A's, and finding herself amongst the popular group of girls in high school. Oh, and she's never had a boyfriend or been kissed before. Not exactly the most realistic protagonist in the world, but she's likable enough despite being a tad annoying at times. After getting settled in, she stumbles across an article detailing the mysterious disappearance and reappearance of 3 female students who inexplicably have no memory of their time gone, but are so rattled by the experience they either drop out or transfer to another school. One would think campus kidnappings would have Nicole practicing a little caution, but it's not long before she's contacted by the kidnapper and warned that she'll be next. Logically, going straight to the authorities is out of the question; Nicole has no choice but to investigate the kidnapper herself. Yes...the story has some issues, but the mystery isn't what kept me playing.
As mentioned previously, the plot is predictable and character routes cliché-fests.  BUT...I couldn't stop reading.  For an OELVN (Original English Language Visual Novel) the writing is exceptionally good.  Aside from a bit of annoying slang here and there, the characters are all well developed with their own distinct voices (something so many of these games lack), and the dialogue is fluid and for the most part believable.  On top of that, I may have caught maybe 2 typos throughout the 4 routes, and that's pretty dang impressive considering how so many games in the genre are littered with typos, misspellings and awkward phrasing.  So, despite my boredom with the overarching storyline, reading through the game was a pleasant experience.
And then there are the boys.  Yes, they're your stereotypical romance tropes, but they're written believably well.  If I had to boil it down to the one thing that kept me playing, it was the romance between Nicole and the guys. Watching the relationships go from acquaintance to friend, and ultimately on to something more, was enjoyable and interesting.  The gradualness of the friendships and Nicole's slow realization of her own feelings was refreshing. Much of the romantic dialogue and situations were hilarious, other parts touching, and some scenes downright steamy.  For an otoge, they hit a bulls-eye with the character romances.  Granted, the premise for getting Nicole and each guy in the same room for the relationship to flourish was kind of boring and predictable, but easily forgiven considering how much I enjoyed the result of those encounters.
On the visual side of things, the artwork is quite impressive for the genre and a highlight of the game. This artist has worked on previous Winter Wolves titles, and I'm a big fan of hers. The style has a soft feel to it which is accentuated by the pastel palette used to color the work; this complements the romantic tone of the story quite well. The character designs are not particularly detailed or inspired, but they're nicely conceived and pleasant on the eyes.  My only disappointment is that we don't get any CG's outside of the character endings.  But this is a small price to pay to have polished and professional looking artwork for the entire game.
Now, to detail the most boring, drudging, soul crushing aspect of Nicole, which is the simulation gameplay.  I generally do not find life sims to be very engaging, but Nicole's gameplay felt so much worse.  You spend a good 80% of the 4 game months picking the same activities over and over to level up your clues in order to further the mystery storyline while also leveling the requisite stat for the guy you're pursuing. And that's it.  You can literally go weeks without a single event scene triggering, and when all I want is to get to the next steamy romance bit, facing days upon days of nothing but the same monotonous activities again and again is torture.  We're not even given flavor text after each activity to spice things up either.  Unfortunately, by the time I realized how mind-numbing the gameplay was, I was already hooked on the feels that I forced myself through for that next romantic "hit".  Thankfully there's a skip button (hidden away in the options menu, by the way, but at least it's there) that helped me fly through things a bit faster on subsequent playthroughs, because I don't know if I'd have survived it otherwise.
The rest of the gameplay consists of visual novel reading with a few dialogue choices tossed in to level up affection with the guys.  Honestly, the game would have been much better as a straight visual novel using dialogue trees to further the storyline, although it would have probably cut the play time down by at least half.  I wouldn't have minded this myself as I feel it would have made the experience MUCH more enjoyable, but I think it'd be hard to justify the $20 price tag for maybe 6 hours of gameplay.
In the end, I can only recommend Nicole to other female players who enjoy otome and a good romance now and again.  Unfortunately, there's just not enough meat to the story to pull the guys in, and I'm not sure most would be interested in the romance aspects which is the game's biggest strength. Still, for a game that was painful to play at times, there are much worse examples of the genre out there.  I'd suggest waiting for a good sale to pick it up.  At the right price it's worth it for the steamy bits alone.
Bottom Line: 6/10

Submerged is the story about Miku trying to scavenge supplies throughout a Waterworld-esque post apocalyptic world to save her brother Taku. water.
Submerged, in my opinion, is an art piece. It's a story of struggle, loss, and survival. Like a searchable painting. Not every nook and cranny has something to find, but hidden through-out are little details that individually may not be significant, but as a whole paint this beautiful tapestry. It's a non combat adventure game with a great aesthetic and a story sprinkled a with little puzzle solving and mystery.
The gameplay is very straight forward, as Miku you traverse this under water city in a small boat. As you explore you will find various upgrades for your boat. Kinda optional in my opinion but it's another thing to go hunting for and will ease your search for answers. The main story objective is to find 10 ration crates. As you find these the story will progress with a cutscene and progress the story along. There is also 60 hidden things to find, several creatures to spot, and other things to find.
The puzzle solving is a series of climbing ledges, climbing vines, and... well it's a lot of climbing. Climbing and boating. That's the gameplay. You climb things, find things, putt-putt around on your boat and try to save your brother. The gameplay on it's face is fairly simplistic. However, as a game without combat you are taking in the world around you.
Some have reviewed Submerged negatively stating it's too short or repetitive. Sure, if you mainlined the story you could get done pretty quickly but why are you rushing to complete a game? If you take your time, search around, and try to take it what the developers put into the game I think you can find enjoyment here, even if it only took you a few hours to complete.
Some minor graphical bugs aside (some textures are weak and there's a little tearing at times) I think Submerged has a lot to offer as an indie exploration title. Just know what you're getting yourself into.

There is a charm and intrigue to Submerged. The game puts you in the middle of a dilapidated, mysterious, city with the goal of saving your brother. Everything in the game has a story, the city, the main characters, even the the creatures. How you go about solving the riddle of the story is left up to you and your pace. The gameplay is rather simplistic as Submerged features no combat. This game wants you to take your time and smell the roses, Searching  to unravel clues and nuggets of information to find out whats going on. The game is gorgeous and designed very well, however because everything is so green, some of the buildings begin to blend together.  The puzzle solving involves an Assassins Creed-esque style platform hopping. This is fine but it becomes repetitive as there is no fear of death or anything that shakes up the gameplay and keeps things new/fresh. The view from the top is gorgeous though, as weather shifts and night comes, you truly feel like your in a ghost city.  There is plenty of things Submerged does very well, from the music, ambiance, and story telling. The only problem is that the game is very simplistic, what you see is what you get. If you like what you see, buy it. It's an enjoyable, calm, experience and great for kids. On the other hand it is tad bit pricey for the amount of gametime/content. I think the game is worth it but some people want more bang for their buck. There is nothing wrong with that. I say buy this when its on sale or do your research!

This one is gray/green and muddy. But lighting is good, there is day/night cycle and weather, and every blade of grass is a 3D model, so, sometimes game is very pretty.
There are technically two stories, about brother and sister, and about the world, told through pictures. They simple, almost primitive. Primitive by design.
Gameplay is simple too. You skim around in a boat, looking for stuff, and climb buildings. Climbing here is more of a traversal, like in “Assassin’s Creed” or “Uncharted” – you just need to find where to go, no danger of don’t making a jump or falling.

Everything feels wrong abut this game. Levels are not as open as they should be, often you'll simply find yourself in a dead end with the only way to go being climbing up stairs. Which of course doesn't mesh with the skates. I might as well not have the skates for unless you're in a slope or have been grinding for a while you hardly go faster than the police officers chasing you. And you trade that modicum of speed you have on them with incredible imprecision over your direction. It's really hard to gain some speed, it's really hard to move around. The game is not snappy in the slightest.
But let's pretend you actually got some momentum. What now ? STOP. Do a graph. Just stop moving. It's time for contextual stick wiggling, harly different from a QTE. It's not very fun, but it is the objective of the game as far as I could tell from these few levels I played. In that regard, it turns the game into more of a platformer as the point is not to build speed but to jump around so that you can reach spots to graph. But again, it's so imprecise I'd rather play a genuine platformer like Sly Cooper.
There is a point system too based on how you trick, but it basically amounts to how long you grind. Which goes in direct contradiction with the tagging objectives that asks you to stop dead in your track, not that it matters considering it's useless and you'll get good grades without even trying. By that I mean that you won't feel like you deserve it and will end up thinking that good grades are actually bad. Seriously. It's that irrelevant. I don't remember any level in the fews I've played that actually recquired you to get a certain amount of points anyway. Why is it even here ?
Let's add to that unskippable cutscene, unsuprisingly dreadful camera, the police forces that feel like they waste your time more than anything else, escaping them stucks you in a cutscene everytime for no other reason but to break your flow so everything about the opposing force, be it avoiding them or escaping them, is annoying, the narrative might as well not be there...
It's not fast enough to be cathartic, it's not precise enough to be rewarding. The levels aren't open enough to give any sense of flow unless perhaps you master them but nothing makes me want to. Graphing is just there to stop you in your tracks. The obstacles on your way are more annoying than threatening. Everything feels wrong. Nothing about it is satisfying.
I want to like this game, I really do but it's all around frustrating... I don't recommend.

In another place, in another time, in a more receptive universe, Kevin Costner's 'Water World' was critically and commercially successful; not only that, but there was a whole 'Water World' cultural homogenization phenomenon. Every film that wasn't 'Water World' was sealed in a vault, every book that wasn't the novelization of the script from the hit motion picture 'Water World' was burned, and every classroom on every continent played the masterpiece on loop. Not since the Pax Romana had people known such peace.
After the weirdly uncontested canonization of still-very-much-alive Kevin Costner, world leaders began unceremoniously running their taps because “climate change was taking way too long.” In a matter of months Earth resembled Costner's magnum opus. Not since the period immediately following the Pax Romana (Crisis of the Third Century) had the world known such instability and amazing shrimp deals.
Enter Submerged.
Submerged is a pretty little indie title brought to you by Bioshock alums, and it shows (aesthetically anyway). Plants are appropriately sway-y, the city-scape you navigate is an eery, decaying extension of the ocean, and the wildlife all have, like, barnacle herpes or something. And it's pretty to boot (not the herpes, the environment). Sunrises and sunsets are breathtaking, and the sea is illuminated by bioluminescent organic nonsense at night. It suffers from that videogame phenomenon of “DON'T LOOK TOO CLOSELY AT THE BAD TEXTURES” and “THOSE BACKGROUND BIRDS JUST KEEP VANISHING INTO NOTHING” but all that's pretty forgivable.
But you're not here to find out about the graphics – you can see them for yourself. You want to know about the story, the lore! Alright!
You're a girl on a boat with your injured kid brother, Taco (the game says Taku or something Oceanic but I like calling him Taco for reasons). After finding a safe spot you set off to provide Taco aid and find out more about the world around you... its story, its inhabitants, its landmarks, and your past. And that's how you're fed most of the narrative. For watching an animal or getting close to a landmark you're rewarded with a pretty Polynesian-style illustration. For getting supplies for Taco you're rewarded with a pretty Polynesian-style illustration of your personal story. And for finding little narrative caches sprinkled throughout the flooded city you get – you get the idea. It's interesting and unique but it feels like so much padding – especially finding picture 23 out of 60 depicting the story of the city. It's also the primary source of gameplay, scaling ruined skyscrapers, office buildings, and hotel; very simplistic in nature.
So is Submerged worth it? It's times like these that I wish Steam had an EHHHH option. It's pretty, it's haunting, and it has, for my money, an excellent overarching message. However, at times Submerged feels like a tech demo. It's shallow, the “grab 70-80 odd images” sidequest gets tiresome (doesn't take too many context clues to figure out what happened to this city guys! I certainly don't need a dozen images of just a building or a dude), and it is short. It's a testament to the idea that it isn't about the destination; no, it's about the journey. But is the journey worth it? Ultimately Submerged's cons outweigh its pros, and that's a damn shame.
