While i totally understand, why this game is so much loved by the players, i sadly have to admit, that at least i cant recommend the game. But when i see, that only around 50% of the people (even now, where the game still cost around 50 bucks) finished the first act, i think that i am maybe not the only one who disliked at least some aspects of the game. So to give you besides all the praising reviews also an neutral review from the side of a player who sadly didnt enjoyed the game as much as many others, i hope that my review, together with the many reviews that love the game, can help you in deciding, if you are the targeted audiance of the game, and if you would enjoy the game.
Because everyone has a different taste, and maybe you will love the game like many others, but maybe the things that i will adress are also very importand for you too. And if this is the case, then maybe this game, while having a very high quality, will just not suit you as a player.
Let us begin with the positive aspects, and their are many of them:
The graphics are just awesome! The graphics allone are already very atmospherical, (like in the mysterious swamp, the view is turning slithly green, a strom on the sea looks dark and dangerous, a sunny day on the beach looks very harmonious etc.) it will be even surpassed by the elemental graphics in the battles: When your fire spells turn the oil into fire, explosions overcome the whole area, your enemys bleeding to death from the necomancer spells, thunders crashing into the water and shocking everyone in it: The battles look very chaotic and awesome in so many ways, and just staring at the battle effects bring me much joy. Everything looks so good in this game, and while it is true, that graphics are not everything, i wanted to give them the praises they deserve, because they are all so perfectly done.
The world is very interesting indeed. Besides the lore of the world that bringes some interesting new aspects into the "clischee" fantasy world, like cannibal elfs  or the possibility to speak to animals as if they would be normal persons etc. makes the world even in such an often used genre like the fantasy genre, a very individual touch. The story is interesting(at least the parts that i have seen so far) and you are always curious how the story will continue. While i was never totally "lost" in the story, and it never gets me very emotionally, it still fullfilles its purpose to keep the player interested. Just when you are a player who really needs a totally deep innovative, and unforseeable story, then you maybe will not be happy from it.
Even better then the already good story is the overall world: The locations you visit look very "real", the citys are full of interesting and different people. Everyone has something to say and i never felt like their are just a few "maincharacters" and a bunch of empy npcs to fill the location. As to the story, you shouldnt expect to much, every character is "just" a very good scripted character so they dont develop the depth of a major Mass Effect Charakter, but also they dont feel like hollows witout any personality.
The gameplay is maybe the best i have ever seen in an classic RPG. The fights (at least in the higher difficulties) really need you to think about your moves, and can be very hard sometimes. Every Quest can be solved in many ways and in generall you have a very high freedom to play the game as you like. You can play (most of the time) as a pacificst, avoiding every battle with your good conversations talents and your stealth mechanics, or as a psychopath who killes everythink that just slithly provokes him. The lonewolf who only fights for his own, or the classical hero who tries to safe the whole word.
But with this freedom comes a very huge problem: The lack of connection between the "worldparts"
Since you are free to do what you want, the game never can forsee how your next movement will be. In one situation you can be the hero who showes mercy to the enemy because you understand his motive and forgive him, and in the next battle you kill everythink that moves. You can first rescue a member of the resistance against the cruel regime, and in the next moment when you are in the outpost of the resistance you can kill everyone inside to get the loot. Their is no "wrong" way to play the game. But this leads to the huge problem that almost nothing of the single aspects of the game is connected.
Let me make an example since just talking around the topic is confusing if you dont exacltly understand what i mean. *minor spoilers ahead*
In the first real act you are trapt on an island where sources mages like yourself are forced to wear a collar that surpresses their power. And also they are trappt in a ghetto, unable to leave the castle and the island. In a certain quest one of the prisoners helped me to destroy the collar so that my source powers are free ones more. But this leads to the situation that now every magister (the guardians of the castle) will see that you have not the collar anymore and will imprison you once more, to force you to wear it again,or attack you if you show resistance. I showed resistance...and in the result every magister in the whole castle did attack me on sight. So i have started a revolution against our surpressers, overcome them, killed them next to the other scared prisoners, opened the closed gates, let the people to freedom....only that they didnt care. Since the daily routine of the prisoners is not connected to the life of the magisters, they will just continue their life as normal. That means complain how hard their life is under the surpression of the magisters, and that they so greatly want to escape but cant, because the guards are so many and the gates are closed...while in reality every guard is dead and the gates are open.
And this problem is in every aspect of the whole game. On a sinking ship i did calmed a few of the shipkeepers so that i didnt have to fight them...but when i found a lifeboat to escape i could safe everyone but them...because they could be already be dead if i just fight them before, and so their life is not connected to the lifeboat so that their is no way to safe these fellas even if you try. Or a leader of the resistance (who cried how many of his good man died in the fight against the supressing magisters) doesnt even say a word after everyone(!) of his camerads died in a big battle, since their was also a possibility that they would be already dead, before the battle starts. And so he just talkes totally normally like nothing has happend while in reality all his friends with which he has fought for many years, just died a few minutes ago.
And this, at least for me, totally killes every bit of immersion that the game would normally develop from such an awesome world. Since you realise more and more, how scripted everything is, and that certain NPCs just react to this quest that they give you, and dont interact with anything else at all (as long you dont attack or try to steal from them) you never develop the feeling that you are "inside" this world and that the world is living around you. But more and more it feels like everything just exists to give you a quest, and stay silent after they have fulfilled their purpose (like maybe a person from an MMORPG, that gives you one quest and then just stands their without any purpose) and since the world and the mainplot are so great and fascinating, it have lead to great frustration to me.
I know that this is not a fault of the game itself since its techically awesome in any sense it wants to be, but i think i just realised in this game, since the experience i get from this game becomes more and more "empty" i think that i am just the wrong audience for this type of very open RPGs. Because for me, the huge amound of freedom just destroys the illustion to be in a real world. And for me this is more importand then 10 options in every quest.

.Story.
You are one angry dragon. Why? Why not.
As your path of destruction spreads, the king of the village you’re tearing asunder will send out different units to stop you until, finally, His Majesty himself appears in an attempt to thwart you.
Let them try.
.Gameplay.
The keys are fully rebindable and, though the starting configuration is a little strange, it works. You use the left and right arrow keys to move, the down arrow key to eat, Z to do a ground pound that’s good for pushing enemies away, X to jump, and C to breathe fire.
It’s through these combinations of draconic talents that you’ll lay waste to the peaceful village before you. Meting out destruction will net you points while eating will keep your angry little friend alive as well as fill his Rampage meter. Once you fill it all the way, the game really shines because, for the brief moment you’re in Rampage Mode, you feel like a real dragon. You’re able to dash, jump, and breathe fire without restriction and it feels very, very satisfying to lay waste to buildings while dashing about and lighting a trail behind you.
Unfortunately, Rampage ends rather quickly and you’ll have to begin filling the meter anew by feasting on the kingdom’s residents.
You can also lay eggs, though I haven’t figured out exactly what adds to your egg meter. Once it’s filled, your dragon will lay a single egg and you have to protect it until it hatches. Once it hatches, you’ll have a little buddy who will attack everything within its reach until it is slain. You can hatch several eggs per wave, though after the third it seems impossible to fill the meter again.
As you destroy more buildings, the king begins to send out tougher units in a sort of story-like fashion. Dialogue is presented regarding the new unit that’s being introduced and it’s oftentimes quite amusing.
The game continues on like this until you destroy 100 buildings and then it’s off to the next stage to do it all over again. The stages vary slightly in background and the units that are introduced seem to be re-colourings of units you see in the first stage--one of three, as of the most recent patch (August 13th).
.Atmosphere.
The music of Dragon Rage is perfectly conductive for destruction. The effects that punctuate your rampage—the crunch of buildings caving in beneath your mighty feet; the whoosh! of air as you leap over the heads of those foolish enough to try and stop you; the crackle of flames as they leave your belly in brightly coloured gouts—are all very satisfying as well.
The cutesy graphics give a light-hearted feel to your warpath. I mean, really, how seriously can you take that face? The jumping, fire-breathing, and lunging-to-eat animations all look great. My favourite effect is when you enter Rampage mode and the screen is awash with scarlet while everything else is reduced to black silhouettes.
.Longevity.
If you’ve been reading other reviews, you’ll note that the game can take anywhere from 10-15 minutes to complete. Yes, there are now three stages with varying difficulty, but they do nothing to add to the base gameplay. There’s nothing to unlock and no real reason to keep playing except for those of us who enjoy hunting achievements.
I can’t agree with the asking price of 6.99 due to the rather small amount of content.
.Pros and Cons.

.Bottom Line.
I can recommend Dragon Rage as a game because it’s a fun way to blow off some steam. I cannot, however, stand by the asking price. I’d say anything around 1-3 dollars would be fair for the amount of content it currently offers.
If you’re looking for a meaty game to sink your time into, this title isn’t for you. If you’re the type to revisit a title just to tool around and destroy things, Dragon Rage will offer you up a satisfying, bite-sized experience.

I'm not good at writing reviews, but I feel like I have to give this game one, given how much fun it was. I just finished on Tactician difficulty the first time after having put in around 120 hours of work and I just have to recommend it for anyone who is interested in RPGs and the likes. The amount of content put into this game is astonishing, which in itself is, in my opinion, pretty damn good.
You can select from a lot of different classes and races, which have their own unique strengths and playstyles. And here's basically where one could write a novel about team composition, what's strong and what has better synergy with one another. And so on. Larian did a good job adding this much depth to the already nice combat system of the predecessor.
About the story, I won't spoil anything, but suffice to say: It's amazing. Your companions are interesting. The places you travel to are as well. The NPCs you meet along your journey are fun to interact with and almost always useful, be it in terms of selling you equipment/spells or giving you information about things you might wanna know.
The mechanics of the game are pretty nice to play and experiment around with. The variety by which you can approach battles is quite high in number as long as you're creative. This in turn, again, depends on your group composition, so selecting your option wisely has to be a given, especially on the highest difficulties.
About difficulties, I did struggle quite a bit on Tactician difficulty, since it was the first time I was playing the game. It might seem a little crazy what kind of bonuses the enemies get in terms of armour and HP, but I found them beatable by indeed exploring every little place on the map there was, speaking to almost everybody to get that little extra bit of experience and equipment which might just be enough to beat the next tough battle. As such, it would probably be best to play the game on Classic beforehand, to get an idea of the mechanics and so on.
And that's pretty much it. I enjoyed it a lot and probably will, still, in the future when trying out different compositions and what not. About the Arena mode and Game Master mode, I don't know, since I haven't tried them yet.
tl;dr: If you're a fan of RPGs and got the money, buy this game. I'm sure you won't regret it. :D

Unfortunetly I think they had the wrong vision when creating this game. They very much focused on Multiplayer, while Peter Molyneux and his creative vision always primarily focuses on the singleplayer. I know they took a lot from DK2, not from DK1, the first one of them being also the game Peter no longer worked on.
That doesn't mean it's bad ... I mean I played much more DK2 than 1 too, but I think the devs of WFTO really ♥♥♥♥ed up the game balance ... by and this might sound crazy at first ... by trying to make it balanced.
I think they really hoped for some type of esports recognition. The addition of potions and other things really is imo indicative of that.
They also completly ♥♥♥♥ed up the defences and trap part of the game. They made it all lock away part of your mana, which means it's COMPLETLY 100% USELESS. You NEVER want to build traps anywhere in your dungeon except right besides your dungeon hearts, because of the open-ended nature of the maps in this game. It's not bad that the maps aren't linear, but you really don't want to waste your precious mana which can be otherwise locked away for Ember Demons and IMPS and keep in mind you ALSO still want to have spells.
So really by trying to balance it for multiplayer, they completly and utterly took all the magic out of the game. The abilities of the creatures also just reek of that mentality. When reading them I felt like this was some sort of MOBA (which they probably thought could happen on their game engine). In Dungeon Keeper 2 units had interesting abilties, some of them were useless, some were nice gimmicks like turning into a bat as a vampire, others were insanely "OP" and could down an enemy in one go. But they were all intersting.
I never even bothered to learn the different abilities of the creatures, because despite the Devs trying everything in their power to do differently, the Death Ball (massing your creatures all together with the rally flag) still Trumps everything else and with sufficent numbers you can just destroy everything. Some doors take annoyingly long to take down, espeically in the campaign where the doors of EVERY ♥♥♥♥ING room have to be SUPER ELITE Doors. Even though I have some slight OCD I didn't bother to destroy them all in missions usually.
Okay what else needs to be talked about? The Graphics are♥♥♥♥♥♥ DK2 had the blocks not be entirely straight, especially when unclaimed, but for some reason the graphics of today don't allow that. The game needs all that processing power to light up all the particle effects WHICH EXIST ON EVERY SINGLE CLAIMED BLOCK. Your Dungeon looks like a ♥♥♥♥ing Disco Ball. I still remember playing it when it just came out and the game was way too dark, especially outside your claimed area. Funny how things change.
Also the creatures of today all look like copy-pastas from each other. The graphics also didn't cut it to maybe give some variance to them? I guess they tried to do it with the Gnarlings, but that is unique mechanic to the.
Oh and for a Dungeon Sim, the game has precious little caring for your creatures. I remember how my Bile Demons created an enormous shortage of food, because those fat ♥♥♥♥s really spend much time just eating away. The Dungeon Sim mechanics were unfortunetly already pretty hollow in DK2, but WFTO doubled down. There are no interesting mechanics to speak of. They didn't innovate at all. We could have had little private mini dungeons for particular dangerous dungeon dwellers, maybe even with special door codes ala Evil Genius, so your own minions don't accidently wander into their lair. OR MAYBE THEY DO!!!! Wouldn't that be an interesting mechanic? To have a Big Ogre Creature eat your low level goblins?
But yeah. Despite what faults Peter Molyenux has and I am not an apologist, I have a love-hate relationship with him, he often has very creative ideas and delivers either average games (fable), which are still fun and have a unique charme or completly broken games with major features missing (Black and White 2), he still tries to innovate. This cannot be said for WFTO. They added no new mechanics to the Dungeon Managment Genre. They casualized it and tried to make it esports compatible. This development really doesn't sit well with me.
I can still play the campaign of Dungeon Keeper 2 and enjoy it, just play around in the comfy levels, which are unfortunetly not difficult at all. Peter Moleynuex's games are notorious for being way too easy and missing a difficulty slider and this game is no exception. But while the campaign levels are easy as hell, they are unfortunetly not comy and that is also why this game simply does not hold up.

The Nostalgia is strong here.  For anyone who played and enjoyed the Dungeon Keeper franchise there is a lot here to enjoy.
Building your dungeon is still fun and engaging, working out what rooms attract what creatures is also fun.
The Graphics are sharp and clear, if a little dark in places, the sound is excellent and the controls are easy to learn, wether you've played this type of game before or not.
However there are a few downers:
The Levels themselves, while fine, often do not allow you to build the dungeon of your dreams due to the restraints of the terrain around you (impenitrable rock) or that you can mine a few squares before you suddenly go into a new area which is really strangely shaped, so, if like me you enjoy creating sprawling dungeons you're out of luck.
Also Combat feels lackluster, there is something missing, and often it comes down to sheer numbersd and creature levels to succeed.
Finally, there are the creatures themselves.  While some of them are quite interesting and engaging (the Chunder for example) a lot of them seem to be poor imitations of their Dungeon Keeper parents and don't, at least for me, feel as engaging or fun as they should do.
Overall it is an excellent attempt at a Dungeon Keeper type of game, let down only marginally by clunky combat and level design.

The level- and puzzle- design of this game is absolutely superb. Each level showcases some novel way for the different mechanics to fit together; not a shred of level is wasted. As far as I can tell, none of the puzzles are easily broken, either, whether with ninja moves or unconventional puzzling. The levels themselves are also very challenging; particularly upon nearing the latter third of the game.
A few things are unfortunately still desired; a more lenient physics engine (jumping is somewhat fiddly, as is stacking blocks, as you'll see from many reviews), a better menu (options should come BEFORE savefile selection!), more levels (only 40+8 bonus), and possibly a better redesign of the final level.
The number of mechanics is sometimes overwhelming, too. In addition to the 4 different guns and the zapper, there're also bombs, grapplable boxes, light boxes, heavy boxes, polarized boxes, lanterns, impact-toggled switches, lasers, colour-mixing puzzles, ice, glass, barriers that objects can't pass through, barriers that put out lanterns, barriers that arrows can pass through but you can't... Suffice to say, you may find yourself trying to recall what exactly a green dashed barrier does, and how it's different to a blue dotted barrier.
If you like puzzle games, this is definitely a good one I can recommend to you; it's up there along with English Country Tune and Snakebird in terms of pure gameplay. It is definitely worth the 4 GBP, whether on sale or not. But be prepared to spend more time on it than you might think, and be prepared to wish for more by the time you finish.

"Submerged is a third-person combat-free game in which you explore a mysterious flooded city and discover the beauty of desolation in vast outdoor environments. You take on the role of Miku, a young girl who has brought her wounded brother to the city in their small fishing boat."
You are presented with the problem within the first few minutes of the game as you step off of the boat holding a young boy; your brother. Already the story feels heartwarming and heartwrenching. I can't go into details, as this is largely a story-driven game, but I can say a few words regarding the story. It's mature, it's macabre, but there are many interpretations and thoughts you can have regarding the story. Nothing is ever explicitly told, just shown. There's a story to Miku and her brother, but there's also a story about the city and the world.
Tying in directly with the story is the world; the environment. A vast city awaits your exploration, but it's one that is a maze of skyscrapers and ruined technology. Not only that, but the world is flooded to an unknown depth. The nature has reclaimed practically everything, and you'll learn more about that as you discover 'secrets', or hidden drawings that fit a timeline of events.
Initially the world might seem dead, but that is not at all the case. Various creatures roam the world, and some even interact with you. Many times throughout the course of gameplay you'll have a pack of dolphins following your boat, or even a whale trying to get by on his hunt for food. You never feel alone playing Submerged, but that doesn't make the eerie feeling of desolation and destruction go away. There are multiple mysteries to uncover, and exploration will solve them all. Trust me, I want to say more but it would spoil too much!
The only reason this deserves a category is because the soundtrack is so beautiful and I hope that it becomes available for download. Seriously, it's so atmospheric and incredible! Uppercut Games, make this happen!
The gameplay is largely what you make of it, much like Journey. You cannot lose, there is no combat, and there are no time limits. Those who expect an action game should look elsewhere, though that's not at all a negative comment about the game. Everything is so visceral and relaxing with playing Submerged. Each building is small challenge to navigate and the stunning visuals always provide you with a unique and exemplary view on the world with each wall you climb. Gameplay is simple, the controls are are obvious, and controlling Miku is simple considering you can't fall off or die.
A game like Submerged is an experience, but in a different way a typical FPS or casual game is. A game that gives you the tools for a good experience is a dangerous type of game, but usually attracts those who like story-driven, thought provoking games. As a whole Submerged is just stunning and beautiful. Unreal Engine 4 is such a fantastic and versatile engine, and Submerged creates a wonderful, living world to spend a few hours or more.
There are only a few categories I can score Submerged by, but I believe that the few categories I can score it by make this game more than worth the time and price. The beautiful visuals, splendid soundtrack, and deeply ambiguous story of Submerged entice you into a surreal experience that you will NOT forget!

LogiGun is the 2D side-scrolling cousin of Portal I didn't know I needed.
The basic premise of the game - you shoot fancy guns. They all do neat and interesting things to help you interact with your environment; and although homage is paid to the FPS-style puzzle rules set down in Half-Life and Portal, the gameplay elements are unique and to not copy from those games.
The controls feel very loose at times, and I still get annoyed that the jump mechanic is set default to the "W" key rather than the spacebar. Additionally, the story seemed very one-dimensional. However, these minor irritations do not detract too much from the size and scope of the campaign - 40 playable levels plus a short epilogue to cap the story arc. There are also bonus levels and a map editor, so that you can make your own maps and upload to them for other people to try out.
Despite my complaints about the controls and the storyline, this puzzle game was worth the money I paid for it. This is a puzzle game done really well, and fans of Portal will feel right at home with this great game.

Short, but very emotional and relaxing indie game created by former developers of Bioshock. The setting is similar to Enslaved, but more depressing - the world is flooded, only parts of the highest buildings are visible above water, all covered in plants and seaweed. Your brother is seriously wounded and you need to gather some medicine and rations for him from the roofs of the buildings. To get there you use your boat and telescope (to locate interesting objects and mark them on your map). Then you climb up and search for hidden stuff.
Submerged combines TPP exploration and some light platforming elements, though no skills or good coordination are needed, as it is impossible to fail here. You don't jump, you just move across ledges, pipes and branches and try to get all the secrets on your way to the top. What is more - there is no combat or violence in this game, but it contains some minor scares and sad moments - think of Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons or Journey. The story is told without any words - the only text you see is your objectives.
There are no technical issues with the game and it's optimized well, but you can feel the low budget. The world and character models look fine, but animations are unrealistic and jerky and platforming elements seem too easy and repetitive (thus boring for hardcore players). Soundtrack is lovely, though, as well as the atmosphere.
If you like exploration games and simple, but touching stories - try it, you should not be disappinted.

According to Steam, I have played this game for 555 hours. I have never played a game which came close to this one at holding my interest.
There are so many different possible ways to play, it never gets old.

The Good:
- Excellent story telling, ME1 was good but the level of immersion and depth of the story and options go much deeper in this sequel. Bioware really knew how to build a good scene, from a heroic jump into the Normandy down to a death of one of your beloved teammate. At no point will you ever feel like you've been cut off from the first game. In my opinion it is the strongest aspect of Mass Effect 2.
- Optional major quests feel more relevant and interesting. They are presented with out shortage of cut scenes, intricate stories fleshed out in brilliant dialogue.
- Improved combat map layout. ME2 allows flanking thus making the shotgun more viable than the first game.
- Inclusion of clips (ammo system) in the game. Limiting the use capacity of each weapon forces the player to be more tactical about the weapon they choose for certain enemies at specific locations. ME1 fostered the abuse of 1 strong weapon particularly the sniper rifle, leaving other weapons sort of unappriciated.
- Better controls over teammates. The player can now designate each team member to specific areas of the combat field, thus improving the over all tactical approach.
The Bad:
- Terrible in-combat weapon selection. The 'rotation-system' is just not best for PC gaming. This part of combat feels as though it was just purely adopted from the console controls with out any consideration to the PC gaming norms.
- Being trapped on top of a box or any "supposedly" inaccessible area by accident is a total inconvinience. This issue is something that should have been patched out. Minor as they are, they do break immersion and certainly annoys the player.
Recommendation:
BUY IT. This game is a perfect marriage of action game play and story, a testament that a brilliant developer need not sacrifice story for a good gameplay and vice versa.

To fix the save file crash problem , you are gonna have to do this manually . Download HxD Hex Editor ( google search ) . Install HxD and use HxD to open up the jet set radio . exe launcher . On the left hand side of the HxD program you will see a list of offset Hex-Codes. Look for Hex-Code 0021D800 , when you reach the Hex-Code look to the far right and locate the word "save" in lower case letters. Click on the "s" and type "SAVE" ( no quotation marks, all capital letters ) . The word "SAVE" should be in red replacing the "save" in lowercase letters. Save the file and play the game without this issue .

It's sort of a spiritual successor to Star Wars Galaxies, crafting is vitally important... but you don't necessarily have to do it yourself. There's no "Weapon Shop" or "Armor Shop", there's only the very rare rewards and drops or players who have crafted these things and put them into the economy. You will inevitably run out of ammo and your gear will fall apart. You need to participate in the economy somehow just to survive.
The actual gameplay is sort of FPS-styled but rather than moving away from the point-and-click WoW style MMO interface... it just adds this other layer where if you don't multitask you'll miss all your attacks while ducking into cover and popping mutations and bandaging yourself up. You still HAVE to go through the ordinary stuff, but the skill curve goes up a bit for being a good shot at the same time.
The skill layout is almost Anarchy Online in its open-ness and complexity........... until you realize that years of lazy balance and reactive patches have rendered half the stats and skill trees completely useless and cookie-cuttered a lot of things. It may jump back and forth from patch to patch.... but mostly going to limit you to a LOT less variety than advertised. Still, the things that DO work are generally pretty fun.
The first two sectors are easily the best MMO areas I've ever played, very detailed and lovingly crafted. FULL of content, you can wander off in any direction and stumble into something interesting... After S2.... not so much. Also not sure why they cut the starting towns down to three from... eight or ten or something. Streamlined or stupified, hurt the newbies most.
There is absolutely no pay-to-win in this game. You can pay for convenience or you can pay for custom appearances... but there's nothing that gives any real advantage past the Freemium level. Most of the marketplace items end up on the auction for anyone to buy with in-game money also, but pure free players are limited to how much of that they can carry.

I'm revising this review after finishing the game finally, and my opinion has not changed.
Jet Set Radio to me is an example of when nostalgic blinds people into thinking old or unique premiss in games will make them automatically good.
While the graphics in this provide a colorful setting for Tokyo in many places, it starts to become a problem when the limitation of graphics in your games start to affect the actual gameplay of it. This becomes clear when trying to race in the game and the back drops give no perception of how far or close you are to an object, due to it being one image rather than separate objects. NPC models in this game are laughable when compared to the player model's graphics that it make it seems they did not even try.
One of the biggest faults in this game is the camera controls. For a game that makes you jump in very high areas, the camera will constantly clip under you. Certain times you make jumps, there will be a provided replay function, while usually this would be fine, the fact the replay happens clearly 2 seconds AFTER you make a jump, makes disorientating time when the camera goes back to the original place. This really becomes a problem when you are tying to escape mobs and the replay messes up the flow of gameplay.
The gameplay itself can be very infuriating at times, especially when games earlier than it (such as tony hawk games) nailed down the formula perfectly. This is clear when the grinding in this game is automatic rather than a dedicated button to grind, leading to mishaps in accidentally grinding when trying to jump to specific areas. There’s no way to simply dismount off of a grind either so when I try and get off I am thrusted forward into a jump instead. Jumping from curved areas is also buggy, leading to your character to either jumping straight up and doing nothing or actually performing a trick move. Stairs are also a challenge in the gameplay itself, this doesn’t becomes a problem till the later levels where you have flying enemies shooting you. When you are walking up stairs you are at the mercy of bullets hitting you with no way you to avoid getting hit, since jumping is even too slow to avoid getting it. A great game. But it seems they ran out of resources at some point mid-development.
Nice story, nice graphics, a lot of quests, none of the quests is repetitive, all the voice actings, and all that. The game itself is fantastic and exceedingly immersive as I've spent around 200 hours to finish just the first playthrough.
However, it is apparent that they rushed on finishing the game from somewhere like 2/3 of the way. The most noticeable evidence, which a lot of people on the discussion forum complain about, is that somewhat rather many quests will not properly be completed. For instance, even if you've done everything and the quest log also says so, the quest remains uncompleted and say something like you abandoned the quest, when you move to the next area. The next problem, from my experience, is that I've noticed some slopinesses here and there throughout the game. For example, some dialogue options are just null, which means the game (or npcs) doesn't recognise the dialogue options and just quit the conversation. For another example, there is a quest in an earlier chapter involving an npc which implies there is more to be found in later chapters about the npc, but nothing ever mentions anything about the npc as if she never even existed, even if the npc has been on the same boat (literally) to the very end of the game. They are not like game breaking bugs, but still, annoying and feel like that their care for polishing the game has been started decreasing at some point.
Overall, I'm not saying like the game is bad or anything like that, it's just that I've noticed these small things (maybe big?) throughout the game and they were annoying. Consider it as a small complain. But still, it's a great game and worth every penny, and that's why I'm giving it a yes to 'Do you recommend this game?'. It's been a great experience and well spent over-200 hours. I highly recommend the game. If they do some patch-works, I think it would be safe to call it a masterpiece. :D

This is the first game in a long time that felt like the person who made it actually wanted to make a good game. So many times developers and companies will rerlease cynical, lazy, uninsipred time wasters that are just trash.
But this game is different, this game has loads of imagination, the monsters are original, the campaign is finely tuned between challenging and fair, the narration is beutiful, the tone fits the setting of you being an evil underlord from the void, this game is very well thought out and just packed full of fun things that most other developers would not think to do.
Take for instance prisoners, now in this game you can capture fallen enemies and imprison them in your dungeon. Now most people would sit down and say "ok lets make it so you can execute them in interesting ways and you get gold or some♥♥♥♥♥♥whatever." But these guys said "♥♥♥♥♥ your supposed to be an evil underlord!" So they gave you a ton of options for what you can do with prisoners. Yes, you can execute them, but you can also convert them to your side, turn them into gold statues, throw them into your arena and have them fight to the death, you can throw them into your crypt and turn them into ghouls, you can put them in your sausage maker and turn them into food for your minions.
The people that made this tought of almost everything, and itss so wonderful to see someone realise the potential of being an evil underlord. And when it comes to your dungeon, there is a surprising lack of micromanagement. For the most part your minions will keep your dungeon up and running, all you have to do is oversee construction expansion and invasion. also the finances of course. I actually like this because it alows you to sit back and appreciate you dungeon, you can stop by the torture chamber and listen to the wonderful screaming for a while, I personally love the screams of the beast master the most. Oh yeeah you can torture your own minions too, the screaming and begging is very satisfying. But be careful because you might accidentally kill them.
Not only all that but this game has a ton of unlockables, not just DLC, but actual unlockables for getting achievments. I love this, it gives purpose to the achievements and is something you can actually go for instead of just paying outride for new dungeon themes you have to earn them, which is awesome. It gives a ton of replayability to the campaign, and you can also brag about it.
All in all this is a very well thought out, well balanced, very replayable game that is just plain fun to play, and I cant wait for them to make more. definetly pick this one up.

I saw this game on Greenlight, and thought it was the most fun-looking thing I'd seen in a long time--
I was
. Make no mistake, this game was a pile of fun to play, and eating that cowardly king was probably the most satisfying thing I've done in a long time.
When I saw
, I mean that the game is a great laugh, extremely cathartic, and a barrel of laughs all at the same time. However, getting the poor creature airborne isn't the easiest thing in the world, and I never did figure out how to keep Her Hugeness aloft for any appreciable time. It would have gone a long way towards avoiding a good chunk of the damage I took trying to obliterate the village.
Which I did, in fact manage to do. The controller worked beautifully, even if it does prefer the D-Pad to the left analog stick. The rampage mechanic was entertaining, for both me and my viewers-- I could almost hear the screams of triumph as I ate that cowardly king during the last one.
He sent his daughter and wife out before he could be buggered to put in an appearance.
The story here is very basic: You're a huge hungry dragon that need to eat and lay eggs. The village down there looks tasty. Time to go do both.
It starts off easy: You have villagers to deal with, a rare few have hammers. Afterr you've torn up the place a bit, the King sends a horde of sword-wielding knights in to help. This goes on and on, until you get above 75 or 80 buildings destroyed, after which the Princess appears. A bit of carnage later, and the Queen turns up.
After they die, the King finally gets off his corpulent backside, and drops in to get eaten as well. However, this isn't until you've very nearly finished obliterating the last of the buildings that were your objective. Each member of the Royal Family has a buff they give the troops: Princess for attack, Queen for Defense, and the King grants both.
Needless to say, they were crunchy, and good with ketchup. Or was that blood from the cavalry and wood chips from all the catapults? I can never tell.
At $6.99 US full price, I get the impression that the dev is leaving money on the table. It's a great game, and a worthy successor to Sonic the Hedgehog running off a cliff when I'm trying to deal with added stress. Well done!

When I first reviewed the game, I gave a "Recommended" review. This time I'm not and here's why:
[Gampleay and controls]
Pros: It's pretty fun, with very interesting weapons and hulls. Game-play is fast-paced and you respawn pretty quickly too. Controls are pretty easy to get used to, if you play with mouse and keyboard typically, although I would recommend playing with keyboard only without the use of a mouse, if you decide to try this game out, because the camera turns instantly, but your turret takes time to synchronise, creating it harder to aim... that's already a con, isn't it? Hh boy!
Cons: It has officially become Pay2Win. Before, it was very insignificant, where you could get up to 50% more damage for your turret, at the expense of some extra armor or something, while most other players would get less. This time, things are different. The module system has been ovrhauled, and you can play against people who have modules of much higher upgrade than you. There are 3 tiers and those tiers determine in terms of tier to match players with a similar sum of tiers, but nothing is done in terms of upgrades of the respective modules to prevent Pay2Win.
You'll lose most matches unless you pay, you'll lose because your team mates are all noobs while your opponents are all pros, unless you buy your way through. Oh, and you can't change any of the controls, to my knowledge, even though the main intent for the game being downloadable was done in order to allow for you to choose controls.
[Balance]
Well... there really are no pros here; it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Bottom line is that most long and mid-range weapons are pretty decent or very powerful and most short and close range weapons are weak or unbearably weak in comparison. The fact that there are modules that make it even harder for certain, if not all close and short range weapons to fight (thermal protection and radius-based module disabling module) much more often than they are a problem for mid and long range weapons, just furthers the imbalance. Ricochet weapon is by far the most weak weapon in the game; has average damage up to 45 meters, is basically♥♥♥♥♥♥for the other half of the distance that its projectiles can reach, projectile travel speed is slow as ♥♥♥♥, ricocheting targetting is non-existent, so, unless you're shooting inside a tunnel, your projectiles will most likely shoot in the air instead of hitting the opponent and the weapon only has 12-projectile mag before it starts shooting slower due to very slow reload speed. Its counterpart, Twins, while a♥♥♥♥♥♥weapon too, is better, because it has no shooting limit, despite having 15m max damage distance reach.
[Aesthetics]
Pros: Some pretty cool effects and you'll find some of the skins are pretty cool. One particular type of mention for this would be the XT skins, but I do have some criticisms down below for these types of skins.
Cons: The skins are counter-intuitive for camouflage, so I've had no incentive to buy them. If I can look cool while maintaining camouflage, count me in, but if the camouflage is ruined DUE to looking cool, then I'll pass.
Coatings are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t; it's basically a paint specifically for getting a different colour than that of your hull, but sold as a SEPERATE ITEM. It also makes tanks look like clowns or some of those Sonic and My Little Pony fan-made characters drawn on devian art.
Most other skins, like Gold for example are simply cheap re-colours of existing type of skin that you get for free once you level up. Like what the ♥♥♥♥?! Also, some effects like the fog in Massacre are cheaply implemented, to a point where if you look from certain angles in the match, the fog becomes basically invisible.
Oh, and gloom has been removed completely and shows no signs of return (basically glow on pieces of lighting), not even for Ultra settings, because god knows why. In other words, the effects are pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥, and for whatever reason they still use 2D grass, while having 3D grass on maps at the same time. Doesn't look good when you notice it. There's nothing in regards to the graphics that would actually make the game look gourgeous. Most of this♥♥♥♥♥♥has been done in the past, even though people keep boasting how its graphics are magnificent. There's bearly any breakable structures, there's nothing like weather effects or you squishing the ground due to snow, mud or a pile of sand, none of that. The game has dynamic shadows on higher graphics settings, but that's already been done in the game's predecessor Tanki Online, so what's there to boast about that?
[Map design]
I admire, to an extent, the design of some of the newest maps. I find that Massacre, Ares and West Prime (to some extent) look realistic in their setting. The other maps are just ones taken from the previous map, without much of any layout changes. The game only has ~10 maps, and when you play with matchmaking, you can't really choose the map, nor whether you want to play TDM or CTF in any way. I like the concept of matchmaking, but I'd rather it be optional and even then have the player given options to select from to determine what kind of battle they'll be assigned to, so they don't, say, end up in a map for long-range weapons while having equipped a short-range weapon and they don't have any long range or mid-range weapond on their presets that they have unlocked.
[Introduction]
It's♥♥♥♥♥♥ You fist play against bots, which are weaker and who's AI makes them much less skilled than you. You have no way of getting out of the introduction indication that forces you to do certain things. You get a new account created automatically now, but you don't get a password for the account, and if you log out of it without attaching an e-mail address, you can say bye bye to the account, as there's no way of setting a password without having an e-mail address attached. First off, Tom Baker! He narrates certain parts of the game and also voices one of the characters - not a main character, but an NPC that shows up here and there throughout the game (Tetsu). When I learned that, I had to pick it up immediately, regardless of whether the game was any good or not. Aside from the fourth Doctor, the game is also fully voiced with cutscenes, NPC chatter, and dialogue options.
Sudeki is from 2005 and it shows. The graphics are a bit primitive, about the same level as World of Warcraft, although the art style is different. It has a more Asian vibe. It's actually a very pretty game, with bright colors, dazzling particle effects, and great character designs.
It's also an obvious console port, with no mouse control within menus, a checkpoint save system, and limited options. The default POV is third person with no Y axis control, but certain skills require first-person view which does allow you full X & Y angle control. Ranged characters play in first-person by default during combat, then switch back to third-person when moving around out of combat.
Combat is fluid, and plays differently for each character. Some have combo moves which aren't too complicated (L/R/L, L/L/L, R/L/L, etc.), others have various weapons you can switch between during combat for various effects. There are also spells and special powerup moves you can activate. Combat pauses while you select these from a menu, and they include cutscene style animations with epic effects. This makes it feel a bit like a turn-based RPG like Final Fantasy VII when you trigger those off, which is kind of fun.
There are shops and save checkpoints scattered around here and there. Weapons and armor can be upgraded with runes to add various effects like damage shield on armor, or extra crit chance on weapons, things of that nature. The game-world is composed of corridors divided by zones. There is no jumping, and sometimes you might encounter an invisible wall where it looks like you should be able to go a certain direction, but you can't. In this way, the setup reminds me a bit of Kingdom of Amalur. You can go almost anywhere, although some areas are blocked off until you unlock them through the story.
Speaking of the story, it's actually quite good. The characters are interesting, there are quite a few subtle jokes and innuendos thrown in here and there, and it has a lot of personality. I didn't want to stop playing but alas, sleep beckons. I look forward to playing through some more, as the game is actually quite fun. For the price, it's very solid entertainment. You just have to overlook the dated graphics and console feel.

Sudeki's a “But… if…” game, which are always the hardest ones to review. The “but” comes from a handful of mitigating factors: it’s fun, but easy; interesting, but derivative; initially engaging, but soon begins to feel rushed. Every positive facet of Sudeki comes with an accompanying drawback.
The “if,” of course, is that if you like action-RPGs, there is nothing in Sudeki that will actually harsh your mellow. It’s not a bad example of its genre by any stretch of the imagination, and is often really entertaining despite its flaws, presuming that you like the genre in the first place.
Sudeki is set on a world of the same name, which warring gods have split into opposing realms of light and shadow. The game begins in the kingdom of Illumina in the Light realm, where a soldier named Tal splits his time between defending the countryside from berserk Shadow monsters, flirting with the princess Ailish, getting yelled at by his father, and being the lone survivor of any mission he’s sent on.
In the aftermath of a battle, the god Tetsu appears to Tal, and lets him know that an end is coming; the current troubles between the Light and Shadow worlds are just the beginning of a larger struggle. Tal, Ailish, a demihuman warrior named Buki, and Illumina’s head scientist Elco have been chosen by the gods to combat the forces of the Realm of Shadows, whether they like it or not.
Sudeki will frequently allow you to control at least two of your characters simultaneously. Like Knights of the Old Republic, any PC who’s not under your direct control at the moment is controlled by the CPU; unlike KOTOR, you move your active character in real-time. Tal and Buki are short-ranged melee fighters, controllable in third-person and attacking via a timing-based combo system, while during a fight, Ailish and Elco move and shoot in first person.
You can switch between the members of your current group at any time using the Black button, which is excellent for micromanaging difficult battles. Each character brings a unique mix of skills and statistics to the table; Tal is basically a meatshield, Buki is a mobile attacker, Ailish wields spells and high-damage magical staves (one of her later weapons is not so much a magical cane as a two-shot rocket launcher), and Elco provides covering fire using a variety of pistols.
The fun of Sudeki is largely in the combat. A battle’s usually a chaotic melee, full of flying projectiles, charging opponents, devastating spells, and unpleasant surprises. A lot of people have claimed that Sudeki is a button-masher, and if you want, you can hammer on attack buttons all damn day. If that’s your kick, go to it.
The reality is that Sudeki's combo system is actually designed to punish button-mashing. Tal and Buki’s melee combos depend largely on timing, forcing you to land two quick hits in preparation for a devastating finisher or a series of juggles. Anyone who’s trying to get through the game just by hammering on X or A isn’t going to do as well as a player who studies opponents, looks for an opening, and lays into them with a careful string of hits.
Meanwhile, Ailish and Elco’s job is to hang back from the melee and rain death upon anyone who isn’t looking. The more powerful their weapons, the more recharge time they’ll generally have between shots, which means you’ll need to dodge and weave to stay on your feet. Once again, you can just hold down the trigger and spray death at your enemies, but the low hit strength of the weapons with a high rate of fire means that you’re really spraying minor annoyance.
Out of combat, each character has a further unique ability which allows you to discover secrets and solve puzzles. Tal can push around local designated Shoving Objects, such as crates. Buki can climb up walls using her claws, Elco’s rocket pack lets him fly as long as there’s a yellow crystal handy to power it, and Ailish possesses Second Sight, allowing her to penetrate and dispel illusions.
When you level up, you can spend advancement points to raise each characters’ stats and teach them up to six skills. In villages, you can further improve a character by welding magical runes to his armor or weapons, providing power boosts, special abilities, or immunity to status attacks. (The latter’s important, since everyone and their mom in Sudeki can inflict status ailments on your party. It’s not unusual to have two or three going at once.)
This is usually the point where I ineptly segue into discussing a game’s flaws, but aside from some dodgy character design (I hope you like Buki’s♥♥♥♥♥ because thanks to the gods of Sudeki, you’ll be staring at it for a long time), Sudeki plays just fine. The biggest problem it has is that there isn’t enough of it.
For one thing, Sudeki is dead easy. Part of this is because Elco gets his best weapon about four hours into the game. With a little work and a few levels, he’ll be popping conventional enemies like a grape with one or two shots. This comes in handy, since Elco gets one of the hardest fights in the game all to himself -- Sudeki’s bosses always seem to contrive a method to make sure you fight them one-on-one – but it also means that any group with Elco in it skates through combat.
You can also easily get all the best skills early on, since none of the spells or abilities in Sudeki come with a prerequisite. You can easily grab all the stat-boosting or protective skills first thing, then use them at the start of any fight to stack the odds in your favor.
In addition, any given boss can be defeated with the use of a simple trick, which looks more like a glitch than anything else. Every time you use a skill, your character enters an invulnerability window that lasts until the end of the move. There’s at least one boss fight where you can completely ignore all of its attacks and instantly counter, as long as you keep casting spells.
Combine that with a few runes, some decent weapons, and Ailish’s tendency to obliterate anyone who looks at her funny with Celestial Circle, and Sudeki's main characters wind up looking less like heroes and more like exterminators.
In addition to being easy, Sudeki is ridiculously short, clocking in at twenty-five hours max. For a game that was purported to be the first real epic RPG on Xbox, this is almost incomprehensible.
Playing through the endgame, one wonders if Sudeki was meant to be far longer, but was rushed to completion. Many plot threads are abandoned or tossed aside, including a major life-changing event right before the final battle. Both Tal and Ailish have major issues that simply aren’t resolved, involving his father and her mother, and Elco is the focus of a major plot twist right before the finale that, unfortunately, doesn’t wind up meaning anything.
It’s a fun game, and it’s not a bad game, but it’s over right when most RPGs are just getting started.

The world isn’t just a dull canvas on which to haul trailers either, and there’s a definite sense of life within the game world — which isn’t necessarily true for past games with the word “simulator” in the title. Pedestrians walk the streets and stand around building sites, and many of the construction yards, supermarkets and industrial facilities you find yourself driving past actually function as delivery and departure points for other jobs.
It’s true that the game world in American Truck Simulator feels a bit small, as you only get the two scaled-down US states of California and Nevada to begin with. Nevada is actually classified as free launch DLC, and there were only two trucks included when the game first launched, thanks to licensing problems with manufacturers like Volvo.
Anyone who buys ATS will get the next DLC expansion for free, which will add the state of Arizona to the game which effectively increases the size of the game world by a third. It’s likely more states will be added gradually over time as they are built, though it’s not clear if any more of these will be free.
Though three trucks and two states might seem like a rough deal, the game is only $20. In a world where most brand new games cost three times that, while many similarly-priced indie titles provide far less in terms of scope and sheer playtime; it feels like pretty good value. It’s also actually cheaper than the price its predecessor, Euro Truck Simulator 2 launched at  which is still normally priced a few dollars higher.
The inclusion of a carefully-chosen list of Internet radio stations is a stroke of genius, as it removes the requirement to license music while providing a geographically-accurate list of stations to listen to while on the road. There’s pretty much every genre catered for, but it’s the hard hitting classic rock anthems that sound best on 18-wheels. I even found myself leaving on songs that I’d normally never listen to, and I’m not entirely sure why. You can import your own music if you really want to, but it’s more fun to mark a few favorites and flick through them.
After you’ve purchased a truck, you’re free to make modifications to it. Some drastically change the look of your rig, like buying a new cab or fancy paint job; others seem utterly pointless like new door handles and upgraded wing mirrors. This is an entirely optional way of blowing all your cash, but I’m sure glad they added so much variety.
You may have already written ATS off as just another boring simulator for nerds, but you’d be wrong. You don’t have to take my word for it either.

In a nutshell for those who don't want to read much: WFTO is like Dungeon Keeper 2 but better; It isn't an RPG which changed direction in development to cash in on DK2; It isn't a city management game with fantasy elements; It isn't even ashamed to be compared to Dungeon Keeper.. The devs seem proud that people find it a better version of a game that they themselves loved.
The creation of this game is what happens when a group of guys play DK2 and get so annoyed that the story ends there that they made their own story that doesn't get shelved.
Sadly this game's popularity is falling - A lot of people played this game to protest EA for that horrible Dungeon Keeper mobile game. As people calmed, this game lost its playbase surge. Shame because the developers are really nice!
The graphics are quite unique to me. They're like 60% cartoonified, but with enough realistic appearance such as antialiasing and pretty effects that you can feel the improvement from older dungeon games.
FAVOURITE THING:
Dungeon Keeper 2 had just one playable dungeon theme. For 99% of the game all you saw was 'red horde versus white knights'. But WFTO has
and worker looks, which I have fantasised about for years!
Technically just having two themes would be an improvement - The ability to have a distinct corridor culture from your opponent is a huge thing. But there are now tons, it's very rare that on 'random' my enemy has the same theme as me, and even then it's no worse than in DK2.
Over time you will have a preferred combination of colour, dungeon theme and worker skin and you will FEEL like your very own Underlord. I myself use this techy Mayan appearance (Mira theme) in orange, with Dwarven (DLC) workers and I genuinely feel like I'm an overlord simply unseen during the campaign.
LEAST FAVOURITE THING:
Some parts of the game, like
are just totally boring and redundant to me personally. Unlike in some dungeon games, training units is free.. So why would I pay 1500 gold to brew an experience potion? In a room far less useful than say a prison? The point at which I'd be buying potions would be when so rich that they don't dent my funds... At which point I'd rather have a mass of level 10 units and put money towards their payday.

Dragon rage is a game similar to the classic Rampage series. You’re a dragon and all you have to do is cause chaos. The game has very cure art-style and some nice music. The game however is way too short, and I am talking like 20 minutes to complete the game short. It is fun though but I think the developer could’ve added a few more levels.
The graphics looks pretty awesome with a cartoony art-style. The screen looks sharp and crisp. The dragon and people are super cute as well.  In the sound department there isn’t much, the background track is okay, nothing too fancy. When you go in rage mode the track changes into metal-type music. The sound effects are pretty nice too.
Basically you’re a dragon who is on rampage mode. You have to destroy a certain number of buildings and kill anyone who gets in the way, including knights, archers even the royal family itself. You can do certain types of moves including dashing, which will knock anyone in your way like a bowling ball. You can jump, stomp or breath fire down on the people. You also get many bonuses spawning and collecting them will give you food, points etc.
You have a health/hunger meter, whenever the dragon breath fire on people or stomp them it takes this bar down and to fill it up again you have to eat people. Throughout the game you have to manage your eating and destroying at the same time. When your health bar gets full you go into rage mode. In this mode the background gets all red and you can only see your dragon’s silhouette. You can dash infinitely in this mode and jump really high and breath fire faster too. Basically you can cause much more mayhem with this rage mode. Once in this mode the health bar starts depleting again and once the bar is empty you go back to the regular mode.
There’s also an egg meter which when it fills up the dragon will lay an egg. You must protect the egg for a certain time and dragon babies will hatch from the eggs. These little monsters will aid you in destroying everything that exists.
When you start off no one is attacking you. Once you start causing chaos the king will send knights to kill you and if they can’t stop you, archers will arrive. Later the king sends catapults, magicians, horse riding knights and many other types of warriors try to stop you. They even build walls so the dragon cannot move freely. the princess and queen come at a certain point in the game. They give defense bonuses to their armies. Once you destroy the king and 100 buildings, the game is over and you have won.
A short gameplay clip can be found below:
The game itself if pretty fun. Think of it as a stress reliever. If you’re angry with some work stuff or real life, you can sit down and take your frustration down on the poor people of the kingdom. $7 is kind of steep though for this short of a game so you can always wait for a bigger sale.

I played this originally when it first launched many years ago and found it extremely underwhelming back then. It was very clearly still in development with debug messages all over the place and was just generally janky.
So I put it aside and completely forgot about it.
Then a few days ago I saw the complete pack on sale and decided to give it a shot again.
Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ it's so much better now. Now it truly and most definitely is the spiritual sequel to Dungeon Keeper 2. Everything from the astounding levels of voice work put into the game to all the little details here and there. The main campaign is fun enough but the expansions add so much to the game.
Let me list some of the things I just love about what they've done:
1. Some of the missions are just amazing. For example, late in the vanilla campaign there is a mission where you fight three other AI dungeon keepers (or Underlords in this). If this were a vanilla RTS or even the older DK games, it would be a fairly tedious affair as you fight on three sides. Here, it's made so much more fun by the fact that all three of these guys who prior to these were completely unknown to you, have complete personalities and banters. They constantly talk to one another as they fight you and act like how they talk. The greedy one is more worried about mining gold than fighting you. The brutal conquerer just straight up rushes you before even he is even prepared. And there's a schizophrenic dual personality guy arguing with himself on one side. It's frigging glorious.
2. Anytime you like when you're on the campaign map, you can go to a realm called your Home Realm where you can basically just build a sandbox dungeon. It has (almost) no impact on the main game itself and at first I was kinda scratching my head why it's even there... as there are better sandbox modes in the game. But the dev team made it so the superb announcer actually converses with you inside that mode. I don't mean like random statements which he usually does, but he will reflect on the current situation in the campaign and what you've done so far. And it's not just one off too. There's usually quite a few things for him to say and it increases your immersion tenfold in the whole scenario.
3. You can unlock dungeon themes are you progress, which you can use in the non-campaign modes like skirmish, my pet dungeon, crucible, or whatnot. These sound minor but the dungeon themes are really well done. They're magnificently different from one another. Remember earlier I talked about those three AIs you fight in the one campaign mission? Well, you can have all their themes and then some. The gold hoarder is my favorite with gold floors, walls, imps, etc. all very well done. They're not just simple reskins, which I love.
4. The announcer. This is interesting. I of course love his original voice back in DK2 and DK where it was more.... subdued and low key. He always sounded kinda disinterested in the whole thing. In fact, some of the voice lines which I think were recorded earlier in development actually sound like that. But most of the lines are delivered in a new way. More fiery, more passionate. He sounds way more like he owns you. I like both, but it can get kinda weird when they intermingle, which can happen sometimes.
That being said, holy♥♥♥♥♥♥he knocks it out of the park. They put so much work into him. He has so many, SO MANY, voice lines. And to make things awesome, they made it so after every mission there's an appendix at the bottom of your mission report that includes all the new things you encounted that game. And then if you click on them, you can hear what the announcer has to say over every single one. Jesus christ the passion they put into this.
The only time I didn't like his performance was at the end of the final mission. First he sounds super anxious and surprised over what's going on. Like, not sarcastically surprised but like his plans are unravelling. Then he acts all smug and "that was totally my plan all along brah". Dude, you're not fooling anyone.
-------
I could go on, but this "review" has really gone on long enough. But I think if there's a case to be made for a dev to get money for their passion project so they can keep making their passion project... I think this is it.
Highly recommended.

Summation: Never has jumping been so frustrating, nor stacking blocks so difficult to pull off.
I wanted to like this game, I really did. And honestly, the game designer did a pretty good job. The mechanics aren't new or spectacular, and in general, there's only ever one way to solve the puzzles, but a puzzle game can't have everything.
Of the mechanics it does have, I can speak positively. The guns - most easily described as platform, crossbow, grapple, and magnet - allow for some interesting and actually challenging puzzles, and even if the game's nothing to look at visually, ordinarily the core gameplay at work here would signal a thumbs-up from me.
But- and given my non-recommendation, you knew there would be a "but"- the controls and physics are wonky. It's fine for my character and the objects to be somewhat floaty, if it didn't make setting up the more elaborate platform solutions frustrating to the point of rage-quitting. I'm not talking about puzzle difficulty here - I'm talking about the very simple aspect of control, which any game that uses platformer elements should implement properly. No matter how often you try, your boxes will slip, slide, perform mind-bending dances and fall off of the platforms you have spent minutes - nay, hours - placing them onto. And then you will have to try again.
And again.
And again, and again, and again.
The ratio of hours I have spent attempting to place one box on top of another box/platform while in mid-air, or attempted to carry a box over my platform-gun's tiny platforms to the number of hours I have spent actually playing the game is probably 1:1, maybe 2:1. The character becomes easier to control as more time is spent on the game - so depending on your speed at solving puzzles, you may become an expert before reaching the stages in which mid-air stacking is necessary - but it should not be required to spend 10 minutes solving a puzzle and 30 minutes trying to stack boxes. Even with practice, that is my experience at the end-game levels.
As to the levels themselves; I can only say that experiences shall vary. Most of the puzzles were not very difficult, although several of the later puzzles would have made me feel justified in my purchase were it not for the control issue.
I cannot recommend this game until the physics and controls are fixed. That's too bad, because the designer really did come up with something clever and created some interesting puzzles.

I appreciate this game, but some troubles with the puzzles and the UI leave more to be desired.
The adventure game this one reminds me of is Beneath a Steel Sky.  The graphics are horribly pixilated, just as games from that era were with audio and voice acting to make up for the lack of graphical attractiveness.  And it does make up for it in those areas, the characters have parts that are well written and well performed with a very human story to go alongside it.
The story is one I can appreciate.  The story follows two brothers, one trying to escape a station after having his memory wiped several times and the other trying to find the station and rescue his brother.  I liked it, the reveal happened a lot earlier than the real reveal and the major reveal becomes a lot more predictable the longer you go on through the game.  However, the writing is self-aware of its own predictability and manages use it as part of the build up -to the expected result- without insulting your intellect.  Instead of happening with an unexpected bang, it happens with a silent drone of acceptance, which I thought was what the author was trying to get and fits in with the environment they were building.
Most adventure games tell stories of odd worlds and go out of the way to say how different this world is from the one we live in.  This game tries hard to explain the world with experience and view we can relate to, emphasizing the people without dwelling on the sci fi, dystopia, or technology.  From that standpoint, the game is a lot more serious than most of the games filling the adventure genre.
The UI and puzzles hold the experience back somewhat.  The puzzles follow the standard point and click or dialogue variety with some machine operation and event type obstacles alongside it.  The gunplay they added to the game was clunky and annoying to do.  It's easy once you manage to figure it out but it feels like something to pad the length of the game.  Some of the puzzles also have this feel, as if they were made just to lengthen the game by making you repeat content and without adding to immersion.  The UI also soured me.  It is not terrible, but some of the user unfriendly conventions of early adventure games were adopted alongside the art style.  I did have some problems trying to figure out how to use items in my inventory together, something infrequent in this game and I wish I gave more thought to the tooltip telling me how to do it the one time I had to during the game.
In all, I'd say it has the bones of a good adventure game and is at least as good as the games it emulates.  Unfortunately, the UI, gunplay, and some of the puzzles leave the experience feeling clunky.  A good find for adventure game fans, less so for everyone else.

I loved Majesty as a kid, and hoped that I might continue to enjoy its sequel. Though the sequel has a pleasing interface and lovely graphics, it got the main aspect of the game wrong. This game is not challenging in the sense that it tests your skills and wit in order to properly establish your kingdom to deal with various tasks; instead, the game is outright impossible. Specifically, there are two levels near the beginning of the game, one in which you are to kill an ancient dragon accompanied by an endless horde of serpents, and one in which there are sewers around your palace that incessantly spawn rats and ratmen. BOTH of these quests are supposed to be intermediate quests and take place after you beat a handful of beginning quests (ironically, these are extremely easy and also extremely short, note my total playtime), but BOTH of them are impossible due to the fact that they are always demolishing your city from the very beginning of the quest. In Majesty, there were certainly quests with hordes of enemies, but very few of them were at the very beginning of the quest, and even so, hordes came in waves, to give you enough time to rebuild. What's worse is that I cannot play any other quest because Majesty 2 offers only linear-based progression, unlike Majesty, where you could complete almost any quest at any time. Not to mention the fact that Majesty 2 features far fewer quests than Majesty + Northern Realms, and you cannot continue playing after a quest is finished as you could in Majesty. I did NOT purchase the expansion packs for Majesty 2 because I wanted to see if the base game was any good first, and frankly, it did not live up to my bare minimum expectations.

Let me start off to say that I recommend this game and no, I was not paid in any form to write the review.
Conan Exiles has started off well in EA compared to most survival open world games like Ark and Rust. The devs focused first on making sure that it was playable early on. They try to iron out the bugs and optimisation problems as they go along with their regular twice weekly updates; this was unlike Ark where the devs were more interested in adding as much new content all the time.
Conan has a bright future as in it already has a basic story that is clearly seen which gives it some uniqueness (I am aware that the story will be expanded on in future updates).
Now to talk about specific things that I have categorised:
ANIMALS/MONSTERS
Pros:
- decent mix and variety
- good models
- okay AI
Cons:
- need better AI, there is no food chain; everything makes you number one priority to kill; hyenas aren't in packs etc
- not enough peaceful creatures - just deer/antelope/gazelle and bunnies
- which brings me to the next point of needing more variety of animals and monsters (something I know will be worked on)
- crocodile occasionally loses its animation when running towards me
STRUCTURES AND BUILDING
Pros:
- great variety of cosmetic things to build
- good variety of specialised building structures like sloped roofs and the ability to build triangular or circular
- mostly well-functioning snapping
- love the ability to stack foundations
Cons:
- needs lower tiers than sandstone like wood and thatch. It is impossible to start PvP unless you have late game weapons and explosives
- as mentioned earlier, there are occasional problems where it will say "failed to place" unless you rotate it to another position and back; also unable to easily stack sloped roofs without tricking the game by building temporary walls
- anything on top or attached to a structure when replaced with a higher tier structure is destroyed (swap realism for convenience)
RESOURCES
Pros:
- good and simple variety
Cons:
- bark harvesting does not scale with better picks
- despawning radius from foundations is ridiculous... Way too long! Why are there different distances for different things? NPC despawning radius is like 15 foundations at least compared to stone which is 4-5
THRALLS
Pros:
- sweet idea and good variety
Cons:
- taming pauses when logging out or out of the area - same applies to crafting things in the crafting stations
- need to have a better interaction system with them like being able to turn them passive, upgrade their gear etc
- need better AI - prioritise enemies better (my archer was more interested in shooting rabbits than to shoot enemy players that were standing still in front of my base)
- I understand that thralls shouldn't be allowed to be placed too close to each other as they could clog up the area but please reduce it by a foundation length as this complicates putting them on floors directly above or below others and if you are a new player with a smallish base, it's not fair to beimg restricted to perhaps maximum 2 thralls as they will be easily dealt with
Thank you for putting this game on EA for all of us to enjoy. Good luck Funcom!
