Mr. Triangle's Adventure is a delightful RPG in the style of FF that offers tons of mandatory as well as optional content, a total recommendation!
Mr. Triangle's Adventure is a game that was made over the span of four years, and a person can develop many skills and grow a lot as a person in such a span of time. While Mr. Triangle's Adventure begins as what looks like a juvenile game about beating up evil vegetables, by the end there's a much more serious plot that actually justifies and explains a lot of the elements that seem goofy on the surface.
Just as the game seemed to get better as it went along plotwise, with plot threads and characters growing increasingly complex and intruiging, so it did artwise. Although the first few areas are not exactly much to look at, the first dungeon in the game is simply a large corn maze with few landmarks, the further you get into the game the more diverse and well-designed the towns and dungeons become. The first town you find might just be a plain, pleasant little grassy town inhabited by fungi who live in giant toadstools, later on there's a magnificent city in the sky, a lost city in the depths of the ocean and a city straight out of the future to explore at your leisure. The dungeons get similarly more interesting, going from wheat fields and caves to cyberspace, bizarre realms and whatever the final area is supposed to be.
Even the music only gets better as the game keeps going. The first volume of the OST is already solid, but the second volume is definitely my favourite! The game really expands its scope in many ways as it keeps going on, and the music does a great job of keeping up, strongly adding to the scenes. I urge people to play the game with the music on since it's definitely tailor-made for this game.
The one part of the game that feels like it's on a solidly even level all throughout the game is its core gameplay. As you keep playing the game keeps throwing interesting new enemies and bosses at you, as well as a ton of optional content and sidequests to do! This is definitely a game you'd want to 100% as the sidequests give some truly great items for their completion, some of which are in fact so good that they make the final stretch of the game seem like one of the easier parts, which considering the difficulty of some of these sidequests is a suitable reward. That said, it does feel like the player gets access to a variety of equipment that raises HP after a certain point which makes the survivability of the game in general less of an issue which was a shame.
All-in-all Mr. Triangle's Adventure was a really enjoyable experience and it certainly was worth checking out! I have beaten the free version from RTG before, and this Steam version promises to add new content and refine the existing content, and that for the very affordable price of one euro/dollar.
There's just so much heart and spirit to this game, and I love the way how it's just so stuffed with content and how it doesn't just take the lazy route where it would have been so easy to. There's a ton of unique sprites for all the townsfolk, there's interesting minigames, there's even a dungeon with a whole separate artstyle and retro music! The game could have omitted most of these features and it'd still be a complete game, but then it'd not be the Mr. Triangle's Adventure I grew to love! I would honestly recommend this game to anyone who is into RPGs like Final Fantasy or just anyone looking for a fun game in general, it's definitely an accessible game and I really hope people will see it for that rather than judge it for daring to be goofy!

If I were to describe
in one sentence, it would be, "Wow, this game is ridiculously hard, but it's also really fun and the soundtrack is awesome."
The first thing you should know is that this game is
unforgiving and very likely to turn away beginners. I would normally recommend trying the tutorial, but even that is hard as all hell until you figure out how to consistently loop around the stage. Oh, and if you think the tutorial is difficult, just wait until you see the actual game! The gameplay consists of your character of choice roller skating around the various districts of Tokyo-to and spraying graffiti upon every kind of surface imaginable (yes, you can even cover the game's initial antagonist with graffiti, and it is HILARIOUS). Each level is absolutely merciless, to the point that I once got stuck on an early level for what felt like an eternity. There were many times where I stopped playing the game for days at a time out of sheer frustration, but it's that very frustration, as well as a drive to improve, that kept me coming back. It's the kind of game that pisses you off just enough to make you want to keep playing, and the feeling when you finally complete
a really hard level is just incredible. Even if you've never played
before and you're having a really rough time with it, you have to persevere and rely on your own skill to get further in the game, and you'll end up feeling much better about what you've accomplished as a result. Except chapter 2, that part really does just suck.
The story is exactly what you'd expect: you've got the rebellious skaters/graffiti artists who want to express their freedom through their art, and the crazy police force that tries to stop them through any means necessary (such as shooting them on sight without hesitation and even calling in mother♥♥♥♥ing armed helicopters with god-damn homing missiles). It's over-the-top in the best way possible, but it also really makes you consider who the real bad guy is. Sure, graffiti is often meant as vandalism, but when people want to express such an art form in a restrictive society, what else is there to do? At the same time, the police may be attempting to stop this violation of the law, but are they any better than the so-called "criminals" when they're taking measures far beyond reasonable legal punishment? Play far enough through the story and you just might find an answer.
Next up is the soundtrack, and DAAAAAAAAAAYUM, is it good. It and the rest of the game are an excellent representation of the "turn of the millennium" between the 90's and 2000's, much like
(and interestingly enough, the two share a song, being "Dragula" by Rob Zombie). Hideki Naganuma is the main composer, with several other artists such as Deavid Soul, Richard Jacques, and Guitar Vader making contributions as well. My personal favorite is "Rock It On," as it serves as the perfect theme for this game's story of a revolution upon a legitimately evil government. If you're wondering why I chose the words "legitimately evil," then you're just gonna have to
In conclusion, I recommend this game if you're a hardcore motha♥♥♥♥a and you love awesome games with amazing soundtracks.

Excellent game for those who like the single player experience of a jrpg dungeon crawler.
Focus lies on tactical decisions in battles. The story is nice and holds everything together, but is not as elaborate as those in for instance a Final Fantasy game.
You create a hero and pretty early in the game you make your party of 6 warriors, with a lot of customization. Choose among 8 classes. Multiclass to up to 5 classes at once. And all classes are useful!
Pro's:
- Long game, im at 30 hours and I expect to be half-way or a bit over
- Replay value in the decisions you make for which special powers and classes you will use.
- Expansive customization in the creation of your party. Mix and match it together the way you want!
- Difficult game! The world is status quo, and if you bring a wrong setup or are underleveled, you will die quickly.
- Grinding can be done fast with the fast battle mode, where your heroes and monsters all hit each other in rapid succession. A great way to save time!
- I love the music and art. Music is vocal and orchestrated, gives great atmosphere. Art is a mix of anime and realism in a healthy mix.
Con's:

This is a great branching visual novel, another winner from Hanako Games.
Presentation overall is quite excellent: writing, music, art, all well done and interesting. The characters are all pretty enjoyable and the theme of mystery and political intrigue, suspense, and all the surprises along the way really make for a great  little tale.
One of the common problems with many visual novels that try to have a lot of different routes/endings is that the dialog can often overlap in places where it is used regardless of route, and sometimes it won't fit in well with the recent events of a particular route. The worst instances of this will even be immersion breaking and contradict things that have just transpired in one route but not another. The Royal Trap for as many possible routes and branches as it contains has surprisingly little of this common problem, and for that should be commended.
There are plenty of possible romance routes, and even a couple of same-gender romance endings tucked away in here for the fans of yuri/lesbian couples, which is always a welcome addition in my book, and generally just a nice thing to see being represented.
I think one of the things that this game does particularly well is meaningful choices and consequences. There are a lot of interwoven mysteries as the plot thickens, and it seems frequently throughout the tale you are faced with decisions that can change your favor with the various lords and ladies, allowing you to switch allegiances and change where your loyalties lie.
With all the variety of options and choices, it feels like in any given playthrough you really only see a small fraction of the game's content, and with each time you try a new approach, you can't help but wonder how much more of the game there is left to uncover in the other routes you haven't aimed for yet.
There are of course many shared scenes and events across different routes too, but there are also quite a few ones that are unique to the particular route you are taking as well, so it feels like a good balance and mix of both. It keeps you wanting to come back and try new routes to see more of the game, and somehow they managed to keep it all flowing smoothly between scenes and routes too. It's pretty remarkable.
Definitely recommend this one. There's a lot to like here for anyone who enjoys a bit of suspense and mystery or just a good solid visual novel.

With many games, appearances can be deceiving. Many times, this leads players to feel disappointed and betrayed. However, there are also occasions in which we are lucky enough to stumble upon a fortunate surprise, in which the game's marketing just doesn't live up to the actual thing.
This is the case with The Royal Trap. Although the preview emphasises the otome side of the game, that is but a mere aspect of it. The main point in this game is not wooing hot guys, but guiding the protag, Madeleine, through a series of unexpected events and unveiling the mystery behind shady monarchs with ulterior motives. Although all 5 routes end up in some sort of relationship, they are so diverse that only 2 can be seen as your standard otome stuff, and even those lack the cringeworthy/fanservicey moments most dating sims offer--probably because, instead of seeing the game as a cash cow, the devs actually care about their story and characters. The enticing plot and interesting structure becomes even more entertaining when added to a captivating cast and a protagonist who is strong and well-rounded, not just some empty ghost for players to project themselves onto (she reminds me of Quinrose protags).
The cast is also diverse for LGBT folks out there looking for representation:
On the playability side, the game offers plenty of choices and most are quite intuitive, making it easy for the player to figure out what to do and how to reach most endings on their own. On the downside, there is no history button and the art tends to be inconsistent. It is obvious that the sprites and CGs were not drawn by the same person, but while the CGs are coherent (and beautiful!), the sprites are a mess. Some look good and detailed, some look like rushed, colored sketches. This may get in the way if you pay as much attention to the visuals as to any other aspect in the novel.
In the end, despite having its shortfalls, The Royal Trap is a very good game overall, and while it is a VN, I would not call it an otome game. It goes much beyond that and offers a diverse range of characters, relationships and endings (that don't always involve romance!). Definitely recommend it for those who enjoy a good story with well-rounded characters.

TL;DR: I'd only recommend this if you're really into the genre and/or get this at a really good discount.
Basically this is Victorian Age Mary Sue Simulator 9000. You play as an attractive superintelligent dutifull ninja in a pretty dress that excels at analyzing complex situations and their possible consequences. But you also have deep feels. Your flaws: You can't sew. That means you are sometimes unsure if you're woman enough. Or something.
It's an ok game. I'd recommend it if there weren't so many overthetop positive reviews already that do nothing but hype this game as if it were the next Hamlet and Julia of Monte Christo or something. I guess if you're really into the genre and desparate for MOAR OTOME, then yeah, you'll like it. But if you are looking for a good branched story where every story path you follow leads you to a better understanding of a complex plot then.. well.. no, not really. They are genuinelly good and touching moments, don't get me wrong, but a lot of it also feels either kind of forced in (like the same sex "romance" option that changes your character from "I have superdeep secret feels for oscy oscar because he's supercute and perfect and this woman is not trustworthy and should be put to jail" to "oh yeah let's run away together mid story because.. fudgepaper this,I'm a free spirit now. I'm not just a talented smart superninja, I'm also a born farmer, now that you mention it".) and very convenient (there's not one, but two princes who'd basically bail you out of a dungeon after talking to you for exactly 5 minutes. After you broke into their rooms. And then didn't talk to them in 4 chapters/2 days. Yes, you are just that charming intelligent wonderful superninja'ish that they can't stay away from you).
I think a lot of potential is just lost after the first half, when you're basically stuck to nearly solely interacting with the "allience" of your choice for the most (especially if you choose Gaston or Nazagi) while the other characters introduced just quit doing anything because the abscence of your magical sexy ninja cleverness takes all motivation for action away from them. Seriously if you on the other hand don't choose their routes, Nazagi and Gaston will either disappear or make a cameo at best. Basically as soon as you're set to a route the game really tries hard to squeeze your character from "oscy oscy oscar, why can't i be born a princess and marry you and eat miso soup with you every morning" to "oh my this new and unusual situation is actually more than i could ever have asked for" and "meh, oscar and i couldnt stay close forever. it was never meant to be" within 2-3 days. So if you wonder "hmm what would X have done if I wasnt there to do Y at time Z".. they'd have sat in their room and stared out the window. Whee.
If you're really into the genre, don't feel kinkshamed, though. Everyone is entitled to their guilty pleasures. You might really enjoy this game. I thought it was kind of meh. It's not terrible by any means, but there're certainly better games out there.

Without a doubt, The Royal Trap is one of the best visual novels that Hanako Games has ever produced, if it isn't one of the best VNs in general. I played this game first when it came out on the developer's site and got very immersed in the story. As others have already explained the basic storyline, I won't repeat that. Rather, I'll point out what I loved about this game and why anyone who is fan of visual novels should include this one in their Steam library.
First, the story is fantastic. It is one of those rare ones where the female protagonist is actually smart and has quite the personality. The flaw in some VNs is that the female protagonist is a clean slate and can come off appearing like an idiot. However, that certainly isn't the case here. You play as Madeleine Valois, a valette (assistant) to the prince of a small kingdom, and her job is to have her prince presented before the princess of another kingdom and make him appealing enough to be married to the princess. In the world of The Royal Trap, it is the women who have the power because they can hold property while the men have to compete for the privilege of sharing that power. Of course, things don't go exactly as planned and there are definitely hiccups along the way. But enough about that, as I did state that I wouldn't reveal the storyline. ;)
Along with the story, the artwork is beautiful. The background art was completely redone for the Steam release. Although I liked the background art before when the game first came out on Hanako Games, I absolutely was in awe when I saw the new art here. All the extra effort to make the game as wonderful as it can be certainly paid off.
Also, I liked how not all of the paths are necessarily romance paths. Personally, I wouldn't classify this game as an otome one because not all of the paths are romance ones. There is a friendship path (although you sort of have to go on a romance one to get to the friendship path) and another path that can kind of be interpreted as a romance or friendship path, depending on how the player chooses to see it. Most of the paths have a bad, normal, and happy end so there's definitely replayability value. That's one of the factors I take into account when I decide whether it's worth it to buy a new VN. There must be plenty of replayability value for me to want to go back and choose another path, make different choices, etc.
If there are any negative points in this game, I'll list a couple. First, there are a few typos that I noticed although they were mainly on one path. However, these could easily be ignored if you can get very immersed in the story. The other negative is that there is a LOT of reading at times. Madeleine will state out her thoughts in long text (in a monologue fashion) and people playing may have mixed feelings about that. I liked reading the texts and getting to learn about Madeleine's thoughts and feelings but then I can see how others might tire or not have the patience to read long walls of text.
Overall, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who's a fan of visual novels and definitely anyone who's a fan of Hanako Games. They've made great games in the past and this one is definitely a keeper. :D

While there isn't a lot that hasn't already been addressed in other positive reviews, I feel obligated to address some of the negative reviews I continually see regarding the game's difficulty.  Like any strategy-oriented game, Divinity Original Sin 2 requires quite a bit of premeditation before entering combat to guarantee success (outside of Tactician mode anyway, more on that later).
The game expects you to use the tools it gives you in each encounter though the largest issue I've seen is when you enter a new section of the game.  Before you go exploring to much it's almost mandatory to address the guaranteed difficulty creep by checking out any and all new gear/skillbooks/potions etc are available in whatever new social area you encounter.  With the game's economy being what it is, having one character geared toward thievery and another set up with a significant amount of barter goes an incredibly long way toward alleviating the need to almost constantly upgrade your gear when entering a new section of the game.
The point I'm making is that the game gives you all the tools you need to address any gear issues you might have the moment you set foot in a new town. This goes for skill books as well as there is no limit to how many books you can learn as long as you have the commensurate ranks in the associated skill and sufficient memory slots to equip them.
Anyway, the TL;DR of all that is the game gives you all the tools you need to PREPARE for difficult fights so long as you actually use them.  All that said, the AI isn't a slouch.  It can and will abuse whatever environmental things are to hand and the devs have set up a great many of the fights to favor the enemies.  This means that as a player the onus is on you to think about the party you want to put together before just trying to breeze through the game.  There are so many ways to make strong characters in D:OS 2 that they're almost limitless.  What you CAN'T do and expect to be successful is to just blindly charge into every fight and new situation with your d*** at full mast (just a turn of phrase, no offense intended ladies).  If that's the playstyle you're after there are a dozen Diablo clones or ARPGs out there that are better suited to that frame of mind.  D:OS2 has a turned-based system for a reason and is incredibly rewarding just so long as you apply some forethought to engagements. In fact, it's easily the best RPG I've played since the early 2000s in terms of gameplay.
Panning a game for being difficult is a non-starter, especially when it's only as hard as you make it by lack of planning. Unless, of course, you're playing on Tactician mode.  If you're doing that, you deserve whatever mental anguish you're suffering from because that is almost entirely designed for masochists who like to sit bare♥♥♥♥♥♥♥on a saguaro cactus.  If that's you, by all means, buy stock in razor blades or whatever but I would seriously hope to not see any complaints about difficulty.

This is Cthulhian mythos horror done right. Definitely worth playing to 100% completion. This game is worth every penny if you love the slow burn of a Lovecraftian style mystery that will linger in your mind for a while. *Emphatic encouragement of Cthulhian spooks done right!!*
Plus, the soundtrack is great for giving the spooks in your own day to day situations. RPGs? Check. Board Games? Check. Halloween? Check. Romantic Dinner for two? Double check!! :D
Bonus note: the Devs are still paying attention to the discussions, so if you have a problem, they at least are still around to help, even while they have new stuff in the works. I got stuck and wasn't sure why and they helped me out without giving away the puzzles, so good on them. I am looking forward to their next game, The Quest Giver, in the hopes that it will satisfy my budding inner GM.
***Kinda SPOILER-y soooo, don't read if you don't want to know.***
And in case anyone thinks this is empty praise, I will point out it's "flaws" (which aren't really flaws but things you may not expect.)
-This game is relatively short. (There are several "levels", so don't stop the first time you hit an end screen). It's not annoyingly short and does have some replayability to it (but after you have 100% that replay might be a few years down the road), but it isn't a 30+ hours of action kinda game. I liked that about it. It stuck to it's story, kept it simple, and didn't feel the need to over do it.
-If you aren't paying attention, you can skip the nuanced changes in each invocation. This adds to the ambiance so do NOT skip dialogues/inner dialogues until you've played the whole game at least once. (You'll know when you get to the actual ending.)
-The actual terrifying "I don't want to go into the next room. I'm about to cry and shut off the game" level of horror (that I absolutely had during the 1st invocation) doesn't last the entire game, but Lovecraftian horror doesn't usually work like this anyways. It's more of a slow burning, nagging curiousity that makes you want to go back and stare even longer into the abyss even if you know you could die, which this game gets down like a BOSS. So even though it is inspired by Silent Hill, it is not FNAF levels of constant fear and tension (which if you are expecting this, you will be let down). But like I said earlier, it IS the lingering Cthulhian kind of unsettling that you want from a Lovecraft-horror game done RIGHT. Cannot stress that enough. :D

A game that was surprisingly good for how simple it looks. Wait surprised me in how effectively it used lovecraftian themes, such as the idea that humans are insignificant and cannot comprehend the greater nature of reality. This is executed extremely well and is not just expressed by making all the bad guys fishmen.
Wait has multiple endings that happen based on what you do at different points, and almost every acheivement for the game is a secret ending or weird side-story. That being said, the choices you make are hardly clear and this detracts from the game a little, as you have to play the whole game over and over to get many of these endings and results. For instance, you are given an opportunity to leave a tool, or keep it, seemingly at random. If you keep it, you miss out on a potential ending. Thats a strange concept, especially since you are given an opportunity to drop it later but if you try to, your character simply refuses to do so.
The puzzles, while usually pretty obvious and clear, sometimes are just you bumbling and reloading a save in an effort to try and get through an area with all things intact.
And finally, since you cant restart on just any night, you need to play the game 4 or more times to get all the endings and the whole picture, and thats IF you dont miss anything on any of those playthroughs. this can get very boring if you are like me and dont like doing the same hour long sequence 5 times just to see a new text box.
Overall, not a game I regret buying. Was nice and creepy, and to my surprise you can in fact die and there are foes in this game to avoid and run from. The multiple endings will appeal alot to many gamers, but it feels like an artificial way of increasing play hours to me. The game took an hour and a half for me, going intentionally slow and redoing things to see what happens, and subsequent playthroughs will be shorter naturally. Buy it on sale and you will not regret doing so, especially if you love the atmosphere of drowning that lovecraftian works give off best.

While the game released in early February 2016, I decided to wait to write my review until the rescaled map and a 4th truck were added to the game. Here we are, 9 months later, and I've got some things to say...
This game is not for everyone, but for people who enjoy relaxing trips through the open roads of the United States, while hauling cargo from point A to point B. The graphics aren't what you would find in most modern games, but that's not exactly the point. In American Truck Simulator, you are tasked with delivering cargo through California, Nevada, and Arizona (other states to come later), while following the laws of American roadways.
It's a simulation game, so while some may find it completely boring and not at all entertaining, others find it calming yet fun. Trucks can be slow or quick, depending on the model, engine, parts, and trailer/cargo. American Truck Simulator (like Euro Truck Simulator 2) supports keyboard/mouse, various controllers (I've tested Xbox 360 and Xbox One, both of which worked), steering wheels (such as the popular Logitech G27), head-tracking devices (such as TrackIR), and even virtual reality headsets (such as the Oculus Rift).
No, there's no official multiplayer, but the popular modification TruckersMP allows you to truck around with friends, showing off your different taste in trucks, paint jobs, liveries, and even wheels.
PROS:
- Great variety of cargo to haul
- 3 states (California, Nevada, Arizona) with more to come in future DLC's
- Map that has been scaled to ensure long hauls feel long
- 4 awesome trucks (Kenworth T680 & W900, Peterbilt 579 & 389)
- Great customization options for all trucks
- Support for many input devices
- Support for third-party modifications
- Support for Steam Workshop content
CONS:
- No official multiplayer (check out TruckersMP)
- Slow production
OVERALL RATING: 8/10

An excellent little gem of a game with minimal game play but excellent atmosphere and interesting, if cryptic story line.
I will echo what many other reviews and say ignore the RPG maker tag if this usually puts you off - it's irrelevent as this game is all about the story line & atmosphere.
You play the part of a person in a 2D world, based mainly about an apartment block where you move about, interacting with objects to try and solve the puzzle about what is going on around you as mysterious events take place.
The controls are simply the arrow keys to move about, the return key to activate an object and the escape key to escape from some dialog screens.
I found the few puzzles I came across pretty straight forward and easily solvable.
When you interact with an object there is usually some text displayed but there can alternatively be a picture displayed or audio played. There is no real time pressure in the game; you can largely play at your own pace.
The game definitely has a Lovecraftian feel about it and I was never certain I really knew exactly what was going on but got enough of a gist about what was happening to keep me intrigued and interested.
A single play through took me less than 2 hours and I'm not a particularly fast player. There are apparently three possible endings and I would imagine I'll play through this game again to experience all of them.
This is certainly one of the best games I've played in 2016 and better than many AAA titles I've played.

So, i'm extremely torn in writing this review.
Ultimately, i am giving a thumbs up because it was sold (in sale) at a very, very, very reasonable price. If i spent the full price, i would be probably a bit disappointed.
I'll try to explain.
I'm a huge fan of DK/DK2 - so i am obviously biased and very hard to please.
That said, WFTO has a few issues that needs serious addressing.
- the game is, in my opinion, too easy. I only had to restart a level twice. All other levels, including the final one, went smooth as butter and it felt like the AI was not even a threat.
- the level design is pretty much bland throughout the whole campaign. The fact that your creatures never fight among each other (which led to interesting way to plan and build your dungeon in DK1/2) allows for you to simply cut huge rooms and build stuff togheter, and simply put a few traps in the outer layer of your dungeon. I never had to send back a creature, just get everyone you can in your dungeon and send a huge wave of minions at the enemy. All levels (iirc) have gold shrines which give you infinite gold. Big no-no in my opinion.
- the campaign story is pretty much straightforward and doesn't really stick with you, or at least, it didn't with me.
- lacks the charisma of a reaper. But that's me being nostalgic :)
- a few stuttering here and there, but the developers said they are working on a fix which apparently is due to the unity garbage collection system. Not their fault but damn it's annoying!
- you get about 10h of gameplay for the vanilla game. It's a bit expensive in my opinion if you do't buy it while on sales, but YMMV
That aside:
+ the game has a huge nostalgia value. It's clear the love the developers have for DK and they clearly spent a lot of development effort into making it as similar as they could to the original material
+ still gets a few chuckles due to the dark humor
+ it's still fun to dig tunnels
+ you get about 10h of gameplay for the vanilla game. Okay if you buy it in sale.
A warning though: it looks like the multiplayer is dead. I tried twice, and i only found two lobbies. This almost made me tick "no" in the recommendation box, but this is not the developers fault.
I will buy the DLC (which continues the main campaign) when it goes on sale, and will update !
I am pretty sure, however, that younger player who never put their hands on DK1/2 will LOVE this game :)

SpeedRunners is a fantastic racing game that you can play alone, against bots, or online with other players. It's high-speed, fun, and uses familiar things like item-boxes and attacking opponents, like you might see in games such as Mario Kart. However, it never feels like it's trying to be a knock-off. It's uniquely enjoyable.
It is played vertically looping courses. The game has several pre-made courses, but fan-made courses are also available. It will even show you the top played fan courses of the day to try out in the select menu.
There's a good selection of starting characters and many more you can unlock by just playing the game and getting experience. I was pleasantly surprised that they do in-fact handle differently. And characters unlocked later aren't necessarily better than some of the starters-just different. Want to keep playing as "Speed Runner" through all of your races? No problem. You won't be at a disadvantage.
There is a story-option that teaches you some of the basic tricks of the game, but the best way to learn quickly is to play online. There are always some nasty people here and there, but that's the internet-not the game.
One thing to keep in mind when you first start if you play online: You will lose. A lot. The learning curve is very steep. Luckily, you'll get to know the courses and how to handle obstacles fairly quickly. The online opponent finder matches you with your "level", which is nice so you’re not up against advanced players on your first rounds. The games are quick and you'll always want to play...JUST ONCE MORE!
Definitely recommended.

An interesting take on RTS.  You don't have direct control of your troops.  Instead, its more like an MMO simulator.  You build guilds for warriors, rangers, and rogues.  Then they wander around on their own, killing monsters, collecting gold, spending it on potions and equipment in your markets.  You can try to direct them, by setting quest objectives, gold for attacking targets or exploring areas.
+ Music
+ Intuitive UI
+ Good tutorial
+ Fantasy setting
+ Sean Connery: Royal Advisor
+ Group units into MMO style parties
+ Carryover heroes between missions
+ Visual upgrades for buildings and units
+ Units levelup, learn abilities, and collect gold
+ Peasents build buildings, tax collectors gather gold
+ Each building of the same type costs more than the last.  An interesting way to encourage build variety and unit limits, without putting simple hardcaps on them.
+- Decent graphics, considering its age and genre
+- You can't build walls, though you can build guard towers
- Gold gathering is far too slow, usually idle waiting for it to collect
- Game gets crazy hard on some Expert campaign missions.  I'm not sure its even possible to beat them, unless theres some mechanic I'm missing
- Being able to freely place buildings is a bit clunky, hard to tell where they'll fit in, would be nice if they could snap to a grid, at least optionally.
* There is multiplayer, but I've never tried it.  It's run by GameSpy, which I'm not sure even exists anymore.  Maybe LAN mode still works, if you have friends.

Majesty 2 takes everything that made Majesty 1 great and does it worse. Objectively speaking the game has way less in it, is more limited with hero variety, less in-depth when it comes to hero A.I, and a myriad of other flaws. I'll break down the systems.
Town and Management:
The biggest change to come is how stripped down the buildings are. A lot of the miscellanous building like the gardens, fairgrounds, and various other buildings are completely removed. You are now limited to only one marketplace, trading posts have to go in specific locations, you cannot have more than three of any hero building, temples may not only be built of specific spots.
Having a cap on the amount of things that can be built isn't a bad thing, but having an arbitary cap takes away a lot of the fun. Especially when you can only have a very limited amount of heros. This also means that a lot of the fun in trying quirky builds is also gone.
Building Placement:
This will quickly become a major issue. Each building requires space larger than what the model indicates, but gives no indication of how much room is required. In the original each building had a green ring that indicated how much space it required so you know when a building couldn't fit. Now it is a guessing game and will have you asking "Why can't this be placed here".
Heros, A.I, and Interactions:
Heros are pretty dumb this time around, and while in Majesty 1 they have tendencies and preferred tactics (Rangers covering barbarians, Clerics following Warriors) each hero is much more indepenant which really takes away from the feeling that these were clans with backstory and personalities.
The voices are also pretty weak but not because they are bad, but because there isn't enough variation. Heros sound very similar to each other and lack the variety that the original game set.
There is some good sides though. The reward flags are not much better having the option to place defensive flags that reward heros for defending a section, fear flags that ward heros from wandering off into a dangerous location. There is also the ability to set default values for each flag so the player doesn't have to spend so much time mindlessly clicking to increase the reward value.
Also, one hero from each mission can be carried over to the next scenario with all their ability and gear (though they are expensive to recruit). This means that you might actually care about the lives of your heros. Each hero also has different stats within a set range meaning that every hero is actual different.
If this seems like a harsh review, it might be. Is this review uncalled for? No. This game is exactly how to do a sequel badly.

One of my fondest gaming memories was starting up Majesty 2 for the first time. My wife was out visiting family, I had the whole evening to myself, and a bottle of wine to pass it with. I spent hours building little kingdoms, glass in hand, shouting at my little virtual peasants like the tin-pot monarch I've always dreamed of being. Needless to say it was a magical evening, but much like the hangover I nursed the next day, Majesty 2 turned out to be far more trouble than I expected.
Just as the classic that spawned it did, Majesty 2 casts you as the sovereign ruler of a fantasy kingdom, beset by all manner of foul beasts. In each scenario you build a settlement out from your keep, consisting of inns, markets, guilds, and workshops, all in the service of enticing heroes to your cause. As king, you can't take on evil directly, but you can hire mercenaries to do all the dirty work for you. The result is a real-time strategy game with very little direct input, aside from constructing your town.
You do have two tools at your disposal to direct your little champions, though. As king you can place bounties on monsters or dungeons to reward those who conquer them, or on locations to encourage exploration. Your tiny heroes are more inclined to go for larger bounties, which you pay from the taxes and profits from your markets and shops. It's a clever economy, with your heroes collecting gold to spend in your town, which you then use to expand and place your bounties. There are plenty of new units and upgrades to use as well, which will be refreshing to veterans of the first game, as well as a new party system for making more effective groups of heroes.
What isn't so refreshing is the difficulty curve. Like I said, my first evening with Majesty 2 was amazing. The introductory levels do a fantastic job of bringing you up to speed on managing a kingdom. Your heroes will level up and conquer the maps for you, and you'll feel like good King Henry himself living large on your victories and riches. But not a dozen maps into the game, the wheels come completely off. You'll start running into scenarios where dragons ravage your town without any recourse, or hordes of monsters descend on your keep before you can field any experienced heroes. It's an incredible brick wall of frustration to smash into after such a promising start, but even with the open scenario map there's no way around it. After a certain point, every map is an uphill struggle against absurd waves of enemies.
It's a colossal shame, too, because if not for the crushing difficulty Majesty 2 would be a huge improvement on the formula. The interface is cleaner, the upgrades are more varied, there's better balance to the defensive buildings (assuming a reasonable challenge), and the presentation is excellent. The look of the game cribs a bit from Warcraft III in a good way, with detailed 3D models and buildings. I really enjoyed the sound design in particular, with some rousing music and a hilariously not-Sean-Connery narrator. But alas, 'tis all for naught if you can barely beat even the middling scenarios. I wish I could recommend Majesty 2 as strongly as I do the first, but the fact is that you're not going to get more than two or three hours out of it before it pummels you into uninstalling.

Love/hate review - only extremes. Extremely good, and extremely bad.  First, the extremely bad: The controls SUCK.  In particular, having the run/take cover/use being the same control (the space bar, instead of having run being the shift key like most other FPS games for example) definitely killed me far more times than anything. So when you find yourself screaming at Commander Shepherd that he's an idiot, and you've smashed multiple monitors, no - it isn't you. It's the game controls.  To say this is a huge negative to the game is an understatement. It really took away from the game and made me shut it down more than once.  It was even worse in ME3.  When the controls make you want to just walk away and stop playing, that's not good for the reputation of a game!
That having been said, the graphics were awesome, and the world you're immersed in often makes you just stop and take a look around at the scenery.  The storyline and game concept itself was not to be bested by any others out there. It was nothing less than phenomenal. The attention to detail was incredible, and made the game what it was: having a story behind every single planet in the systems was no small feat, yet there it was - that's attention to detail. The building up of the mystery in the main storyline really drew you in way better than a movie, or even a book in many ways. I got the game based on the recommendation of others as having one of the best driving storylines out there, and it certainly lived beyond its reputation. Well done to the writers.  Giving you the options of delving into a ridiculous number of side missions which include bringing you in to the very personal lives of the many characters, and each story an awesome one in its right, again - just attention to detail that really made this game stand out from all others.
Then to top it all off, what happens in ME2 affects what happens in ME3!  Genius scripting all around.

7hr review:
Bottom line you are paying $40 for a vita port.
Look the games mechanics are not awful, its got complexity to some degree, and it appears very complex on the surface.  Some of the battles are hard if you take the games flow as straight forward (get a mission then go do it) once you learn you can counter that difficulty by running though a level 5-10 times farming that difficulty kinda dissapears.
The combat is the worst aspect of the game, its RPG maker style.  No animations and your portraits block smaller enemies.  Casters can only cast magic, so they basically sit there worthless defending until you have a battle deemed worthy of using them...ive found a front row of fighters or knights and a back row of all rangers and a cleric does just fine, in fact excels vs a diverse group since you dont have a bunch of casters defending.  Standard attack is the norm and theres a fast battle option that removes the battle from the battle.  Youll use this 99.9% of the time.
Combat is hard because sometimes the game throws a curveball enemy spawn at you that youll run from, you get a skill right off the bat to instant escape.
The class system seems awesome but since skills are not really needed, i dont see the point tbh.  I dont think it would change the fact that youll use standard attack and fast battle for just about every non boss fight....and normal fights you might need something extra...well just use your flee battle skill, leave the dungeon and save, come back and its now a spawn that you can auto-battle though.  Difficutly gone.
Most of the difficulty seems in the fact that its an old vita port.  UI and the lack of auto save is what makes it hard.
Story seems decent, artwork is fantasic...but the first person 3D dungeon crawl mode feels more like a windows 98 screen saver...again...rpg maker feels.
Its voiced over in japenese which is appealing for some.
Gear is extremely basic.  Nothing more than hit chance and damage.  Unique gear has nothing unique about it.  Youll be hunting for that spear +1 for +1 damage then once you get that youll want the spear +2 for an extra 1 point of damage....zzzzzz.....
Yes you can cutomize your character portraits....cool...if you want to get into that for a vita port game.
Im recommending the game, steam has so few games like this (other than the giant pile of steaming rpg maker games made by players...this feels like an rpg maker done by professionals but still an rpg maker game eventhough its not)
Wait for a sale....this is a $5 game at best.  Its a great jrpg in terms of artwork, music, and style (other than the 3D first person dungeon crawling which are tiny little maps with nearly no style)
Honestly if i hadnt left the game running while i went shopping id probably have refunded it and waited for it to be on a steep discount after figuring out the basics.  Still...for this type of game, and for the lack of options for this type of game, its still a thumbs up...just dont pay the full price...not sure what orfice the heads of the devs are up to keep this game full price on this platform so many years after it was new.
At least mod it so the controls are displayed for desktop PC, take the effort to make combat at least on par with phantasy star 2 from sega genesis, you know have a basic animation based on weapon and character...and figure out a way to save progress without having to leave the game running mid storytime....after about an hour straight i needed to run to the store but was in the middle of "cutscene" which is just jap. voice over + english text and close up still pictures....but had i closed out id have lost an hour straight of work and then would need to relive the story part again...so i just left it running.
I think with some updates to the right platform, some updates to modern QOL, and some super basic animations for combat...and maybe puitting something interesting on gear...and this game would be a $40 game on steam.  That wont happen though.
Buy this game at full price if you are a jrpg junky that likes the artwork (its really fantasic btw) and voice overs and story over the mechanics...and enjoys a game that isnt overly easy...eventhough i feel its just as easy as any other jrpg ive ever played (grind and over level and stomp everything but then have to figure out a boss fight)
This really plays like vita port...unfortunately....and has combat production values that a good artist with rpg maker could reproduce (probably better than they have done with this game tbh)  Otherwise the complexity is just throwing fights you cant win and need to recognize as fight you must run from, and boss fights with a gimmick.  The gear is boring, the classes are boring with a few classes being curiously useless for 99% of your fights...and the handicap from being a port that wasnt meant for a pc is a struggle at first.
Not awful as i made it sound here, but, for $40...i feel these devs are not from japan but rather fantasy land.
Ill update if something changes..depending if i feel that the games path changes from the standard overlevel and stomp everything....which i would gladly enjoy every second of if the loot i was farming was interesting.
This game just seems so close to classic just a few tweaks, a bit more depth, and a bit of animations....its got a feeling while playing that is greater than what your actually doing...somehow.

RPG Tycoon is a very promising, solid, good game at its core; with several unique & original twists & variations of the RPG, Simulation, Town Building/Management Genres, that are all nicely & effectively tied together & implemented, to make up an overall, fun & enjoyable gaming experience that youd hope for & want & expect from a game like this, that can keep you glued to it for hours at a time.  The game has come a long way since its early days, with continued support, updates & content added at a reasonable pace, with yet more work to be done & bugs that may or may not pop up along the way, but also with a diligent & friendly Dev that has stuck with it since the beginning & continues to update, modify & bug smash along the way & is routinely responsive & listens to his community.
The foundation the Dev has laid down for this game has always been solid & the RPG, Simulation, Town-Building/Management aspects incorporated into this game has always had lots of potential from its early days & is mostly why Ive kept a good eye on it since then.  It looked promising enough back then but I was on the fence for several months, hesitant, mostly due to the critical reviews, while still checking back on it periodically.
Eventually though, enough time went by & after keeping an active interest & a keen eye on it, & seeing continued progress, development & improvements & watching his YouTube vids, I felt like this was a guy that was truly into his work & committed to seeing it through.  So I finally decided to give in & I bought the game..played it & have had many hours of fun with it since then.
Since then & along the way, many things have continued to be added, updated, improved upon & expanded; some things becoming bugged, some things unbugged; all at a consistently reasonable rate; all of which is the standard norm for Early Access games with a small team.  Its just himself & I think maybe he collaborates with 1 or 2 others.  Rinse, repeat; its an ongoing process, but one which the Dev has continued to see through on an acceptable basis.
Aside from his normal To-Do list & agenda of updating & progressing the game over time in his own visions, hes also been receptive to the posts people have made with bugs/suggestions, etc; as evidenced by the past posts from myself & others here & the change-logs & resulting game-play changes that followed.
At one point, due to having a vested interest in this game; since its something very different & so nicely encompasses so many cool & different traits from other games & genres that I really like & since Ive always really hoped to see this game in completion someday; in my haste, I hadnt seen any Account activity or Discussion Forum posts from the Dev in about a month & a half, so was worried that the Dev might have gone bye-bye as too many of them far too often do, with EA games these days...but he promptly & politely responded, simply pointing out he always keeps a watchful eye, just not always from the Dev Account, which actually makes sense in hindsight.
On that note, occasionally there will be the random/rare person that posts bugs/suggestions or w/e & then a week or 2 or more goes by without a response from the Dev & that person becomes upset or says stuff like, "Oh the Dev must not care". etc;  Which to be fair to them, up to a point, thats understandable.  I even jumped the gun myself once.  Its not unusual...& in fact is sadly half expected anymore with EA games, for the Dev to bail on a game, or just not be at all involved with the community.  But I can personally & honestly state, thats just not the case here, to this date.  He is just one guy & has his own personal RL stuff going on, just like many of us do & works on this game in his free time, which all things considered, seems like he must generally make a point to set most of it aside, to attend to this game.
Also, he does personally respond to posts, just not every single one & not all day, every day.  I personally can relate to that, as Ive got a super busy schedule myself, sometimes too busy & have to prioritize the stuff I want to do VS the stuff I need to do, & even stopping all that to do something simple, like respond to a text or email, can add more to my plate then I can already handle at that time.  I think a lot of Devs here on Steam fit into that category, as most of them arent full time programmers/game-designers & their game isnt their main source of income.  Some Devs dont bother to read &/or respond to their customers ever, but this Dev does fairly often.  And to me, as long as that level of customer service/interaction continues & the game keeps moving forward in a positive direction as its been; thats all that matters to me & all I care about, to warrant supporting this or any Dev, that demonstrates that on-going level of commitment.
The last time Id put any time into this game was appx 2-3 months ago ( from time of this review @ Dec 17th 2016 ) & had been wanting to play the game again after the last few updates/bug fixes & try out the new DLC.
So recently I was able to play several hours off & on over the last week.  Started a new game, after buying the new DLC.  Everything was running smooth & working great at first, with a few minor bugs like; every time saving & quitting then reloading save game, the same few tutorial help boxes popped up, like if youre starting a new game.  Or while paused, clicking expand land, you hear the SFX of game like it was running even though visually, the game still appeared paused.  Nothing big or game breaking at all.
Some more problematic things started to occur later on tho, like upon saving & reloading, most NPCs were unhappy & leaving, with no indication there was a prob prior to saving & quitting.  To be fair, Dev has a thread stating if you have probs be sure to erase that data which Im not sure I did this last replay.
Despite any bugs or probs along the way, I have faith in this Dev, from his past actions, not just words & promises like some Devs can do.  My honest opinion is, if you like what you see advertised here from the games Vids & Description, then you cant go wrong buying this game.  Its pretty much exactly/mostly what youd want & expect from a game like this.  Its not however a super duper in-depth game.  And its not meant to be & doesnt have to be to still be fun & enjoyable.  Nor is it on the shallow end either.  Overall its more of a mid-depth semi-casual gaming experience with several aspects that are still nicely in-depth, with other aspects to still keep you on your toes & wanting to continue to play, manage, grow & expand your kingdom.
Bottom line is, this games been in development for a while now & continues to progress steadily, considering its from an Inde Dev.  Depending on the current state of the game & where its at, you may experience a relatively bug-free game, or you may be in the middle of a recent content update with the inevitable bugs that follow, which TBH, yes can get frustrating.  But thinking about it... Why does one get frustrated with something in the first place, instead of just not even caring or thinking twice about it & instead just walk away?  Cuz you care about it.  Cuz you like it.  Cuz theres some part of you that has a vested interest in that thing to begin with lol.
Which is ultimately a testament & compliment to RPG Tycoon & what it does right & why its worth most peoples time even now, & especially once its 100% finished.  And which is why Im still glad I bought this game, even tho it has some polishing to do yet & hopefully a few more features/game-play additions.  I look forward to the future when well see this game in its fully realized, finished state.  ( :

Gemini Rue is a fun revamp of the old point n' click experience wrapped up in a twisty, turny sci-fi narrative.  The game spruces up the traditional mechanics by adding slight touches of combat, standard detective sleuthing and other elements, among it's primiarly pixel-hunt littered narrative.
While the graphics are in an old, pixel-based style, they are suitably grimy and dirty for the setting, which makes it work.  No amazing visuals to be found here but more of a classic look that kind of called my memory banks back to Shadowrun, Syndicate and other classic games.  The story is solid with some choice based dialogue and optional achievement objectives, but in reality this game is very straightforward.  It's all about figuring out what to find, where to use and thusly where to go.
The story itself was awesome and even though a few of the twists lingered in the back of my mind like, "Oh, that's who that is...that's what's happening," I still found myself pleasantly surprised here and there.  That whole begotten city, sci-fi touch really did give me fond memories of playing through Shadowrun SNES about 5 times in a row.  Some have complained about clunky gunplay but I was able to win every duel without a hit on medium difficulty on my second playthrough.  Could have probably done it on the first but was still learning the ropes.  The shooting/chase sequences helped to add variety to the standard puzzles and lengthy story expositions.  The thing about the game's story is that once it hooks you, it hooks you.  You'll want to find out what happens and then play it a second time to see if you can notice how things were going to play out.
Controlling two characters for a portion of the game was also a nice touch, and I enjoyed the fact that the majority of the gameplay in the two main locations was different enough that it further freshened up the experience.  Also pleasing was the fact that the majority of the dialogue was done with voice-acting, and even though an amateur team did the work, they did a pretty good job of bring the gruffness and vulnerability to the characters that required these different emotions.
With all of that said Gemini Rue isn't without its flaws.  It took me about 8-9 hours on the first playthrough examining every little thing and over-complicating the puzzles, but once you figure everything out as well as how to be a successful gun dueler, challenge is a pretty moot issue.  This game is not that tough.  My second playthrough was completed in barely 3 hours, so if you are a really keen player with adventure games (I'm a big rusty, getting my legs back), you have the potential to rip through this game pretty quickly.  Most of the times that you will get stuck is because you will completely overcomplicate the solutions.
More depth in the game would have been welcome...some different guns, some unique character attributes, ability to upgrade your skills, etc.  As a first outing this was not a problem, but there was definitely potential for this game to go in REALLY deep.  The experience as it was, wasn't shallow but at times you I felt like I was wishing for all of these other things to crop up in the training experiences which would become tools Azriel could use to complete his missions.  Still, it was mostly satisfying in the way the adventure unfolds and you'll want to keep playing to see just how things go down in the end.
I'd like to write a longer review for this one but it's honestly a pretty simple, easy game with a complex story.  If you get stuck at any point, I guarantee it's because you are thinking about the puzzles too in-depth.  My second playthrough really illustrated to me how short and unchallenging this game really is.  I only missed one achievement and I didn't need a walkthrough to figure anything out.  Most of the times I was stuck was just me creating these elaborate solutions of how I needed to solve a problem.  With that said, Gemini Rue is definitely worth playing for point and click fans who enjoy some other accoutrements to that style of gameplay, yet I can't help but feel I played a game with so much more potential.  Hopefully, there will be a sequel and if so I will definitely support it.

I absolutely adore this game.  It's so intense and so amazing; from the story to the characters, to the art. I just loved it all.
The story, regardless of which route you take, is rife with twists and turns.  I always ended up surprised by events that transpired.  The endings were all unique.  Yes, there were a few similar occurrences, but that comes down to the overall plot of the story more than anything.  The routes themselves had quite a lot of similarities (again because of overall story), but there were enough differences and new experiences in each that it never felt repetitive.
Now, the beginning is a different story.  The choices you make in the first four chapters ultimately decide what direction the rest of the story will take, but besides a few things here and there, the actual happenings are the same no matter what.  It's kind of just a REALLY long prolog in my opinion.  Still, it wasn't all that bad.
I really liked the cast of characters in this game.  They were all completely unique and interesting.  I believe they were also well-rounded.  And, depending on the choices you make, you get to see quite a bit of depth in their character.  Of course, I preferred some more than others, but that's bound to happen in any game.  The actual design for each was also unique (and very pleasing to the eye).  Some games have a cast of characters with a lot of visual similarities that make it hard to distinguish between all of them at times, but not this one.  I adored the art style and artistic designs used for each.  The art really added another layer of depth to the uniqueness of each character.
I highly recommend this game.

I've enjoyed this game so far, though honestly a majority of the enjoyment has come from unlocking achievements rather than the content of the game itself since it's fairly simplistic once you realize how to make money on the base game.  Most games of the tycoon or city builder nature have multiple resources competing and impacting your progress, with selection of stats to grow being very impactful to your success.
In RPG Tycoon, the only really significant resource is money and everything else is tiertiary at best unless your aiming at unlocking specific achievements (which is what I've enjoyed doing!).  A single resource isn't necessarily a bad thing, however there's also only really one effective way to get that resource, and that is quests.  Within a single game, you'll come across the same quests multiple times, and while it's nice the first playthrough to see what the alternative choices would get you, it gets a bit grindy.
As your heroes grow, so does the amount of gold quests give.  This also keeps your settlements happy, so you don't need to choose between doing quests and having your heroes help around town since the answer is always do quests.  This results in the game getting a bit on the grindy side, but since I'm usually playing it while doing something else such as cooking or waiting for something to compile, it doesn't bother me as much as if I were trying to sit down and stay focused only on the game.
That said, I liked the game though it's very simplistic (nothing really matters but money, even though the "Grow Your Kingdom" tasks make you feel like you might have something to do other than run quests over and over again to grind out more money.  The only decisions you really make early on are avoiding going into severe debt early on because you don't know to grind quick quests and epics for cash yet.
The idea behind this game is great, but the execution still needs a bit more work and polish.
I'm hopeful the game will continue to improve with updates since it's been updated rather frequently recently, so I am currently recommending it!
EDIT:
I also agreed with the reviews about a number of bugs that break the game, but that said when I came across an issue, it was fixed within the next update after I posted a review about it, so I can't really complain too much there.
As a result, I'll be buying the expansion & update my review later.

After loving ME1 I looked forward to ME2. So I got it when it came out years ago. I rebought the Deluxe edition here on Steam to try it out, thus the reason for the short game time. However, it is not the ultimate version due to politics between EA and Valve. But I will start with the game itself. ME2 is a fantastic game, and while I kinda wish they would keep more of the sci-fi approach, I really enjoyed the cheesy B action movie story. The music is great, the action is awesome, the characters are lovely/cool/badass. The combat is smoother than in ME1 although they also dumbed down (or streamlined) both the skill tree and shooting (there are ammo clips now). Still, they start with an impressive intro and you almost don't get bored through the whole game. I miss the planet exploring too as it got replaced with launching probes which gets really boring. Don't want to spoil anything so I'll just say that the threat from the first game is appearing again so you fight through various scenarios up until the grandiose final suicide mission. Some squad members join again but most of them are new to keep it fresh. Unfortunately two are DLC characters which makes them less relevant and not that immersive inside the story. Origin ran away with the other DLCs as there are a lot of them you just cannot get through standard means on Steam. The whole trilogy deserves to be played but sadly ME3 is not for sale on Steam, again only on Origin.  But the main game can easily stand by itself - it's fun with fluid combat, epic story and is a worthy sequel, in many regards even better than ME1.

While i totally understand, why this game is so much loved by the players, i sadly have to admit, that at least i cant recommend the game. But when i see, that only around 50% of the people (even now, where the game still cost around 50 bucks) finished the first act, i think that i am maybe not the only one who disliked at least some aspects of the game. So to give you besides all the praising reviews also an neutral review from the side of a player who sadly didnt enjoyed the game as much as many others, i hope that my review, together with the many reviews that love the game, can help you in deciding, if you are the targeted audiance of the game, and if you would enjoy the game.
Because everyone has a different taste, and maybe you will love the game like many others, but maybe the things that i will adress are also very importand for you too. And if this is the case, then maybe this game, while having a very high quality, will just not suit you as a player.
Let us begin with the positive aspects, and their are many of them:
The graphics are just awesome! The graphics allone are already very atmospherical, (like in the mysterious swamp, the view is turning slithly green, a strom on the sea looks dark and dangerous, a sunny day on the beach looks very harmonious etc.) it will be even surpassed by the elemental graphics in the battles: When your fire spells turn the oil into fire, explosions overcome the whole area, your enemys bleeding to death from the necomancer spells, thunders crashing into the water and shocking everyone in it: The battles look very chaotic and awesome in so many ways, and just staring at the battle effects bring me much joy. Everything looks so good in this game, and while it is true, that graphics are not everything, i wanted to give them the praises they deserve, because they are all so perfectly done.
The world is very interesting indeed. Besides the lore of the world that bringes some interesting new aspects into the "clischee" fantasy world, like cannibal elfs  or the possibility to speak to animals as if they would be normal persons etc. makes the world even in such an often used genre like the fantasy genre, a very individual touch. The story is interesting(at least the parts that i have seen so far) and you are always curious how the story will continue. While i was never totally "lost" in the story, and it never gets me very emotionally, it still fullfilles its purpose to keep the player interested. Just when you are a player who really needs a totally deep innovative, and unforseeable story, then you maybe will not be happy from it.
Even better then the already good story is the overall world: The locations you visit look very "real", the citys are full of interesting and different people. Everyone has something to say and i never felt like their are just a few "maincharacters" and a bunch of empy npcs to fill the location. As to the story, you shouldnt expect to much, every character is "just" a very good scripted character so they dont develop the depth of a major Mass Effect Charakter, but also they dont feel like hollows witout any personality.
The gameplay is maybe the best i have ever seen in an classic RPG. The fights (at least in the higher difficulties) really need you to think about your moves, and can be very hard sometimes. Every Quest can be solved in many ways and in generall you have a very high freedom to play the game as you like. You can play (most of the time) as a pacificst, avoiding every battle with your good conversations talents and your stealth mechanics, or as a psychopath who killes everythink that just slithly provokes him. The lonewolf who only fights for his own, or the classical hero who tries to safe the whole word.
But with this freedom comes a very huge problem: The lack of connection between the "worldparts"
Since you are free to do what you want, the game never can forsee how your next movement will be. In one situation you can be the hero who showes mercy to the enemy because you understand his motive and forgive him, and in the next battle you kill everythink that moves. You can first rescue a member of the resistance against the cruel regime, and in the next moment when you are in the outpost of the resistance you can kill everyone inside to get the loot. Their is no "wrong" way to play the game. But this leads to the huge problem that almost nothing of the single aspects of the game is connected.
Let me make an example since just talking around the topic is confusing if you dont exacltly understand what i mean. *minor spoilers ahead*
In the first real act you are trapt on an island where sources mages like yourself are forced to wear a collar that surpresses their power. And also they are trappt in a ghetto, unable to leave the castle and the island. In a certain quest one of the prisoners helped me to destroy the collar so that my source powers are free ones more. But this leads to the situation that now every magister (the guardians of the castle) will see that you have not the collar anymore and will imprison you once more, to force you to wear it again,or attack you if you show resistance. I showed resistance...and in the result every magister in the whole castle did attack me on sight. So i have started a revolution against our surpressers, overcome them, killed them next to the other scared prisoners, opened the closed gates, let the people to freedom....only that they didnt care. Since the daily routine of the prisoners is not connected to the life of the magisters, they will just continue their life as normal. That means complain how hard their life is under the surpression of the magisters, and that they so greatly want to escape but cant, because the guards are so many and the gates are closed...while in reality every guard is dead and the gates are open.
And this problem is in every aspect of the whole game. On a sinking ship i did calmed a few of the shipkeepers so that i didnt have to fight them...but when i found a lifeboat to escape i could safe everyone but them...because they could be already be dead if i just fight them before, and so their life is not connected to the lifeboat so that their is no way to safe these fellas even if you try. Or a leader of the resistance (who cried how many of his good man died in the fight against the supressing magisters) doesnt even say a word after everyone(!) of his camerads died in a big battle, since their was also a possibility that they would be already dead, before the battle starts. And so he just talkes totally normally like nothing has happend while in reality all his friends with which he has fought for many years, just died a few minutes ago.
And this, at least for me, totally killes every bit of immersion that the game would normally develop from such an awesome world. Since you realise more and more, how scripted everything is, and that certain NPCs just react to this quest that they give you, and dont interact with anything else at all (as long you dont attack or try to steal from them) you never develop the feeling that you are "inside" this world and that the world is living around you. But more and more it feels like everything just exists to give you a quest, and stay silent after they have fulfilled their purpose (like maybe a person from an MMORPG, that gives you one quest and then just stands their without any purpose) and since the world and the mainplot are so great and fascinating, it have lead to great frustration to me.
I know that this is not a fault of the game itself since its techically awesome in any sense it wants to be, but i think i just realised in this game, since the experience i get from this game becomes more and more "empty" i think that i am just the wrong audience for this type of very open RPGs. Because for me, the huge amound of freedom just destroys the illustion to be in a real world. And for me this is more importand then 10 options in every quest.

If you like point-and-click investigations, this game *may* be up your alley, and I add that caveat for one reason. I absolutely loved this game. Not only do you get to take on the (primary) role of a cop named Azriel Odin but you also get the opportunity to play as many other characters in a story that finds its way together from many seemingly unconnected strands. The only reason I warn you about playing this is because it's not a simple puzzle-solving investigatory game; it requires--it some cases--a LOT of thought, if you aren't following a guide that spells it all out for you. Not all of the puzzles are obvious, and most of them are much more difficult than you'd expect, ranging in difficulty from "no-brainer" to "it's been thirty-five minutes, what am I supposed to do with this thing?" Aside from one instance of faulty direction (you'll know what I mean when you get stuck on the lock-pick puzzle), the game is not to blame for your inability to solve the puzzle. It's to blame for forcing you to think outside the box, to examine every possible option, to go over all the things you might normally take for granted in the gaming world: in this instance, it requires you to pay close attention to details you've gained along the way. Everything is important to one degree or another and it bears mulling these details over time and again. Second, in the same vein as the aforementioned difficulty, this game makes you think--not just about puzzles but about the story, as well. I absolutely do not want to spoil this game for anyone who has an interest in playing it, so I'll refrain from citing any specifics. I think it is a very well-made game; I think it is a very important game for people to play, if they are willing to pay attention, think, and take something away from it, that is; and I think it's the kind of game that will make you almost forget you're playing it--it sort of sucks you in like a sci-fi space drama, but without all the added bull involving large scale galactic battles and strange species invading this planet or taking over that mining ship, etc. It focuses on the people and their stories, but above all, it speaks to the human condition in a profound way I've rarely seen in video games.
I would whole-heartedly recommend this game to anyone who is willing to take the time to listen to what it has to say.

While the game released in early February 2016, I decided to wait to write my review until the rescaled map and a 4th truck were added to the game. Here we are, 9 months later, and I've got some things to say...
This game is not for everyone, but for people who enjoy relaxing trips through the open roads of the United States, while hauling cargo from point A to point B. The graphics aren't what you would find in most modern games, but that's not exactly the point. In American Truck Simulator, you are tasked with delivering cargo through California, Nevada, and Arizona (other states to come later), while following the laws of American roadways.
It's a simulation game, so while some may find it completely boring and not at all entertaining, others find it calming yet fun. Trucks can be slow or quick, depending on the model, engine, parts, and trailer/cargo. American Truck Simulator (like Euro Truck Simulator 2) supports keyboard/mouse, various controllers (I've tested Xbox 360 and Xbox One, both of which worked), steering wheels (such as the popular Logitech G27), head-tracking devices (such as TrackIR), and even virtual reality headsets (such as the Oculus Rift).
No, there's no official multiplayer, but the popular modification TruckersMP allows you to truck around with friends, showing off your different taste in trucks, paint jobs, liveries, and even wheels.
PROS:
- Great variety of cargo to haul
- 3 states (California, Nevada, Arizona) with more to come in future DLC's
- Map that has been scaled to ensure long hauls feel long
- 4 awesome trucks (Kenworth T680 & W900, Peterbilt 579 & 389)
- Great customization options for all trucks
- Support for many input devices
- Support for third-party modifications
- Support for Steam Workshop content
CONS:
- No official multiplayer (check out TruckersMP)
- Slow production
OVERALL RATING: 8/10
