I voted positive on this game because of its potential. That aside I reccomend waiting till a few more issues are worked out. If you have played ARK: Survival Evolved or Rust (though I have not played Rust so I can't confirm that) then this game will be easy to pick up on. It is the same basic concept. Stranded in a harsh and unforgiving enviroment that you now must survive in. Collect resources, build a base, spec your character in certain stats, raid other bases, create a guild/tribe, etc. All the hallmarks of a standard survival. So what sets this apart? Well aside from the gimmicky endowment and breast size meter, what sets this apart is the storyline. If there was one. It's kind of there at the moment but more of it will become avaliable as more content for the game is release. Another fun aspect is choosing which religion you want to follow. There's Set, Yog, and some other one that looks like a Zeus rip off. Each one provides you with different benefits as you level up the shrine of the god you choose to follow. Gain enough favor and you can temporarily become the enbodiment of your choosen god to reap hell upon your foes. Third unique aspect is agressivley persuading (enslaving) NPC characters, or thralls, for various tasks. Depending on the thralls roll and level will determin the bonus they provide (warriors, artisans, priests, entertainers).
Pros:
- It is a fun game with a good replayability factor that you can easily sink hours into without boredom
- Building is pretty easy. There is less of a collision issue with placing structures when compared to ARK
- Devs are ontop of their game (no pun intended) in fixing current content as quickly as possible while acknowledging erros that still need fixing
- There is enough skill points for a player to play solo effectivley.
- Plenty of servers to choose from
Cons:
- Still some glaring bugs that make pvp base raiding a joke (explosive jar exploits). Until those are fixed building a base is almost pointless
- Devs attempt at multiple PVP modes almost worked. Specifically PVP Relaxed. Its not. Players can and will be agressive. (ok this is more of a warning than a con)
- No defense against players in avatar form short of being in avatar form yourself. (at the moment)
Overall a fun game with a  lot of potential. Not a lot of cons and of the ones mentioned two of them should not even be an issue for much longer. Just note that it is still in early access and will remain in e.a. for the remainder of the year as the devs release more content and patch issues. So take what issues you run into with a grain of salt. If its a reoccuring bug then report it. OH and while you can play solo, it is best played in a group.

5676. Those are the numbers on the wall of your apartment. The whole story from
revolves around those four numbers. Benjamin currently living in the department sees them every day. He tried to erase them but nothing worked. It seems as they are magically fixed on that spot on the wall. And then one day he comes home from work and the numbers for the first time ever have changed. And with this change his world will be turned upside down.
is mostly a text- and story-driven adventure game with some puzzle elements thrown in. Most of the puzzles are solvable with a bit of logic and intuition. Most of the time although you are running around in the apartment trying to figure out the larger picture of what is happening. The game is hereby divided into short day and night sequences.
Ignoring the simple graphic the game has a suspenseful atmosphere for two reasons: The first is that there is the possibilty to die. It doesn't happen to often and you can restart at the last save point (rarely more than 5 minutes of play time back) but you can die. So you are always fearing for your life. The second reason is the lack of information and you need to play to the very end to get the complete picture. After 5-6 day and night sequences the game will reach its conclusion. And after this you will notice directly (and it is stated on the shopsite as well) that this is not the end. With the second cycle you then start to feel a bit like the protagonist: Was it like this before? Somehow this seems strange? Can I change the result?
is an interesting game and the overlaying storyline is good enough to get you keep going to the end. To play through all cycles you need probably around 6-8 hours if you don't rush like a mad man. If you are trying to get the achievements (and you didn't look them up before starting to play the game) you probably need another two hours. I would recommand that you play through the complete game without prior information. After you have finished it you can return to earlier cycles in order to collect missed stuff. All in all I think the game is recommendable although you should not expect much of a game but more of a horror novel with interactive elements.
PS: If you have questions just post them here and I'll try to come back at them as fast as possible.

Wait – Extended is a psychological mystery horror game. It aims to provide a lasting horror experience that doesn’t rely on jump scares but the fear of the unknowable.
The game claims to be influenced by the works of H.P. Lovecraft, however it doesn’t so much show its influences on its sleeves so much as it wears a “I Love Innsmouth” shirt and a Cthulhu facemask. You follow the experiences of a man who every night experiences strange horrors that force him towards some unforeseen goal. The world becoming more and more warped as the numbers burnt into his wall tick down.
Wait is made in the RPG Maker engine, which may immediately put you off but if To the Moon and Stray Cat Crossing teach us anything it’s that we shouldn’t judge a game because it was made in RPG Maker. However, almost as a consequence of this, the game play itself is not very engrossing. Move around and explore to pick up items to rub on other items to advance the story.
The story itself is pretty solid. I’ll avoid spoilers but at first it seems fairly run of the mill Lovecraft horror. Strange things happen that nobody else seems to notice, there are hints at all-powerful beings and grotesque creatures chasing, you but always just out of sight. It’s only when you finish the game for the first time that a lot of it is revealed and you see the depth hidden within it. There are five different chapters, where each one is similar but distinctly different alongside side stories and plenty of hidden secrets. It’s also got a fantastic soundtrack that fits perfectly with the unfolding mystery.
The game does fall down however when it comes to the protagonist. He seems far too complacent, and it breaks the feel of the game. Pushing through to the later playthroughs can prove a lot of effort if you’ve not been immediately grabbed by the story and in all honestly a lot of the story feels somewhat generic.
Wait did not leave me with anything in the way of a lasting sense of dread or fear, but then again neither did any of Lovecraft’s works. Perhaps its best not to take the relatively low score that I have given this game at face value. This is a game that is well made and interesting but rather esoteric in its appeal. For some people I think this is exactly what they’re looking for, and if you love a bit of psychological horror then you should absolutely give this game a look. For most people however I’d say that this game is a safe pass.

Pretty much the very definition of an open-world RPG. Cyrodiil is massive, and is a joy to adventure through and even too look at. There is a lot of detail in the world and it is clear that a lot of time and love went into making an authentic looking, immersive fantasy world. That being said, the most important part of any RPG is the depth of the character customization and leveling, and Oblivion does a fine job at that. You can choose your race and change your appearence with a good amount of customization. The skill customization is deep enough to be able to play as seperate playstyles as a nimble theif who is great at lockpicking and a bow, a knight who wears heavy armour and wields massive battle axes, or a magic using mage. Having your skills level up the more you use them just makes sense, and has your character develop naturally, evolving on how you're playing the game without breaking up gameplay. The other most important thing in any RPG are the stories and sidequests. There are enough sidequests to make your head spin, and a lot of them do have interesting stories to tell. A lot of them I don't want to give away, so you'll have to find them on your own. There is also a great amount of items you can find and loot. From different weapons like swords and axes to different sets of armour, there's a lot to find in this game.
Now for the things it didn't do particularly well. The story of the main questline isn't really that interesting, atleast to me. It just felt too predictable, and the segments where you actually travel into Oblivion itself were all really boring. The beautiful thing is, however, if you don't like the main questline, you can just skip it. An open-world game this massive is also prone to have some bugs. There are not a huge amount of them, just enough to warrant a mention. There are also a number of quests that aren't too captivating, but again, with this much content, you can't strike gold everytime.  There also seem to be a lack of voice actors and actresses in this game. There can't be more than ten of them; you will be hearing the same actors speak for totally different characters constantly. Combat also isn't the deepest thing in this game, it's usually just mindless swinging at enemies until they die first. Ranged combat with bows and magical spells fare a little better, but not by much.
Now, this is the Game of the Year edition, so it comes with the two major expansions for the game. Knights of the Nine I didn't particularly care, mainly because I didn't find the storyline particularly interesting and it didn't add very much content-wise. Shivering Isles, however... holy crap. That's one of the best expansions to any open-world game ever with a very interesting new world, lots of interesting stories to tell, and overall just tonnes of new content.
This game is worth your time and money. Nothing beats going on an adventure that you craft yourself, and Oblivion does a fantastic job at that.

Ive owned this game 6 years, and having just finished another play-through i thought it time to write a review :p
I return to this game often. it is one of the best RTS ever imo. The twist of only being able to indirectly influence your "units" (via a flag system of rewards that you have to pay for) makes it refreshing and stand out from the pack. Replayability is immense due to the randomise set-up option. Your units are heros (individual archers, warriors, mages, healers etc) that level and gear up as you progress through any given mission. You can also carry over up to 3 of them to subsequent missions. Once you research the prerequisite you can organise them into parties of up to 4 individuals (i use classic tank/healer/2xdps). The game looks beautiful, plays smooth and bug-free, and never fails to satisfy. The voice acting is extemely well acted and the lines well-written and amusing.
i have two small gameplay dislikes:
1) all the heroes have to physically gather at the selected inn in order to form parties. while youre waiting for the correct  last member to arrive the rest of your settlement is vulnerable (and it can take a while).
2) The building placement is affected by the corpses (represented by amusing little gravestone markers) of fallen enemies. You have to wait for them to despawn before you can place a building. bear in mind theres constant spawning of rats from sewers and skeletons from your graveyard withing your settlement almost "from the word go", this can be quite irritating as your trying to lay out your buildings.
Other than these minor gripes, the game is an absolutle joy. a real gem. I can not recommend it highly enough to a wide variety of players and play-styles. In my opinion is an unsung and hidden gem amongst a lot of over-hyped garbage. I am sure you can pick it up for peanuts in a sale, but iirc its very cheap even at full price.
Highly, highly recommended. You will certainly get a very good return for your money.

TL;DR - While Majesty 2 doesn’t quite live up to the promise of the original Majesty it still delivers hours of fun. Worth buying for fans of the original game or the strategy genre in general.
Majesty 2 remains true to the gameplay of Majesty - instead of building up an army and marching your soldiers to destroy an enemy’s base, you have to construct a small town around your castle in order to ensure that the heroes you recruit have all that they need to be successful. Heroes can’t be controlled directly, but their actions are a reflection of their class (e.g. Rangers like exploring, Rogues like to steal) and of the rewards banners that you put up. While the original game had only two flags (attack and explore) - Majesty 2 adds a host of others, such as a “defend” flag. Veterans of the original will also notice a few tweaks both major (temples can only be built in certain locations) and minor (paladins are now men) to the gameplay.
Unfortunately, a few drawbacks keep Majesty 2 from fully living up to its potential. The game is fun, and it's nice to see Majesty get a visual reboot after all these years, but some of the quests inch towards the tedious - particularly in the expansions. The AI is also not very good, and convincing your heroes to do your bidding somehow seems to be harder than in the original game.

I'm not saying that the game is bad just that i don't recommend it and here is why:
- For long time now this game does not qualify as "historical" or "medieval". It's pure fantasy. Or folklore, to be more precise, and i'm talking about the core game with it's official DLCs and not about mods. It's more of a spiritual successor of Darklands than the first Crusader Kings.
- There are too many random things going on to be called a strategy game. There is too little control over your character and future characters - your children. Things just happen and you just react to situations. And things happen absolutely at random without any reason or logic. This means that if you are lucky then you are going to be successful and if unlucky then your game can end only few years in. This leaves no room for any strategies.
- The game is way too hard. Yes, it's complicated as well but even after learning the game it's still hard. Half of your neighbors, vassals and even your own ruler is going to plot against you from the start of the game even when you are nobody and haven't offended anyone.
- The AI is absolutely s**t. I suspect that the two previus points: randomness and hardhip are supposed to hide the fact how stupid the AI actually is. Because maybe if you have enough problems to deal with you might be actually thankful when AI screws up. Well, i am when my random enemies fail but when my own vassals are screwing my realm up then i don't really appreciate it.
- Every patch fixes some bugs and then creates new ones.
- Ironman is broken one way or another. Most of the time saving won't work and you have to get your desired achievement in one playthrough. Yes, that's still true unfortunately. Because of all the random s**t that can break your game any minute, this can mean countless retries.
- Developers "fix" things that were never broken. This also means that some achievements were more easy with some patch but nearly impossible with next one.
- Instead of leting you the player play the game the way you want, what sandbox originally used to mean, you are forced to play as devs want you to play.
Since you can easily mod everything to your tastes it wouldn't sound too bad if you wouldn't be forced to play ironman for achievements. Besides i'm giving my opinion on the actual game and not on bugfixing mods.
- This brings me to next point - There are never ending achievements with each patch. Some might like that - i don't.
- Some shady political ideologies creep in.
- No more reasonable sales for ancient DLCs. I used to be able to buy extra copies not only the core game but also older DLCs with reasonable price. Well now that i'm not promoting this insanity i'm not going to buy any extra copies obviously so not too big of a loss i suppose.
- Reading through the EULA you don't know if you are valonteering to install spyware on your computer with this game. The language, besides being in legalese, is too vague to determine what exactly you are signing up to. I can't find any official post to clarify this either.
Maybe one day when they finish the game and put it all on sale for 90% - 95% (like Firaxis did with Civ V) then maybe there is something.
At this point, in my opinion, there is no reason to get even the vanilla CK II. Not even for 75% discount.
Now you see constantly 5k to 10k people playing this game. This means that with already available mods or with your own modding skills you might be able to get this game playable. But if you look at the achievements and how "many" people have gotten the most basic achievement as getting married then you realise that vast mayority of players are not playing the vanilla game.
So this game CAN be good but be prepared to wait until your favourite mod gets fixed after yet another patch.

It’s taken me nearly 18 months to finally getting around to playing RPG Tycoon, during which time it’s passed through Steam’s Early Access, had its full release and most recently released its first DLC entitled ‘Supply & Demand’.
RPG Tycoon is a city builder at heart played from the perspective of a Ruler who resides over a Kingdom. For their Kingdom to prosper it’s the Ruler’s job to make his settlement appealing and attractive for heroes to visit. Heroes they can hire to then send out on quests to earn gold, happiness and fame for the Ruler’s Kingdom, so that in turn the Ruler can expand and improve their Kingdom.
Simple, right?
Well… no.
The game starts as a simple concept, which soon spirals into a deep interconnection between buildings, heroes, gold and happiness. Want a hero? Build a house for them. Now the heroes want paid. Send them out on quests, etc. But then the heroes want paid more as they level up from XP gained from quests, and such is the fame of your heroes that other adventures now visit your little kingdom and they want food, drink and entertainment. So, you find yourself having to build a Tavern, which makes an income from the visitors. Now your heroes are tired and low on health from manner quests, so you need to build a Medical Tent.
Somehow, you’ve managed to get through the first year comfortably. Your Kingdom is happy, your heroes are doing well, your Tavern has levelled up. However, your town is looking shabby and the visitors aren’t happy about the lack of decorations. They’re also not happy about other ‘things’ and for me this is where the only real issue I have with the game starts to show – there’s a distinct lack of visual feedback on what’s making visitors and your settlements unhappy.
The lack of feedback makes it difficult to entirely understand how to improve your situation and stop your Kingdom going from being content and happy, to suddenly depressed. As far as I’ve experienced so far unhappiness is the only end-state in the game. Perhaps there’s a lack of money ending too, and perhaps your settlements get raided, but I’ve never actually made it that far. Three to four years in-game time is as far as I’ve managed before the sudden 0% happiness drop.
A brief check of reviews and Steam Discussion group shows you there are bugs still in this game, which isn’t a crime by any means (even if some people have taken umbrage at DLC being released before old bugs have been fixed). The positive is that the game’s developer, Matt Gambell is very active on both Steam and Twitter to answer and reply to feedback on the game. So, in an environment where indie devs are often criticised by some for hitting early access too soon for a quick cash grab, it’s refreshing to be able to see an active developer who communicates with his player base and is keen to fix bugs.
In fact, during the time I’ve taken to think and write about my experiences with RPG Tycoon, Matt Gambell has released an update that fixes an issue with Finance Happiness that was causing a drop in happiness rating. Yet, bugs remain, as shortly after starting a save game a few issues showed themselves including; rival kingdoms had reset & a complete game freeze.
As you might expect from a title containing ‘RPG’ the game does have some basic RPG and tabletop elements to it. Heroes have attributes, which are used in quests (ranging from quick to epic) to gain fame and fortune. Yet the game lacks one essential element of any RPG or tabletop game and that’s a basic set of rules and glossary for the user to follow and understand. That’s not to see that the game doesn’t provide information, as it does in the form of hero screens and quest descriptions. It just lacks the explanation of what those attributes do, and how they’re used in quests. There’s no real bridge between the game design and the user’s experience. It’s mainly left to chance, prior understanding and just a little bit of luck.
The little snippets of info and feedback that translate the developer’s thinking and reasoning behind the game’s mechanics into something the user can understanding (without giving the magic of the game away). At times I found the quest requirements unclear, and at times felt like I was guessing at what resources I should take on quests with me. Without a doubt I was guessing which slot they should go in to. On the plus side the game keeps a history of which combinations of items you’ve used on quests, so it does provide a small amount of feedback to the trial and error approach it pushes you into.
I’m sure there’s a hope from the developer’s point of view that the text quest provides enough information for the user to know what to take. A similar approach is used when you’re offered a multiple choice situation during Epic Quests. There’s no real feedback or insight provided other than the quest text. So when it comes to choosing an option, you’re once again sort of just left guessing and hoping for the best. A roll check is then used to see if you meet the requirements, but the UI doesn’t actually tell which attribute was used in the roll check.
So with all of that in mind I’m left feeling that RPG Tycoon perhaps left Steam’s Early Access a little too soon at the cost of detail and polish. The base of the game is there, it’s just missing the smaller details to make the game more user friendly. You can enjoy the game’s current state; it’s presentation and soothing music, certainly make it a relaxing game to play and of course with a bit of time invested you will start to understand how to play.
It’s certainly a nice idea, and one I hope gets the polish it deserves to make it more user friendly, as as far as I can see that’s all it’s really lacking.
A fun game, with an active developer that just needs that little bit extra to be fully enjoyable.

I spent 99% of the time dicking around exploring the map.  In many other games I wouldn't have had a great time doing that because the map would end or there wouldn't be anything particularly interesting to find.  In say, Skyrim, there would probably be a cave with generic enemies to kill and that would be all.
In this game though, there was always something utterly magical to find.  I helped a rat and a turtle living in a cellar find love.  I talked to and killed evil scarecrows and helped a succubus escape a twisted hellscape with her lover.  I broke into the cellar of a kindly old woman who offered me a loan after her cat told me there were suspicious types down there and found debt collectors who turned into demons when approached.
Yet the most magical thing of all is how natural and meaningful it felt.  As a I naturally progressed through the game's story, I ran into so many bits that rewarded this idle and almost obsessive exploration.  Indeed, the story is so wonderfully open ended at times giving such simple yet broad goals that the only correct thing you can do at times is explore and lose yourself in this magical world that Larian has made.
Despite the broad nature of most of your goals the story still manages to remain present and intelligent.  Oftentimes it will surprise you by popping up at the most unexpected moments with new twists and turns in the most natural of fashions leading up to a conclusion that is both epic and satisfying.
At the beginning, your goal is simple: escape Fort Joy.  The game gives you little to no guidance on how you might do that yet you'll never feel at a lost since you'll discover so many possible ways to escape just by naturally exploring your environment.
This is easily the best game I have ever played.  There is so much magic, so much attention to detail, and a utterly brilliant and punishing battle system to boot.  It will be a long, long time before a game ever comes close to how good this game is.

A friend of mine told me about this game and said that I should check it out cause I would probably like it. I didn't check for a week but after some more time I took a look. 10 minutes after first checking out the game I bought it and here I am, almost 100 hours in the game.
The game is huge, we played the first act for 20+ hours, and there are 4 acts! The gameplay is very interactive and feels great, you can, for example, create a puddle of acid and set it ablaze!

The only 2 things that I dislike so far is the fact that a few quests have a tendency to bug out making you unable to complete the quest. Also the mages in this game are kinda underwhelming. Physical characters are much more potent. Im hoping they'll take a look into that.
All in all a great game and possibly one of the best rpgs ive played so far. I would recommend this game to anyone who likes to play rpgs and being able to play this game for months to come.

I just finished 2 yesterday.
P.S This is probably my first review, please forgive me if I'm grammatically incorrect or anything like that.
But starting where I left I off, Wow. Just wow. It's hard to describe how much fun I've had playing this game. This easily is in my favourite games of all time. Let me explain why, with Pros and Cons so it's easier for me (without spoiling the game of course).
Pros:
-The characters.
Much more interesting than the characters in ME1. Although like ME1 they develop as you go along in the story which is great, because my opinions on a lot of these characters changed over the course of the game. As well as the antagonists, it is much more than just good fights evil. These characters made me test my morality quite a lot in the game.
-The story.
Yes the goal is straightforward, as identified when you start the game. But it's just more than just that goal, it's the people you meet. The people you help and the people you become friends with. That makes the journey truly great. The ending was also freaking great, I didn't expect what happened in the ending.
- The Paragon and Renegade System.
Although I went for a pargon playthrough, there were a couple of times which I had chosen renegade choices which I may have thought were right in my opinion. Unlike ME1 where it was easy to get complete paragon, I feel here my choices were more morally grey, rather than black and white. Also although not related, I felt ME2 was a lot more mature and darker than ME1 which made my whole experience a lot better.
- The world
Unlike ME1, the world is bustling with life in ME2. There are so many interactive things around the world and this includes going around talking to random people, doing some sidequest or even listening in a conversation or event that is occuring. I liked how the world change accordingly to my actions no matter how big or small. NPC's would respond or act differently around me when I would make certain actions, which shows the effort they put into making this game.
Cons-
- A few glitches here and there, but otherwise pretty well optimised. The game only crashed on me a few times.
Overall: I have practically have no faults with this game. Mass Effect 2 is now one of my favourite games of all time and I will never EVER forget the characters I interacted to within this game and the game itself has a special place in my heart.

Chocola Fudge Brownies
Ingredients
½ cup unsalted butter, melted
1 tablespoon cooking oil (olive oil or coconut oil are fine)
1⅛ cup granulated sugar
2 large eggs
2 teaspoons of vanillas extract ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)
½ cup all purpose (or plain) flour
½ cup unsweetened cocoa powder
¼ teaspoon salt
Preheat oven to 175°C | 350°F.
Lightly grease an 8-inch square baking pan with cooking oil spray. Line with parchment paper (or baking paper); set aside.
Combine melted butter, oil and sugar together in a medium-sized bowl. Whisk well for about a minute. Add the eggs and vanilla; beat until lighter in colour (another minute).
Sift in flour, cocoa powder and salt. Gently fold the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients until JUST combined (do NOT over beat as doing so well affect the texture of your brownies).
Pour batter into prepared pan, smoothing the top out evenly. (OPTIONAL: Top with chocolate chunks or chocolate chips.)
Bake for 20-25 minutes, or until the center of the brownies in the pan no longer jiggles and is just set to the touch (the brownies will keep baking in the hot pan out of the oven). If testing with a toothpick, the toothpick should come out dirty for fudge-textured brownies.
Remove and allow to cool to room temperature before slicing.

I've never written a review before, but I think this game deserves one.
I really, really enjoyed this game. It just isn't like other horror games, in which some creepy visage jumps in your face and makes your liquids run. That's not real fear, it's just a scare.
Sure, „Wait“ has some small heart-stopping moments, like sudden noises and such, but that's not a main feature in my opinion.
It's more about the things you can't see or grasp.
Is someone there? Did I just hear something? Creatures that just stand still without any reaction, looking at you...that's what I personally fear the most.
Our protagonist is experiencing horrible nightmares in his own apartment and needs your help to find out what's going on, although all he wants is to go to work and eat his salad afterwards.
What I love about him is the way just accepts things. Furniture is changing is his apartment while he is at work and he can't do anything about it. So why panic? Somehow he calms you with his pragmatic attitude in the midst of these unsettling nights.
After some play time you really get into the story and want to hunt every breadcrumb of information, which can be found in any object.
If you're too lazy to explore and try different things you'll probably miss out on most of the fun, so be observant, as no information is useless.

This is one of the best games I ever played. Not just among RPG-Maker games. And here is why.
The storyline is so unique and complex it makes everything come alive. The music is so skillfully made and placed that it absorbs you completely and creates a wonderfully fitting atmosphere. The amazing amount of detail the developers put into this, making every little object click-able and hiding this many secrets, stories, lore and references behind everything, it blows my mind.
Another reason I love this game is cause it doesn't give me the feeling of being spoon fed everything. If I gain an Achievement I had to actually do something. If I solve a riddle it's not always plain obvious. This game isn't hard and can be played casual. But having it on 100% is a real accomplishment, and fun.
And like you turn of the lights for a good movie, please do so for this game. There is close to no jump-scares but there is lots of amazing, wonderful, creepy, feeling in this. A lot of games from the so called horror genre could learn a thing or two from this title in term of using other elements of fear like feeling alone or powerless, the unknown and all the others.
And for everyone who likes H.P. Lovecraft this game is a must. The Elements of his world are clear to see in this game and yet it doesn't feel like his but like their story. I believe if he was alive he would applaud this game.
And the only thing I can say about this game directly without spoiler. If you have not played it through several times you have not seen half of the game.
In appreciation of this masterful piece of game art I recommend this highly as on of the secret treasure of this years game releases.

Due to the events that happened in the past, an apartment is locked in an eternal limbo, haunting present and future occupants into obsession, an obsession that will lead them to a damning death if they ever found the truth.
Currently, a young man by the name of Benjamin Moss resides in this cursed abode. No matter where he moves, the walls and rooms of this cursed place grip his very being, making him restless and hollow. Stained on his walls are the numbers, “5676.” Are these numbers linked to the mysterious, paranormal activities occurring in his home? Desperate for answers, he begins his search for the truth but will he drive himself into madness in the process?
---
It consists of solving puzzles in a form of riddles and the occasional searching for items to proceed forward through the story, e.g., hammers for destroying brittle walls.
The appearances of the threats are mostly scripted, and they don’t chase you around so you are free to take your time and absorb the environment. There isn’t much to explore anyways but certain events change to an extent depending on the number of your playthrough. For example, there’s a part in the beginning of the first run where you have to mess around with a circuit breaker (the power cuts off). The same thing happens in the second playthrough, however, instead of going to the breaker, you must exit the apartment to complete this sequence. They are small changes but they keep the game fresh and increase the replay value.
There are also a couple of alternate endings, but I only found two of them for now. I will update when I find more or when the developer confirms the number of endings.
---
The scare factor of the game, on the scale of 1-10 (1 being, “me looking for something to scare me but couldn’t find it, no matter how hard I tried” and 10 being, “I ♥♥♥♥ my pants, I should’ve worn a diaper”), I rate Wait- Extended a 4, “the game tries.”
I would say that certain parts are creepy but Wait certainly is more story-driven rather than scaring its players. Since the threat isn’t present all the time, the game relies on sounds and narrative to set the atmosphere. I did notice that some of the background sounds are reused sound assets. I recognize them from other games.
---
It is a RpgMaker game so I think most people know what these games look like. I didn’t run across any gamebreaking bugs or crashes but I did have a problem putting the game on fullscreen. After several button pressing later, I found that F5 seems to toggle the fullscreen and windowed mode. I don’t play many RpgMaker games so this might be standard procedure for them.
---
The game has a slow start and the plot isn’t fully explained by just playing the game one time. It is only towards the end that the story opens up. I do like how certain actions dictate what the ending will. The Steam page says there are hidden storylines. I have no idea what they are but when I find some time, I will be playing around with the game to scour for them.
My first playthrough took me an hour and subsequent runs might take another hour, depending on how long you solve puzzles. I think the game is interesting enough to keep you playing because the plot twists are handled well. Just don’t expect a scarefest.
---
For its price range, $7.99 (has a small discount, $6.79, at the time of this review), I recommend this game. It isn’t expensive and there’s a nice story within its walls. Thanks for reading!
---
Pros:
- Story-driven
- Has different alternate endings
- Has replay value (events will change, depending on the number of your playthrough)
Cons:
- Reused sound assets
- Switching to fullscreen is a bit annoying (I’m just slow. It took me awhile to realize F5 does this)
- Not as scary as I would like
---
By the way, if you have some time, watch me fool around in Wait - Extended.

I will admit I like the game in it's current stage but I love these type of games.  If you hate crafting, survival, and a decent challenge stay away from Conan Exiles.  If this is your thing and you're willing to deal with Early Access and finding a well managed server you will really enjoy this game.  I recommend a well managed server because the Official Servers get wiped here and there with little to no warning.  I'll admit that I was angry more than a little bit but a friend was running a server and since then I have enjoyed my time on the game.  From here I'm going to go over the Pros and Cons:
Pros:
- Decent size map with a lot to explore
- Character customization is decent
- Leveling with Attribute Points and Crafting Points
- Choose recipes to be able to craft based on level
- Many decorative items to make your base look lived in
- Decent combat with a few different Weapons and Armors
- Religion done in an interesting way or choose not to
- Capture Thralls to defend your base and help craft things
- Plenty of PVE with risk at all levels
- Constant updates and performance fixes.  Almost getting them daily.
Cons:
- You select a Race but doesn't effect anything
- Weapons need a more separate amount of damage to make them worth using
- A larger selection of armor so everyone doesn't look the same
- Thralls are only a decent threat and the AI needs some more tweaking
- Pathfinding needs fixed for almost all animals.
All in all I am giving the game a 8/10 and I feel it's worth a buy if you want to support it.

It's an unashamed old-school grid-based blobber, with many little modern conveniences.
And it's not a particularly hard one at that.
You have a party of 6 people, and you run around on a variety of dungeons, fighting enemies, collecting loot and beating the snot out of bosses so you can collect McGuffins to advance the plot and get special abilities.
There are 4 ways to run into monsters.
Ambushing is done in certain spots of each dungeon, each ambush attempt has a greator morale cost (5, 20, 35, 50, etc), and toughter enemies. You use these same morale points to invoke special abilities you unlock with the same mcGuffins.
In each ambush attempt, up to 6 groups can pass by and each that passes increases the chance that they'll get first strike by 20% - this is very dangerous so you should avoid passing on the groups early on.
Each group generally consists of a tougher mini-boss monster and some weak cannon fodder to act as meatshields for the boss. These mini-bosses escape after several turns and take the loot with them.
Ambushing is your main source of equipment and loot in general in the dungeons, and the best way to fight enemies in quick succession if you want to grind levels.
As for combat, your party of 6 is divided into a front row and a back row; the first triplet in front, the second in back.
There is a lot they don't explain about combat, eg that you can use a whistle ahead of time (it'll light up the whistle icon at the bottom) to prevent bosses from screwing up your party order once. The spell casting UI also completely sucks, I had to google how to get to my wizard's attack spells.
You issue the actions you want your party to take, and then they're "applied" either normally or fast. Several prompts show up for each action, under normal mode, you advance 1 prompt per press of a button (you can also hold it), under fast mode it'll just skip through all the prompts rapidly. After a while I found myself just quickly tapping through and relying more on sounds and the simple animations to tell me what is going on over actually reading the prompts.
However once you reach the mid game, you'll tend to just stack up +Hit and +Avoid (you can see the current values on the portraits on the top right), and pair it with Force Guard so that enemies don't dispel them to their originals levels, and there isn't much strategy left.
The one thing I don't like about combat, is just how heavily levels factor into it.
For example, if your character is level 15, and a monster attacks and it does 200 damage (just about a OHK), but you can barely hit him and do pitifully little damage. But if you level up but with no real change in equipment or stats, he now hits you for considerably less and you can do a reasonable level of damage to him.
Combat does have a fairly strategic layer to it, and you do have a lot of tools at your disposal (and you unlock more and more over time).
If you can overcome the level gap, the main game isn't hard at all.
Dungeon design leaves a bit to be desired.
I do wish they could've added a bit more in the line of puzzles, but I suppose not every game can be like Etrian Odyssey.
Every dungeon has its own unique theme and feel, and usually a unique gimmick as well.
As a few simple examples
The story is fairly rudimentary and serves more as an excuse to progress from dungeon to dungeon. The characters are likeable enough and there's more than enough dialogue and exposition to allow you to get attached to the characters.
I have heard that the developer will be doing significantly more writing in future titles, I for one hope they don't because there is really nothing wrong with this level.
A lot of the dialogue is also voiced, and with Japanese voice work to boot (that's a big plus for me).
Also the translation is absolutely awful, not that I expected better from anything published by NISA, but shame on you all the same.
The best parts look and feel like a fairly literal translation taken out of google and tidied up a bit for grammar, and the worst parts are either incomprehensible or completely misleading.
The last bit plagues a great many useful items and skills!
For example, you can carry Dolls with you to save you from insta-kill attacks.
Some of them contain this in their description: Item loss rate UP.
Nearly everyone would think: "oh, I'm going to lose items if I carry this with me, oh dear!"
What that property actually means, is that there's a very good chance that the item won't break after saving you from disaster.
The character system is fairly simple and rudimentary.
Most of the depth comes from your class selections, and then your selection of cross-class skills.
I do like how your characters' ages factors into your survivability.
I also like that your reserves slowly level up and make some money for you.
As most know, there are 2 distinct art styles available, which affects the portraits of the characters you meet, and the CG scenes you get to look at during crucial moments of the plot.
First is the Type A art style by Yoko Tsukamoto, this is a more realistic/gothic art style, and despite some of the scenes looking rushed and incomplete, it's just oozing soul, personality, and atmosphere.
Second is the Type B by En Okishiji, it's banal boring generic animu moe blob rubbish; Okishiji is clearly a talented individual, but his artwork is a terrible fit for the game, and is in general just soulless, bland, and sorely lacking in details.
There is no mincing words about how bad Type B is, using it is like watching anime with dubs; if you want to do that, all the more power to you, but I just want you to know you have absolutely awful taste.
As for how lacking in detail type B is, just go look at Rui's portraits as an easy example.
In Type A, you'll notice several very distinct and unique features, such as her eyes looking like a lizard's. This detail (that is actually very important to her character) is completely absent in the type B art.
The locations themselves aren't that great, the models are low poly and the textures are fuzzy, but do keep in mind that this game was also targeted at the Vita.
The music is also fairly decent, it's never going make it into my top 100, but it never got on my nerves while playing.

Look, Dungeon crawling Japanese RPGs are meant to be difficult, they are meant to be hard, but in most cases you should be able to overcome the situation with smart play and dedication. Which is why I want to shoot Stranger of Sword City out of a cannon, burn the cannon, and then burn the ashes. When it comes to inconsistent gameplay mechanics, out of nowhere situations that screw you, and elements that just extend gameplay for no good reason, Stranger of Sword City is at the top of the list.
Frustration is what is in store for you if you play Stranger of Sword City. Unless you follow a guide. This game is very particular about how to fight in battles, how to get equipment, etc. Anytime you go off the path (a path mind you that you don't know, and the game can mislead you on), expect to be punished with a lot of grinding to make up for it. And This is the Citizen of Grind City. You don't know grinding until you've played a dungeon crawling JRPG, but this one feels like one of the worst in terms of grinding. I mean, you can just look at the hours played on this one. And you're probably wondering “Dragnix, why the hell did you continue to play the game if you hated it so much.” Well, when I receive a review copy and start it and promise a review.....to me it's a promise that I have to keep. Even if it literally kills me to do. And my god, on several occassions Stranger of Sword City had me throwing my hands up and yelling out as many swears as I could possibly think of. And more that haven't been invented.
Look, the base concepts of the game are solid in terms of the battle system and the complex combat. There's a good game underneath the surface, one that will challenge players out there. But it's so bogged down with other elements, that you'll find yourself drowning before you can really enjoy them. Spend you time looking at other games in the genre, because Stranger of Sword City is not one I can recommend.

A number of Wizardry-alikes get made, but it's a minefield even in this well-trodden ground. Too easy, too random (aka Wizardry IV :P), too self-referential, too many random mechanics, too cheap...but the folks at Experience have proven some of the best at this old game, and SoSC is one of their best.
Stranger is on the harder, more traditional end of this company's effort; the music is epic and operatic, the monsters and the portraiture are moody oil paintings, the story is grim and mature, and the difficulty is definately nasty and intolerant of mistakes. This is a boon for those who don't usually like how the player characters of their J-DRPGs tend to be on the cute side.
The character building system is well-made, providing a great sub-classing system that is at once both full of synergy yet not absolutely mandatory. Getting all of that with so few of them is really smart. I also found the Divinities system a highlight, allowing you to go with some real decision-making reguarding how you wanna fight and build, and allowing some "tug of wars" with the bosses. The Ambush system wasn't as rough as I expected (I expected rote grinding but it was great in small bursts with that delectable DRPG risk/reward).
I did have a few problems with how automated combat works, how numbers flew up behind forward rows, and hotkeys function but these are minor quibbles.
Altogether, this is a seriously great DRPG and a good buy for anyone looking to get another one experienced.

Stranger of Sword City is one of those old-school Dungeon Crawler games inspired by Wizardy and the old Might & Magic games - but it's polished and innovated on the old formula a fair bit.
It trades some of the typical 'grindiness' inherent in the genre with fast paced (though still turn-based) combat and an addictive class-building system where you get to multiclass and transfer select abilities from one class to the other.
This leads to pretty amazing combinations. Picture the Samurai's ability to keep attacking until he gets hit by a counter-attack combined with a ninja's evasion - or a ranger's infinite concentration length with a warrior's 7-hits while in concentration genocide.
SoSC also isn't afraid to give you a decent bit of counters against the RNG that is king in so many dungeon crawler games. Many games in this genre rely on enemies abilities to debilitate or even insta-kill your characters... these are all present in SoSC, but there's counters available if you've played and built your characters cleverly against every single one of these - and while there's stilla decent amuont of grindy 'trash' encounters, most combats actually require a decent bit of thinking before you press the 'commit turn' button.
Your main way to improve your characters, asides from leveling up, is of course gear progression - and here also, SoSC innovates with the 'ambush' system, where - provided you can find the ambush spots in dungeons, you get to pick a fight seeing the reward type and the enemy you'd have to fight for it.
'Hrm, lvl 20 demon for a rare katana, or a lvl 5 bunny for a few common helmets?" type of deal.
Oh, and fairly rare in this type of game, there's 3 seperate ending paths that diverge quite a bit in your final resolution.
That said, SoSC still relies quite heavily on grinding it's content to keep your characters of a sufficient level, which I had little patience for (and thus evaded by checking 'recomended levels' on the wiki, and cheating my characters up a level or two per dungeon, rather than grind through the trash for extra hours for the same effect).
That didn't stop this brutal game from murdering me a whole bunch of times, but I still greatly enjoyed the journey.
If you like old school dungeon crawler type gameplay, I'd say Stranger of Sword City feels instantly familiar, while still being innovative and very much 'it's own game'. Highly recommended.
If you *don't* care much for dungeon crawler style games though - give it a miss. Nothing here takes it far enough outside of the scope of it's genre to appeal.

This mmo gives off a feel of Borderlands and Ryzom (Another, older, mmo. Google it.) smashed together.
Skill system: 6/10
Personally, I like the skill system, however, I feel like it's tied to the single currency of AP too much. You need AP to raise mutation levels, skills, tradeskills, and stats. (Which take 5 AP points to raise a stat by 1.) The game offers sub-level ups, so you gain 3 AP points per sub-level up, and it happens multiple times before you actually go from level 1 to level 2. You can get a lot of AP points this way but they all drain out by the time you're done spending them. The ability system can also be steep, for example. I wanted to do sonic manipulation and empathy for my mutations. However, both of which take 43-48 points in empathy or sonic manipulation to get the first skill. That's a bit tough. Now add in your skills and stats, and disregard tradeskills. It makes it difficult to pick and choose what you need. With all this stuff going on, you really need to know what you want to do with your skills before you spend any.
Combat: 4/10
Average hotbar combat with left click as attack and right to activate a spell or use your second gun/weapon if you're dual wielding. Headshots do more damage, etc. You have your standard Health, Stamina, and Gamma (mana) at your disposal in combat. Nothing special here.
Gameplay: 7/10
I found the world immersive and fun to explore. There's tons of places to explore, however the constant need of awareness of danger kept me on my toes. There's a lot to do, and it can get pretty hectic when you accidentally get into the nasty mess of 5v1 combat. If you like post-apocalyptic worlds like this one, I think you'll like this game. The game is completely classless, too, so you can customize what you want to do; ranging from crafting, to guns blazing, to a post-apocalyptic ninja, etc. The only other MMO I saw this done was in Ryzom.
Technical Stuff: 5/10
If you're looking for a pretty game, don't bother with this one. The game is sorta old and you don't even need an overkill PC to play it. There are some graphical issues (for me anyways) but they are minor and shouldn't impact the gameplay much. Some of the scenery hitboxes are a bit larger than they should be, and on a rare occasion, you might see an enemy run through walls, but it's pretty a solid game from a technical standpoint.
Final Average Rating: 5.5/10
Other Comments: The game is best played with friends. I don't recommend playing solo.

This is a game in hindsight I can't see me ever paying $10 for, though the joy for me was getting this game when it was first put onto Early Access at a reduced price and watching it gradually grow with features being added (and bugs coming and going and often at times coming back again in later builds which was extremely unusual)
I really don't feel this game is finished, as in I don't feel it's ready to see the light of day of 1.0 just quite yet.  It still feels like a mid to late BETA.
That being said however of the time I have spent with this game and pushing through some of the most infuriating game-breaking bugs during Early Access I did enjoy the game albeit it getting somewhat repetitive in the late-game.
The concept surrounding the game is great and has been tried by other developers with varying degrees of success and I feel this one lands in the middle of the road.  But even with my nitpicks and complaints I often find myself coming back to it from time to time, especially after an update to see what's been added or fixed.
However since coming out of EA the joy has started to slowly slip as I don't see frequent updates being pushed out, and I have to ask myself frequently is a game really all that great if the joy I mainly get from it is BETA-testing it?   Well... yes and no, as long as the ends justify the means and the finished product is all that it can be or more.
In truth though I actually look forward to the DLC to add additional content, though I'm crossing my fingers that it's either extremely affordable or free.  If it's free then I can turn a blind eye to the price of the base game itself as long as the content of the DLC holds up.  If it's $7-$10 DLC then most absolutely either wait until on sale or just avoid altogether until it hits the inevitable $1 bundle.

Game crashed before the tutorial was able to be completed. Occasional user interface (UI) elements persisted on the screen after a menu was closed, the only way to clear the screen was to quit the game and reload. Questing is tedious with a lack of polish to the interface. The hero management interface is broken and only half the intended features seem to work. The item systems is just barely working at this point resulting in game breaking bugs and lost inventory.
This game is a unique twist on the classical RPG formula where instead of playing the hero, you manage their city. There are no monsters to battle, but you can train your heroes to improve their base statistics, solve quests to gain followers and cash. The ability to send multiple heroes in a party on epic quests is also fun. Sometimes a sub-quest involving the vanquishing of a villain appears or substantially better loot is to be had. The town has special buildings available once a certain level of experience is obtained.
Sending your heroes out on a quest involves a somewhat unique screen where you have to select six pieces of equipment they will take on their journey. This is interesting at first since each piece of equipment has a priority and some does nothing to assist the quest. As the heroes quest, more equipment and missions are unlocked. Once the equipment is placed in its correct priority slot, the mission results in better rewards. Unfortunately, the next time a hero goes on the same quest, this entire setup must be repeated. It gets tedious after a while since ultimately there are 30 different pieces of equipment available and the selection screen is limited to what it displays so there is a lot of scrolling involved. Understandably, the developers added a history screen and indicators to what equipment may be useful, though frustratingly they have this on a different "history" screen which causes a lot of back and fourth between the two windows.
The hero hire screen allows a hero to be hired. The statistics attached to each one has no explanation to what they are for resulting in either a lookup on the internet or just selecting randomly. Once a hero has been hired, they wander the town doing nothing unless they are actively on a quest. Once back from a quest they will be tired or injured. They must be selected on the main map screen and directed to the healing facilities. The hero management interface is broken and telling a hero to go heal from that screen results in the hero ignore the command. This is especially frustrating if there are many civilians exploring the town since it is hard to find a particular hero in the crowd. However, the training options from the hero management work, so get them guns son.
There seems to be a nice collection of fun items to acquire over the course of a game. Some improve the city, some are equitable on heroes. Unfortunately some of the biggest game breaking bugs come from items. Certain city improvements (rugs and pots) can be used to improve vendors in the game. After making an improvement, the item doesn't disappear and can be reused multiple times. After nearly five minutes upgrading all the vendors millions of gold were added to the treasury every time anything was purchased. Once the upgrades to the city were finished, any items left in the inventory were missing.

Next thing worth mentioning are the visuals. This game was originally made in the year 2000, thats 14 years ago, and it STILL looks good to this day. Sure, some of the textures may be a bit lacking and objects may seem a bit blocky by today's standarads, but for an HD re-release of a game thats 14 years old, it holds up really well.
The game play is really fun as well. The game has a really good flow to it, seeing as it relys heavily on your momentum. Sure, some say the controls are a bit clunky and the auto-grinding can be a pain sometimes, but once you get used to it, those things stop being an issue (for the most part). Grinding down a railing,, jumping off to wall ride, doing a backflip off of said wall onto another railing, all while spraying graffiti and avoiding helicopter and tank fire still feels as awesome as ever.

This is a grind game, plain and simple with a pay-to-win structure but fortunatly no pay to get anything is involved. Hopefully it stays that way. It has good music and graphics, however it all but stops there sadly.
That being said, the game is based around 3 characters. It is a running turn by turn style play where you control the placing of the 3 characters, the items in their inventory, potions, and special abilities.
You progress through the dungeons and side quests fighting wave after wave of monsters with little reprieve. There is NO saving in this game. Once you start a dungeon or side quest you either quit and restart or you finish. There is also no progression save other than unlocking new forms of your characters through the side quests.
There is an in game store in which to use 'gold' or 'crystals' to purchase new unlocks such as characters, pets, or preperation store upgrades. Gold is obtained through finishing (or dying) in quests (dungeons and side quests). Crystals are obtained through finishing a dungeon only.
This game has a lot of potential IF the developer would add a little more to the game, such as the ability to adjust full screen or windowed, sound/music on or off, back story, actual quests, and other possible options to make the game a little more immersive. As it sits, I give it a reluctant thumbs up, mostly because as a 'grind game' it is decent.

Your crew is fun and has enough variety; some are also characters that you can romance; although if you try to romance them all, you will cause a mess; and if you prefer one character over the other; you will see the consequences in the other, which will change behavior toward you.
Setting up the team is a matter of picking the right elements; each one has pros and cons; and you may want to recruit all of them, to try them out and see which one works best. Also the more you create a relation with your team, the more abilities they will unlock.
The decisions you make, does not really affect much, beside the type of points you get. Paragon is the "bad and good" system; each action is either considered bad or good; and your aspect also reflect if you are more of a good guy or a bad guy. I did not find any sort of penalty for being bad, nor I did get extra points for being good, so just play as you see fit.
Graphics is still good for today's standards; it won't win you if you care only about outstanding texture quality and hyper detailed models, but overall if you get sucked in the story, you will enjoy the graphics.
Sound is also very good; with great effects and marvellous music; some pieces are really outstanding.
Controls are fine; it is a classic cover shooter so you know what you get. I did play it with mouse and keyboard; so I can't say how does it work with a gamepad.
Overall it is a great game, still, even today. Andromeda may be the latest cool thing, but so far, I still prefer the old "trilogy".

Hanako Games has been a remarkable name in the otome genre for quite some time now. As being one of Hanako's later games,
is a marvelously elaborate adventure of royalty, politics, romance, intrigue and alliances in a fantasy realm - and probably Hanako's best game yet in my personal opinion.
Our story revolves around Madeleine Valois, a noble born young woman coming from an insignificant family, raised to attend Prince Oscar of Ocendawyr as his valette - a companion, an advisor, an agent and a maidservant. For the occasion of Princess Cassidy's
- a celebration for the coming of age and a hosting various suitors to secure her future - Madeleine accompanies Oscar to the neighboring kingdom of Gwellinor. Considering the validity of a female heir is the central power for royalty in this setting, an already fierce race for the hand of Princess Cassidy is on. Yet, Madeleine will also find herself in a web of intrigues threatening not only the integrity of the crown, but the security of her own and her companions. As dangerous gossip concerning many secrets runs within the halls of royal palace, Madeleine tries to choose her allies carefully for her own means. Will she manage to dissolve the web of intrigue, or simply become a part of it to survive?
Overall,
is one of the best otome games both in means of an original setting and story elaboration that I've ever seen. The world and its various ways are depicted befitting 16th century power politics through heirs, names, titles and land with many anecdotes appropriately arranged into a unique setting. All characters are portrayed well beyond skin deep with profound personalities and background. They all are depicted with certain demeanors to establish certain means with unique abilities; possessing dreams, aims, insecurities and hopes which makes every one of them interesting and credible as a personality, breaking out of common stereotypes. Even the most ordinary of them possess their own depths with well written story elaboration.
Our protagonist, Madeleine is most certainly not our everyday shy and helpless heroine. She is a relatable and able personality with her stature, her training and her character. She is a smart and strong young woman who keeps both her wits and her charms about her. An incredible social player with an ability to observe, analyze and assess situations in the blink of an eye. She is calculating with a novel sense of duty and responsibility, yet she still carries her own worries and desires for the future silently. Her chosen interactions are various and always consistent with her traits. Our job here is to reveal what part of Madeleine's substantial personality will become victorious by the end through our choices. Each and every ending you may acquire feels probable and satisfying with the given personality, which is a masterful feat to accomplish in this genre.
For display purposes, artworks are genuinely beautiful anime style and CGs themselves are various with suitable expressions. There is no voice acting for any part, yet the soundtrack already establishes a rich and driving atmosphere through a gripping narrative - both describing actual events and commentating on Madeleine's train of thought. It's like reading a really good story with beautiful pictures presented on the side.
The game has 15 different endings - and a truckload of choice options - presenting alternatives for Madeleine's future and each one sheds some more light to the secrets within palace chambers. I'd highly recommend playing
for every otome gamer and for whom would appreciate a good visual novel about court politics. Enjoy!

In
, you play as Madeleine Valois, valette to prince Oscar of Oceandawyr. This basically means that you keep the young prince out of trouble, spy for him, protect him and his interests, fight for him, and even die for him if necessary. The two of you have a close, playful relationship. As Oscar's royal duties take him to a nearby country to attend their princess' birthday celebrations, you of course accompany him. But inbetween making the princess fall for Oscar (and do you really want her to?) and sneaking through the hallways of the palace, you come across a deadly royal plot...
+ The music is very atmospheric
+ Every character gets a bit of background in their route
+ A relatable, strong protagonist
+ Its theme, style & feel of courtly intrigues
+ 15 different endings, 4 romanceable princes
- The two rival princes are not incorporated properly into the story if their path is not chosen
- Not able to explicitly romance the ladies
- The odd style discrepancy between the static character art/portraits and the big "event" art
- Courtly intrigue is not that complicated
It's a solid visual novel/otome game that also focuses a lot on the protagonist's personal development and feelings, and allows you to make choices that lead to many different endings (though not all of them differ that much from each other). The plot or trap at the core of this plot is not
complicated or interesting in the end, and I found Madeleine's personal quest for a new life actually more engaging. The CGs or event art was very pretty, and I enjoyed that art style quite a lot more than the normal static character art.
Also! There are quite a few female characters in this game (Dolores, Princess Cassidy, and Colette), and you can become friends with all of them. Some art also includes Madeleine holding hands with them, building a life with them, etc., but it NEVER becomes explicit that you can actually romance them or be in a proper relationship with them. Like, what?? You give me all these cute girls (one of whom is explicitly into ladies), but I cannot make them happy in a romantic sense? :(
Anyway, though this is not my favourite visual novel/otome, it is a very enjoyable one if you enjoy its theme! There's also much to be said for its female protagonist, Madeleine Valois, whose character is truly explored in the game.

Voice acting is uneven, but serves its purpose. The music is quite good, but is sadly rather sparse.
And now for a list of complaints:
There's a pretty good adventure game here, but it's sadly obscured by interface problems. If you are an adventure game fan who can look past some of these warts, you might be able to have a good time with Gemini Rue.

I drove over the road back in the 70s and 80s. To be honest, I miss it. I have been an avid flight sim fan for decades (started back in the DOS days) and thought I would give ATS a try. For the most part, I love this sim. If you are thinking about purchasing it, there are a few things you should know. First, without at least a steering wheel and pedals, the game is almost immposible to play. I started by installing the trial version of European Truck Sim and tried driving with a mouse. Forget it... it's almost impossible. I then tried ATS with the flight yoke that I use with my flight sim. That worked better, but was still a tough go. I finally bit the bullet and purchased a Logitech steering wheel/pedal combo and it works like a dream. If you are serious about persuing ATS, plan on investing on some decent add on hardware.
I generrally am really enjoying this sim. It's well built and runs flawlessly. The level of immersion is so real that once, after I lit a cigarette, I looked over to my left to roll down the window lol. I have TrackIR that I have been using with my flight sim  (FSX - Steam Edition) and it integrated right into ATS allowing me to look around as if I was actually sitting in the cab. I love it!
That being said, there are a few things that I find difficult to get used to and seriously detract from game play. First, the AI traffic can be really annoying. AI vehicles block your path, pull in front and slow down extremely quickly. When turning, if you pull a little too far into the intersection, the AI traffic will stop so close that you can't make the turn. If you have vehicles behind you, you can't back up and eventually find yourself in a gridlock. I have learned to stop well behind the stop bar and wait for traffic to clear before turning.
Next is the Interstate access, both entering and exiting. The off ramps are at a 45 degree slope. If you are in a line of cars and have to stop before getting to the top of an inclined off ramp, plan on stalling a few times before getting to the top until you get a hang of the clutch. The on ramps have about a 150 foot long acceleration ramp. This takes quite a bit of getting used to while attempting to merge with such a short accel ramp.
Finally is the parking spots. I have about 1,500,000 trucking miles under my belt in real life hauling everything from lowboys with heavy and oversized earth moving equipment to dry boxes, refers, and flat beds and never have I seen places that are so tough to get into or out of as some of the spots in ATS. It's a challenge, but rewarding once you get it.
All in all, despite it's foibles, I really do love this sim and look forward to playing when I get free time.

I always dreamed of building anything that moves and shoots, I remember building starships in Minecraft, but those couln't move, when I joined steam, I found Robocraft, I liked the game at first, but not anymore with the stupid crate system, I stumbled upon Machinecraft after looking for a sandbox machine building game, and when I looked at the workshop, I knew I hade to give it a shot, I played it and it was like a dream come true even though I wasn't good at it.
The developer is Japanese and he does not speak English, he uses Google Translate, so the translations are, pretty terrible, servers have a maximum of 30 people per room, and there aren't many people online at the same time.
So here's the part why I don't like it and cannot recommend it anymore: an update came changing HP calculation to "surface area to volume", this reduced the HP of my space battleship from 17k to 6k, not too long after that, and update strongly reminicent of Robocraft's "fast and formidable" came out, setting a speed limit on all builds, with 500 km/h being 100% HP, now it is either to go fast and have paper thin HP or to be horribly slow with a decent HP, then, an update to wheels broke many old wheeled machines (I didn't have any), then a recent update removed BOSS_ and broke my space battleship. This makes me question: is the developer following Robocraft?
Anyway, that is just my opinion, I'm running out of good machine building sandbox games to play, and I really wish the [DEV] would read this and take a step in the right direction.

When my friend first opened me to the idea of Paradox games, I wasn't convinced. Civ 5, while an engrossing game, quickly began to bore me. I thought strategy games were not my thing. But my god, I was hooked two hours into EU4. These are some of the most engrossing games I have ever played - they are heroin level like Skyrim or Minecraft. Personally, I find the greatest allure to be the historical factor. It's satisfying to, say, defend the Norman invasion of England and rewrite centuries of European politics or kickstart an independent Netherlands 500 year early.
Along with that, the game stands apart from other Paradox titles in its personality. The focus on dynastic family lines leads to oft hilarious stories of woe and success. (I'll never forget my pitched battle for control against the seven year old duchess of York in my first game as William the Conqueror.)
Complaint wise, the heavy DLC in this game and others irks me: (Want to play a Muslim character? DLC! Pagan? DLC! Indian? DLC!) It limits a huge portion of the game to those who are unable to pay 100+ dollars for it and all the DLCs. Although, this game is definitely the worst example of this practice. Wait for a sale on the base or the DLC collection.
Nevertheless, I HIGHLY recommend for everyone at least remotely into strategy.

It's a pretty game, that starts of fun, but then the grind and tediousness starts to wear in.
You can’t save in dungeons (In fact you can only save at the base), so when you die (Which you will, as enemy’s have one-hit k.o. attacks) you will have to either reset and lose your progress, or wait a ridiculous amount of time for them to heal up, forcing you to use other characters, setting them behind on the grind for them to die again.
There’s no fast travel to the dungeons, in fact once you find a dungeon that’s inside of another dungeon you have to go to the previous dungeon to find the entrance. There are items that let you escape, but they are limited. Now each dungeon has a teleporter, that allows you to teleport to that part of the dungeon, or leave from there. Sound great right? Well there’s a catch, randomly a boss will reappear and guard that point, when that happens you CAN NOT teleport using that. You have to go back, fight the boss, redoing part of the dungeon. Of course this happens after you leave a dungeon so if it’s a teleport that you need to use, have wasting your time.
It’s a shame because this game had a lot of neat features that could have made it great, but in the end there’s so much stuff that I feel is added just to make the game feel longer than it is.

It's not that NIGHT Into Dream is a horrible game, but it's a score attack game that really shined because of a company reaching the 3d plateau.  Yet this game is still highly rated and the honest truth is I can't tell you why.
Maybe it's nostalgia.  People seem to reference a story, I don't know if that's not available in my version of the game or if they're just sniffing glue and watching the wall between levels, but this game lacks quite a bit.   There's no real tutorial, and honestly after learning the "depth" of gameplay (get 20 gems quickly, hit the big bad, repeat 4 times and then kill a boss)   there's not much end of one, but I also don't feel a need to really continue playing the game.  After beating 6 levels, the 7th is locked behind a gate to get a higher score, so I can either replay the levels, that I really didn't enjoy the first time, or go play something else.  I chose to play something else.
The issue for me is the levels are beautiful and colorful and linear.... It's a 3d game where you can't go in the direction of the camera so everything you see behind you is quite... pointless in my opinion.  It's just graphical fluff, the gameplay is just fly around try to combo things, and like I said get 20 gems and hit the enemy, then do it four more times.  There's minimal variety.  The big interesting pieces is the bosses which are all different, but you have two choices, either die while trying to figure out the patter (and go play the monotonous 4 enemies again to get another chance)  Or look up a guide, and find out how simple these bosses are.
Worse most of the bosses don't give you a hint whether you're hitting them the right way or the wrong way, a lot of time it's just repetition but repetition of something that doesn't feel like you're doing anything to them.  So even if you are killing them I don't know if there's a way to tell without looking it up or just trying long enough to win.
People love this, but... I don't know, I feel there's not a great way to track your progress without finishing the part of the level you're on, the controls are fluid in game but the menus suck, the bosses are annoying until you understand them but they don't assist you at all about that (remember when bosses wouldn't even flash when you were actually hitting them)
Honestly I just didn't find it entertaining for more than an hour or two.   I found running 2-4 minute stages to getting to a boss a chore more than a joy, the levels are all rather similar with only one or two interesting moments, and while the bosses were great, there was very little rhyme or reason to why they are my enemies.  I find it hard to recommend.
HOWEVER If you played Nights back in the day, then this game is for you.  It's still nostalgic, it's still amazing, I just don't think there's much here for a new player of the series and as such I have to say I can't recommend it.   Definitely try out some of the more interesting games such as Space Channel 5, or Sonic Adventures but I just can't really recommend this game.
