To put it simply, Machinecraft is like Robocraft crossed with Besiege, only you can build literally anything with very few limits in place.
Want to make a tiny box that murders everything? You can.
Want to make a flying, transforming laser toaster? That too.
Want to build a super accurate car with ALL of the details? Go right ahead!
The possibilities with what you can make in this game are limitless
However, nothing is perfect. This game has two drawbacks; the first of which being the barebones tutorial.
The tutorial is in Japanese, so the only option is to use the subtitles in your native language (usually not translated that well, but it gets the point across).
Once you're done with those and you have a basic idea of the controls, you can start looking at the sample machines (in the _samples folder) to get an idea of the functionality of each aspect of the game.
Did I mention the Workshop support? You can download a huge number of machines built by the community, and either play with them as they are or dissect them and see how they work.
So all things considered, the barebones tutorial isn't that bad.
The only other drawback, I would say, is the number of players. There aren't that many people playing, but those who do tend to play quite consistently, and you'll start to recognise names and make friends very quickly (most players can be really lovely). Plus, as people are trying the game the community is expanding and the game is becoming more populated.
The reason I say this game is like Besiege is not only the fact that individual sections of machines (bodies) can be destroyed, but also the freedom to assign any functional part to any number of assignable buttons, at your convenience.
There is DLC available for this game, in the form of a £7 'donation', in a way. Upon purchase, you gain access to two cosmetic parts: the stamp, and the emitter.
The stamp works by allowing you to paste one (or several) custom image(s) (up to 512x512 pixels, for obvious reasons), onto either the chassis blocks, the whole machine, or just a widely configurable part known as a box, which is simply a giant, or tiny, customiseable cube.
Any questions, feel free to comment on this review and I'll try to answer them.

I'm not quite endgame yet, but I'm definitely far enough in to offer an informed opinion. I HIGHLY recommend Fallen Earth for the compelling stories (even the side quests are pretty captivating at times), advanced crafting, and outstanding player base. Since you've heard rants already, I'll clear up things I feel the other comments got wrong instead:
- This is a post-apocolyptic RPG, but beyond that it has little in common with Fallout. The crafting in Fallen Earth is much more advanced and takes longer (days, sometimes). The V.A.T.S. combat system we know and love from Fallout is not used. Most importantly, the actual story is completely different. So if you want F2P Online Fallout, you're going to miss the mark a little.
- It is nearly impossible to "accidentally wander into" a PVP zone. You will be warned if you approach one and the map marks it with a glaring red zone. In the off chance you're blind enough to wander into one, players above that zone's max level are excruciatingly penalized for being there. So don't worry, you aren'y likely to be killed by another player until you're ready.
- Admittedly, the game is hard to get used to without a guide. There's no sugar-coating it. You know what they say about learning to ride a bicycle, though.
- Finally, while this is just my personal opinion, I think it's hard to consider crafting a hassle when you can literally keep playing while you craft. That engine your building will continue its construction while you shoot blight wolves and collect scraps.
Enough from me, download and try it. I certainly didn't regret doing so.  9/10

NiGHTS into dreams is a decent PC port of a classic Saturn title. Made by Sonic Team was all about making the levels you could speed through quick but have fun with repeated playthroughs. A bit more arcade-y than the famous blue Hedgehog, this is yet another unique idea by Sega that deserved quite a bit more love than it wound up recieving. While Saturn games are becoming increasingly hard to obtain, thanks to Steam it is fairly simple to go back and see what all the fuss is about. If only Sega would do this with more of their titles.
Pros:
* Decent remaster of a reasonably hard to obtain Saturn game.
* The more you play the more fun it is the mess around in the levels.
* Simple oldschool gameplay that is both relaxing and fun, but reasonably challenging to get A ranks.
* Levels are fun to revisit and play around with, incuding the A-Life and high scores.
Cons:
* Extras from Christmas NiGHTS, such as Sonic and Reala not included in the Christmas NiGHTS content. Shame since those are some of the things that made Christmas NiGHTS so cool to begin with.
* 90s level structure means it is a bit short by modern standards.
* While the visuals have gotten a facelift, the camera hasn't.

This is a great game but you need to know who this game is for.
Here are the notes I have that you should know before you purchase:
1. Death is not necissarily perminant but it is VERY time consuming.  Loading after losing a character is a valid but the game also has a mechanic where you can swap out the character for HOURS and get them back later.   So you either lose time from your last save or you swap out the character and try not to get its replacement killed before they are ready to come back.
2. Items are uncommon.  Buying things from the shop is expensive and rarely useful.  Most of the time you get better doing Ambushs.  You may not get much better than a single point of damage improvement for your character for an hour of grinding.
3. Levels are slow.  You will be grinding your levels.  Between havinging to be careful and how slow you gain exp per fight be aware that the you will not be speeding your way through this game.
4. The game seems to have a steep entry curve.  The game is significantly harder early on than it is once you have developed your team and got some divinities to use.
5. Save often.  If you forgot to save before you enter a Labyrinth I recomend tunning around and going back to save.  The game loads quite fast and the loss of a minute or two is worth it.
6. This is a port from the 360 and Vita.  This game is not the most up to date PC graphics or even PC game mechanics.  But it is a good game.
If any of the above points bother you then there are plenty of other games out these you may enjoy better.  If you don't mind the points above and you like Dungeon Crawler RPG's you may find this a fun entry into your library like I did.

Alright, this game has beautiful images but is amateurish in its presentation.  In short the gameplay isn't so good.  The story is blah, nothing special but not horrible.
The problem with gameplay isn't game breaking but it's frustrating.  The inventory isn't sorted for you so it becomes a complete mess over time.  You are forced to have three characters in the front row unlike you opponents, meaning that they will attack, almost exclusively, your weakest character.  Making all your weak guys in the back row move forward and get slaughtered.  The game doesn't explain certain aspects during the tutorial leaving you to figure it out, such as what all that greyed out stuff on your screen is about.  The easy area you start in only becomes easy once you've attained level 5 and had a few of your characters die a few times.  To some that may seem like a great challenge but really it's just poor design, having monsters spawn in in random numbers, one to nine, and with a level varience of 20, it's pathetic.  One fight you could be fighting one level eight monster and the next nine level twenty two's.  You do not level up very quickly either so that level five is going to take some time.  Grinding is very center stage in this game, you get little money over time leaving you with little options when it comes to purchasing items in game.  Items are very rarely dropped by enemies so you must conduct hiding actions in set up areas to ambush large monsters to steal there treasure chest, but you must be quick as they will run away after a few turns.  I really like this feature, but it feels like it may have been included so they could more legitimize the horrible drop rates.
Ultimately this game feels like they delibrately made leveling up and item gains slow so as to provide fluff for a game that otherwise wouldn't be terribly long.  Add to that the rather random difficulty of battles and this whole game feels like it was made by people who didn't know what they were doing.
In conclusion, it will frustrate you but it's not horrible.  Buy it on sale, or buy something else.  Anything over twenty bucks for this game is really not worth it.

At first I was quite concerned with my purchase of this potential game, as time has progressed I have started to notice that among my other early access games with the exception of Gnomoria and Banished, this particular game has now grown to a state where I consider it worthy and playable for an extended amount of time. I particularly am impressed with the amount of new things a hero can do while another does the generic questing. The settlements have now become far more interactive, the shops serve more purpose than just money farming, and the inventory system now seems much more efficient at relating to the player what exactly they have and what it is good for. There are quite a few things left for me to really explore in this game, however it does seem familiar to another game by Kairosoft which I also loved called Dungeon Village, but even so this game is quickly surpassing that in terms of activities and gameplay especially the questing which allows you to choose your type of destiny instead of just accepting what there is already.
for my obligatory rant however, I must say that the interface and specifically the ability to click on a specific object like a dirt road to delete resulted in my accidentally deleting an accessory shop, I would ask that with the opacity option maybe a more refined targetting with my cursor is desired. Also another petpeeve i've developed is with the arbitrary award system at the end of the year. In dungeon village the village and its heros in particular are awarded medals which are actual items that can be used to improve a hero's stats across the board. I'm not suggesting that exact thing but I would prefer something other than numbers and letters at the end of the year as this just does not add anything special to the game for me in particular. Lastly, and remember I have not played through the entire game since the last update but I feel as though the random events could be more than just global modifiers maybe something more interactive or under your control or the option to attempt to control the event would be preferable than just accepting the event as is. I suggest maybe also adding something similar to the dice roll system from epic quests allowing your heros to not only quest for settlements but to have the chance to maybe protect, improve, prevent, etc options for a global modifier event. If they fail the event is worse, if they succeed they improve the modifier, if they do nothing it remains the same as it currently is.
Anyway I will be returning to play this after work, and the game as it has now become and currently is, worthy of purchase and worthy of your playtime. I don't know the developer or what he is working with but I saw a pile of crap spread on an empty canvas become a beautiful painting that still needs a slight touch up. Good work man and please continue to do your best and follow your own vision more so than the people who make suggestions because in the end they bought your game because of your decisions and visions and alot of developers seem to bow down to every crappy suggestion that sounds good on paper but damages the core gameplay that originally attracted that same person who made the suggestion to the game in the first place. tl;dr keep doing your own thing, but stay open minded to suggestions that may still be useful or an improvement to your vision.
Edit: Forgot to mention, I love the settlement of Threepwood, I can't put my finger on why but it seems familiar and friendly to me.

This is a passable port of the PS2 remake but it's a big disappointment that they couldn't make the game run at 60fps instead of 30.
This is especially true since they supposedly lost the source code & decided to make the PS2 version from scratch, which should have been a chance to improve the game.
In that sense it's actually a downgrade from the Saturn original whose 2D backgrounds ran at 60fps, though everything else was still capped at 30.
In fact the port has poor frame pacing which introduces a juddery feel even for a 30fps game.
The controls and mechanics also feel like a step down from the Saturn original, even after a patch added analog movement support.
The remake does improve the graphics, up to roughly the standard you'd expect from a good Dreamcast game & widescreen support is added, but the draw distance is still poor. You also have the option to use the original Saturn graphics, which disables widescreen.
It's a shame that the Link and Time Attack as well as Sonic into Dreams are missing from its version of Christmas NiGHTS.
Sonic's level is easily the least important cut since it plays poorly but it's still content that would've been nice to see preserved since it was the first real taste of what would eventually become Sonic Adventure.
The Link and Time Attack were fun challenges & it would've been especially nice to see more of them with different layouts. That's one of the few things the Wii sequel did right since its Octopaw stages are rather similar to the Link Attack concept.
I think the game itself still holds up well but as a port or remake it's disappointing.

TL:DR - 7/10 Stranger of Sword City is my first dungeon crawler game and I'm quite enjoying it. It gets surprisingly fun and intense at times, with the only downsides being the sometimes insane difficulty spikes and the weird save system where you have to abandon wherever you are, trek back to the capital, and save. Which means you then have to trek all the way back. Definitely a JRPG in that regard. Definitely worth a purchase if it's on sale and you're curious.
Overview:
Stranger of Sword City is a JRPG dungeon crawler. As a new player to the genre this basically means that you build a party of 6 people and traverse the world in first person moving on a grid system. As you move through the world combat occurs through random encounters, which occasionally spawning 'Lineage' monsters. These Lineage monsters are basically just unique enemies that carry inside of them 'Blood Crystals', which are needed to boost you and your chosen God's power.
It's worth noting that these Blood Crystals are also what move the story forward. So you need to make decent use of your Journal > Lineage List to make sure you haven't missed any in an area (as far as I know you can leave one or two behind, just be sure to gather as many as you can to hit the story chapters). Unfortunately this is also where the game can get frustrating at times due to the difficulty spikes and grinding involved, but more on that later.
Story 8/10:
The game starts out with you travelling on an airplane that mysteriously gets teleported from another dimension/world, where it crash lands. Shortly after you learn that you are a 'Stranger' (a human from Earth that has significant power in this other world) and meet Riu, the Commander-in-Chief of the Stranger Guild. Riu then explains the world to you, your power, as well as introducing you to the other characters who then set you off into the world to test out your power and train you.
I'd estimate I'm roughly half way through the game at 30 hours and the story has kept my interest. I think the story is engaging, the characters are interesting, and the world itself - whilst distinctly JRPG - is also worth your time. The plot does a good job of holding your attention by slowly unraveling the mystery that is the source of your powers, the blood crystals, and why you're in this world. The political jousting between the 3 main factions are definitely unique and each has a strong pull to side with them. The game very much operates on a 'there is no right choice, only choice itself' mechanic, which is a nice change and definitely something that holds the game up.
The story is effectively broken down into 'collect x Blood Crystals' to advance, which occasionally changes 'clear this area' or 'slay this'. It does have a contextual reason for doing all this though; the problem is that occasionally it can feel like you were told something, started it, came back the next day... and there's not really a detailed log of what you're supposed to do. So sometimes you can feel a little lost if you're not familiar with the genre. For example: I had received a key to unlock a new dungeon area, except I couldn't use it. I was told I could, but I couldn't. The reason was that I hadn't gone and defeated a boss in a totally unrelated section of the world. The problem was that I was trying to not to fight that boss because I needed more levels to fight him effectively, and I wanted to grind/explore a new area rather than tread familiar ground.
Gameplay 7/10:
The core gameplay mechanics for Stranger of Sword City comes down to building a party of 6 and then pitting them against the world. The classes can have several different 'jobs' which determine their roles in combat, such as defense, attack, support, heal, magic, etc. The classes all play differently and each have their own place in the world. None of the classes feel worthless, which is a good thing. It's worth mentioning that depending on where you are in the world you'll need to take a cleric/wizard due to certain support abilities they have, though.
Each class and job has specific skills and abilities they can use, which you gain through leveling up each character. The powers do get more powerful and interesting as the levels go by, but it can take a very long time of you wishing you had a certain ability, only to get it 6-10 hours later.
The good thing is you can 'auto-apply' skills/abilities in fights to quickly end both your and the enemy's turn. This enables you to blast through the same old fights.
The downside to combat/gameplay is two-fold:
1. The goddamn saving system
If you want to save this game you either have to retrace your steps all the way back to where you entered the dungeon, or use a very expensive butterfly to teleport back to your capital where you can then hard save the game. So if you fight for an hour, and get randomly wiped out, all that progress is lost. Pretty old school. This can be a very frustrating problem because sometimes you'll be fighting in an area with enemies that are your level, just below, or just a bit above. Then suddenly a enemy with 15-20+ levels on you will appear out of nowhere and they will start one shotting you if you don't escape. There are teleport points in the middle of levels, but it can be a struggle reaching them when you're new to an area.
There's a particularly annoying boss fight that is a real struggle about mid way through the game. You defeat her, only to be taken to another stage - without being able to save - where you then fight a second boss who is even stronger. And he will start one-shotting you immediately. All that progress wasted, pretty brutal (and annoying). It just means more, and more grinding, which you know, don't pad games out this way please.
2. The difficulty spikes
The game itself is pretty hard as standard, you've got to be prepared to do some grinding to just make it somewhat easy. This isn't too much of a problem because there are a quite a few large dungeons to fully explore and clear, so you're not quite grinding since you're experiencing something new each time. But there are some fights where you've gotten as far as you can in the world without endless grinding and you just hit a brick wall of difficulty. It's not even about skill, if the boss senses weakness in levels/hp/abilities it'll just start KO'ing at will without mercy.
So you're forced to grind to stand a chance, and even then you'll scrape through. The strange thing is that after that bit the difficulty will go back to normal levels, it gets frustrating and tiring.
Combat is nuanced and there are many tactics and strategies you can use, but you've also got to build an understanding of how certain enemies fight. It's interesting and each new enemy that's introduced keeps you involved enough to keep going through what can at times be a grind.
Graphics/Art 7/10:
If you like that modern Japanese art style, the game is very well done. The character portraits are skillfully drawn and the painted backgrounds/environments in set pieces help pull you into the story more. The game engine itself however... well it's just there to run the combat system I guess. The game engine environments aren't pretty, but to be honest any PC can run this game and it is a dungeon crawler from the PSP, so you can't expect Unreal Engine. The engine graphics do the job, sometimes that's all you need.
Conclusion: 7/10
It's a fun game that will hold your interest and is definitely worth picking up on sale. At full price it's a bit expensive though if you're not familiar with the dungeon crawler genre. If you're curious just as I was pick it up when it's on sale, it's a good buy and it will keep you entertained so long as you overlook the difficulty spikes, the frustrating save system, and the forced grinding.

I came for the trippy atmosphere and stayed to chase A-ratings on every stage.
My first exposure to NiGHTS was a cameo in Sonic Adventure where NiGHTS, the androgynous jester fairy, flies Sonic through a psychedelic dreamscape with trance music playing. The level was colorful, fun, and compelling in an enchanting way -- which brings me to this enhanced version and port of the 1996 game!
NiGHTS Into Dreams pulled me in with its warm setting and upbeat music as expected. Two outstanding tracks include the DnB tune "The Dragon Gave Out a Loud Scream" with a likewise, screaming saxaphone and the "Message from Nightopia" track used in Sonic Adventure. However, what engaged me most were the score-attack mechanics. Controls were simple once I understood what was going on, like driving a super-simplified car for the first time. Next comes racking up points. It feels so satisfying to nail a 25+ combo from flying through rings and orbs at a fast pace. After getting that far, I would feel an adrenaline rush to keep the current string going.
I had some frustrations when it came to boss battles, and it's not about the bosses themselves, but the clock and punishment. Each boss requires a different strategy to beat it, and some are less obvious than others. By the time I learned how to deal with said boss, time was too short to defeat it. When you lose to a boss, the entire stage is over, meaning you must start from the beginning. Not too bad, seeing as the courses prior to the boss take 8 minutes at most but it gives you a shot to get a higher score.
One other complaint is that any mode of movement that was not flying was not as fun, because it took more control of my character than I wanted it to. The worst was a rail platform that slams into NiGHTS and battled with my attempts to swing NiGHTS toward required orbs.
My complaints are however outweighed by enjoying the rest of the game and a fantastic soundtrack to boot. This one is highly recommended, especially since it goes for little over a US dollar during some sales.

One of my favorite recent indie purchases. I replayed some of my favorite paths several times, in the same way I'd reread a short story I liked. The writing is rich and deep - which should be a given for VNs and so often is not. The Prince and Princess premise seems very cliché, but that's only on the surface; once you're past the prologue and the first four chapters, the story goes into highly surprising directions.
Pros:
. Music is fantastic, and works very well with mood of scenes
. Most (though not all) of the characters are well developed and nuanced; their strengths and flaws flow logically into their actions and reactions.
. Well written story and interesting world. I particularly loved the concept of matriarchal inheritance the authors created. Land and wealth are inherited from mother to daugther only; sons get support and a title but no actual inheritance, and so are put in the position of having to win a bride in order to take any kind of place in society and help her manage her estate. Now, getting away from Ye Olde Feudal Europe setting is always appreciated, but this in particular put an interesting spin on story, world and character motivations.
. The main character is fairly well rounded with both strength and weaknesses. Though I just wish she'd been allowed to kick butt and take names just a BIT more often...
. The last path I took was Gaston's, because I didn't like what I'd seen of his character. And his story may not be for everyone, but damn, at the turning point, I actually had a small tear in my eye. It's...surpisingly effective.
Cons:
. Throughout each path, you have maybe 20 choices all told, and only half of them matter. If that. Do NOT play this game because you like complicated every-choice-has-a-consequence game. Once you choose one of four paths, your impact on the game as the player, other than not getting your PC exiled or killed, is actually fairly minimal. THis bugged me at first, but then I decided to treat this like an actual visual novel rather than a real Choice Of type game.
. THough the visual side is pretty limited, actually. THere's a few slides you can get in each path which are very pretty and sometimes quite touching, but most of the time you're looking at fairly bland scenery with sprites standing motionless and talking heads at the bottom. Standard fare for visual novels, true, but not the best part of this one by any means.
. A few choices have pretty weird consequences. Just thinking about a guy is going to make him show up...? A good save/load, backtrack and auto-skip system allows you to fairly quickly undo anything you might regret in hindsight.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 is a pretty good games with a lot of flaws, some of which are just simple bugs that can be patched out. Other issues require some serious rewriting or restructuring of how the game's story and progression works for these aspects to really shine. So, lets get down to it.
The Good:
-The combat is a lot of fun for a turn based game just because of the amount of freedom you get to interact with the battlefield and the enemies you face. Need some cover from ranged fire? Turn the puddle at your feet into a steam cloud with a fire spell. The boss went first, and it ran away towards a high cliff out of the reach of your melee characters? Teleport it down right in the middle of your party and go to town.
-The story and world building is solid, and kept my interest throughout the game. The companion character quest lines are all interesting and tie in to the main story in a cool way for the most part. You have the ability to be a villain if thats your thing, too.
The Meh:
-Skill crafting seems a bit lackluster at the moment, as hybrid skills don't take into account what skills you put in outside of its school and the required school level to use the skills.
-Companions don't really interact with each other, they only interact with your avatar, which kinda sucks if you're used to Dragon Age style back and forths between characters in your party.
-Gear scaling in the middle to later acts is really wacky. Sometimes a 1 level difference in an items required level to use will give you a massive increase in armor or damage stats.
The Bad:
-Mild spoilers: In all fairness, the last act in the game just flat out sucks for large stretches of it, and theres a lot of things that contribute to it being annoying to plow through. First off, theres barely any indication where you're supposed to go throughout the entirety of the first half, which led me to wandering around the tiny city that composes the entirety of the last act, trying to figure out how any of the quests in my quest log were supposed to interact with each other. There are bugs that make some of the fights that take place in the city almost impossible to complete unless you have one spells that clears surfaces, due to the enemies being able to respawn in a surface that for some reason is in a wall. Also, for some reason performance takes a steep dip when you get to the last act, with my consistent 60 frames on my GTX 1050ti dipping to about 15. My last grievance with the last act has more to do with my lack of consistency in remembering to autosave, as theres a lot of instakill and softlock scenarios that happen throughout the last act that don't have predesignated autosaves in areas beforehand, causing me to lose a lot of progress on reloads. Oh well.
-There are a lot of quest and achievement triggers that just don't go off, leading to a lot of quests not completing in your journal.
Overall, I really liked D:OS 2. While the last act sours the experience a bit, the rest of the game is so stellar that I would still highly recommend this game to anyone who likes turn based rpgs, or coop games in general.

Gemini Rue is a point and click adventure game with sparse and limited fighting mechanics in various stages of the game that takes place in a dystopian sci-fi future that could be inspired easily from movies like Blade Runner. As it is expected, you explore the environment and interact with people and objects in order to solve puzzles and eventually proceed. There is also an item called the communicator which lets you communicate with various characters throughout the game but also provides you with all the necessary information and mission status.
You play the role of a man named Azriel who was an ex assassin but now has left his past behind him and works as an officer against the organized crime which is run by a mafia-like group called the Boryokudan. Your formal mission is to aid a man who later helps you on your true mission which is to acquire information about your lost brother Daniel. After infiltrating the Boryokudans and reaviling that there is a secret facility where people are sent there to have their memory whipped out and re-trained to become criminals and that your brother was sent there, you gather your crew and set a new mission, rescuing your brother.
The storyline despite being short is quite compelling and there are nice twists at the end as expected. The overall theme of the game is nicely expressed through the art style with retro like graphics and atmospheric music. However, I would really prefer it if instead the 16 bit overlay the visuals were a little more detailed. In comparison, the audio quality is really impressive for being an indie game. The audio logs are rich and clearly there was put a lot of effort into it. So, the audio and visuals are not side by side in my opinion.
All in all, Gemini Rue is a solid adventure game following the steps of the classic ones, yet it feels fresh and modernized. All friends of the adventure genre should definitely try out this game.

I'm a student enrolled in truckdriving school. This game has been rather instrumental in demonstrating some of the proper maneuvers and whatnot in regards to semi-truck driving. Reading about a "button hook" turn and actually getting to kind of see it in action through simulation are two incredibly different things. The game has been incredibly helpful in allowing me test a lot of things out, although it is obviously by no means a substitute for being behind the wheel of an actual semi.
CONS
---I find the weigh stations to be far too simplistic and serving relatively little to no function ingame. You pull in on the scale and you automatically pass the gross weight. I think that it should be possible to actually end up being overweight, then the weigh stations would actually carry with them the dread that most truck drivers face. Afterall, the purpose of the weigh station is to find truck drivers who are hauling overweight loads and put them out-of-service. For drivers who -are- overweight, more rural routes to try and bypass the weigh station as certain... rogues tend to do, would also be excellent.
---The speeding fines are ridiculous. I mean, I obviously know the game isn't NASCAR simulator or something. I'm playing the game for the purpose of trying to get an idea of how the trucks handle around turns. With that being said, the truck will on occasion speed up going downhill or the speed limit might change faster than you can safely slow the truck down... and you end up getting slapped with a freaking fine for being only like 3 - 5 miles over the speed limit. (A fellow steam user has pointed out that this is actually pretty realistic though.)
---Gameplay becomes repetitive. Mods that add in a multiplayer mode do help the replayability, but at the expense of no AI traffic. Neither of these two things are that big of a deal for me, but it might be for some other people.
PROS
---It's possible to go into settings and try to simulate how the airbrakes function in the real world. I've found this to be fun to tinker around with. It's an example of one of the many little features that the game includes that you can toggle on or off depending upon how serious you are about your overall simulating experience.

---AI drivers will perform hilariously ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥gish maneuvers just like in the real world. No, I don't mean that they're horrible drivers or incapable of following the law. They instead do something that's pretty common with a lot of drivers I've seen in Georgia. They'll be in a hurry to pass you, merge in front of you and cut you off, and then you'll see them end up jumping on the exit and speeding up to the stop sign. Like IRL, the AI drivers are sometimes in a hurry to go nowhere. Having to react to crap like that really puts the perception distance + reaction distance + braking distance rules into effect to avoid creating an accident ingame.
I'm still experimenting with a lot of stuff ingame, but these are some of the pros and cons I've found in regards to how "realistic" the game is on a whole. I definitely recommend this game if you're into that sort of thing. It's more of a learning experience, more than anything, but it can be pretty fun too at times.

*They removed the sheets of enemy and hero stats, now the stats are simplyfied to; Attack, defense, armor, magic def, ranged def,

Despite some infuriating aspects I really enjoy this game.
It is Dungeon Keeper reborn for a new age and I love that. Im also a huge fan of the added complexity and depth introduced by potions and the construct system for example.
The game is being constantly updated and that always seems to help. The version im playing now is VASTLY superior to the one I played in 2013.
One of my biggest frustrations has always been and continues to be the combat. Its. SO. Frustrating. Whther you're trying to claim one tlie only for the AI to drop their entire army on you or not being able to really tell which of your minions are good at what in combat so you resort to just throwing them all at an enemy. I like the units but the more esoteric naming leads to a lack of transparency in the power of certain units DK kept its classes relatively simple for a reason, while I love the creativity of the new creatures, it doesnt strike me as a good idea game design wise.
The other biggest frustration...and this is just a horribly bad design idea all round as far as I can see. Is that you can no longer pick your creatures up if they are not on your territory. This has led to me having to slap my creatures to death on mroe than one occasion as there is a lot of creatures that roam freely into enemy territory and will stay there....fighting....until they die....giving the enemy creatures free experience. When killing your own creatures becomes a valid strategy....something has gone horribly wrong. I can understand it being there for Multiplayer, but in Singleplayer its just annoying.
Im marking it as recommend because I do love what theyve done and what theyre trying to do. And I have confidence in the developers to fix issues. However my experience with the game is mostly frustration due to the combat at this point. Other reviews mention the frantic pacing and the lack of time available to actually....keep a dungeon, this does hold somewhat true in places, particularly the main campaign. And I think this issue is exaspartated by the frustrating combat whenever a foe is actually encountered.
Thats my only issues really, fix up the combat to be a bit less "throw things at them" and let us pick up our goddamn creatures when in singleplayer.
When it comes to updates maybe the developers should focus less on adding new game modes and fixing fundamental issues that - in my opinion - have existed since day one.
And this is a very personal thing to me....but I loved the slight colour tinge/grade on the dungeon in Dungeon Keeper 2 and Id love to see that in WFTO, something that makes it less....brown.
Apart from those (not insignificant issues). Yeah. You can have a lot of fun with this. I do :p

Before establishing Steamified I had many discussions with friends over what I wanted the site to accomplish and what developers and publishers I would like to forge relationships with. One of my closest friends is an RPG aficionado who practically begged me to get Aldorlea Games on board. The publisher, he advised, was one of his favorites because they gave indie RPG developers a chance to be noticed as well as developing some of the more popular and better RPGs on Steam. He pointed out the fact that their Millennium series was one of the more popular RPG franchises on the platform. However, it’s just a simple fact that some developers and publishers take a bit longer to get to work with. Sometimes you need to demonstrate a portfolio before a company will take notice. This was the case with Aldorlea Games. We simply had to put up some quality early content and have some positive feedback from developers and publishers that we were working with before they would come on board. However, once they did come on board with Beyond Reality they have been supportive.
Initially it was an older title that I was hoping to work with – Beyond Reality had yet to be released – so I was taken aback when they asked if we would provide some exposure to their latest title. They decided to jump in from the deep end with us and for that we’re appreciative. Beyond Reality is one of the best titles that Aldorlea Games have published to date. That it is the first game to be developed by EternalShadows Studio speaks volumes to the talent of their developers. The premise of Beyond Reality has you taking on the crew of  the Alpha Omega Company in a game world where science meets magic. You must find the secrets behind the realities of life that your crew has always known in order to put an end to a war, pollution and to rewrite history.
The introduction to the game sets a fantastic tone for the entirety of the game. Many RPGMaker games I find can suffer from hideously slow beginnings that provide poor attempts at offering a tutorial at the costly expense of establishing a good story. The developers have found a way to provide both simultaneously. Beginners to RPGMaker games will be able to pick up the whys and the how to’s of the engine very easily while seasoned veterans will be able to immerse themselves into the game play very quickly making it an ideal game for both levels of gamers, a rare treat indeed.
I’ve long been a fan of games that tackle real world issues head on in a way that is not overbearing or out welcoming but hammer home points that they want to make in a succinct and intelligent manner. The game handles the topics of science and pollution with aplomb. I was definitely skeptical at first as to how this would be tackled as the topic of pollution isn’t one that is very often covered in gaming. EternalShadow Studios weaves the important points that they want to make into the story line of the game in a thought provoking and succinct manner that pushes the strengths of the story without ever taking anything away from the game. I appreciate that as a rare feat of excellence.
What a pleasant surprise to see a different graphical and artistic style than regular RPGMaker games. From time to time developers will attempt to offer some innovation to the artwork in games and to be different. There is a tremendous amount of risk associated with innovation in gaming and the result much of the time is an unfortunate one. However,  I really do enjoy the artwork in this game. It provides a different tone and level of ambiance than other games do.
I want to take a moment to offer my appreciation for the early option to choose fantasy or modern character names and there are even examples provided of some of the main characters in the game. This was a very nice touch. Often times I find fantasy names to be grating. It was nice to have the choice to play as Blayze instead of Le’tainafae (the latter I made up).
At full price Beyond Reality sits at $4.99. Until the 16th of January the  game is $3.49. I argue that Aldorlea Games could easily have set a higher price for the game as I consider the game to be a quality purchase even at full price. At the sale price you’re laughing. If you’re in any way an RPG fan then there is much to like about Beyond Reality.

The original Majesty game was great fun and occasionally challenging, then comes Majesty 2 which breaks the entire concept and turns it into a frustrating mess where trial and error are par for each repetitive level.   The biggest problems with Majesty 2 is the fact that the game is exceptionally grindy for a so-called Fantasy Kingdom Sim...which it isn't at all.
You can barely get a minutes breath without being constantly attacked by swarms of monsters attacking you from every angle, whilst your so called heroes are usually all dimwitted or just plain greedy especially when a high level monsters appear, and it doesn't take long for some nasty ones to appear....base defenses are completely useless, they are destroyed extremely fast so most missions are really only beatable if you zerg - zerg - zerg all the objectives as soon as possible, any focus on building your kingdom is a waste of time and ultimately will cause you to lose as soon wave after wave of ever increasingly difficult monsters start attacking your town.
The biggest and most game breaking issue with Majesty 2 is severe balance issues,  some missions feel like they rushed when they were designed, or perhaps lack of sufficient playtesting?    Overall, Majesty 2 isn't really that 'hard' per say, its more like finding one strategy for each map/mission that works and sticking with it, usually every other method results in  failure and frustration for the player.

If you’re looking for an example of an RPG Maker game done right, you’re going to enjoy this game.
Beyond Reality is one of those games that manages to take a fairly simple set of systems, and do them well enough to stand out. I wouldn’t say it’s a challenging game by any means, but there is enough exploring and battling to make it worth a play.
Plot-wise, I was hooked in pretty quickly by the intro, and the rest of the game did a nice job of carrying the story. I always had a pretty good idea of where I was going, and never ran across any problems when I took a little time to explore. A major thing I noticed is that the characters could’ve used a little more development, though. I got enough of a sense of them to understand most of their personalities, but not enough to grow attached to any of them.
As far as graphics go, this game definitely lands on the better end of what you’ll find in RPG Maker. The mapping, while not always spectacular, was done well, and you can tell there was thought put into each location. There are a lot of little things that enhance the atmosphere, too - footprints in the sand and snow, splashing in the water, etc. - just a few little touches to compliment the scenery. I appreciate that many different packs of graphics were used and combined, so we weren’t stuck staring at the default graphics. The character sprites weren’t anything particularly exciting, but they fit the portraits and settings well.
I had a bit of trouble with battles early on, but that’s on me for not keeping track of equipment upgrades. None of the fights weren’t exactly challenging (I rarely lost a character), but the front-view system was put together well. If things are getting too easy, you also have the option of avoiding enemies or running away, if you want to. I never found the battles tedious enough to run away from, though.
Besides that, the music and sound effects were chosen well, though nothing particularly stood out to me. The attack/battle start sounds do get a bit annoying after a while, but that’s mostly because the same sound is used in a lot of RPG Maker games.
Overall, if you’re looking for a short and sweet RPG, you won’t be disappointed.

I love the cover art/promotional material for this game, but man...
*PROS*
- Sleek GUI/Menu
- Attention to detail (footprints, added effects, etc.)
- Lovely mapping (for the most part)
*CONS*
- Poor story progression/character development

: You're thrown into this game - and so many random things happen within the first 15 minutes you're going to have next to no clue what's going on. A bad dream with no relevance really, a girl in a crystal (where that came from I don't even  know), an S-Rank spell that transports you back in time and disingenuous reactions to that situation just made me go "uh..." - I mean, it just all seems so poorly fleshed out/cheesy. And why is the "most powerful mage in the world" far less powerful than your second recruited mage?
- Dialogue needs some polishing.

: It's not awful, don't get me wrong - but there's a lot of repetition and name-dropping which makes the dialogue rather boring at times. My advice to the dev is to implement some flavor text/exploration-based text throughout to strengthen the lore/situational awareness (like why Asha was in the crystal...that happened far too quickly).
- Bugs. Mostly with passability (having to restart game because the guard won't move past you in Herador) - but I had a script error in battle that I wasn't able to replicate.
- Boring battles

: The "attack, get hit" repetition goes on far too long in most battles - maybe they get better as you progress and unlock new abilities? I'll have to see...
I was really excited for this - and kind of sad that it fell so short. I'm going to continue playing - and hopefully I find some charm/a reason to fall in love...but as it stands right now - I can't recommend this one.

First off, I've played this game a few times already, so it's great to finally see this game on steam.
Pros:
Good Story - I like the characters and the general idea of this title. It's thought provoking and while some improvements could be made in character development, it doesn't take too much away from the over all experience
Music - Now I know this game doesn't have any original pieces but none-the-less, the tracks were well chosen.
RPG Maker - I myself am working on an RPG Maker game, I make this a pro because it's always good to see a decent or good RPG Maker game make it onto steam. Is this the best RPG Maker game? No. But, is it worth the purchase price, sure! You can tell from the mapping and the story that a lot of thought and work went into this title given the engine it was built in.
Cons:
Character Development - the game is fairly short, and the orignal was even shorter. The developer did a great job extending the story line for this version of the game but it sometimes feels like the charcters could use more depth and weren't... filler. But, again, not the worst by far out there.
Mapping - "Wait, didn't you mention mapping in your pros?" Yes, I did. as good as the mapping is in this game, for a commercial product, and I thought hard about this, it could be better. By that I mean, lighting and atmosphere. It lacks in those departments and I know the power of RPG Maker is limited, but there are solutions to this problem. I suggest the developer to consider some broader techniques for his future projects, especially commercial ones.
Battle System: I personally don't like the battle system as much as others, and the animations are pretty copy and paste. I would prefer to see a little more effort in this portion of an RPG. It's no where near as bad as MANY rpg maker games that I've played, but since this is a commercial product, custom animations and a more unique battle system would have been a nice touch.
Overall, I recommend this game. Having played the orginal and a couple versions of the current copy, it's not a bad game. The asking price is fair for something that can be finished in 5-7 hours. I'd love to see what the dev can make with a newer engine and some custom resourses!

Like several other reviewers I´m put off because this can hardly be called a strategy game anymore.
Yes, the developers were extremely unlucky with their campaign, Heart of Gold and lots of Steam-workshop-levels are much better.
But the major problem for me is that fighting Empire is just boring because it´s always the same. Gets worse if you encounter lots of traps: They don´t do much damage, but it takes you ages to get through if fortified with Ramparts. Personally, I just send my Archon there to destroy them, do something else and take a look after an hour or so how my attack goes. How about more trap damage and less resistance?
Dungeon Keeper 1 was fun for me when I played against a good AI-keeper because different to Empire other keepers could surprise you. You had to be quick to get rooms, neutral creatures, gold etc. without letting your defences down. Of course, the Dungeon Keeper AI was just♥♥♥♥♥♥ But you could write a skript with events for each map to determine their behaviour, ressources and to let them respond to your strategy.
WFTO doesn´t give you any of those possibilities. The AI will always try to dig to you and attack you, even if it is seriously weaker than you. No chance to set it to "builder", "defensive" etc. So it´s always the same: Rush to train your creatures, build rooms to get good fighters, wait to retaliate the first attack and then destroy your opponent. Very boring. Might be better if you played against 2,3 or 4 AIs, but I´m already glad the game runs more or less on my brandnew (!) system if I play against 1 on a medium map (basic system requirements far more than matched). The developers obviously didn´t want us to be able to turn off at least  some of the most ressource consuming features like light effects, smoke, distortions... So be really careful: Unless your computer was made for gaming and is rather new, you won´t be able to play at least two third of the maps here on Steam.
But even on these small or medium maps the game play isn´t much fun. Personally I think it´s a good idea to have Siege Shrines that allow you to dig through enemy walls if you´re playing with Replacement Earth. Otherwise it would be really frustrating. But I simply don´t understand why you and the AI are able to dig through walls even without, provided a little time. And it finally gets totally ridiculous if an Underminer, a low (!) level construct, can wipe away enemy walls in quite a range. So just don´t bother with fortifying your dungeon, it isn´t worth anything. It´s arm-as-fast-as-possible and clash, no other way of playing possible.
Building a dungeon is fun because of the nice graphics and challenges provided by the terrain. For me it´s the part I like best in WFTO. But I haven´t discovered DK-Features like "Lair Enemy" which forced you to build your dungeon differently according to the creatures you get in order to avoid deadly arguments. Would have been really nice to have Food Enemies, Tavern Enemies and so on instead of always building the same standard-dungeon. What ever happened to Sorcerers killing Imps so you had to place your Library really carefully?
Different to DK you have more possibilities of micro management here, but I can´t really handle them: If I place a Cultist in the Sanctuary to pray for gold so I can build faster, it will often simply return to the Library and I only lost research time. Maybe I´m doing something wrong, but I finally gave up trying.
Creature management is the next big issue that puts me off. Lots of different creature menues to choose, but no possibility to have the classic-DK-menue where you had an overview what your creatures were doing, who was idle and who fighting. Sometimes I´m unable to pick creatures from the menue if they are fighting. Earth tiles under the buttons get accidently clicked all the time. Impossible to keep creatures in your Hand of Evil while you perform other tasks. Absolutely no idea what to do with angry creatures: In DK I could put them into the Temple to cool down. Tried to give them gold, but my Hand of Evil is always in line of sight so I mostly miss. Couldn´t see that much difference if managed though. Now I just transform them into gold (most times accidently transforming innocent creatures around as well due to very laggy gameplay). So there´s no real motivation to level-up my creatures, it´s easier to replace them if needed. Therefor I finally gave up playing with Vampires, too: Bad enough that they kill your valuable prisoners if you´re not quick enough (or gameplay laggs too much), but I can´t find a way to keep them occupied without Guard Posts, so they always start feeding on my other creatures - and they complain all the time! No total number of creatures (own and opponent´s) to tell you if it would be wise to attack. Or to give you an idea how big your army is, because in big maps they do not all respond to rally flags. Even on small maps I can´t flip through my different creature types (due to laggy gameplay?): Menue always simply jumps from the first to the last creature. This way I can´t really play with Beasts because I can´t pick them up for the Arena.
And, of course, no battle menue. The only thing to give you an overview while fighting in DK with the possibility to cast spells directly on specific targets. So now just hope you´ve got more creatures, send them to battle and pray to the Gods of the Underworld. Strategy? No, action seems more important. Lots of screams and lights and keepers trying to desperately hit enemies with lightning-bolts without any success because the game jumps more and more frames. How about hot keys for spells also? At least that would stop the screen from scrolling all the time you try to cast a spell and the game already lags like hell.
In several posts the developers tell us that the game is so ressource-devouring because of all the waypoints your computer has to calculate for creatures. So it definitely was a good idea to have heroes not always heading for your Dungeon Heart but simply staying where they are. But on the other hand the developers take any chance from us to reduce possible paths - f.e. by making walls indestructible without a Siege Shrine or by my most favourite trick in DK: Build a Temple- or Guard Post-tile directly next to water or lava and the height distance will be too big for non-flying enemies. That way you can (provided with Lava or Water Traps) even create one-way-roads.  So how about a Step Construct?
And if you want to have really thrilling competitions with other keepers instead of one big battle you should give us the opportunity to fight several small battles at once to weaken the opponent. WFTO goes a step into that direction by introducing shrines and Titans. But the game needs much more of that! Make a Titan Shrine as the only place where players can summon a Titan. Make shrines that greatly expand your mana or increase your mana regeneration. Make rooms that cannot be built but must be discovered. And then give us back the old Invisibility Spell for our Imps, so we can annect and instantly sell all these valuable rooms if not guarded by creatures who can detect invisible enemies! That would be a way to really bring DK into this decade.
And, last point: What was the idea to make dungeons  almost completely independet from gold? Nice to have rituals and spells for gold in the beginning because they really speed up building your dungeon. But training creatures should always cost gold! Only then is there a chance to starve out your opponent. Only then you are forced to keep digging into new regions instead of just staying at home to build only Beast Dens and throw your beasts constantly into Arenas.
Obviously the developers expected very different things from a DK-remake than me, but I couldn´t find out what exactly, apart from impressive graphics and sounds. Looks to me like they had so many ideas that they lost their golden thread.

This is actually a pretty enjoyable RPG! The story was interesting enough to keep me engaged, and the gameplay was quite fun.
The story has a time-traveling element to it and I always like those. It may be a bit slow after the intro, but after you get through a few dungeons (which are comfortably short enough), it picks up the pace. The game actually gets better the further you play, and I especially like the scenes toward the end of the game.
Battles were quite fun, despite the simple turn based battle system. Most battles don't last very long, so you won't get bored of fighting. Fights are balanced well, a bit on the easy side but it does have its challenging moments.
There are also no random encounters, and encounters are placed around the map instead. This gives you a choice whether you want to fight or not. It makes exploring much more comfortable.
The spacing of the map areas are also nicely done, it doesn't feel like it's tedious to travel. This is also helped by the fact that enemies are on-map and you can try to run around them but they do chase you! (quite a bit effectively IIRC)
The scenery is well-done, various climates from snow fields to deserts. I also like the little details such as effects when you step on certain terrain such as sand or shallow water, and you leave footprints and splash the water, respectively.
There are a few puzzles here and there which are simple enough to understand (you won't get frustrated), and there are sidequests which include hunting for certain monsters, and they drop valuable equipment. They're quite fun to do.
The character art is great, and the music sounds beautiful and fits well, especially in the final scenes of the game. That was EPIC.
I suggest to play the game using the highest resolution, so you can see the entirety of the maps and have dialogue efficiently placed (it looks much better that way).
Overall, this is a pretty good RPG Maker game. A simple one, yet fun. I'd recommend to give it a try.

Nights into Dreams is a score attack game that is overflowing with 90's Sonic Team creativity. Unlike the later game Nights: Journey of Dreams, there are no cutscenes or minigames in NiD. The goal of each level is to free your four ideya from a device along the track by putting in 20 blue orbs before time runs out, all while racking up points. After the fourth ideya is brought back to the ideya palace, players face that level's unique boss. The game does not tell you how to beat these bosses, and the level will have to be replayed from the beginning should you run out of time. I suggest looking up the boss battles if you really struggle with them. Beating the boss quickly is ideal, as it will increase you multiplier (up to two times the the score from thr main stage) and earn you a higher rank (F being the worst, A being the best).
This is a great game if you don't mind repeating levels to get better at them. The levels are beautiful (keeping in mind, it is a 32-bit console era game) and creative, the music is wonderful and varied. The complete lack of instruction can be irritating before you learn the game but after that it's very straightforeward and just a matter of figuring out how to improve you score. I would very highly recommend playing this with a controller with a joystick instead of with a keyboard. Seriously, save yourself the frustration on this one.

This is Dungeon Keeper 3.
It retains the charm and familiarity of the original games; you tag the earth, imps mine out rooms, a host of evil creatures are attracted to your dungeon, plenty of heroes are killed (or tortured) and the always welcome tones of Richard Ridings (the mentor from DK1 & 2) will once again guide you on your way to conquering the underworld.
Only there’s more of everything this time around. More creatures to attract and convert, more rooms, more traps, and the addition of potions, rituals and constructs. There are more game modes alongside the main campaign, including crucible mode where you can fight endless and increasingly difficult waves of enemies, there are sandbox and scenario levels (and you can create your own in the map editor) and multiplayer and skirmish levels.
And the developers are still working on more, pet dungeons have been announced and are going to be added soon and who knows what might come after that.

Beyond Reality is a very solid rpg that follows the classic style ---- featuring the same mechanics and the same elements but with a different visual style that works very well and is easy to learn and get into the game immediately.
Several choices are offered at the beginning to suit your personal taste including screen size and even the selection of "fantasy" or "modern" names for your characters. So make your choices and get into an interesting, imaginative, and absorbing story.
As you begin you are taken back 2000 years in time to a land called Jastamune to resolve the complications of the conflict taking place ---- not much time to ponder the why, just start the quest through differing locations such as caves, mines, forests, and castles ---- all of which have different treasures and secrets to find. You can fight the battles you choose among the many types of enemies or escape (if you're quick). You'll want to explore very carefully, though, to find all the treasures containing weapons, money, potions, etc.
Scenery is beautifully done, and the music is varied and excellent throughout the game.
So give this one a chance ---- especially at the very reasonable sale price ---- and you'll have a winner. Recommended, for sure.

(this is the first time i've played this game)
NiGHTS into Dreams is a beautiful game. There's just something about flying around as NiGHTS that just feels so... good. Collecting those orb things, making loops with the ribbons... it's just really nice.
That being said, there are some issues with the game itself.
Firstly, the lack of tutorial. I'm playing this with a keyboard (no other alternative), and I spent 10 minutes working out how to move and attack. It just dumps you onto the menu. No opening cutscene, not even a bit of dialouge, no explanation as to what you're supposed to even do in the levels. I know this game is supposed to be vauge, but c'mon! At least explain the controls!
Secondly (and I know this was probably due to the programming limitations at the time and the fact that 3D games were kinda a new thing in the original verson), the animation of the two children is just kinda... ridiculous. It looks really weird. I'm playing the re-mastered version, and I dunno, it just kinda irks me that they didn't even bother to make it look less derpy.
Finally, the boss fights. No explanation as to HOW you're supposed to defeat them - again, I get the game wants you to figure out this stuff by yourself, but with an extremely tight time limit and no explanation, it just frustrates me that you have to restart the entire freakin' level if you run out of time.
Also the time limits but that's because I'm the kind of person who completely forgets about objectives and always gets lost and distracted by beautiful maps.
Anyway, that over, this game is... an experience. Even with all my issues around it, I still highly recommend it. It's just the feeling of flying around in a crazy dream world that I've never experienced in any other game.
Lastly, I think it'd be better played with a controller (as it was designed for a console), and I would recommend for first time players to look up a guide to familiarize themselves with the controls before starting if they wanted to.

TL:DR- If you like the JRPG combat format, this is the game for you.
(First Reaction- game not yet complete)
Aesthetics-
The aesthetics of this game are miraculous. The game has two sepparate art directions you can choose from. First is the gorgeous artwork of Tsukamoto Yoko, a realistic style that breathes life into the characters. You can also choose the artwork of Oxijiyen, whose artwork leans on a cartoonish style. The ability to choose between these two, and the fact that you can choose both simultaneously, allows the player to choose which style(s) that the player wishes to explore the world with.
The art for the world is not quite at the same level though. Backdrops in fights are interesting, but not near the level of finese Tsukamoto gives to the characters. While difference areas of a dungeon do have their own backdrops, there is no variance in a single area. This matters because the game requires grinding in order to efficiently progress. The world, it feels, is one of the most neglected characters of this game.
The art for the dungeons is abysmal. The texture quality is terrible, a quality that is amplified due to the quality of the character art that is visible while traversing these dungeons.
Gameplay-
The Gameplay is twofold. There is no innovation on the surface of this game: it appears as a standard JRPG. What sets this game apart is the power the player has over the characters. The player has complete control over every member of the party, allowing the player to choose the class and stats of all party members. Characters may also have their class changed, which allows the character to take the knowledge they gained from their previous class, and use some of that with the new class. This system allows for the intellegent creation of hybrids, allowing each of your characters to truly develop into someone who can rightfully claim themselves as a member of the Chosen One's party.
The system may be fantastic, but the controls for the game are awful. The PC port is lackluster, with very little attention given to allow comfortable controlling with Mouse and Keyboard. The clanky controls really detract from the game: f.e. menus that do not have a leave option, so the player has to press Esc to return to a previous menu.
Character creation is absolutely awful. Additional Starting Stat Points for characters is based on an RNG roll that is weighted towards low stats. This does not add to the player's experience in any positive way. Either the player sinks a lot of time attempting for a high roll, or the character that is created is objectively weaker than a character that got a higher roll. This is only multiplied by the fact that the player can maintain a roster of 16 player created characters, all of whom may vanish due to the permadeath mechanic present in the game.
One point that may be a con against this game for some people is the grind. I lost my very first playthrough, on the first lineage (without Riu), because I did not grind levels and gear. I have had a blast grinding for gear and levels, due to the "hiding" mechanic, but this is not the game for people who do not enjoy the JRPG combat style, as you will be need to grind many a trash mob with the system.
Narrative-
The story is very stereotypical. You play as The Chosen One, who entered a fantasy world due to mysterious circumstances. It is your duty to fufill your role as a chosen one... we get it.
The interesting part of the narrative are the characters. Specifically the other Chosen Ones and the Vessels. These characters have great personalities, and the voice actors do a really good job embodying these personalities.
Unfortunately, the great freedom the gameplay gives the player hampers the story. The MC may be a silent protagonist, but the MCs companions are emotionless puppets who have no effect at all on anything. They are merely there to aid the MC accomplish the role of a Chosen One.
Music-
Uninspiring. For me the test on a soundtrack is "Would I buy this sepparately?" and the answer is a stern "No." No single track stands out, and I find myself listening to other music while grinding.
Verdict-
If you enjoy the JRPG combat format, this is the game for you. Otherwise, you may want to pass it up. Obnoxious controls, lackluster dungeon art, and really terribly designed character creation put stains on an otherwise enjoyable JRPG experience.

I liked this game A LOT. Intuitive, intriguing, humorous, relatively well written... You should note that even though this is a "choose your oen adventure" it's still predominantly a visual novel. It's a lot of reading, and not a ton of choice making (especially in the first half). All the same, it's quite enjoyable. Although there are (I think?) 15 different endings/tracks, there are only four that are REALLY different-- the others are variations of the four; however, with every track you take you get a bit more of the story, so you do have to complete pretty much all the endings for the the full circle of the plot. The characters are charming and unique to themselves, and each route is pleasing in a different way. (Gaston's was my favorite; very odd and humorous.) The main character is well-rounded and intelligent-- -something that I like to see in a female protagonist.
The replay-ablity is pretty good. The first and the third chapter (which are story heavy) are nearly the same no matter the track, so they can be a bit tedious to get through, but the other 8 (or so?) will be different. The soundtrack is lovely; the art is strong in someplaces, and just sorta ok in others. This is also definitely not a dating sim, as many visual novels are. Several of the endings have a romance attached to them, but its hardly the focal point of the game.
My first playthrough took me about 2.5 hours. I'm sure you could go faster if you are more focused than I was (I was on a train with many distractions.)
I paid full price for the game, I do not regret that. I would do it again.
For people wondering if this is like Long Live the Queen: No. Its not strategy based for one thing. The emphasis on this is all story, not survival-stat-building. However, the quality I would say is the same.

Gemini Rue Review
A Noir-sci-fi point and click adventure game, Gemini Rue is the project of sole developer Joshua Neunberger. headlining hand-drawn backgrounds spanning several planets and locations, and an expansive story, Gemini rue has won numerous awards for its story and style.
The story drags you in right from the start, beginning with a man in a chamber (i won't say any more than that) and then immediately switching to someone waiting under a shelter in the rain. The atmosphere is thick, accentuated by the quiet Noir soundtrack and the ever-pouring rain. The puzzles are good, with the occasional frustrating pixel hunt.
With two story threads, and the ability to switch between them, the game never really gets boring; if you get tired of one character, you can easily switch to the other. The game has voice acting, which is surprisingly good for an indie game. The dialogue is decent, and the pixel art suits the game.
Once you have finished the around 6-7 hour story, you can enable developer commentary, which gives you an inside look at the development process as well as some funny bloopers. I played first on Windows, but i decided to try developer commentary on mac, and discovered how buggy it was. The cursor stuck to the edges of the screen, you had to option-click for right click, and you couldnt scroll your inventory. Now for the pros and cons list.
pros:
+Excellent atmosphere
+great, engaging story
+passable voice acting
+decent artwork and style
+good developer commentary
+ambient noir soundtrack
+different main characters
cons:
-slightly clunky interface
-some puzzles are mindless pixel hunts
-buggy on mac
final score:
9.5/10

I'm a student enrolled in truckdriving school. This game has been rather instrumental in demonstrating some of the proper maneuvers and whatnot in regards to semi-truck driving. Reading about a "button hook" turn and actually getting to kind of see it in action through simulation are two incredibly different things. The game has been incredibly helpful in allowing me test a lot of things out, although it is obviously by no means a substitute for being behind the wheel of an actual semi.
CONS
---I find the weigh stations to be far too simplistic and serving relatively little to no function ingame. You pull in on the scale and you automatically pass the gross weight. I think that it should be possible to actually end up being overweight, then the weigh stations would actually carry with them the dread that most truck drivers face. Afterall, the purpose of the weigh station is to find truck drivers who are hauling overweight loads and put them out-of-service. For drivers who -are- overweight, more rural routes to try and bypass the weigh station as certain... rogues tend to do, would also be excellent.
---The speeding fines are ridiculous. I mean, I obviously know the game isn't NASCAR simulator or something. I'm playing the game for the purpose of trying to get an idea of how the trucks handle around turns. With that being said, the truck will on occasion speed up going downhill or the speed limit might change faster than you can safely slow the truck down... and you end up getting slapped with a freaking fine for being only like 3 - 5 miles over the speed limit. (A fellow steam user has pointed out that this is actually pretty realistic though.)
---Gameplay becomes repetitive. Mods that add in a multiplayer mode do help the replayability, but at the expense of no AI traffic. Neither of these two things are that big of a deal for me, but it might be for some other people.
PROS
---It's possible to go into settings and try to simulate how the airbrakes function in the real world. I've found this to be fun to tinker around with. It's an example of one of the many little features that the game includes that you can toggle on or off depending upon how serious you are about your overall simulating experience.

---AI drivers will perform hilariously ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥gish maneuvers just like in the real world. No, I don't mean that they're horrible drivers or incapable of following the law. They instead do something that's pretty common with a lot of drivers I've seen in Georgia. They'll be in a hurry to pass you, merge in front of you and cut you off, and then you'll see them end up jumping on the exit and speeding up to the stop sign. Like IRL, the AI drivers are sometimes in a hurry to go nowhere. Having to react to crap like that really puts the perception distance + reaction distance + braking distance rules into effect to avoid creating an accident ingame.
I'm still experimenting with a lot of stuff ingame, but these are some of the pros and cons I've found in regards to how "realistic" the game is on a whole. I definitely recommend this game if you're into that sort of thing. It's more of a learning experience, more than anything, but it can be pretty fun too at times.
