You will run at a high level player only for him to kill you immediately without being able to process how he did it, and it will inspire you to be like him.
Chivalry is a game about mechanics. It throws away any subtle advantages through a perk system prevalent in most modern multiplayer games.
This is a game more about swinging your sword - you must try to get past your opponents block while maintaining your own, all while a battle rages around you.
There's something worth playing here for both serious and casual gamers. The combat depth is simplified and more forgiving in large scale fight sequences, while it can ramp up to an extreme as fewer people are involved.
Being team-based, individual skill matters a lot less. You may get a large amount of kills or have the highest score if you're better, but it doesn't guarantee a win. In this game your just a single foot soldier among many.
If you want to improve the depth of the combat goes much deeper - reverse overheads, ripostes, dragging, matrixing, spin attacks and more.
You counter the maneuver he used moments before to cleave you in two - a brief pause emerges in acknowledgement from both parties, you feel pride in your actions and from your nemesis - only for reality to snap back where you're the victim another move you've never experienced.

This game is still in development, its features are simple and limited at present, however it is quite an enjoyable game and its current simplicity only helps it as it makes the game accessible. I have focused mostly on the solo-co-op experience and so far and have enjoyed it greatly.
Graphically the game is very beautiful from the character model details to the world map, you will be greeted with desert dunes, oases, canyons, and ancient ruined civilisations.
Combat at this time is very simple, think Elder Scrolls but without the magic, but no doubt will be fleshed out later down the development pipeline.
Base building has been a treat for me personally, can be a tad annoying with block placment, but like the game its simplicity helps, gather a few rocks and logs and off you go with your imagination to bend this world to your will. You can build in and around your enviroment for example I currently have a fortress built into the side of a giant rock protrusion and have since built an altar to my patron deity on its plateau and then decided to expand said base into a nearby formation now dominated by a colossal tower that i some times brood atop of as i gaze over my domain as my thralls toil far below.
Speaking of Thralls, this game features a slavery system were you attack npcs all of whom are hostile subdue them by non lethal means bind them and like Conan in the movie put them on the Wheel of Pain, and break them to your will. From there you will apply them to their profession. Some are cooks and as such speed up cooking times, Tanners for leather work, blacksmiths for weapons, and armourers for armour crafting. Fighters and archers can be used for defence of your homestead.

Gemini Rue is an excellent Point and Click adventure with a low res, grimy, cyber-punk aesthetic.  The look and animation of the game remind me of old games I used to play on the Amiga, in a good way.  The sound design is well done as is the voice acting, though it would have been nice to have some variety in the lines that get repeated often.  The puzzles in the game are generally relatively simple, but this is for the best as it keeps them from causing too much interruption in the story which is the highlight of the game.  In the game you play the part of several characters, and at one point can even change between them to complete portions of their story in whatever order you choose.  That is one of design strengths of the game, like pretty much any game in the genre, the progression is basically linear, however there are different paths which must be explored completely to allow you ultimately progress through the story, but you can complete these paths separately or work on one them move back to another then come back to complete the first.  This both allows the game to move more naturally as you don't feel like you are on rails most of the time; and allows you to do something else and come back to it if you get stumped in your progression.  I'm not the best point and click player and often have to refer to walkthroughs to complete them.  I did have to do this two times, and in both cases it was very small objects in the environment which I didn't realize were interactive that stumped me. I liked the low res look of the game, but the pixilation probably aggravated these objects not standing out.  If there were a system to highlight the objects that were interactive, that would help to eliminate that issue.  Yes, that would be easy mode, but if I could only turn easy mode on when I really needed, it would interrupt much less than having to leave and do a Google search.  The only other minor gripe I have is that you cannot view your item inventory without first finding an interactive object.  If you like point and clicks it's a must play, if you don't then you'll find it less aggravating than most.

Quest Run can be very difficult, and you will no doubt encounter plenty of complaints in that department.
The game is also centered completely around luck.  Many times, if a potion drops, you will live.  If it doesn't, you will fail and have to start over. Any strategy on your part is a moot point.
Another complaint is the unlockable "upgrades", which are usually a hindrance.  "Can I please re-lock the vampire class?"
But this game's main failure is the gigantic length of time each quest takes.  There are no save points during gameplay, so each quest you undertake is a huge investment of time.  If you fail the quest, all of that time is wasted and you start over from scratch.  In our current climate of short gaming sessions and frequent save points, this game is completely tone deaf to the demands of modern gamers.
Only someone with enormous uninterupted time on their hands should consider playing this game.  For everyone else, the fun this game provides does not equal the time investment it requires.  In that respect (fun/time), this game is a laughable failure.

This game has a lottttttttttt of problems.  Probably more than any game should ever have and still get a recommendation.  Despite all it does wrong though I enjoyed it.  So much is bad, it's kind of hard to even find a place to start.  I guess the graphics are as good a place as any.  They are atrocioussssssss.  You want to make a retro adventure game, fine, I'll allow you to go as far back as Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis or Laura Bow and the Dagger of Amon Ra.  For god sakes though, don't go back to Maniac Mansion or Monkey Island.  I'm just exhausted of these terrible super retro looking games where it's all just mashed together pixels.
This actually leads to one of the other major problems of this game.  The puzzles are pretty much all terrible.  Almost every puzzle relies on the fact that the game is so graphically bad that you can't see what's on the screen.  So congrats, it's certainly retro in the sense it's a pixel hunting graphical adventure game where I have to slowly scroll across the screen searching for the one pixel that will tell me what the object I'm looking at is really supposed to be.  So overall I'd say this has some of the worst puzzles of any adventure game I ever played.  One literally required me to put my foot in a hole in the wall to reach up to an electric socket.  First I couldn't even tell it was a hole in the wall, nor that an electric socket was above it.  Simply terrible.  The game also has very poorly implemented combat, it's awkward and no fun at all, just put the game on the easiest level of combat to spam threw it.  I don't know why they put that in here.
The voice acting is also pretty rough.  I guess the main female and male characters are alright, but barely.  Everyone else really sounds stilted.  I assume they actually didn't have voice actors and just found friends to voice these parts.  It's probably the worst voice acting I have ever heard.  I almost wish they didn't have any voice acting, probably would have made it better.  I did enjoy the character portraits that popped up anytime someone talked though.
Despite all those problem I still really enjoyed it.  Mainly it came down to the story which although extremely predictable, was still fun.  It's basically a cross between Cowboy Bebop and Blade Runner.  This game probalby would have been an excellent film or anime.  The music is superb and really gets across the noir futeristic atmosphere the game is trying to get across.  Likewise the planet of perpetual rain looks fantastic as far as the graphics go.  Probably the atmosphere more than anything else saved this game from me not recommending it.  It's a treat to explore this world and I wish they had more stories in this universe.  Preferably with better graphics and farrrrrrrr longer.  This is easily 6 hours, maybe 7, which is crazy short in my opinion.  12-15 hours would have been more to my liking for this game.  So although I'd recommend it I really don't think you should spend much, I almost want to say only play it for free, but the work that went into this does deserve something.  #Worth $2.00

If you're looking for a dungeon crawler, you could do a lot worse than this. Great visuals and music, challenging baddie whomping, and interesting mechanics abound to keep the player interested.
Dungeon crawling has become a Japan-dominated genre and Stranger of Sword City is one of many dungeon crawlers to come from Japanese developers that's worth a playthrough for both newer and older fans of the genre.
It is worth noting that while some reviews state this game is extremely difficult, it's actually much easier than some other staples of the genre. Despite your level being so much lower than that of the enemies in Normal mode, you aren't expected to grind endlessly. Most of your grinding comes down to ambushing enemies for loot. You are not meant to be at the same level of the enemies you come across.
There's a lot of good to be said about this game. Fans of super old-style dungeon crawlers may want to give this a pass because it lacks the complexities and extreme difficulty of some older titles, but as a modern dungeon crawler it's hard to not recommend.
If you like Dungeons and Dragons, you'll like this game.

One of the best games ever, and the best game in the Mass Effect series. At its core it's a cover based third person shooter. It's also an RPG, but only a light version of it. You choose between different classes and you are able to upgrade the abilities  of your character and your crewmates. The gameplay is much more refined than in the first game, and I feel like you can skip right to Mass Effect 2 and still enjoy it. The universe of Mass Effect is perhaps the best gaming universe I have ever experienced. So much thought went into the planets, the alien races, the lore and the politics of the universe. You will lose yourself in it, and really care for the characters.
The gameplay itself is mainly a linear cover based shooter, but it is really engaging and polished. You have the ability to pause in the middle of a fight and use different abilities by your character or your crew, you can also order your crew to move into different locations to give you a tactical advantage, this is mandatory at higher difficulties. The game offers quite a few different enemies with different strengths and weaknesses you can exploit, and you can take advantage of this with different crewmembers' abilities. This brings an extra layer of depth to which crewmember you bring on the mission. Each mission is linear, with light exploration. But all the missions are directed very well, with different outcomes depending on your choices and the crewmates you bring on missions.
The main game has a good length of about 18-24 hours depending on how much extra stuff you do. There are several DLC packs of varying quality, with the best definitely being "Lair of the Shadow Broker". These DLC packs will add at least 6-8 hours combined.
Seriously, do yourself a favor and play this amazing game!!

Updated Review
Here is an update of the game. I have now spent 86 hours and am really loving this game very much. Here are more interesting features of this game
1. Rolling for hours for optimal bonus points.
It has been many years since the Wizardry games, that I have been so actively trying to roll for the dice for my starting characters. You are given a choice of different age (10-99) which will affect your life points and bonus points. Bonus points also varies greatly due to random dice roll, and can vary from 4 to 17, for me. Supposedly there are people who can roll 30, but that has NEVER happened to me after 100 tries. However, 17 bonus point is enough for me to built an extremely powerful character, that can max out their primary stats at level 8. Wow, talking about the great difference rolling makes in this game!!!
2. Planning and implementing Class Changes.
You can have a team of 6 members and are allowed to change classes 5 times during the game
(10 class changes if you include newgame+). This make for very interesting strategic decisions that you can make. You have to plan way ahead. It make sense to select the race and maxed out the primary attributes base on the FINAL class of the team member.  For example, if your final class is a Wizard, it make sense to set the race to Elf and try to maxed out intelligence to 33, even  if your starting class can be a Cleric or a Dancer. So foresight and planning is a MUST in this game, which make it really interesting.
3. Playing cautiously and keeping on your toes.
This game really keep me on my toes, because I team members can lose life points anytime they are knocked unconcious and may turn into butterflies (the game way of telling you about PERMANENT death). This is exerbated by the fact that you can only save at 1 location, which is inside the stranger guild. So,  whenever I pick up some nice loots or gears, I have to worry about NOT dying until I make it back to the guild. If any of my character dies or fall unconcious, it is a necessary game RELOAD for me, thus wasting hours of gameplay, or lost of certain precious loot. I am playing at beginner's difficulty and it is still that challenging and FUN.
4, Farming massive XP from respawning monsters.
This is a wonderful feature of the game and is really fun. It is just not mindless hack and slash, but careful playing. You can actually get a humongous amount of XP if you keep the last respawning monster alive until he calls for allies and then you can kill him. I have heard of people who got 70,000 XP in a fight through careful gameplay. There are battles that can take hours and become extremely profitable. However, there are time when I was tired and got one of my team members killed after hours of XP farming. If I use my oldies team (age 60+) that has 1 life point, I will have to reload the game due to permanent death and waste the hours of farming. If I use my young team, they are not as powerful. All these considerations are interesting strategic tradeoffs that you need to consider, making this game really FUN.
So, here is my update after 100+ hours!!! This game is really fun, and I will give another update after another 50 hours or so.

Speedrunners: Gotta go fast
Do you like racing games like Mario Kart, 1950’s esque artwork, superheroes, well designed video games, and having fun? Well, my friend, then SpeedRunners is for you!
Because it’s all of those things wrapped into one really well made package.
SpeedRunners is a racing game, first and foremost. The setup being that various superheroes are racing to the scene of a crime, or emergency, and trying to beat each other there! At least that’s what I got out of it, the game is light on story; but it honestly doesn’t need it, the gameplay is what shines here. And boy, let me tell you, it really shines. This game is polished. It’s incredibly smooth, responsive, and just feels good. Like peeling the plastic off of a new cellphone.
And surprisingly, SpeedRunners is an Early Access game! It’s still in Beta! I continuously find myself being shocked at just how good this game handles. It feels like a full fledged release, and I give the developers, DoubleDutch Games, credit because SpeedRunners is fantastic. This is in part because of the wonderful ‘track’ designs present here. A good racing game is crippled if it doesn’t have fun courses, which SpeedRunners delivers on. There are twelve or so levels, and only two that I dislike. That’s a pretty successful margin.
Now, unlike any other racing game I have played, SpeedRunners involves… running! Who would have thought, right?
And despite being a foot race, SpeedRunners maintains an excellent sense of speed. Four players all running at breakneck speeds trying to usurp each other. Throwing missiles, freeze-rays, hooks, and crates left and right hoping to trip each other up. The highs are high, and the lows are looooow. Being in first place, getting hit by a missile, tumbling around and ending up in last place-- and then dead-- is jarring. You’ll get mad at your friends. But when you do it, it’s oh so sweet.
Each race is an elimination race where each ‘lap’ continues on until only one runner remains. Other players are eliminated by advancing far enough ahead that the edge of the screen touches someone. Then they explode, are out of the race, and the screen’s border progressively closes in until it’s just a tiny rectangle big enough for two players. This requires you to memorize the tracks very well, because at that point you’re almost literally playing blind.
It gets real intense real fast.
As with most multiplayer games, SpeedRunners is best with friends. But the game also offers some really, really, good bots that actually offer a decent challenge. And it has a very active multiplayer! I’ve never not found a game, which is great… Although I have occasionally run into some particularly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥y people… But it is the internet so that’s to be expected.
I beat another player using the hook, this game’s equivalent of the ‘blue shell’, and he promptly told me in all caps to leave the game and engage in sexual congress with myself. I called him out on this, and he told me I was being rude for using the item. I proceeded to handle this situation quite poorly. But that’s another story!
Internet antics aside, SpeedRunners is fantastic and certainly one of my favorite games of 2015. Even if it came out in 2013. 2013’s 2015 racing game of the year.
SpeedRunners is just a joy to play. Even alone. And for $15 it’s a total steal. There is tons of content in this game, with like a billion different Runners and like ten skins for each one. They also have workshop support so that the community can create levels… Sadly I have only played a few workshop levels that even come close to the amazing quality of the developer courses.
I will wholeheartedly recommend SpeedRunners to anyone looking for a cool local co-op game. Or, hell, anyone looking for a competitive racing game.
It’s that good.
Seriously, go buy it. These guys deserve the support.

No, really. It's very good at what it's meant to do. MachineCraft is a very open sandbox where people can design to their heart's content, where the only barrier is their mind.
It has a glaring problem: appealing to a large portion of its potential audience. This is caused by many things:
1. Accessibility - No, I don't mean paywalls. Remember when I said "the only barrier is their mind"? It shows up pretty quickly, and the game will feel like rocket science right off the bat. Yes, people can and should learn eventually, but it's still very difficult to learn and master.
2. Combat - When people look at this game and compare it to Robocraft, they think about combat. MachineCraft combat is far from perfect. A lot of the mechanics are off, and simply are not balanced.
3. Niche - This game is the living definition of "niche game". People are thrown off because of how different it is from other games and struggle to enjoy it.
4. Graphics and Sound - Both are key culprits. The graphics are far from perfect, having flat (and mostly nontextured) models. The terrain seems fuzzy to me, and the blocks themselves are only colored. The sound hurts your ears often.
I myself see MachineCraft having great potential, and therefore give it a thumbs up.

If you have a lot of imagination, and love to make stuff that's highly complex - you'll love this game.
If you liked the mechanical parts on space engineers but hated how they never worked properly in space engineers, or how much of a pain making movement sequences was, then you'll DEFINATELY love this game, as the joint system is absolutely fantastic. Sequences can be set to assigned controls making walking mechanisms a doddle.
You're not even really limited by blocks, as you can sculpt blocks or even use box, capsule, hemisphere shapes that aren't even limited to the grid size, position or orientation. You really can make anything.
Look up some machinecraft videos and you'll see it's amazing for building potential.
Criticisms:
1) Playerbase isn't all that big. This is probably partly down to it just not being well known but also that on release the game couldn't handle more than 50 players per location. Not sure if this was ever solved, but it isn't an issue anymore due to the playerbase size. You'll still find 7 or 8 people on a server though if you look.
2) No sensor blocks in this game. You can code in LUA outside the game which will allow you to do sensor type actions, but this is likely outside of a lot of peoples capability. On that point though, the LUA does allow you to do a huge amount of things if you know what you're doing.
3) Learning curve - there is a lot of included samples with the game to get you started, but still fairly difficult to get into and understand.
4) Special features such as MOD maps and LUA code are not documented in english, if you get into the very top end features of the game later you'll have to put the instructions through google translate and have to do a lot of trial and error. (you really dont need to do these to get some really advanced stuff out of the game though) LUA scripts can be reloaded ingame though, so those are fairly easy to experiment with.
EDIT : I've played this game since version 0.49, well before it got on steam - so my play hours are probably in the thousands!

I will begin this review with the statement that I have more hours on the Game of Thrones mod than I do on the vanilla game. The game itself is not bad, if you are the type of person that can get immersed into roleplay, it is great. If not then it may be a bit on the boring side as a large cunk of the gameplay in my opinion is roleplaying and growing attached to your character/dynasty. You are crafting a story, not so much conquering kingdoms in this. The freedom that it presents you is amazing. You can largely do as you want, within reason of course. However I will go onto to say that playing on a laptop or on a smaller screen is extremely not recommended. There are a lot of menus and other promts that take up a lot of screen space and smaller screens quickly become clustered and it becomes more frustrating than fun.
Many people speak of the DLC in a extremely bad way. I'm not entirely disagreeing with those people. If you have read the reviews then you have doubtlessly seen many such negatives reviews about it. Well here is the thinka bout the DLC, most of it is stuff that you will never use. Do you want to play as a Muslim ruler? Do you want to play as an Indian ruler? Well then great, you will want the DLC. Not having it though is largely irrelevant. I will proceed to state however that the expansions are great, but the DLC itself is not. There are many clothing and other types of DLC. If a person has bought the Old Gods expansion then that player should have the clothing and appareances DLC native for that region by default instead of paying for an additional sum. Yet even this is still largely irrelevant and does not effect gameplay.
This game has been out for a good while and it is great that the Developers are continuing to add onto it. At the time of this review they just released the Horse Lord expansion. This is years after the game was released. They have gone from only having Western Europe in the game to the edges of Western China. The amount of content that they have added is staggering. If you don't own the India DLC then it doesn't really matter. If you are playing as a Western Europe ruler and eventually your territory extends that far then you are allowed to conquered it.
The game is huge and also has a large community of modders. Many of the mods are hands down some of the best I have ever seen (Game of Thrones and Lord of the Rings topping that chart). The amount of content is fair. If you are insistent that you want the whole game with all of the expansions and DLC then pick the game up on sale. Each summer and Christmas sale it goes down to about $35 with all the DLC included.
I would definitely recoomend this game. Especially if you are a Game of Thrones fan.

I really wish I could completely recommend this game. I really would. After all, It's Jet Set Radio. It was one of the classics on the Dreamcast back in the day, and I remember spending hours upon hours playing through this game.
In the very rare chance you don't know what this game is, Jet Set Radio is a fun, simple action game where you skate around with some rather advanced inline skates and cover the somewhat futuristic city of Tokyo-to (not Tokyo, mind you, Tokyo-to, a re-imagined version of the more well known Japanese city) with graffiti while avoiding the overly hostile police, using tricks such as grinding on various rails, pipes, and power lines, sliding on walls, and flipping through the air to avoid being caught (and even spray up your targets in mid trick). The challenge ramps up as the police get even more aggressive, bringing in SWAT teams which use tear gas and machine guns on you, and even missile launching helicopters to end your run. On top of that, some targets you have to spray up take multiple passes, where you need to move your analog stick in various half and full circles in order to complete: the more time you take getting them done, the more of the chance the fuzz will catch up to you. And you also have rival gangs to contend with as well, who at the start of the game are invading your turf and causing you problems here and there. All this is being narrated by a wild haired DJ by the name of Professor K, who keeps you up to date with what's going on, as well as providing the music you will be listening to during each level via his pirate radio station that gives this game its name. Despite how threatening and oppressive I just made the game sound, the tone and feel is actually rather whimsical and comic, and it comes off more like a light hearted cartoon than a dark edgy take on urban graffiti culture.
Everything I remembered about it is still here: the bright and colorful cell shaded graphics, the interesting city locations to skate around in, the over the top characters and enemies, the simple way to link up tricks while skating around, the rather cool looking graffiti you can collect as you play, and of course, the fantastic soundtrack, . The fact that it's now in HD is a plus, and the few bonuses they throw in, like some tunes from Jet Set Radio Future, and a documentary, are a nice addition.
This game isn't perfect however, and it's now time to get into the negative things about it. For one thing, the controls haven't aged very well. They can be rather floaty and imprecise at times, especially when you are trying to pull off a quick jump off a rail to another one in order to grind away to safety... only to miss for some ridiculous reason and end up falling a long distance and taking damage from that. Or there's hitting a wall which cuts short your momentum, forcing you to back up and speed up all over again, costing you time (each level is on a timer, by the way), or getting shot by the cops. Another problem is the camera. This game was made back in 2000, and those who played games back then should remember how much time we spent fighting the evil camera in games. It's not as bad here as other older games of the time, but there are enough moments where the camera spazzes out that will make you grind your teeth. Those two things combined with the ever aggressive police can make the game feel cheap at times. But those things aren't enough to make me hate the game; there's enough good here in the gameplay and setting to offset those problems...
... that is, if the negatives I mentioned were the only things that were wrong.
The main thing which makes me hesitant to fully recommend Jet Set Radio is one major bug that for the life of me I can't understand how it made it past quality control: the inability of the game to save your progress. No matter how far you get, if you turn this game off and come back to it later, you WILL be starting from the very beginning again. Even though the game actually has a load function, and it does have a save file that records the last time you played, it doesn't matter: it will still start you at the very beginning. Your progress just doesn't get saved, no matter what you do. This pretty much breaks the game: unless you plan to do a marathon run of it, or keep it on in the background and never turn it or your PC off until you beat it, you're just not getting to the end in one sitting. Jet Set Radio is at least an 8 hour game, and that's just if you're going through the main story without getting any of the extras (such as extra artwork to spray up the city with). I doubt the average person will be willing to go 8 hours nonstop just to see the end.
What adds insult to injury here is that this bug has been present since the game first was offered on Steam... and that was back in Sept 19, 2012. That's a little over 2 YEARS AGO(at the time of this review). How do you have a bug like this remain unfixed for 2 years?? And this is SEGA we're talking about, not some first time independent company that has no experience with putting games out. That Sega would just leave this unresolved for a game that it considers one of it's classics is just beyond me. That Steam would let them get away with it angers me even more. It doesn't matter that the game only costs 5 bucks... I've paid less for other games that were made by developers who had the decency to not sell a broken product.
There used to be a fix for this that entailed getting a PIRATED/CRACKED VERSION of the game and switching out the .exe file in your game folder for the cracked one. I'm pretty sure I don't need to get into how that is just all kinds of wrong (not to mention adding more fuel to the fire that is the whole video game piracy debate). Seriously Sega: what the hell??
However, I found out later that there was a simple fix one could do with a Hex editor, where you basically open up the legit .exe in the editor, and change the word "save" to "SAVE" in a particular column, and the game will load your saves correctly. Now, it's great that a solution has finally been found, but think about this: if it's that easy to fix, then why in all 7 hells has Sega not bothered to implement it in all this time?? And they want money from us? Yes, I know it's just 5 bucks, but I've paid less for indie games that had more attention paid to how well they functioned than this. And the fact that the consumer has to be the one to fix this rather than the company selling the game is bad customer service, period.
So despite Jet Set Radio being one of those old games that I remember fondly, and despite the fact that I think that it looks and plays fine on the PC, I just can't in good conscience recommend that anyone buy this game without pointing out this one glaring flaw. I don't care how cheap it is: you shouldn't have to pay money for what is essentially a broken game. The fact that people out there actually DID recommend it, despite the fact that you CAN'T SAVE THE GAME is appalling to me, especially since it hasn't been fixed in over 2 YEARS. Sega should have had this fixed by now, and Valve should have been on them to do just that from the beginning. I stated before in my original version of my review that people should save their money until Sega fixed the game, but considering how easy the fix is, and the fact that I feel the game IS a decent classic worth playing, I feel more comfortable giving the game a TENTATIVE thumbs up. Honestly, one shouldn't pay for something broken, but when you get it working, it's a good time.

A boring, tedious, poorly controlled copy of Spelunky.  Almost the entire game consists of either waiting for a block to break (due to excessive number of hits required) or just running back and forth to the surface (there is no quick travel and your backpack fills up FAST).
PROS:
-Basics are all there (upgrades, mining, "caves" with loots, etc)
-Underground area seems to be pretty big (I went down to 1200 ft but nothing really happened)
-The voiceover sounds great.
CONS:
-NO MAP. Seriously?
-Extremely repetitive having to backtrack to the portal to get to the surface, especially considering how tiny your backpack is. You will be running back and forth *ALOT* (probably 1/3 to 1/2 of the gameplay is just this).
-Very slow mining. It takes 14+ swings to destroy an iron ore patch (lowest ore) with the 2nd level pickaxe. FOURTEEN swings per block !!
-Controls are awful (especially combat).
-Character will fly sometimes when you jump but not other times (not a major issue as fuel is prevalent).
-Plot makes no sense. Characters will mention things you've never heard of.
-Nothing actually happens? You just grind ores to upgrade your gear and go further into the mines...thats it? There didn't seem to be any new mechanics introduced, there was basically 1 enemy type (its size just changes), and the tiny bit of plot there was made no sense...

NiGHTS Into Dreams is a brilliant game that was a relatively large part of my childhood. Playing it in HD with this Steam release is a huge nostalgia trip. Unfortunately, I'm not sure how good people may find it if they never played it in its Sega Saturn heyday.
That being said, it's still very quality. In NiGHTS Into Dreams, you control a flying character who is able to manoeuvre themselves up, down, left and right along a preset plane in a 3D level. So the game curves you around and chooses where in the level you go basically, but you can backwards/forwards, etc. (It's sort of hard to explain, I'd recommend watching a YouTube video)
The idea is that in a given level, you have to collect 20 "blue chips" (glowing orbs) and, once you've done that, activate the "ideya palace" (which is this machine-looking thing that acts like a start/finish line). You must do this four times, with the course changing each time you've completed this task. After this, you are teleported to the boss. It is simple in practice, but very hard to master, and its in-game score system goes very well with Steam leaderboards.
The music is varied and amazing; it helped shape my current day love for video game music. The visuals are very vibrant and complement the music perfectly, in my opinion.
With this Steam port, you are able to fully customise your controls (which are pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ by default so do that as soon as you get the game), and the game gives you an option to play with the updated HD port or the original Saturn graphics (very big difference).
All in all, I'd rate this game a solid 9/10, maybe 8/10 if I try to subtract the nostalgia value it has for me. Before doing anything, I'd recommend you look up a video for it and see what you think.
Thanks for reading! Appreciate it.

I find it unfortunate that Sega had flailed about so badly after their glory days of the Sega Genesis, and  I admit to an uncommon difference of opinion that I found Sega much more compelling during its declining days of the Saturn and Dreamcast.  To be sure, the Saturn was ineptly engineered, but it possessed a handful of absolutely beautiful gems that were not to be found anywhere else.  Among them, Nights Into Dreams.
The beauty within Nights isn't about any one thing, but the experience taken as a whole.  Gameplay is simple time-trial courses, but the whole "child's dream land" themepark combined with the grace of acrobatic flight is positively surreal.  Each of the end stage bosses is its own deviously crafted challenge.
I was ecstatic when Nights first came to Steam, as it brought Nights back from an obscure past of long dead gaming consoles for more people to enjoy.  Understand that for all my gushing -- I had played Nights quite a bit back in the 90s.  These days I find myself with more games than free time (hence my rather low time investment in the Steam version).  However, I remember Nights on Saturn as one of the greatest of classics, and the Steam release is fully worthy of that memory.
Nights is not the kind of game that will appeal to everyone.  "
" type of gamers probably should keep on sauntering.  But!  For the gamer that appreciates a great video game much like a museum curator appreciates Vincent Van Gogh -- look no further.

One of the best games ever, and the best game in the Mass Effect series. At its core it's a cover based third person shooter. It's also an RPG, but only a light version of it. You choose between different classes and you are able to upgrade the abilities  of your character and your crewmates. The gameplay is much more refined than in the first game, and I feel like you can skip right to Mass Effect 2 and still enjoy it. The universe of Mass Effect is perhaps the best gaming universe I have ever experienced. So much thought went into the planets, the alien races, the lore and the politics of the universe. You will lose yourself in it, and really care for the characters.
The gameplay itself is mainly a linear cover based shooter, but it is really engaging and polished. You have the ability to pause in the middle of a fight and use different abilities by your character or your crew, you can also order your crew to move into different locations to give you a tactical advantage, this is mandatory at higher difficulties. The game offers quite a few different enemies with different strengths and weaknesses you can exploit, and you can take advantage of this with different crewmembers' abilities. This brings an extra layer of depth to which crewmember you bring on the mission. Each mission is linear, with light exploration. But all the missions are directed very well, with different outcomes depending on your choices and the crewmates you bring on missions.
The main game has a good length of about 18-24 hours depending on how much extra stuff you do. There are several DLC packs of varying quality, with the best definitely being "Lair of the Shadow Broker". These DLC packs will add at least 6-8 hours combined.
Seriously, do yourself a favor and play this amazing game!!

Gemini Rue is a retro-style point and click adventure set on an incredibly atmospheric and stylish backdrop with an engrossing story and deeply challenging puzzles. It has all the hallmarks of classic games within the genre and is of a quality that puts some big-budget modern games to shame today.
You assume the role of two characters in this intertwining story;- Azriel Odin; a former assassin who is searching for his brother whilst looking for personal redemption for his past; and a mysterious hospital patient named 'Delta Six' who's memory has been wiped for reasons unknown. Your job is to collectively discover the secrets that exist in this bleak, corrupt and crime-riddled world and provide a resolution to your characters's plight. As the narrative develops and the story unfolds; you will be hooked. For such a simple 2D game; the story is truly absorbing along with the fully-voiced characters each with an intriguing personality.
The user interface is also extremely well implemented which is pivotal as this game demands complete precision in the execution of tasks and puzzles. It is incredibly complex at times and you will be forgiven for having to look up the occasional solution but it is a testament to the developers on how to create a challenging, thought-provoking and engrossing game.
If you're a veteran of the genre, a fan of adventure games or just looking for a story-driven title that offers a rewarding challenge; Gemini Rue is absolutely unmissable. It captures the essence of classic games perfectly and delivers a powerful and intriguing experience throughout. One of the best titles on Steam

Alright, I usually do not bother writing reviews because I either feel 'meh' about a game or it is already so popular that every gamer knows about how good/bad it is. This game is different.
Let me start by telling you how I got this game. At first, a recommendation popped up on my Steam Store page telling me about this release. I thought "Wow, another RPG game like all the others..NEXT." Boy was I wrong.
A couple days later, while watching one of my favorite streamers, the guys starts up this gem, telling his viewers how he's always loved Divinity for their approach to RPGs and the content ingame. He starts a new game with a friend, both controlling 2 characters and after the first exploring, dialog, and subsequent disastrous fight I was hooked.
I picked up the game a couple days ago and dove right in on Tactician difficulty (hardest if you don't count permadeath mode). At first I got trashed by every enemy, forcing me to rethink my battle approach. You actually need to consider positioning and tactics: can I sneak up behind him or not? can I go to this high ground with my ranger or is that oil barrel going to make me a roasted piece of meat? what are this guy's weaknesses and what do I equip to take advantage?
With all these 'run in without a thought, fight, win, repeat' sort of games in the last couple of years, D:OS2 truly stands apart from most of the RPG genre. The game does not take you by the hand, telling you where to go, what to do, how to do it. I'm absolutely loving it and I'm barely past the first Act. All this from a developer team that had quite a hard time a couple years ago, said f*** it we'll do without a publisher company, found love on Kickstarter and brought us this marvel and GOTY - for me at least. That's right Larian, I read up on you and wish you all the best!
You can stop reading reviews on it now. If you enjoy the concept of an RPG, buy it and try not to play through the night without realising you started after dinner almost 12 hours ago.

This game feels and plays like the more classic RPG's of the past. Just look at games like Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights and Larians own Divine Divinity and you'll know what I'm on about. The first Original Sin was good, but this is something else, something more polished and fun to play.
Unlike many newer RPG's, this game doens't have that much handholding. It lets you explore the world and figure out things by yourself without much obvious spoonfeeding. Also, your actions have some weight on how things play out. Don't save a seemingly unimportant NPC early on and it might come back to bite you later on.
The world itself is quite interactable. Not only are there loads of things lying around for you to rummage through and steal. There are also plenty of environmental effects like puddles of water or blood giving you the chance of electrifiying it and anyone standing in it. Oil can be lit aflame, as does poison. You can let it rain to douse the flames, creating steam. Obviously your characters will also get wet because of the rain. A campfire will then again warm up your characters. All these effects are certainly fun to mix up and don't feel that gimmicky like in the first Original Sin.
Lastly and quite importantly: the inhabitants of the world feel quite alive, the story unfolds nicely, the dialogue is top notch and your party members are delightfully in depth.
Highly recommended for any RPG lover. Otherwise still a rock solid game.

Cons:

Nearly every player is lagging and that causes the game to glitch very often. There is nearly no game in which you can play normal - oh well I guess you can always play solo or against bots.
I don't know the devs background, but I guess he is just a beginner and should work more on the netcode. As example for bad implementation is the ping ingame. Normally ping should measure the round-trip-time (rtt) and is really easy to calculate, but he is using his own version of ping which probably calculates the time between the current and the next network packet. This causes the ping value to jump and stutter - and this is also true for everything else sent over the network. Gameplay is jumpy and everyone teleports around.
One gametype with around 15 standard maps + workshop maps. You can use items to slow down enemys and use boost pads to gain speed. That one gametype is running around in a map that loops all the time. Your goal is to be 1st and then get so fast and far away that the other players disapear at the edge of your screen. The screen is always based on the 1st player.
This "edge of your screen" thing is kinda cool, but here is the big downside:
Since the screen is based on the 1st player: Falling is winning! Once you are 1st, try to jump down somewhere so that other players can't keep up!
That means other players can't keep up because they are slower, far away or noobs right?
No they can't keep up because you jumped first - thats it. Why you ask? Because falling is so fast, that everyone else is still at the edge, while you are already at the bottom.
So I lost serveral times, just because I was 2nd place for a little bit (to gain speed) and then got out of screen.

I never played DOS1, but I received a copy of this game for free to stream on Twitch. I can't tell you how happy I am to have received that copy. This game is truly one of my favorite games of all time.
For years, I've said that Fallout 2 was (and still is) my favorite CRPG of all time, but DOS2 is pushing for a real close second. This game really takes me back. It is just packed full of content in a way that most new RPGs just can't hope to deliver. I mean it when I say "content" too. So many new RPGs seem to mistake filling their open world with mountains of garbage to be content. I love FO3, FO4, and Skyrim, but there's no denying that the vast majority of their open worlds were just pointless crap. That isn't the case in this game.
I should honestly wait to get further in this game before leaving a review, but holy crap, there is just so much to see and do. I've played over 50 hours, and I'm only about a quarter of the way through the game. Even then, I'll need to replay this at least a couple more times just to feel out a few of the other strong story possibilities. The options in the game are ridiculous.
If you're a fan of CRPGs in the vein of Baldur's Gate, Planescape: Torment, Fallout 1/2, etc. you will love this game.

Hey everyone and this is my review about the game!
This is a Real time Strategy game.
There are many resolution sizes available.
You can choose between Fullscreen or windowed mode.
Able to Disable cutscenes.
There is a master volume slidebar with a %.
There is a Sound volume slidebar with a %.
There is a Music volume slidebar with a %.
There is a campaign volume slidebar with a %.
There is a mentor volume voice slidebar with a %.
Able to toggle Subtitles.
There is a mouse sensitivity Slidebar available.
You are able to change the controls on the keyboard.
There are some different languages available.
There is a Map/Level editor.
There is an online multiplayer and there are still some people active.
Online multiplayer does NOT require Ip Port-forward stuff.
This game brings you back to the deepest dungeons of the underworld. Where you have to Attack, Build, explore, Dig and loot the dungeons.
You will have to protect the "Dungeon Core", Once a dungeon core has been destroyed the game will be over. You start with some workers which are mining halls in the dungeon and claiming tiles.
You are able to build on the tiles that you own. Each unit will need a bed, Food, Gold and ofcourse the requirement to be able to summon them. You are able to use spells, finding artifacts, shrines and sins.
Sins are required to develop new buildings. The campaign mode has a build-in Tutorial and it's good explained. Each Campaign level has 3 achievements. Each minion has their own happiness meter.
The happiness meter has to stay up in the positive, or else they will become unhappy and eventually even rebelling. Unhappy units will have a penalty in their effectiveness. Rebelling units will attack your own minions and you can't control them.
There is a tutorial and it's well explained.
The text and subtitles are totally voiced over. (So everything from the game).
You are able to go inside of an unit and play him in first person.
Workers and units are able to level up.
Workers will try to rescue fallen allies or other corpses.
Workers will try to steal the land and territory from others.
Able to make Rally points.
You can slap units to increase their effectiveness. But their happiness and health will be draining.
Has a minimap.
Has a Tech-Tree.
Commentary is sometimes funny.
Text font could be small.
There is a Campaign, survival and Skirmish mode.
Minions/units are able to become unhappy and eventually even attack your own units (Rebelling).

I like this game a lot, event though it's still very much in developement, it's still enjoyable. I always enjoy finding games that have some new twist to them and this is one of them. It's a game about kung-fu rabbits,as a like to say (eventhough it has dogs, rats, cats, and wolves also). though it lacks in super combo moves, ang the ability to shoot lasers, and what not that you might see in other games, you know which ones i'm talking about that say theyre all about martial arts and such, but honestly, im happey this game lacks in that stuff. it keeps it real... or at least as real as "kung- fu bunnies" gets. This game really stands out to me for a few things, it's fighting with phisics, sceletal structure, parkour, dynamic AI, how damage is shown, armed combat vs hand to hand, and last but not least the ears. Now when I say that this game keeps it real, i mean really real. I say this because of the fighting with phisics I mentioned. what this meants is that when you get hit, its not a set amount of damage that is done, its all in how you get hit, where you get hit, what you get hit into etc. and they do an outstanding job with this. for example, lets say that some one punched you in the arm, of course you arent going to die, if they punch you in the leg you will probaably be fine, but once they hit you in the head chances are, you're going to die. Also  moving into to sceletal structure at the same time, if they do hit you in the arm or leg enough, it will break that bone and you will be considered defeated. also like i said what you get hit into, if you get round house kicked in the side, you might be able to roll it off, but if you get round house kicked into a wall you're taking some damage from the kick and that much more from the wall therefore doubleing your damage and potentialy causeing your enemy to hit something critical and most likely defeating them. Also, parkour was a great addition thanks to some of the things you can do. You can wall run, do flips over stuff, ledge grab just about anything you should be able to,  and more. this is great in combat if you use it well, for example, if someone is chasing you, you can wall run up the wall, jump off (even do a flip off of it if you're feeling styleish ;P)grab a ledge pull yourself up and fluip off and "leg cannon" your enemy. also what sets this game appart is the dynamic AI. in this game, if you dare button mash, you are almost guarenteed to lose, if you just keep swinging at your enemy you will lose, if you never throw a punch, you will lose. The AI will learn any patters you make or tendencies of yours and will adapt, you must continuously change your fighting style and mix things up or else, chances are, the AI will catch on. Moving on tho combat and how damage is shown more.most of the time, damage isn't shown. you just have to guess, but often times there is some blood you can see dribble down you character and drip (bonus point to that because, you dont always bleed the same way) although it's easier to tell with armed combat vs unarmed, in unarmed since it's all blunt damage it's almost impossible to tell whereas in armed combat, unless you get hit with a dagger it's a instakill. with daggers it may take a few swings (depending how you use it).  If you do get hit by a dagger, it's easier to judge damage due to showing externally, you can get scratched just about anywhere and it will show, also if heavily damaged, your character may go slightly limp and grasp his chest/ the injury. my point is, it's realistic how it show damage, you cant always see it but sometimes it thows up quite well, but unlike some games, it wont show up the same way every time. then moving on to combat a little more, theres armed and unarmed, for both you can parry/ block or counter hits, you can perform stealth kills, etc. unlike most games though, any weapon you hold you can throw it aty your enemy, and if theyre good enough they can catch it (and vise versa). However armed combat for he most part is hit block hit block, for unarmed it's a bit more interesting such as something that goes: you punch, enemy counters by pulling your arm in attempt to flip you on your back, you then notice this and counter by pulling your arm back and return the favor with a punch to the head, but you were too slow and they ducked and kicked your legs out from under you, you are critically hurt but prevent furtherdamage by rolling it off, the enemy then tries to kick you again but you grab his leg and flip him backwards, before the enemy can recover from being thrown onto the ground you curb stomp them and end the fight. this is the awesome combat in the game in addition to the parkour type stuff I said before. lastly, like I said, the ears. this is really small but I love it, little things like ears or tales move and flail in accordance to witch way you move. To wrap this up I would like to appologise for this giant unatractive wall of tet, typos and all. I highly recomend this game, get it when a sale comes but it is the finest hand to hand combat I have experienced in a game to this day (unless im totally blanking out wich I doubt). It's still in developement but its still very enertaining. (and if you're up for a challenge fight and revieve your enemies so they are even more adapted to your strategies).

This game is one of the best F2P games I have ever played, and the biggest F2P game I have ever played.
+The game world is huge. It spans over sectors and the overall map is bigger then triple A titles such as GTA V and Just Cause 2.
+Character customisation. When you start the game you have the ability to change the appearance of your character, and during the game you can equip things that can add benefits and features, like dusters or combat suits.
+Clans and teams. In game there is a team system that people can join into so that you can complete a mission together, and some missions require that. The team system also allows voice chat. There is also a clan system that works like normal, and the clan has a special "clan vault" that they can use.
+Mega server. All players are on one server, but it works due to the map size.
+Vehicles. The game has various mounts, such as horses and even giant mutated chickens, along with motorbikes, ATVs, dune buggys, and more.
-Microtransactions. Since this is a free to play game, it is a given. You can buy almost any item in the game on their store. But I do not mind doing this from time to time, as I enjoy the game to the point that I want to support it.
-Graphics. They aren't very good. Good news for people on lower end PCs like me, but for somebody running a machine that costs as much as a small family vehicle, not so much.
-Voice acting. Barely any of it... at all. It is really BAD, it just isn't common.
-Buggy. Some bugs will occur in the game, but there is usually a fix. Usually.
TL;DR: This game is a pretty fun first person post apocalyptic online RPG. Possibly the only one of its kind. If you liked Fallout, you should try it out. If you hated Fallout, you. I reccomand this game for anyone, really.

I have played an inordinate amount of this game. If you like Civ and like diplomacy with lots of other nations and like shifting maps, then this is a great buy. The combat isn't great and the interface is horrifically unintuitive due to the complexity of the game. You need to invest time up front to lose a couple of two hour games to learn what the heck you're supposed to be doing at any point, but once you do, you find one of the deepest and most rewarding games out there.
Immense amounts of fun to scheme against others, get involved in or suppress civil wars, arrange marriages, attempt to mentor and breed good traits into your kids, and grow as a county/duchy/nation/empire. Huge amounts of fun just to see what the rest of the world gets up to on its own, far away from you. Different cultures and religions play quite differently from one another, which adds to the replay. It's fun to keep large countries or empires from fracturing, which keeps the game engaging even after you are larger than your rivals in the world.
Lots of additional content makes for a fun game, but it's preposterously expensive as a whole. Wait for it to go on deep discount, as it does at least every time that a new expansion is released, and you'll get more than your money's worth.

One of the best games in my possesion, if not thé best game. It is an awesome dynasty simulator where you can, more or less, do whatever the hell you want. Wanna be king of a giant kingdom? Unite some lands and you can! Wanna be a murderous tyrant, and see how long you will survive? You can! Do you want to marry hot ♥♥♥♥♥es, love em and leave em, and foster many children? YOU CAN!
Honestly, the game is like Europa Universalis in many ways - many people make it their goals to conquer large lands and stuff, but the key difference is that EU is a war game with diplomacy aspects, where CK2 is a diplomacy game with war aspects.
I'd even go as far as saying; no, it's not a diplomacy game, it's a roleplaying game. Because nothing says roleplaying like your king going insane, becoming a lunatic, and banning all pants. Or becoming the antichrist, and having armies lead by witches. That's all pretty cool, right?
PRO'S:
* Nice graphics for this type of game. Better than EU4.
* Have I mentioned the artwork? Holy hell, look it up.
* Roleplaying aspects are well written.
* Multiplayer capability. Your friend gets a genius heir? MURDER HIM.
* Endless replayability. Especially with the character creator. Want to be a Christian lord in year 800 Sweden, to see how long you can go? Do it. Want to be an Indian in England at the start of the game? Why not?
* The DLC seem pricey at first but, they do add loads of content. Add to that the (pretty much) mandatory sales that go on and you can get 120+ euro's worth of content for not even the price of an AAA fresh-release game. 40 euro's, if even that.
* There are a lot of mechanics, and they are quite complex. Not ''omg my brain hurts'' levels of complex because tooltips always tell you what to do. More so you're talking about vassals, relationships, blood ties, incest (INCEST? yes incest) and inbred children, lines of succession, cultures that allow certain things others don't, religions that work differently. It's a wonderful colored world that is your playground.
* Death can be fun in this game. And I've only ever encountered that before in Dwarf Fortress.
CON'S:
* Okay, it's not the best graphics. But that's not why you want to get this game, to begin with.
* Some of the roleplaying aspects, while fun, they don't last long. There are very few ''story'' events which unfold over longer periods of time. Even way of life didn't add many.
* Well, the DLC are pricey. Not OMG 30 EURO pricey, but more so there's quite a few of DLC so it adds up. My advice, get the game on a sale. Not because it's not worth it's price, but because nobody wants to shell out 120 euro for a game.
* Some of the game elements are a bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t-y. You can take on west Francia, and middle Francia, which make up most of modern day Europe, who together have barely 6.000 troops, but some random peasant can start a rebellion and spawn 10.000 men to fight you.

But the DLC model is ridiculous. AI in the game use the mechanics which come with the DLC. For you to use it, you got to pay, alot. I understand it cost time and money to put out these expansions. I understand the people at Paradox need money to buy food and diapers and DLC's for other games on Steam. But there is a limit.
For example, $15 gets you an expansion into India where you can play as a Indian lord. Great! Except India was updated into all games when the DLC came out and is in the base game if you buy it now. And all those Indian lords use mechanics that came with the DLC. So what do you get? The ability to use something which is already on the game you own. Additionally, you need to spend another $1-$3 (per pack) for skins, music and clothing for the region which you just bought. If you want your Indian lord, who will play out his scenario regardless of whether you shelled out $15 or not, to look like an authentic Indian lord, you need to pay more money on top of the money for the DLC.
Additionally, the DLC's require each other to enjoy fully. The Indian DLC lets you start around the mid 9th century, about two hundred years before the base game. But only if you have the Old Gods DLC. Which again comes with its plethora of pricey aethestics (not neccessary but criminal not to include).
I would not mind the DLC's if they were truly expansions. However, not only does the AI use many of the DLC mechanics but you can actually see (but not use) many of the mechanics in game (i.e. the retinue system). The DLC's are not expansions. They are Paradox's way of holding you hostage and daring you to spend money.
The base game is still fantastic. 93% positive reviews,DLCs notwithstanding, is a testament to the fun you still can have. Gameplay wise, the depth is absolutely insane and will suck you in. The DLCs are definitely not needed to have fun or enjoy the game. Yet $220 (and counting) in DLC for a $40 game is unjustifiable. Especially when many of the mechanics seem to already be implemented. Sadly, this is becoming more common among games. If the system changes, I will change my review. Unfortunately, I believe Paradox has gained the greedy trait.
TL;DR: Fantastic gameplay ruined by only getting 18.2% of a game ($40 game / $220 in DLC)

This is a game very near and dear to my heart. In fact, it's what I consider to be my all time favorite video game. I first played it a little as a child at my cousin's house. Then, when I was in middle school, I borrowed said cousin's SEGA Saturn for two whole years JUST for this game, and only returned it because he eventually asked for it back. In recent years, I've gotten some of my friends interested in this game as well. So naturally, I have a bit of a biased opinion towards this game. Even so, I will try my hardest to leave a fair review of it, and will try to address how it stands from a gaming perspective, as well as an HD remake and PC port perspective.
The premise is as follows: Two children who are struggling with their personal aspirations in the waking world find themselves in the dream world, teaming up with a flying jester to stop the Lord of Nightmares from acquiring enough of a type of dream energy that would enable him to enter our world. The plot is a bit weird yet simple and creative all the same, and the feel of the game captures that quite well. On top of that, the characters, while equally simplistic, are harboring both the same goals and doubts many of us have also experienced at their age, and over the course of the game, they are made to confront and attempt to overcome their personal demons, with two moments in the final level really capturing those elements of their journey. The gameplay is unique, distinct, and really does capture what it feels like to be in a dream world with its visual presentation and the music found throughout the game. The difficulty can be pretty hard for newcomers, though some may get the hang of it pretty quickly. It's pretty simple and straightforward, but performing well, especially for getting higher scores, can be quite challenging. Once you've gotten the hang of it, though, you could probably beat the main game in one evening. That being said, it is VERY replayable and addictive, and I often find myself coming back to play it whenever I've had a rough day. After all, we usually go to sleep so that we can relax, rest, and have the physical, mental, and emotional strength needed to confront the ordeals of tomorrow, and at least for me, NiGHTS into Dreams helped me do that at a time when I needed it most.
As an HD remake, the game gives you the option of playing all of the original game's levels with either the original graphics or a far higher resolution. And let me tell you, the HD graphics are breathtaking! In addition, the remake also includes a special winter themed level that was included in the Christmas NiGHTS version of the original Saturn game, as well several other time and date based elements introduced there. However, the multiplayer versus mode that was in the original game is inexplicably missing, along with a lot of other bonus content found with the Christmas NiGHTS game. Having played the Xbox 360, PS3, and Steam versions of this game, the only real differences I have noticed are that the PS3 version has slightly longer loading times which happen more often than either of the other versions. Beyond that, though, I haven't found any noticeable gameplay differences, so you can't really go wrong no matter which version  you pick.
Regardless, this is a game anyone can enjoy (heck, it was originally rated K-A, or Kid to Adult, when it was released on the Saturn), and for good reason. My own history with the game aside, it is just the right blend of relaxing and intense: beautiful graphics, creative stages, simple yet addictive gameplay with just the right amount of challenge, a story that is easy to understand and characters who are easy to identify with, and an absolutely wonderful soundtrack. I would highly recommend buying this game and giving it a shot, especially if and when it goes on sale. You will not regret it. Thank you for taking the time to read this, and sweet dreams!

UPDATE:
Now that I'm 16 hours in, I have a better feel for it, and my opinion hasn't changed.  The game is pretty well balanced and playing on normal difficulty (which is still nice and challenging), I haven't run into any ridiculous difficulty spikes (outside of the random encounters that toss enemies at you that are 20+ levels above your party).
There are some cheap tactics in the enemy AI, like criticals and requiems (basically unavoidable instant death attacks if they land) which will annoyingly cost your party members significant recovery time.  This detracts a tiny bit, but once you learn which monsters do these things, you can take some preventative measures by buffing your avoidance, but it's not always a guarantee.
There are a few OP skills, some of which you can get pretty early on.  Ninja's illusion, for example, while not directly OP in terms of damage output, its effectiveness at avoiding all kinds of damage to your party members makes it difficult to not use every turn.  There are also a few class/skill combinations that allow you to crush random ecounters a bit too handily.  Overall though, this doesn't detract from the enjoyment of the game.
The overall message of this review remains clear:
(goodness, what a long winded definition)
Based on a 4 hour initial playthrough, this game is definitely for anyone that enjoys party based, turn based dungeon crawlers.
Combat is turn based in the form of rounds, highest agility with the highest chance of going first.  Party member size is six, so you get a good variety of classes/skills going on in a group.  You can also change classes whenever you feel like after paying a fee, and you retain any skills you learned from the prior class which you can equip on your new class (there are limited slots).
It's pretty obvious that this is a port, as the graphics aren't all that great depending on the resolution you use (the higher, the more muddy they get, running at 25x14 it looks simply okay).  There are no issues with fonts, but the character overlay and info boxes in battle do look a bit too large when running fullscreen.  There is both western and weeb art, so fans of both can use whichever they like.
The game is nice and difficult.  I'm playing on a normal playthrough, and while I haven't had any deaths in the party, I've been extremely cautious in avoiding them due to the life point/permadeath system.  If your members die too many times, they are gone for good, so it's best to play it safe and leave a dungeon to get healed up/identify items/sell.
I'll update this more as I play through further and can offer a better review, but so far in the first four hours, this game is a godsend for those who love turn based dungeon crawlers!

Please visit
to see the full in depth review with pictures and video.  Due to the word limit I cannot post the entire review, so here is a basic summary of the game as I see it.
I have been pondering how to write this shorter summary of this game.  Given that I have written quite a bit already at the link above, I am trying to determine how to condense it.  Yes, I was given a copy of this game by NIS America for review purposes, and yes, I heartily recommend this game to anyone who is looking for a solid, enjoyable First Person Dungeon Crawler experience.
But there are issues, and these are things you need to be aware of before jumping in.  Firstly, there is no handholding here.  The game explains very little, giving you the barest of explanations about mechanics.  It has a UI that had me confused frequently (where do I find the bloody Slow and Avoid spells...9 hours later I find the tabs for spells).  What are these icons in the middle of the screen at the bottom for?  Why does it take so long to grind out levels?
Despite these faults however, I kept playing, and I honestly enjoyed it.  The story is a tad threadbare but unlocked in a unique way.  The factions you have to work with are interesting.  The music is PHENOMENAL and if I had a way to get the Soundtrack I would in a heartbeat.  The art work and artstyle and sprites are unique and fun.  The combat, while basic, is entertaining (Seriously, a Samurai using Carnage Front gets hilarious) and the mechanics involving permadeath and class changing are unique.
Also, the dungeons are very interesting.  Each has a unique feel to them, from a container yard full of bandits, to a snowy forest that spins you around and has hidden pathways, and a secret underground temple palace with teleporters and false walls, each felt different enough to be fun.  I got far enough to unlock the second set of dungeons, which included an underwater temple, a ghost city, and a mining complex, but due to the difficulty of grinding XP I havent had a chance to go further.
Seriously, the encounter rates are so low it can take an hour or more to gain a single level.  It gets a little absurb.
If you can handle the hardcore nature of this game, and are wanting a great dungeon crawling experience with some of the best art and music I have seen recently, you cannot go wrong with this game.

Stranger of Sword City is a DRPG - which means a lot of fighting, a lot of dungeons and a lot of loot. All of that, is pretty damn good... except the shell it's put in, is one that looks years outdated.
Full Video:
Summary:
As always, check the video for the best possible impression
While I enjoyed this title's core gameplay loop quite a bit, it needs to be said first and foremost... it looks outdated as hell. This is obviously a game from 2014 that was released for a 10 year old piece of hardware… But it’s coming to the PC and here we expect our dungeons to look pretty.
While the overall static art, portraits and monsters look great, the lack of animations, combat effects and otherwise barebones “extra’s” very much detract from the visual experience of the title.
Now, the game is pretty difficult, but while that normally isn’t an issue – other games are hard! – The problem of this games grindy nature, forcing you to level new characters repeatedly to have a healthy pool of characters to switch around does also detract from the gameplay loop of running dungeons.
If you can live with the sub-par graphics and if you enjoy leveling a variety of characters through the same dungeons then this game offers a few things that are damn good.
The gameplay is pretty great. With a large variety of dungeons, monsters, items, classes and many methods of combining them together. Coupled with a unique and interesting twist on the perma-death mechanic it gives the game a sense of adrenaline during combat, while not completely messing you over if a character in your party dies.
The story and world, coupled with the artstyle are damn good. Grim and dark isn’t normally something I feel in an Anime-style RPG, but this game has it down to a T, making me notice that the world they live in isn’t nice and they just have to deal with it. It’s great atmosphere.
The story has a nice level of depth and dominions that allow for a lot of exploration and various plot twists.
It’s a game for the lover of the DRPG and JRPG, and it does a great job at that. But it’s not a perfect game, and comes to the PC already visually outdated.

Gemini Rue is a fantastic and immersive experience. Despite a half-baked combat system (which the game could have probably done without) and some frustrating moments of pixel-hunting, most of the puzzles are logical and rewarding. The story is unpredictable, psychological, and well-paced.
The art design is some of the best I've seen from such a low-resolution game and the soundtrack is a Blade Runner-style blend of noir jazz and eerie atmospherics.
Although the game itself is rather short, the world it creates feels genuinely ominious, and I hope that Wadjet Eye Games will revisit this fascinating universe in the future.

I'm not sure what it is about sitting in a digital truck and driving across the American southwest, makes this game so great, but something just does it.  It brings back memories of road trips I guess.  You and the open road, much like in this game.  It some how emulates that feeling.  Just you, and the wheels rolling beneath you as you pass road signs pointing in various directions, several small towns, and the occasional big city.  A nice experience is also the radio streaming you can do, whether listening to country, classic rock, Christian, jazz, or what have you, you can find a music station to listen too.
Let's start how this game is for everyone right away though.  You are trying to make it big as a truck driver, and this game goes in depth when you can finally afford enough money to buy a truck, and start expanding your business, hire drivers.  It becomes very fun watching your money grow.
The environment to start with in this game keeps improving with each new update.  I plan to update this review as time goes on, because new locations are being added, and re-scaling of the world.  As of writing this, California, Nevada, and Arizona are complete.  Arizona is so far the most visually appealing as the SCS crew keeps getting better at designing America.  I personally can not wait to see their take on the Pacific Northwest, like Washington, Oregon, Idaho, Montana.  Should be awesome to see how they improve over time and make the diverse landscape of America.  Visually beautiful?  There has never been a moment yet in this game, but they have improved since California on how to make things look more realistic and cities seem more alive.
Overall, if you want a game that isn't about action or frills, but want a relaxing game to sit back, enjoy, and take in the sites, I would say this is it.  Especially if you like trucks.

Unlike its contemporaries, which incorporated more simulator-esque aspects into their design with indepth skating mechanics that sought to emulate their real-life mechanics, Jet Set Radio is at heart an arcade game. It plays fast and loose with the concept of inline skating, even automating aspects like grind tricks to further simplify the controls.
It doesn't lose any difficulty as a result, and this is a game that
you learn how to play it.
This isn't the best port. Graphical glitches objects popping-in are the norm, bugs are everywhere (I encountered a particularly annoying one where my game refused to save until I just gave up and reinstalled it), and the new tutorial gives vague and in one occasion flat-out wrong information required to complete it - as well as skipping over integral parts of the gameplay such as wallride jumping.
It's nearly unplayable with a traditional keyboard and mouse scheme, there's no level select for retrying story missions, there's no retry level in the game itself (you simply have to exit back to the hub to retry a level), and the game doesn't display the requirements for high rankings or even how scoring works.
Despite all this - and despite it being really important that you know all this before purchasing - I absolutely recommend playing this game. That wonderful experience of mastering mechanics you'll initially suck at, learning the levels inside and out, the famous OST and the sheer amount of style that this game exudes make this a game worth more than just buying, but a game that's worth getting pretty bloody intimate with.
So get with it, so you too can understand UNDERSTAND, UNDERSTAND UNDERSTAND, UNDERSTAND UNDERSTAND THE CONCEPT OF LOVE.
