I remember as a kid going to local Toys r Us toy store and playing the SEGA Saturn demo kiosk for what seemed liked hours. It was either the pitter patter of Sonic R or the mystical trance of NiGHTS. Those days, those times, that dumb young me? Amazing and hypnotizing stuff that has it's place in game design history. But ol' Father Time did a number on my whimsical memories of the game. While the port is plenty fine technically the game just isn't all its been built up as these past decades. Sometimes cult classics are best left as fond memories. I was happy to have the chance to revisit the game from my past but it simply wasn't a rewarding or fun experience. The game boils down to spamming the A button for 90% of regular levels. The boss battles bring something to the table at least. But aren't very intuitive if you've never played games from the past or grew up on them. I just didn't find it fun and I more or less beat the game out of spite which was mercifully a mere 2.4hrs (only challenge left after the story would be 'A' ranks on each level). Sure its nice to finally say 20 some odd years later that I did beat it, but I kind of wish I never came back and still had those rose-tinted glasses on with the fond memories.
Which all makes me hesitate to even recommend it to fans of the game. And I really can't recommend this game to somebody who would need to be scouring the reviews for information on the game. The price is right if you're feeling frisky. No recommendation here though.

Every night, all human dreams are played out in the two parts of the dream world - Nightopia and Nightmare. In Nightopia, distinct aspects of dreamers' personalities are represented by luminous colored spheres known as Ideya. However, the evil ruler of Nightmare, Wizeman the Wicked, is stealing this dream energy from sleeping visitors, in order to gather power to take control of Nightopia and eventually the real world. To achieve this, he creates numerous beings called Nightmaren, including two acrobatic jester-like, flight-capable beings called NiGHTS and Reala. NiGHTS rebels against Wizeman's plans, and is punished by being imprisoned inside an Ideya Palace, a gazebo-like container for dreamers' Ideya.
One day, Elliot Edwards and Claris Sinclair, children from the city of Twin Seeds, go through failures. Elliot likes to play basketball, but is challenged by kids from another grade and loses. Claris wants to sing in a play but is overcome by stage-fright in front of the judges. That night, the two of them arrive in the dreamworld and suffer nightmares about these incidents. They escape into Nightopia and find that they each possess the rare red Ideya of courage, the only type Wizeman cannot steal. They release NiGHTS, who tells them about dreams, Wizeman and his plans, and the three begin a journey to stop Wizeman and restore peace to Nightopia.
NiGHTS into Dreams... is split into seven levels or "Dreams", each divided further into four "Mares" and a boss battle. The levels are distributed equally between the two child characters; three are unique to Claris, three to Elliot, and each play through an identical final seventh level, "Twin Seeds". Initially, only Claris' Spring Valley and Elliot's Splash Garden are available, and successful completion of one of these unlocks the next level in that child's path. Previously completed stages may be revisited to improve the player's high scores; a "C" grade in all the selected child's levels must be achieved to unlock the relevant Twin Seeds dream for that character.
Various acrobatic maneuvers can be performed, including the "Paraloop". Flying around in a complete circle causes any items within the loop to be attracted towards NiGHTS. The game features a combo system known as "Linking", actions such as collecting items and flying through rings are worth more points when performed in quick succession than they are individually.
After completing the four Mares, you're transported to Nightmare to confront one of Wizeman's Nightmarens, and you have two minutes to defeat the boss, the time taken contributing to your total score for that Dream. After defeating each boss you can play a level again, and choose via the menu which boss to fight.
The game keeps track of the moods of the Nightopians (harming them will displease them, for example), and it features an evolving music engine, allowing tempo, pitch, and melody to alter depending on the state of Nightopians within the level.
Combining original graphics and gameplay with beautiful soundtrack and atmosphere, Nights into Dreams... is considered by many the best Sega Saturn game, as well as one of the best games ever made.

Gemini Rue is an smart, interesting, and worthwhile little point and click adventure game. I hadn't played the genre for quite some time before this, but there was something about a cyberpunk noir dectective title that I couldn't avoid. And it delivered. The ambiance was exactly what I was looking for, providing a deep sci-fi mystery thrown over a gritty urban locale. Mix in a decent soundtrack reminiscent of a mellow jazzy detective story combined with Mass Effect or BladeRunner and it hits all the right beats.
The story was woven brilliantly; you playing the part of Azrial Oden, ex-assassin on the hunt for his missing brother. I found myself following the pace very well, putting the parts of the mystery together on my own just as the story was delivering the outcomes. This meant, at least to me, that the story was smart, but not too smart. The gameplay is similar enough to other point and click games however the use of Azrials commlink to call associates or the terminals being used to look up vital information kind of gave the sci fi narrative a much more immersive feel.
I guess a for and against this game would be it's length. If there was one complaint I would have it's that the story was a bit on the short side and that I didn't get to see enough of this universe. One or two other locations to further flesh out this world would have been great to see. I finished the game in around 8 hours at a pretty relaxed pace, not completing all (maybe a third) of the achievements. This to me was a bit too brief but the tight story and atmosphere more than make up for it.
I thoroughly enjoyed Gemini Rue. So much so that I'm looking to try some of the other point and click titles from Wadjet Eye Games; the next being the Blackwell saga. If your looking for a good point and click game with elements of noir detective mystery combined with a great sci fi angle, then I'd suggest giving this game a try.

It's a point-and-click adventure game of the older variety (puzzling puzzles and all), which, for some reason, puts some people off from the very outset. Assuming you're not from that group, however, you will find a game with a pretty unique and intriguing story, accompanied by a very fitting noir atmosphere (I hesitate to call it cyberpunk, though similar themes are employed) and well executed retro graphics. On the other hand, the story and the atmosphere are the good parts of the game.
Why do I say that? Well, even when it works the controls, particularly those for shooting, are a bit of an annoyance. The game would've been better without those action sequences, but alas, they're there and can be endured. The main complaint, however, is that the game is rather buggy in game-breaking ways. There are workarounds, but it still makes it a bad product. For example, on Windows 7 x64, the first thing one has to do is to turn the Steam overlay off, or else any alt-tabbing or shift-tabbing means that all dialogue will be in fast-forward mode, making it impossible to follow the plot. Resonance, another game from the same developer, has the same issue, so at least I kind of knew about it.
Next, after a restart my saves just disappeared. Turns out this can be fixed by moving them from \SteamLibrary\steamapps\common\Gemini Rue\reslists\Saves
to \SteamLibrary\steamapps\common\Gemini Rue\Saves but why should I have to? Oh, and the escape key needed to access the menu sometimes stops working, at which point one should apparently realize that hitting shift first helps. Oh well, at least I didn't have to patch the game with specific versions of DLL files, but that reportedly happens too.
Now, if you are willing to subject yourself to all of that, there's a nice, really well-voiced sci-fi story in it for you.  If not, you're probably just being sensible. Either way, I can't really recommend paying full price for the game. Sales level prices, yes, but perhaps only to fans of the genre.

Western 1849 is a short game, but the gameplay is surprisingly good. In each of the six locations, you can move your character between four different points within the map. Your choice of position will depend on where the bandits are located. So if you have a bandit on the far left of the map and you are on the far fight of the map, you can’t shoot him before you move closer to his location. Gunfights start to become tricky when you have several outlaws in different positions. Some are waiting on higher ground (like on a roof) and others are hiding behind chariots, barrels or rocks. You can only take them down (with your gun and rifle) when they are in the open or leave their cover, unless you have a stick of dynamite. When five or more of them do this at the same time it can lead you to a quick death, if you are not careful. To help you out, the enemies you can’t see on the other side of the map will be identified by an exclamation point on your screen. If the exclamation mark is white, this means the bandits are still hiding but when it becomes yellow they are out of cover and ready to shoot. Each time you take one bandit down without being hit, it will increase your multiplier points; but if a bullet reaches you, it will restart the countdown. Also, if are an incredible gunslinger and shoot enemies at a fast pace, it will activate a rage mode where you become invisible for a while.

I've had this game for awhile now. Its one of those games that I want to love, but just can't.
Here are a few reasons why...
1. Stability is an issue even now, almost a year after Early Access opened. Funny thing is: stability has actually gotten worse
2. The  UI is terrible. Confusing and counter-intuitive, you'll likely find yourself clicking around in menus trying to find things for several minutes
3. The game is largely all dicerolls. Its unclear how to influence your odds
4, Missions are arbitrary and pointless. There is no reason to read the text. It doesn't even tell a cohesive story
5. Its not clear what the game is about. Is it about hero management or city building? And what's the deal with neighboring towns (some you're competing against, and some you're just visiting). It doesn't seem like the game-maker has a single vision for the game, but rather has a few visions for a few different games and kinda just taped them together.
At the time of writing this, the game isn't worth your money (August 8, 2015). However it *is* still early access, so I might have to modify these words eventually.

If you're looking for a positive review, then you're in the wrong place, HOWEVER, if you're here for a tremendous chicken Stir Fry recipe, THEN LOOK NO FURTHER!
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan and heat through. Serve with noodles.

The armor system is shoehorned into this game in such a way as that many class combinations that are natural in most games of this type are useless; and there is no documentation warning people of this.  SImply put, you don't want to be doing both magical and physical damage at the same time, because you are then required to force your way through both armor types; there is no good reason to do this.  The result is that many skills simply don't work together, and the clusterf#ck is worsened when you attempt to pick classes and skills for  your party; only to find out later in the game that you chose wrong, and are now underpowered.
The problem is that they forced this beta idea into the game without testing it properly, and documenting its effects.  The result is that you get to restart over and over and over again until you figure out what works with what.
Paying money to beta test a product is an extremely anti-consumer business model; especially when the game has not been released in 'beta' mode.
Short version:  don't bother with this pay for beta release until at the very least guides come out explaining how to build your party properly.

I never leave reviews, but I can't let this game get burried in an avalanche of childs who don't have patience with something that was clearly labeled Early Access.  I leave this review with 300 hours of gametime now.  I've seen this game inside and out.  So you can trust I have an educated opinion.
Pros:
1.) Far better than most "early access" games when they first launch.  Within 2 weeks they've imrpoved so much of the issues that you wouldn't even remember day 1.
2.) Great universe, gentalia everywhere, and the same survival package you'd expect from most survivals but it works.
3.) Fun combat that definately can see improvement, but I love the direction its heading.
4.) Pretty great building mechanics, especially with the ability to build mostly anywhere you want (this can lead to a con see cons)
5.) A large beautiful map that is amazing to explore
6.) Brutal NPC's (when they dont lag) that can be a fun fight everytime
7.) For a early access title, its well polished on the client side and has lots of features already
8.) Avatars :) (also a con see cons)
Now I don't wanna seem like a blind fanboy, this game DOES have its problems that need to be addressed:
1.) Balance, this is the killer @ the moment.  The endgame is fairly unbalanced, in fact, most tiers going up to level 50 are unbalanced and need to be addressed quickly before people grow too bored.   Explosives need to be buffed, there needs to be a 4th tier of weapon that can damage t2 AND t1. We need raid ladders.. badly.  Mesa/unraidable bases is really bad for the meta atm.  This plays into the ability to build wherever you want.  Being able to take a raid ladder and counter this brings the best of both worlds.
2.) Avatars :( While they are super cool they need to be balanced.  There's a lot of ways they can do this.  a.) make them able to be damaged (by thralls, other avatars, and even your teamates arrows/weapons if they dare) b.) allow your altar to cast a spell on your base, if you have the mats to summon an avatar, and somone else is summoning one on you while your offline, your avatar will come to defend your base to potentially ward off complete annihilation.  c.) increase the cost of avatars, they really aren't that hard to come accross.  Some combination of these needs to be in affect in order to balance avatars
3.) A few exploits in the game that need to be addressed (will keep them quiet)
4.) This is from a server admin perspective PLEASE give us more tools from the admin side.  Rcon would be the most important, along with clan management tools.  Mods need to be able to auto download from the server as well, because there are some good mods available but no admins want to run them with out auto download
There might be some details that slipped my mind.  But these are the most pressing cons and the most amazing pros.  This game is going somewhere.  It has a ton of potential and if funcom sticks to their deadlines and the promises they claim for this game then I have no doubt in my mind this will be up there in one of the best Survival MMO's available on the market.  Give it time mates, I remember early ARK, I remember early Rust.  This game in its infancy already proves to me that it will carve a niche into the survival market.
Some impatient people may need to give it time, but if you are a TRUE early access tester, this game is a blast.. especially with friends!!

Just like with it's predecessor, Mass Effect 2's strong suit is the story, however this time around, the story telling and presentation have been upped quite a bit. Everything feels a lot more cinematic and dialog animations feel more organic than they did in ME1. Granted, there isn't that much that drives the overall plot of this trilogy forward.
It basically serves as a build up for ME3. However what will stick with most people are the multitude of characters you'll meet along the way, most with their own backstories and quests. Just like with ME1, I'd say that the best part of the game is just talking to other characters and enjoying the scenery.
The combat and leveling system has changed quite a bit, in some ways for the better, not so much in others.
The awkward and clunky combat of ME1 has been replaced with a relatively standard 3rd person shooting system. Think of it as "Gears of War with skills".
The leveling system has been quite stripped down. You no longer level up things such as weapon accuracy or Charm/Intimidation. Now all you level up are your skills. Whether or not this is a good thing is up to you. I kinda liked the more intricate system of ME1 but I understand why they changed it. It makes things simpler and not having to level up accuracy means that weapons feel less clunky to use from the get go.
However as a whole, I'm still not a huge fan of the combat system. Sure, most guns and skills are mos satisfying to use, but just like Gears of War, most scenarios devolve into a sluggish cover war, where you take peak shots from the same piece of cover until all enemies in your sight dead. This is especially true if you're playing on higher difficulties. It just slows down the pace of the game. It's also kind of a shame, because some stages have interesting level design, but you only really make use of maybe 5-10% of a room during a fight.
So, just like with ME1, combat is a means to get you forward in the otherwise enjoyable story of this game. But it is probably more servicable in doing so than ME1 was.
Overall, I'd absolutely recommend this game if you at the very least enjoyed ME1's story and want to experience more of the Mass Effect universe. If you hated ME1's combat system, you might actually get some more enjoyment out of this game.
I do however highly recommend that you actually play ME1 first, as this is a direct continuation and not a whole lot gets explained to you. Also, you can import a completed ME1 save file into this game and have all of your choices affect this game, creating an overall more personal experience.

Overgrowth is a game where you play as a rabbit fighting and free running through the worlds that have been supplied by the company that is making the game (Wolfire) or the public.
These maps have many different variants in what you can find in them. Some might have no enemies and require you to run and jump across the maps doing various free running maneuvers to get to the end of the level. Others might supply you with enemies for you to fight head on or slowly take them out as silently as possible.
The free running flows nicely and allows you to access many different cracks and holes in the map assuming you know the correct way to use the free running mechanic. by holding spacebar you'll be able to run on a wall horizontaly or vertically. by tapping the spacebar again you will jump in the direction the camera is pointing. However if you want to jump off of one wall, run on another, then land on top of a rock you will have to use the shift key to chain together these maneuvers.
The fighting in Overgrowth is fenomenal. Speed is essential when going head on into a fight, more often then not if you look away for even a second you will find that most of your brain is splatterd on the closest wall. Combat in this game revolves on left click to attack and right click to block. Attacking is as simple as holding down left click and letting the game attack the enemy while you tap WASD and SHIFT to change the type of attack you will throw at the enemy next. Blocking and avoiding attacks is much more difficult. To block an attack you have to tap the right mouse button at the right time to avoid you being thrown accross the room. Doging applys using tapping the movement keys in the direction you want to doge, again having to hit it at the right time.
Problems I have faced while playing this game have been more present in the combat than anything else. Blocking and avoiding attacks are the biggest contenders. Since this is a 3rd person fighting game the view you will be playing in will vary. Often times the angle of the camera is dependent on how well you can see the enemy attacking. Because of this the doge mechanic tends to be hard to judge. When you facing the enemy head on the keys that you will use to avoid an attack will be AS and D. When looking from the side the keys you will use are WS and A. But when you find yourselfe between views knowing what button combinations to press to avoid attacks is hard to judge, and I find my spine broken much more because of it.
Another problem I have with the fighting resides in the blocking. When in combat to block an attack you hit right click. But it is un-clear wether you tap the button when the enemy is going into the attack or about to hit you.
My final problem with the combat is when fighting with weapons, specifically the smaller faster weapons such as short swords spears and knives, the weapons move much faster than anyone to react beyond "Oh crap.".
Overall the game is an incredibley fun and fast game to play and I highly recomend it

Very good, nearly great.  The big draw here is the noir science-fiction story.  A point/click adventure without a decent story is useless, and Gemini Rue is interesting if you are into futuristic urban dystopia.  There is a good bit of suspense, but also a lot of do-this-so-you-can-do-that linearity that will frustrate you if you get stuck, because there's nothing else you can do until you figure it out.  The best part of the game in my opinion was the part where you could switch between two characters, so if you did get stuck, at least you could switch to the other character's storyline until you were ready to go back and tackle the other point in which you were stuck.  Eventually it all comes together nicely with a satisfactory ending and some fun easter eggs along the way.  The voice acting and sound/music effects actually add to the suspense and game atmosphere, so that's a big plus.
I am not a big fan of the pixelated art style, or my cursor getting momentarily stuck every time it ran into an edge of the screen (hit escape until the menu centers, and then hit it again - you should have your cursor back).  If you aren't into point/click, but the theme interests you, you should give Gemini Rue a go.  Don't know if I'd buy again, but recommended for a playthrough as a good change of pace from action games.

Alright, I don't have thousands of hours in American Truck Simulator but I would call myself a fan, everyone who doesn't own this game or Euro Truck Simulator 2 will have a hard time being a fan. Generally the trucks handle good for what they are, as a fan of many racing games it was an awkward step in driving a truck but I have a general interest in them so it wasn't hard to learn how to corner or brake distance. But you will need an interest in big trucks overall to want this game for any reason other than a relaxing driving game.
I'll start with the good. American Truck Simulator or ATS, is a job based simulator (like all the other simulators) that focuses on the driving aspect of driving a tractor trailer or normally, truck driving. It's a relaxing game, while I wouldn't say you could sit back and relax like you're watching a movie, it's easier than racing games. You still need a good sense of driving and a few years of driving would mentally help. Though if you're young or don't know how to drive, it's not going to be easy.
The game does simulate driving a big truck very well, the sound is close to what you would naturally hear though I would personally prefer had the rumble been louder and the world enviroment sounds, they do have sound but you can't hear it unless you're in the cinematic camera which zooms way out or some type of wind which sounds cool while driving on a windy day. Though there isn't any weather effects other than thunderstorms / light rain. I wouldn't mind a bit of snow or fog.
You can't get out of the vehicle, there's no documents to sign or papers to write on like an actual big truck job, which I find alright. I personally wouldn't mind a bit more depth to the job itself but I don't see the use in that. One thing I kind of wish for is an actual job mode or some sort that forces you to work for the same company and work at certain times of the day. This game gives you the ability to drive for the same company once you have learned all the locations, overall it's just choose the highest priced load near-by you or best price per distance and you're set. I kind of want to give myself a bit of a idea for what I would do or want to do.
There is the ability to actually build your own distrabution company, but for the most part it comes down to buying a second truck, hiring a driver from the company management on the pause screen, and keep driving. It's not really in-depth about it and you can't see the drivers of the trucks you gave them, most trucks I buy personally are customized, when I want to use another truck I usually let an employee drive it and I don't ever see them on the road. It kind of sucks that the world is static while you're the only one really growing.
The game doesn't have any music you can listen to over the road, no preset stations, you'll have to manually put music into the folders or have an internet connection to play the radio stations that are coded into the radio, though they have a high bit rate and lag more often than not. I would just use one of the music players online.
Alright, for the general bad. I like these games though, I'm not trying to bash the devs or contradict myself, but these are things that should be realised. I'll say this outright, the "bright" minds at SCS need a mental check-up, to put it in the nicest way possible. I've been following ATS since its announcment or atleast an announcment for close to a year before its realease and on the day of release, the game gets an update, what's the update? It's DLC, it's corn cutting DLC. The game only shipped with one truck and one state, I mean what the donkey's tail SCS? The news the day after release was "Nevada DLC is FREE!" well no sewage pipe. The game only had one truck and California the moment it was on the store. If the game only had one state and you had to pay for everything else, you bet your boy howdey SCS would of heard something.
SCS has some of the worst DLC practice I have ever seen. Your simulator games are good for driving, but all the DLC of Euro Truck Simulator 2 is dumb, I'm really trying to be nice about my words. I have only seen one developer that does this and that's the devs of Payday 2, you're paying for things that either should of been in the game or free in general. Simulator games for some reason are starting to do frog licking things. They're selling small peices of content for dollars on the pennies and the bigger content for a lot more than they should be. I'm not willing to pay five bucks for the future states that are being added (the only states in ATS are California, Nevada, and Arizona), how much will they charge for all 50 states? If they can even make Alaska and Hawaii work. But for real, three bucks to change your steering wheel or colour your rims? You can get the small peices of DLC for free if you have a certain ammount of time in the game AND have an account for their website, but the DLC should be free for everyone, not a timed offer for people who have a "World of Trucks" account.
Also, if you're expecting the cities and towns to be detailed with each city having highways that connect across every mile, drop that expectation. I live in Las Vegas, there's a Las Vegas in the game. I was really excited to drive in my own city in my dream truck, well duck me, right? Las Vegas in the game barely resembles Las Vegas in real life. There's only one area in the city that looks like the real city at all. A lot of buildings were recycled, while they don't have the name of the casinos (for copyright) at least make the cities feel like actual cities. Generally there's only one highway in each city. The Arizona state has two in the main cities but they just cross paths for the long trail. The cities feel like larger towns than they do busy day and night traval destinations. I wanted to see San Francisco, which is better detailed than Vegas, San Diego, which looks like a joke, and Primm, which isn't even a town. It has at the most, eight buildings.
I'm not gonna go into much more detail, overall the game just focuses on driving and that's it. You can't customize your truck as much as you could in Euro Truck Simulator 2, but there will probably be a DLC in the future that will make you pay for fuzzy dice in your cab. I could probably get real fuzzy dice to hang on my mirror in real life for the same price as the DLC and have a bit more bang for my buck.

I think this is one of the greatest science fiction point-and-click adventure games you could find on steam. It's got old school pixel graphics and just great voice acting all-around. The puzzle elements are also a lot of fun. The story behind Gemini Rue may seem derivative. It's set in a universe like the TV show Firefly and it's movie counterpart Serenity, it has the tone and feel of Blade Runner and has the plot of Total Recall. But it never made it bad. It's just taking the good stuff on what I like about science fiction.
You play as Azriel Odin, an ex-assassin that is looking for his brother on the planet of Barrucus, which is part of a Gemini Star System, a system that won it's independence after a war and is now run by a crime syndicate known as the Boryokudun. The other character you will get to play is Delta-Six whom is a patient of a mysterious facility. This is all I can say about the story without going into spoilers.
Throughout the game, you talk to characters, solve puzzles, do detective-like work to learn about things and occasionally go on shoot-outs. There's an interesting shooting mechanic in the game that you will learn how to use.
All of the characters in Gemini Rue are well written and feel real. The philosophical themes of identity and memories are also explored in this game and is pretty much what the game wants to explore and talk about. There are a couple downsides of this game. Some of the puzzles are little too difficult and the fictional universe that is offered in Gemini Rue remains mostly unexplored with the exception of a single city on one planet and a facility somewhere else.
But I recommend this game to Science fiction, cyberpunk and story adventure fans. It's definitely a must-buy!

tl;dr version: game still in alpha (incomplete, buggy), but now in an acceptable state as far as early access games go.
edit 10/17/15 review update
When I first got RPG Tycoon many moons ago, it was just awful. One of those early access games so early in development, it felt like a gyp. It was like that for quite some time up until roughly the second half of 2015. That's when the developer finally got serious working on his game. I've seen RPG Tycoon grow and mature over time to a point where it is now showing promise and potential to be a decent albiet simple and crude management simulator.
In my previous review, I  did not recommend due to how unstable it was and a memory leak that slowed the game down so much it became unplayable.
Since then, those two issues are gone. I now recommend RPG Tycoon!
Well, as an alpha anyway.
RPG Tycoon is far from complete. Some features are still obviously being worked on. There are still annoying bugs you can't avoid while playing. Game is in need of balance tweaks. Loading save games still has a high risk of causing something to glitch out. Visitors still tend to get frozen in place and never leave.
But the game is now in a state that I can call playable. Its pretty okay for what it is too.
Basically if you've been eyeballing this game thinking about buying it, I'd say its safe to buy now. The developer is now supporting their game and updates are churning out more frequently. But, obviously, if you're one of those types who can't stand unfinished/buggy games steer clear for the time being. RPG Tycoon has a long way to go still.
Heaps of fun, would recommend. If you want a singleplayer game thats a bit different and to shoot up a load of dudes then this game is for you.

Update: SCS has come out with the map re-scale. However, it is in BETA, and as such there are some bugs and design inconsistencies. Therefore, I will not do a review on this nor change my rating until the map is fully supported. I believe that is only fair to the game designers.
Positives:
- Trucking in America
- If you're looking for relatively fast deliveries, this is the game for you
- Picking up and dropping off trailers is much harder than in ETS2. The trailers and trucks are larger, and the maneuvering space much tighter
- Modding community
Negatives:
- Much smaller map scale in comparison to ETS2
- Limited number of models of trucks to purchase
- Very limited stock choices for truck customization
- No significant updates to graphics
- Very slow release of significant updates to the game by SCS
- Many of the routes become repetitive due to the small scale of the map
Updated 11/2/1016 - SCS has finally added a new truck design, the Peterbuilt 389. Now this is the beast I've always thought about when it comes to American trucking. Huge, powerful, noisey - hey, it can't be beat! Thank you SCS for adding it. Now I'm just waiting on the long promised map rescale.
------
SCS's American Truck Simulator (now on referred to as ATS) is a fun little game for the first few hours. After that, it becomes rather monotonous. Billed as the sibling to European Truck Simulator 2 (ETS2), on the surface it seems to be the case. However, scratch said surface and you will find stark differences.
The first thing one notices is how small the maps actually are. In ETS2, the distances feel real, and a 19 hour delivery really feels like one. However in ATS, the distances are extremely scaled down. The same 19 hour distance feels like a short jaunt. A side effect of this is that the main routes become common place and thus quickly end up being rather boring.
The next issue is the lack of truck designs to purchase. Compared to it's older sibling, the choices the player has in trucks are very limited. (Update: as of 11/2/2016, SCS added the Peterbuilt 389 free to owners of ATS) To make matters worse, stock truck customization is extremely bare bones. I remember when I first played the game, I eagerly anticipated leveling up so that I could unlock more customizations. I was sadly disappointed to find out that there were hardly any at all.
Now to be fair, SCS has added a few (namely tire customization), yet that was also applied to ETS2, so there really wasn't anything extra special for ATS. They have also added steering wheel customization (very basic), but again that was shard cross platform.
Another issue is the graphic quality of the game. It seems that they used the same engine on ATS as that which was already present on the years old ETS2. So in essence, one could almost consider ATS as a stand alone ETS2 DLC. As an example of how outdated the graphics are, a friend of mine recently saw me playing and commented on the "legacy graphics" he witnessed.
I also find SCS's speed of delivery on important updates equivalent to molasses running downhill on a cold day in winter. They promised a few months ago that they were working on a re-scale of the playable map to make it more like ETS2. This was due to the playing community's justifiable outcry. However, other than a few screen shots, they have produced nothing. Indeed, at the time of this review, the last status update (a few screenshots) they had given was on September 5th, almost a month and a half ago. They also claimed that due to successful sales of their products, they were able to hire a larger team of developers. However, one would not be faulted to wonder if they simply hired playful primates. Is it one developer and a monkey working on these updates? SCS is extremely quiet concerning this.
The player community has also been constantly begging SCS for new truck models, and at first, SCS seemed to indicate that they were pursuing licenses for them. However, it has been an extremely long time since they have mentioned anything in regards to it, causing one to wonder if they have silently abandoned all effort in the matter. (Update: as of 11/2/2016, SCS added the Peterbuilt 389 free to owners of ATS)
The one huge offering that ATS has is its modding support. What makes the game enjoyable for many players is the numerous mods that game enthusiasts have created (lighting, weather, mechanics, new truck models, map revamps, etc.). If it weren't for these, I honestly wonder if ATS would be as popular as it is today (other than fanboys who'll support the game no matter what).
As someone who has played well over 200 hours in ATS, and who has at times really enjoyed it, I am forced to decide whether of not I would recommend this to a friend for purchase. When it comes down to it, I cannot recommend it at it's full price. Perhaps when it goes on sale for around $5, then I'd say to grab it up. However, as the product is today, the slow speed of development and updates by SCS, the sub par graphic quality, lack of truck choices, and a few other issues, I really don't think it's worth the full asking price.
In the end, I give it 3.5/5 stars. It has it's fun moments, and has potential. You really do feel like you're driving a truck (as long as you have the correct mods installed), and at first the routes are fun to drive. Unfortunately, it turns repetitive awfully fast.
(note: I have changed my review score from a 3/5 to a 3.5/5. The reason being is the release of the Peterbuilt 389 on 11/3/2016. Why not any higher? While I am thankful that there is one more truck model to drive, it still does not address the fact that the maps scale is quite small, nor the lack ot stock truck customization. It also does not address graphic quality nor speed of significant updates. I still cannot recommend this game at its non-sale price as no new truck model will salvage the game from the primary issues I have already documented. Map rescale will greately change my recommendation, and one can only hope that it happens soon.)
* - If/when SCS updates the game, I will also update my review

The best thing about this version of Jet Set Radio is that it DOES include the soundtrack and levels from the NTSC Dreamcast version (most ports I've seen cut those out). That means you get Grind Square, the best level in the game, with Rob Zombie, Cold and Professional Murder Music blasting while you soar through the air spraypainting apache helicopters from one powerline to the next!
Seriously though, if you can't get your hands on the original Dreamcast version, this is the next best thing. The graphics hold up great in HD (so long as you don't pay much attention to the wood-block pedestrians), the controls with a gamepad are slick, and the potential to mod the game for custom grafitti tags opens the floodgates for your own creativity. And if you've never played Jet Set Radio before, $5 gets you a wild and brutally challenging experience with a culture straight out of MTV's best years.
One warning: This is not a long game by any stretch. You'll easily finish a playthrough in one sitting if you know what you're doing. At $5, the game is basically a dollar an hour of story. Thankfully, the extra tasks such as collecting all graffiti souls, unlocking all characters and getting JET on every level are so brutally tough that completionists can attack this game for weeks.

This game is terrible. Anything you may have liked about the first Majesty has been changed for the worse or altogether taken out of the game; I'd make a list, but it would take entirely too long. Big defects of this game:
-AI is terrible. Characters hang around the castle area more often, accomplishing nothing. Flags do little to motivate and when they actually manage to catch the attention of a hero, the hero usually rushes to his death - they are either too stupid to run away or, more likely, one of the  unimaginative monsters are overpowered and heroes have no chance against it.
-Stories are poorly thought out or are nearly the same as quests found in the first game. It seemed that the developers focused more on the mildly humurous jokes made by the advisor/narrator and less on anything novel or interesting for former Majesty fans. Even if you could get past the monotony of the quests, there are only a handful of quests available.
-Finally, the largest problem in my opinion is the fact that every quest other than the tutorial, regardless of the supposed difficulty, is nearly impossible to beat without finding loopfole or cheap trick to finish th mission. Now, I'm not saying it's annoying because it's a difficult game, I'm saying that I have repeately run into situations where, had I not already attempted the quest several times, I would have had no chance of surviving regardless of the tactics or steps taken. Amost every quest I've played allows you a mere minute before waves of rats, skeletons or even more powerful creatures bombard your town. If you manage to take care of them, there's bound to be another directly after that one. Basically, every monster spawning point continously creates monsters who, instead of wandering aimlessly as was seen in the original Majesty, run directly toward your town to assault buildings or heroes. The sheer amounts of these monsters is astounding. And after a small number of in-game days, your city will be filled with sewers and a graveyard that also spawn large numbers of monsters. Basically, these monsters that aren't even a part of the mission's plotline truly ruin the mission at hand and cause the player to focus on defending the city for the majority of quest. Only once EVERY creature spawn point has been destroyed can a player even BEGIN to focus on the quest itself.
Tha game seems like it was thrown together with little thought put in to the story or the ease of playing the game; I wouldn't be surprised if I found out that it was never even tested before release. I know this review probably just sounds like the rants of a noob who can't deal with the difficulty of the game, but I honestly think that this is one of the worst games I've ever played. Actually, writing this review has gotten me so worked up, I think I AM going to list all of the problems, little and small, that I've found so far:
-Poor Artificial Intelligence
-Too many monsters to deal with -always attack your town
- The quests are nearly the same quests found in the original game
- Few things are explained or have tips; If you haven't played the first one, you probably won't know what is going on
- Fewer buildings and types of heroes
- Can't control which buildings should be taxed/ repaired
- Many areas of the map cannot be built on - No apparent reason.
- There is no more "seriousness" to the plotline as told by the advisor. Everything is a less than hilarious joke, usually about the same apparent alcoholism the narrator suffers from.
- Everything in the game has a cartoonish/ childish look to them
-Quest opening screens scroll through seemingly unrelated and aesthetically displeasing screenshots
- Player can only build a limited number of buildings of a given type. This means a limited amount of income and heroes
-Only one marketplace; Trading posts can only be built in predetermined areas.
- Every quest about a single, powerful monster (Giant, dragon, etc.) begins with them attacking your town with no chance to prepare. They then continue to raid our town without relent.
- All enemies are incredibly powerful against buildings. A rat/skeleton or two can take down several buildings if unattended.
- Heroes do nothing on their own: Ranger do no explore anymore, rogues don't steal/ collect chests, warriors no longer hunt, clerics (healers) rarely follow and heal people, dwarves don't build (gnomes don't exist as far as a I know), elves no longer bring in lots of money, etc.
- There is a "party" option which is supposed to aloow you to keep a group of four heroes together, however I could never get the party to accomplish anything of worth.
- The ONLY way to make a decent amount of money is to search for trading post areas, build trading posts and hope that they aren't destroyed during or after the building process (Which they most definitely will be).
- Buildings are weak (or, as mentioned above, the monsters destroy them very quickly.
- Poor attempt at a map editor (too much too explain)
- Camera views are awful - Can't zoom out very far
- Camera panning controls are slow
- Live cutscenes will interrupt any action you are currently doing
- Sewers pop up often and spawn at least three rats at a time in the center of your town
- Many quests require you to convince heroes to go to a certain location on the map. The only way is to use an explore/ defend flag which tend to only attract rangers and rogues
- Rogues are melee and incredibly weak
- The same hero spells/ improvements have to be researched at every building - not a central one such as a library
- "His Majesty's" spells can also be researched multiple times if accidentall clicked, accomplishing nothing but loss of gold
- Annoying voice actors
- Many buildings/monsters have no description
-I've played 6 quests and still can't build many of the buildings
- As new buildings/ heroes are introduced, they're purposes are not always clear or explained
- There is no explanation to what upgrading a building does.
I'm sure there are many more issues I could find or have forgotton to list, but I'm done. Once again, don't expect anything fun or exciting if you decide to buy this game. I am most likely never going to run the game again; my interest in Majesty 2 has died as quickly as it started.

It's really more of an expansion for the original Majesty than a sequel.
The units are mostly (entirely?) the same.  The gameplay is the same.  The hero incentives are the same.  The base building is only slightly altered.
The music is absolutely terrible.  I turned it off after 5 minutes.  The campaign narration and text might as well not be there.  The campaign has no incentive to replay, and the missions are all pretty much the same.  Additionally, the lords system is too weak to be useful or fun.  The standalone single player missions are probably better than the campaign msisions.
The game's interface has some problems.  There is no option to customize hotkeys.  There are not hotkeys for frequently clicked spell abilities.  The camera movement has no insta-move-- only scroll.  There is no hotkey to jump to the last notification message.
The base game is certainly worth the $2.50.
The monster Kingdom expansion is a failure. The monster AI seems to have worse AI than the vanilla.  It can be very difficult to get units to attack or explore at times.  It has typos in several places.  The unit balance has problems. Some missions frequently crash.
I'd recommend staying away from the Monster Kingdom expansion.

I wrote a bad review of this a year back. After coming back to give it another shot I'm going to write a sort-of good one.
Firstly, they've fixed a lot of the issues I had back then (UI issues like the call to arms dot being a tiny thing that was hard to click on, total lack of useful mouseover information, massive glitches)
Secondly as I got further into it I started to appreciate the thought that has gone into it. And particularly the new mechanics that weren't in the original dungeon keeper. A lot of them make sense when considered, like seperating the DK1 horned reaper "strong creature thats hard to keep happy" and DK2 horned reaper "endgame summon monster" into two seperate monsters, the vampire and titans. Or giving a means to assign creatures to the peaceband, so they work instead dropping everything to following the call to arms spell. Smart.
(Tip for anyone coming from DK1 and 2: Dont try to build 5 x 5 rooms immediately like you used to be able to in that game. Theres so many rooms and less space to build them in so its worth planning what you need for the level and starting with a 3x3.
Also I highly ecommend you slow down the game speed, which is a stock option thankfully.)
But it still has one MAJOR issue though, the difficulty curve. You're either storming though the level fairly easily or you're hitting a brick wall (level 4 with its unending waves smacks you out of nowhere after a fairly easy first few levels) it really lacks the twists and surprises that Bullfrog designed levels had.
Pretty much every level has an infinite gold seam, so once you find that, you dont have to budget anymore. Plus you have the option of gold potions, turning your enemies to gold, a spell that literally just gives you gold for temporarily mana etc.
Its too many get out of jail free cards. Again in the old bullfrog games they werent afraid to occasionally lock you out of some of your abilities, to force you to change strategy.
Maintaining a dungeon is really easy since creatures dont fight internally anymore, not even converted hero units. I dont think I ever once had creatures complaining about food even with a 3x3 pig farm feeding a massive dungeon.
Lava only seems to sort-of burn creatures, and plenty of them just dont care anyway. I got the stone bridge well before "how do I cross this lava" ever even became a problem I'd thought about solving.
DK1 and 2 you could NEVER rebuild earth. So once it was mined you were exposed for good. Here you get a spell to do that easily.
See where I'm going with this? The game gives you a bunch of abilities, maybe too many abilities, but rarely tests your brain with them.
The two suddenly-actual-difficult levels where I had to actually think and strategise were the ones I enjoyed the most.
It adds up to a fun DK flavoured novelty, but one without an engaging challenge. If steam had that option I'd give it half a thumbs up.

Ha, Jet Set Radio. This here is the best game of my childhood. My favorite Dreamcast game and, by far, one of my favorite games of all-time.
Jet Set Radio takes place in Tokyo-to, an alternate dimension Tokyo. In this city, for some reason, graffiti and hip-hop are seen as violent crimes or something like that (more on that later). It is also a huge part of that city's culture, where several gangs of inline skaters "fight" for control of the city.
You can play with a group of several characters who are part of a gang called the GG's and you follow their story as they try to graffiti the whole town against different enemies such as enemy gangs, the mafia and the police force. Each playable character has their own style and personality, which also reflected on their way of skating and graffiti. In terms of story, dont expect a masterpiece, but it still works to move the game forward and it is still fun.
In terms of gameplay, the character's movement is hard to get used to. Im still trying to get used to keyboard and mouse controls, but as soon as you get used to them, you will understand why this game is known as one of the classics.
You choose a member of the GG's and you select the level you want to play. When you are dropped on the map, your job is to spray your graffiti on all the marked locations in the map before a timer runs out.
While dashing, jumping and grinding, you will be attacked by the police. The police force acts like Tokyo-to is being attacked by an enemy army so they use everything from normal police officers with a baton to freaking war helicopters to take you down. And, like I said, there are even more enemies than just the police and army. It is a fun challenge, even with the not-so-easy-to-learn controls.
There are also special levels where you are fighting directly against a gang, following them and tagging them to stop them from moving, those are always fun. And there is another type of level where unlockable characters will approach you and challenge you to a tagging competition. In this mode, you will have to pay attention to the challenger's moves and copy them, it is a good challenge and it is very fun.
And now it is time to talk about THE best aspect of the game. The soundtrack. Oh, the beautiful, amazing, funky, FREAKING DAMNED AWESOME! soundtrack.
This game has an incrediby varied choice of songs. There are a lot of different genres, like hip-hop, J-rock, rap, electronic, J-pop, rock and a few more. The songs are creative and they all add up to the action you are seing on screen.
Unfortunately, I don't even know what else to say about the soundtrack of this game other than saying it is amazing and it ties this game perfectly.
Overall? This game is great, honestly. The cel-shading graphics, coupled with the beautiful and intelligent design of the city of Tokyo-to means that no level looks boring.
The feeling of playing with different characters coupled with the different graffiti put in the game (and you can also design your very own ones) WITH the very same design of the levels means that no level is boring.
All that with a soundtrack that will make you stop every now and then (or just leave the game in the character selection menu) just to concentrate on listening to the songs themselves means that this game is a jewel of gaming, a must-have.
Im giving it a 9/10, and it isnt a full 10 just because of the controls being a tad difficult to get used to...

Oblivion is a sandbox game, which means the main map doesn't consist of smaller levels, but the whole land can be explored without a single loading screen. There are also smaller sub-levels—dungeons, cities, houses—which can be accessed from the main map.

Reading a lot of the reviews, negative and positive, one thing that seems to come to light is that the game is buggy. This is 100% correct. The game in its current state is buggy, just like a lot of new Early Access games start out - server issues, game breaking bugs, rubbish AI, exploits, the list goes on.
However, if you find a good server (Yes official servers are an issue, but there are some really good unofficial servers) then you can have a great time, PVP offline raiding is an issue but the Devs are working on this and all the other issues - some people are saying they are taking too long for this, its been ~3 weeks.. I sometimes feel that there is an expectation that things can be fixed with a simple tick box "Oh, Jump exploit? Better untick that and update the game".. unfortunately that is not the case, these things take time.
I bought this game looking for a survival game similar to The Forest (which I love), but one I could play with more people, more focussed PVP and I believe Conan does that. I play on an unofficial server where Base destruction is off, with active admins to stop the base blocking glitches, with monitoring for exploits and I really enjoy the game.
There are lots of issues still to be worked out, AI stuttering on approach of in the distance, unbalanced weapons and leveling with many more that I expect will be found out as the game progresses.
But I stress again.. ~3 weeks in early access... This game has massive potential, and the Devs seem hard at work to make the changes required and requested by the community. I personally look forward to where Conan goes.
So, in my honest opinion. If you're expecting a game without bugs, without exploits, without problems, without instant fixes of those problems, without some days where the game is unplayable in its early access state, without unbalanced gameplay, without all the features that may have been mentioned, without all those things you expect from a full game.. then don't buy it - it wont be for you.
Where if you want a fun, building game with PVP (base destruction on or off) then set a timer for 1hr 45 minutes, buy the game, go onto local server, set all the server options to MAX and see how you find it... IF THEN you like it find an unofficial server, with a good admin and player base... and play it properly - thats what I did. Do not regret spending my money on this.

I didn't want to log off last night, I just wanted to continue exploring, killing and building (I will of course continue my adventure this evening, after I finish work and other rl commitments).
MSI GT72VR 7RE Dominator Pro 17.3" Full-HD 120Hz, Intel Core i7-7700HQ, 16GB, 256GB SSD + 1TB HDD, GeForce GTX 1070 8GB
I was notified on startup that I had an outdated GPU driver with known issues. I ignored this warning because I was eager to play. I should've just taken the time to update the driver though because behold, after 30 mins or so my GPU crashed. After updating the driver I've had no problems.
The game world is just beautiful. I love the stylized graphics, I personally always would chose stylized over "realistic" mind you, it's a fantasy world after all. Timeless. The music is epic, it sets the mood from the start with promises of a great adventure.
You've been left to die on a cross in the Exiled Lands. Conan himself casually strolls by and cuts you down, I was just starstruck and unable to speak to him, I guess that's why he just left me there, to survive on my own. Oh well :) The first thing you need to do is find water and food, so there's pretty much just one way to go - to the river. Gathering is easy, press and hold E as you walk. I picked up some insects and I ate them. With branches and stone collected from the ground I could craft a crude Stone Pick, which I used to kill some turtles and collect wood and bark from trees and stone from rocks. You gain the first levels quite easily, and the levelling system allows you to place skill points in different stats and also unlock crafting recipes. With enough wood and stone I could build my first shelter. When it gets dark at night, it gets really dark, so be sure you craft a torch and you'll need a campfire to cook your food. So when you got your basics covered, food, water and shelter, and your delicate body parts covered by some light armour, now you're ready to explore and fight to survive, build and dominate the world.
The world is already inhabited by dangerous creatures and npcs. Npcs you can capture and break to make them work for you and protect your base! There's quite a lot of content actually, considering this is early in Early Access. Mobs are aggroed from afar, and some come in great packs. It can be a challenge to play solo. I play together with a friend and it's easier, and of course heaps more fun experiencing the game together with others!
Combat and AI needs more tuning, which I'm quite sure Funcom knows and are working on.
The building system is amazing.
So is crafting.
You play single player or invite a friend to co-op on your own system or play multiplayer on official or private servers.
It's Early Access yes, and I'm perfectly fine with donating a few bucks to see this game reach completion (the entertainment value of the game has already recouped my expense imho). And I'm perfectly fine with recommending it to anyone, as long as they all know what Early Access means. Everything is subject to change, there are bugs, it's not finished yet etc etc.
Conan Exiles is an Open World Survival Sandbox game with vast potential. I'm really enjoying it and I'm looking forward to see what the future holds.

It's really more of an expansion for the original Majesty than a sequel.
The units are mostly (entirely?) the same.  The gameplay is the same.  The hero incentives are the same.  The base building is only slightly altered.

The standalone single player missions are probably better than the campaign msisions.
The game's interface has some problems.  There is no option to customize hotkeys.  There are not hotkeys for frequently clicked spell abilities.  The camera movement has no insta-move-- only scroll.  There is no hotkey to jump to the last notification message.
The base game is certainly worth the $2.50.
The monster Kingdom expansion is a failure. The monster AI seems to have worse AI than the vanilla.  It can be very difficult to get units to attack or explore at times.  It has typos in several places.  The unit balance has problems. Some missions frequently crash.
I'd recommend staying away from the Monster Kingdom expansion.

Like many other reviews I give this thumbs up for potential.  The game still needs a ton of work and fine tuning and, frankly, content.
On the PROS side is the basic concept.  Run a village as AI Heroes do all the adventuring.  I have no doubt the finished product will be a good game and worth the money, but I'm holding out hope that it will be a great game that is a steal for the price.
On the CONS side there is a quite a bit wrong or off.  The FTL lite "Epic Quests" feel like random 50/50 guesses.  When it asked me to help a farmer with his pigs 4 times in 4 straight quests I said "yes" all four times.  Wrong each time.  However I have no idea how this matters other than XP not gained.  This transitions nicely into the overall lack of a feeling that my decisions matter other than keeping the town in net gains money wise.  2 hours into the game and I don't even read the quest bits anymore, I just pick and option at random and roll on.  100+ hours in FTL and I still read the text.
The notifications are also super annoying, they constantly pop up to tell me that it is autosaving, which by the way is frequent and necessary, and to tell me a quest is done.  Of course the quest is done, I just navigated a bunch of pop ups telling me the same information.  Again, we are dealing with information that quickly becomes superflous, which is not a great trait for a resource management game to have.
The bonus giving objective queue seems to run out after about 4 sets, though if I remember correctly the Dev noted that is going to be a big part of the next update.
I know I mostly have complaints/critiques here, and I could probably find more.  So why recommended still? Because I really really want this game to be great, it's my first alpha build purchase and I want other people to try it out and offer even smarter feedback than I can.
Thanks for what you are doing Dev, for the large amount of resource management games out there the lack of quality and non-Farmville variety is sad.  Keep working hard and making this game everything it can grow to be!

This game is about as old school as you can get barring text-only, though it proves that there is no such thing as going out of style when it comes to fun.
Story-wise Gemini Rue is a sci-fi noir tale - in the vein of Blade Runner - about a cop searching for his missing brother in a post-war, gangster run corner of the galaxy. It is also the story of a nameless detainee in a mysterious facility where mind erasure and “re-education” are the rule. These two stories run side by side with players alternating between roles, filling in the narrative blanks until they finally come head to head during the game’s climax.
As for the writing, while some of Gemini Rue’s twists, motivations, and dialogue seem hackneyed at times, they can easily be written off as contribution to the game’s pulp roots. The gameplay is mostly solid, with a decent shooting mechanic for the “action” sequences and plenty of point-and-click puzzles to solve. My only gripe is that some clickable objects are very small, requiring one to play “hunt the pixel” in order to interact. More than once this caused me to overlook an otherwise obvious solution.
In the end, Gemini Rue turned out to be a pleasant experience and worth the investment. If you’re a fan of sci-fi noir, classic point-and-click adventure games, or both, you should consider checking it out.

I reinstalled this game on a lark, but quickly discovered why I stopped playing the first time. Level design.
In the first 4-5 missions, the game holds your hand through different objectives. You are expected to defend your town, but can generally work at your own pace.
All this changes after you beat the mage. After that, you have two different missions to choose from. One starts you off surrounded by several monster-spawning sewers (where in previous games you might see one spawn every 10min), and the second mission has a frigging dragon and its spawn coming after you, right off the bat.
The starter 'guard' is never enough to hold back the tide, which leaves you desperately building your guild halls hoping the monsters ignore the defenceless villagers WHO ARE TRYING TO BUILD SAID GUILD HALLS. Of course the alternative is they go after the peasant houses which generate gold. So now you have guild halls, BUT NO ECONOMY TO BUY HEROES FROM SAID GUILD HALLS.
I'm sure I could spend hours sifting through faqs and wikis until i finally have the 'trick', but this runs completely contrary to the whimsical first impression the game gives in those initial levels.
Overall this game is very similar to Euro Truck Sim 2, which in my opinion is a very good thing. With some mods to add more trucks and trailers, this game can offer many, many hours of entertainment.

I'll say it straight away: Jet Set Radio is not for everyone.
JSR has not aged fantastically from its original Dreamcast release. For as much as I absolutely love Jet Set Radio and its successor, Jet Set Radio Future, I will admit it has its share of issues. It's a platforming action game that feels a bit floaty and 'chunky,' for lack of a better word. No matter how carefully you plan out a jump, it never feels like you got it _just_ right. The trick system feels like a lackluster afterthought. And, for a rollerblading game about outrunning the cops and tagging up buildings, it can be a bit slow.
However, even then, I cannot bring myself to dislike Jet Set Radio even a tiny bit. While it may not control the best, it makes up for it in undeniable style and finesse that I've seen almost no other game pull off. The cel-shaded artstyle was one of the first of its time, and it fits the overall theme of the game well. As you would expect, a game centered around graffiti has beautiful pieces, and a wide variety to pick from, at that. Plus, there's something so gratifying about a game that is a giant, flaming middle finger to an oppressive police force in general.
And of course, you can't discuss Jet Set Radio without mentioning its soundtrack. While one or two tracks feel out of place, (I'm looking at you, Dragula and Just Got Cold,) they're completely forgiven by the wild mash of electronic, hip-hop, and upbeat rock that will stick in my mind and music library for years to come.
While JSR may not be the best controlling or longest game out there, it's a game with a superb premise, and a game with a stylistic approach that I don't think will ever be matched in my lifetime. Here's looking at SEGA to rerelease JSR: Future at some point!
(Fingers crossed, but let's be honest, I'm not too hopeful.)

Alright, I don't have thousands of hours in American Truck Simulator but I would call myself a fan, everyone who doesn't own this game or Euro Truck Simulator 2 will have a hard time being a fan. Generally the trucks handle good for what they are, as a fan of many racing games it was an awkward step in driving a truck but I have a general interest in them so it wasn't hard to learn how to corner or brake distance. But you will need an interest in big trucks overall to want this game for any reason other than a relaxing driving game.
I'll start with the good. American Truck Simulator or ATS, is a job based simulator (like all the other simulators) that focuses on the driving aspect of driving a tractor trailer or normally, truck driving. It's a relaxing game, while I wouldn't say you could sit back and relax like you're watching a movie, it's easier than racing games. You still need a good sense of driving and a few years of driving would mentally help. Though if you're young or don't know how to drive, it's not going to be easy.
The game does simulate driving a big truck very well, the sound is close to what you would naturally hear though I would personally prefer had the rumble been louder and the world enviroment sounds, they do have sound but you can't hear it unless you're in the cinematic camera which zooms way out or some type of wind which sounds cool while driving on a windy day. Though there isn't any weather effects other than thunderstorms / light rain. I wouldn't mind a bit of snow or fog.
You can't get out of the vehicle, there's no documents to sign or papers to write on like an actual big truck job, which I find alright. I personally wouldn't mind a bit more depth to the job itself but I don't see the use in that. One thing I kind of wish for is an actual job mode or some sort that forces you to work for the same company and work at certain times of the day. This game gives you the ability to drive for the same company once you have learned all the locations, overall it's just choose the highest priced load near-by you or best price per distance and you're set. I kind of want to give myself a bit of a idea for what I would do or want to do.
There is the ability to actually build your own distrabution company, but for the most part it comes down to buying a second truck, hiring a driver from the company management on the pause screen, and keep driving. It's not really in-depth about it and you can't see the drivers of the trucks you gave them, most trucks I buy personally are customized, when I want to use another truck I usually let an employee drive it and I don't ever see them on the road. It kind of sucks that the world is static while you're the only one really growing.
The game doesn't have any music you can listen to over the road, no preset stations, you'll have to manually put music into the folders or have an internet connection to play the radio stations that are coded into the radio, though they have a high bit rate and lag more often than not. I would just use one of the music players online.
Alright, for the general bad. I like these games though, I'm not trying to bash the devs or contradict myself, but these are things that should be realised. I'll say this outright, the "bright" minds at SCS need a mental check-up, to put it in the nicest way possible. I've been following ATS since its announcment or atleast an announcment for close to a year before its realease and on the day of release, the game gets an update, what's the update? It's DLC, it's corn cutting DLC. The game only shipped with one truck and one state, I mean what the donkey's tail SCS? The news the day after release was "Nevada DLC is FREE!" well no sewage pipe. The game only had one truck and California the moment it was on the store. If the game only had one state and you had to pay for everything else, you bet your boy howdey SCS would of heard something.
SCS has some of the worst DLC practice I have ever seen. Your simulator games are good for driving, but all the DLC of Euro Truck Simulator 2 is dumb, I'm really trying to be nice about my words. I have only seen one developer that does this and that's the devs of Payday 2, you're paying for things that either should of been in the game or free in general. Simulator games for some reason are starting to do frog licking things. They're selling small peices of content for dollars on the pennies and the bigger content for a lot more than they should be. I'm not willing to pay five bucks for the future states that are being added (the only states in ATS are California, Nevada, and Arizona), how much will they charge for all 50 states? If they can even make Alaska and Hawaii work. But for real, three bucks to change your steering wheel or colour your rims? You can get the small peices of DLC for free if you have a certain ammount of time in the game AND have an account for their website, but the DLC should be free for everyone, not a timed offer for people who have a "World of Trucks" account.
Also, if you're expecting the cities and towns to be detailed with each city having highways that connect across every mile, drop that expectation. I live in Las Vegas, there's a Las Vegas in the game. I was really excited to drive in my own city in my dream truck, well duck me, right? Las Vegas in the game barely resembles Las Vegas in real life. There's only one area in the city that looks like the real city at all. A lot of buildings were recycled, while they don't have the name of the casinos (for copyright) at least make the cities feel like actual cities. Generally there's only one highway in each city. The Arizona state has two in the main cities but they just cross paths for the long trail. The cities feel like larger towns than they do busy day and night traval destinations. I wanted to see San Francisco, which is better detailed than Vegas, San Diego, which looks like a joke, and Primm, which isn't even a town. It has at the most, eight buildings.
I'm not gonna go into much more detail, overall the game just focuses on driving and that's it. You can't customize your truck as much as you could in Euro Truck Simulator 2, but there will probably be a DLC in the future that will make you pay for fuzzy dice in your cab. I could probably get real fuzzy dice to hang on my mirror in real life for the same price as the DLC and have a bit more bang for my buck.
Multiplayer is really the only thing that makes me want to play ATS more than the hours I already put into the game, even then online multiplayer is modded, there's no official multiplayer, which might actually be a good thing. I don't know there.  There's no true end-game content either so don't expect anything more than a jack load of money that you won't really spend after getting the trucks you want. It's just driving, more driving and driving. No good easter eggs like the ability to drive a car or a special truck or some special job. It's just the same and the only thing that will advance, is your mental stability to do the same thing any longer.
I do have a lot of bad things about ATS, but overall I'm a simple minded person and I like to relax sometimes with an interest in truck driving. Unless you're me, don't buy this game. I like this game, it's getting a good rating because its what I want to give it. But just take a long hard look at the game and see if driving at a fairly slow speed is what you want to do.

It's a good game. Like really nice.
Technical: Once the game gets going with some complexity expect your framerate to drop quite a bit, it's not unplayable for me personally, but it is a technical limitation of Unity that negatively impacts the game. Only few brief moments where it went under 20FPS.
Audio/Voice Acting: The original narrator from the past Dungeon Keeper games returns, and has great lines and voice acting like before, but is obviously giving a different kind of performance than before, he doesn't sound gleefully evil if that makes sense. For other audio it's pretty solid, some of the minions will utter funny lines to themselves, and they all have unique personalities that make for an enjoyable atmosphere. However this ends up being annoying to hear all these so often, and a lot of the humoerous dialogue takes away from the game. I thought we were evil bad guys, yet I am meant to laugh at my characters.
Gameplay: There are a ton of new additions, spells, a sin system (think tech tree) defenses, mechanics just. Just so much. A lot of people complain that spells don't have use, but I would argue they are very wrong, and a lot of other people seem to agree if the complaint every comes up. Every spell in the game has had some use for me depending on the situation, if I struggle for gold I have a few ways of getting gold, turning a prisoner into gold, spawning gold into the dirt, gold shrine, throwing a potion to make gold. Just apply that to nearly all aspects and you find a pretty open system that you can talor to your needs. In skirmish against AI it's unlikely you will be as pushed to use these, but multiplayer and in storymode I found it useful. For the most part, the gameplay is very solid, everything seemed to work as intended, I unfortunately don't know a good way to write up more about it. It does allow for multiple strategies to win and I like that.
Story: I admire they gave a reason for your overlord forgetting everything in the beginning, and that they tried to give a twist to the story. But it's pretty basic, take over the overworld because the mentor (Narrator) is evil. Honestly that's fine, the missions broke up the gameplay and made the game not feel stale or boring at any point, couple of the characters were actually pretty funny, like the enemy that was shouting out loud his plans of attack and the Narrator insulting him. Game has a hell of a lot of charm. My problem is unfortunately with the ending, while the game builds up this twist a bit, the twist happens with no proper explanation, and then the game just ends. I just finished the last level like 30 minutes ago and I am puzzled, Like the ending just missed some lines it seemed or didn't explain itself at all. It's hard to talk about this without spoiling but the ending didn't have a great payoff to me.
Here is my only real problem, the game has a tone that is definitely not anything like DK1 and 2. It's a lot more light hearted, and the phrase "It's good to be evil" does not work on this game at all. The "good" guys are represented in ways where they are in need of being purged and killed from the lands (they aren't good) and YOUR character and minions never come off as being evil, they utter funny lines, one of them farts constantly, and it's just not the same as DK2, it had humor sure but it was a lot more restrictive. I can't fault the game for this, because it is trying to be it's own thing and that's fine, but I understand where some DK players are coming from. I would have loved a more darker evil version of everything, but that's not something that can be fixed until a sequel.
