Jet Set/Grind Radio is a classic Dreamcast game.
Dreamcast game.
Its soundtrack and style withstands the test of time. Unfortunately, the gameplay itself does not hold up. A certain sluggishness that I had previously attributed to DC controller's analog stick is present here, affirming that it's just the game. Many people will say "it's still the same old thing" just like they did about something like Sonic Adventure, but just like that Sega port, I can't really recommend this.
I love Jet Set Radio in concept, in sound, in what it tries to be. I realize at an older age now though...this just isn't actually that fun to play - or at least it was better on the DC.
I hope Jet Set Radio Future gets a port at some point because that game is far better and lacked the control issues I have with this. It was faster on top of running at 60 fps instead of 30, purely from a gameplay perspective. Still had a kickass soundtrack, had much more impressive levels, gave you the ability to do things like continously trick giving your character speed on a rail. It made grinding more fun. It made EVERYTHING more fun. Possibly the greatest "bundled-in" title for any console ever released.
That is also reviewing JSRF just a little bit as well, but I don't have the ability to do so proper, so I'll do it here.
Anyways, I can't pick a "neutral" option, so I'm going to have to go with a "not recommended".
I remember this being a fun game. I remember getting all the way through it and doing the trials and all that. I remember being excited when it was to be ported.
I feel that some other people might feel the same way if they play it again. The graphics and sound still impresses, but perhaps the experience of having gone through this game is best left in the era it was released in - on the console it was released on. I say this as a fan and not someone against the series. I would probably say the same thing about the GBA version the game as well, which I owned for years: JGR was fun. Coming back to it was not.
That's my two cents. Take it or leave it.

CATS! is a collection of underwhelming "parody" games.
All of the game modes available are just poor remakes of popular mobile game genres.
The first mode being "arcade". This is an infinite runner, and is arguably the best thing this game has to offer, but that isn't saying much. Your character constantly runs to the right, and you have the ability to jump and double jump to avoid obstacles and collect things. The jumping arch feels a bit awkward, and a lot of the jumps will have you spend time off the top of the screen, so you can't see where you are landing, resulting in many frustrating deaths. Although ultimately, it isn't that hard.
The game does a decent job at adding a few new enemies and obstacles every few levels, but it isn't enough to stay interesting for long. I got to the 2nd chapter, and quit after I realised that all of the terrain and objects I had seen so far were just blue versions of the stuff I saw from chapter 1. Perhaps it would evolve more later, but the game didn't grip me long enough to find out.
Also, the animation and art look like placeholder sprites, and don't really match eachother's style. It isn't the ugliest thing in the world but isn't exactly pleasant either. After each run you can purchase some permanent or consumable upgrades to use in your next runs, or purchase new incredibly saturated and ugly colours for your character.
The second game mode offered is "jump" mode.
This is a pretty uninspired rip-off of the popular endless jumping games like Doodle jump. Your completely inanimate character will bounce endlessly, and you can move it left or right to have it bounce off of platforms, to try and get as high as possible. The platforms have no thought behind them, as it seems to be randomly generated everytime with no real rules. Everything is scattered everywhere. There are a few upgrades to collect, which is nice, but they don't feel very useful when the game mode feels so easy. This is easily the most unfinished-feeling game mode.
The third game mode is called "puzzle".
Multiple times, I had trouble even starting the puzzle. I would click on level select and nothing would happen. I had to go to another game mode, quit, go back to the main menu and select puzzle again for it to work. Not a good start.
And all we've got here is a bejewled rip-off. It adds nothing new of interest, and the graphics are once again dull. The levels vary it up a little bit by changing the arena shape, but it isn't enough to stay fun for long.
Accompanying the 3 main game modes, CATS! also comes with 2 bonus modes.
One being "screensaver", where it feels like a cheap version of Nintendogs/cats. You can choose between 4 cats, that stare at you in a certain pose, until you click on them again. You can cycle between about 5 animations, as you watch feathers fall in the background. It's really pointless, and I can't see anyone having fun with it for more than a minute, but I guess it's an okay feature to have.
The final mode is "Pet toy".
Some bugs crawl across the screen, and you're supposed to let your cat play with the screen and smash the bugs. My cat wasn't captivated by it at all, and completely ignored it. Perhaps some people have more excitable cats that will jump at the screen, but being the PC version of the game, I'm not sure how many people are willing to let their kitty scratch at an expensive monitor.
The best part of the entire game is honestly the music. It's cute, and catchy, but sadly is used way too much and gets repetitive.
Aside from the game itself, the behind-the-scenes seem a bit sketchy. This game used to be called Project Cats before it got a rebranding. It originally had one more "hunter" mode, which has now been removed, and is being sold separately on Steam as Cat Simulator.
Not only that, but CATS! obviously has its flaws. Some undeniable ones, yet at the time of writing this review, the game is rated at "mostly positive". Most of the reviews are by accounts with no more than 2 games in their libraries on average, and normally no more than 2 written reviews. They talk about the gripping gameplay and amazing graphics, when it's almost incredibly obvious that these are most likely bribed or bot reviews. Of course there's no proving that, but it seems very fishy.
Regardless of the other reviews, this is my opinion on the game. I'm sorry to give it a negative review, and I hope the developer will look at my criticism and try build upon their game using it, or at least cheapen the price. Currently it is at 10€, which is roughly the same in dollars and pounds. Very overpriced.
I hope you found the review helpful!

The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is a role-playing game set in Cyrodiil, the middle province of the fantasy world of Tamriel. There is no ultimate goal of the game, but according to the main concept, the player has to close the Portals of Oblivion to stop the invasion of the Daedra thus saving the mortal world, Nirn. In addition to the defense of the mortal realm, the Empire must also be saved from inner threats.
Oblivion is a sandbox game, which means the main map doesn't consist of smaller levels, but the whole land can be explored without a single loading screen. There are also smaller sub-levels—dungeons, cities, houses—which can be accessed from the main map.
The game lets you decide almost everything. You can choose how you want to play, what class you'd like to be, where you'd like to head to or what you'd like to do at all. Western 1849 Reloaded is an old-school arcade style shooter with Bandits, Bandidos, Thugs and cigar smokin' Foremen who are all itching to give you a very bad day. The graphics are stylish and the animation simple, yet effective. Bad guys will take up position in cover that often makes them hard to hit with your guns but that's OK because you have some dynamite with which to flush them out. You can dodge from one position to another yourself which can make it easier to hit some of the bad guys as well as affording some cover from the more advantageously positioned enemies. Play progresses in a number of scenes each with 3 waves of bad guys that start out easy but rapidly get tougher and nastier. Watch out for the Foremen who begin to appear during wave 3 of the railway station, they will throw dynamite which can be very unpleasant!
Each enemy killed will increase both your point score and gold earned from bounties and that gold comes in handy for upgrading your weapons and armour as well as extra items for your inventory which can vary from a score multiplying medallion to an uber laser gun and extra ammo. There are up to 21 achievements to be earned and in addition to showing up on your Steam profile these will also unlock perks in game. At the end of each wave you can choose one of 3 randomly selected perks some of which will boost you for the rest of that game and some that will offer a big advantage for the next wave only. Some of these perks interact in unexpected ways with the bad guys often yielding hilarious and sometimes useful results. Although I rarely leave music on in games I found the music enhanced my enjoyment and the sound effects and voice comments from the baddies add to the fun as well
For the price this game gives excellent value for money and is fun to return to now and then when you don't want to think too hard. It definitely reminded me of the old arcade games I used to play as a teenager and the only thing that would improve it would be having a tacky plastic gun in my hands to point and shoot with. Not exactly cerebral then, but highly recommended nonetheless.

Western 1849 Reloaded:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The year is 1849 - inhabitants of the Far West have gone nuts in search of the golden nugget! Gold is the major currency in this era and truly gives a chance to anyone to make their mark in life. But where gold is found, it also attract scumbags to the nearest town. This is exactly what happened to the small, quiet town of Sunset Bluff. So cowboy, we need your help to drive these bandits out of town. Oh and by the way, welcome to the Wild West!
Western 1849 Reloaded is an action/ third person /arcade type of game where you take control of the saviour (sheriff) of Sunset Bluff.
The game offers five levels of difficulty from rookie to champion, but you will have to beat each level to unlock the next one. As a rookie, you will have to eliminate three waves of gunslingers in two different locations which give you a total of six waves to clear. When you reach the champion stage, you will have to clear out eighteen waves in six different locations. That’s not going to be easy!
Western 1849 gameplay is surprisingly good. In each of the six locations, you can move your character between four different points within the map. Your choice of position will depend on where the bandits are located. So if you have a bandit on the far left of the map and you are on the far fight of the map, you can’t shoot him before you move closer to his location. Gunfights start to become tricky when you have several outlaws in different positions. Some are waiting on higher ground (like on a roof) and others are hiding behind chariots, barrels or rocks. You can only take them down (with your gun and rifle) when they are in the open or leave their cover, unless you have a stick of dynamite. When five or more of them do this at the same time it can lead you to a quick death, if you are not careful. To help you out, the enemies you can’t see on the other side of the map will be identified by an exclamation point on your screen. If the exclamation mark is white, this means the bandits are still hiding but when it becomes yellow they are out of cover and ready to shoot. Each time you take one bandit down without being hit, it will increase your multiplier points; but if a bullet reaches you, it will restart the countdown. Also, if are an incredible gunslinger and shoot enemies at a fast pace, it will activate a rage mode where you become invisible for a while.
Well done - you have cleared your first wave! Before you start the next one, you have to choose one of three perks available to you. There are twenty-four of them, from common to legendary, and they are totally random at the end of each wave, which makes this game fun and full of re-playability. Whether you manage to win the stage or die (most likely), stats will be added up and you will receive coins.
With coins, you can upgrade your arsenal and purchase new abilities. You can add up to six of them to your inventory.
Graphically, the game looks great and runs smoothly. If you like country and western music, like myself, you will enjoy the soundtrack.  I prefer the mouse and keyboard rather than the gamepad in this game; I find it easier. I would love to see more than five types of enemies.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good graphics and the game runs smoothly
-	Six levels of difficulties
-	24 perks and additional abilities to purchase
-	Good re-playability
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Needs more types of enemies
A fun, challenging arcade type of game where each of your attempts is different, depending on which perks you choose at the end of each wave.
7/10

I had not played Overgrowth nor Lugaru until Overgrowth came out on steam. I had been following the updates on

It does not yet have a campaign to go off of, but the modding community and the SUM launcher provides good dialouge and many maps to play around with. I will go over some pros and cons of some of these catagories.
Pros:
Fighting- Fighting in this game is awesome. There is no getting the hang of it. You will no doubt get good, but you will no doubt be killed by someone. Although a little clunkly and odd, it has alot of fun potential.
Weapons- Weapons are (At least to me) are very detailed. They shine in the light, and the blood reacts to them. Although not a huge variety, you can get mods that add hundreds more of these to the game.
FPS- Only on a few maps does this game lag. As long as you keep down filtering any computer should be great to run this game.
If you have a bad comp:
Low settings: 40 fps.
Max settings:  38 fps.
Graphics- Not the best ever, but if it stayed this way, no one would complain. Stunning visuals, and again, with no lag.
Blood- One of the most realistic in a game ever. Keep the blood on the full setting, and watch the cut open up, and watch the blood slowly trickle down and drop off you.
Characters- Only nine characters, three of them rabbits. You have the rabbit, female rabbit, civilian rabbit, rat, cat, wolf, and dog. Each one of these each time you pick them is different. The color of the fur and clothes, and even the height and weight will change.
Arena- This is a gamemode (Or a downloaded map) That pits you against another animal while thousands of fans watch. It will show you how popular you are, how many fans are in attendace, and how good the odds are of beating your opponent.
Now come the cons.
Cons:
-No Multiplayer
-Confusing combat
-Very slow level loading times
-A bit of a high price
Overall, I truly would reccomend this game to everyone. It is hands down incredibly fun, and very able to run on crappy PC's.

Western 1849 Reloaded is a great game.
You play the role of a Western gunfighter, who is having a shoot-out with lots of bad guys.
Rush from position to position to get a bead on your enemies, and then shoot them in the head for maximum damage.
Shoot the tin cans for a bit of target practise, or to increase your rage ability.
The bad guys pop up from behind buildings, bannisters, water barrels, and wagons - and they shoot at you in your white hat.
It's a bit like whack-a-mole, Western-style (well, okay, it's a lot different to that, but I think you get my drift).
Depending on how much success you have, you get a load of coins as payment for your fine efforts.
When you get enough coins, you can then buy extras.
You can buy equipment, upgrades, and abilities with your gold coins - and they're well worth it.
There are several stages of difficulty (Rookie, Sheriff, Legend, Hero, and Champion).
When you beat one stage of difficulty, you can then move on to the next one (although you have the option of playing on the easier levels as well, if you want to).
Each stage has several levels (you get a new level each time you move up a stage).
Every level has three waves.
At the end of each wave you get to choose one of three perks.
Choose wisely - the fate of the entire town may depend upon it!
Whilst this game is not as great as a free-range first person shooter, it's still a lot of fun.
If you like Western shoot 'em ups, then do yourself a favour and buy this game for a bit of easy enjoyment.
P.S. As a personal aside, I love the music that plays while you're in the menu.

Updated 11/2/1016 - SCS has finally added a new truck design, the Peterbuilt 389. Now this is the beast I've always thought about when it comes to American trucking. Huge, powerful, noisey - hey, it can't be beat! Thank you SCS for adding it. Now I'm just waiting on the long promised map rescale.

SCS's American Truck Simulator (now on referred to as ATS) is a fun little game for the first few hours. After that, it becomes rather monotonous. Billed as the sibling to European Truck Simulator 2 (ETS2), on the surface it seems to be the case. However, scratch said surface and you will find stark differences.
The first thing one notices is how small the maps actually are. In ETS2, the distances feel real, and a 19 hour delivery really feels like one. However in ATS, the distances are extremely scaled down. The same 19 hour distance feels like a short jaunt. A side effect of this is that the main routes become common place and thus quickly end up being rather boring.
The next issue is the lack of truck designs to purchase. Compared to it's older sibling, the choices the player has in trucks are very limited. (Update: as of 11/2/2016, SCS added the Peterbuilt 389 free to owners of ATS) To make matters worse, stock truck customization is extremely bare bones. I remember when I first played the game, I eagerly anticipated leveling up so that I could unlock more customizations. I was sadly disappointed to find out that there were hardly any at all.
Now to be fair, SCS has added a few (namely tire customization), yet that was also applied to ETS2, so there really wasn't anything extra special for ATS. They have also added steering wheel customization (very basic), but again that was shard cross platform.
Another issue is the graphic quality of the game. It seems that they used the same engine on ATS as that which was already present on the years old ETS2. So in essence, one could almost consider ATS as a stand alone ETS2 DLC. As an example of how outdated the graphics are, a friend of mine recently saw me playing and commented on the "legacy graphics" he witnessed.
I also find SCS's speed of delivery on important updates equivalent to molasses running downhill on a cold day in winter. They promised a few months ago that they were working on a re-scale of the playable map to make it more like ETS2. This was due to the playing community's justifiable outcry. However, other than a few screen shots, they have produced nothing. Indeed, at the time of this review, the last status update (a few screenshots) they had given was on September 5th, almost a month and a half ago. They also claimed that due to successful sales of their products, they were able to hire a larger team of developers. However, one would not be faulted to wonder if they simply hired playful primates. Is it one developer and a monkey working on these updates? SCS is extremely quiet concerning this.
The player community has also been constantly begging SCS for new truck models, and at first, SCS seemed to indicate that they were pursuing licenses for them. However, it has been an extremely long time since they have mentioned anything in regards to it, causing one to wonder if they have silently abandoned all effort in the matter. (Update: as of 11/2/2016, SCS added the Peterbuilt 389 free to owners of ATS)
The one huge offering that ATS has is its modding support. What makes the game enjoyable for many players is the numerous mods that game enthusiasts have created (lighting, weather, mechanics, new truck models, map revamps, etc.). If it weren't for these, I honestly wonder if ATS would be as popular as it is today (other than fanboys who'll support the game no matter what).
As someone who has played well over 200 hours in ATS, and who has at times really enjoyed it, I am forced to decide whether of not I would recommend this to a friend for purchase. When it comes down to it, I cannot recommend it at it's full price. Perhaps when it goes on sale for around $5, then I'd say to grab it up. However, as the product is today, the slow speed of development and updates by SCS, the sub par graphic quality, lack of truck choices, and a few other issues, I really don't think it's worth the full asking price.
In the end, I give it 3.5/5 stars. It has it's fun moments, and has potential. You really do feel like you're driving a truck (as long as you have the correct mods installed), and at first the routes are fun to drive. Unfortunately, it turns repetitive awfully fast.
(note: I have changed my review score from a 3/5 to a 3.5/5. The reason being is the release of the Peterbuilt 389 on 11/3/2016. Why not any higher? While I am thankful that there is one more truck model to drive, it still does not address the fact that the maps scale is quite small, nor the lack ot stock truck customization. It also does not address graphic quality nor speed of significant updates. I still cannot recommend this game at its non-sale price as no new truck model will salvage the game from the primary issues I have already documented. Map rescale will greately change my recommendation, and one can only hope that it happens soon.)
* - If/when SCS updates the game, I will also update my review

If the first Mass Effect veered towards being just Meh Effect, it's easy to say the sequel is an improvement on almost every possible front. While it still includes some bad padding and a few ugly design quirks to be called truly great, it is definitely a very solid game. Indeed the worst part is not in the game itself but in the convoluted and utterly anti-consumer DLC scheme that EA and Bioware have constructed around it. Fortunately the game doesn't feel like it's missing anything even when playing without the DLCs.
+Much more fleshed out dialogue and characters
+Paragon/renegade reactions and choices are often very entertaining
+Makes a nice use of imported save data
+Asides from some terribly low resolution body textures, the graphics still look pretty nice
+Good music that has a lot variety
+Replay value
(+No driving with Mako)
-You have to modify video files
to the level they should be and to skip intro logos. What the heck Bioware?
-Game options seem even more limited and you have to fiddle with .ini files again to get sensible shadow resolution etc.
-Scanning planets gets old really fast
-Doing the same couple of minigames dozens of times is still not good entertainment
-Dialogue system is still misleading and doesn't tell you what will actually be said with each choice. Changes in the paragon/renegade system make following some of the related dialogue options very difficult as Shepard's ability to choose those options is calculated using a very bizarre system that the game doesn't explain in any real way
-Miranda's smirking that never stops no matter how stupid it looks
-There are still missions that don't really connect to anything and have little to no real story and feel like leftovers or practice runs from idle level designers
-Subpar mouse controls outside of combat, most notably a complete absence of doubleclicking in menus and sluggish mouse in scanning mode

Following the release of Mass Effect: Andromeda, I felt strangely compelled (as if by a wizard, but most likely not) to review my thoughts on the game that really made me a lifer on the Mass Effect franchise, for better or for a slow agonising death where every drop of its creativity and magic is drained out, like a mosquito would suck the blood of an African child or an EA Executive would swipe money from my wallet.
Mass Effect 1 is seen by many as the best game in the franchises existence (what I refer to as its honeymoon period) -  there is a feeling of vivid infatuation with all the things it does neatly and how well it captures the "spirit" and "essence" of the sci-fi genre, while all its flaws are overlooked with an "It can do no wrong!" attitude towards it. And while I thought it was a damn fine game, had the sequel followed its conventions to the letter, I wouldn't shed the very metaphorical tears that I do now for the state of the franchise. Basically, to me it was a fun experience but nothing to get hung up about.
With Mass Effect 2 however, there was a definite charm to the game, the characters, the way in which you explored the story behind the games events, and how you acted as they transpired. I concede it is perfect by no means, (show me a game that is) and it is only as good as the entirely subjective opinion one has of it, but on the following things you will not be able to convince me otherwise:
Mass Effect 2 might not have the best gameplay of any game, with basic combat mechanics and AI that ranges from being so handicapped that it draws comparisons to a game of whack-a-mole to so insanely diffucult and overwhelming that you spout explitives and curses like water from a fountain (I'm looking at you Husks on the Reaper IFF mission...GOD) But what it did allow you to do, and do well was to use the powers and abilities of your allies, as well as your own to combat these challenges and think about how you progressed through each mission.
Did this stop us from picking our favourites for every mission? No, not really. Was this broken at times to where certain companions or weapons made the game far to easy? (RE: Bringing Jack along for the IFF mission and the Arc Projector making Donovan Hock a minor annoyance) Certainly, but for the most part it was successful in creating a feeling of teamwork in a game where that was very much the theme.
The story and its characters, felt less like a life or death struggle with a foreign alien power to me, and more like some kind of booze cruise through space, where occasionally, a group of heavily armed yet charmingly disfunctional mercenaries show up and sometimes solve problems (In a very good way, I am supposed to like the characters after all).
With the exceptions where some of the characters from the first game have had dramatic and uncharacteristic mood swings and have left your service, pretty much all the characters are handled well, and for the returning characters far better than they were before. Tali is given a personality this time, and isn't just used as a hub of information on the Geth and Quarian politics as she was in the first game...well...okay maybe some of that is still true, but she is far more likeable this time around and becomes a firm favourite by the end of her story arc here. Garrus adds a few more strings to his bow this time around, as he sheds his skin of being a complete 'yes-man' to whatever Shepard says in game 1 and his flair for independance and sense of duty to his friends is actually showcased in this game and not just something he says he does. I would honestly buy him a beer, and that is saying something because 1. I don't drink and 2. He's fictional.
Other favourites are Jack, Thane and Mordin, and while the former two were clearly invented by someone with a bizarre amount of vague fetishes in one case and a bizarrely specific one in the other (you should be able to figure this one out) They both felt and acted like real people and not the Mary Sues I had been accustomed to player characters and their companions being. Flawed, and at sometimes brutally ugly but you'd trust them to have your back....okay, maybe not Jack but I am totally justified in saying that and you know I'm right.
It is here that Andromeda misses the point. It aims for something of an air of the pioneering spirit and the yearning for exploration that the idea of exploring space gives us fans of the sci-fi genre - The idea that we may find beauty and mystery in the endless black void, or a painful and unusual death and that we don't care eitherway because SCREW YOU I AM EXPLORING SPACE.
In reality what it delivers is probably the weakest experience in this area of the genre, despite being the only one created for that sole purpose. Okay, it has better combat than ME 1, but at any time do I care remotely about placing a radio transmitter on an ice planet because a guy that runs an amatuer News network asked me to? I AM THE PATHFINDER, WHY DO I CARE?
Okay, so they have loyalty missions and a sharp focus on the crew and side characters like in ME 2, but do they matter at all? Does Drack really care if I effectivley give the order that kettifies his finest scouts - Seemingly not as he forgives me a conversation later (You can bet Wrex would have tried to drink my spinal fluid) Nobody really cares about anything and they all seem to get along basically fine, so why am I required to pander to them? In 2, it was because they would probably die and that would screw me over....not so much here.
Okay, It has a better ending than 3. But what game, book, film or television show doesn't. I can safely say, the average level of amusement while playing 3 was far higher than Andromeda, and given how bitter the taste in my mouth still is about that, you must understand the gravity of this statement.
In short, I hope that the following games in this franchise, should there be any learn from this game, in my opinion the series finest hour and don't just borrow themes and references, and copy the core gameplay and story progression from a dull dragons age sequel that killed my enthusiasm for an entirely different franchise they own.
Summary: I loved this game. I kinda Liked Andromeda.
P.S. I actually do think a Wizard compelled me to write this, I was just too embarassed to say so before, Bloody pointy hatted bosh'tets.

This was a potentially awesome game, but it was completely ruined for me by a few poor design choices.
--I really hate the item attacks. The core gameplay here is so fun and deep, all the items do is detract from it. You end up spending more time worrying about who has what item than how to get faster. Plus the attacks are just kind of cheap. You can outrun everybody for the entire round, only to suddenly find yourself in last place or even eliminated because you got hooked or frozen from behind. How is that fun? It's just frustrating and stupid. You can supposedly dodge the attacks, but I found that this was often impossible even when I knew the attack was coming and was prepared to dodge it. It also introduces an unnecessary element of luck with what items you pick up.
--The elimination is too strong sometimes and too weak other times. The idea is that if you can't keep up with everyone else and fall off of the screen, you are eliminated. The problem is you can get eliminated even though you aren't really behind. Sometimes, time-wise you are right behind somebody but you just happen to be off of the screen due to height difference or other factors. Even though you're 3 milliseconds behind them, you're eliminated. Other times, the person behind you has been off of the screen for 3+ seconds and still isn't eliminated. A lot of close matches end prematurely and a lot of blow-outs drag on needlessly because of this.
--There is WAY too much first place punishing in this game. It is so bad that I've honestly wondered if a better strategy might be to try to stay in 2nd place. When you are significantly ahead in this game, the following happens:
1. The camera stays centered on the people behind you. You are at the very edge of the screen and can't see in front of you at all. This makes you much more likely to hit obstacles, land on spikes, miss grapples, etc. Some of this can be overcome with strong map knowledge, but it's still a huge disadvantage. When you are ahead you will usually just screw up more, allowing everyone else to catch back up.
2. You have three people behind you constantly shooting missiles, grappling hooks, and freeze beams at you.
3. The first person to visit an area will often activate shortcuts for the other players. What the hell is that? I got there first, so I create a better path for you so you can beat me? Why? This is really dumb.
Sooo much fun in such an early state, even with the game breaking bugs lol.

As others have said: I really hoped this game would be good, being a huuuuge Dungeon Keeper fan myself.
But even after roughly a year, and patch 1.5, it still feels very buggy and incomplete. I just finished the campaign and feel somewhat dissatisfied...
The game is ambitious, as it comes with a big load of extra tactical depth - at least in theory. It has the Dungeon Keeper feeling but in many many occasions it does not feel thought-through, as there many many features (potions, contructs, creature types, war bands, rituals etc etc) that just rise and do not shine because the gameplay is too hectic and chaotic. Eventually you'll just zerg-rush anyway.
E.g. after 13 (short) levels I still have no idea what the abilities of 95% of the creatures do, since the only way to figure them out is the use the (very very clunky) posession spell - which unfortunately is completely useless apart from that. I used basically only two or three out of the dozen potions/rituals/contructs/defences, simply because I didnt have to (and there was no space to develop a strategy anyway, since there is hardly any time to dig, explore and plan)
All in all, It feels a bit like a dry and chewy Kobe-beef steak:
At some point there were the perfectly right ingredients, but they did not manage to create something great out of it.
Which is a pity

I really want to like this game but it just misses the mark quite badly.
At first glance it feels and looks (albeit much nicer gfx) then Dungeon Keeper 2, the narrator is a nice touch along with the murky audio.
However after a few hours of gameplay it all feels a bit thin, the narrator becomes far too much notifying you of every single little detail and incredibly grating.
None of the minions have much personality and all seem to act the same other then scout units who, well, scout and attack from a distance.
Unfortunately I have to compare to Dungeon keeper as it was claimed to be the successor to it and I will :
In Dungeon Keeper 1 & 2 every minion that entered your dengeon you would carefully select or send back according to what you needed. You would pay attention to them and track their leveling up process and aim to keep them happy.
In WFTO it doesnt seem to matter what enters your dungeon as you can just seem to bum rush the enemy from one end of the map to the other as soon as you have a big enough army (which really doesnt take too long), as the unlockable 'sins' or room/spell unlocks chart pretty much throws all rooms at you within 20 minutes of a skirmish game.
In DK you would have to make a decision at the beginning of a game, Turtle, tech, aggressive or a mix of the 3 again, depending on the situation, sometimes rushing off to the enemy to fortify choke points and then take some time to unlock tech and build defenses, again in WFTO it really doesnt feel like it matters as long as you get enough minions in your dungeon.
Lastly is the actual 'feel' of the game, and theres no real way to properly explain what I mean but WFTO just doesnt feel as kinetic and 'meaty' as DK 1 & 2 did, the units feel hollow and jittery, clipping into eachother while their audio (while very good quality) just seems to either be far to loud or too quiet and cuts off randomly.
Even if I were to not compare it to DK I still would feel a tad unsatisfied as nothing seems to have been properly finished or polished off and  misses out crucial finishing touches that makes the game stand out, and instead appears flat across the board.
I DO WANT TO LIKE THIS GAME, and I keep coming back to it but it is always unsatisfying to finish a session.
I will not talk about stability issues (even though they plague the game and my rig is far better then required..) as that helps no one and I'm sure will ... eventually ... be ironed out.
at £10 it could be worth a look but for full price, I am afraid not.
(note I backed this game from the very start..)

Love it! I was a huge fan of the DKII and i think, that this perfectly fits together with the old DKs.
PROS:
*It feels like a seperate game, with it's own type of style and humor, with quite a lot of new rooms and creatures and not like a new, modified version of the DK series. The gameplay is also improved quite a bit from the old series.
*I love how the spell researching plays bigger role in the WftO, than it did before. And the Titans have replaced Horny.

*The levels do have quite the replay value, (as there are mostly multiple ways to do the levels) especially if you are a freak for the achievements.
*The survival mode. It's quite hardcore in the beginning, but it's also much fun.
*The keepers (underlords) have their own styles and not only colors.
CONS:
*the game performance (as many others have also noted). Once it gets crowded, the performance drops drastically.
*The main story was too short.
Recap: if you loved the old DK2, you'll probably like this one. As i said - it's not a newer, prettier 1:1 copy of the old games, but it is more of a game of it's own.

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW!!!
It's pretty fun for what it is at this stage.  It's almost a city builder, but your resources are your heroes.  You send heroes on quests to earn experience, gold and loot.  You can discover settlements, which you need to keep happy but I'm not exactly sure how to do that.  I've sent heroes on quick quests to settlements "in despair" and actually lowered their happiness.  The game needs to tell you what each settlement is in need of so you can raise their happiness more efficiently.  At this point, it seems to be trial and error.
The variety of different quests is interesting and leaves the door open for even more complexity in future development.  There are villains that are discovered automatically through quests and are defeated by completing "epic" quests.  Defeating these villains earns extra gold and happiness I think.  There are also bandits you can defeat through bounty quests, but bounties expire and there doesn't seem to be a way to remove the expired bounties from the list.  I wish they just automatically disappeared once they expired.
The loot system needs some work.  You get loot and it's stored in your kingdom.  Your kingdom's inventory only shows 8 slots, but, as far as I can tell, you actually store a lot more than that.  I've deleted many items in the hopes that I could keep new loot as opposed to selling it at the end of a quest, but I've so far not been able to do so.  I feel like that's a bug where your kingdom's inventory just keeps spawning random items.  Which is fine, since you basically have unlimited loot, but surely not intentional.  Managing the loot equipped on your characters is cumbersome, as well.  You can equip items on your heroes which increases their stats, but I don't think you can view the equipped loot and you can only equip one piece of loot at a time (so you can't equip both a sword and a shield, for example).  You can change your equipped loot, but you can't see what is already equipped and I'm not sure that the stat bonus changes are reported properly when trying to equip different gear.
It also seems like there aren't many buildings available to actually build in your kingdom at this stage.  I haven't earned a new building in a few kingdom levels and there's really no reason to expand my kingdom further at this point since I've built all the buildings and I don't need more space to build more.  I'm sure those will come in time, but people in your kingdom still complain that there isn't enough to do or enough shops in which to spend money.
RPG Tycoon is an interesting take on the tycoon genre and I look forward to playing it more once it's a bit more complete.  It's one of those games that I could easily see just sucking many hours from my life without me even noticing it.

Coming from the Dreamcast's heyday, this game has excellent presentation and glorious music. Character's become likable just through their idle animations.
Replaying levels is somewhat antiquated. Instead of a chapters function you go through the main game again. You do open up some permanent challenge modes that stay on your available mission list, but for the most part if you want to get sega's triple ratings, you will have to go through them all. It's easy to do on your second run though.
The meat of the game is skating through the city, evading police, and spraying tags. The joy of this is that many stunts are made part of your basic movement tools, especially wall riding, grinds, and half pipe ollies. You face a diverse police force who all have to be dealt with in different ways, but there is nothing quite as worth it as taking down a helicopter with nothing more than an aerosol can.
The camera is set to a cinema mode by default, which gives you time to reaction to the riot police about to mow you down, but sometimes makes it hard to get around corners. If you leave the place where the cinema camera starts or let them get too close it will go back to normal camera, so this minor gripe is avoidable.
The most important difference between characters is whether you want to spray faster, or more slowly for a greater point boost. Both are capable of getting the full ratings through other point sources (time taken and tricks), so it's up to the player.  Going infinite on trick runs is possible if you want to guarantee that you get the rating and look awesome, but never necessary.

I HIGHLY recommended Gemini Rue for anyone who's looking for an old fashioned point and click adventure, with challenging but fair puzzles, and a fantastic story.
Everything about the game's presentation is absorbing. It has an old film noir, Sci-Fi Blade Runner feel to it with gorgeous artwork that feels retro and fresh at the same time. The premise and feel reminds me of a story straight out of Cowboy Bebop, with twists that anyone paying attention to should enjoy. Voice acting and music (very moody and dark ambiance), was also spot on.
I really found the puzzles engaging as well. A lot of point and click adventure games I have trouble getting into simply because their "gameplay" is either much too easy or just too vague in telling me what I am exactly supposed to be doing. I didn't think Gemini Rue had this problem. There were puzzles that were easy solve, and others I had to think about for long minutes before coming up with an answer. The Easter Eggs and achievements spread throughout the game was also a plus for me.
The only problem I had with the game was the fact that it felt too short, and that after all is said and done, the characters are technically confined to two basic areas throughout the whole game when I wished there had been more to explore... But honestly the game did take me quite a bit of time to beat, and as for the lack of a wider world, I just enjoyed it so much that I didn't want it to end.

I really enjoyed NiGHTS: Journey into Dreams on the Wii, for what it was, so I was excited to check this out.
Unfortunately, this game is an odd combination of very easy to clear and beyond immediate comprehension. The camera is so zoomed in (much MUCH more than, say, an old Sonic game) that the wonderful feling of 360 degree flight and linking rings is constantly interrupted by scanning up and down to find the next group of them; there are huge gaps in the level with no leading collectibles to guide you, and it really interrupts the flow of the game, which... seems to be the whole point, the flow. There's no other way to experience that flow except by rote memorization of level routes.
And the mechanics are so esoteric and unexplained (even within the "tutorial", which is just a flipbook instruction manual which doesnt talk about even half of the in-game objects) that your ability to interact with and understand the mechanics is very limited except on, I imagine, far repeated playthroughs after looking through guides. The game's very, very short unless you care about getting high rankings, but I don't know how you'd figure out how on your own considering it's not clear how valuable time, links, bonus rounds, and etc. are to point totals (I got totally mixed results when trying to prioritize one/all).
The HD version doesn't adapt the pre-rendered visuals well; they feel either uncanny or unclear. There are no gameplay improvements I can find in the HD version (like an adjustable camera).
If you like the idea and surrounding aesthetics of this game, hunt down the Wii game; neither are masterpieces, but it's basically this but better executed.

So this is a good game!
As others have said the menu takes some getting used to but apart from that it is very enjoybale.
There are however still quite a few AI issues that I feel at the moment means its not worth the full £30 maybe £20.
However the dev is very good at adding updates so hopefully this will be sorted.
The AI issues noted so far are;
When computer AI kicks to your full-back he will 99% of the time kick the ball out on the full from the 22. Despite being under no pressure.
When your own fly-half kicks the chase is always horrendous and if their 15 runs at you he will normally do very well.
THis is a real pain as the second issue is that turn-overs from rucks are extremely rare and I have Sam Warburton playing 7 every game!!!!!!  I have also on instances driven the oppostion back from my 22 to theirs without gaining possession The issue with this is that the computer can have possession for almost an entire 1/2 especially if you win it back to just knock on! More turnovers are essential.
The game also doesn't notice things like the touch line when running or when a player is blatantly isolated.
For some reason when it gets to 80 or 40 mins even if you are 5m out from opp try line your fly half will kick the ball dead.  Not useful when you are on 3 trys and need the 4th for a bonus point.
When players make a clean break through the line they will often stop and pass to a heavily marked player rather than continuing themselves (this has cost me several games/bonus points)  or they will not give the ball when there is a ridiculous overlap that is guarenteed a score.
It is very intermittent as to whether a player will try to but the ball down between the sticks after crossing the line unapposed,
There also seem to be some really basic back moves that seem to end up with a try.  Especially as some defenders run all sorts of crazy lines that completely miss all the attackers.
Finally the back row never break off the scrum.  This ties into the point above, especially during a blindside move as it creates a ridiculous overlap.
SO in conclusion this is a very good game and I do enjoy it greatly.
However with the bugs/glitches mentioned above I don't believe it is currently worth it's premium price as the bugs glitches do somewhat ruin it, especially when games are tight and you feel like the computer is just cheating you.
Edit: So as mentioned above the dev has issued an update that introduces more turnovers etc to the game that does give it a better feel.  There are still of course other bugs present still but the developer is continuing to update the game and is committed.  If you are considering purchasing this game, stop considering and start buying you will get a lot out of it!

Finally, a rugby title has been released that has some depth and longevity to it.  Having been disappointed with previous management titles released this year, I decided to purchase RUTM 2015 to see if this title could deliver and so far I have really enjoyed playing it.
As with any management game, it requires a couple of hours to familiarise with the UI and screen layout - And like others have commented, this seemed a little clunky at first, but given time I was able to get used to it without any problems.
The number of leagues and players is very impressive. Rugby fans will be pleased to know that both Northern and Southern Hemispheres are both represented, and there is even an editor that allows for players to customise their teams and alter the names of any unlicensed leagues, teams and players.
The match engine is intuitive and allows players to engage with their team and issue orders during a match. Adding Team Calls is a neat feature that can really help to change the outcome of a game.
The youth development and academy system is also something that I am particularly fond of, and it allows players to create a self-sufficient team that doesn’t cost a ridiculous amount to establish.
I think RUTM 2015 has been a promising addition to the management genre and has set the bar for other Rugby games to follow.  If you are a Rugby fan I am sure you will enjoy this game.
Positive Aspects:
* Great player database and leagues to choose from – both Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
* Different match engine approach with Team Calls and issuing orders.
* Great Youth and Academy system, allows smaller teams to be built up over time.
* In game editor which allows for plenty of customisation.
* Lots of tactical options and statistics for players to tweak.
Negative Aspects:
* Slightly clunky UI and menu system.
* 3D match engine graphics could be improved upon.

About 30 hours in I feel like I can make a review for this game.
Being an avid Rugby Union fan as soon as I saw this on the steam market I bought it. Initially the game wasn't great, the menu navigation and UI wasn't amazing, but after playing around with it for a while you get the hang of it and are able to move between sections easily. Whilst the graphics aren't great I don't think that's what this game is about. The in game player base is awesome with great depth. The match mechanics are okay, not a big fan but if you get the hang of the plays and what not it can be quite fun.
So yeah that's a broad look at the game. The killers for me however are more minute.
There's a few big problems IMO. First and foremost is the unrealistic simulated games. You can have a team of 'World Class' players and lose to a team of 'Nationals'. Look I know Rugby and I know you can't count anyone out and what not but this lead to a lot of head scratching from me.
Some players are not up to date; e.g. Duane Vermeulan was argueably the best player in the world this year and he's rated as 'International'. So yeah there's a few cases like that, some players over rated and other underated. Which once again left me scratching my head.
Sometimes I felt as though my team simply sucked for no reason. I would have an awesome back line, they would have a crap one, set my tactics to play a more expansive game, and strangely, I lost. More head scratching...
Overall though it's a fun game to play, if you're not a rugby fan, don't buy this unless it's on sale, I don't feel like you'll get $40 worth of satisfaction. I'll continue to play this game and learn more about the mechanics (still learning!).
Cons
- Confusing/clustered UI
- Unrealistic results
- Some players not up to date
- Bad graphics
- One or two crashes
- Players brought up through the 'Colts' and 'Academy' when selected for international duty don't have a name unless edited
Pros
- In depth teams
- Aweosme development of your players through your teams system
- Accurate coaching system

A charming and beautiful updated classic for those who are willing to give something a little different a try.  Let me address some of the complaints;
First off, yes the game creators didn't quite make the objectives entirely clear (There were no "in-game tutorials" in 1996!) so I would reccomend hitting up any of the player guides available online,  it's not rocket science, and it will open up a really worthwhile experience.
Secondly, the game DOES in fact support native plug-n-play controller support.  Again, this may not be obvious to the unintitated, but if you left-click the game title in your Steam library, it will bring up a Menu.  Select "Game Configuration" and presto, you can activate your in-game controller.   I personally find the Xbox 360/One controller work admirably for this game.
With some of the fundamental complaints out of the way, let me heap a little more praise on this game;  It's memorable, unique, and charming in a way that gamers usually only find in a Miyamoto developed title.  A true classic, and it makes me wish Sega would invest a little more effort in updating it's back-catalog of similar gems.

A budget mix of Nuclear Throne with some of the roguelike mechanics of Risk of Rain.
Gameplay consists of blasting baddies on the way to collectables to unlock the elevator to the next floor of baddies. Similar to Risk of Rain, there's a timer at the top of the screen that raises the difficulty of enemies as it ticks upward, so speed is encouraged. Enemies constantly spawn in on top of you, ruining any tactical feel from the top-down action. Damage done by enemies seems to vary between "nothing to worry about" and "oops you died", rarely striking a happy medium.
There are 3 characters, each with 2 very small skill trees of passive abilities to upgrade. The characters are rather bland. Boris, for example, can hold LMB to shoot, or hold RMB to... shoot faster.
The pixel art visuals are amateurish and unattractive. Obstacles such as crates and tables, enemies, and treasure-containing lockers all melt together in a difficult-to-read blob of dark pixels.
There's no tutorial and virtually no explanation of game mechanics. There's a bartender who allows you to select a drink, which gives you various bonuses. One of these is "Start the game with 2 datacores and 2 void cores." I still have no idea what void cores are, though I think they're the green boxes you find as objectives.
All in all, it feels like an uncompleted Early Access title. With more characters, extended skill trees, a visual makeover, and some mechanical polish the game could be a solid pickup. Ultimately however, you're better off grabbing one of the games that clearly inspired it, such as Nuclear Throne, Risk of Rain, or Neurovoider.

Cons:

I haven't played Dungeon Keeper in more than a decade but as far as I'm concerned this is the spiritual successor that definitely fulfills a niche that needed filling. The narrator has that wickedly eeevil sound, most of the maps are challenging, and the game is just plain fun.
Initially I was frustrated with aspects of the interface and AI but after getting into the game a few levels then going back to the tutorial, I realized I missed a few things that were covered that were integral to playing. Some areas of the interface could use some polishing, like the war flags on the right (which in my opinion should be easier-to-click inlaid icons) but once you learn the keyboard hotkeys they stop frustrating you.
The deveopers also seem to take an active interest in responding to the community and they're regularly putting out patches so thumbs up there.
I'd say the biggest gripes I have is an inability to pause or slow the game; I'm not sure if you could pause in DK or DK2 but it just seems sensible that this should be an included function with rushing maps that have timed waves. I also wish happy minions would follow your build instructions in the order they were assigned rather that engaging in what seems random instructions. You have a wave coming at you in 2 minutes and they've decided to reinforce walls in a useless room rather than dig out the dirt. While you can specify an area for them to focus on, this function doesn't always work nor does it rate high on my useability scale.
I should also add that I've experienced no performance issues whatsoever and the game runs like a dream on my i7 with nvidia GTX 970 with all settings maxed.

This game was released too early. The speculation is that Funcom was on the verge of bankruptcy so they pushed the game out the door half-baked even for Early Access to try to raise money in a hurry banking on the Conan IP to drive sales. It worked, even though the EA market is utterly saturated with "survival"-themed murder-simulators. Funcom sold a crap load of copies and made a lot more money than they'd hoped. I guess that's a "win" from their standpoint, although not so much for the sods who bought the game.
I won't go into the game's many, many problems but I can't recommend it in the current state it is in. They don't have very good QA on their patches, resulting in a lot of anger amongst the player base as stuff is always getting broken. Funcom seems to have learned nothing from the problems that similar games like ARK, Rust, etc have had with exploiters and griefers. The game is so riddled with exploitable bugs and their anti-cheat really doesn't seem to work.
Even worse, the Chinese are getting around Funcom's region blocks to cause havok on western servers using hacks and exploits to overrun PVP servers and massacre the established players there just like they did with ARK and some other similar games. Funcom, rather than deal with the issue, just locks threads complaining about this massive problem.
In short, I can't give this game a thumbs up. If Funcom can:
1) Get some control over their patch QA before blowing up stuff and enraging the population in the process
2) Actually get a working anti-cheat system in place
3) Get a handle on exploits that are making PVP servers a complete joke
4) Block the Chinese from bypassing region blocking
then they might actually have the beginnings of a decent game here that will hopefully get better in time. Right now, it's just a complete sh!t show and it's dropped most of it's active player base in less than 2 months.
Caveat emptor.

Time for a review update. .... I warn you, its a big one.  This game really annoyed me.  The missed opportunity here is painful.
A wasted opportunity.  A game which could have hit a total niche USP and still made a fortune.  An adult game in a market crying out for adult content with truly adult themes and choices in a world where snowflakes have a lot of safe spaces and cry out for an opportunity for emotional development.  Not that I care, but there was a role for this game here. Yet, they missed it. They missed that and also missed the opposite USP of the ultimately gratutious (which would have worked) just as well.  How did they miss this so entirely?
The Frozen North - Free expansion was just launched.  It adds a lot which was previously missing.   Quite a bit more variety in the landscape, which yields a strong sense of skyrim dejavu and it expands the total real estate in the game enourmously.  There is quite a bit more to craft and build adding some much needed content.  It is a very good expansion which this game desperately needed.  Yet for all that. There is nothing to do!
Abolutely avoid the official servers like the plague.  Online play is problematic for many reasons.  Disconnects are still a thing and I find servers with dramatically increased building resilience preferable.   Spending a lot of time on crafting a town, village or fortress which seems to be made of paper and items only to lose them all if you go on holiday for a few days just kills any enthusiasm for the game.  This basically makes the official servers irrelevant. So your choice is play unofficial or buy your own. I did the later.
Having said that, the expansion now makes this a much more viable game.  There is some content, not enough but it does feel less like an Alpha or early beta product in terms of having something to do.
Perhaps most important, thralls are still almost irrelevant in the grand scheme of things and you can walk through a town of thralls and not really slow down.   This, of all things needs to change fast.   Having proper defenders would add a huge amount to pvp which is tragically limited and bland.
Combat - Still incredibly tedious.  One click spam over and over with very little skill of any sort.
The biggest problem is/was, the terrible launch, no one's interested anymore.
The hyenas.  OMG so many hyenas.   They arent funny or quirky at any level, just idiotic.
I do like the building system and crafting a lot. As more gets added this is relatively fun though a bit limited at the moment. You can create some great structures and for me, this is very much the high point of the game.  Building and crafting is great fun and you can do a huge amount.
You can tame thralls and use them to defend your structures.... except, one hit or 2 and they die, even the best of them.  Line em up in a group and kill everything in front of you with a swing or two. So they are ultimately pointless except in huge numbers and even then, the AI isnt clever enough to stop you spliting them up.
Very little content.
Very poor combat (Skyrim without magic).
Those annoying hyenas.
The core USP of the game (thralls.) Adds almost nothing.
Could have been a game mature adudiences would gravitate to just by being less corny and more realistic than general gaming fodder.   It isnt adult at all so it missed what could have been a nice USP.
The official server rules are horrible.  - life is too short to waste forever and come back to nothing for a myriad of reasons.

SpeedRunners, I never thought I would enjoy this game until I actually played it.
It's a high adrenaline game that always forces you to be thinking about what to do next.
But this game has quite a few pros and cons.
PROS:
- Fun
- Challenging but not too annoying
- Unique Characters that aren't just a cosmetic upgrade, but are treated like a whole new person
- Many ways to play, including a story mode.
- The way the game is made, you can play it for a long time and it won't get old
- The game is really rewarding when things start going your way.
CONS:
- Story mode can get a bit boring
- After you have become a complete expert at the game and you don't have anyone to play with, you may want to use multiplayer, which can be laggy.
- The running can get a bit repetitive after a long time.
OVERALL:
The game is really fun at the moment and is great, only dropped down by multiplayer and repetitivity. 8/10

Just think a fallout MMORPG... or S.T.A.L.K.E.R, or any other apocalyptic game, but in an MMORPG form. Pretty self explanitory. But i guess i'll go into more detail with my ever-so-rare pros/cons list.
Pros_
MASSIVE open world that would take more than a full day to travel from one side to the other on foot. (but don't worry, there are horses and vehicles to help.)
A bunch of cool secrets to be found.
Interesting roleplaying potential.
Cool story and factions.
(bonus!) The low playerbase gives a good feel of isolation, really gives that extra immersion of an empty wasteland on a dead earth. Though unlike with fallout, having multiplayer makes the few players you will come across, means no two people will have the same experience, and be able to meet people with interesting stories and characters and such. Makes the dead world feel all the more alive.
Cons_
Intense learning curve.
VERY slow paced leveling and such with a lot of "go here, kill this stuff." Though it does have the redeeming factor of traveling places you wouldn't go otherwise and seeing interesting scenery.
Not too active playerbase, but the ones that are, luckily, are usually the ones that have been there since the beta.
Old game with dated graphics and stiff controls, though it has aged somewhat decently well.
Support died off ages ago, aswell as updates, for the most part.
Conclusion_
Its an old game, but a good one, and worth the look.

For those of you that don't have the game yet and don't know a whole lot about it, I'll explain this more. The game released with one state; California. Which was kind of small. It was nowhere near the expansive size of Euro Truck Simulator 2. But I waited. Nevada came out. It was free! I was down for them making states and adding them for free, that's a good business practice that I can support. The same thing happened with Arizona. I was incredibly supportive of this. The game was fun, and they were adding new places to drive so the game didn't get boring, and I didn't have to pay for the states, which is what any good, decent company will do. This was incredibly pro consumer, and I was all for it. Then New Mexico comes out. And I was, again, excited when my game had an update, so I waited patiently, and as soon as the game was done, I jumped in and started a new game. So you can imagine my surprise when New Mexico isn't available to me. So I go to the steam page and sure enough, they're charging 11.99 for what used to be free! This was already insulting, but it stung even more since I had bought every paid for DLC up to that point in both ATS and ETS 2 to support these guys. But I'm not buying another DLC from these people, not after this. especially not for 11.99

I've put off reviewing this game for a while as it's really quite difficult to express just how good this game is with a simple description alone...Reading some of the reviews around here it seems this is a bit of diversive title with some people saying it's a gorgeous little game and other slating it as an utter bore...I will give credit to the latter group as this title did at times seem a little repetative but it must be said it it's defense that what it lacks in diverse and veriaty based gaming it more than makes up for in terms of evolution of the existing gameplay and it's looks.
NiGHTS into Dreams is a rather difficult sell. the premise is thus. you play as NiGHTS a Jester like figure who lives in the rhelms of dreams, your mission is to fly around the various stages of the level (Which is rail locked to up and down or left and right) collecting orbs that will allow you to free up bigger orbs that in turn will allow you to fight an end of level boss, once all the bosses are defeated you play a final boss level and thats about it. it's against the clock and if the time runs out you turn into a small child and you get chased by a giant walking clock till it games over it's a simple premise but it's crafting more than makes it worth it...the gameplay is simple enough for an introductory player but elevates in difficulty as you go along...it really takes the rail elements and experiments with using them in immersive 3d levels...it's a very experimental game it must be said...
It's also utterly beautiful to look at, with the original sega saturn version or a new remastered for HD version available both look simply gorgeous and it's art Design is a beacon for what was possible in that strange time of evolution in the mid 90's...
Can I reccommend this game? I would say it depends on your preference...if your one for constantly changing missions and wide veriaty or even more traditional platforming elements...I dont know if I can say this game would be for you...but if your open to having experiences and to playing a game for immersion and the more creative elements that gameplay has to offer then I would say give this game a shot, it'll broaden your horizons and may even change the way you think about video games...

I've had some fun with the game, but it has too many flaws for me to recommend it in good conscience. Not only is it difficult, it is unfair, luck-based and has obscure mechanics, making the difficulty a drawback rather than a draw (I love difficult games). The mouse controls are awkward and the keyboard controls are insufficient and insufficiently configurable. Then the gameplay is repetitive and it hardly ever feel like you're making progress.
On the other hand, the art is cute and the system is original. So it might be the game for you if you don't mind bashing your head against a wall repeatedly until you're lucky enough for the thing to break, or if you don't mind regularly getting wiped through no fault of your own (I don't). You also have to enjoy repetitive micro-management (I do).
If that's the case, and if you like puzzling out how things work over many failed runs, you should get this. It was carefully crafted and definitely plays differently than most game of Steam (you're more likely to find similar while looking through flash games).

One of the first console games to use an analogue stick controller and did so wonderfully. A Sonic Team and SEGA classic through and through. More than just a port but rather a respectfully remade tribute to the Saturn's answer to Mario 64. You can switch between the original Sega Saturn graphics or play with new models and textures that enhance the visual quality of the game without changing the artistic direction. This game is fast, bursting with vibrant color and catchy music that you'll never forget. My only complaint is that the game only runs the at the console's original speed of 30 frames per second. If you grew up in the golden age of gaming then NiGHTs Into Dreams should be in your collection.

Welcome to Chivalry brother!   It seems you have decided to take the plunge and dive in to one of my all time favorite multiplayer games.  Tis not an easy game my friends n' enemies and your patience will be tested everytime you log on and join a match.  If you enjoy a maschochistic learning curve where only few will stay and most will leave this game might be for you.   Truth be told I HATED this game when I first got it.  It was hard, people were unforgiving and wacky fighting game mechanics made me want to quit so I did for awhile.  I came back, why you ask because there aren't many decent actual first person melee games to be played and also once you learn this game it becomes a lot of fun.   I would like to address some issue I always see in reviews.
First one I will talk about is the oh so scary toxic community.  From my experience most people are actually nice aside from some like any online game it comes with the risk of playing with D-Bags.   You would be suprised to see how many of these toxic players are actually new players just frustrated with the game.  I see so many new players call people ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and names because there not dominating the board and then call us toxic, it is almost ironic.   Another thing is yes there are some players who have been here for years that are aholes.  I wont name but I have had rank 50+ players try to vote kick me and grief me repeatedly to make me leave the game because how can someone with half as much play time kick my butt.  These players represent our egotistical players, there in every online multiplayer game that has any competitve edge to it, you can't escape it.  The best way to deal with these so called toxic players is to mute them, you can mute anyone you don't want to communicate with so USE IT!  Also don't fall for the Tbag tactic it is merely a pyschological trick to get into your head and make you angry.

The other elephant in the room is the fighting style of chivalry and how it can be manipulated which is generally called exploits!   At this time I doubt Torn Banner is gonna do anything to change it so you must learn how to defend against the onslaught of drags and reverse strikes.  Feinting also gets alot of flak but it's taught to you early in the tutorial so use it if you want and mute people who grief and whine about it.   Back to the exploits, sadly this game is probably gonna stay like this but thats why I love it.  Your weapon is mostly a hitbox that you can swing around and do some fun things with.  Plenty of vets will gladly tell you about dragging and reverses if you show respect and a williness to learn.  I have taught new players the simple concept of drags and their enjoyment of chivalry went up tenfold.  The fighting style of chivalry makes for some intense insane fun though once you embrace it.

Now if you can overcome those two things I talked about you will surely find a fun and exciting time in chivalry.  Remember don't give up and your only defeated as long as you think you are.

Majesty 2 takes an original approach to the tired fantasy-adventurer trope by putting you in control of the town the adventurers visit! Sell potions, create quests, build guild halls and watch as heroes bumble about looking for gold and glory.
The player builds a very basic medieval-style town by placing shops, guilds and defensive structures, while peasant houses, graveyards and sewer exits appear on their own, making for a unique town layout each time you play. Watching the heroes accomplish quests and then spend their hard-earned gold in your shops is immensely satisfying, and the humour is surprisingly effective.
The game is not without a few shortcomings. Your lack of direct control over the heroes will mean that you will occasionally fail time-sensitive quests, and certain missions are in major need of some balancing. On more than one occasion I found myself having to consult online forums to see what I was doing wrong.
Despite these few shortcomings, however, I find myself re-installing Majesty 2 again and again, months after having finished it, just to play it through completely once more.

PROS:
==================================================
+ Freedom to create and build your character/class however you want.
+ Light and Dark Humor every where. It keeps the game refreshing and entertaining.
+ The possibilities of how to approach or win each fight are insane.
+ Tons of ways to combo your skills in battle for devastating effects. Be warned, the enemies can also use this on you!
+ The pickpocket system is both amusing and unique. It is powerful but limited so that you cannot exploit forever.
+ Story so far is decent but the side quests are just as good.
+ The open world is beautifully crafted. Exploring is extremely fun but also dangerous because you never know what you are going to run into be it traps, new quests, hidden loot, hostile enemies (sometimes more powerful than you), and special NPCs.
CONS:
==================================================
- Mixed feelings about the new armor system. More details on that below.
- The loot system can be extremely generous or very disheartening. More on that below as well.
- The crafting system is either incomplete, gutted, or Larian couldn't decide what they wanted it to be.
- I'm still unsure how the dialogue persuasion concept works. Even a character with high Wits cannot succeed when choosing the "Wits" option. Perhaps I also need higher Persuasion points? If someone corrects me on this I will retract this.
ABOUT THE ARMOR SYSTEM:
------------------------------
This new armor system is a mixed bag for me. I am almost certain that Larian implemented this system to prevent players from abusing CC-Chains on every single fight.
After playing 100 hours, I've noticed that the armor system really forces you to build your party towards maximum damage output. The faster you can break the enemy's armor, the faster you can CC them, and the faster you will win. If the opposite happens and the enemy breaks your armor first, then you are become vulnerable. So the best answer is to build your party to put out the most damage in the fastest possible time. It is also ideal to focus two or more characters on the same type of damage (physical or magic) in order to break armor as fast as possible. Having a balanced party can work but it is less effective.
ABOUT THE CRAFT/LOOT/SCALING SYSTEM:
------------------------------------
I believe the crafting system in DOS2 got gutted and was partially left in the game. Maybe Larian is planning on fixing it in the future but I'm not sure how they screwed this up considering they had pretty much fixed everything in DOS: EE. You are still able to craft potions, scrolls, runes, and some generic equipment but we're no longer able to enhance our gear with souls, elements, bow strings, whetstones, etc...
The loot system for the most part is fine. You will find all sorts of gear throughout the world but everything outside of Unique Gear is purely RNG. But it gets really annoying when you don't have a rogue character and you keep getting daggers from Ornate Chests.
The scaling in this game is also very questionable. While the first part of the game is seems very polished in terms of balance, the game takes a very steep drop off (or spike) in terms of numbers scaling when you get to the second act in Reaper's Coast. Between the levels 10-20, the scaling of gear and enemy health/damage is bonkers. This forces you to keep your gear up to date every  level or you will get wrecked in battle.

The Conan theme stil feels lacking beyond the initial cutscene. The most recent dungeon is a step in the right direction but it really feels mostly like fighting wildlife, while the real Thomas stories were pretty much set in the Cthulhu universe, with all its eldritch horror and weird exoticism.
Crafting mostly lacks depth, there's a few basic materials that get crafted into tiered, upgraded versions that require you to harvest more of them.
Environments are pretty and there's multiple biomes with some variation in flora and fauna, but absent are the magnificent, impossible cities and the vast treasures of Conan lore.
The game really has two fatal pitfalls right now: One, it's not terribly deep (combat is rudimentary and difficult to manage as the physics are wonky and the FPS drops quickly, crafting isn't very interesting, no real complex dungeon raids or adventures/quests), and two, most servers have serious balance issues. Once you're level 50, the god avatars get reasonably simple to farm, and it gets to a point where nobody can really build anything without it getting torn down in short order. PvP is good and I expect my stuff to get destroyed in a competitive server, but there's really just no point in base building or training up fighter thralls as god-avatars are everywhere and there is no counter to them (especially since most players just wreck your stuff when you're offline). Unless you and several well equipped friends happen to be logged in and at your base for the 60 seconds it happens, there's just nothing you can do to stop somebody destroying hours or days of work. And the game doesn't even tell you who did it. There are PvE servers, of course, but it makes fortifying and recruiting thralls pretty pointless and enemies/resources are always despawned because there's nothing to keep the server from over-building.
