This game is incredible. The sheer variety of things to do (and ways to do them) is on par with classic CRPGs like Fallout 1/2.  The writing is also very well done, including work by Chris Avellone and other genre luminaries.
The combat is intense, strategic, punishing, and widely varied.  If you go in the wrong direction, or face too strong enemies. (Aka, trying to just kill all of your prison guards instead of escaping the prison in another way) you will almost certainly die.  But, if you carefully optimize your builds and strategies, even seemingly impossible odds can be overcome.
To top it off, the entire game can be played in up to 4 player co op, either online or in splitscreen. The co op in this game is some of the most creatively implemented I've ever seen, letting characters work together or compete against one another depending on the characters and circumstances. As has been said before, this is about as close to a tabletop roleplaying game as I've seen on a computer.
OH YEAH, almost forgot: the graphics are amazing. Really, this game is beautiful.  If you like RPGs, this is quite simply a must buy.

UPDATE:
Having finished the released Story mode and the earlier release of the Lugaru Story (transitioned into the new engine), I still recommend the game, though it feels like more of the same from Early Access.
The characters and environments have been much improved and added to.  The workshop also allows for plenty of new content.
Unfortunately, the Story is told roughly through small fixed levels.  Luckily, there are some nice checkpoints throughout (useful for some of the more frustrating platforming sections), though some of them are too generous (there were a few times I died, only to find that I had stuck just enough of a toe into the correct area to load from the point I hadn't reached).
Other times, the combat was a little too brutal, with a mob of enemies grouping up on you; hit and run tactics seemed to work best, but if you get cornered, I found there were several times that I was just stuck, no matter how much I wanted to roll or jump away.
Overall, I would say it is worth it, but you need to get enough experience to accept the system, but give yourself enough breaks that the little hiccups don't weigh you down.
--------
ORIGINAL (Early Access):
While the game is still in early access (at time of writing) much of the basic game mechanics are in place, and they work very well: the platforming-parkour makes scaling the environments fun and filled with energy, the combat is fast and incredibly satisfying (even when the computer manages to take you out with a single blow, it will be from a brutal, spine-breaking blow that will leave you cringing and not feeling cheated), and the characters are animated well.
Currently, the game is just a collection of maps and scenarios, but you can also download user-created content or create your own with an in-game editor.  As for an actual story mode - not yet.  Also, while there is some same-system multiplayer support in the form of a single-stage versus map, online multiplayer is not supported (hopefully "yet").
I have nothing but praise for what this game is doing, but here are the only warnings I have for prospective buyers:
1) You might be able to toggle it off (I personally don't, so I can't confirm it), the blood in the game might be disturbing to some.  Many a person who saw the Watership Down animated movie might have flashbacks.
2) The game is labelled as "Furry" and you do play as animal characters, although the game does not (at writing) take the game down the shameful paths that are associated with that infamous genre.
3) The content is somewhat light without an actual story mode.  If you get tired of running around in the environments and fighting in the arena mode, then you will have to wait for another update before you might think of returning to the game (an issue fairly common with these early access games).
In Conclusion
If you aren't turned away by the content of the game, you will love the quality put into this game.

Played Enter the Gungeon? Felt like it was a bit too slow? Needed things ramped up to eleven? Wanted more *thump* to your soundtrack? Maybe add a bit of persistence to the mix as well? Void Raiders has your back. This crazy Russian infused twinstick roguelite takes a lot of the core concepts and then just turns *everything* up to eleven, visual effects, colours, music, screenshake, you name it.
It's a bit like if someone decided Pacman and Enter the Gungeon needed some time in a hotel room with LSD and Viagra, and a "Best of Barry White" album, and this is the result. It's mayhem, beautiful, barely controlled mayhem, and it's entirely hilarious. You have next to no idea what's going on half the time as there's a ridiculous number of projectiles whizzing about in the later levels, you're reacting quite literally on instinct as you simply go "KILL EVERYTHING!", and well, that's about the size of it.
There's lockers you pilfer using credits that rain down from the sky like it's AdVenture Capitalist, giving you various statistical buffs to keep you more or less alive as you work your way through the ever increasing levels of madness, eventually running into bosses who SUDDENLY require some level of thought because their guns go from "Slightly dangerous" to "OW OW OW MY FACE".  I was going to compare this to another game that uses the same kind of stat system - Hero Siege - but that game is NOWHERE near as crazy, or fast paced. This thing is in a league which sits near things like Ubermosh and proper bullet hell type arrangements.
Between runs there's a simple talent tree setup to steadily increase the starting power of each of the three Void Runners (I'm not sure if there's more you can unlock, or more planned, there needs to be, this game deserves ongoing support), there's a relic vault you can unlock persistent buffs for your runners once you've kekked a few bosses, the bar allows you to choose starting buffs or tweak what kind of things you get out of the supply drops, and the whole thing has this wonderful sense of ongoing growth and expansion that keeps you coming back for "Just one more try", because you'll always be getting stronger, even when you lose.
The enemies are simple bullet sponges, but they fit the themes, and they're definitely not to be underestimated, there's some that are deliberate "Wolf in mook clothing" types that WILL near as damnit one shot you if you're dumb enough to not pay attention to their wind up animations. The Bosses demand respect, naturally, and health and ammo is not as frequent as the credit rain that comes along through the levels.
This game is a gem that deserves your attention. It's a russian infused, vodka laden gem that's entirely bonkers, and if you love twinsticks, well, this one will certainly grab you hard and not let go, just be ready for a fast and furious ride, because good grief, it hits top gear right out of the gate, and then it gets *faster*. If you like sedate games, run, run fast, this game is anything BUT sedate.

Overgrowth is ambitious. In fact, I've never seen another openworld game quite like it. In it's present state, this game has tremendous potential and requires community support to see that potential realized. I feel that many Steam users have been spoiled by more polished alpha state games and expect the same from Overgrowth. This title is a reminder of what an EARLY ACCESS game really is. Developers bring their games to Steam in Early Access looking for community support to shape the game into something they want to play. This game is perfect for that concept. At the time of this review (update 206), Wolfire is focusing on the campaign mode for the game. However, there is plenty of room for change while the game remains in alpha. I highly recommend this game to anyone who finds it appealing. Everything this game has to offer is out in the open and plain to see. You are getting an openworld close quarters combat simulator. The physics are impressive, and the character models are a welcome break from the staples in the fantasy genre. If you are expecting a polished, complete game, stop looking at early access titles. Only get this game if you are willing to support Wolfire and see this game reach completion.

So you start off the game by selecting one out of three characters and then pressing start to begin your dungeon run (no hold your hand tutorial :D). From here, you will be shooting up monsters, gaining xp, activating your character's special abilities, collecting credits, gems and coins, dodging sniper bullets, buying items that help your run, unlocking dungeons, racing the clock, fighting bosses, and you'll die...alot, but your death is not in vein! Cause as you level up by defeating monsters, you get skill points to spend to your characters tree! You'll also be rewarded with credits. Credits in the game buy you items in that run. Items like chainsaws give +3 damage! A rocket drone follower can shoot some enemies for you! Sythes can increase your critical hit chance, and all of these help you defeat bosses! Bosses and enemies in the game each of thier own unique attack, learn from thier timing and abilities and use it to your advantage!  Choices you make along the way affect how far you'll be able to get, decisions can make or break your game so choose wisely.
As you progress through dungeons, you'll be finishing objectives. In a normal room, the objectives lead you to a point on the map where you'll find a power cell or cube, these items can be used to go through special dungeons that have enemies that drop gems , coins and other special currencies! These guys can be used to upgrade your characters gear! Your shield, armor and headgear all boost the stats of your weapons and abilities to let you get even further down the dungeon. On top of that, as you get better and better, and begin to defeat bosses, you'll unlock the artifact vault! This vault will hold up to 3 items for you to bring to each and every run, you unlock each of the three spaces by defeating the first three bosses. And when you thought it was over, there is a lone invader on the character selection page that changes a huge part of gameplay! You can select 1 of 5 options that do things like make health packs and ammo drops stronger, elevator store discounts, replacing supply drop with a teleporter strike and a couple more. TONS of stuff in the game to keep you busy :)
While the game is a rogue-like, one of the things that shine through is character progression. The first site of this progression comes with leveling, as you destroy monsters you gain exp, and can build up to lvl 10 on each character,(which in my expierence takes around an hour or so to do with each character). For each level up you gain a point in your character's skill tree, these skills greately change how the character plays, some skills can give bouncing bullets, and others can give a drone companion,  you can get up to 10 points, while there is 14 different skills, so this means you have to choose wisely when picking skill points and test others out to see what works best for your playing style, of course, you can reset these skills whenever you want and re-distribute your points to get a different feel to the character.
While you go through the floors that require item payment of neptune's dungeon, you will find item drops different from regular credits, like gems and coins. These items can be used to upgrade characters weapons in each of thier respective menus. There is alot of items to go through, and I would say it takes at least 10 hours to get all the characters to thier max, and thats only if you are super grinding.
Choices in the game really can take you or break you, buy that mystery item for 25 credits or save it to pick from 3 you can see, in the elevator? Do I want to get the drink that gives me extra ammo or health, or change out my supply drop with an orbital strike? The game gives you decisions all of the time, to unlock the next level or not, character skill tree choices, buying items, picking a drink from the tavern. You have to experiment all the time to see what best fits your playstyle and what could take you past the next boss :) And thats one of the best aspects of the game!
+ Randomly generated dungeons
+ Choices affect your run greatly
+ Lots of items
+ Characters that have different playstyles
+ Character skill trees + upgradable gear
+ Individualistic bosses and enemies
+ Great sci-fi atmosphere
+ Nice soundtrack
+ Steam achievements + trading cards
- Only 3 different characters to play as
- No real story or background to characters
Void Raiders is a stunning quality rogue-like shooter with multiple aspects of character progression, a time based diffiuclty, a wide array of unique items and enemies, and is great to look at. While the game can feel a little grindy at times, you are always trying to beat your last run and learn from previous decisions. The experimenting and learning is what the game is all about. There are tons of item drops in the game with different abilities, and tons of enemies with different attacks. The game sadly only has 3 different characters to play as, but they each have different skill trees and have a unique gameplay shift then the others. For the low price of the game, Void Raiders gives players tons of replayability and a unique expierence of a blend of genres. A gem for rogue-lite lovers and still an amazing game for the rest of us.

Void Raiders is a fast and action pack, arcade top-down shooter with a very flashy theme. The game offers a few playable characters who have their own playstyle and skill trees, as well as some equipment upgrades. The game also offers purchasble passive items to players during levels and after a level has been completed. Visually the sprites and level design are well-done, and the amount of level and enemy variation is quite high. Granted I've only made it to level 6 as of writing this, but there is a lot to look at and I do mean A LOT.
So much so that it may be a deal breaker for some people. Things can get hectic really quickly and sometimes it's very difficult to proccess what is going on on the screen when bullets start filling it up. That might just be me and my unfamiliarity with these games, but at times it's quite bullet-helly. Ontop of that the rooms in the levels tend to be quite cramped and small with a lot of terrain that can sometimes be hard to tell if it's solid or not. I had a bit of trouble distinguishing what I could walk on or hide behind.
Despite the few personal issues I've had with the game, it is a very solid game. Would totally recommend for its price.

Before anything else, let me explain the game. You own a kingdom. Why? Who knows. You build stuff (taverns, shops, barracks, etc.) in a large-ish grid of grass and trees. You attract people into your kingdom, in hopes of them buying some stuff from your shops, like your average tycoon, although as of yet it is a very small focus. The big focus is on quests. You send your heroes on certain types of quests (rescue, vanquish, deliver, etc.) in certain other kingdoms. You allot some points to certain categories, and they're on their way. Thats pretty much it. Build more, quest more. Thats kind of all it is now. Now on with the rating. First of all, if I could rate this game N/A, I would. This game is simply unstable. There are many many bugs and imbalances. The developer himself said the game cost almost nothing to make, so I truly think the game would have been shed in a far better light if he waited to release it on early access. Although it is on the right track, its hard to recommend it as it is. Here is a pros and cons list, with that out of the way:
Cons:
Unbalanced
Buggy
Sensory-depriving color pallette, nothing but green and brown and gold highlights the whole game.
Somewhat repetative quests, with sliders that seem to do nothing (unlike the ever-important sliders in GDT) EDIT: Sliders are now gone, and are replaced with... nothing? Now its worse than before, but not stealing something anymore.
Slow progression, esp. in building.
Once money (sorry, 'gold') goes below 0, its game over. No exceptions or anything, just a game over screen.
Heros slowly die, with no apparent way to heal them. You even get a healing potion store, but not for them I guess. EDIT: This is aparently now fixed
Klunky UI
(keep in mind that almost all of these cons are things that can very easily be fixed by tweaking some numbers and code, so its up to the developer to make things right, for me atleast.)
Pros:
Interesting and unique graphics (though they could still use quite a bit of work)
Despite monotony, still quite fun.
Things to research,
Shops to run,
Not much else to say.
I recommend this game because it is absolutely on the right track. If everything goes as it is, this game will be good. I can't disrecommend this game because of unforseen bugs and unbalances. While the developer should have released it a bit later, he very well might not have gotten any playtesters, therefore not being able to find any of those bugs or unbalances. The core game is fun, and thats all I'm looking for. So overall, I'm cutting this game some slack. I'll probably only play it briefly after the large updates every few weeks or so. The developer very honestly says he will work as hard as he can to finish this game, but anything can happen to one lone developer. A caring, involved developer like this is what this game needs to be fixed. I just hope he will. As of now, the current update, wait to buy, but you eventually should.

Chivalry: Medieval Warfare is an interesting take on FPS melee combat set in the medieval era during a war between two rival factions. As you would expect, a great deal of the game is melee with 3 of the available classes being melee-only (save for throwables) and one ranged class. One of the interesting aspects of Chivalry is that you have a great deal of variety in your swing via different keybindings (overhead, thrust, swing) as well as a few other alternate attacks. Additionally you can parry incoming attacks by looking at them and hitting the respective key and you can even cancel an attack mid-swing to fake out your enemies at the cost of stamina. This allows for an interesting meta between attacker and defender which ultimately comes down to reading their “body language” and/or gauging the situation to see which move is most certain to wound them without risking too much.

This game is one of the best I have ever played. I unfortunately wasn't able to get it back when Jet Grind Radio came out for the Dreamcast, but even on a keyboard and mouse, this game is ludicrously fun.
Each level has been masterfully crafted to highlight all aspects of the game, from perfectly timed sprays as you fly past a target in Kogane, to the grinding and roof jumping of Grind Square.
The tone of the game is matched perfectly by its brilliant soundtrack, spanning many genres but remaining consistently high quality, and always perfectly complementing the gameplay.
As far as gameplay goes, the mechanics are unique and imaginative, but there is a bit of a learning curve. You can skate around each level as you please, grinding, riding walls, doing flips, and jumping around to get to several optimum graffiti locations, often painting over that of a rival gang. The physics feel nice and smooth, if a bit floaty, and precision is required, making it somewhat tedious to get around without an analog stick, but if you have a gamepad there shouldn't be much trouble once you get it down. The actual graffiti is done either by rotating an analog stick or mashing the arrow keys in what's similar to a quick time event, but with the only time being the police or the level timer. Without a gamepad, this can be frustrating at times, but it isn't too much of a hassle once you're accustomed to it.
Now go buy this one of a kind gem and enjoy! Oh, but do yourself a favor and don't play the tutorial. The beginning of the campaign will be more than enough, and you REALLY don't want to have to deal with the tutorial. Just trust me on this.

One of the greatest games of all time. NiGHTS definitely deserves a little more recognition for the beauty and creativity of the game. Controls are easy to learn, and I'll often find myself playing for hours at a time trying to beat my old scores or just releasing steam with a boss run. The characters are colorful, easy to love, and full of personality! This is a feel-good game!
I'll be honest, the first time I saw NiGHTS as a young gamer raised on Nintendo consoles, it was in the NiGHTS into Dreams pinball table alongside Sonic in Sonic Pinball Party for the GameBoy Advance. Needless to say, having just recently been introduced to Sonic, and having a mindset that most girls didn't play videogames, NiGHTS appeared to me as SEGA's lady-Sonic character... the feminine colors of pink and purple hadn't always appealed to me.
Many years later, revisting some of my older games, I picked up Sonic Pinball again, and I thought to myself: "I remember the NiGHTS table having something the Sonic one didn't: Bosses! You're older and much more skilled now, so why don't we give this a go?" After a few practice rounds, I'd cleared my way through all 6 tables, their Nightmaren bosses, and eventually unlocking the secret NiGHTS "Twin Seeds" table, which led to my first encounter with (and triumph over) Wizeman the Wicked.
I was hooked. I wanted to learn about the REAL NiGHTS. After finding very few videos on Youtube over the original NiGHTS into Dreams, I did my own research, and found the game was available on Steam for just $10. At this point in time, I didn't have a Steam account, nor was I interested in TF2 or Garry's Mod, Counter-Strike, any of these legendary titles I'd seen friends playing in the past.
That's right:
The whole reason I made a Steam account was for NiGHTS.
So the next time you see me on your team in TF2, or the next time you see me post a Garry's Mod animation, you can thank the whimsical dream-jester, and the geniuses who've brought it to life.

Do I recommend this at $20? No. At $10 or 15$? Yes, I would. I did buy it at $20 out of boredom, due to it seeming like a nice complement to my new real life job which gives me a different persective on trucking, but I am a bit disappointed with the game.

And if your goal is to play online, you'll find no more than 230 players on the USA server on average, which is hardly a replacement for the AI traffic that will be removed when you play with the multiplayer mod. There will be times when you pass through a city on routes, and see not one single vehicle on the road. That's a very lonely experience, despite playing online.
With that in mind, I suggest playing the American edition offline, with the REAL logo mods for the various signs, trucks, icons, etc to make the game seem like the real world. There's also a nice economy boost to speed things up (by slightly cheating), so you wont get bored before getting your fill of the game's world. You should definitely download the user-made Volvo truck model too. It's very impressive. I hope we see more trucks added by users, as it seems the developer is more focused on Euro's edition.
The experience otherwise is fine. It's no racing game. Play it casually, relax, take in the sights, listen to the internet radio stations, try to abide by laws for some challenge. The experience is fine that way. The graphics engine sucks though. Despite my GPU and no CPU cores getting taxed to any real degree, the game often chugs at 30fps in cities for no reason.

Overall if you think that's a kind of a game you'll enjoy playing on a PC then go for it, but personally I didn't enjoy it enough (mostly because of the frustration from random side of the game) to recommend it.

Mass Effect 2 is the peak of the Mass Effect series, offering an incredible ensemble of characters with high quality writing and voice acting. The narrative and world building of Mass Effect 2 is mostly communicated through these characters, whom you are introduced and acquainted through recruitment missions, loyalty missions, squad chatter, and individual conversations on the ship.
To my dismay, some of the RPG mechanics from Mass Effect 1 have been toned down or removed entirely. There is no real loot system and the skill tree from the previous game has been simplified. However, the ability to roleplay in conversations (Paragon vs. Renegade) is still there, along with the added mechanic of conversational interrupts.
Customary to most Bioware RPG games, you can customize each squad mate’s abilities and loadout. During combat, you can optionally pause and issue squad commands. On the higher difficulties, it’s incredibly satisfying to chain squad abilities together to overpower the enemy’s defenses.
Pros:
•	Great characters that make you feel invested in the universe
•	Fantastic side missions and quests – some of which don’t rely on combat
•	Solid writing and voice acting overall
•	Varied level and city design
•	Improved combat system that encourages tactical squad play
•	Conversation system allows for some choices/roleplaying
•	Worthwhile (although overpriced) DLC
•	Amazing soundtrack
Cons:
•	Main story arc takes a backseat in favor of the character-driven side missions
•	Skill tree is simplified and too combat focused
•	Morality system is binary (Paragon vs. Renegade); few gray areas
•	Planetary scanning is a chore

This game feels and plays like the more classic RPG's of the past. Just look at games like Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights and Larians own Divine Divinity and you'll know what I'm on about. The first Original Sin was good, but this is something else, something more polished and fun to play.
Unlike many newer RPG's, this game doens't have that much handholding. It lets you explore the world and figure out things by yourself without much obvious spoonfeeding. Also, your actions have some weight on how things play out. Don't save a seemingly unimportant NPC early on and it might come back to bite you later on.
The world itself is quite interactable. Not only are there loads of things lying around for you to rummage through and steal. There are also plenty of environmental effects like puddles of water or blood giving you the chance of electrifiying it and anyone standing in it. Oil can be lit aflame, as does poison. You can let it rain to douse the flames, creating steam. Obviously your characters will also get wet because of the rain. A campfire will then again warm up your characters. All these effects are certainly fun to mix up and don't feel that gimmicky like in the first Original Sin.
Lastly and quite importantly: the inhabitants of the world feel quite alive, the story unfolds nicely, the dialogue is top notch and your party members are delightfully in depth.
Highly recommended for any RPG lover. Otherwise still a rock solid game.

The following will be my in depth review of MASS EFFECT 2. I have placed 35 whole hours into this beauty of a sci-fi shooter, and I feel I have amased enough experience in the game to make a decent review on it. Keep in mind this is my opinion, and however I feel about the game may not accurately reflect how others feel. Also this review will contain MAJOR SPOILERS about the story and other aspects of the game so be warned. With that in mind, let's get right into this!
Table of Contents:
1. Thoughs on Story
2. Gameplay
3. Graphics / Art Direction
4. Final Score / Final Thoughts
----------------------------------
1. If you want a full review of the story, then I suggest you read up on it via IGN or another game review site. This section is meerly my thoughts on the story. Personally, I think the story is pretty well developed. The beginning scences where you get sucked out of the ship and die really sets the mood for the rest of the game. While its kinda weird that Cerberus spends a TON of money to revive you and the Alliance basically doesn't give a crap, it doesn't hurt the overall feel. What I also like is that the story doesn't have a choke hold on the game. You hop into the action within the first 10 minutes of the game, which is something I feel that many games don't do. Sometimes game stories spend the first hour of the game's time and bores you out of your mind. MASS EFFECT 2 doesn't do that, and I'm happy it holds off. The height of the story BY FAR is the ending, where everyone can basically die any second if you don't earn their loyalty earlier in the game. In my playthrough, I lost Miranda at the end, which prompted me to look up how you lose people. Apparently you there are a lot of ways you can lose people, and I feel pretty lucky I only lost one person. However, I felt AWFUL about losing her, and this is something the game does really well at the end. They make you actually care about your companions and I like that. Overall, the story is well constructed.
2. The combat in this game is awesome. Combining the sci-fi aspects with the fps will always impress me. I love the abilities they give you and how one ability doesn't trump all the enemies in the game. To truly succeed in this game is to find the right balance of abilities, and I like that. Of course there is shooting mixed in, and they did the fps part fine. I mean how can you get that part wrong anyway? All you gotta do is make sure you can point and shoot and the game is okay already. What I do like is that you have many choices of what gun to use. You have at least 4 weapons to choose from at any given moment, which gives you many options in terms of how you want to take people down. Combine this with the abilities, and you've got yourself a million and one ways to kill someone. I also heard you can combine abilities like pull and throw to make them more effective, which is great. You can bring 2 members of your crew at any given moment, and you have a pretty wide arrangement of teammates to choose from. From guys that can light enemies on fire to people who basically use the force, you have a ton of options on who to be your partners in crime. Now the enemies you fight aren't always super unique from one to the other, however, there are enough different enemies for it not to get really boring. They nailed this aspect of the game.
Okay, now that we are done with that, lets talk about the other gameplay parts. Outside of mauling anyone you see, you will explore many planets in the game via your ship on the galatic map. There are WAY TOO MANY planets to find and I mean WAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAY too many. Now this may sound overwhelming, and believe me it can be at some times, but you can't physically land on every planet. Some planets you can only scan for resources on, and others you have a very brief landing on to kill some mercs or fix some stuff. Other than that, there aren't many planets that you actually explore, which is fine because having all those planets to explore would make this game REALLY big. However, they just don't do much besides add 10 minutes of gameplay where you shoot up a few guys or fix some random machine. The exploration aspect is cool, but I feel there are too many planets to find. At the end of the game I found examining every planet I found a chore.
Now lets talk about the skill tree and upgrading / customizing your assets. The skill tree is like any old skill tree: you level up, obtain skill points, and apply those skill points to a... well... skill tree. Now the tree in this game is not as big as others, in fact, it is kinda small. But I feel this doesn't hinder the game. Instead of giving you 50 skills to choose from, they give you 4-6. I feel this helps the player focus on what they want in their characters, however, I also think the skill tree is smaller than it should be. I also feel that the bonuses from the tree don't really help that much. I didn't see a big difference from one stage of the tree to the other. The same can be said for some of the weapon, armor, and ability updgrades. While some are helpful, like increasing the carrying capacity for ammo, the upgrades that increase damage or shield protection don't make much a difference. Now the ship upgrades are crucial to your crew surviving the end of the game, so I HIGHLY suggest you get those. You can also customize your armor by actually changing what armor you wear and by changing its color, which is something I really like. And since we are talking about customizing, you can customize Shepard at the beginning of the game. These options for Shepard and the armor are very extensive and I like that. However, I think both the tree and the upgrades could have been done in a better way. It is a minor flaw, but they just didn't sit right with me, especially the upgrades.
Last gameplay portion to talk about is the reputation rating. Shepard can either be the good guy, a paragon, or the bad guy, a renegade. You are free to choose which you wish to be, I personally chose to be a good guy instead of being a stuck up prick. Either way, I'm not sure if these ratings affect much other than the ending. If you choose to be an ultimate♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and not care about your crew's loyalty, prepare for A LOT of people to die at the end. Other than that, it just affects what you say in dialouge to other people. You mainly get paragon or renegade points through dialouge, and believe me when I say there is WAY TOO MUCH dialouge. This is about the only real problem the game has. The amount of dialouge this game has makes me cry, literally. There is about a 1 page paper's worth of dialouge for every interactable character, especially with your crew. They will just blab on and on about whatever they wish. The good thing to take out of this is that there is a lot of detail to the game, but I think they overdid it a lot a bit in this department.
3. I am not much of an art geek. Likewise, I am not much of a graphics geek, but this game was made in 2010. The graphics aren't fantastic, and you can tell at some points. Seeing pixelated walls isn't a great feeling, but again this was made in 2010. I can let that slide. The overall art direction of the game seems a little too much of the norm. Not at any moment besides some of the cool lights you see on the galatic map did I say, "This game is pretty." The whole setting is sometimes devoide of colors besides grays and even the other colors aren't very bright and... er... colorful. But it didn't really bother me either, so as i said, I'm going to let the graphics pass.
4. I give MASS EFFECT 2 a 9 / 10. The game does what it came out to do, deliver you an awesome sci-fi fps experience. While there are a few problems, namely the amount of god dang dialouge, the pros outweigh the cons. The game isn't short either, which can be good and bad. If you like shooting up bad guys in space, I highly suggest you grab this gem of a game.

I heard about War for the Overworld when I was looking to see if the old Dungeon Keeper games had been put on Steam. A couple of reviews I read said that WftO hit on all the things that made Dungeon Keeper great and I am going to have to agree. It hit every bit of nostalgia that I was hoping to get out of playing Dungeon Keeper again.
There was a good variety of rooms, units, constructs and spells. Not all of the levels were "destroy this other person's core building'". It lasted me about 15 hours to beat the campaign on my first try and this was with me having to restart levels multiple times because I made poor decisions about my dungeon layout.
The only negative I would have is that the AI was very passive and barely attacked for the first third of the campaign and then suddenly got ratcheted up to 11. I then came across a "kill room" design that I used for every level after that because the enemies were never smart enough to break a wall somewhere else. Instead they would just walk through a room of death that they couldn't possibly survive. In general, combat is the one thing I would love to see improved in a sequel. Merging RTS unit controls like from StarCraft would be my dream because currently you just plant rally flags to draw your units and cross your fingers that your numbers are bigger than the enemies.
If you are looking for something to scratch that Dungeon Keeper issue look no further. You have found it. Simply buy this game and enjoy the ride.

War for the Overworld is a deformed beast. It has the bite and snarls that we expect it to have, yet even the most phlegmatic of eyes can’t help but notice the sores and pus leaking from its skin. There’s also the hacking cough and the tendency for its knee to give out when it climbs a set of stairs.
Personification aside, yeah, WtO is a mess. One that’s enjoyable much of the time, but there’s little point in ignoring that Early Access didn’t do its job.
As the spiritual successor to the much-loved Dungeon Keeper 2, WtO carried a lot of high expectations during development. It spawned a game that is mechanically identical to its predecessor, with all the usual charm and humour enunciated by its canyon-throated narrator. There are lots and lots of new structures, units, and rare items to find in the bowels of the Earth, and the A.I. does a competent job of keeping you on your toes during Skirmishes. Plus, there’s a (mostly) fun campaign and even a budding custom-map community.
So, you can still carve out a big dungeon and terrorise mankind, only now you can do it with more options. What’s to dislike?
It’s a technical mess. Units getting caught in doorways, defences malfunctioning, units warping, God-awful FPS when things get even slightly hectic. Take a look at the screenshots, then the Unity logo. This is not a graphically beautiful game, nor is its engine complicated. It’s DK2 with more content. DK2 runs like a dream on my computer. A successor with slightly brighter graphics and some new features does not justify this hot mess. It’s bad, bad, bad, and although it didn’t ruin my enjoyment, it can’t be ignored, and there were at least five occasions where I had to reload a level due to performance deterioration.
Unity is not a monstrous game engine and WtO is not Crysis. This unpolished state is the result of developer negligence. Nothing more.
There are some other frustrations, too. Though the campaign is mostly fun, some levels are designed to irritate you. Two in particular, one an ambush mission and the other a defence one, left a sour taste in my mouth, where strategy was thrown out in favour of reloading the level and spamming specific units until you reached completion by sheer luck. The bonus mode, Crucible, also gets plenty boring after some time, since you’ll soon reach a point where your defences are so impeccable that all you need to do is sit tight and watch the enemy die out. There are design imperfections that a re-visit to the drawing board might have fixed.
WtO is still a fun game, but despite years in Early Access, it was released in a damaged state, and it is still in the same state. If you can bear dealing with less than sixty frames and the occasional visual displeasure, WtO would make a fine addition to your library if bought on sale. It’s good, but it continues the Dungeon Keeper legacy rather meekly.

This game is one of the best I have ever played. I unfortunately wasn't able to get it back when Jet Grind Radio came out for the Dreamcast, but even on a keyboard and mouse, this game is ludicrously fun.
Each level has been masterfully crafted to highlight all aspects of the game, from perfectly timed sprays as you fly past a target in Kogane, to the grinding and roof jumping of Grind Square.
The tone of the game is matched perfectly by its brilliant soundtrack, spanning many genres but remaining consistently high quality, and always perfectly complementing the gameplay.
As far as gameplay goes, the mechanics are unique and imaginative, but there is a bit of a learning curve. You can skate around each level as you please, grinding, riding walls, doing flips, and jumping around to get to several optimum graffiti locations, often painting over that of a rival gang. The physics feel nice and smooth, if a bit floaty, and precision is required, making it somewhat tedious to get around without an analog stick, but if you have a gamepad there shouldn't be much trouble once you get it down. The actual graffiti is done either by rotating an analog stick or mashing the arrow keys in what's similar to a quick time event, but with the only time being the police or the level timer. Without a gamepad, this can be frustrating at times, but it isn't too much of a hassle once you're accustomed to it.
Now go buy this one of a kind gem and enjoy! Oh, but do yourself a favor and don't play the tutorial. The beginning of the campaign will be more than enough, and you REALLY don't want to have to deal with the tutorial. Just trust me on this.

Great Rogue-type twin stick, very addictive gameplay, and I haven't even listened to the soundtrack yet.  All the best stuff from my 80s and 90s arcade upbringing in one nice package, I haven't had this much fun since Ikari Warriors.  Do yourself a favor and buy it, and support this good effort.
Edit:  I add this part at the end in case any other developers read reviews for other games to try to understand what makes something so popular or attractive to users.  I would say this developer pays an appropriate amount of attention to the visual effects, not so much that they ovewhelm or that the game loses focus, but it makes a really nice "paint job" on top of great mechanics (which seem very well-tweaked).
A lot of other games, including ones I have bought but not played lately, seem almost to this level, but are just missing that extra variety in the color palette or visual effects to stay up to date with modern games.
Here's a hint -- if the visuals on things like Bejeweled look head and shoulders better than your game, it needs some shine.  This developer used relatively low-pixel 8-bit style graphics and gave it the right shine to make it do its magic, with very simple yet effective art.  I consider this game to be a model for other developers in its class, and feel very happy with my investment, to the point that I have shown it to coworkers and family.  Kudos, and may your competition learn from your efforts.

A niche if there ever was. A vibrant, hip, stylized skate-park playground. This is a Japanese game, thick and thoroughly, in art style, story, characters and text. A short play through the main story (about 5-6 hours for first time) but a good chunk of variety that many would benefit in their libraries. The game play is precursor to Tony Hawk games: dropped in street neighborhood with a few tasks to carry out while pulling skate tricks on the environment. In this one, you have to spray your skate gang's graffiti across the walls of the city while avoiding the increasingly over-the-top police force, which ramps from dogs that chase you down as you try to tag a sidewalk, to jet-pack secret agents with M16's. Controls feel wonky at first, but you'll pick up the movement and flow of the character after a level or so. It's flashy on its own, but your own skill and creativity make this game a beauty to play.

The reviews don't lie, this is one of the best sci-fi stories you're going to experience in any medium. The story itself is not outrageously innovative, but the subtle way the characters are woven into the intrigue captured me in a way most other games don't. The puzzles are logical without being completely obvious, and the story progresses at the perfect pace. Great game.

Do I recommend this at $20? No. At $10 or 15$? Yes, I would. I did buy it at $20 out of boredom, due to it seeming like a nice complement to my new real life job which gives me a different persective on trucking, but I am a bit disappointed with the game.
This is a much smaller product compared to Euro's counterpart. I knew this going in, but realizing that there is literally only 3 trucks to pick from is still a shock. That's hardly enough to be called a "simulation" of this career. You'll find yourself covering what little landmass they offer very quickly, as well. And if your goal is to play online, you'll find no more than 230 players on the USA server on average, which is hardly a replacement for the AI traffic that will be removed when you play with the multiplayer mod. There will be times when you pass through a city on routes, and see not one single vehicle on the road. That's a very lonely experience, despite playing online.
With that in mind, I suggest playing the American edition offline, with the REAL logo mods for the various signs, trucks, icons, etc to make the game seem like the real world. There's also a nice economy boost to speed things up (by slightly cheating), so you wont get bored before getting your fill of the game's world. You should definitely download the user-made Volvo truck model too. It's very impressive. I hope we see more trucks added by users, as it seems the developer is more focused on Euro's edition.
The experience otherwise is fine. It's no racing game. Play it casually, relax, take in the sights, listen to the internet radio stations, try to abide by laws for some challenge. The experience is fine that way. The graphics engine sucks though. Despite my GPU and no CPU cores getting taxed to any real degree, the game often chugs at 30fps in cities for no reason.

Mass Effect 2 (ME2) is the sequel to the amazing Mass Effect (ME1). In Mass Effect 2, you play as Commander Shepard and recruit 12 powerful squad members (2 from DLCs) in your team to fight against the enemies. Compared to ME1, the features in ME2 have been tremendously improved and polished. Since I have played ME1, expect to find a few comparisons in this game review.
- Breathtaking cinematic cutscenes (So many feelings and goosebumps)
- Beautiful music (More goosebumps)
- Skippable conversations
- Character and armor customization
- Great story, unforgettable ending
- Additional squad members (badass, mysterious, crazy, and funny individuals)
- Same ammo used for all weapons (except heavy weapons)
- Improved HUD screen and power wheel
- Squad movements associated with key bindings (no more via HUD)
- Enemies protections are color coded (barrier - purple, shields - yellow, armor and health red)
- Space/Galaxy exploration
- Progress status on space exploration
- Interesting dialogs (Some of them are funny)
- Shorter loading time
- Purchasable mementos and pets for your cabin
- No more annoying elevators
- Two mini-puzzle to unlock research and credits
- Any classes can hack now (not only techies)
- A few intense time limited missions
- Missions can be continued after finishing the main plot
- Pursue a romantic relationship
- In-depth encyclopedia (Codex)
- Arrow pointer in map
- Tutorial at the start of the game
- Introduction to newer species (Drell, Batarians, Vorcha) and creatures
- Variety of alien species and enemies
- Emphasize teamwork
- Access to Cerberus Network (You'll get extra weapons, armor, missions and one more squad member)
- Fewer skills/abilities (but it is fine since you have many squad members)
- Weapons stats no longer exist (but weapons can be made stronger via research)
- Specific weapons for specific classes (e.g. Infiltrator cannot use assault rifle) (but preferable than those in ME1 where weapon’s accuracy was affected)
- Difficulty in reaching level 30 (possible if ME1 character is imported, completed all missions and DLCs, or continue a new game after first playthrough)

- Other expensive DLCs (you'll need Bioware points to purchase them)
- DLCs not sold in Steam
- Mako missions replaced with probes
- Possible wastage on buying probes and fuel (I did)
- Scanning planets could be dull and repetitive over time
- No running, only sprinting
- The "Press 'F' to Finish Mission" blocked the dialog wheel
- Failure to connect to Mass Effect 2 server error (popped up every single time after starting the game)
Overall, the good outweighs the bad in Mass Effect 2. If you are a fan of Mass Effect or if you love action role-playing, sci-fi adventure and exploration, then this game is for you. Mass Effect 2 will definitely be one of the games where you will cherish the feel good moment. You will wish to replay it in the future to experience those nostalgic moments again.
Note: Be prepared to feel empty after you have finished playing this game because I do.
A tip for those who are reading until this far, pay a visit to Uranus and launch a probe if you have not already.

I really like this game.  This is an RTS.  You build a few shops and build guilds where you can build "heroes".  All your units are heroes.  The more buildings and heroes you have, the more taxes you get.  Here is where the game gets original.  You have no (direct) control over the heroes.  They wander about and do as they wish and buy goods from your shops (gaining you more money).  To get them to do what you want you have to bribe them.  Want an area of the map revealed?  Put a dollar amount on it, the more you put on it the faster it gets done and the more heroes show up.  The tricky part is that unless they are close to enemies you have to bribe them to attack them or to defend your buildings or attack an enemy building.  I would have played all the way through this game except for an absurdly hard level that is timed and forces you to memorize the map.  The collection is worth 20 bucks.

This game was just godly, the choices, the dialogue, exploration and combat.  The story, or stories more like, was truly engaging as was building a connection with the characters.  And with the choices to create my own, I did just that, an avatar to interact with the world set together by the true gods.  I quite enjoy the presence of sophisticated types regardless of how rude they may be, along with my affinity for lizard-like races, chose to be a blue ocean in the form of a lithe lizard, who with a mixture of bow and magic, controlled my enemies, and aided my allies.  On my journy was my three companions who have more than proved their friendship.
To begin was the vocals of the group, Lohse who with her mastery of summoning, most disconcerning interest in electrocution along with her words of encouragement(and madness) made for a friend worth staying in the back with and babying the rough'n'tough boys when they've had too much of a spanking.
Then theres the Beast who, in-spite of being quite short, excelled at movement, cutting down enemies as quickly as knocking them onto their♥♥♥♥♥ and with being a dwarf and a pirate no less, was enthusiastic, joyous and free as a dwarven pirate should be, whilst Lohse was the voice to the song, the Beast would always be the first to sing along.
And last, but definitely no least was the understandably arrogant Red Prince, tamer of flames, a true beefcake to my slender form, and as brutal with the shield as he is with his sword.  And somewhere along the lines his "Fire" met my "Water" and together created steam if you know what I mean, sure he was destined to another, but this here was the closest thing to true love.  Hm, but how far exactly did that "love" go, if you catch my meaning, meh, a fan-fiction to keep to my own.
But the hardest part about all of this, the story, your companions, was saying goodbye in the end, to say, this is it.  To end the journey and part ways with those of which you have made it so far with was quite heart wrenching.  I almost didn't want to say goodbye, but a story has to end.  For me, I would have wanted to keep playing after the epilogue, to be a god and explore the world as a one-lizard band.  Maybe even return to the Ancient Empire, see how everything fares with the Red Prince, share a few drinks, and reminisce upon our old adventures.  Perhaps we even get the whole gang together for another adventure, just like good old times.  But to say goodbye, to say goodbye was so hard, to part ways with friends, those who have been together with you through so much, is always hard, and sometimes, imagination alone isn't enough to mend the emptiness filled by adventures, especially ones with those you have melded with.

I guess this is more a tale rather than an actual review, or perhaps it is a review in the shape of a tale but even with the very small flaws in this diamond, I shall cherish this game for what it accomplishes.  A good story, a world full of surprises and secrets, and a band of friends I would forever play god with til' the end.  But I demand nothing more from Larian studios for they have made their sacrifices to deliver something no triple A game developer could get quite right.  I shall see to it that I myself create new adventures, because with the tools Larian has provided, we can all become story tellers, and we can all be pathfinders for our own adventures.
-10/10 ...Would definitely adventure again.

It's good but there's a few things that need to be improved.
What I missed the most from the DK games were all the little details that were put into creatures' personalities and traits. For example, you couldn't have spiders and flies share a lair because they hate each other. Bile demons hated skeletons because they're fat and skeletons are skinny so they wouldn't work together. A level 10 demon spawn becomes a dragon, a tentacle only comes if you put a lair next to water. There are DK ersatz characters in this game, like a succubus instead of a mistress, but they're not fleshed out much. I do like how, for example, the Auger is a slow creature, so you have to think about the layout of the rooms he uses so he doesn't have to walk too far, but most of the other creatures are attract and forget, which means you don't have to be particularly good at designing your dungeon. You just build things and wait.
Fights don't have a lot of strategy to them because all of the creatures feel the same. The ghost in DK1 for example, was a weak creature which could reflect magic and blow away enemies using wind, so you'd use that creature in certain situations. The bile demon was AOE, the warlock was ranged healing, the mistress was a kiter, the hellhound was for picking off runners and imps, the orc was a tank. There's not much of that here, you don't really need healers because you generally have so much mana that you can just heal creatures yourself. The creatures' offensive spells all feel the same. Everything feels bland and overpowered.
The lair and treasure room don't attract creatures and their shape doesn't matter, so you can just slap them down anywhere and forget about them. Boring. Make them do something.
The world map in DK1 was really cool, the way it was hand drawn and changed from good to evil over the course of the game. The one in this game isn't as interesting.
Still it's a good game and all but they need to take another look at DK1 instead of DK2 and see what made that game good.

It's been what? 15 years since dungeon keeper 2? I really wanted this to be a worthy sucessor after bullfrog was torn apart, but instead we get something reminscent of it, picking up one or two jokes from the DK twins (micro piglets).
The game itself works, but the dungeon keeping charms are just painted on - and they rub off quickly.
Compared to the desaster that was dungeons 1 & 2, this is closer to the original series, but it's still not understanding it.
Where you struggled in dungeon keeper to design your rooms for maximum performance using halls and hallways, you tear down everything in here until you happen accross a gold dig to fill your pockets - and the game suffers for it, as frame rate drops are happening all over the field.
It seems the devs want you to make one huge hall, as the pathing system is really the worst part. Whereas the enemy goes straight for your heart whatever you do (often times right into stacked traps) as if scripted, your own hirelings are too stupid to find doorways and start complaining: No money, no food, no sleep, etc.
The premise and promise is there, but the parts are too rough around the edge and won't fit together right, always feeling crooked and angled.
Nostalgia is a hell of a drug, but this game will make your trip down nostalgia lane a bad one- you're better off going through your storage, looking for that CD with the red frog on the label.

Pretty fun game. I really enjoy the atmosphere and the narrator is fantastic. Certain parts are fairly dumbed down compared to what you would expect in a typical RTS, but I don't consider that a bad thing (in fact I would say it works great in this kind of game). Your minions are mostly automated and will do their jobs and train themselves but as the underlord you can of course micro them as much as you want. I also find the idea of you as the dungeon master having a mana bar as a resource to cast spells, build defences, and hire workers pretty unique as well.
Now that's not to say the game doesn't have some problems. Even though your minions are autonomous they are sometimes kind of stupid and don't sleep, eat, or get their paycheck quick enough and you'll often get messages that they're unhappy. This can usually be solved by just clicking on them and dropping them into the area they are lacking in but I don't really think you should have to do that when you don't have them assigned to anything.
The worker flag is kind of irritating too because you can either force all workers to work on an area (sometimes I want like  2-3 still working on the other side) or you can let them decide what to prioritize and sometimes they'll just dig walls or run off to another task instead of placing all the floor tiles down while I'm waiting to make a room. Note that this may just be me not being good enough at the game to figure out how to assign workers properly.
The economy system is kind of wierd too. You get unlimited gold from workers mining these "gold shrines" which are big rectangular boxes. I think if maybe gold acted like mana where you could mine a big chunk of it, but it wouldn't start recharging until you stopped mining it for awhile it might be better? I'm not sure. This isn't really a major complaint but it's something I dislike.
Overall, the game does have a number of issues, but nearly all of them can be overlooked or are very minor. I do highly recommend trying out War for the Overworld because it does feel really unique to play as an actual bad guy for once. The gameplay is solid and so far the campaign has been a very enjoyable experience.

While I love this game with my heart and soul, I can't recommend this game to ANYONE. First off, this is a free to play, MMORPG with more numerical values in skill points and microtrasactions than are reasonable in an MMO, RPG or not. If you are one of those people who can keep tabs on their progress every 20 seconds great, you 'might' like this game. Secondly, crafting takes the longest it should ever take you. Building a gun in the game takes about as long as a machine might take to calculate the numeric value of pi. I sat waiting for literal days, waiting for crafting items to finish. Third, after finding most of the beginning quests, you struggle to find more, leading you to take hours on the crappy little ATV you spent 5 days (real-time) to make, running strait into a PvP field, dieing instantly from a stray bullet or an overpowered NPC. Last but not least, there is the problem of buttons. I have never played a game where every key on your keyboard + keys you don't even have is/are used in game to perform simple tasks such as turning left.
I don't want this to sound like I'm griping about this game, but its just something where if you can deal with organized chaos you may have a chance to play this game, otherwise, stay clear of this game.

So far so good. I already like this infinitely better than Nuclear Throne, which it is very similar to in terms of combat and weapon sounds, because it gives me a chance to not die quickly over and over again because it actually gives me some♥♥♥♥♥♥♥hit points. Nuclear Throne gives you 8. This game gives you 100+. That is the single only reason that I found NT challenging. Despite giving you so much hp, this game is challenging. Enemy bullets travel fast (too fast), enemies travel fast, and they respawn infinitely on each stage and they respawn often. And that is one of the biggest problems I have with this game is that enemy projectiles travel too fast. You cannot avoid gunfire and will always take massive amounts of dmg. It really does need to be toned down if they want this game to have any shelf life. And I'm not bad, most gunfire/lasers are just unavoidable. The objective is to collect four pink things in the level then the elevator is ready and you backtrack to it to go to the next stage. The game gets increasingly hard from very easy to hard and so on, exactly like in Risk of Rain. Another thing that makes it more enjoyable than Throne is that you can get permanent character skill upgrades, like crit chance and the ability to have a gundrone. K&M controls work great and you even get a nice red laser to help you aim in case you lose your crosshair in the action which you will like in most top down shooters.
Graphics
The graphics are done well although they need to be cleared up because the rooms can get confusing as to what you can or cannot walk over/around. I am often wasting bullets shooting into a pillar that blends into the background or I have to try and decipher how I want to navigate a room while ten guys are wailing on me with lasers.
Sound/Music
Awesome! I love the music and the gunfire booms loudly.
There are some things I hope get fixed up, like how on one stage I was staying locked in one room and running out of ammo because the little white ninja slice guys wouldn't quit respawning and running at me. They need to tone down those guys respawn rate and make them take a little less dmg to kill. Also when the girl character runs out of ammo she just simply wont fire but once every few seconds making her only useful if you have energy for her special move and get lucky and get a ammo drop. The other big problem is that end of level rewards are useless unless you can stack them multiple times. The problem is that the game gets hard very quickly so that's not going to happen and even if it could, end rewards are random. Double end level reward bonuses to fix this.
It's an early access game so of course it needs a lot of work, such as a better UI, better menus, more instructions, more options, more content, more coherent level design for less confusion, more clear item buying during a level so you don't miss it, character improvements, slow down enemy bulets, lessen respawn rate, more clear goals, more varied goals, explanation of why I need to use green build credits to enter certain side areas, and so on. So far they are on the right track and depending how much they put into this game it could turn out awesome.

Fun and frantic top down sci-fi shooter with three playable characters.
Amazing soundtrack that really gets you pumped up to do some damage.
Upgrade your characters as you try to survive.
A perfectly done rogue-lite experience.
Character upgrades carry over, but you can also get power-ups that only last each game you play.
Stack your bonuses to gain increase in health,damage,credits etc.
Enemies attack in waves while maintaining small spawn points throughout the map.
Make your way through each zone to the guided items that will open up gateways to more difficult areas.
Multiple levels/areas.
Some blood and gore.
Intense action that ramps up in difficulty as the run progresses.
Lots of replayability.
A variety of pixelated goodness as each area has it's own unique set of enemies and theme.
The game runs pretty smooth even on my low end processor and graphics card.
Both keyboard and gamepad work well, each bringing a separate experience.
It's as if Geometry Wars met Call of Duty, Re-Loaded and Doom and were in the setting of Mass Effect.
(Yeah, that's the conclusion I came to. It's open to interpretation though.)
All in all, I would highly recommend this game.

This is a first impression of the game and I will probably write more about it later.
Void Raiders is a top down mouse-aim shooter-RPG with random level layouts and item drops, persistent character progression and lots and lots of bullets.I played a pre-release alpha build and was immediately enamoured of it, and for five bucks, this early access build is an excellent foundation. Though it lacks plot or characterization of any kind at present, it has good enough music and spritework to convey a sense of style: a dark, neon-lit, occasionally rain-soaked metropolis on... Neptune?
It has three playable characters- Boris the Brawler, Tina the Gunslinger and Gudrun the Bladedancer, and of the three thus far I have had the most success with Boris, whose upgrades slowly turn him into a bullet-spewing tank. Tina puts out even more shots with her dual guns and has an entertaining special ability that causes her to spray bullets everywhere around her. Gudrun, with proper use of her blade-dashing and bullet-reflecting, is surprisingly survivable, and has a shotgun for when her sword isn't enough, but if you can't effectively use her sword to intercept incoming shots, she's by far the most fragile of the three.
Stages are split up into floors. On each floor you must obtain a certain number of key items, either these metal boxes with pink lights or these glowing green datacubes, before the elevator to the next floor becomes available. Enemies respawn endlessly, but you get xp for every kill. They drop cash, ammo and the occasional health pickup. Cash can be used to purchase stat-boosting (more damage, higher crit chance, health back on critical hits, etc) items from in-level vendors, one item per vendor, and you also get a choice of three items to buy between floors. However, you don't know what you're getting if you buy the in-level items, and in roguelike fashion, these items are lost when you die.
There's another review on here mentions the somewhat sluggish player movment, noting that you often have no choice but to "take the hits", and I'm inclined to agree, but if anything that's the game's only real shortcoming apart from not-yet-added features. However, I personally feel like the current level cap of 10 for each character is a tad low- admiteddly, leveling only gives you skill points, with the actual stat increases instead coming from upgrading your armor using components earned from defeating the bosses. I can only hope these upgrades have no cap, or at least a high one, as the game still becomes very difficult in later stages. Interestingly, I noticed that the difficulty increases not per stage but rather at certain time intervals in the length of your run- if you waste time, things will only get harder, but you might miss out on extra funding and items.
I've played a lot of roguelikes and am glad to see another one with character experience and skills that carry over between runs. I hope that, like Rogue Legacy, or Galak-Z's arcade mode, victory in this game is an eventuallity, or at least a reasonable possibilty as in Ziggurat.

This is one of Sega's gems, and certainly one of the Saturn's best games.  The PC version is almost identical, which means don't expect next-gen graphics.  This game was originally written for a 32-bit machine, and the PC port shows its age.  However, this is still a "must play" game.  Totally original, bright, colorful, and a blast to play.  Older gamers will "get it" right away, but younger players may try to play it like an adventure game...  it's not an adventure game.  It's actually like a race against the clock to rack up as many points as you can while flying around a 3-D "track."  Once you've collected and deposited 20 blue Ideya orbs, they'll turn gold and you will want to use the remaining time to collect as many gold Ideya orbs as possible.  This will ensure high scores.  Each world has about 4 different tracks, and you'll be judged A, B, C, D, or F according to your score.  Then you'll face a boss, and each one has a different weakness.  Sometimes it's difficult to determine what you're supposed to do to defeat them.  This game actually would've been right at home in the arcade, in my opinion.  It's wonderful, and every gamer should give it a try.  (It was created by Sega's famed Sonic Team & Yuji Naka, the creator of Sonic The Hedgehog...)

This is my first review, so keep that in mind.
I got it as a gift from a friend (he showed me a list of games and I chose this one, because it was a mix between noire cop shows and sci-fi weirdness) and let me tell you I was not disappointed.  I grew up with point-and-click adventure games and this one was clearly different, if only because the object you use to move foreward don't seem contrived or out-there at all.  No rubberband-and-carrot boomerangs to kick-start a bunny generator so it can release bunnies to form a fluffy bridge to cross.  Nope.  Need to stop a guy from shooting you?  Right click on him, left click on gun, dead.  Need to open window? Right click on it, left click on foot, etc.
It only took me about 3 days of on-and-off play to finish this with just a bit of difficulty.  This game is very good at giving you all the tools you need to succeed, you just have to be paying attention.  Nothing the game makes you do seems trivial.
The story was very well written and I couldn't find any holes in it.  No one breaks character and they're all very unique.
Learning not to use WASD and instead click the screen to move around was a little strange, and sometimes I had trouble moving the characters where I wanted them to go, but it didn't bother me that much.
BONUS: If you're someone who likes references or easter eggs, there are a TON of Battlestar Galactica references in this game. I won't give them all away, but the person who created this was clearly a fan.

The result is that many skills simply don't work together, and the clusterf#ck is worsened when you attempt to pick classes and skills for  your party; only to find out later in the game that you chose wrong, and are now underpowered.
The problem is that they forced this beta idea into the game without testing it properly, and documenting its effects.  The result is that you get to restart over and over and over again until you figure out what works with what.

Short version:  don't bother with this pay for beta release until at the very least guides come out explaining how to build your party properly.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Note: Void Raiders is currently in Early Access. The version reviewed was released 17-MAR-2016 (including hotfix).
Void Raiders is a hectic science-fiction twin-stick shooter with rogue-like elements and great pixel graphics.
Graphics - Void Raiders has mostly great pixel graphics with a technological theme. It doesn't quite look like cyberpunk, but there's a definite sci-fi feel to everything. From the "Lone Invader Tavern" that makes up the sparse main menu, through the handful of different level styles, character and enemy graphics are solid quality and well animated, while levels are made up of interesting objects, albeit laid out in only a limited number of ways.
Once the action starts everything gets a bit hectic. All of the guns fire bright pulses of colour, rather than bullets, adding to both the science-fiction feel of the game and the action on screen. At first it feels a bit cluttered and overwhelming, but you get used to it after a while, and begin to appreciate the chaos all around you. The screen shake effect adds to the atmosphere.
Graphics options are all but non-existent. You can change the severity of the screen shake, and there's a "not available yet" setting for particles, but you won't find resolution settings, levels of detail, or anything like that on the settings screen.
Sound - Original grungy techno music with a heavy beat infuses each level, encouraging the frantic action present in every level of the game. Sound effects are mostly good, with a few different gun sounds and suitably booming explosions. There is an odd beep, like the sound of a pinball bumper, that feels a bit out of place when you collect items, but overall sound is good.
Gameplay - Void Raiders is a frantic twin-stick shooter, with WASD for movement and mouse for aiming your character's gun and shooting, but unfortunately it doesn't yet support controllers (although that is a planned enhancement). You choose one of three characters, who all start out feeling pretty similar, and on each level you race around like a nutter blasting at anything that moves while you collect objectives and try to reach the elevator marking the end of the level.
Enemies respawn frequently enough that you'll typically run out of ammo if you just try to stay still, so the game keeps you moving constantly, dodging incoming fire, evading melee enemies, and raining death around you. Enemies sometimes drop health, ammo, or cash. The first two simply top up your ailing health bar or increase your ammo reserves, respectively, while the third adds to your cash stash, enabling you to buy upgrades that increase statistics, or add some other beneficial effect. I think I've seen about a dozen such upgrades, but I don't know how many there are in total.
You can choose from one of three characters when you begin, and when you die (which will happen frequently), you can either continue on with your previous character (minus upgrades) or you can return to the Lone Invader Tavern and start again with someone else. The tavern also lets you spend skill points, earned through levelling up each of the three characters, on various skills and bonuses from each character's skill tree.
There's no tutorial for the game and instructions are minimal, so you may have trouble getting into it. Once you get the hang of it, though, and you've upgraded a character a couple of times, the game really starts to shine.
Pros:
+ Great atmosphere
+ Great pixel graphics
+ Good soundtrack: both music and sound effects
+ It's grindy, but it's fun grindy, due to the lasting character progression
+ Different characters evolve to be significantly different to play after spending a few skill points, increasing replayability
+ Achievements
Cons:
- Only three characters, although there may be more coming
- There's no story or introduction provided, so the characters' goals are completely unknown
- It gets a bit repetitive; would be great with some more added goals or even character development side quests
- Achievements seem to be a bit bugged, with some of the "Complete xxx level" achievements not always unlocking
- Terrible quality writing for the in-game text (e.g. "ADD A DROP OF LEVANDAR TO YOUR BATH", or "ON NEPTUNE NOONE CARES YOU SCREAM", or the level called "MOANSTERY")
- Still a few small interface issues, such as opening up the options menu when you have a character open in the tavern, or the tooltips being partially hidden by the mouse pointer (see screenshot in my profile)
Void Raiders is a quality rogue-like shooter that, to me, is what Early Access should be all about. The core game is completed, and there's obviously been some fine tuning already performed, and a lot of effort and love put into it. It still needs more content and a bit more polish to really shine, but even as it is now in Early Access, I see no reason to not strongly recommend it. It's a fantastic, fun game.

Bliss.          Combine smash hit games Nuclear Throne and Risk of Rain and you get Void Raiders. There are two excellent systems at play that make this game work. First you have the temporary character upgrades/pickups during the gameplay. You are able to purchase one of three upgrades between randomly generated levels and these stay with you until you die. They are pickups such as a thorn halo that hurts enemies close to you or an increased critical chance. These are welcome but incremental, almost anemic, upgrades. They help once you stack 5 or more of each but initially they won't do you much good.
The second system that makes this game work is the permanent character progression. You start with 3 selectable characters and as you play with each they level up. Upon levelling up they get skill points that you can apply to two different skill trees for each character. These are serious improvements and you will likely die a lot at first with each new character. However, once you apply 2 or 3 skill points your character becomes a death-dealing, apocalypse wielding, mayhem spitting machine. To take it one step further for you progression junkies, there are 3 equipment upgrades as well. While beating levels you will earn four different resources and each hardware upgrade uses 2 different, very rare, resources. This will likely be the slowest upgrade path and it seems to be an odd choice at this point given that they appear to be fairly week changes.
This is early access though and the game isn't without it's potential improvements. To be a true classic it needs to tighten up the controls/responses. A real SHMUP needs lightning fast movement and tight controls. The game currently is a little swimmy and the shooting feels off, inaccurate. That might be due to the impossible cursor/aimpoint that is lost in the oversaturated graphics. I'm not a graphics snob and I love pixel art as much as the next guy but I find the lighting, color choice and minimalist art to hurt the experience a little. At the same time the individual art is charming at times and shows real talent. I just think the art direction could benefit from more consistent style and a little more restraint on light effects.
