I got this game gifted to me and decided to try it (I also had the option of using it in a group giveaway) because the concept looked interesting to me. At first, I wanted to wait until more time had passed before doing this review, but I really don't see much potential here.
If you like RPG-based management of mercenary heroes and your own village, you might like this game. More likely, however, you won't.
The aesthetics are okay - very simple, blocky graphics that remind me of games you could easily find on gaming websites like Kongregate and Newgrounds. The music is decent, but can and will get annoying fairly quickly.
The controls are easy - lots of clicking on menus extremely remniscent of Game Dev Tycoon (GDT). Many reviews for this game point Game Dev Tycoon as a source of inspiration for this game, however, you could honestly think of this as a much weaker, boring attempt to pay homage to GDT. There isn't really a tutorial function, but everything is pretty straightforward. For some strange reason, dirt roads are very expensive to make (not cost-efficient at all), so DO NOT make any. They don't really seem to do anything either. The learning curve is minimal, but wonky. There are combinations you can do when sending your heroes on missions - for example, certain villages prefer certain missions, and every mission requires you to select "attributes" to put your skill points into (ala GDT).
Mission example: when you send your hero on a supply run for village x, you can decide to put a few points in horses (seems to speed up mission completion time), weapons, food, and conduct (seems to do absolutely nothing). Or, you can choose to allocate points to bravado, to scouting, stealth, and aggression. Depending on how "compatible" your mission, selected village, and allocated points are, you will accumulate points in "loot," "influence," and "damage" (again, ala GDT).
The higher your loot value, the more llikely you are to receive items (ex: weapons, shields). You can sell these all at once or equip them to your heroes (they can only equip one item at a time) for stat boosts. Influence and damage values affect how many followers you will receive/lose after mission completion. I think followers add to your money-generated-over-time, which comes from things like potions being sold at an alchemy store. You also gain renown after completing missions, which is used in combination with gold to purchase building upgrades like more buildings (many features are incomplete or locked at the moment).
During missions, you will be presented with 3 scenarios (they are always the same) where you must select a "strategy" for your hero to use (ex: be confrontational, talk your way through, or work around it. Again, depending on what you choose and its compatibility with your selected mission, you will gain points in the 3 main mission counters (loot, influence, damage).
This game is clearly in early, early access, and I strongly recommend you do not get this (or at least wait until it's released as a finished product). You cannot sell items once you decide to keep them (the sell option is grayed out, so you have to pick "sell" right when you complete a mission and are shownn the loot screen if you want extra gold). You can find new villages and missions with the "explore" option, but it just unlocks more boring, tedious artificial-game-lengtheners.
Honestly, if you want to play a game like this, I STRONGLY suggest you turn away and pick up Game Dev Tycoon instead.That game at least has a lot of variety and aesthetics for you to enjoy.
At least for now, wait to see how this develops (if you are really, really interested). Even if you are dying to try this, I implore you to wait until it is out of early access.
Do not recommend.
Cheers,

Overall, Warframe is an amazing game. Not just an amazing free game but of any game. I'd easily shell out 60$ if I had to to play this game. But what specifically do I like so much about this game? I've made a brief list of the major pros and cons of the game and you'll see why.
Pros
*Gameplay is fun and doesn't get repetitive thanks to the huge arsenal of different frames and weapons
*Fun to play with friends and supports up to four players in a group
*High quality and stylised graphics
*FREE!
*Events and relics help to distract from some necessary grinding but even without them grinding is not a big deal as it's fairly easy to obtain any necessary materials aside from possibly ones from the void
Cons
*Story is fairly boring in my opinion but is also completely optional as in you can do those missions but ignore any story relevance they may contain and just continue to progress
*There is grinding but as I previously mentioned I didn't mind
*Music wasn't memorable at all which is kinda a shame because the sound design for everything else is fairly decent
*There are times where I got confused but this can be fixed simply by looking at the wiki or asking the community (who are all extremely nice and helpful)
In conclusion, as a free game I'd give warframe a 10/10. Comparing it to all games I'd probably still give it an 8.5 or 9/10 just because the major drawbacks of this game either didn't personally bother me that much or could be fixed with simple solutions. I hope this was helpful to anyone on the fence about trying Warframe! See you in there Tenno!

Compared to newer entries in the Trials series, Trials 2 feels incredibly dated. Its lack of polish, unrefined and floaty physics, and just general quality-of-life features show just how far RedLynx have come over the years. This is a very barebones game, but it was necessary for the devs to get to the point that they're at now. As it stands, this is a decently fun little time-waster, but the Miniclip sponsorship signs in the background show you exactly what kind of mindset you should approach this with.
Overall, I recommend skipping this version and picking up Trials Evolution or Fusion instead. Or, you could even play their mobile app, which is also very good.

I guess it's time for my review!
Stability / Polishing / Performance:
The game is not crazily polished, but it works well and has no major bugs as far as I was able to tell.
It's performance is compared to other games rather underwhelming, but it should work on most systems.
Graphics:
The graphics aren't all that great.
The texture resolution is good, the overall quality of the textures is also fine.
But when it comes to complex lighting effects the game doesn't necessarily match today's industry standards.
However it doesn't look "ugly".
Gameplay:
The game is very detailed when it comes to the controls.
The physics aren't so bad given it's not aiming for damage models or any fancy stuff.
It shows it's muscles when it comes to simulating a lively AI driven traffic world.
Eventhough the AI sometimes acts outrageously stupid, there are few games one could compare this game with, but I'd dare to say the AI here is still the smartest, given that (nearly) no other game tries to accurately simulate normal every-day traffic! (even GTA with a much higher budget has NPCs blowing each other up just by accident - this doen't happen here)
The game also has a little background simulation going on for the player's company, which I'd like to recommend to focus on in later titles, since it shows some potential in my opinion.
Models / Game World:
The truck models are very detailed and look nicely, if you don't look too closely at the big headlights you can mount at the bumper and the roof of your truck (those have just a plain texture).
The AI cars don't look too shabby either.
The game world itself is a little lack-luster.
Eventhough they made great improvements compared to the previous title, it's still partially in medieval-ages of game development with sprite-based distant flora and some simplistic general design.
Cities don't consist of much more than a few steets.
However I believe the game has something to it.
You could consider it to be one of those "zen" games that you can just use to relax while playing.
It has a progress system, a (downloadable) multiplayer and steam workshop support, which already addresses a whole bunch of the previous critique and if you feel adventurous, you should look around on the internet, there are plenty more other mods that address even more things of the game - I believe there's even one or two complete game world replacers   and add-ons out there.
It is a game about filling up bars, and when you fill all the bars, you win!

Playing Trials 2 is like going to a restaurant, and ordering the chili.
First, you're impressed.  It's pretty good!  The meat is tender, the onions and beans are flavorful, the broth is robust.
Then, the cook comes out and adds some Cayenne pepper, to give it just a little spice.  Superb!  Well done!
And then the cook comes out again and adds some more Cayenne pepper.  Well, I mean... why?  It's quite good the way it is.  You can still taste the other ingredients, and it's not bad, but things are kind of getting overwhelmed by the spice.
And then the cook comes out once more and dumps a gallon if Cayenne pepper into your dish.  Now you're irritated, but you know there's good chili in there, right?  You take a bite, and try to ignore the spiciness, but even when you find a great big chunk of meat or something, all you can taste is spice.  Spice, spice, spice.
Difficulty is good in a game.  A little spice is more than nice.  But when your game's gimmick is that it gets so difficult that you can no longer taste the enjoyable stuff, well... what's the point?  Who wants to eat THAT dish?
A bad chef is one who sucks at chili.  An unforgivable chef is one who ruins good chili.  The same goes for game devs - good game, ruined because some idiot was all like "XTREEEEEEEM MEANS HARD, RIGHT?"  I will not be purchasing any games by Red Lynx again.

A worthy sequel of Mass Effect.
This game has much more humour in it. Many new, great and diverse characters (and old ones too). I really liked their interesting and rich backstories.
More side-quests.
All environments are different and more varied compared to the first Mass Effect.
There are no inventory or item drops. You just upgrade the core items (sniper, heavy pistol, heavy weapon, shotgun, assault rifle, submachine gun) with the modifications you find in missions or stores. [Enemies only drop ammo]
The action is more fun and varied.
The main story is not on the same "wow" level as the first Mass Effect tho. Just a few plot twists here and there. But still, it fills many gaps that were left after the first Mass Effect and expands on it.
The only thing I didn't like in this game was a simple and annoying bug (It made me press F5 much more often, because I really didn't want to replay the same things if something went wrong). Your controllable character tends to get stuck above objects. You never know when this will happen. I just learned to avoid walking/running near the edges of objects... But still... very annoying. Especially during missions.
And a tip:
if you want to unlock the framerates and get rid of the harsh/pitch black/dark shadows, paste this in your GamerSettings.ini file.
You can find the file here: C:\Users\%username%\Documents\BioWare\Mass Effect 2\BIOGame\Config\GamerSettings.ini
Just finished Mass Effect 3. What an awesome last game of this trilogy. Really recommend to get it on Origin. You will not be disappointed at all.
The very first minutes will make you say: "oh crap, the sh|t just got real!".
The animations and gameplay are much more fluid and responsive than in Mass Effect 2. The sound effects and the massiveness of the enemies/surroundings leaves you in awe.
The graphics improved too. Weather effects (storms, rain, dust, etc.) are gorgeous.
I think this game has the best dialogues between the characters in the series. There are so many good and funny remarks/situations.
Didn't experience any game breaking bugs or crashes. Just some tiny glitches, but nothing bad really.
I don't know why the ending was so criticized by the media and players.., I really liked it (just don't shoot anything at the very end, just a tip ^^).
What an awesome trilogy. One of the best games you can experience to this date.

Changing to Negative, after waiting months with no improvements beyond more land, that offers no real extra purpose other than to gather different materials solely for building. At this point, if you have played other survival games, this is the same, where 90% of your content, focus, and progressional goals are aimed at building.
As this game is a Funcom game, you can expect it to be much less than it would be in the hands of a more skilled company, a company that is better at understanding the desires of gamers, and understands "fun" a bit better. There are a few key points that you would hope are improved upon greatly here, in order to make it stand out from the rest, but 6 months in and the hope is fading fast (referencing combat & exploration). As it stands, there is no purpose to explore, and it doesn't take long to see it all once, as the map is rather small. Combat is still super basic, and shields still can't take more than a few hits. The A.I is still as derpy as ever too.
There is no taming (yet), and instead they have thralls. They are passive NPC's placed on workstations to improve crafting speeds, lower resource consumption, or a few let you craft extra stuff. Again, the only real purpose here is to further enhance building, by making it faster. Other than that, you are in a primitive world that is rather small. As you have to run on foot, you can cover most of the world in 10 minutes of running.
Thralls are knocked out with a club, brought home, and turned into slaves. There are different occupations for them that allow benefits such as reduced materials cost on crafting or increased crafting speed, or for other purposes such as entertainment and removing that corruption debuff. There are different levels to a thrall, currently ranging from 1-3, and legendary versions. Some also provide the ability to craft unique weapons that you can't otherwise.
There is a lot of balancing that needs to be done. A prime example is arrows, it takes a lot of materials just to make 10 higher level arrows, or for an extremely cheap cost, arrows that are almost as good can be made via the Set Religion. The same can be said for healing potions which take 10 aloe plants currently for 1 potion, or 1 harvested human piece for 1 potion of similar strength through the Mitra Religion which is much easier. Some upgraded armor is nearly worthless when comparing the cost difference between a lower version. It takes 300+ arrows to kill a black rhino, of course you can't fight him in melee doing that, so you sit on a ledge for 10 minutes shooting him.
Oh, arrows also suddenly don't shoot, consuming your arrows. This issue persists as you keep swapping between weapons each time to fire a single arrow, or relog to fix.
The adventure component is neat, the caves/dungeons/zones with corruption will be one of the most interesting elements if they are enhanced upon. Currently there aren't many or they don't serve much purpose, but they offer great potential (key word being potential, this is looking doubtful). The map size isn't all that large, so hopefully it will be greatly increased with lots of those mentioned corruption zones incorporated (but based on the Northern expansion, this is looking to be false). For now, much of your time will consist of leveling, which most people just do in a single large village as that offers the best EXP. If you aren't leveling, you may be out exploring for a while, although this won't last super long. The rest of the time is spent hunting those thralls like a Pokemon or building.
One of my favorite things to do in a survival game is building. Immediately I could see that the building flexibility are far more user friendly than say, Ark. Using the mousewheel allows you to turn objects with ease or cycle placement, and if you hold shift + mousewheel, you can even raise/lower the height of what you are placing (assuming it isn't a snappable). There are some bugs with this current free placement at times, and my only complaint is that gates use 3 foundation spaces rather than 2 or 4. This is a key piece of info to consider if you are making a symmetrical base as it was a bit late for me. Those who enjoy decorating will appreciate that there are more than 5 pieces of interior decor, such as carpeting, furniture, tapestry, flags, and some other bits.
We are still missing triangular roofing though, and glass tier stuff (despite glass being in-game). The building stuff looks decent though, the primary positive I will award it. However, we have dyes now and still aren't able to paint our buildings, that is a big problem.
Combat is the other prime staple many will wonder about. Right now it is a somewhat simple hack and slash. Shields break too quick against melee to be functionable but are great at blocking projectiles. The dodging system needs some work to be more reliable. For the most part you will circle an enemy while whacking it or sidestep while shooting. There is great potential for more in-depth combat later though which could really make this game shine, but at this point, it is rather unexciting as there are better combat based games.
To make this worse, the A.I remains derpy since 6 months, with next to no improvement as animals and NPC's teleport around on screen, and you are suddenly dead from melee hits when they weren't near you.
I don't recommend it as it is a Funcom game, and they are proving to really screw everything over (applicable to all their games). They make one poor decision after another, don't know what players want (We got trebuchets instead of taming / settlement system / purge.. trebuchets are useless to all PvE players, while the others would be for all). We also got 50 emotes, why that was a priority over real content, who knows?
As it stands, the game lacks content worthwhile. We are about 6 months in out of the 12 month EA period forecasted by Funcom, and it isn't looking good in terms of content. We got a bit more land to explore, and more stuff to craft for building, but no real content that would make you actively explore dungeons, or have any sort of end-game focus. Comparing it to ARK briefly, there is nothing like end-game bosses that have an important purpose, or taming that consumes your time, or anything else really. You can go level up, and build. To give credit, their building stuff does look decent, but we have dyes & no way to paint them, so that is a problem.
Personal experience score: 3/10
Story: N/A/10 - There are several bits of lore and a few bits of exploration based lore. Much is still a work in progress with some NPC's set up for an artifact collection system down the road, whether it actually makes it in is the question
Sound: 4/10 - It needs more atmospheric music and there are audio bugs to work out such as the sound cutting out briefly constantly.
Graphics: 6/10 - They look good and a bit different, definitely not realistic. The images in the photos were most likely done using enhancements or Nvidia Ansel. There is a strange ghosting effect currently occuring of all objects when moving, from weapons to landscape.
The new northern content is heavily unoptimized though, where you can run ultra @ 40fps in the desert with a 960, you can run medium @ 25 fps in the north.
Controls: 6/10 - Simple and nothing complicated, the method for dodging could use a bit of work and there are some bugs to work out with what you are currently holding not swinging or the long stall after switching weapons at times. Archery needs some work too as the arrows aren't working as they should, and simply don't fire. Most of the issues are just bugs currently
Game Length: 5/10 - You end up realizing all you are doing is leveling to build a better house, no other real reason to play.

I'd really like to congratulate the development team on their successful execution of creating a true successor to the Dungeon Keeper franchise. This game has all the loveable bits of the old Dungeon Keeper games:  creative uses of units; unique storytelling with compelling voice actors; well-balanced encounters; immersive, stylistic graphics; and several modes of gameplay outside of the campaign.
So much of the game manages to be nostalgic and novel at the same time, as old favorites find themselves repackaged with new mechanics. Classic rooms like the Prison and Torture Chamber synergize in new ways, as you now not only have the option of just converting captured units to your team, but you can use captured units to spawn a spirit that will scout and clear the fog of war, or you can use that same spirit to confer experience to your own units. Don't want to even use the Torture rack? Well, now you can use a spell to turn captives into gold--that's right, you can directly monetize a successful KO!
Back in Dungeon Keeper, my least favorite room was the Guard Post, but WFTO provides a Garrison instead. Units can be asked to keep there, but WFTO implements a stat boost for fortifications and defenses within the area of an active Garrison. So, even if a unit isn't standing watch, it provides a massive stat-boost to your basic defenses, so, for me, it's one of my go-to rooms any time I need to leave traps to watch a space.
There are huge improvements to the overall mechanics of Dungeon Keeper II, particularly when it comes to passively leveling your creatures. Rooms do not place direct limits on what level a minion can reach, instead, a minion can train as much as they want, but there are diminishing returns on their training investment as they level up. The Training Room, now rebranded as a Barracks, no longer has a gold-per-xp charge, so passive training is free but time consuming. To skirt this cost in DKII, it was common to build a Combat Pit exclusively and drop units in, wait for them to KO, then wait for an Imp to drag them back. Instead, now units that are KO'd in the pit simply respawn on the edge of the Arena and walk back to bed--no more micro-managing Imps to make sure your level 9 minion doesn't die because the AI failed.
Another significant change that stands out is the use of wall space. DKII incentivized forethought in room placement by providing additional use-props (torture wheels; training dummies; casino games) on the wallspace. WFTO breaks from this however, meaning there's no loss for failing to construct a room with all four sides--which is great for those moments where you accidentally dig into some, pock-marked terrain--but there's also no explicit reward for carefully considering how you're going to place room X versus room Y (implicit rewards are, for example, increased defensability).
Overall, I'd say that if you loved DKII, you're going to love WFTO. The experience may not be entirely bug free--cinematics for the first campaign did not seem to flow, animate, or transition correctly for me; I ran into a bug with the Aum on level 7 of the regular campaign, where the level just wouldn't end (fixed by restarting level); and I regularly ran into the stutter-bug at high dungeon populations (fixed by Saving the game, actually; I don't know why this consistenly helped)--but the frequency with which these problems happen is low enough that it's not going to affect the outcome of your playthrough, and their offense is so minor in comparison to the extent of the accomplishment that, when you walk away, you're not even thinking about them.
WFTO is not only a successful successor (*sunglasses emoji*), it's an improvement over the original, hands down.

Set In a distant future dominated by conflict following the collapse of a vast solar empire, you are a Tenno and the power of the Warframes is at your command. Warframe is a fast paced action shooter with a wide array of weapons and characters creating diverse play styles to explore. From the moment you are set free by a mysterous persona known as the Lotus and told to escape the clutches of an militaristic authoritarian faction known as the Grineer you are immersed in a complicated geopolitical landscape which spans from the savage beauty of Earth to the frozen wastes of Pluto. Everyone has an agenda, what is yours?
Hidden threats and challenges await players who seek them out, scripted boss encounters, world changing events, deadly bounty hunters will impede your exploration. As your understanding about this universe grows, rich story based missions will reveal secrets and hidden dangers you had yet to discover. These missions feature cinematic cut scenes, character development along with new gameplay elements for players to master and put to use against their foes. Warframe features a wide arsenel with hundreds of weapons and dozens of character classes to explore and an expansive drop, crafting and resource system to learn and utilise.
Players can customise their character and weapon power level through a Mod system. Mods are cards with statistical changes that alter or add to the base permamters of the item they are placed in. Mods can be obtained from drops from defeated enemies, through mission rewards or from factions. Mods are reusuable and level up when fused with a resource known as Endo enhancing thier statistical properties even more but at an increased cost of power drain. Being careful with your equipment's limit power is a challenge to be overcome with experience as you try to maximise your potential. With a limited number of Mod slots and a finite Energy Pool available players will have to learn to make sacrifices as they gain a wider collection of Mods to choose from, the rarest and most powerful requiring serious commitment to seek out and obtain.
Since its launch in 2013 Warframe developers Digital Extremes have applied 22 major updates to the game, and hundreds of smaller content patches and fixes. Adding new environments to explore, new mission types to participate in, new game play mechanics to learn they have continued to challenge themselves by expanding the game into bold new directions but always with a message of continued future commitment to polish and refine the game.
As a free to play game it isn't surprising that Warframe has a Market and a Microtransaction currency. What is suprising is how largely fair the system is. The Market place is filled with items that can be purchased immediately with real money via a currency known as Platinum. However blueprints to craft much of this equipment can be purchased with Credits, an in-game currency earned by playing the game. Requiring components or materials available from playing and sometimes coming with a heavy time to craft these Blueprints are a primary source of obtaining new equipment for all players. Most non-craftable purchases are non-essential cosmetic based, or boosters that speed up acquisition of experience and resources. The only outlier seems to be slots for equipment (Weapons, Warframes and Comapions). With a limited number of slots to start with, newer players who put in enough time might find they quickly run out available slots to store equipment. You can always sell equipment you don't care for, but a new player might feel obligated to purchase Platinum to expand their arsenal size. A dedicated player can circumvent this by learning to harness the power of the Player Trade economy, that enables one player to trade Platinum to another player for a items. Equipment slots are some of the cheapest purchases available from the Market, making it relatively easy to obtain enough Platinum from trading to purchase more slots. The fact remains though that this Platinum needed to enter the system from the purchase made by another player in the first place. The overall experience of Warframe is not diminished by the Microtransaction system however it may seem unfair or slow for an inexperienced player who has not yet grasped the strength of trading.

Once referred to as "an art game before art games," by IGN, Jet Set Radio holds a special place in my blood-pumping chest organ.
A cult classic with colorful cel-shaded graphics, set in a delightfully Japanese Dreamcast-era overworld.
You're a roller-blading gang of misfits who spray graffiti on the walls of a neo-Tokyo to stick it to the establishment. 'The establishment' being SWAT teams, helicopters and trained assassins who are out to murder you, punk. A ridiculous, unforgettable concept with an unforgettable OST by Hideki Naganuma to match (one of my favorites of all time).
The gameplay is simple and accessible, and the level design compliments the series staples like wall rides and rail grinds usually well; players with experience will get the most out of the world. Nothing groundbreaking. There isn't much difficulty, the story is exactly as shallow as you might expect, and the mechanics are short of anything great, but I've always found all its shortcomings forgivable. JSR was never mechanically amazing, it just has a lot of style. Unsurprisingly, it's a Sega game.
I'd imagine Jet Set Radio wasn't remade to fix control bugs (although it does hammer out a few) or to revamp the levels; it was remade because people fell in love with its music and artstyle. It's pretty hugely inspiring in terms of how soulful a game can be. Controls can be sluggish and jumps can be difficult due to poor rail/platform placement, but the spirit that this game shoves in your face is unrivaled. Where else will you hear the line, "we're riding high on a smooth stream of supersonic sounds!"?
This game is as much a statement as it is a piece of entertainment; the hella funky rebellious mischief we all need a part of.
I won't tell you to play it, but I will tell you that it's the most radical game you'll ever miss.

I must say that Tin Star must be one of the most story-rich, narrative driven games that i've ever had the pleasure of playing in recent years. An all without graphics, or sound! That really says something. To tell the truth, i hadn't played an interactive novels before this one, and from now on, i'm comparing every one that i DO play to Tin Star, why? because of the narrative, that's why. In an interactive novel such as this one, especially without graphics or sound, you have to hold the players attention in some way. If you don't, than you've failed a designing the game. However, Tin Star had me hooked all the way from the begining to the end. The writer, Allen Gies has immense talent for writing, and i commend his work. The style in which he delivers each new situation is always engaging, though sometimes feels a bit forced. And with that, let's get into the very few flaws of the game. First of all, the characters. Now, don't get me wrong, I loved the characters in Tin Star. They were very well writen and had diversity, but, their character buildup is very steriotypical. For instance, you've got the stoic cowboy, the renegade gunslinger, the eccentric prospecter, etc. However, like i said before, the way in which they were written makes up for it. The spelling could use some correction, but that's just more nitpicking than anything. And lastly, the ending. The ending feels really forced, and afterwards, you are presented with a lengthey epilouge that tell you what your character did after the ending, instead of letting you play it yourself. I can understand this for the other characters, but for the protagonist, it doesn't make sense to me. One of the negatives to having a simple, white canvas to write a story on is that your eyes start to get annoyed if you look at it for too long. Tin Star has the same problem. When i'm playing a game, i want to be told an engaging and thrilling story. Not be blinded. People with sensetive eyes will not enjoy the experience. I suggest switching to a more eye-freindly backdrop like dark blue, or something. Unfortunatley, ther's no way to change this yourself. And those are really all the negatives. Most of them are really nit-picky things, but negatives nonetheless. Every game has them. All in all, I really reccomend that you try this game. Especially if you want to be told an engaging story with many branching paths. I will definetly be trying more CYOA games, and Zombie Exodus is next!

"Somewhere in Asia, there is a city that cannot be found on any map called
Tokyo-to, but everyone just calls it Tokyo. The two hottest thing on the
streets of Tokyo-to are the punks wearing magnetically-driven in-line skates
powered by newly developed netrium batteries, and Jet Set Radio, a pirate
radio station manned by the DJ, Professor K, that plays nothing but non-stop,
hardcore music."
Probably one of the many hidden gems found on Steam, with a cheap price of £3 I went into this game with nothing to lose and none of the nostalgia of playing the original version. Within the first minute I found myself pleasantly surprised at how well it the themes of the game was explained and executed. The introduction cut scene quoted above highlights the key features of the game from the get-go; in-line skating and music, combine these two with the tough streets of Tokyo-To, it's interesting characters and its never ending struggle of territory through graffiti tagging between the resident street punks known as "rudies" and you get a refreshing story with an insane amount of replayability.
Gameplay
The city of Tokyo-To is spilt into three areas where each gang located in their specified area, allowing three short and rather quirky before a more serious and sinister main plotline is revealed. Most levels will have you spraying graffiti at specified locations in a given area while an unfriendly police force are constantly trying to take you out and rid the streets of the rudies. As you tag more places, the opposition will become more agressive in stopping you, so you might want to plan at which points might be risky to tag once the tanks, helicopters (and even trained assassins) decied to step in. Minor gamemodes are implimented in order to get a variety of play throughout the streets. All levels are timed so you want to score huge points through speed, tricks and graffiti in order to get a better ranking and unlock certain secrets.
The music is what really what hooks you into the game, probably the finest i've ever seen in a video game, it includes songs  from J-pop, hip hop, funk, electronic dance music, rock music, acid jazz, trip hop. Inlcuding some well known songs from american artists as you leave Tokyo-To and enter what is essentially New York. Its something you need to hear for yourself in-game or even on Youtube.
Mechanics
The stats are pretty simple only having three which detetermine health, skills as a skater and how hard it is to perform actions to tag areas (which will earn more points.) Having said that there is a huge roster for you to unlock and try out to see which specific stats suits you best. Tagging a place requires spray cans which can be found anywhere around the level, this comes with a varing limit depending on what character you have chosen and you will definetly want to carry as much as you can or else you will find yourself wasting time.
The weight and feel of the game is fairly well made as you are always in control of your character as they jump and grind, allowing you to master movement quickly and focus more on the actual game. Performing tricks was a bit of a turn-off for a few people as it is all automatic jumping on a rail or wall will iniciate a form of grind, grind tricks are done by staying on the rail, grinding air tricks are performed simply by jumping at a fast enough speed and half pipe tricks require you to jump at the right point. This was primarily a concern as people (inluding me) compared this to its sequel Jet Set Radio Future, which was more engaging when doing tricks.
The game has a really nice cel shaded which gives off comical and colourful environments which are easy on the eyes and is a nifty technique to get a good looking game without sacrificing those precious framerates, therefore the system requirements is fairly low compared to other dreamcast ports.
Seeing a game as good as this so cheap might be because of the fact that not many people know this and I highly suggest you try it out, you will not be dissapointed.

If you care about the amount of gameplay you get for your money at all, this game probably rates higher than any other game. (Last I read, the
player had over 500 hours on this game.)
Crusader Kings II is a strategic game where you spend most of your time looking at a big map of Europe cut into little counties, but it is
different from a game like Medieval II: Total War.  Whereas in those games, every nation had rigid boundaries and an entire nation was a distinct, unified entity, Crusader Kings II focuses upon the feudal system of governance, and especially its hereditary system of succession.
You are not a nation, you are an extended family through the ages.  You may start as King of England, but lose the throne in a succession war, only to wind up inheriting the Kingdom of France, instead.  It is a game of political machinations more than warfare.
You can't just declare war whenever you want to, you need to, by hook or by crook, manage to get a claim to that land you want to invade.  Battles are relatively quick and hands-off (play that Total War if you want to manage the troops directly) but it's the space between wars that makes the game interesting.  To get that claim, you probably need to find some way to get the princess of that land in your bed (or your son's bed), and it's this medieval bloodline plotting that make up the meat of the game.
For that matter, you don't necessarily need to declare war to gain land - just marry into the family that succeeds a throne, and make sure that, one way or the other, your chosen heir also manages to be the chosen heir of a target kingdom, and the kingdoms will be unified upon the death of your current character and the current king of the target land.
Likewise, just because you gain land doesn't mean you can keep it.  You need to delegate land out, and succession laws can fragment your kingdom so much that you see hard-conquered lands slip out of your grasp by inheritence without your consent.  EDIT: And since writing this, Conclave has come out to add complexities to keeping your nobles in line.
Worse, while whomever you give land will be quite grateful for the first 20 years of their rule or so, their children will have no gratitude for the gift of land your father gave them, and will likely be burning with ambitions you have to keep in check.  Every few decades, your character ages and dies, and succession wars and civil wars are the primary way the game keeps your over-arching ambitions in check.  Rather than letting a large empire mean that no external threat can challenge you, and no internal threats exist, the larger you become, the less vulnerable you are to external threats, but the more vulnerable you are to internal ones. You spend more and more time trying to find a way to bludgeon the rebellious nobles and religious minorities into line.
If you get tired of games of Total War, and don't bother completing them because, once you are the strongest power on the map, there's nothing to do but steamroll everything else that stands in your path, then CK2 is a great remedy to this.  (You can still make a world-spanning super-empire, but it's much more interesting to try to keep it when the owners of that land still fight you when you plant your flag there than to just have them mutely pay taxes to you and have assumed loyalty to your cause.)
It's a game that's just hard and realistic enough to make the things you do actually feel like you're thumbing your nose at history.  You can play an Irish earl, rise to High King of Ireland, and conquer England.  Or play as the West Africans, and conquer the Muslims and convert them to your pagan faith.  Being a norse viking that captures the pope and sacrifices him to Odin is always fun.  (And nabs the Holy Smoke! achievement.) And if you do it with an unbroken line of Viking empresses, all the better.
Mods are also a high point: Play the Elder Kings mod, based upon the Elder Scrolls, and conquer Cyrodiil and beyond as an immortal or vampire, using magicks to summong hordes of demons when under threat. There's an A Game of Thrones mod, as well, and mods to turn the game into something like a space 4X game.
DLC still comes out for the game, as well.  While more than a little annoying to be nickled and dimed, the trickle of new content keeps the game fresh and new achievements are meaningful challenges, requiring players to take up historic underdogs to rise to glory.  Getting a full board of achievements is extraordinarily difficult, but enjoyable for the challenge they provide.  Compare this to Activision, Ubisoft, or EA, where you buy iterations of the same game every year, and throwing down $10 for another year's worth of life in a game is well worth the price.

I didn't realise that classic adventure games could be so immersive! I enjoyed latest Telltale work, but I would hardly place them in adventure genre. Gemini Rue on the other hand is a real classic point-and-click adventure game, though you could say that the biggest flaws and offenders of the genre were left out. You won't find any illogical obstacles and puzzles, pixel hunting or absurd item combining.
What you get is a great sci-fi noiresque story, where you are a detective looking for his lost brother on some god-forgotten planet. Later the game opens up and lets you switch between the two main characters, the detective and the missing brother. It really does feel like you're detective, getting dirty and doing the groundwork: asking around, getting true identity of people, searching information about them in database. Top this with action sequences where you can cover and shoot at your enemies and you really get an exceptional adventure game. Voice acting and writing is astounding and the story itself is intriguing and suprising. All of that in a indie game made by the handful of people! I did enjoy the visual style of the game and I think it befits the game, but I guess some people could argue that the resolution is too low.
Overall, superb game, highly recommended. A great reminder that the adventure games are a great way to tell a story and don't have to be obscure and plagued with bizzare puzzles.

Gemini Rue's a cyberpunk-noir point-and-click adventure game in the style of Lucasarts' classic catalogue.
It's well-written, features a couple of standout voice performances--I particularly enjoy Azriel--and almost none of the cringeworthy, "developer's brother's friend in a closet" stuff you might expect from what was formerly a student project. You'll see some of the plot coming before it does, but the game raises some decent, Intro to Philosophy-level discussion material about what makes us all human.
The pixel backgrounds are gorgeous, and the soundtrack's apes Vangelis' Blade Runner score in all the right ways. Moody saxaphones back up Azriel's rain-soaked journey into his past; clinical synths bounce and settle underneath Delta-Six's retraining in the mysterious Center 7. Everything comes together to form the atmosphere that is perhaps Gemini Rue's strongest asset.
Gameplay-wise, the puzzles feel good and about as hard as they should. The combat mini-game isn't a high point--though it's neither frustrating. If you're an old hand with adventure games, you'll probably clear this in 4-6 hours. At worst, 10.
Enjoy it as you would a good book over a couple of rainy afternoons.

Gemini Rue is a solid adventure game, probably the best one I've played in years.
It's well rooted in the point and click genre, but it uses a few mechanics that are a bit unual alongside the tried and true arsenal: a communicator which you can use to interact with other characters and/or computer terminals, a combat mini game (somewhat similar to the one found in the Indiana Jones series) and the ability to play with multiple characters. These are nothing new, but they are used well and break the monotony that sets in from hours of pointing and clicking.
The graphics are good (but the pixelated look may be a problem form some) and the art direction is great, there is little confusion about what to do, everything is cleverly hinted at. Sadly, this makes the puzzles seem a bit easy, but on the good side there are very few instances of pixel hunting and when is does get used it makes perfect sense in the context of the scenes.
The first part of the story is very good, I liked the mood and the mystery surrounding the events, sadly the big twist becomes apparent about halfway through the game and I kept hoping for something out of left field which never came.
Overall it was a good experience, with great music, great voice acting and a nice, although predictable, story.

I'm more reviewing my thoughts on the game than my personal experience since I haven't personally played it much. I originally saw this game from someone playing it on YouTube and it looked great, I think it was in beta back at the time.
It's a different take on the team deathmatch style of games, where everyone is just running around and shooting. This game is fun because it still has team deathmatch, capture the flag, or storm the base types of game modes, but the way fighting happens is different than most games. I'm sure by now you've seen that the game is fought with medieval weapons, like spears, bow and arrows, halberds and other large bladed sticks. Of course you're still running around killing people, but this feels so much more fun and different than most games, and the kills are more satisfying because you actually cut off people's arms, legs, or heads depending on the weapon and where you strike. Speaking of that, it's not just like you have a sword and you click a button and swing it, the angle you're facing/looking really do make a difference and the weapons swing in a way that makes sense, rather than just hitting whatever is directly in front of you.
Overall tons of fun to play/watch someone play, and if it's something you think you would like, it's worth getting.

A worthy sequel of Mass Effect.
This game has much more humour in it. Many new, great and diverse characters (and old ones too). I really liked their interesting and rich backstories.
More side-quests.
All environments are different and more varied compared to the first Mass Effect.
There are no inventory or item drops. You just upgrade the core items (sniper, heavy pistol, heavy weapon, shotgun, assault rifle, submachine gun) with the modifications you find in missions or stores. [Enemies only drop ammo]
The action is more fun and varied.
The main story is not on the same "wow" level as the first Mass Effect tho. Just a few plot twists here and there. But still, it fills many gaps that were left after the first Mass Effect and expands on it.
The only thing I didn't like in this game was a simple and annoying bug (It made me press F5 much more often, because I really didn't want to replay the same things if something went wrong). Your controllable character tends to get stuck above objects. You never know when this will happen. I just learned to avoid walking/running near the edges of objects... But still... very annoying. Especially during missions.
And a tip:
if you want to unlock the framerates and get rid of the harsh/pitch black/dark shadows, paste this in your GamerSettings.ini file.
You can find the file here: C:\Users\%username%\Documents\BioWare\Mass Effect 2\BIOGame\Config\GamerSettings.ini
Just finished Mass Effect 3. What an awesome last game of this trilogy. Really recommend to get it on Origin. You will not be disappointed at all.
The very first minutes will make you say: "oh crap, the sh|t just got real!".
The animations and gameplay are much more fluid and responsive than in Mass Effect 2. The sound effects and the massiveness of the enemies/surroundings leaves you in awe.
The graphics improved too. Weather effects (storms, rain, dust, etc.) are gorgeous.
I think this game has the best dialogues between the characters in the series. There are so many good and funny remarks/situations.
Didn't experience any game breaking bugs or crashes. Just some tiny glitches, but nothing bad really.
I don't know why the ending was so criticized by the media and players.., I really liked it (just don't shoot anything at the very end, just a tip ^^).
What an awesome trilogy. One of the best games you can experience to this date.

Being a sim/RTS hybrid sounds a little weird but that’s what it is. You don’t directly control your units, they control themselves. What you do is choose what kind of units are created and attract them with rewards. It’s a very neat concept and plays out pretty well (aside from the final level which is flap-jacking hard!). It has pretty slow pacing and suffers from the same RTS elements where you start each map at ground zero but if you enjoy either half its worth a go.

If you haven't played this game, or are on the ropes about tactical rpgs, so to speak, I would like to, admittedly, persuade you to give this game a shot. It's one of those games that comes about once in a few years, that scrubs away all of your distate of how modern "triple A" games *usually* are.
You are not just some outcast with no opinion, nothing to say who goes along with whatever everybody else is doing; you have a particular obligation to not only the people relying on you in the game, but your personality and persona as a whole. This world is dripping with ooze waiting for you to delve deeper and deeper into it. Will you stop the cycles of old-way religion, leaving the rest of the world to have the chance of repeating their behaviors? Or, perhaps, you might continue the perpetual divination of beings who are "destined" for greatness. P.S., there's *plenty* of grey areas here, folks.
While some might say the story is overwritten and verbose, I consider it a good thing to try to break the limits of storytelling. "Politics change, but stories, they never change." -Stephen King

I don't write many reviews, mostly because I give a very large margin for errors in a game.  However, this one has gone too far.
I understand this is early access, and this review is to tell anyone reading to NOT purchase it at this time.
Wait for the following at the very least:
1) They update their system specifications.  I'm running above their recommended and was still freezing up at random intervals at minimum graphics settings.  System specs are supposed to show what is needed to perform without dropping frames across all common instances.
2) They eliminate whatever unholy memory leak they've currently got.  Just on loading up, I'm noticing this thing eats twice as much resources as similarly-graphical games.  Over the course of my few-hour gaming session, this more than doubled, basically preventing anything else from running.
3) They fix their initial log-in cinematic.  Every bloody time I've tried to open this game, it plays that same, unskippable 2 minute cinematic.  Since windowed mode is also busted, I can't minimize or unfocus to cease hearing its repetitive lines.  I've resorted to taking off my headphones and walking away each time I've opened this game.
Sure, there's a bunch of critical balance issues as well, each of which effectively ruins the game for everyone new.  For example:
-Territories are extremely abusable, meaning new players have literally nowhere to build because some guy stuck a single block of foundation within some large radius.
-NPCs can break walls that players can't.
-Certain build strategies are literally impossible to raid.
-Players are capable of blocking spawnpoints, such as iron or thralls.
But I understand that early access means these are commonplace events.  What I cannot forgive is inadequate memory usage.  If you're on the fence or your machine is more than a year old, I recommend avoiding this game.

First off, let me say that this is NOT an Ark reskin. Too many people have gotten away with saying that.  Ark is a good game, don't get me wrong but the only thing they have in common is the engine that made em.  Before Ark came out, the survival genre was purely Zombie survial, but both games stepped out of this shell and are truly original survival games.
2 of the biggest let downs for the game for me is combat and a design that encourages you to play with groups so bad it makes it dann near impossible to be successful and be able to make/do everything solo.
The game has kept getting better since launch and what gives me hope and let's me know this game won't be in early access indefinetly is that the Devs have at least some credibility with previous releases and most of all, they listen to the players.  If players don't like something, they modify it.  If they mess up (like every game developer does) they address it and take care of it quick.
So yes, I recommend it. Is it perfect? Not yet, but I have faith in Funcom and I think you should too.
P.S. Funcom hit me up personally so we can discuss future plans for the game. :)

Oh boy yes do I reccomend this game. The Combat system is a clever mix of Third/First Person Shooting/Melee like Skyrim or Fallout with some Tab Combat like WoW when casting Mutations (Basically spells for healing, damage and support) so you can choose to simply ignore one play style over the other or use a mix of one. If you want to dual wield two, one handed melee weapons or guns then go for it, the game allows you to even use a one handed melee and gun at the same time, basically filling melee and range in one go.
BE AWARE though that the mouse buttons are backwards, to use the weapon in your right hand click the left mouse button and vice versa. I haven't found a way to fix this without it affecting interactions with the world so my advice is don't change it.
The only flaws are the sound and beginners confusion. I personally found the ambience quite annoying and the game is very quiet out of combat but I suppose you could call it relaxing.
At the beggining of the game you follow a simple tutorial dungeon (with good voice acting) and then you get to pick one of three starter locations that tailor to how you would like to play.
You have a few starter quests which thankfully come one at a time but when you leave that slice of starter land and head into town then you'll find there are lots of quests that need doing. They don't appear very cleatly on the mini map so look hard and you'll notice little hazard symbols like the desktop icon bare visible on the mini map. Those are quest icons.
I did notice that the starter areas seem to follow a similar story at first, just in a different landscape.
One thing that really confused me was Tradeskills. I'm sure once I devote more time to the game and decide what kind of character I want to be I'll understand it better.
If you want a nice little MMO that puts the best features of WoW and Fallout into one then have a go...

NOTE: This game is Free to Play, as a result of that fact, take this review and all others with a grain of salt as you can basically play it yourself, and I encourage you to, so you can see with your own eyes. Infact, do just that instead of reading this review so your opinion will not be weighted by my own.
So this game is basically Boom Beach in a lower quality. In the very beginning, you are greeted with an on-rails tutorial segment that everyone that isn't Supercell does with their Clash-like or Boom Beahc ripoffs... usually.
As a note, this game will be treating it as just that; a boom beach clone.
So after playing it some more after that point, I've found that you can add segments onto your island, though I feel this limits defensive possibilities, you can't cancel upgrades, change resolution, make the game fullscreen or change hte UI screen size, and most of all... units that deploy have no collision with the environment's rocks, and with eachother, which doesn't make much sense since there's always multiple entry points to any base.
Looking at the unit list, there is definitely alot to be unlocked and aimed for, and due to the fact that nothing requires a level 10 or higher HQ (It's called a Command Bunker, but bear with me.), I'll assume hte level cap is or may be Level 10, even if temporarily. Also alongside units are even more buildings to get, most of which are gained before HQ 7, which also might be the level cap right now or for all time.
The game at first has one resources; Supplies, which I assume you get more resource types later on.
I didn't play for long since... Well in my honest opinion, boom Beach jsut leaves a better impression.
I would suggest that the game's unit collision (while deploying, when deployed I don't care) is adjusted to be there, at least with the environment as it just looks bad. I also would at some point put some more work into the grapical design, it looks pretty basic for what (i think) is a completed product.
I also would strongly advise allowing players to skip the tutorial.
Altogether, the game left a fairly sour first impression with me, so I will rate it...
4/10. The game does seem to have some good, unique-ish elements like island expanding which is slightly cusomizable, but it needs work before I personally would call it passable by any means.
It's free to play, so maybe you'll enjoy it more, just get past the tutorial and act as if you just started playing.

I guess it's time for my review!
Stability / Polishing / Performance:
The game is not crazily polished, but it works well and has no major bugs as far as I was able to tell.
It's performance is compared to other games rather underwhelming, but it should work on most systems.
Graphics:
The graphics aren't all that great.
The texture resolution is good, the overall quality of the textures is also fine.
But when it comes to complex lighting effects the game doesn't necessarily match today's industry standards.
However it doesn't look "ugly".
Gameplay:
The game is very detailed when it comes to the controls.
The physics aren't so bad given it's not aiming for damage models or any fancy stuff.
It shows it's muscles when it comes to simulating a lively AI driven traffic world.
Eventhough the AI sometimes acts outrageously stupid, there are few games one could compare this game with, but I'd dare to say the AI here is still the smartest, given that (nearly) no other game tries to accurately simulate normal every-day traffic! (even GTA with a much higher budget has NPCs blowing each other up just by accident - this doen't happen here)
The game also has a little background simulation going on for the player's company, which I'd like to recommend to focus on in later titles, since it shows some potential in my opinion.
Models / Game World:
The truck models are very detailed and look nicely, if you don't look too closely at the big headlights you can mount at the bumper and the roof of your truck (those have just a plain texture).
The AI cars don't look too shabby either.
The game world itself is a little lack-luster.
Eventhough they made great improvements compared to the previous title, it's still partially in medieval-ages of game development with sprite-based distant flora and some simplistic general design.
Cities don't consist of much more than a few steets.
However I believe the game has something to it.
You could consider it to be one of those "zen" games that you can just use to relax while playing.
It has a progress system, a (downloadable) multiplayer and steam workshop support, which already addresses a whole bunch of the previous critique and if you feel adventurous, you should look around on the internet, there are plenty more other mods that address even more things of the game - I believe there's even one or two complete game world replacers   and add-ons out there.

Even though the characters move as if they are stuck in a constant lag, I still liked the character design and artwork. It's cute with enough detail.
Games will hardly feel the same as there are different upgrades per run, making you either superpowerful or struggling to stay alive. It's rewarding when you're strong, and intense when you are on the weak side. There is also a random event where you migt get a bonus or you get something bad happening. This also adds to the game feeling fresh and different on each run.
This game has wanted me to smash my keyboard more than a thousand times. It's infuriating when you're having a semi good run and BAM! All monsters oneshots you in three seconds and it's game over. There's no possible ways to win certain runs unless you get the exact upgrades you need.
While hitting the monsters is automatically handled by the characters, you have to rearrange them on the field to make weak characters stay out of powerful enemies way and make casters be able to attack the correct monster. Even though you can slow down the combat to a certain point, it doesn't eliminate the fact that sometimes you have just a few seconds to swap out your characters before they're literally oneshotted by the enemy. Some characters can't survive well against certain monsters, so you literally have to move them within 2 seconds that the monster appears on the screen. Sometimes this happens at the very start of the game. There are so many times where my characters are taking massive hits because I am struggling to manage spellcasting and moving them to the right spot. I wish there had been a setting to turn off the automated system and let you select a choice without a time limit.
Most fights, I find myself constantly hitting the heal button and tossing potions around, because the characters are taking so massive amount of damage. Sometimes my characters are near death and I just barely manage to get them back up in health. Other times, I miss by half a second and they die. This is my least favorite part of the game.

I'm recommending this, but not.
But why, you may ask? You have so much time in it, surely it's got something going for it?
It does. Thing is, the game is pretty much an excersize in unrealized potential. The environments look samey, until you go out of your way and find lovingly crafted areas people will never bother with.
The combat is clunky, if functional, and regularly gets screwed with by poor skill and item balancing.
The setting is actually surprisingly good, and there actually is an underlying story that you can play through at your own pace that is, shock and awe, actually pretty genuinely interesting, especially for your average scifi buff.
Noticing a theme? There are some wonderful ideas, but for whatever reason, they just never quite pushed them far enough. The game is sandbox-y enough to be impressively wide open, but they didn't quite cut away from MMO Theme Park syndrome.
The crafting system is amazingly wide, allowing you to make damn near everything in the game just from things you can get yourself, except for the necessary endgame things that require asinine boss grinding or broken pvp point grind.
Honestly it's getting depressing to talk about. It's one of those things that could have been flat out amazing, and for whatever reason, it just falls short. Still, it's the only modern MMO I've been able to stomach for any length of time, so there's that.

I have to admit, my hopes were set way too high when I bought this game. I assumed that it was going to have open worlds with differently dispersed enemies and weapons, as well as open-world style gameplay. When I got in-game, I found the Start menu to be extremely simplistic, which, in my opinion, is a good way to navigate easily. As I entered Campaign mode, I was thrown off by not one campaign with open-world gameplay, but 3, with set objectives for each. After discovering that I could not play 2 of the campaigns, I chose Gladiator, which forces you to fight for an infinite amount of time with infinite amounts of matches. Once in-game, I found it to be extremely buggy, with simple combat controls (LMB is the only way to attack). The graphics were alright, however, I found it annoying that the most common attack is a kick. Soon, the controls made more sense. I discovered how to duck and roll around like a wheel. Countering was difficult, but fun. The enemies were ridiculously difficult to defeat, but I got a 'kick' out of the ragdoll of their bodies and cheapshotting the other rabbits by throwing spears at them as soon as the match starts. Eventually, I found that you could revive all rabbits, including yourself, by simply hitting X. I used this to stay in the matches, even after I had died. Soon came the 'Lightning Key', as I called it, which allows your rabbit to send out a lightning bolt from his chest, instantly killing all other rabbits. I used this to get my skillset up to well over 2000. I had over 4 quadrillion fans, and my rabbit's apparel was completely black. The enemies were bugged by this point, being larger than the building itself, and simply put, a large mass of glitched black. They were impossible to defeat, and could kick me infinite distances. I crashed the game 4 times before I gave up this cheating lifestyle and moved on to beat all of the challenge missions, which, surprisingly, were ridiculously easy. This whole review may seem like I'm bashing on this game, but that is not the case.

When gamers talk about classics on the Dreamcast, Jet Set Radio is a title that is often brought up with misty-eyed nostalgia. The vibrant visuals, diverse soundtrack and anarchic spirit struck a chord with critics and fans back in the day. Unfortunately, while the the art direction and audio still hold up remarkably well, the gameplay doesn't. Most missions consist of you spraying graffiti over a designated number of hotspots in an area within a certain amount of time. So far so okay, but once you've sprayed a certain amount of graffiti, the police come and make completing the mission an exercise in tedium and frustration. Other missions task you with copying a rival skater's moves, racing them, or spraying them with enough graffiti. The controls and camera just aren't tight enough for the demanding challenges that the game throws at you. You'd think that with such a lack of precision that the game would be a tad forgiving towards minor mistakes. That's not the case. One jump a little too far, one minor bump against a wall, or one little brush against your opponent can cause you to fail. There's no option to restart a mission if things aren't going well; you have to either wait for your opponent to beat you, or go back to the garage and go though the entire mission briefing all over again. Completing these tasks feels laboring when it should feel fun, clunky when it should feel tight, and frustrating when it should feel liberating. If you loved the original, these objections won't matter to you. If you haven't played this game, I'd recommend you check out either the superior Jet Set Radio Future or Tony Hawk Pro Skater.

I don't know if this guy was going with a Furry Fandom when he though about this but I must say I love the fact i'm not a human when I go around kicking a$$ in it, and then getting my a$$ kicked by other rabbit/wolf/cat/dog/robot Wahey, but it's pretty damn fun.
PROS:
Combat System: I popped into this game not knowing what to expect, and then my face hit the floor and I realized I had some work to do.  This is a combat system like no other, this isn't Button Mashing 101, you actually don't swing when you hit LMB, you have to get up close and hit it, and with each directional button you hit when you swing you do different things, like a roundhouse kick, a jab, hook, roll away, etc.  So if you go into this game expecting to mash buttons and win, you are gonna be on the floor with your neck broken fairly quickly.
No humans, just animals: There are no humans in this game, just anthro bunnies/wolfs/cats/robots/dogs, which is a different change, and probably a huge A+ when it comes to the Furry community, which I am part of.  But I really like the fact it isn't just "Another human" this guy is actually putting something different in place of what a character usually is, and I like it.
Classes: There are other classes, as I said the wolf, cat, etc.  The wolf is basically a one hit kill for the bunnies, as for the others I haven't tried yet, I like the Rabbit too much.
The Ninjas: Every class is apparently a Ninja, I guess that would make sense since they wallrun, hop REALLY HIGH, with the amazing fighting skills and the ability to throw a spear/sword at a opponent and get a 1 hit kill off of it.
No stamina/health bar: I like this honestly, you just kind of have to guess if you are about to die or not, since they don't bother you with a little health bar, plus you don't really have little stamina, as far as I know you have infinite, but you kind of have to watch how much blood you lose, especially when it comes to weaopns
Weapons: There are weapons in this game, and I really love them, despite the fact you can 1 hit kill if you throw it at them from behind or throw a spear at the opponents head, I got into some really heated sword battles that lasted several minutes or longer, and damn they were really fun too.
Feel like a total bada$$: The title speaks for itself, when you start rolling around punching, roundhousing, jump kicking, and slicing everyone up I felt like the Master of weapons untill I got constantly kicked while rolling, but it was nice while it lasted.
Wounds: If you get wounded by a weapon he actually holds near the wound with a hand if he has a open hand, I just think it's a neat little feature to notice that you are injured, like the ammount of blood pouring out of you wasn't enough already.
Different maps + Arena: I love the Arena even though on ocassions I get totally screwed over with how laggy it can get in that stupid arena on slight ocassions, but there is different maps to run around with and explore, with enemies you can fight so you can do something.
Responsive controls: I feel as if when I hit something it actually DOES what I want, instead of me hitting a button and it just kind of does whatever it's supposed to, problem though is with some weapon fighting the Roll doesn't really want to work on ocassions, and I don't know why.
Challenges: There are many challenges to do and they are pretty fun, I only did a few like kill a few enemies with just your fists, I'll have to try the rest later on.
Different skins/clothes: Each animal has different clothes, mainly the Bunny though, like there is a Assassin like outfit if you hit the "1" key a few times it changes his color, clothes, and clothes color, so you can be the one you want.
CONS:
REALLY long loading times: Half the time the levels take FOREVER to load, yet I get around 300 frames, I don't think it should take several minutes to load up a level that I've played several times over and still take me 5 minutes to load up.
Constantly kicked: As I said in the pros I'll explain abit more, I was playing on a Dune level and I found a rabbit to fight, he kicked me down, I rolled, he kicked me WHILE I was rolling and then I snapped my neck, then when I tried to go back and kick the s%*t out of him he did it AGAIN.  I think the roll needs to be a little bit tweaked, maybe when you roll you can't get hit untill the moment he starts getting up or something? That way you get some time to get up and get your thoughts together, as well as be able to fight back.
Jumping Physics: These are really weird, I was jumping around and had to jump back to where a enemy was cause I jumped away, he litterally did a 0.1 milisecond turn and had a s@%t ton of momentum and jumped all the way back, which kind of struck me as off, it's also weird to jump around a enemy cause you can't really turn all that well which feels kind of weird.  It doesn't help that when you land on a slope he instantly turns to go down the slope and moves down, so if i'm on a small ledge and jump and land, i'm most likely gonna fall off.
Not much after a while: After you do the maps and arena a few times there isn't a whole lot left, there are challenges but even then it feels like it needs something, I say a Randomly generated map or something, just click a button, it randomizes a map and enemies with terrain and you go around exploring it to see what you can find.
WHAT I THINK:
I think this game is really fun and can have a lot of potential, and I feel confident it's gonna go somewhere in this guy's hands, he's already shown a lot of potential with just the combat system and the way it feels to roll around and fight instead of just another game where you press buttons and hope to win.  The game gets a 7/10 It needs some work and some additions but it's pretty f$#%ing good for what "I" was expecting out of it.

You don't see very many games set in the Old West, so when one comes along, it's a novelty.
Tin Star is a Text Adventure, although not in the same sense as Zork, Moonmist, Planetfall, etc. In those games you actually had to type out commands to interact with the world, whereas Tin Star has pre-defined choices. You often get a bunch of options to choose from, but even so, you're still limited to whatever the author programmed.
In this sense, Tin Star resembles the Choose Your Own Adventure book series, which ran from 1979 to 1998. Anyone who grew up in the 1980s and early 1990s likely spent hours with different CYOA novels. I know I did.
The story of Tin Star follows a man or a woman (you can select your gender, name, and sexual orientation) who was saved from execution via hanging and made the sheriff of a small town. During the game, you get to meet all sorts of individuals, many of whom can be either friend or foe depending on how you interact with them.
Unfortunately, I can't delve too much into the story without ruining it, but I can say that there were a number of plot twists. Unlike some AAA titles that advertise "your choices will matter," Tin Star actually makes good on that promise.
There are no graphics, music or sound effects of any kind. This means you'll have to use your imagination to conjure up the imagery, but given that the author provides plenty of information, that's not too difficult.
One minor benefit to a total lack of audio is that you can easily play your own music in the background without it interrupting anything or being interrupted by the game's music/sound effects.
The system requirements are so low that even a PC that's over a decade old could run Tin Star. So if you have an older machine or an underpowered laptop, rest assured you won't have any problems here.
I do have a few "issues" with the game, however.
1. The visuals consist of black text on an off-white background. While that's a fine setup, it'd be nice if the player could choose their own text and background colors. I know some people prefer using a dark background and lighter text, especially if they're playing in a dimly-lit room.
2. As far as I can tell, Tin Star only saves your game at the end of each chapter, and only then if you tell it to do so. This is because you can replay the chapter if you want to try something different, which is nice, but it also means you have to start that chapter over at the beginning.
3. There's only one save file. If you start a new game, your old save will be written over. So if someone else in your household wants to play Tin Star, make sure you back up your save or that they have their own Steam account and use family sharing.
Bottom line: It won't win any awards for being flashy or technologically impressive, but what it does have is a good interactive story with meaningful choices and interesting characters. I'd recommend Tin Star, especially considering it's only $4.99 USD.

Overall, a nicely put together story and gameplay which I enjoyed.
It has some rather unusual elements in a modern Point and Click though - you have combat scenes and you can die in this game. The combat to me feels rather cumbersome - I usually don't play point and clicks in one go due to the puzzle solving nature of it, so have combat in different parts of the game makes me go 'uhh what was I supposed to do again?'. After playing through the whole game and going through the second time, I revisited the tutorial and realized I've totally forgotten about the aiming bit (pressing control button to trigger an aim) and have been shooting blindly, although I managed to get through with my blind shooting. Dying isn't brutal as the game reloads from an auto-save point upon death (although it's better to have your own saves as well to lessen the steps between the auto-save point and the action).
This game has a 'hardcore' kinda feel to it, in a sense that it makes you do one step by step. Like if you wanted to open a door, you MUST walk near it and then open the door. However, I do like the fact you can kick things as well as addition to the normal 'see/talk/pick up' mechanic.
The voice acting is good, and I like the mood the game sets. The little touches in the game like how well animated the rain is, and the sound of the rain gets louder when you open the door to the rain outside is pretty immersive.
Definately a recommendable game if you like a decent storyline, atmospheric mood, decent voice acting despite dated and not-so-great graphics. If you do play this game, I encourage you to save alot as you can have different solutions to certain things in the game and missable acheivements.

The story in this game is good, but the gameplay is what kills it for me. The areas you venture through are basically point A to point B with a maybe one or two different ways of getting there. The environment looks cool and all, and the game does a great job of looking like a futuristic world, but you can't help but feel like you're in a hallway that leads you to your goal. Which is fine, but at least give me a few ways of getting there. The main reason I can't recommend this game is the gameplay. While the story, voice acting, and dialogue are all great - the gameplay is lacking. Firefights are just tedious and boring. I usually use the sniper to take out the idiot enemies further back, then the pistol or assualt rifle for the ones closer up. Still the combat is so dull and unchallenging. I'm sure it probably gets better later on in the game, but I'm over 6 hours in, and it just isn't doing it for me. The squad abilities are cool and all, but the fact that you can finish almost all firefights without using them at all lets you do just that. So the abilities end up being flash instead of a necessity. There are little things that bug the hell out of me. For example if you decide to switch to the sniper rifle, but accidentally click on the grenade launcher, you have to switch to the GL and then switch to the sniper rifle. Even thought the game is basically paused, you can't cancel your mis-click and re-click on the weapon you wanted to switch to. Then the AI on the enemies isn't the greatest. They'll stand near the edge of cover, and you can easily shoot them. But instead of moving away to protect themselves they just keep taking fire until they poke out to shoot or die. Also, they pop out to shoot on a timer it seems like. The enemy AI is so predictable it takes away any difficulty.
The game is positively received by most, so you should probably give it a shot anyways. But I just wanted to share my opinion. Personally I dislike the game, but that doesn't make it a bad game. The story, voice acting, characters, environment, are all great, but the gameplay leaves me bored.
