NiGHTS Into Dreams is art. Plain and simple. A true classic for the SEGA Saturn. This HD remake does justice to the original (and even lets you play the original as well). It also includes Christmas NiGHTS, a now hard to find Christmas version of Spring Valley and the Gillwing battle that was included in a Christmas SEGA Saturn bundle in Japan and was given away free in stores elsewhere.
The only downside to this HD release is that it does not include Sonic the Hedgehog into Dreams, which was Spring Valley + boss fight against a reskinned Puffy to look like Doctor Eggman that was included on the Christmas NiGHTS disc. This was actually Sonic's first polygonal appearance, and it's a shame that it was not included here.
Other than that, you get the HD remake as well as the original, Christmas NiGHTS as well as a concept art and image gallery. A great deal, and a must have for fans of NiGHTS and SEGA everywhere.

A dystopian cyberpunk point-and-click indie game with atmospheric art direction and excellent sound design.
Playing as a former assassin you're placed in the raining wet city of Pittsburg at night. Throughout the game you uncover more details about your mission and backstory, picking up details from characters and items within each area.
While the gameplay is quite linear and less opaque than some point-and-clicks, situations sometimes require a bit more experimenting to discover the correct way to progress. Some of the scenes could also have been more fleshed out in the variety of things to be interacted with, as some locations felt they could have used it.
Altogether Gemini Rue is enjoyable if mostly for the art and soundscape, especially the latter which carried the game for me. The hand-drawn scenery and sprites suit the game's dark vibe and are clearly drawing (no pun intended) from cyberpunk influences.
One minor issue I had was with the voice casting. While the dialog can tend on the cliched side I felt the voice acting could have been better cast, with many characters lacking an immersive delivery. The protagonist however is better suited to the voice, and is easily the best match.
The game is quite short,  and can be completed in a sitting or two depending on how much time is spent on progressing through scenes. I completed it in Steam's Offline mode, so my actual play time isn't displayed publicly (note to devs: make it work for such singleplayer games).
For those looking for a similar experience I'd highly recommended the Hideo Kojima classic Snatcher for the Sega CD. The voice acting, characters, dialog and humorous respite work together to make a very well-rounded and satisfying game.
In short, I'd recommended Gemini Rue to those looking for a short, well-made and atmospheric cyberpunk-esque fix, and are open to the point-and-click style of gameplay.

The greatest sleeper hit I've seen in a long time.
Seen nothing on this game, somehow, but it's been around for a bit now. I enjoyed Starmade, Robocraft, and at some point, the basic Minecraft experience. Yuck.
Long story short: MachineCraft lets you build vehicles. Land. Air. Sea. Space. All done very sandbox style (vs Robocraft's questionable tech tree and grindy research to just get a reskin of a part) with MUCH more dynamic mechanics than some other titles (robocraft and starmade, in my case).
Wanna have folding guns? Great, get some hinges and cannons. Want a blowback action tank cannon? Slip in a piston and some locking blocks, hook it to a fire button and let that baby RIDE! Wanna make a plane? You might have to experiment, but I made a flying van that's a car, sub, and plane all at once. Two days into playing the game.
Amazing entertainment. Incredible vehicle and mechanic building action. Honestly, I can't think of major improvements off the top of my head. You can even do private servers for messing around, and there's very little stress in the game... Just, well, fun!
Edit: After playing a couple hundred hours of this game and becoming a god, all I can say is MachineCraft is the future.
Machinecraft is to mechanical building what minecraft was to open worlds. The possibilities are limited only by what your experience, clever engineering, and of course imagination can dream up. I've found countless ways to improve, streamline, and overclock tech, and I still keep finding more.
Put simply, this game's content isn't about progression or stories or competition. It's about what you can dream, how you can do it, and how you can challenge yourself to make it better. The depth and progression you experience as an engineer is a skill you will pat yourself on the back for and an outlet you will expres yourself in.
Logical or artistic, both find root in this game, and it is as much an outlet as it is a social and competitive experience. I would say this game is beyond words, but I just lugged a couple thousand at you probably, so I digress.
Cons: Addicting to all hell. I'm taking out my warning. You can moderate this game, but the first couple days will be hard.
The premium for this game isn't about edge or about fun stuff, you get a freaking smoke emitter and preference if servers overflow. But you know what? I bought the premium anyways. The guys that make this are damned champions, plain and simple. They've worked for my dollar and then some.
10/10 would buy just because again. And I'm a frugal man.

The graphics are cute/cartoony. The music is not terrible, but not great either. Pretty much standard fare. Thing I'd take issue is, theres nothing Ive seen so far for this game to have the tag of "RPG".
Theres no story to speak of (that Ive found yet anyway, granted I've only done 3 missions). Basically, theres a map with different missions you can choose. Choosing a mission gives you a brief description of it. Such as "Protect the princess" or what have you. Then it goes right to the battle.
It looks like your typical JRPG, with your PCs on one side, enemies on the other. Each PC can only attack the enemy in front of it, except for certain items or abilities allow you to attack others. Each PC has a special ability that it can use based on the type of class it is. Attacks are in real time and keep going whether you want them to or not, as soon as a time bar is filled, the attack is made). Items are randomly dropped into a 4 slot thing at the left, when a new one drops you lose the one in the 4th slot. They are anything from weapons and armor, to scrolls that raise your level (NOT as big of a deal as in a real RPG) and potions with various effects.
So enemies come in waves, with up to 3 on screen at different time. The final wave is a boss and there is a couple points in each mission where either you get to choose something good (healing, a good random item) or bad (cant gain exp, slowed down ect)
Its an ok tablet-style casual game, but besides the fact that the classes are traditional D&D classes and you gain EXP which makes your characters better, theres *nothing* about this game that could be considered an RPG.
I'd call it casual, maybe strategy. Based on the fact that the fun lies in switching your characters places to take hits and knowing when to use your special skill and who to put items on. But definitely not an RPG at all.
RPG =/= fantasy setting.

This is one of those pseudo-HOG games. There's a lot going on and it takes a while to work through, but it mostly isn't looking for hidden objects. For someone who really just wants a series of find-the-objects-in-the-beautiful-scene puzzles, this game is mostly distraction.
WARNING: Minor spoilers ahead. Really minor, for anyone familiar with this style of game.
If you really like connect-the-tubes/wires/strings puzzles, this is probably a great game for you. There are a lot of them. Plus a few put-the-objects-in-the-right-order puzzles, a jigsaw-style puzzle or three, and a few do-things-in-the-correct-sequence puzzles. Surprisingly for this style of game, there are no line-up-the-concentric-rings puzzles. But yes, there is a puzzle where you repair a forge, then use it to create a part of a key.
The hidden-object puzzles are all very short, very easy, and all reuse the same backgrounds at least twice. To make things worse, there's a HOG aspect that might not bother others but really bugged me: The HO puzzles contain multiple copies or variants of the same objects. For example, one puzzle required you to find a small lightbulb in the scene. There was a red lightbulb, a blue one, and a green one; any of them worked to satisy the puzzle. Other objects in the same puzzle were singlets. Why the copies of some objects?
There is an overabundance of "plot" to the game. It's a bit of a whodunit. Which would be fine, except solving the mystery takes up a lot of the game time, and the mystery is both contrived and obvious from very early on, particularly considering how convoluted it is. Nice try, but it detracts from the overall game, rather than add to it.
This game suffers from typical logic issues: Areas in early parts of the game that need to be returned to and searched much later on--for no apparent reason; areas and objects that clearly are part of puzzles yet can't be clicked on early in the game, but suddenly become active when needed; objects that can be picked up but that have no clear use for a very long time; etc.
The most frustrating part of the game is far too much "action fussiness". For example, at one point, you need to break a window to reach an object. You have a crowbar and a pipe wrench. The crowbar doesn't work to break the window, but the pipe wrench does. OK, sure, that makes total sense.
But if these pseudo-HOG games let you use the dang crowbar for all of the puzzles, the games would be a lot shorter. Open a locked suitcase? Crowbar. Chip away ice? Crowbar. Clear rubble? Crowbar. Pull a curio from a flaming fireplace? Crowbar. Emergency electrical fuse? Crowbar. That's... 90 percent of this game.
As with many HOG-like games, there are oddball locks galore. You often times are carrying tools that could break open the locks, but for one and only one lock do you break it open rather than hunt for a special key--and that one time, the tool used is, well, surprising. Wouldn't be my first choice.  (Hint: it isn't the crowbar.)

The character creation thing is nice, especially the customizable face thing. If you try it, you'll like that it seems like a game for grownups, e.g. the guys & girls are sexy & they make real stories & have arguments & decide things & so forth. It is a heteronormative game: generally guys think about sex with girls, & vice versa, & actual sex does happen as part of the gameplay, just as a heads up to any concerned parents out there. The team dynamic is good in this & is generally a two, three or four-person thing, & it is a well made thing even if it is a bit corny.
As far as inspirations go, it makes me think a lot of Star Trek in that things are a bit on the happy-go-lucky "cheesy" side of things. The aliens are clearly just people with different faces or like different skin tones or with fake pointy ears on & so forth - not very convincing! As a matter of fact, now that I think about it a little bit, it sort of seems like a sci-fi Final Fantasy game, but for young adults instead of tweens. It makes me think of Final Fantasy VIII, if anyone can remember that far back! That was over ten years ago now. I might be getting old! I'm thinking specifically of the university dining hall scene that happens about 20 minutes into the gameplay. It is at least superficially similar to the sci-fi classic novel "Ender's Game" by Orson Scott Card, a favorite of mine.
Gameplay is very linear, as other reviewers have said, & i'm ok with that, that's fine - open-world 3rd-person games like Shadows of Mordor & Mad Max seem to tend to devolve into a sort of a "hunt & scrounge around" type of gameplay that I'm tired of. I want clear goals, a mission & achievements. There is a gay character in Mass Effect 2, a sexy alien, & a creepy loser hacker. The majority of the action takes place on an alien spaceship / what seems to be an engineering office building
In conclusion, I endorse this game & would buy it again. It is just being set aside for now because I bought a different video game called Aliens vs. Colonial Marines, if anyone is curious, & I WILL get back to it! I have an extremely high opinion of Mass Effect 2, WOULD play it again, and WILL in just a bit here, do NOT lose hope of that happening at all costs! It is NOT too nerdy for me or too corny

This is about as close as we are ever going to get to Dungeon Keeper 3, and I'm ok with that. EA proved it can not handle the stable of franchises it owns, so a spiritual successor comes in to fill the role proper. The game is almost identical to DK2, but it is ever so slightly different. Rooms are still dripped through the story missions, but you reasearch sins instead of rooms and spells. The sins can unlock different perks, spells, and constucts on a upgrade tree. In single player the unlocks carry over mission to mission, and multiplayer either starts off at 0 or at a base level. We also have an alchemy lab and a workshop that have their own special potions and constructs and most rooms have some interactable prop that determines their behavior. My favorite is the messhall prop that allows you to grind up anything and feed it to your minions. The campaign is pretty good, but one glaring, cart-stopping blemish arises during one mission where you control a small group of creatures with no dungeon core to defend. It took some getting use to the controlling of creatures without picking them up and flinging them at their target. The banners are♥♥♥♥♥♥poor during navigation more complex than a stright line or right angle. I ended up using the possession spell for most of it, and even then the other creatures didn't want to explicitly follow the leader. Other than that though it is pretty much DK2, so if you loved Dungeon Keeper like I did, pick it up. It is a vast improvement over Dungeon Keeper Mobile *shudder*.

It's not that great. No animations for gear shifts, No 3 stage jake brake. Can't own trailers, economy is really unrealistic, AI for NPC vehicles is attrocious, collision detection is really bad. The game crashes all the time. All the time. When I boot the game I have to turn down my volume because the opening animation is way too loud, and I then have to turn my volume back up to hear the game audio properly. No log books. Police fines are draconian and add nothing in terms of animations or any kind of fun, scaling your load is incomplete, no readouts for axel loads. Can't slide tandems, or 5th wheel. CB is consmetic only, no toll roads, ezypass etc. No truck wash or dirt system. Most of the guages are there just for show such as oil temperature, etc and the underlying systems are not simulated. Most of the controls in the cab are cosmetic only. The engines behave stupidly and don't match what happens in reality. It's not uncommon to be doing 3000+ RPM in top gear to go 60MPH. No pre-trip inspections or maintenance other than pulling into a garage and clicking ok. No diff lock. No Flags, beacons or signs. No load securement, no RGN or stepdeck. No fuel slosh in tankers. Handling is not affected by road conditions or weather. No permits. No bridge authority, no pilot cars. This really doesn't even attempt to replicate trucking. Obviously made by people that know nothing about trucking and didn't even try. And the maps are too small, and don't feel like America at all and look like a cheap cartoon. No pedestrians, no residential houses, no farms. There is not a single river or bridge aside from the bay area bridges. Trucking landmarks such as the donner pass, or any pass are not included - which is a crying shame because they are the more challenging and interesting aspects of trucking. This is not a simulator, this is a casual, badly executed incomplete alpha and a blatant cash grab. Don't buy.

I haven't even touched Jet Set Radio until just a few days ago, maybe 3 or 4 days before this review, and I regret not getting my hands on it until now. The absolute best part about this game is its design. Between the cel-shading and the vibrant colors, this game is astonishing to look at even with its low-poly models and slightly aged textures. It definitely looks like it's been touched up a bit, and even then the game has aged wonderfully. The soundtrack goes along with its aethstetic perfectly with turntablist hip hop tunes, electronic tracks with backing guitars, and a singular pop-punk track thrown in there for whatever reason, but even that track fits in.
The game's story is simple, nothing notable in the least and most of the time gets over-shadowed by the humorous and lighthearted dialogue in the cutscenes. The gameplay, however, is where the game takes a hit. It's not so much that the game itself is difficult, but it's that the controls are a bit clunky and sometimes frustrating. The way the game punishes you for getting too close to a challenger you're supposed to tag a group or race an opponent is the biggest flaw, with issues like inconsistencies with tricks and enemies that you just can't shake off being minor in comparison. It's easy to get past most of the flaws with a little experience. The game is that it's fairly short with about 6-8 hours of gameplay and a five dollar price tag, it's not that big of a deal in the big picture.
With that said, I think this has to be one of the greatest deals on steam. Five dollars for a completely unique experience you will not get with any other title. Less than most titles on steam, and less than most things period. Buy a copy of this game right now, and maybe buy some copies for your friends. If this game goes on sale for 50% off or less, then buy copies for all your friends. 9/10

Warframe is a 99.9% FREE online Co-op vs AI game!
You control a Warframe. There are over 20 Warframes to choose from and they all have unique themes (Fire, Berserker, Stealth, etc.) and special powers (Fireball, Warcry, Smokescreen, etc.).
There are hundreds of weapons for your Warframe to use (Rifles, Snipers, Shotguns, Launchers, Pistols, Swords, Axes, etc.).
Every method of killing your enemies is perfectly viable. I have the most fun when I use all the tools available to me. For example: I'll use my Fire Warframe to burn five enemies, then I'll use my shotgun to shoot another six, and finally I'll use my sword cut up the rest!
You will always have access to 99.9% of the game's content (except cosmetics) without needing to pay any real money. If you want cosmetics, you have the option of spending real money on Platinum (the game currency) or you can just trade other players the in-game items you earned for Platinum. I've played over 3,000 hours without spending any real money because I just sold in-game items to other players for Platinum and then used that Platinum to buy cosmetics.
Warframe has pretty good graphics, but doesn't actually require too much from your computer. Warframe updates pretty frequently, so there is always something new and interesting to do.

Mountain Crime: Requital is a murder mystery Hidden Object game where you play a doctor who finds himself trapped in a hotel with guests dying around you. Initially you try to help the guests as a doctor but as more backstory reveals itself, you start trying to solve and prevent murders before you eventually realise you might not be there by accident.
The graphics and sound are a little dated but otherwise good enough. The voice acting is ok, and the animations are terrible! (Particularly where characters walk around the scene, they look as if they were modeled on a ape walking around on two feet.) There is plenty of story and backstory, most of which is revealed in text format through letters and clippings, so if you tend not to read text or skim over it, the story might be lost on you. The puzzles were easy for the most part, and there are plenty of HO scenes although most of them are quick. There's a map that shows actions needed and locations but there is no fast travel.
Overall, the game is above average thanks to it's story which tries to be a little original and not follow the tired "find a loved one missing due to supernatural events" that most HOGs can't leave alone, and the only real annoyances are the large amount of back tracking you need to do, revisiting the same locations again and again, and for the first half of the game, it feels like you only carry one item in your inventory at a time, the item that you need to progress to get the next item, and so on ... if you can get through 90 minutes of that, the game opens up a little. at over 3 hours to complete, it's a nice length, not too short and not too long. HO fans will enjoy the story and the difficulty level suits players new to the genre.

In
you play as Dr. White, who just received a phone call of a patient from the White Wolf Hotel. Upon reaching the hotel, your patient, Mr. Grey has been bitten by a poisonous snake, and the evidence points towards murder. Every single resident of this hotel is suspicious, and it's up to you to find out what really happen, as the number of corpses starts to piling up!
Another adventure and this time, heavenly inspired by Agatha Christie's works, although not even close of reaching its cult status.
sure did tried, and the result is amazing, but it's just not easy to create and portrait a plot with major impact. This title brings a fantastic plot where the player must pursue tips and evidences towers the real murderer, before more lives are taken. Throughout the game Dr. White keeps finding pieces of information to construct a case and solve the ultimate puzzle of why the murder is taking the lives of the residents of the White Wolf Hotel. This is a well implanted feature, as the player doesn't really need to find such notes, but once you're deep into the story, all the information counts towards the player enthusiastic search for the truth. Not every game regards this option as a guarantee feature, and not every title really offers a satisfying game where the player feels like an authentic detective.
All the characters hide something, and although you learn that fast enough, it's still no reason to stop them from being interesting and mysterious.
White Wolf Hotel hides many secrets and finding them all will be a treat for any adventure fan out there!
The chosen designs for
follows the category of horror mansions, minus all the ghosts, spirits or any monster, everything else is included, especially the isolated atmosphere that makes this thriller even more intense. The player can expect heavy rain effects, lonely and abandoned paths through the basement, interesting and very well decorated bedrooms, a beautiful backside with plenty of areas to explore, and much more!
Hidden Object scenes are interesting and offer a new and intuitive system by identifying the objects by image and not by their name. These scenes are very fast to complete and not boring at all.
Overall puzzles are easy to medium difficulty, and everyone should be able to complete them, as they are intuitive and fast paced!
There are no game modes to change such as difficulty or extras to pick, but it's well represented in terms of difficulty, and in terms of resolution, displaying perfectly well for HD monitors, which was very rare in 2011.
is a must for any adventure fan, with beautiful visuals and a great plot to follow, and although midway through the game everything becomes predictable, it's still pretty fun to sit back and watch everything comes together.

Overgrowth is a game I heard about on YouTube. For those of you completely unsure about what this game is, essentially its a physics based martial arts/parkour simulation/sandbox/proof of concept that's available as early access for 30 dollars. Normally I wouldn't recommend spending that kind of money on an early access game, but I believe that Overgrowth is worth it, even if it's just to help fund the rest of devolopement-Wolfire Games is highly devoted to making sure this game is amazing before any kind of full release, and they update it frequently. If you arent quite sold by the idea of a highly realistic physics based martial arts combat+simple, intuitive parkour, then maybe you WILL be sold by the fact that you have immediate and easy access to a functional and easy to use editor, letting you do anything from making a simple sky arena, to an entire city, to a custom parkour course. If you arent the most creative then you can still play in the arena- sort of a self contained campaign/ minigame letting you climb the ranks, gathering fans and increasing your skill rank. There's also a challenge mode in the works, though none of levels seemed to be fully functioning- and there is also a campaign menu, hinting at two campaigns outside of the arena, neither of which is playable. All in all, I'll go ahead and re-state my earlier statement; Overgrowth is worth the thirty dollars, and if it isn't worth it to you right now, it seems like it absolutely will be in the future. In its current state, Overgrowth gets a score of:
6/10
please keep in mind, that Overgrowth still isn't anywhere near full game status, but it's still loads of fun as it is, and I fully believe that it will become so much better in the weeks, months, and maybe even years to come; getting onboard now is something I recommend. However, don't just take my word for it, I highly recommend going over to YouTube and looking up vids on it to be sure before purchase.

This game.  *sigh*
You play an aggravatingly dense doctor surrounded by a host of grating, forgettable characters in a mountain resort. A storm has wiped out the road. Everyone starts dying and it's up to you to figure out why. The reason for all the death and Saw-like traps is pretty obvious to the player after a few puzzles, but not to the aforementioned toaster-dumb doctor.
2.5-3 hours of playtime will get you through this plodding story full of LAUGHABLY AWFUL voice acting / character animations. The story is presented in a piecemeal manner through poorly written newspaper clippings, letters, guestbooks, creepy photoshopped family portraits, etc. Once I knew how it was going to end, I pretty much just went on auto-pilot while the protagonist obsessed over watching the news.
What's sad is that the artwork in the game is above standard, and the HOG puzzles themselves are well-designed. There's evidence that this COULD HAVE been a good game.
Unfortunately, there's only a small selection of HOG scenes that are further watered down by reusing the same locations several times. The other puzzles in the game were either a) far too easy, b) poorly explained, or c) glitchy. And the fact Dr. Dense felt the need to comment on almost EVERY SINGLE PUZZLE that he was sick of "tricky locks" made me wish he'd fall in a woodchipper.
If you want to ruin friendships, this is a great way to do it and laugh all at the same time. Highly recomended.

After that you get a boss which is essentially a puzzle of "how do I defeat this?" They seem to be rather short.
How you play is even strager. You actually only move on 1 plane at a time (up, down, left, right). There are set paths sometimes which you can branch on to be on a different plane, but it's not just open. You can fly, so it's not really a platformer. But it still feels a lot like Sonic but with many less enemies and no challenge to the actual stage.
It is very colorful with decent variety to the very small amount of distinct stages which is nice.
But in the end, I didn't find this fun. I never exactly felt challenged. There is essentially no story (you can read it as part of the "How to Play" menu if you'd like, but I almost immediately forgot it since it doesn't actually feel like it is anywhere in the game). Without story, the gameplay has to carry it. And the gameplay isn't fun to me.
If you do just want an arcade-y point grabbing experience with pretty good music and interesting visuals, you could do much worse. If you want a game where your actions feel like there is a point or that points don't actually provide happiness, go somewhere else.

People say there are two sides to every story, Gemini Rue takes that to the next level. Its a sci-fi point-and-click story game with a film noir feel to it.
There are some elements to the game in which you have to solve puzzles and/or small problems but they can be solved in a matter of minutes if you just think about where to go next.
You can choose what you can say and ask other characters, you can even lie to other characters if need be to get what you need in the end. There is an inventory system that can hold a variety of items like keycards, that can be used to access certain areas and/or resources in-game.
It also has a very unique combat system where the playable character can take cover, peak out and shoot at enemies, and even take deep breathes for a good old-fashioned headshot.
If anyone is looking for a game with a story, try Gemini Rue out.

Just going to write a short review that, albeit positive, will include some caveats to consider if you're unsure of purchasing the game.
First off, I really like this game. I have 100 hours in it after 2 weeks of it being available, and that speaks louder to the game's qualities than anything I could write here. There are select few games in the same vein I like more than it (STALKER: SoC, Witcher 3, Fallout: NV are 3 off the top of my head).
The caveats I mentioned are essentially all pertaining to bugs. This game has a lot of bugs. People may not realize there are a lot of bugs (or possibly don't care) because of how low quality a lot of AAA games come out to be, but that doesn't really excuse the problem here. The biggest offenders for bugs encountered are quests breaking. There were multiple times throughout my time where quests either broke, or stopped being updated in the journal so I had to use outside resources to figure out what to do next. Sometimes NPCs break, sometimes the pathing breaks. Obviously this is a long game, so for a majority of the time bugs won't effect the experience. These are still very relevant problems that need addressing, however.
In short, it's a really great game. But if you're on the fence about a purchase, I would suggest waiting until there are more bugfixes.

Blending elements of noir and science fiction, Gemini Rue delivers an interesting story wrapped in old-school graphics and great writing. Fans of old Sierra and Lucasarts games will feel right at home.
The atmosphere can be summed up in one word: oppressive. Rarely have I felt so unwelcome - which is good! The music and sound design are top-notch. However, the voice acting sometimes seems to be a bit flat. The pixelated (but by no means ugly) graphics definitely are a throwback to the "golden age" of adventure games. Don't let them discourage you, the visuals aren't everything. The combat is clunky, but generally not a huge bother.
It's the puzzles that make an adventure game. In Gemini Rue they're very intuitive and neither too easy nor too hard. Some of them can even be solved in multiple ways, which I felt was a nice touch and shows how much thought was put into making this game. A developer commentary is included, giving further insight into the authors' minds. There are some visual bugs, but nothing gamebreaking.
Overall a very enjoyable game, even if you're not a fan of the genre. Definitely worth the price tag.

Complicando todo demasiado, tiene muchos tipos de monedas, tienes que sacar certificados para hacer cosas como plantar un huerto o conseguir un barco... Vamos la burocracia llevada a los MMORPG.
Recomiendo probarlo a los que gusten de los MMORPG y quieran probar algo gratis, yo creo que se puede jugar perfectamente sin gastar un duro mientras no te vayas a meter en el PVP que creo que está muy roto. I'm on the fence about whether to recommend this one, but since the overall review score right now is very positive, I decided to give it a thumbs down as balance. It's not exactly bad, but just kind of lackluster.
The hidden object scenes are generally simplistic - no more than 10 or so objects to find by silhouette, and in many of the scenes there are multiple valid instances of some of the objects, any of which apparently counts as finding it. The puzzles are all pretty standard, and those also often seemed like simpler examples of the type. For example, one of those "move past gears to rotate paths into place" puzzles, where there were enough paths to move back & forth around the gears that there wasn't any real challenge to it. So, gameplay-wise, probably best suited for those without much experience with hidden object games.
The story is usually the least interesting part of these games for me, and this is no exception. It's a bit of a confusing mess, but only because it's presented non-chronologically. Once you've gotten enough pieces of the story to start seeing it, it becomes very predictable.
Also, I ran into one technical problem with a "traffic jam" style puzzle near the end of the game (I posted a thread about it in the discussions here). I suspect this was caused by running the game on a 3840x2160 screen, because it seemed to be having trouble aligning the cursor. I eventually had to just skip that puzzle to continue on.
Overall, I'd say this is a decent enough way to kill a few hours if you get the game in a bundle or something, but I don't think I would bother buying it on its own.

is the first 'hidden objects game' I played. I'm very familiar with the 'point & click adventure' genre but the idea of hidden objects never appealed to me because it sounds like a pixel hunt.
I have to say
mostly plays like a point & click adventure game: you collect items and use those on items in the game world to advance the story. Occasionally, you'll get a 'hidden object' screen in which you need to find some items but they're always hidden in plain sight, so there's no pixel hunting involved. Even then, there is a hint button. If you really can't spot that last object on the screen, it'll point it out for you.
The story is a basic detective story. You're a doctor who's called to a hotel to examine a patient but when you get there, it's clear a murderer is on the loose. So you start an investigation by examining the hotel, its residents and its surroundings.
I liked the setting, the mystery and the way the problem-solving needed to be tackled. The solution to advance the plot is always logical if you think about it. There are some puzzles to be solved, too. At first these are very easy, but in the second half of the game they can be pretty challenging.
You're never stuck in this game: if you don't know where to go or what to do next, you can click the hint button. If you can't solve a puzzle, you can just skip it. In both cases, there is a time restraint: after clicking the hint button, it needs to 'recharge' before it can be used again, and it takes some time before you can skip a puzzle, so in both cases the game does encourage you to try before giving up.
Without using spoilers, the story turns out to be a pretty basic detective story but it's interesting enough to want to discover what's going on. On the other hand, the 'personal story' of the main character turned out to be very cliché and became pretty predictable towards the end.
All in all,
was a positive experience of about 4 to 5 hours. It certainly isn't a mind-blowing, life-changing experience but it is worth its price. If it's on sale, I think you shouldn't even doubt and buy the game if you're into 'point & click adventure' games. I'm not sure if it's a good 'hidden objects' game because the hidden objects scenes were quite easy and because I can't compare it to other hidden objects games.

Bought this on a whim. Wasn't sure what to expect, but was very pleasantly surprised.
What you get is an entirely text based, 10 chapter story where you develop your character as a US Marshal in 19th century Nevada. After some introduction, you start each chapter in the hub of your town where you decide what to spend your limited time and very limited money on, and then something happens that needs a Marshal. The mission of each chapter has a nice variety, ranging from quiet investigations to big skirmishes, and the real selling point here is the choice it gives you on how to approach every thing in them. Generally after some investigating things get drastic and you have to make a series of choices based on your skills, knowledge, and character. With about 4 or 5 and sometimes 8 options for every bit, I never felt too pressured to do one thing or another. The amount of 'just shoot them' options make renegade Shepard look like a pacifist.
Behind the all text is a very RPG like skill system measuring your abilities, alignment, and relationships. It never explicitly says that you fail or succeed at something due to these values as well as never explicitly says when they're checked like in Fallout, only when they increased. I liked this, it gave some immersion and made me think about what the Marshal could do, rather than what numbers said he could do. I rolled a Lawful Good persuasion gunslinger and when I did those types of things, they worked, but when I tried to build something or wrestling a bear, I was up a creek.
The story gradually built up, with the connections between the chapters being revealed more towards the end. The final ending I got was a little boring, I really just went up to someone, arrested him, and that was it. I probably could have gotten something more interesting if I decided to do more shooting and less talking, and it didn't help there was a weird period of nothing between big action finale and the actual ending of the story. However you do get a full rundown of how your choices made a difference and the ultimate fate of your town and the cast that does give closure.
Mechanistically, the text engine used is bare bones looking, but works fine. Conversations are in a layout that should be recognizable to anyone whose played Mass Effect but much more concise, and the 'asking for information' prompts differentiable from 'threaten and shoot them in the face'. I wish they gave it an interface little flavor though, sometimes it felt like I was just taking a really exciting customer service survey.  Some say there's some poor grammar, but unless your an English major this probably won't bother you alot, I never noticed. If, for example, you were just bothered by 'alot', it might be an issue.
One note: There is permadeath, but only if you 'accept' the fatal mistake. You lose a cosmetic point at the end of the game, but that's it. Additionally, you can save and reload at the end of chapters. Progess is save automatically.
I got 6 hours out of one playthrough, asking every question possible and restarting a chapter a few times to get a better ending. I'd expect another run would be shorter with reading less background, and probably it would take about 4 playthroughs total to see the outcome of most things major. That's quite a bit of game for $5, if you don't mind reading it.
tl;dr: A very intense customer service survey set in 19th century Nevada about making good choices.

Mountain Crime’s repetitive nature and terrible voice acting hides a good idea of a murder mystery. If there were more puzzles and if the hidden object scenes would last more than 30 seconds, it could have been a really memorable hidden object game.
In a secluded resort, the seemingly colourful cast of visitors slowly get killed one by one. But as our investigating protagonist gets to the bottom of the crimes, he learns that these victims are actually connected by a very old, heinous crime.
Or, in other words, Mountain Crime: Requital is essentially a hidden object reimagination of Agatha Christie’s famous novel, ‘Ten Little Nig
gers’ (nowadays usually called ‘And Then There Were None’), only with horrible voice acting and a rather half-hearted and lazy ending.
Still, for the most part, the game is somewhat enjoyable. The puzzles are really fun and even the silhouette-based hidden object scenes are decent. But they are few and far in-between, as most of the time is spent by endless backtracking—which, without a quick travel feature, makes the game boring way too fast.

After all this time, NiGHTS into Dreams remains a unique action cult classic, with a strong arcade influence. The non-pervasive cutscenes may be heavily dated and rather cheesy, but fans of score-based action games will find a lot to enjoy here.
Initially, the colour schemes may cause confusion while reading the levels, and there's no helpful tutorial to introduce you to controls or goals, but once you've discovered how the scoring system works, and have adjusted to the visuals, the game can provide hours of fun. You've got the option of Saturn graphics or "HD" graphics, and I'd recommend the latter, particularly if you're playing on larger screens. While the game does have intro and outro videos, there's no real narrative interrupting the play either; NiGHTS is a game you can pick up and play for short or extended periods of time depending on what fits your mood.
The HD release includes Winter NiGHTS into Dreams (i.e. Christmas NiGHTS) too. Fans may get an extra dose of enjoyment from playing Splash Gardens, decked out in a Christmas theme, listening to Jingle Bells as they play. Other additions include a gallery of unlockable art work and photos.

It's a rather tough call to recommend (or not recommend) this game, because personally I feel it fits kind of in the middle and much of your enjoyment will come from nostalgia.
So, WFTO is essentially Dungeon Keeper 3. After a rough early access and subsequent buggy release, over 1 year later the game still has many issues, but at least the devs have listened and made improvements.
That being said:
- The "cursor" while stylish is still very unprecise
- The game still has some bugs in it (most notably health bars of my minions keep disappearing despite the option to do so not being enabled. This is a serious issue, because the game requires you to use healing powers, so it would be great to know which minions were badly damaged)
- The framerate absolutely TANKS, which is unacceptable for such a mediocre looking game. It should not hog so many resources on a powerful system
Now on to the actual review:
- Graphics: As said before, the game doesn't look particularly good. It's a better DK2 with improved lighting, better models, higher resolution, flashy effects, etc. But the basic models, etc. still look like 10 years old. Let's not even talk about the animation quality. It's just comedic.
- Sound: Oh, where to begin. The voice acting is SUPERB, everything else should be thrown onto a garbage pile. Combat sounds blend together into 1 big mess, while constantly being interrupted by "your minions are being slaughtered" or "xyz has died" or "your minions are rebelling", etc. And not to forget the ever present new years rocket when one of your minions levels up. Or the sound effect of your necromancer killing an enemy. OMG. Just get rid of 80% of the sound overlap or make them less annoying. It's a serious problem.
- UI: It's "ok". My biggest issue is with the warbands UI. This is extremely clunky. Unit control is a nightmare in this game. I mean, you don't even have direct control, but oh my...it's just messy.
- Gameplay: If you liked DK 2 you will like this one as well I guess. The game consists of separate elements.
1. Excavate a proper dungeon and mine gold
2. Build rooms to attract minions and do other stuff (rooms with 4 walls are more efficient I think)
3. Be sure your minions have everything they need (food, beer, place to sleep more or less is all they require).
This is the strategic management part of the game, which is followed by:
4. Click on a banner to send all your minions, previously created warbands or a certain type of minion (e.g. beasts) to a rally flag where they will try to defeat your enemy and not get horribly murdered in the process. Your minions are♥♥♥♥♥♥stupid. Combat is chaos. Eh.
5. Cast "heal" as often as your mana allows you to
6. After 2 minutes "delete" the rally flag so your minions won't rebel, because they are hungry or tired or whatever (if they are still alive).
Seriously, low level minions die like flies. And the only other spell I found really worth using was lightning bolt, when I was fighting enemies on my own turf, because it is cheap, does damage and stuns the target. Spells also have no cooldown. Of course there are more spells, but micromanaging spells and picking out single units in the melee is kinda not worth it. Just heal your minions or zap the enemy.
Apart from that you can also "research" new rooms, spells and traps. Traps are in my opinion one of the biggest wastes of time in this game. At least in the late game. They die almost instantly to level 10 creatures, even with a fort that heals them and makes them stronger. They are also expensive and "lock" some of your mana away. Rarely worth it. Focus on doors instead. Certain minions need to be working in certain rooms in order to create traps, doors, potions, rituals, or research, etc. You get the idea. If you want these minions safe when fighting or just to resume their day to day tasks, you can assign them to a "peace band", which is fidgety as hell.
Story and campaign: Since the initial release the campaign was heavily adjusted. Levels that were apparently a nightmare 1 year ago are now a pushover. I had to restart 2 levels at one point, because they caught me off guard. Apart from that the levels are really easy for the most part. They just take a while to complete usually. A difficulty selector would have worked wonders here.
All in all it's a fun little game, but it's definitely something you need to really love, so you can overlook all its flaws. The bad performance and the terrible battle controls make me wonder why anyone would want to play this game in Multiplayer. Also, we have 2016, why the hell is there no auto save feature? Get it for a discount perhaps. If you really want a new Dungeon Keeper. And of course you can still possess your minions, though it doesn't seem very worthwhile to do so most of the time.

I stumbled upon this when I was looking for an adventure game with an intriguing story, which is what I found and I'm glad I did.
Gemini Rue is a noir science fiction retro point and click adventure with a twist.
The first part of the game lets you switch between two characters: A cop with a dark past trying to find his brother, and a brainwashed prisoner trying to escape a rehabilitation facility.
The second part is the well executed conclusion of both of those stories.
The setting and ambience fit the overall theme very nicely, and the game does well in making you care for what happens to the characters.
The rare combat sequences are fun and don't feel, as one might fear in a point & click adventure, out of place at all. The soundtrack and voice acting is great too.
Everyone looking for a serious, thought-provoking story in the form of an adventure game should not ignore this gem, which is my new favorite non-comedic point and click.

TL;DR = Must be willing to commit MASSIVE amounts of time to progress, while fighting against RNG, and P2W disparity. Game would be fun if crafting wasn't an RNG grindfest, if it wasn't so gear dependent, and if P2W, Subscriber, F2P gap wasn't so vast.
The time listed on my steam page is inaccurate to how much time I actually spent playing it (a little over a year when it first came out).
This game is plain and simple pay to win (P2W) unless you have vast amounts of time to commit to the game in order side step the glaring disparities between subscribers / cashshop champions / and those playing for free. You can still play the game F2P but are SEVERELY limited by labor points and their regeneration. Even if you are subscribed it doesn't fully alleviate you of the true P2W nature of the game.
However, PvP is a cluster♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of stealthers and the gear differences between casual, hardcore, and P2W players is most rampant in this aspect of the game. Even as a full tank in plate, max level, and in the pity gear they give you for coming back I was being 1 shotted by DPS classes. The PvP is fast paced, but by that I mean that if you don't have a dedicated healer you will probably die in less than 5 seconds. Medium and Large scale PvP, you are basically dead as a nonstealth melee fighter. This is good and bad because it encourages you to stay in the backlines and protect the group but at the same time gets boring when you are just waiting for stealthers to pop out.
This game is 100% gear dependent and the success of making gear and being able to upgrade it or it being the type of the gear you are making to compliment the class you make is all RNG. This means you could have to make the same piece of armor hundreds of times before you are able to craft the piece to the highest level possible. This means that even if you have all the materials necessary to craft the armor to top tier, RNG can leave you spending days, weeks, months trying to craft a single piece to maximum potential. Of course this can all be made easier if you buy stuff for IRL $$$ but even still does not give you a guarnatee, only a slightly higher % margin to succeed. Even then you need the labor to craft what you need so unless you are P2W you wont have enough labor to get done everything you need to.
To own land you either have to subscribe or commit a vast amount of time juggling resources and what not to keep and maintain the land by generating taxes. This juggling becomes more and more of a time commitment the more land you have. The more land you have the more resources you can make to generate gold or for crafting.

I'm so glad I got this game as a part of a bundle. Even with the low price, I would advise you to stay away unless you're okay with mediocre gameplay, horrible storyline, and cheesy acting.
First of all, the gameplay wasn't bad; I'll give it that. The puzzles are decently challenging with the offer to skip and ask for hints on what to do next. That's all fine. For most of the puzzles, I didn't need the hint or skip buttons because they were simply too easy for me. I actually found myself using them to get through the game faster. There isn't much hidden object searching in this game though, so if that's what you're looking for, search elsewhere. The HOG system for this game isn't great; I'd rather the system in Mystery Case Files. The items are shown for this one and they usually don't even look the same when you find them because of the angle they're in.
The storyline, however, was out of a soap opera. It made no sense and there are way too many holes in the plot. Oh, someone's dying? Great, let me just solve a bunch of puzzles before I save his life even though in real life, he would be dead in 2 minutes. The cheesiness is REAL. The brought in a bunch of random characters for no reason and made some unnecessary choices to bring the story forward. The game DRAGS ON just for the sake of being longer, not because of storyline. And even with the dragging on, I still finished it in under 4 hours. It was just an unpleasant 4 hours.
The acting is cringeworthy. I muted the game pretty much the entire time I played because I couldn't stand the voice acting. The ambient sounds of the game were fine, but that's ALL you can hear. There's music once in a while, sure, but it was the same damn music each time and it's not even great music. Just decent, although kind of reminiscent of Goosebumps the TV Show.
Overall, I give this game at most a 5/10. The story makes absolute no sense, gameplay is mediocre, and acting is really horrible. The only thing keeping the score up is literally only the mediocre gameplay and mediocre graphics. I'd rather play a Nancy Drew game or Mystery Case Files.

Don't go out of your way for this one. Even if you got it in a bundle, don't bother. It's boring, predictable, oddly-paced, and leaves much to be desired on many levels. And while I've certainly played much worse, the cons heavily outweigh the pros here, and it's just not worth wasting 3 hours of your time.
Don't get me wrong, the game is not a 100% farm-fresh steaming pile. It sports some great background art, and a couple of game mechanics I haven't seen in HOPAs before (or since, considering the game is over 5 years old now), which would normally be a good thing. But they were ultimately too underwhelming in practice to be redeeming.
I was actually looking forward to playing this, too. But after a mere 15 minutes I was bored out of my mind and wondering how long it would take to complete, and if it would get any better or more interesting. It didn't.
You're a doctor who gets invited to a shady hotel in the middle of nowhere to treat a patient. But after the road washes out and traps you there along with other guests, the game dives face-first into a shabby murder mystery plot that felt less like an interesting story hook and more like like someone decided it'd be a cool idea to throw together out-of-context ideas from a few Stephen King novels, elements of
, and characters that may as well have been ripped from a bad Agatha Christie fanfic - topped off with a predictably weak "80's soap opera" style twist. The actual story that emerges from such an unholy union somehow manages to be mildly creepy enough to raise an eyebrow at, but it falls apart very quickly - in large part because of the writing.
The dialogue and item/scene flavor text are laughably dense, sprinkled with gems like "I prefer my freedom, but I'll take a cup of tea", or "I need to unlock this door" when looking at a suitcase. The protagonist is also
an idiot. You can practically hear the "WHOOSH" sound as clues and glaringly-obvious deductions fly over his head. None of the other characters are remotely likeable either, nor do you ever learn enough about any of them to care.
The overarching plot that our bumbling hero finally pieces together...well there are enough threads lying around to build a decent story, but the game doesn't package or sell it well. Sure, the 'mystery' is unravelled (even though you could call it from a mile away), but there simply isn't enough to tie all the people and story snippets together without resorting to a Deus Ex Sherlock "
" monologue at the end. The abruptness of the ending also doesn't help. I could overlook that if it at least played out as if there might be a sequel, but it doesn't. The scene following the Sherlock speech is strangely bittersweet (I give it points for the sheer level of irony), but just when it seems like it could get interesting, BAM, credits. No wrap-up narration/closure. I guess the weird conversation at the end was supposed to function as one.
Ok, enough about story.
I wish I could say that the hidden object scenes make up for the game's other weak points, but sadly they don't. I'll start with what they do right though.
+ Objects and clutter fit the scenes, and are things you'd expect to find in those areas, albeit placed a bit haphazardly.
+ Objects are smartly hidden. You're not given much to find, but some of it actually presents a bit of a challenge.
+ Multiple valid versions of objects. If you need to find a screw for instance, there may be 3 or 4 screws in the scene. In most HOPAs, you'd be expected to match the exact silhouette, or pick the one that's "most screwlike" (more common for mistranslated stuff). But here, any one of them would be fine to use. Two completely different-looking ties? Either one would count for the one tie you're supposed to find, even if it doesn't match the silhouette. It's basically adding more fitting clutter objects without being a troll about specifics.
But:
- Every scene has only 8 related objects to find (e.g. parts for a lawn mower)
- The 'lists' are not in text form, or even silhouette. Just grayscale versions of the items.
- All scenes are revisited at least once, some up to 3x over the course of the game
Seems like a short list, but the 8-items-only thing is a serious bummer. There's so much potential in the art style and background detail, and it's wasted in the name of making the scene as relevant as possible. That's a good thing when it comes to staying on track, but those silly lists are the reason why we play these games in the first place. Even if 75% of the items are totally nonsensical for what the protagonist needs, it's the hunting part that draws people. What fun is a "hidden object" game if it actively aims for as few hidden objects as possible?
Puzzles were far too easy. I solved several of them completely by accident, and only one or two required any thought. The puzzle window also poofs the second you enter the last move/digit/etc, so for some of them I didn't even know what I had accidentally gotten right. I also usually like to get a mental picture of the solution, so it was annoying to not even have enough time to hit the screenshot key (really, it's that fast). But that's a more personal nitpick.
I haven't laughed so much at the way characters move through scenes in a long time. Picture someone making a stop-motion walking animation using Barbie and Ken dolls (up to and including stiff limbs and Ken's abnormally wide shoulders), and you get the idea. (Okay fine, they're a BIT more fluid than that, but honestly not by much.) People also slide around the floor as they walk, tilt oddly when gesturing or holding things, and generally look like they're about to tip over.
I've also never seen such a jarring discrepancy in scale between actors and background. For instance, when the sheriff does his Ken-waddle into a room and stops near a pair of women's high heels, it shouldn't look like he could easily fit both feet into one and still have room for a small puppy. Character scale, perspective, and angles are so ridiculously wonky in front of such meticulously detailed backgrounds that it feels like a mashup of completely different games.
Unremarkable at best, grating at worst. There are a few spots in the game where there's a short loop of audio that I'm guessing is supposed to simulate things like outdoor critters, workshop noise, or whatever ambiance they were going for. But it gets annoying very fast when the clip is barely a few seconds long and on infinite replay.
Some SFX didn't seem to match their origin, and sounded weird or 'off'. Similar issue with the music. It tried to be suspenseful in some really strange places when nothing was going on. I ended up turning it off because the combined dissonance was starting to irk me.
Voiceovers were..ok I guess. Nothing bad, but nothing that stood out. Though it did add to the funny factor when characters were speaking AND moving ridiculously at the same time.
I'd say Mountain Crime comes off as a decent effort at producing a HOPA that at the very least takes itself seriously enough to keep everything as relevant as possible to the story they came up with. Most games at the lower quality end of the genre can barely boast a storyline, let alone a coherent one. So I give the devs props for that. The backgrounds are lovely (seriously guys, keep that artist on your payroll), and I'd love to see some of the more unique gameplay features of this title expanded on in the future.
But ultimately I would
say this game was 3+ hours of my time well spent. I was bored after 15 mins, and remained bored till the end.

This game, what can I say about this game. It is, effectively, my childhood in a capsule. Developed by Sonic Team, back when that was still considered a good thing, the parallels to a sonic game are definitely there, with chip collecting, high speed gameplay, and short but sweet boss battles feeling very similar to a traditional sonic from the Genesis era. The primary difference beyond theme is that there is an emphasis on aerial maneuvers and acrobatics as you float through the dreamscapes. It's not enough to simply go fast, you're meant to go fast with flourish. I originally played NiGHTS and the special holiday demo Christmas NiGHTS originally back on the Saturn, and the re-release does a lot to keep the charm and innocent magic of the original.
There are two graphical modes, the HD-Remaster and the classic Saturn graphics which, thankfully, share the same gameplay progression. The new HD mode looks quite nice and definitely makes a more modern, easier to stomach version of the game for people who might not carry the same level of nostalgia for the franchise, but I found myself playing through with the Saturn graphics most of the time, at least for the first run though. While I have not quite unlocked them yet, Christmas NiGHTS is also available in this release, which I believe was also given the same HD/Classic mode treatment. The one thing I found absent was the Nightopian collection (a small gallery of Nightopians you've come across in the game) but I'm hoping that will potentially be unlocked along with the Christmas NiGHTS portion. The rest of the gallery however appears intact and contains the all important Music selector.
All in all for newcomers NiGHTS provides a a weird little game that's fun, colorful and can just be picked up and enjoyed without worrying about investing hours of playtime or unlocks or anything like that. For those with a previous history with the game, its a unique portal back in time, which brings with it the same sense innocence and wonder the game has always drawn on.
Update: While I can confirm the Nightopian Collection did make it in, Christmas NiGHTS only unlocks as a remastered version without the Saturn option. They're still great levels though and easily the most memorable part of NiGHTS.

Gemini Rue is a pretty standard point-and-click adventure with a fantastic plot. It appears to be a straight and to-the-point point-and-click adventure game telling a story in a no-nonsense dystopian future involving a detective searching for his brother imprisoned within a testing facility. But when you learn that the facility is for rehabilitating criminals by wiping their memories and starting them with a fresh slate, it begins to make you question what makes us who we really are.
Despite being fairly low-res, the game does look good. However, it does not cooperate well with multi-monitors, the Steam overlay, and alt-tabbing. Also, the save system stores saves in two separate locations depending on how you launch the game. The actual point-and-clicking is fairly standard, but there are a few points in the game involving some really sub-par combat that the game could have gone without. These broken systems all make the game's presentation feel a lot cheaper and incredibly fragile to run. I'd rate this game higher if it wasn't for these issues, but they were so prevalent that it bugged me every time I played. If you can overlook functional bugs, definitely see your way through this game for a fantastic finale.

Mass Effect 2 represents a subtle shift in focus, tone, and overall feel from the first game, while improving upon it in many ways and adding a bevy of likeable characters and episodic stories to flesh out the universe. Continuing as your imported Shephard, you find yourself a part of the terrorist organisation Cerberus, with a new crew, new Normandy 1701-A, and new mission to take down the enigmatic and hitherto unmentioned Collectors.
While the first came was a slower, earnest affair, Mass Effect 2 feels amped up, more action-packed, and more impactful. The story is significantly weaker as your primary enemy is set up sloppily in the opening moments and their threat is largely resolved by the end of the game. There are also a total of 6 story missions while the bulk of the game is comprised of recruitment missions and loyalty missions, personal, episodic side stories that for the most part feel very unique, are well written, and provide great opportunity to role play and make impactful decisions. Each is somewhat isolated from the main story, and you can do them in almost any order. Some are mandatory and others not, though people may die if you miss content. Particular standouts involve Tali's loyalty mission in which she is on trial, Jacob's investigation of his father's crash site and sinister developments that have occurred there, and Jack's emotional return to the place that made her what she is. Weak elements include some weak characters (Jacob himself, certain Normany crew) and a very distinct segregation from the events of the first game. Minor decisions are carried over (e.g. random NPC you won't remember comes back here) while larger decisions and actions (e.g. proof of the reapers, who survived Virmire) have negligible impact. Cerberus, isolated cells of terrorists in the first game, are here represented as a sprawling, well-funded organization and one that Shephard quickly accepts working with. This is somewhat addressed in-game, but feels off, and the fact nobody else is investigating the reapers is flat out ridiculous. Also, as with Star Trek Into Darkness, Mass Effect 2 cures death itself but never mentions it again or uses to restore the deaths of main characters, any of whom can die based on your choices at the end. While a nice feature that makes the terrific final mission very intense, this means that those characters by design cannot have a huge impact in the larger story, as they may or may not exist beyond this game.
Gunplay feels tighter though, multiple locations are incredibly well-realized, and some side missions continue threads started in the first game and concluded in the third (the geth, the genophage).
All that said, Mass Effect 2 feels like playing through a fun sci-fi series that builds toward a great final episode, but is entirely swept aside by season 3.

Excellent port. One of the best re releases for a Sega game period.
The gameplay is pretty much similar to Sonic. You fly and pass through rings, and you have two forms of attacks. The spin, and the para loop. To do the para loop, you simply move NiGHTS around in a form of a circle, and with the para loop, you can use it to defeat bad guys and get bonus points.
The music in this game is fantastic. One of the best soundtracks for Sega games, and I cannot get enough listening to the theme when fighting NiGHTS and Reala.
The controls are smooth, but as for graphics go, it can get disorienting when moving around, thinking you are able to move in 3D, but it's designed to be in a 2D perspective. When you play the game, you will know what I mean.
All in all, its a good port, but if you are not sure, I recommend you buy it on a sale.

40 hours of playing NiGHTS into Dreams. All I can say is I ABSOLUTELY LOVE IT!
The gameplay may look boring, inane, or weird but if you give it a try, I promise you will love it. If you are a SEGA or Sonic fan, you have no excuse not to purchase it. It should be illegal not to buy it if you adore sonic.
NiGHTS will always be my favorite game. I've never had so much fun playing a video game.
The soundtrack is just gorgeous. The album version is better! It comes with two alternative songs for each level.
The gameplay is difficult to explain, to be honest. Your objective is to collect 20 orbs as fast as you can. With the reminding time, your goal is to gain as much points as possible by flying through hoops without losing your chain.
My only comaplains are the boss battles, 6 long levels (around ten minutes long) and locked at 30FPS. In addition, I did not like the boss battles. They may be advance during their time, but I found them ambiguous to beat.
However, eventually, you will want to try again and again to beat your scores. NiGHTS has that feeling like playing a Sonic game.
It comes with bonus features like the SEGA Saturn version and a remastered christmas theme of Spring Valley.
Overall, if you see this game on sale, its a must purchase game. You will love it!

So I had played warframe on the PS4 about a year or so ago and only gave it a minor glance.  Upon trying it on the pc, I regret not giving this game a chance much sooner.  It is not only a prime example of what a good F2P economy can be, but it also shows just how much a development team can accomplish when focused on specific features within the game.  Combat is amazing, with dozens of options open to players, and more unlocked as you progress through the game.  A deep lore that unlocks as you naturally progress, and systems so deep that you can spend hours working on them and feel like your scratching the surface.  The major selling point for me though has been the community.  I've played countless other online games and have had interactions from ok to downright vile and toxic.  I've grouped with dozens of people I've never met before, and everyone has been friendly, willing to help and amazing to talk too.  I look forward to many more hours with this game, and to see what they come out with next.

Extremely well-written point and click game. I personally find this game superior to Telltale's The Walking Dead in terms of storytelling. It has good pacing. Being a point and click certainly helped as there are no filler scenarios. There no sudden surprise wrap-up endings. The story's twist isn't cliche, and not entirely expected or unexpected.
Aesthetically, the use of dark colors and constant rain give it a sort of noir detective feel and the retro look kind of aids with the game's overall themes. Being science fiction, you can expect discussion about identity, which the game discusses very well and gives you a lot to think about. It doesn't end in a clean manner and does not shove morals down your throat. The soundtrack is a mix of trcks that sound very sci-fi in nature, and some somber jazz tunes.
Most puzzles were pretty straight-forward, though the combat mechanics feel a little out-of-place and take some getting used to. The gameplay isn't what makes the game attractive though. If you're looking for a game with an excellent story, you should definitely pick up Gemini Rue.

I've spent waaaaay too much time in this game whether modding or playing it.
This game certaintly has a hard learning curve but once you understand it the game is incredible.  I recommend choosing the Canary islands and speeding up the game for around 30 years and then saving and reentering as a random person in the world.  It is incredibly satisfying seeing the insanity that is possible and slowly working your way up the ranks.
Even aside from the world the game brings, if you don't like medieval Europe then get a mod that is a post-apocalyptic North America or Skyrim or Game of Thrones.  You can add magic, werewolves, and many other assortment of Fantasy beings.  There's a mod that completely transforms the game into the space age.  Counties are now worlds and it adds a ton more content with all new cultures and religions.
Even better than all that, if you don't like a small part of the game, even part of a mod, you can just take it out.  The coding language is incredibly easy to grasp and you can remove or change pretty much everything in the game.  The only real downside of the coding side of things is the fact that there aren't really many guides out there and the ones that are out there are kind of lame and lack support.  That is all forgiven by me though as you can easily reference other mods and the game code itself to see how they do things.
To add even onto that the console in the game is well done with numerous commands.  If you want to cheat you can cheat and if you want to play legit you can play legit.
I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who has some time and the small commitment to learn the game.

This is a pretty fun game, but its got some issues.
Its Ark with a different gimmick.  Instead of dinos there are Thralls, which are NPC slaves you have to kidnap.  There is also religion, which has some fun mechanics including the games ultimate siege weapons, Avatars.
The other parts - gathering, building, levelling - are very similar to Ark.  Conan does these parts a tad better if I had pick.
The devs are extremely active.  They have heeded players, patched daily at the start, dropped a large patch a few days later, and they are focusing on the right issues.
As for issues for concern, there are a few.  The tech is primitive (which I love) but so is the combat (which I do not).  They added some mechanics (power attack, dodge, main and offhand weapons, throwing weapons) but most of them dont add much or aren't useful enough to do over spam clicking.
Its pretty fkn laggy, but its also early in the early access.  They have already made steps forward here but if this really bothers you I would advice waiting.  Desync, FPS lag, latency, its all there!
The raiding is... I dont know man.  Im not sure its ever going to be fun or add much to the game.  You have to either build a cheese base on the tip of a mountain or you're getting foundation wiped.  Lots of people getting wiped so hard they leave the server/game.  Of course there are PvE servers, servers with base damage turned off, and solo-play if this really offends you.
ANYWAY pretty fun game.

2013 review:
Though I haven't finished the game, I really enjoy playing it. It has huge nostalgia factor for those who've played on Dreamcast, but even if you didn't (like me), the artwork, music, and map designs give off a feel that's jazzy, urban and futuristic all at once. Something about it seems timeless. I also love the soundtrack, which is an amazing and a core part of the game.
One cool thing about PC version is that you can import custom graffiti into the steam app folder. I got a real kick out of that. I mention analog stick because the controls port horrendously to PC, so USING A GAMEPAD IS A MUST. You can, however, fullscreen the game resolution to 1080p.
Your goal is to go around tagging the city--and occasionally, other gang members--while performing jump tricks to rack up points. All you're doing is tagging and exploring within a time limit, so sometimes it gets tedious. Also, there is no variety control-wise besides using the analog stick to spray paint since "tricks" are performed automatically while jumping. Other ways to earn points is to find Soul Graffiti emblems. Some of them were difficult to grab and made me ragequit.
Overall, it's a silly and charming game that's still pretty fun despite being so old. I'd say get it when it's $5 or less.

This game is cute, charming, and polished.
Why the thumbs down, then, you ask?
The answer is that the game, while cute, lacks strategic depth and is not worth the $30 price point. The rooms are unbalanced and there is a clear setup to spam in order to win every game. The maps and scenarios are not varied enough to feel like a new game each time. It leverages upon nostalgia for dungeon builders past and does not substantially innovate. There are some QoL issues: for example, feedback loops are tenuous and it is not always clear why a dungeon inhabitant is unhappy.
I think that this game may become worth it at the $15-20 price point, since it was quirky and kept me entertained for a little while. If you're into this sort of game, I would recommend waiting for a sale.

The first thing I learned about NiGHTS when I first played it is that it is virtually impossible to explain what it is through text or even videos. It is just so far from anything else out there that there's no base to compare it to. The reviews and gameplay videos I'd watched beforehand had done little to give me a mental image of what it actually is, so it was still largely a mystery to me when I finally got to try it.
My best attempt at an explanation is as follows: it's an arcade-style pseudo-platformer which revolves around semi-free flight through a 3D environment on a shifting 2D plane. You collect floating orbs with the goal of gathering 20 of them as quickly as possible, which allows you to break open a bigger glass orb once you find it and enter a bonus mode in which you try to collect as much stuff as you can and return to the start (the 2D path forms a convoluted loop) before the timer runs out. Each time you do this, the 2D path which you travel along will shift to incorporate different parts of the 3D world. After completing 4 such paths, you leave the main world to fight a boss; the faster you defeat the boss, the more your score will be multiplied, and the better your letter grade for the world will be (with one of the game's 100%-completion goals being landing the A rank on every level - which is no easy task!).
Recommended if you're looking for a break from the norm that won't be a huge time-consumer. That said, it might be good to wait for a sale, as for all the incredible uniqueness it offers, it is sadly quite short with only six normal levels and a seventh shorter level.

I honestly cannot believe that I'm writing a negative review, yet here I am. The first two acts are incredible, beautifully polished and complete. The third act starts to get a bit weak, having a tendency towards very specific paths to continue, unlike the previous acts which give immense freedom in how you play and your choices mattering. The fourth act is nothing short of a trainwreck, critical pieces of information being easily missed (a book lying on a table in a completely optional area) and in one case, spoiling parts of the plot itself by giving me incorrect journal entries.
Ultimately, if you can put aside the huge drop in quality as the game progresses, it nets to be a fantastic game, unfortunately, I'm not one of those people. The later acts were nothing but pure frustration for me, and by the time I had finally finished, I had forgotten about the fun that I actually did have in the previous acts.
In short, since there isn't a mixed option, I have to recommend against it, but if you can get over the quality drop, it's well worth the price, otherwise wait until a sale.
