Amazing RPG, very engrossing in all aspects.
Great story, likeable characters, combat makes you think, and decent loot system.
Two big gripes about the game
1. Loot progression is somewhat borked. It's not very noticeable mid game, but early (levels 1-5) and lategame items (levels 18 to 20) are extremely level dependent. Even Divine/Unique level 18 gear is sometimes not worth keeping over merely rare level 20 gear as the raw defensive or offensive stats are simply subpar. Same goes for early game gear. You won't be able to fight necessary enemies to progress through an area without equipping your party with a certain level of weapons (actual rarity doesn't seem to matter).
2. Awful skill bar managment. Not customizable, and gets extremely cluttered in the midgame to endgame. Newly acquired skills seemingly fill up whatever blank spot is left on the bar. Need some options to customize what goes on the bar and what does not.

Pros.
- A lot, and I mean a LOT, of customization.
- Simple stage building.
- Several different gamemodes.
- Quite a lot of technical variables for building.
- Rather nice community.
- The samples can quickly teach you how to use every part in the game, and how to build things like mechs and walkers.
Cons.
- Finding servers is a gamble. Most of the time, I'll only ever find two servers open.
- The combat isn't very-well developed. It seems all combat-based servers are entirely free-for-all.
- Not a lot to do in singleplayer.
- The optimization needs a bit of work. Dropped to 10 fps on a server with ~20 players, most using reasonably medium-sized machines.
- You can expect your stuff to break from each update. Played before it was on Steam, transferred a rather-complex artillery tank to the Steam version, only to find that weight and piston strengths were changed, effectively breaking the main gun on the tank.
- The descriptions of certain functions and parts can be
vague at times, but this is most likely from machine translations.
I really like this game, but I do not find it to be a replacement to Robocraft, not in the slightest.
Overall, 7.5/10, because it can still use some more polishing.

The first question many people ask is whether or not this game is better than Ark. It is in many ways and not in others. The visual experience is far better in this game and even though it was just released not too long ago, in my opinion the graphics of Conan have already surpassed where Ark is at.
In Conan Exiles, instead of taming Dinos like you do in Ark you will go out and knock NPCs out that will become known as a thrall once you break their mind. They can be placed around your base to protect it and will attack anyone that isn't you or in your clan. I was intrigued by this feature when I started playing and it is AWESOME. It's so hilarious  running up to someone, knocking them out, and then tieing them up and dragging them away to your base to become your slave.
The building in this game is much better than in Ark and it is SO easy. If you are on a server with base settings and no gathering multipliers and can take a little while to get the materials you need but in my experience I had a base up that could protect the stuff I gathered effectively in about 30 minutes.
If you haven't played Ark before buying this game there is a learnign curve and some people will have a difficult time figuring out the game. But, for the ones who did come from Ark, this is literally almost the exact same inteerface and you will have no trouble getting started.
So far, the community has been great and are very forthcoming in answering any questions that I may have. Nobody has destroyed my base while I was offline ( Although this may just be that I was lucky in the server I chose).
Finally, there are quite a few bugs in the game. But it is still in early access and the devs have been very fast at fixing any bugs that are discovered and reported to them. Within the past couple of days I have seen 2 updates roll out one after the other fixing significant bugs and adding new content. It's always a good sight when you see an active development team that actually listens to its customers and wants to see them satisfied.
I recommend buying this game and I hope to see you in the wasteland exile. :D

A noire sci-fi thriller point-n-click which asks the question; what makes us who we are? Our memories? Our environment? Our friends?
Assassin turned cop, Azriel Odin, seeks to find out what happened to his brother in New Pittsburgh after the Gemini War.
Delta-Six wakes up in a mysterious facility alongside other patients. Having no recollection of his past or his identity, he must find out why he is in this facility and how he can escape.
The player can take control of both characters at anytime (except for the beginning) until he is finished that "chapter," if you will, only to switch back to the other character to complete their "chapter."
The puzzles can be difficult, but never tedious. A few may be frustrating or rely on small items within the environment, but still very doable if you pay attention to detail.
This roughly 8-9 hour game starts slow, but when it picks up, it picks up hard and fast. A definite must play for anyone seeking a great story and/or a noire/sci fi game. 9/10

There is FAR too much to say about Oblivion to do it justice, so I'll say it in terms of total gameplay: try approximately 225 hours.  That's how long it took me to get through the main quest because there were too many interesting side quests and caverns or bunkers to raid to stay away!  The game is presented so well and really gives you a sense of being in an alternate world.  My main complaints are that it's buggy and crashes somewhat often; that combat in upper levels can sometimes be tedious because the stronger enemies level up with you; and that it can be really hard to get started because it's so vast and so open, with little in the way to guide you.  That's part of the fun, though; for the most part, you can just pick a quest or a path and go with it.  Play it for a few hours, and I can almost guarantee you'll be hooked.  It's definitely a great way to get ready for the new sequel, Skyrim, as well.  Oblivion is one of the great RPGs of our generation, and of gaming as a whole.

As you escape the first dungeon and you are free to explore the whole continent of the imperial city, you know that you adventure will be grand!
As most Elder Scrolls games the main story has some hick-ups from the start. You are just a messenger and the main characters really do their best to keep you as emotionly detached as possible.
But as the main story progresses you explore the land and more side stories manage their way into your path. These stories really are so lifely and bring more depth to the world as a whole.
The gameplay is solid, but lots of people keep telling me "Morrowind was much better".

For me, this happened in Morrowind, but in Oblivion they got rid of those "useless stats" as I call them. For it greatly improves the gameplay.
Last but not least a flaw, is the character creation, for a game that revolves around you as a character, the creation of it is abysmal. The more you tweak the more chance you have to ruin your character. They really improved this in Skyrim.
Overall I grade this game a 8,5/10

A fun game, although I felt the ending was rushed and disappointing.  I got a few hours of play for less than a dollar, though, so I'm not complaining too much!  The storyline kept me guessing on a couple of points, although the 'twist' of who the protagonist is became obvious fairly early.
I enjoyed the puzzles, and most were not too difficult although I had to use some trial and error for a couple.  The hidden object scenes were a little different from most other games of this type that I've played - instead of working from a list, there is a 'wheel' of objects to find that will result in either putting together something you need, or causing something else to happen in the scene that reveals your objective (I did have to laugh at the hot air balloon!).  In most scenes there were several similar objects, so you had to find the right one - for example you need a glove, but there are a few gloves strewn around so which do you choose?  As far as I can tell there were no penalties for misclicks (and there are no achievements), so if you have trouble there's no harm in clicking all the gloves!
All in all, a fun game for the price although I would probably recommend picking it up at a discount if you can.

Recommending
is a difficult task because, well, it's aged... not so well in certain aspects. Oblivion was an absolute treasured jewel in my childhood, so it's easy for me to look past the potato graphics and outdated gameplay, but just as I have trouble playing
, newcomers to Oblivion can expect trouble as well.
The main problem is the biggest: its gameplay. There's no getting around it: combat sucks. It was servicable then, but it's horrendously outdated at this point. Your sword feels like a foam toy from Walmart as you swing around chipping away tiny bits of health. You'll find yourself knocking hundreds of arrows just to kill one leveled monster, making the corpse look akin to a pin cushion. In essence, weapons and combat have no weight. It's seemingly straightforward (you swing your sword at an enemy) and there
a level of depth (in both combat and magic combat), but overall, it isn't a very exciting experience.
Art styles can make or break a game, and, thankfully, Oblivion's graphics are painted with a very warm pallete. Unfortunately, the game is also ugly as sin--especially its much made fun of models. Besides the rather ugly graphics, the world itself is a bland collection of plains, hills, and trees, trees, trees. The diversity just isn't really there, and while it was extremely exciting back in 2006, it isn't too impressive now.
All of this negativity, yet there's a thumbs up. Well, that's because Oblivion is still an utterly
RPG that, if I may be so bold to say, has some of the greatest writing found within an RPG. It's obviously not
level writing, but the sheer creativity found within the questlines and side quests is astounding. Seriously, with quests ranging from entering a painting to rescue a trapped artist, to investigating a string of vampire murders when the victims aren't vampires at all, to being locked in a mansion with five other guests, all of which you must murder yourself, to a grand heist pulled off on the jewel of the Empire, Oblivion features a wide diversity of interesting and unique quests that are well worth your time.
As I mentioned before, there is depth to Oblivion hidden within its mechanics. The ability to craft and create your spells, to combine various levels of enchantments to create bizarre results, to mixing and matching ingredients to fuel interesting potions--Oblivion will let you fight with a sword and shield, but it allows you to go as deep as you want to twist combat into a feeble matter.
Overall, Oblivion is a deeply flawed, yet well written and mechanically detailed RPG experience that should be experienced, should you be brave enough to fight through its rather mundane combat and outdated world. Over ten years and I will vehemently defend that this game stands up stronger than even
and
in terms of interesting writing and quests.

An absolute classic from twenty years ago, this game essentially was a fore-runner to Total War, having both a strategic campaign screen and a RTS tactical screen (as primitive as it was) for battles.
Strangely enough, coming back to this after having played Civ 4 Colonization, it dawns on me that the Civ 4 Colonization formula is basically identical to Lord of the Realms 2 (population doubles as economy and military, direct control over agriculture, buying mercenaries from either your home port or your army creation screen, etc.). Had Civ 4 Col been made in 1996, it would have been awesome, but alas.
Lord of the Realms 2 is the grandparent, conceptually, of a number of games today. Total War especially owes a lot to the ideas of Lord of the Realms 2: strategic screens that lead into tactical screens, city management, random events (Black Death, finding extra grain, etc.), and even very rudimentary diplomacy were all present in Lord of the Realms 2 already back then, and most of these ideas quickly found their way into the basic Total War formula.
Lord of the Realms 2 is probably as important to PC strategy gaming as Quake was to FPS games, or Final Fantasy was to RPGs. In all these cases, these games weren't necessarily the first of their kind, but they introduced key mechanics, ideas, or quality standards that became visible in almost every game in the genre that followed.

"If there's one game I regret never creating, it was "NiGHTS".
—Shigeru Miyamoto
For those of you who never had the Saturn, NiGHTS is one of the handful of games from that era that represents the glory days of SEGA and Sonic Team. The colors are vibrant, and the soundtrack is cheerful, unique, and quirky with some tracks being surprisingly ambient. The story is told without words using only music, cinematics, and imagery.
In game, you control the titular androgynous character who flies around on a twisting and turning track, sort of like one of those remote controlled racecar tracks. The controls themselves are simple and effective. NiGHTS has it's flaws, the biggest offender being the camera which will sometimes have trouble keeping up with NiGHTS or will "cleverly" hide point collectibles in such a way as to make you fly at an awkward angle to be able to see them.
Overall, NiGHTS is a very charming unique game that is worth a try .This HD remake also includes bonus content in the form of  Christmas NiGHTS, which is a fun little remix of one of the first stages.

Probably my favourite game from the Sega Saturn/PS1/N64 era; perhaps even my favourite game ever! The game is simple in concept; you play as Nights, an androgynous jester that inhabits the land of dreams, and assist 2 children in collecting "ideya", which represents a core personality trait such as courage, kindness etc...
In gameplay terms, this means starting in a 3D level as one of the children, with Nights locked in a magical cage behind you. At this point you may explore a little, but there is a strict time limit represented by an alarm clock that will attempt to wake you up and end the dream. Once you walk to Nights you will fuse with him and can then begin collecting ideya.
This is played out via the 2.5D mechanic that was popular back then; though the levels are 3D Nights' flight through the levels is set, with the player moving left to right collecting 20 ideya and depositing it in a cage to release the aspect. Rinse and repeat a further three times along different routes through the level, and then fight a boss.
It is an uncomplicated design and there are only 7 levels total, but the main focus is on score attack so there are plenty of opportunities to replay the courses and improve. What elevates the game to classic status is in the overall design; the levels are dreamlike and varied, and each course throws up interesting twists, such as rollercoasters, or Nights transforming into a toboggan on the snow levels.
The music is absolutely phenomenal; transforming from soft and ethereal to driving and dramatic as levels progress, with a cute theme song to top it off. This complexity earned the soundtrack a comparison to Disney by several reviewers at the time.
The game also introduced the A-Life system, which was eventually expanded into the Chao of Sonic Adventure. Creatures called Nightopians populate the levels, and your interaction with them can change their attitude towards you and eventually change the level and music in subtle ways.
The story is minimal but effective; a simple introduction for each child detailing the reason for their nightmares and an ending cinematic for each also, plus an extra scene when both child's levels have been completed. All the scenes play out without voice, so the story is entirely visual. Despite this, it manages to have a very touching end that truly fits the "Disney film" aesthetic that was reference by reviewers.
I heartily recommend this title; I imagine that it will not be as enthralling as it was to me as a child, but the core mechanics still stand up to scrutiny. This release includes updated textures from the PS2 rerelease of the game (only in Japan) so it is not strictly HD quality, but the bonus "Christmas Nights" game that was given out in '97-'98 as a demo of sorts is included, and is jolly good fun at Christmastime, especially if you have children.

The Good: You'll carve out your dungeon from the cavernous earth and build various rooms to attract minions through gateways to do nefarious functions. Libraries attract warlocks, barracks attract gnarlings and so on. Some extra features for better micromanagement of your dungeon have been added like flagging certain important minions to ignore war banner calls as well as control groups to better focus your evil armies. Still, a well stocked dungeon will mostly take care of itself, the imps marvelous in their task of stomping out any lumps. New tabs and functions have also been added allowing you to gain alternate functions from dungeon keeper utility (i.e. restore earth to pretty up your dungeon or plug holes), various potions you can brew to various affects, and sanctuaries to charge diabolical rituals. There are also Titans, super units to help defend or destroy encroaching enemies, allowing to spearhead bastions your rabble cannot otherwise reliably take on.
The Bad: There is a sort of tech tree (The Veins of Evil) added and while I can see its function in multiplayer, its placement in singleplayer was rather odd. You unlock points (Sins) at your library, but often I'd have more points than I could spend and the new things I'd unlock could feel haphazard at times. While the dungeon takes care of itself, it still has the same problems as previous Dungeon Keeper games that things might actually be screwed up and you'll have no notion till it's far too late. Or conflicted AI--though usually behaved when a war banner was down. Minions are back to being instantly dropped without worry about fall recovery (ala DK1) but when fighting enemy Underlords could exhibit the problem of a fleshy combatant vs an AI on how well they can micro. Still, I only needed to retry a few missions a second time and the overall campaign clocks in at around 13 hours. Unfortunately it seems a bit short and that they should have spaced it out more or had more interesting side missions. Also the ending is kind of lackluster.
TLDR:
Overall I'd give it an 8/10. A must have for fans of the old Dungeon Keeper but still a number of flaws remain.

There's not much on the market for co-op, turn-based games. This game is much more fun with a friend, but it is wrought with bugs and poor design decisions. I am playing on tactician mode.
For one, being on high ground is advantageous, but enemies seem to be able to melee strike you despite being 15 feet below you.
Secondly, it seems like every single enemy type has some sort of teleport, jump, strong melee attack, and a ranged attack. So every fight is the same (minus differing terrains). You can get to high ground but everything can reach you and hit you without much trouble. There are crocodiles that throw magical boulders and dogs that shoot bolts from back-mounted crossbows. Every humanoid seems to have the polymorph flying ability. Making all enemy types essentially the same doesn't make the game "hard," it just makes it stupid. How can I employ strategy when everything can fly and shoot me from wherever they are?
Third, line-of-sight seems to be screwy. Many times, I will be on high ground with no line-of-sight on something below, and yet that something can still shoot me in the face with arrows.
Fourth, the physical and magic armor system make it impossible to crowd control off the bat. Everything needs to be damaged first. It blows that my partner does physical damage and I do magical damage... it's like whittling away at two different health bars for the same monster.
Several other issues, but these are the most glaring ones. I would wait until this game gets some more patches in before shelling out forty some dollars for it.

The reason why I got this game in the first place was because of seeing the screenshots and hearing the stories of the adventures you could end up having in the game. The game ugh, the game has its moments but as much as it pains me to say this, the game is just innately flawed and broken that it takes away any fun from the positive aspects of the game.
So what are these positive aspects then. Well the aforementioned adventures and stories you can have. I distinctly remember in one of my multiplayer sessions the legendary scandals and rambunctious activities of King Arkantos and Duke of Lancaster. Playing spy against neighboring kingdoms and engineering the fall of empires. It was a jolly good time, even some of the less notable stories and adventures bring back fond memories of the game and has obviously made me come back for dozens of hours on end to see if they would give me the spark of enjoyment in the game. This can stem from those adventures or social engineering dynasties, both of which are incredible in depth and sheer fun factor. However...
… The game is fundamentally flawed in other areas. So let us start with the elephant in the room: Combat. To put it short, it sucks. To put it a little longer, its worse than
navel combat, and thats saying a lot since
naval combat/AI is one of the worst implemented features ive ever seen in a video game. In
, if you have more troops you win, no depth, no worrying about composition, no real difference other than remembering that heavy troops are marginally better than light troops for obvious reasons. In other lesser games, this might be alright, but for a game made by developers who are known for making complicated in depth strategy games with in depth combat systems, this is something that needs to be called out.
Another thing that needs to be called out is the RNG in the game. RNG is pervasive in video games, but no where has it been more obvious as this game, its almost as bad as
in this respect. Whereby everything is on an RNG dice roll and you cant control anything essentially, you just need dumb luck to get you through the game. For a strategy game, this is bad. Strategy games are about taking control over forces and leading them to glory, prestige, victory, even despite sometimes overwhelming odds all the while using your own wit and intelligence to accomplish this goal. But in
, just by creating a larger stack of troops will win you any battle, and you have next to no control over your kingdom because its too busy being determined for you with die rolls in the background.
While I hate making comparisons between games, I feel like it is inevitable with this game. Most of the game's mechanics are so dumbed down and simplified it gives you no control over how you truly manage your realm. Heck, even
had more options for how to control your kingdom than this game, and that was a “visual novel-esque” game. While on the opposite side of the coin,
has better realm management and combat mechanics. I might hear you say that EU4 doesnt allow you to control your individual government members. While this is true, you dont play as the government, as you play more of an overseeing entity (There was a steam review that jokingly referred to you as a wizard), so you let the government take care of the micromanagement. While in CKII you ARE the King or Queen, but the game sits idly by and doesn't make you feel like you are truly the one in charge of it all. Maybe it was this way for “historical reasons”.
But then why does the game always play out in an ultra ahistorical mode, where the muslims and the norse take over all of europe. Im not saying it has to play out like
here, but even events and balencing to make the game take on even a seemingly historical edge would be a great start to making it more bearable. Instead you got the Muslims and Norse attacking everything that moves, and certain “historical characters” who do not die when they should very well be dead. The game lacks any sort of balance in any sensable area. Nothing to push the game a certain truly historical route, and making it so those “historical dynasty” characters live forever.
Honestly, this is a dynasty simulator. Its not a strategy game, or a kingdom management game, its just a game about simulating your dynasty. Despite what the storepage tells you, it never plays out like that in my experience. The game's cons drain any fun the game can give you, and end up leaving you with an empty husk of a game, where all you got left is your dynasty, and bah now you got pneumonia and died.

Shorter Version:
This game attempts to compete with Robocraft's design and fails miserably at it. The GUI is hard to understand, even with the F1 help menu, building isn't as easy as it should be and controls are even worse. To top it all off, some weapons are just overpowered and some are very underpowered.
Your machine can only fire in the direction that your bot is facing if you're using a blaster, making it difficult to get those excellent shots. Lock-on rockets always tend to hit the ground, even if the opponent is grounded the entire duration of the projectile flight.
Longer Version:
1. GUI. The graphics interface looks like it came from an old Flash game. When the game starts you have a bunch of buttons on all sides of the screen, all with words. In the center is a 'MachineCraft' logo and your currently selected machine. When you click on the 'Link' buttons in the bottom, it brings up a bunch of tutorials. We all love tutorials right? Well turns out that 'Link' actually meant URL Link. That's right my friend, it opens up YouTube videos! It's sort of a let down that you have to watch a video in order to learn to play. Players that prefer in-game tutorials will not be pleased.
2. Building. Clicking on 'Build' takes you to the building garage. If you didn't do the tutorial your first look would will have you going 'huh?' Once you start to build your own machine, you might get confused with the interface. I know I did at first but I soon got used to it. One thing that is great about the game is that you can customize just about anything. A not so great thing is you have to customize simple things such as if a wheel should roll or if a hinge should be allowed to bend. My first and only build was a Launcher Tower. I skipped the moving mechanics and decided I only wanted to build a building but I added the launchers so I'd have some kind of weapon. Plus they were pretty. Another thing I don't like is that when I went to test the tower with rotators attached, guess what? I forgot to tell the rotators they need to... you guessed it... rotate!
3. Mobility. Maybe adding an anti-gravity device to the tower wasn't such a bright idea. But I became determined to make it hover. Turns out a **** looking structure won't stay upright. I was saddened when the tower tilted and became limp. After a while I gave up and decided to use thrusters. Thrusters, my friends, are a pain in the ***. Not only do I need to tell the bottom thrusters to go up, I need to put thrusters that will know to go down and every other direction. With a thin tower and not much room to place other thrusters, I scrapped that idea and gave up with adding something to move the tower around. If you like to tell your movement devices what they should actually be doing, this game is for you.
4. Combat. So I get into this match with a bot and I'm all like, I'mma kill you! I load up those plasma rockets and before I could fire. My tower blew up. I looked at the bots life, looked at mine. Look at the bots machine, looked at mine... thin was not the way to go. So I decided to use the pre-made bot to try combat. Match started and I'm so used to looking at my target with a crosshair that I didn't even notice there was no crosshair. I fired but the cannons shot forward. I turned the machine and fired again. Okay so the starting bot doesn't have **** for aiming. I found the button for plasma and decided to use that. Plasma fires at full energy, heads to the bot, the bot glides on the ground, the plasma hits the floor. I shot another, plasma hits the floor. So I'm like, great. My weapons took a♥♥♥♥♥♥on me. If you're one of those players like me and you prefer your weapons not to be stupidly dumb, this game is not for you.
5. Multiplayer. I went online to play. Turns out there's not many people who do play online and the ones who do sit afk. Maybe it was the time I was online or maybe not many people actually play this game. One thing is for sure, if you're expecting to go head-to-head with someone. Expect a lot of 'show your machine off' rooms.
Overall I would not recommend this game to anyone. It has a few great things but not enough to weigh out the bad things.

I'm going to be honest here; I didn't like the first Original Sin.  I found the combat surprisingly clunky, the "two protagonist" playstyle akin to mashing action figures together as a child and the NPCs bland and empty.  Just everything about it wasn't as good as the raving crowds claimed.
This?  This is amazing.  This is so far one of my favorite PC RPGs I've ever played...and I'm old enough to remember the original Ultima and Gold Box DnD games.  Most areas and quests have multiple solutions and you're not really punished for taking one over the other.  There are a few areas where lockpicking is basically required but besides that stealth, conversation or brute force are typically viable options to dealing with a problem.  Combat feels tactical (something most RPGs frankly don't really do anymore) with your choices in positioning, abilities and terrain manipulation meaning the difference between victory or defeat more often than just pure stats.  With careful planning you can beat groups of enemies better geared and higher levels than you, though it's still unlikely as one lucky crit can one shot a character.  There are very few mindless "throw away" battles once you leave the tutorial island.  Almost every encounter will be an actual fight for your life.
There are some areas the game can be improved further.  While your companions will pipe up more and put more of their character on display than the original, it's not quite enough.  The process in which it happens is sterile and lacks organic interaction.   Instead of the NPCs talking as if the other NPCs were standing around them, they spout their one line and that's it.  If, say, the Red Prince spoke to Fane or Sebille during the journey it would go a long way to viewing them as characters instead of interchangable henchmen that happened to have a  bit of backstory or a sidequest attached. So yes, as much as people like to♥♥♥♥♥♥on Bioware...this could benefit by being more like Bioware in that regard.
Another complaint is I never feel like I'm at the point I'm supposed to be at with gear.  I consistantly feel like I'm a few levels behind with my armor and health offering a totally negligable amount of protection with some enemies wiping my party before I even get a turn.  I don't even know how the game can really "fix" this other than perhaps tossing in an NPC somewhere explaining that each level gives shops DRAMATICALLY better gear and the difference between level 10 and level 12 is roughly 150% increase in defense.
Oh and do ignore the publications out there that act like plaiyng Undead is sooo hard.  You literally NEVER have a reason to not be in full armor and you can easily heal from poison damage and poison potions.  It's really not a challenge at all.
Edit and Addtions:  I had originally complained at some poor coding regarding playing a non-origin character and how playing an undead PC made the game think you were Fane leading to some broken quests and ridiculous immersion breaking dialogue.  It seems since launch most of these issues have been patched and some major story moments have been reworked.  It's disappointing they were in the game at all as I can't fathom why anyone would WANT to play as an "origin" companion instead of a real character and why playing a real character would end up being so buggy but...that's just me.

Gemini Rue is a short but impressive retro-style point and click adventure game. It presents itself in a very Blade Runner/Cowboy Bebop-ish style, which clicks well with the fresh storyline and atmospheric music. I'm a big tower defense fan and this is a very solid tower defense game. Certainly near the top of all the ones I've played. Probably the best 2D one.
I'd say if you like tower defense games then it's arguably worth the full $10 price. On sale it is 100% worth it.
+There is a good variety of towers/ traps.
+There is a fairly large selection of maps (most of the map is shown in one of the screenshots), which can be made bigger with workshop/ mod maps.
+Almost no flyers (-they add flying enemies on the last two maps >_>)
+Every map has an endless mode.
+Unlocking endless requires being a level with 6 difficulty modifers so it encourages repeat plays.
+Difficulty modifiers for increased XP and variation of play.
+There is a modifier which decreases difficulty so for those who want to just have some fun or for if a level is proving particularly difficult you won't get locked behind a level to progress. You can always go back later and replay any level with more upgrades/ unlocks.
Some design choices that make me appreciate this game more than most.
+Calling waves early gives 50 gold bonus regardless of time so doesn't push you hit next wave as soon as it appears every time for maximum bonus.
+There is no mechanic that leads you to hoard gold. You get it you spend it.
+The upgrade system doesn't tie you down into using specific towers. It's more tied to progression and XP where you can change around your tower upgrades every map.
---There are flying enemies in the game.
-8 difficulty modifiers is a decent selection but more would certianly be nice.
-The way endless mode is set up many of the towers become entirely useless to have in your loadout.
-Some of the towers quickly feel inferior to towers you get later in the game, especially on later levels. Originally created for the Sega Dreamcast back in the year 2000, Jet Set Radio has been brought back out into the wild with a revamped HD version.  Has this game stood the test of time or are things from this era in gaming history best left alone?
The story is a very simple one, you play as a member of the GG's, a group of youngsters in the city of Tokyo-To who fight other groups in the many locations in the game world. Your goal is one of expression through dance, music, and graffiti.
The design of the game is that of a very simple one. Pressed by time you go around tagging up different parts of the city to expand your territory all the while escaping the clutches of the police. The game also invokes a sense of style in how you go about your mission. It isn’t just enough to tag up the city but to make sure you look cool while you do it.
The gameplay is one of an intense cat and mouse. Finding the areas you need to tag while being chased by police, dogs, helicopters, and tanks (not all at the same time, mind you). All the while the sands of father time slip down in the hour glass. But, before you can tag anything you have to gather spray cans which are spread around the different levels. Each of the characters you can choose from has a certain amount of graffiti they can carry as well as a certain amount of health and skill for pulling off tricks. When finding an area in need of some graffiti, you enter into a mode of a series of quick time events. In these events you swing the left analog stick in a specific direction (specific button presses on the keyboard). If you are to mess up the event you lose a can of graffiti in the process, but when you restart you start back at the beginning.
After clearing a section of the game in the single player campaign, levels will become opened to the other three modes of the game.
: a mode in which you spray paint (tag) the streets.
: a mode where you earn as many points as you can (i.e. do as many tricks as you can) until time is up.
: in this mode you pick a person from your group to race with someone else in your group.
Bringing in something completely new to the scene (at the time), the game shows off its cell shaded graphics which give the feeling of playing an anime/manga. Accompanying the new graphic style is a diverse array of music ranging from j-pop, hip-hop, funk, electronic dance, rock, and acid jazz. The graffiti in the game was the work done by several artists, most notably Eric Haze who contributed several pieces including the game’s logo.
The game also has a nice level of replayability with online leaderboards for all game modes (including the campaign). Jet set radio also has unlockable characters of the different gangs you go up against, as well as a few other surprises ;].
I would highly recommend this game to any gamer, it just oozes cool.

Better late than never. This game is such a deep and intriguing adventure.
I have had this game on my "to play" list for years, and I have started this game 5 times from the beginning, But couldn't get into it.
I did not play Morrowind when I first started with Oblivion, so without any form of refference I delved into Cyrodill.
AS the intro starts, Uriel Septim speaks to you with his nice dark voice and the epic music starts to play, this game feels magical. After creating your character (more on this later in this review) you may choose you star sign and class. Both choices really differentiate your character.
As you escape the first dungeon and you are free to explore the whole continent of the imperial city, you know that you adventure will be grand!
As most Elder Scrolls games the main story has some hick-ups from the start. You are just a messenger and the main characters really do their best to keep you as emotionly detached as possible.
But as the main story progresses you explore the land and more side stories manage their way into your path. These stories really are so lifely and bring more depth to the world as a whole.
The gameplay is solid, but lots of people keep telling me "Morrowind was much better".
Yes there are some spells removed, some things added like the conversation wheel to make people more happy. As a gamer I like to build my own characters, but sometimes there are so many stats to keep track of, that you lose yourself in it.
For me, this happened in Morrowind, but in Oblivion they got rid of those "useless stats" as I call them. For it greatly improves the gameplay.
Last but not least a flaw, is the character creation, for a game that revolves around you as a character, the creation of it is abysmal. The more you tweak the more chance you have to ruin your character. They really improved this in Skyrim.
Overall I grade this game a 8,5/10

In Mountain Crime, you play as young Dr. Phillip White, who receives a mysterious phone call and travels deep into the mountains to help an ailing man at a hotel resort. But, upon arriving, you soon find out that something sinister is taking place at this sleepy residence.
You can compare the story to that of the 1980s film Clue, but with slightly darker undertones.
No, really, you play as a guy who goes into the middle of nowhere and everyone else (except for you) is a complete and utterly clueless fool. Murder in a big, beautiful mansion, the works.
The only difference is the fact that you're a beefy doctor with a penchant for solving puzzles and...Well, the cheesy ending; but the game is pretty fun to play so I won't spoil it for you!
+
I've played quite a number of HOGs and I was pleasantly surprised by the unique spin in this one.
Instead of going through hidden object scenes full of stuff that has to be picked through to cross off a list, there's a ring of six or seven items that, once filled in after finding and dragging the items into the bubbled ring, will create or repair a useful tool or key item to progress the story - like a vacuum cleaner, blow torch, etc.
This aspect of the game alone was very refreshing and less time consuming compared to the repetitive formula that other HOGs use for gameplay.
Puzzle-wise, though, I'm happy to say that there's a good variety to play with; though, I think more would've been appreciated because the HOG scenes can be a bit tiring after awhile.
My favorite aspect of the game was exploring; the hotel has a large number of rooms and each one has its own theme and unique charm. The hidden documents, weathered walls and furniture made me wonder just what kind of history the place had.
Sadly, I feel that the story was a bit too predictable and fell short of its potential towards the end; but it was really fun to play and the game is sold at a great bargain - so I got what I wanted.
I'm not so sure if Mountain Crime has replay value, but I will say that this is something that HOG fans can enjoy.

A murder mystery written like an early Agatha Christie novel, presented like an Alfred Hitchcock movie, with the solvability (and continuity) of an Ellery Queen mystery.  Engaging, intriguing, heart pounding.  Keeps the gamer enthralled and guessing until the end.  I felt like I had read a thrilling murder mystery without actually any reading involved.  Excellent pacing with just enough time to almost catch your breath.
Storyline: Dr. Philip White (one dark and dangerously stormy night) is called to the newly renovated White Wolf Hotel to examine and attend to a Mr. Grey.  When he arrives, the bridge washes out leaving him stranded.  He discovers there is no Mr. Grey and a hotel filled with other guests also invited to this grand opening by Mr. Grey.  (And Then There Were None ~ Agatha Christie, anyone?  And no that is not a spoiler.) The mystery begins when the body count begins.  Who is Mr Grey? Does he even exist?  Why are these people here, unknown to each other yet have a connection?  What is that connection?  And why this requital?  As the body count rises, the answers are revealed.
Gameplay:  Hidden Object puzzler with point and click elements.  The hidden object scenes instead of being find lists, are picture finds (somewhat like a silhouette).  The HO scene opens and small pictures form a circle of the things or pieces needed to be found.  Not as easy as it sounds since the objects needed to be found blend into the surrounding objects (which are appropriate for where the scene is).  For example looking for desk items, on a desk covered with items typically found on a desk.  Also there are generally several of the same item and like a matching game the gamer needs to pick the correct one.
Puzzles: Sliders and logic, or maybe better stated: logic sliders.  For example the typical moving of X number of one color object to the opposite side of a board/grid while the x number on that side are moved to where the other color is.  Typically found on locks.  Also there is the finding of keys, which are usually found behind some type of logic slider puzzle.
The Point and Click element is just as important to the story and in true point and click fashion there are plenty of puzzling obstacles to overcome.  However this element is so intermixed with the Hidden Object aspect it is hard to tell the two apart.
Note: No map (not needed), no penalties for game hints or puzzle skips.  No achievements but trading cards for those who care about those things.
Conclusion: Enthralling and believable murder mystery, and like all excellent murder mysteries when the pieces start to fall into place, it is an avalanche.  Definitely worth full price.

Recommending
is a difficult task because, well, it's aged... not so well in certain aspects. Oblivion was an absolute treasured jewel in my childhood, so it's easy for me to look past the potato graphics and outdated gameplay, but just as I have trouble playing
, newcomers to Oblivion can expect trouble as well.
The main problem is the biggest: its gameplay. There's no getting around it: combat sucks. It was servicable then, but it's horrendously outdated at this point. Your sword feels like a foam toy from Walmart as you swing around chipping away tiny bits of health. You'll find yourself knocking hundreds of arrows just to kill one leveled monster, making the corpse look akin to a pin cushion. In essence, weapons and combat have no weight. It's seemingly straightforward (you swing your sword at an enemy) and there
a level of depth (in both combat and magic combat), but overall, it isn't a very exciting experience.
Art styles can make or break a game, and, thankfully, Oblivion's graphics are painted with a very warm pallete. Unfortunately, the game is also ugly as sin--especially its much made fun of models. Besides the rather ugly graphics, the world itself is a bland collection of plains, hills, and trees, trees, trees. The diversity just isn't really there, and while it was extremely exciting back in 2006, it isn't too impressive now.
All of this negativity, yet there's a thumbs up. Well, that's because Oblivion is still an utterly
RPG that, if I may be so bold to say, has some of the greatest writing found within an RPG. It's obviously not
level writing, but the sheer creativity found within the questlines and side quests is astounding. Seriously, with quests ranging from entering a painting to rescue a trapped artist, to investigating a string of vampire murders when the victims aren't vampires at all, to being locked in a mansion with five other guests, all of which you must murder yourself, to a grand heist pulled off on the jewel of the Empire, Oblivion features a wide diversity of interesting and unique quests that are well worth your time.
As I mentioned before, there is depth to Oblivion hidden within its mechanics. The ability to craft and create your spells, to combine various levels of enchantments to create bizarre results, to mixing and matching ingredients to fuel interesting potions--Oblivion will let you fight with a sword and shield, but it allows you to go as deep as you want to twist combat into a feeble matter.
Overall, Oblivion is a deeply flawed, yet well written and mechanically detailed RPG experience that should be experienced, should you be brave enough to fight through its rather mundane combat and outdated world. Over ten years and I will vehemently defend that this game stands up stronger than even
and
in terms of interesting writing and quests.

The best tower defense game I played. It feels like a very fun sandbox to play in: it has a 2d physics that can be hilarious, the traps and defenses are interesting and often have a powerful feel to them - using is satisfying. Somehow that physics engine makes those dungeon feel more alive, when it get's very crowded and massive amounts of enemies are pushed over the edge, it's awesome.
While it's very fun, it also feels well balanced and upgrades are well done. Using various "mutators" to reply the levels with added difficulties opens whole new field to replying old levels (for example, you can add one that gives you just one health instead of 20, or adds health/regeneration to enemies, etc - those will give you experience multipliers, so adding more can make it crazy hard but also give insane exp). So you can develope interesting combinations/strategies for earning extra experience needed to boost your defenses even more.
Also, various consumables (traps you put on certain spots "on the fly", and wait for the timer to reset so you can place some more) make it more dynamic, and adds yet another layer to possible strategies, as you can choose only one type of consumable for a given battle.
But honestly, just see this game on youtube if you are not sold already. If it looks awesome to you, well it plays very awesome too!

Another decent hidden object game, but as with many in the genre it has its problems, which while not game breaking annoyed me more than normal, but overall it had an interesting enough storyline and the gameplay was fairly decent, so still a fairly decent game overall, especially for the fairly neglible price (especially when on sale).
The story has you as Quincy MD crossed with MacGyver trapped at a hotel during a storm where you almost died getting to your rich new patient. People start dropping like flies around you and you have to investigate and try to stop the killer before he runs out of victims. The plot is a bit of a mixed bag, a lot of it is shown in news clippings and details of the history of the hotel and all the people being killed who all seem linked back to an arson a couple of decades previously, so you have to race to uncover the identity of the killer. At one point there is the hint it might be an interesting denouement in the nature of identity/memento or some other psychological thriller, but in the end it feels more like a daytime soap plot (except for the body count).
Still that part is okay enough to provide the background for the gameplay, so that breaks down into the hidden object scenes which are of the construct an item style of HOG, which is where you go all MacGyver and construct all sorts of items from things found in one place, so at one point you collect a safecracking kit (and then proceed to use the screwdriver to take the entire safe door off ignoring the rest of the kit you painstakingly searched for), some sort of miniflamethrower, a hot air balloon (because you didn't want to just lift/push the basket off the item you needed).
While very inventive it all feels pretty bizarre (more so that normal for the genre even, which is pretty bad by and large). The imminent peril of people dying of snakebite, or being strapped into a chair at the mercy of the killer, and then you go around repairing a globe, or a piano, most often just to get common household tools - that you generally discard after one use so there can be another convoluted puzzle to get yet another screwdriver or whatever later in the story. You rarely get any explicit story hints of why you should be interacting with these objects, just they are the only things on the map which can be interacted with left, so that must be where the latest essential tool can be found.
Anyway that gripe aside the scenes play fairly well and feel somewhat naturalistic, the puzzles also tend to be unexplained - I guess the hotel owner likes messing with his employees and forcing them to play puzzles to open doors and otherwise do their job. No wonder all the staff seem to have disappeared before the story starts. The puzzles themselves are mostly fairly easy, with a reasonable variety, but the controls are frequently wonky and things don't always move how you want them to - this even forced me to skip one puzzle as I couldn't move the piece far enough right to finish it. There were a couple I found more difficult but I think it is more down to me being bad at those types of puzzle (the 4 shape overlapping rotating puzzle right at the end being the main one). Of course with no achievements you can actually use the skip/hint buttons if you really get stuck without it forcing you to replay it later to get the last couple of achievements (and forcing you to find a way to do those puzzles or consult a walkthrough anyway).
Overall it is a recommendation, especially given the price, but don't expect too much, it has a lot of flaws to go with the good points. Also I laughed out loud (literally) immediately after freeing the Senator from the chair - I don't think this is the intended reaction...anyone else do the same?

An old abandoned hotel, a monstrous storm, a mysterious invite and lots of murder...it's like the movie Clue only not as funny.
You play Dr. Phillip White and you've been summoned to a hotel to help a person in need. Then a storm hits and your car crashes leaving you stranded at the hotel. You'll meet lots of characters but honestly none of them matter since they all fall over dead like flies. The amount of murder in this game is just ridiculous. It honestly got to the point where I'd expect to find a dead body in every room. However, the story itself isn't bad but it quickly takes a predictable turn and the ending is down right hilarious. I laughed out loud at the end just shaking my head.
Of course, the game doesn't intend to be funny. It takes itself seriously. The voice acting isn't perfect but it's passable. The graphics are dated but not hard on the eyes. The game play is where the game shines. I enjoy the hidden item scenes because you go into each one with a list of items to find that go together to form something actually useful. So no finding random gum wrappers or etched hearts. The mini games are very standard fare; sliding puzzles, memory puzzles, pipe puzzles, etc. They're fun but some are a bit vague when it comes to instructions.
The game lacks achievements which is a shame but it also makes playing the game more relaxing. It's an old game at a cheap price and a good one for fans of the genre. Though the story isn't amazing it's funny and I enjoy laughing while playing a good game. So I say you should buy it and give it a shot.

I do recommend this, but only by a slight margin. This game is multiplayer only, and it's all about PvP combat. However, even if that's what you're into, you may not want this game in particular. There are a lot of...interesting/unrealistic techniques that people past Rank 15 use to win. For example, the backwards overhead:
It looks dumb, and it honestly is dumb. It should be removed from the game, yet it still hasn't been. Then there are other dumb things people do like swinging their weapons 360 degrees. When people do it, it also looks dumb and is dumb, and should be taken out.
It should be mentioned then when you use the feint (act like you're going to attack then cancel), which is an actual realistic combat technique, people get really upset with you. That's right, people get mad at you for using a legitimate mechanic, but it's A-okay if you use some convoluted dorky technique. Overall, I'd say the community is slightly better than the TF2 community, but there's still plenty of cancer. One guy got upset at me for saying that Oblivion had better combat than Skyrim, and hurled insults over it. Also, if you like being an archer, prepare to be picked on. There are jerks in the community who will kill archers and only archers, not to mention verbally abuse anyone who happens to be an archer (especially a skilled one).
Despite all this, it's still fun to play. Think of it as Monty Python: The Game, and you'll enjoy it. The gore is goofy (you can punch a guy's head till it explodes), the battle cries can be funny, and it's really just silly action. If you're looking for a realistic medieval combat game, this isn't it. However, it's still a good game. I got it on sale, and I suggest you do too.

The Dungeon Keeper has come....er, I mean the Underlord!
Back in the day, I was a HUGGGEE fan of Dungeon Keeper, that game was my jam! When Dungeon Keeper 2 came out, I of course got it, played it, beat it (many times) and then after enjoying the end cinematic, I patiently yet excitedly waited for DK3!
Well, long story short and of which I'm sure a few of you can relate, DK3 never came and turns out Bullfrog closed up shop and with each passing year, DK 3 became a pipe dream, but one I longed for.
Many years later, I was on Steam and I saw War for the Overworld pop up and I did some reading about it. It was meant to be a spiritual successor to Dungeon Keeper and even received endorsement from Peter Molyneux himself and they had even secured the original narrator from the DK series!

First off, this game is absolutely FREE so you lose nothing from trying it. Probably one of my favourite Source mods in existence and still has a very active playerbase and forum community. Before the game was placed on Steam, I'd play this religiously so my hours would probably be closer to the 200-300hr range. Anyhow, the thing that sets this game apart from others is that in certain gamemodes, it actually has two styles of gaming...
Infantry (FPS):
The standard mode with classes that have upgrade paths that you customize as you earn experience for contributing to your team. The team can be broken down further into squads that have a squad leader that earns and selects power-ups for well-performing squads. Powers like squad revive can turn the tide of a final ticket push. Under vehicle maps, once a vehicle factory has been built by the commander, all infantry units are capable of building AND CUSTOMIZING the tanks they take into battle, from the weapons that are mounted onto it to the type of amount of armor on the vehicle. The tank battles are the bread and butter of this game as each weapon you're capable of mounting has armors it's good against and ones that it's not. Weight, slots, and cooldown put realistic restrictions on the tanks so you don't have a tank with 5 nukes strapped to it and make the tank battles all the more engaging. Additionally, each class has different upgrades for different vehicles (such as additional cooldown, artillery feedback, etc) that could really give you the advantage in battle.
Commander Gameplay (RTS):
Theres a steep learning curve, especially against people who have been playing this game for over 5 years. However, once you've got everything else down -- like what weapons are good to research and best way to play each map for each faction -- the commander is the single most powerful player in the game. Each team starts the game voting for a commander. From a top-down view, the commander guides units, places buildings and defensive structures, and determines what technology to research -- much like a typical RTS. However, unlike a standard RTS, your infantry units are actual players who chose how they contribute to the team and provide feedback to the commander on what's working or not.
Tl;dr: Awesome game with massive tank and infantry battles and RTS gameplay for advanced players. Also the game is free.

Recommending
is a difficult task because, well, it's aged... not so well in certain aspects. Oblivion was an absolute treasured jewel in my childhood, so it's easy for me to look past the potato graphics and outdated gameplay, but just as I have trouble playing
, newcomers to Oblivion can expect trouble as well.
The main problem is the biggest: its gameplay. There's no getting around it: combat sucks. It was servicable then, but it's horrendously outdated at this point. Your sword feels like a foam toy from Walmart as you swing around chipping away tiny bits of health. You'll find yourself knocking hundreds of arrows just to kill one leveled monster, making the corpse look akin to a pin cushion. In essence, weapons and combat have no weight. It's seemingly straightforward (you swing your sword at an enemy) and there
a level of depth (in both combat and magic combat), but overall, it isn't a very exciting experience.
Art styles can make or break a game, and, thankfully, Oblivion's graphics are painted with a very warm pallete. Unfortunately, the game is also ugly as sin--especially its much made fun of models. Besides the rather ugly graphics, the world itself is a bland collection of plains, hills, and trees, trees, trees. The diversity just isn't really there, and while it was extremely exciting back in 2006, it isn't too impressive now.
All of this negativity, yet there's a thumbs up. Well, that's because Oblivion is still an utterly
RPG that, if I may be so bold to say, has some of the greatest writing found within an RPG. It's obviously not
level writing, but the sheer creativity found within the questlines and side quests is astounding. Seriously, with quests ranging from entering a painting to rescue a trapped artist, to investigating a string of vampire murders when the victims aren't vampires at all, to being locked in a mansion with five other guests, all of which you must murder yourself, to a grand heist pulled off on the jewel of the Empire, Oblivion features a wide diversity of interesting and unique quests that are well worth your time.
As I mentioned before, there is depth to Oblivion hidden within its mechanics. The ability to craft and create your spells, to combine various levels of enchantments to create bizarre results, to mixing and matching ingredients to fuel interesting potions--Oblivion will let you fight with a sword and shield, but it allows you to go as deep as you want to twist combat into a feeble matter.
Overall, Oblivion is a deeply flawed, yet well written and mechanically detailed RPG experience that should be experienced, should you be brave enough to fight through its rather mundane combat and outdated world. Over ten years and I will vehemently defend that this game stands up stronger than even
and
in terms of interesting writing and quests.

Mountain Crime: Requital is a game where you play the worst doctor in the world as people all around him fall prey to the stupidest, most easily avoidable deathtraps imaginable. (Seriously, imagine Saw, if the traps were designed by an idiot, and managed to ensnare even bigger idiots). There's a big mystery about an old resort where a bunch of kids burned alive that the hotel you're in was built on, but all in all the plot ranges from boring to hilarious, without any detours to interesting.
The hidden object scenes are okay. The main mechanic is you're searching for objects by a given silhouette (although sometimes the silhouette doesn't match with the item, so thanks, game). A few scenes are repeated, but at least they all have the gimmick of ostensibly using all the items you find to acquire the needed object to advance.
The regular puzzles are okay too. No real stand-outs; just typical HOG fare like "Slide the blocks around until the one block can escape", "Turn the pipes so the liquid can pass through", "There is a combination lock, but you saw the solution so it shows up in your journal", stuff like that.
There were a lot of cute little animals, including a prominent squirrel guy in one puzzle that had big ol' cutie ears. There was also a moment when the character you play as was standing next to an exploding gas stove and seemed completely unaffeted. The ending is hilarious.
All in all, it's a fun game, and definitely worth a shot.

Hello, hello! We are together for a review of another HOG again! How marvelously different and interesting, is it? No, of course it isn't. This is our millionth HOG, and after a while they all end up resembling one another. Still,
is one of the better ones out there, with an interesting enough scenario to establish a sense of curiosity.
We here have Dr. Philip White, who receives an urgent phone call in the middle of the night, which asks him to attend a patient at the White Wolf Mountain Resort, in a really bad storm. As any self-confident wise guy with no common sense spared, he travels to middle of nowhere to attend said patient, only to find a murder-mystery. All communication and transportation is cut off, hotel guests are dropping like flies and there is a sick ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the loose who treats all this chaos as an elaborate game. It seems that everything is connected to a bigger crime buried in the past. "But what crime?" asks Dr. Philip White, and starts his investigation like any Scooby Doo wannabe.
Cute, huh? Don't be deceived by my mockery. Our protagonist is a naive sod, but the story itself and the connection between hotel guests are a mystery worthy of uncovering. As for the game itself, graphics are pretty good. Background design is interesting and there are many, many lockboxes, automatons and hidden doors around. If I'd visit this hotel in real life - without a murder-mystery present, of course - I know I'd love to spare a week or two there. Character animations look pretty until they start talking. Then with the tongue-tied voice acting and clumsy lip synch, the atmosphere crumbles. It's like a really fine looking lady with no smarts. You'd love to look her all day, as long as she doesn't talk.
Puzzles, I hear? Oh, they are good. There is a balanced combination of ordinary ones, and 'just annoying enough to stall you off until you were about to give up' ones. HOG scenes are very neat, with open and distinguishable items, with more than only one item of the kind lying around. Each HOG is designed to gather pieces for a machine of sort that you're trying to fix, so you can reach another item of use. This way, items laid around kinda make sense, which is rare in this genre.
All in all, this is a fine HOG, but I'll attach a warning. This game is included in a Hidden Object Bundle 5 in 1 in Steam, so if you have the bundle already, there is no actual need for you to buy this game. You already have the game within the bundle. If you don't have it and are even mildly curious, go ahead. Gonna end up with 3-4 hours of decent HOG fun. With this said, my work here is done! Good gaming!

PROS:
- Massive cities compared to Euro Truck; took me about 5-10 minutes to simply get out of Los Angeles.  Not complex road systems like GTA, but large areas of city scenery
- Police patrols instead of traffic cams.  If a police car sees you speeding, you hear sirens and they flash their lights, and you get a ticket.
- Finally, since it is North American road rules, we can turn right at a red light and not get penalized for it!
- Weight stations add a little immersion, don't know what affect they have on gameplay at this time however
- Truck interiors seem much more realistic now, may be just because they are familiar interiors with analog gauges.
- New trailer delivery system - you can choose at the gate to a) Auto-park the trailer b) Park the trailer in an easy spot c) Park the trailer in a difficult but percise spot, all with different XP bonuses
CONS:
- Very few truck brands, and therefore probably fewer models
- Much smaller map than Euro Truck at this time, only includes 3 states (Nevada, California, & Arizona).  I'm assuming they plan to expand on that.
- UI, main menu, sound effects, and in-game HUD are all direct copies from Euro Truck - no originality.
- American trucks with the extended front (rather than the flat, rectangular shaped trucks) are much harder to drive at high speeds, takes longer to get from point A to point B, especially on twisted off-roads.
- Very unpopular with multiplayer mod, no more than 100 people on at a time on NA or EU servers, as opposed to 2400 on ETS2.
OTHER POINTS:
- Already tons of mods out for the game, including trucks, trailers, graphics, gameplay, and more.
- swood american music

This is one of those games with huge potential, which is sadly ruined by pay to win model.
Game features big open world and 2 factions on three different continents. Factions are race locked, and you cant even communicate with each other until you learn the other's faction language. Game mostly relies on trading, so there are boats, gliders and cars, used for fast transportation and delivering trade packs across continents. Trading has a bit of micromanagement behind it too, some items have cheaper selling price if the NPCs are overstocked, and selling price varies from zone to zone. Each delivery carries a risk because any other player can attack you and steal your items, even players from your own faction which can become special third faction - pirates, if they do too many crimes. There is even the jail where other players can judge criminals' sentence after they are caught. Sadly trading routes are controlled by people with maxed out gear who will kill you almost instantly on sight. Although it does make it a very interesting hide and seek game.
Another interesting aspect of this game are its classes. There are 10 different skill trees and you can use 3 of them at same time. That makes it 120 different combo-classes, they even have its own names. Each skilltree is leveled individually, and you can unlock all skill trees on a single character. This is really good if you dont like making alts and want to play one character only. Skilltree changes are very cheap and so is the respec.
Open world world pvp is common, there are some players who like to gank too, but most of time if its newbies you'll just pass next to each other. There are also zones where pvp isnt possible at all (starting ones mostly) where you can also trade but its rather a time waste and not that profitable. Other ones are in war state at certain times of day, although the wars are not impactful on the zones themselves (NPC and everything else stays the same, its just that players gather around to fight) unless you are passing through and might get killed by other players.
There is also housing, although its locked behind 'Patron' which is a paid membership, but it can be obtained with ingame gold by buying tokens from donator players.
Crafting is good, a lot of items to craft and materials to gather, although all these actions consume labor points, which have really bad recovery rate for free to play players and only recover while you are online, unless you have Patron which gets you double recovery speed, double cap and offline recovery.
One of the issues are the players who make dozens of bots they use for trading and labor.
Its very hard for new player to breakthrough because there is very little pve content to earn money on and they are forced to be fodder in pvp, or use stealth and hide all the time.
I really like this game, but unfortunately there are just too many issues that cant be overlooked.
Pros:
- big open world
- nice skilltree class system (120 different classes)
- very unique trading feature
- gliders, boats, cars, skateboards
- naval warfare, it is also very enjoyable to sail
- big pvp wars
- alot of different items to craft, and materials to gather
- housing
- nice looking world with exotic places
- a lot of interactive vanity items, you can even make music sheeths and play custom music on it (although you have to write the composition with in game notes, you cant just use), there are different instruments for it too
- fresh start servers are nice idea
- there are nice events and free boost packs on most of bigger updates
- you can build guild castles and control certain zones
Cons:
- pay to win
- very little pve content, game is mostly based on trading and pvp
- very hard for new players to get good gear, everything is controlled by p2w players
- players using multiple accounts (bots) to mule more packs at same time/ or as laborers (labor points)
- labor points
- new fresh server released just one year after last one, which is just making it a bigger cash grab
- although there are alot of classes, it breaks down into few meta ones more or less

Dreamcast held a diverse collection of colorful & creative exclusives during its lifespan, with Jet Set Radio being the most popular title that wasn't ported proper until over a decade later. Finally on PC with the original soundtrack (minus two tracks), JSR is a flashback to older game design featuring expansive, diverse levels that reward exploration, an eclectic electronic soundtrack that blends genres fluidly, and the creation of a new graphical rendering style with cel-shading. The level design is excellent, with many hidden routes and shortcuts which are integrated into both escape and chase sequences, making even recycled maps feel fresh. JSR's soundtrack is incredibly diverse and creative, adds to the uniqueness of the experience; combined with the colorful character cast, the introduction of cel-shading, and the varied gameplay, JSR feels like its own world, a unique spin on the early 2000s Japan.
While the main story isn't exceptionally lengthy, it's worth picking up just to experience this one-of-a-kind game; JSR is truly an innovative and unique experience that is highly recommended for anyone with a gamepad.

PROS:
- Massive cities compared to Euro Truck; took me about 5-10 minutes to simply get out of Los Angeles.  Not complex road systems like GTA, but large areas of city scenery
- Police patrols instead of traffic cams.  If a police car sees you speeding, you hear sirens and they flash their lights, and you get a ticket.
- Finally, since it is North American road rules, we can turn right at a red light and not get penalized for it!
- Weight stations add a little immersion, don't know what affect they have on gameplay at this time however
- Truck interiors seem much more realistic now, may be just because they are familiar interiors with analog gauges.
- New trailer delivery system - you can choose at the gate to a) Auto-park the trailer b) Park the trailer in an easy spot c) Park the trailer in a difficult but percise spot, all with different XP bonuses
CONS:
- Very few truck brands, and therefore probably fewer models
- Much smaller map than Euro Truck at this time, only includes 3 states (Nevada, California, & Arizona).  I'm assuming they plan to expand on that.
- UI, main menu, sound effects, and in-game HUD are all direct copies from Euro Truck - no originality.
- American trucks with the extended front (rather than the flat, rectangular shaped trucks) are much harder to drive at high speeds, takes longer to get from point A to point B, especially on twisted off-roads.
- Very unpopular with multiplayer mod, no more than 100 people on at a time on NA or EU servers, as opposed to 2400 on ETS2.
OTHER POINTS:
- Already tons of mods out for the game, including trucks, trailers, graphics, gameplay, and more.
- swood american music

Gameplay 2.5/5

One of the best and most enjoyable games I have played in the last few years. It’s very similar to Dungeon Keeper, but it has more features and potential. The basics are the same, dig out your dungeon and unleash your creators on your enemies. The creators are unique and beautifully made, with their own habits. Lots of new rooms, traps and magic to discover, with additional rituals.
The story is well made, typical concur the over world story, but a few twists and with humour. The Champaign was enjoyable till the end; however, the ending did not give me the closure what I wanted. It was well planned all the way long.
The game has a lot of extras, one of the most popular ones is the map editor, where you can create your own map.
To summarize it up: The game is really enjoyable, with lots of Dungeon Keeper like features. Anyone who misses the game should defiantly try this.
On the downside, game has a few bugs, but they are continuously fixed by the developer. Crashes can spoil your mood, when you forgot to save before. It would be nice to have an optional auto-save.
If you want to play a good God Game, and torture humanity to extinction or just want to crush another evil Lord, this one is certainly one of the bests!

Pretty good story and worth a purchase for any dedicated point-and-click adventure fans, but Wadjet Eye's other project, the Blackwell series, tends to have better puzzles and mechanics. Gemini Rue will probably have you checking back and forth to a guide not because of how difficult the puzzles are but because just enough of them are solved via pixel hunts or by disregarding conventions of an adventure game that you will have a hard time knowing which ones just need some creative thinking and which aren't worth hammering through. E.g. one puzzle is solved through trial and error while a similar puzzle before it is not. The former's similarities to the latter will make you think trial and error is a red herring approach. Another puzzle involves relentlessly talking to an NPC who doesn't respond -- but how does a player know to do this when they're similar to the many other NPCs who don't respond and AREN'T part of a puzzle? They're minor annoyances that can be solved by having a guide on hand, but it takes some of the fun out of adventure gaming.

ArcheAge is a MMO with a lot of potential. It offers a world where other players affect your game experience. It lets gives players the opportunity to help and hinder each other as much as they want. The best aspect of this game is the way it encourages players to form groups in order to complete more difficult tasks and affect other groups of plays. From making guild that are designed to keep you safe from other plays, to making guilds designed to take your profit form other guilds.
ArcheAge can offer some great experiences to they players but has high costs. Since a lot of the experience focuses around the interaction between players, it makes characters strength become a mayor factor in the enjoyment. If the player does not feel that they have a fighting chance and can not affect the outcome of interactions, they will not get they enjoyment that the game offers. In for the player to have sufficient character strength to affect player interaction, they will need to spend a considerable amount of money or time on the game. The amount of time required to play without paying money is about that of a full time job. The amount of money needed to feel have sufficient character strength can vary since, the players uses real money to acquire in-game money. This is done by using real money to buy subscription and selling it ingame to other players.
ArcheAge is an expensive game in terms of time or money.
I could only recommend the game to you, if you are without a job or willing to spend a lot of money.
