I don't really feel like recommending this game. While I guess it showed some potential as a small indie game, I wasn't impressed by it. It's not that it's terrible, but it isn't good either, it just... is.
The gameplay, to begin with, isn't very good. It's pretty much a sidescroller, something reminiscent of a 90s beat 'em up, although with guns rather than fists. You start on the left, progress to the right, killing everything in your path, that kind of thing. The thing is, there isn't a lot of enemy variety (and even then, most of the time it's just a different skin with the same "attacks"), and the guns themselves are pretty weak, while the knife does great damage. However, taking enemy hits does a great deal of damage, and sometimes you get hurt just by standing close to an enemy, without any contact. There's also an unlocks store, but you can pretty much complete the game as it is, in less than an hour, and the money you might earn in a single playthrough can get you a handful of new guns only.
The story is pretty bare bones. There's an interesting idea behind it: you're playing as a German soldier from WWII, who ends up helping the Allies agaisnt the SS, who're trying to use an alien artifact to take over the world. However, there's little to no dialogue (which is all text based, by the way). Even then, I think I can give them a pass on the story department, as many games with a similar gameplay had little story to them.
As for the soundtrack, it does its job, I guess. Nothing really remarkable about it.
I guess that's all for this game. I'm giving it a thumbs down because I don't feel it's worth it enough to upvote it, and there's no "neutral" score.

Short, but worth the asking price. Finished up first play through and will definitely play through another time or two. Now for the run down.
Ruiner is pretty accessible with a straight forward control scheme. Dual stick ala Robotron, Smash TV, Apocalypse, just to name a few. Though let's not make the mistake of thinking of the control options as limited. Ruiner's controls are not a left stick move, right shot only. There's a little more meat to the controls than that.
The gameplay is frenetic bordering just at the edge of total choas. Fire fight visuals are well timed and reinforce that heart warming feeling of tiny people running around on fire missing limbs and/or exploding! Good times... Runier contains several different weapon types. Ranging from run of the mill machine guns to burn your face off laser weapons.
The skills / abilities trees can be configured to provide an RPG style boost to charater stats. New abilities can also be acquired and expanded in this section. Skill / ability tree points can be reassigned at anytime during gameplay, making for some interesting gameplay variations.
Solid performance, 2560 x 1440 @ 60FPS. The controls whether controller or keyboard and mouse feel good overall, though when using a wired USB x-box controller a few weapons hit felt ill timed. A minor issue that doesn't effect the overall playability of Ruiner.
The story of Ruiner is direct and serves to further the gameplay in a narrative sense. Yes the story could be deeper, but the story did exactly what it needed and nothing more. Clear and concise. Sort of a neo Tokyo vibe as told in a William Gibson fashion. You, the player are dropped center stage into the action and the story advances rapidly as you catch up.
Ruiner's sound track had me at the loading screen. Chill, down tempo, lo fi cyber punk all the way. A few heavier tracks exist though a little too machine oriented for yours truly and those tracks normally come into play during battle scenarios. The sound track wraps up Ruiner in a gritty neon red and black dented metal box with a purple neon bow and a note that reads "Hello Darkness".

With almost 100 hours in, I can say that this game is both fun and frustrating, but also neither forgiving or boring.
It's Early Access, and while a lot of people seem to forget that, a lot of the community does not. It has (just like other EA releases before it) it's bugs and glitches and exploiits, but nothing is severely gam breaking; no show stoppers. While this is true, Funcom has been absolutely awesome in patch releasing, community interactions, and as transparent as they can be. They have a steady presence in the Conan Exiles subreddit, providing feedback to the community.
Whether you want to play solo or co-op on a private LAN server, open your server to others, or even (as I have) setup a dedicated server for anyone to play on, you can always find a place to play with others. There are currently ~11k community servers online
, and this number is fairly steady. This is both PvP, PvE, or a mix of both. A lot of admins (such as myself) are active and truely want to make sure their servers offer a fun and intersting experience.
The game has a learning curve, and it's a bit jagged at this time. Some things are intuative, especially if you have played any of the other high-profile survival games currently out. Some things, not so much, though this has already shown to be be a) something they are working on and b) part of the survival aspect; you have to learn quick or die to the elements.
I gladly recommend this game, though with a warning: if you must have a complete, polished game, then you should wait. If you're like me and you like finding the bugs and writing reports, you want to be part of that process that makes helps the dev make a great game, and you like being an early adopter in spite of what issues come with that, then this is the perfect time to hop on the bandwagon.

Content Overview:
The description is truthful, it combines strategy with FPS. If you don't mind a few players in the commander and in general who tend to treat the game a bit too much like ARMA, this game is right for you.
The commander vehicle is the key to every game. You lose it, game over, other team wins. End of your sad, sad story of hardship. It lets you build things like refineries and barracks. It has some armour, so don't worry about it spontaneously combusting. As long as you don't go into the water like a dumbass, you should be fine.
Which brings us to the next sub-topic: Buildings.
A variety of buildings exist, including...
Refinery: Produces resources for your team to use. Your entire infrastructure depends on at least one of these existing. Don't lose it. Can only be build on corresponding resource nodes.
Barracks: Lets your team spawn and change class there. Very important.
Armoury: Lets your team regain health, ammo, and allows them to change class.
Vehicle Factory: Self explanatory. Allows your team to construct vehicles. More on that later. If you don't have one of these soon, you're probably gonna lose.
Repair Station: Repairs and resupplies friendly vehicles.
Radar: Allows your team's commander to research new technologies that advance your team's vehicles, or some other things. Also reveals enemies within its range. If you lose this, it either means:
A: Your comm is♥♥♥♥♥♥and doesn't know where to place buildings
B: An enemy managed to slip past your defenses and destroyed it
C: You're losing. Welcome to life, folks.
ML Turret: Stands for Missile Launcher. Can also be built by the engineer class. Only attacks vehicles and buildings.
MG Turret: Stands for Machine Gun. Can also be built by the engineer class. Only attacks infantry.
Walls: Self explanatory. Can also be built by the engineer class.
Engineer exclusive buildings:
Camera: Reveals enemies in its line of sight
Radar: Reveals enemy vehicles in a certain range
With all that, onto the next can of worms, vehicles. I'm not going to go into detail with these. If you want detail, there are plenty of guides on the community page.
Light Tank: Also known as the AFV in the Brenodi Empire.
Medium Tank: Also known as the Tank in the Brenodi Empire. A (debatedly) more powerful version of the light tank.
Heavy Tank: Most powerful (debatedly) tank in either team's arsenal. Can equip (yes) nuclear rockets.
Artillery Tank: Fires extremely powerful artillery shells over long distances. If you're not careful, a few of these can completely anihillate a base.
APC: Equips machine guns and grenade launchers. Can also act as a spawn point.
Jeep: An unarmoured, but fast vehicle with no weapons.
I'm not going to go into any more detail then that, but I'd definitely recommend this expansive and unique mod on the Source engine. Development is slow due to lack of funds, but if you like it enough, I'm sure you can help remedy that.
With that said, good day.

I feel this is an alright puzzle game, and for the price totally fine, but...
Well, I wish the puzzles were designed rather than generated. The procedurally-generated puzzles are presumably all possible to solve, but they lack a certain "elegance" to them that hand-designed puzzles would have. There were a lot of puzzles near the end where the solution involved outright burning moves or continuously selecting the same direction with a 4 or 5 line of squares, as well as making some moves that felt really counterproductive. A lot of the puzzles lack "forced moves" after a certain point which leaves you having to do a lot of trial-and-error to figure out what works and what doesn't.
I like that in general you can micromanage different sections of the board and if you solve one section of the board it's very likely that's the only way to solve it, and the puzzle concept is definitely a good one, though it does feel like it gets a bit repetitive by the end, even with only 49 puzzles. But ehh, it's still a good game, just not one I imagine I'll return to.

This is Battle Islands, a ww2 based "free-to-play" game, where the player will have his/her own island fortress, it's basically a singleplayer strategy game online, and with singleplayer I mean that you can't see your friends/enemies play but you can still fight them when they're offline. In Battle Islands the player have to focus a lot on both defense and how to attack the enemies. You can have as follows:
Land units i.e. soldiers, jeeps and tanks.
Naval units i.e. gunboats, warships and submarines.
Air units i.e. fighters, bombers and torpedo bombers.
In this game you'll be using supplies and gold as a currency. Supplies is used for the most e.g. training units fortifying structures, upgrade/promote units and structures and also buy stuff. Gold can be used to buy supplies and camouflage (camouflage is used to be hidden from other players so they can't attack you). The player can also buy gold with real money if necessary, but it's not needed since you eventually earn gold throughout the game.
Battle Islands is a game that craves a lot of patience, so you better find yourself something else to keep you preoccupied while waiting, unless you buy gold to boost the gameplay. Your armies can be used to both attack other bases, as well as defend you own. You can also build different structures, like factories, supply depots and rigs to get extra supplies from. Barracks, ship yards and hangars to get your attack troops from. The basic defense units comes from the camp, harbor and airfield. You will also be using machinegunners, howitzers, anti-air guns and sea forts to defend your base.
In battles against players you'll take and lose dogtags, dogtags tells how experienced you are in battles against other players, and if you've been attacked a lot.
There is a campaign of 30 levels where you can loot some supplies. If you're a beginner I would recommend to fight the campaign first, but you won't earn any tags from it.
In Battle Islands you'll spend a lot of time on upgrading your stuff, blasting other players bases and move around structures to create a stable defense.

After 150 hours spent in the game I feel it's about time I write a review.
Oh boy, this game was a blast to play. As far as Tower Defense games go I feel it has a reasonable level of difficulty, though some levels – such as Shallow Grave or The Mountain – can be pretty brutal if you're unprepared.
Every trap can serve you well in defending your dungeons, even the humble Dart Trap and Spike Trap you start the game with. By leveling up and using the gems obtained to upgrade your traps, you increase their efficiency – more damage, faster cooldowns, or lower cost. Mixing and matching your loadouts and set up was half of the fun for me in Dungeon Warfare. The other half admittedly came from playing with physics traps like the Push Trap and Spring Trap, knocking hapless heroes into the abyss or pools of liquid and hearing them shout in dismay before disappearing.
The game gives you plenty of flexibility in how you approach a level. There'll be pits you can try tossing enemies into, or using Spring/Push traps to launch enemies into spiked walls for an instant kill, and with the varied traps all being fairly balanced and useful, the combinations of traps and upgrades brings quite a bit of variety into how you play. Sometimes replaying the same map under a different loadout can be quite fun.
After you've cleared enough levels, you can start using Runes to increase the difficulty, as well as increasing your rewards. This can be a good method of leveling up to be better prepared for later maps like The Mountain.
Eventually you'll want to take a look at the included Map Editor. It's fairly straightforward and easy to grasp, and making your own maps or downloading those made by others further adds to what you can do during your time playing. Making maps of my own and trying to beat them has been a lot of fun as well.
The music is also fairly nice, especially the opening theme that also sometimes plays during your time defending your dungeons.
All in all, I really enjoyed Dungeon Warfare, and its sequel that's on the horizon is looking like it'll be quite amazing.

This outcome somewhat shows that first 2 hours are really important and that Valve knew what they were thinking when they chose 2 hours mark for refunds.
The  biggest downfall of this game is that it doesn't feel like a game, but more like experiment that worked to a degree, because at the end of the day, it shows how imporant first contact with the game, or anything for that matter.
You won't feel anything by playing this game - you just go from puzzle to puzzle and you will find that everything has its place, like it was programmed by a machine and not human beings.
This game is a platformer based around Tetris - you make shapes out of 4 blocks and you get from point A to B. That's it.
Graphics are ok, music is unmemorable and the only track that stands out is the one from final stage, but worst part are the floaty and delayed controls. More on that later.
First half of the game is actually pretty easy, because it puts most emphasis on puzzles, but like some indie games, when the designers run out of ideas, they throw you a curve ball and it looks like many indie devs share the same idea. Limbo? From cute platformer to crappy game of twitch reflexes and pixel perfect precision. Psychonauts (don't even get me started on that), Magrunner, Stealth inc? Same thing, throwing curve balls or completely changing the rules to artifically prolong the game.
Turning puzzle platformer with inprecise, floaty and delayed controls into Super Meat Boy (well, maybe not that hard) is not a smart idea and it only annoys players, especially since this game is unforgiving and one small mistake most of the time will end up with you restarting level all over again. It is annoyance, but levels are really short if you know what to do and you just have to be on your guard.
There are no surprises in this game. It just comes and goes. First half and chocolate HB bonus are ok, however you will feel nothing. As much as I don't like Eversion, that game at least had one gimmick surprise. Here it's nothing. It is not engaging and not relaxing, but at the same time not boring. It is just something else. Sadly, steam doesn't allow "mixed", so I just have to say "no". Shame, really, because I love puzzle games and I really wanted and trired to like this one, but can't.
Even though the price is low and you will play it for 6-7 hours, it won't leave an impression on you or give you any motivation to even complete it (I guess 5% of owners finishing the game is proof of that). If you really want to feel that hollow feeling of a soulless game, go for it, because it is better than staring at the empty screen. If you will get it from some cheap bundle, go for it. Overall, though, you're better off getting Stealth Inc or any other game.

Man. I jsut finished Ruiner and let me say: it is great.
Pros: The aesthetic, the soundtrack, and most importantly the gameplay all come together to make an unforgettable experience. While not as hard, the comparisons to Hotline Miami are definitely earned. The top down, quick as lightning bullet hell fights are always engaging - if a bit samey at times, though towards the end they start throwing a lot of interesting mechanics in. The visuals really give you a sense you're playing through a stylish cyberpunk action movie and there are some genuinely great setpieces. The abilities you can unlock really come together in interesting ways, and by the end you're basically a death machine (amongst other, far more powerful death machines, mind you) and I found myself hooked on the combat until the very end, which brings me to my cons:
Cons: My only two complaints are that the story is incoherrent for the most part towards the end, and it's short. Too short, in fact, to the point that the ending feels incredibly rushed and sudden. I thought I was maybe halfway done, but it all wraps up somewhat sloppily, and I definitely did not get as much of a chance exploring the city as I would have liked. The story isn't incredible at any point mind you, but I was at least engaged and understood what was going on and my so-called "motivations" for my actions.
All in all I would recommend this to anyone who loves games like Hotline Miami or Furi, and anyone else who want's a challenging, visually bullet hell game. Now if you'll excuse me, I need to go start new game +.

Before going into this, I'd just like to say that I've never played the "Dungeon Keeper" games that inspired this one, so I'm not wearing the rose tinted glasses of nostalgia.  That being said, I think this may be one of the most fun games I've ever played.  While there is a bit of a steep difficulty curve (I'm looking at you, level 7), and the campaign seems a bit short, It is still an enjoyable experience.  The deep, varied, and strategic gameplay, combined with a strong visual asthetic and a dark sense of humor, make this game feel fresh and enjoyable, even on repeated playthroughs.  The devs still seem to be active, so we can (hopefully) expect more content in the future.  The online multiplayer and Workshop support should help tide us over until then.  Plus, there is a sandbox mode where you can create and grow a dungeon with virtually no limits, and then test it against waves of invaders.  I've speant an embarassing amount of time in this mode.  It's sort of like a combination of a fish tank and your father's train set, but with more evil.  This game is a good expereince on its own, but it will really appeal to fans of the original dungeon keeper.  It's basically what the third game would have been if EA (Electronic♥♥♥♥♥♥ hadn't turned it into a terrible "pay-to-win" phone game.  Dig out tunnels, build rooms, attract monsters, contruct defences, fight enemies.  Heck, they even got the guy who did voiceovers in the original to come back.  Anyway, it's a good game that's worth your time and money.

A fantastic tower defense, with captivating pixel art and a plethora of unique traps.  Use the hex trap and turn single enemies into frogs, or use the bolt trap that does a lot more damage to the larger enemies.  Use a grappling hook trap to pull enemies down a pit or into lava, or use a lot of flame traps to stack burn on enemies and wipe out large crowds.  The game also has consumables, which are essentially spells which do different things.  Place an egg on the ground, that when cracked spawns a minion to attack creeps, or use the midas consumable to turn enemies into gold, stunning them and making them give more gold on death.
The games upgrades are also interesting.  Consumables can be upgraded to gain new effects on use, towers gain cooldown reduction, damage, or many other things.  The final tier of each trap offers a completely unique upgrade to each trap, and that fully upgraded trap can only be used once on the level.  The final level of the slow trap makes the slow trap deal 1 damage per second, which can be used in a chokepoint to conquer levels with ease.  These unique consumables, upgrades and large amount of various traps allow you to play however you essentially want.
The game features workshop support (not many levels are actually on the workshop, sadly), runes for each level (make levels harder and get more exp), and a survival gamemode which works on any level.  Last for as long as you can with increasing difficulty, but your limit on max level traps is increased, so more strategies are opened.
Buy Dungeon Warfare if you are a veteran of tower defenses, or a newcomer to the genre and looking to find a fantastic game.

A nice little puzzle game that doesn't overstay it's welcome but does entertain and deliver solid gameplay.
I really like Blocks that Matter, it's a clever little puzzle/platformer that does both things reasonably well, while the platforming could be a little more polished at times (there's a few times it's a pain) and there's levels that try to focus too much on platforming (timed/chase levels) overall it's a clever little game.
The core of the game is your creators need your help.  You're the little Tetrobot and you run around the level trying to save them, gaining powers and abilities and work your way through 40 levels.  40 actually different levels.  While some levels are similar and the controls don't change too much the game does change quite often, and doesn't clump similar ideas together too much.
For instance there's dripping lava that's an instant kill, once this appears you'll see it every so often, it's rarely the core of the level, but it also doesn't just have 10 of these levels in a row and then you rarely see it again.  Instead it's layered into the game as it gets progressively harder.  Ice blocks, locks, and falling blocks work the same.
The abilities Tetrobot uses is good too, they keep changing and a few of them create very solid puzzle elements and resource management.    The main abilities though are drilling blocks, and then placing those blocks back in the level four at a time to build platforms.
The interesting thing is there's 3 main different types of blocks you can place, Sand falls down, Wood burns, and the rest of the blocks just exist... There are a few others but this brings me to my big problem with this game.  It's a very inventive game but most of the blocks just "look" different, they don't react or feel different, it's a shame because it's a very clever game, but I don't understand why they needed so many different types and looks to blocks that ... well so many of the blocks don't really matter, sadly.
However there's a wealth of content for completionists here, there's at least 60 levels and I think a bit more.  There's 40 main levels, but then each level has a locked box that needs to be gained which most will challenge the player as it requires extra steps and then a "star" for each level which requires the player to have more than a certain number of blocks at the end of the level.  Both of these are reasonable challenges though will challenge most gamers.  This addes to the longevity of the game, and without looking up spoilers will keep players around for hours.
Overall I recommend blocks that matter if you like puzzlers.  It's a solid puzzler with a familiar face of tetriminos and an interesting new twist on them that is well worth picking up.  Ultimately I give it a recommend, because it's a fantastic experience.

RUINER is a great game! It combines fast-paced combat with an awesome cyberpunk aesthetic.
Many people compare the combat to Hotline Miami, however, I find the combat in RUINER to be much more in-depth. The RPG aspects of RUINER allows the player to earn a variety of different skills that can effect the playstyle from extra dashes, explosive and stun grenades, to the ability to exchange energy for health. The vast amount of abilites that are available will allow for numerous different playthroughs and will prolong potential playtime.
The story of RUINER is simple, yet effective. You are looking for your brother and for the people that hacked your brain. With the assistance of a hacker known only as "Her" you carve your way through the layers of a dystopian city, killing anyone standing in your way. The story doesn't take itself too seriously, it doesn't warn the player of the dangers of technology or of corporations, the story is simply a set-piece for the violence.
The art-style is probaby my favourite style in a video game to date. Reminiscent of early cyberpunk anime such as Ghost in the Shell and Akira this is a game with equal style and substance. Character designs are well drawn and each and every environment is lovingly rendered.
Finally the music is stunning. Deep bass and synth is common throughout the soundtrack, my personal favourite being SLEEP PARALYSIS by Sidewalks and Skeletons. If you are a fan of Cyberpunk or Hotline Miami this game will not disappoint!

PROS:
- Lots of great core gameplay for creative players. With the introduction of equilateral triangular foundations, you can make *triangular structures*. This is the first time I've seen this in any type of survival game. With this, you can combine triangular foundations with square ones to create very interesting pieces of work. Being a creative player myself, I had so much fun just building.
- PvP and PvE is similar to Skyrim. Some people would consider this a negative, but I very much enjoyed Skyrim's simple combat system. There's stamina to keep track of while battling. You can dual wield, use a sword and shield, or use bow and arrows. Most of this comes down to who has the better stats, but it is possible to outplay your opponent if you really get into this game and have the right build.
[[UPDATE: With the combat update announced, combat will only be getting better from here]]
- There's lore. Actual lore to pick up and read or listen to. There's NPCs you can talk to--or kill, if you want to (though they'll respawn). All in multiplayer as well. I'm incredibly interested in the world of this game and hope to see more lore pumped out in the future.
- The game is gorgeous. The hair and body physics are out of this world. There's nudity for *both* genders, and *both* have customizable body parts (breasts and♥♥♥♥♥♥♥sliders). It's strangely immersive, and I say strangely because I've never felt "immersed" in a survival game before. It's immersive in the same way, again, Skyrim is immersive.
- Character customization will always keep your character realistic looking (unlike ARK), but you can still have some ugly♥♥♥♥♥characters if you'd like to be ugly. I'm hoping they add more body customization options in the future, and more facial ones. Can never, EVER have enough customization options.
- Servers follow this "tagging" system. So if you have a PvP server that's more relaxed and friendly, maybe a little goofy, you can select PvP and "relaxed" as its tag. Or maybe you have a PvE server that has no bonuses and wants to stay true to the vanilla gameplay, you can filter it as such. Or maybe you have a hardcore, ultra-serious PvP server where you want to focus solely on tactics--you can tag it as such. It makes filtering the type of servers YOU want much easier. Only downside is that the server list takes a long time to load up...
- [[June 23, 2017]] Free expansion has been announced, expanding the map severely and adding an entirely new biome. Climbing is going to be added to combat height restrictions, ultimately changing the PvP meta, and combat is being revamped. A lot of great changes are coming and I'm going to throw in the towel and change this review to a positive. It WILL go back to negative if the devs bail or do something generally incredibly stupid.
FIXED:
- Horrible lag for low end, even middle end, computers. For those who have mechanical drives, DO NOT GET THIS. Buy an SSD and install this game on that SSD. Otherwise, load times will take 10, even 20, minutes. I wish I was joking. I bought an SSD, which is currently on its way, just to combat this game's load times and hopefully have an easier time with other games in the future.
[[UPDATE: Currently have the game installed on an SSD and it loads so much faster]]
- Not sure if this also applies to mechanical drives vs. SSD's, but loading in players' buildings takes a while. This is while you're *in* the game, too. And it's the worst if you're ever getting raided, but you can't do anything because the game is freezing trying to load everything.
[[UPDATE: This seems to have been optimized]]
- PvP is imbalanced. Currently favors the raiders, and there isn't much to do in terms of defense for your base. The only way to ensure a solid defense is to set your base on a tall mountain, and delete the stairs when you log out. That's it. No counterplay for raiders, but otherwise you'd have no way to counter them if they raided you anyway. The game needs more options to help defend against other players, beyond this "thrall" system which is pretty imbalanced currently (though a great idea if they tune it up more in the future).
[[UPDATE: With the announcement of climbing and the combat update, it seems this will no longer be an issue, but we will see. It will go back into cons if huge problems persist.]]
- PvE doesn't have much to do beyond building and killing stray NPCs/mobs. There's bosses, but not really any loot to get from them as far as I know. Surely something good will be added in the future, though. I hope.
[[UPDATE: There is lore to collect, which can give animated poses like Surrender, Blow Kiss, Seduce, etc. Great for roleplayers or just to use to goof around. However, there is still little loot to be had for PvE, so as great as this addition is, I'm afraid this is still a con.]]
[[UPDATE 2: The new free expansion adds better AI for NPCs and loot actually matters now, so PvE is pretty much fixed in my eyes.]]
CONS:
- None at the moment besides minor nitpicks.
I'll try my best to keep this updated as the game continues its early access. Let's hope Funcom actually allows the game to leave it, though.

This is my favorite video game of all time. Ignore my playtime, I've played this game consistently (even to this day) since it originally released long before I played it on Steam. I've played this game at least fourteen different ways and I always, and I mean ALWAYS, find something in my next playthrough I hadn't noticed before. This game is as short or as long as you want it to be. You want to focus on taking down the Collectors and nothing else? Go right ahead. You want to kick back, relax and explore the galaxy in front of you at your own pace? Go right ahead. You want to go romance your favorite companion only to hear him say "Can it wait a bit? I'm in the middle of some calibrations"? Go. Right. Ahead. The story is superb, the gameplay is straightforward and you can customize your character and armor to your liking. This is not a game, this is an experience. I assure you, you will play this once and instantly want to play it again. Your choices truly matter. This game doesn't have an illusion of choice, no, you make a choice and it will come back to bite you later on. (Example: You don't want to upgrade your ship's shields for when you assault the Collector Base? I hope you've at least decided to get some heavy plating on that bad boy. Otherwise, you're in for a rough ride kiddo.) Hell, any of your companions can in fact die permanently in the final assault. And if they die, I hope you don't expect to see them miraciously reanimated in Mass Effect 3. They're dead because of you kiddo, and now you you'll remember that for the rest of the trilogy if you decide to import your character and choices in Mass Effect 3.
So my question for you is... how will the galaxy remember YOUR Commander Shepard?

Jet Set Radio is a stylized masterpiece from the little known console known as the Dreamcast. It was one of the very first games to use cell shaded graphics. Which it uses to build it's aesthetic of a futuristic Tokyo. If you never played this game before you will probably dislike it like I did when I first started.  I didn't want to quit playing it on the first try so I played it for 2 or 3 days to see if it would hold my attention. I now play it on the IPAD, PC and PS4 on the daily basis because it's very entertaining once you understand the mechanics.
In short, you have to build your military might by attacking online rivals, completing battle campaigns, upgrading your factories, oil rigs and defending your resources from invasion.  The players  whom have the best offensive and defensive strategy rise quickly via upgrades, promotions and joint battle operations.
If you don't like waiting you have the option to buy gold bricks which allow you to avoid long waiting periods associated with crafting your offensive and defensive measures in order to engage in more intense battles. Gold is rewarded to all players after their meter reaches 100% and they move on to the next level so this is completely optional.
The game gets better as you progress and build a stronger military to handle both offensive and defensive measures. Eventually you will want to form an online alliance or create your own. This will allow you to team up against stronger rivals whom will grant you many more rewards if you are successful on the battlefield.
There are some frustrating issues with the games like tanks ignoring enemy fire even though you send in 5 tanks to handle business in the general area. Another issue is bunker soldiers shooting through buildings and destroying tanks and soldiers that are clearly at a safe distance behind a fortified wall ect ..
The artificial intelligence could be a bit better but overall it's still a fun game to play overtime.

This game is a lot of fun. It can be a little challenging (ok, a lot) with all the bully commanders and tyrants out there pummeling your humble defenses and farming away your hard earned crates. But, that's one of the reasons to like the game - the challenge and strategy required to preserve your stockpile long enough to advance to the next level and achievement. It can be a little disturbing when your supplies get taken away, especially just prior to the implementation of upgrading your units and defenses. I'd whine and cry a little more if I wasn't guilty of doing that to others myself - after all, it's WAR! And even the mighty lion and the fastest cheetah go for the weakest prey. Why fight someone your own size to risk great loss when you can pound a lesser army and take all the booty you want. Ever hear of Sun Tzu? It's a great game, loads fast, functional and free to play, The developers are happy to sell you gold at a fairly reasonable cost which can be used to purchase massive amounts of supplies. . .but where's the fun it that? Only a weak-minded, cowardly, punk-axx, spend-thrift little sissy/bully would need to do that. Also, it can be very helpful if you have the availability to log on for a couple minutes about every hour or so, but you can also go days and weeks without doing so and still find yourself in pretty good shape since no one can actually permanently destroy your base - you just lose crates and dog tags. Give it a try, it's cool. And, you can also draw really cool pictures of the islands and units in a makeshift birthday card to your girlfriend when you forget about her, add a quick rhyme and a clever poem about your gameplay and how it in no way compares to all her talent and beauty, and then she'll love you even more and appreciate all your efforts in the game while she's making dinner and cleaning up around the house. (She's smacking me in the back of the head right now - I gotta go) Play the game.

So I've finished the game and it really was an awesome game, but it has its flaws and there is a big drop in quality after the first two acts, but I still consider this an approvement over the divinity original sin, which was a wonderful game. So any fan of the previous title should really try this one. I'm sure there are plenty of review, which highlight the positive aspects of the game, I'm not really good at that, so I'll just let you know, that I've enjoyed the dialogues, the combat, the characters, the magic and the overall RPG elements.
Fair warning, the game has a lot of bugs still, personally I've encountered just one potentially game breaking bug, which had to be solved by running away while using unarmed civilians as distraction, if that haven't worked I would have to load a previous save, god bless their souls (not the godwoken, I've let them to die and never looked back). But the most annoying bugs concern the journal entries, which track your quest progression, they do not update correctly, which is really irritating, since the story and your choices should be really important part of this game and the journal should reflect that, but that is unfortunately not so at this moment. Hopefully this will be fixed in the future updates. Because it really takes away the joy of completing the quest, when the journal indicates afterwards, what a horrible person you are for not finishing it.
I have two more things, which I would like to mention. First thing are the elves, the terrible desing for the elves, I don't mind that much, that they have necks like girrafes or that they have wrinkled skin, what bothered me the most are the armor design. You take a plate armor, put it on human, lizard and undead with small changes, you put it on a dwarf with a little bigger change, but you put it on an elf and you get half naked person with something which looks like roots on the chest area and two oversized pauldrons on your shoulder. In the end they look terrible and you can't even hide it with armor, because the armor doesn't cover them. I guess it is a price you have to pay for their very usefull abilities. Second thing is splash effect, because the developers really wanted you to enjoy their system of elements everything has to have some splash effects, so the elemental play will be everywhere. It can get really tedious to controll the enviroment effects, in the end I preferred to use physical weapons over amazing source skills, so I wouldn't have to deal with splashing a bit of fire over poison and start a chain reaction, because there is always some oil and some other element elsewhere, god forbid you hit enemy with elemental skin, which makes them bleed element, causing another chain reaction.
Therefore I do recommend the game, but I would suggest you to wait for a bit before playing. I will certainly wait for them to fix the issues and then replay the game with different origin and more importantly with mods, so I can enjoy the game to the fullest.

Now before I start, I just wanted to say... "YES! I get that a lot of people say that Archeage is P2W! But that doesn't mean it isn't worth a try!"
Let me expand on that:
Archeage is free to play. I only played 12 hours, and within that time frame, I realized that the game is actually pretty good. Though there are so many other features that this game has that it would be impossible for me to tell someone to not give it a good try!

Disclaimer – I am a Kickstarter backer of this game and huge fan of the original Dungeon Keeper
1) Essential - buy it NOW

3) Avoid
Time to complete – 17 hours to complete campaign
Played multiplayer? No
Worth revisiting? Yes, will probably come back to play the DLC and try out some skirmish
Best part – Takes that oh-so-awesome Dungeon Keeper formula and adds new twists and mechanics to keep things fresh and exciting. Some of the new additions don't quite hit the mark (useless, overpowered or duplicated function) but on the whole I liked the majority of the new stuff.
Worst part – The game has some technical problems, particularly on the last two levels of the campaign. Expect frequent 1 second long freezes, big fps drops during battles and crashes requiring a restart of the game. Smaller maps run pretty much flawlessly.
Summary – When War for the Overworld was initially given it's 'full' release I was disappointed with what we got and found it a far cry from the Dungeon Keeper series which inspired it. However, huge credit must be given to the developers for listening to feedback, making improvements, squashing bugs and making WftO into the game that was promised. I still do not hold it in such high regard as DK1 but it definitely rivals DK2 and most importantly has the 'feel' of a Dungeon Keeper title, which is not an easy thing to pull-off. I do not regret supporting this project on Kickstarter and I am a happy backer!

It baffles me how much P2W Archeage is.
If you run 4 accounts with stipend and vocation buffs that is 4380 labor x 4 accounts. Ofcourse you need to have a good setup to use that much labor. Lets say you have 2 freighters and can run dry that labor in 3-5h which is PURE GRIND.
You get 17520 labor in total in 24h. Lets assume you have max commerce which makes pack craft and trade in around 72 labor. 17520 / 72 = 243 packs. With optimal route and minus pack costs you make around 10-12 silver profit a pack. Which is roughly 3k gold if you have max commerce on all 4 and get 12 gold profit. And I did not even include the APEX and stipend expenses which are 3k per account.
3k gold is 3.3 APEX in EU which is 25£ or 29€. Or 15€ from shady gold sellers.
And to get a gear score of 6k requires you to spend around 200-300k gold if bought from AH.
TLDR: You need to play 3 months straight with perfect setup running packs 3-5h a day. Or you need to pay 1.5k € Just to get within the gear curve. And 6k gear score is bare minimum to not get 1-2 shotted.
So this game is only for rich people unless you like being a slave in the game and earning 5$ a day.

This game is surprisingly fun for how rough around the edges it is. TL;DR: I would recommend it for any fans of Everquest era MMOs.
The Bad.
The game is quite buggy. Clipping is poorly executed, and often you will find your character hung up on a pebble or a random hill slope. Once, upon logging back into the game with a character I was previously playing, all of their inventory was erased. Just gone. Sometimes quest NPCs get stuck in solid objects where you can't click on them to get a quest. Some enemies are undamagable, because they are stuck in some kind of permanent stasis.
The game doesn't seem to have any cogent plot. Granted, I didn't play deep into the game, but for the first four hours, the quests were just randomly generated grind quests. There was no story. No explanation for why the castle is surrounded by spiders, skeletons, skeletal mages, gargoyles, evil mushrooms, elf witches, goblins, ratkin slaves, elementals, and strange beasts. Those are just all things that are out there, hanging out, waiting to be killed (again, like old Everquest zones).
The Good.
The progression is actually well paced and satisfying. Even with a full erasure of my inventory, I was able to buy some basic gear and keep on levelling. I chose melee as my skill, so levelling didn't involve tough decisions. And the levels and gear upgrades really made a difference. The game also had a simple crafting mechanic that offered some valuable item upgrades as well.

What, you want more? Ok then. The idea of Dungeon Keeper series, which this game continues, can be seen in the store page for this game. Instead of leading your hero through a dungeon, defeating monsters, here the roles are reversed - you are planning out a dungeon, training and commanding monsters to fight invading heroes, meeting the various needs of your monsters in the process. All of this is accompanied by appropriately dark humorous lines from The Mentor (the same voice actor that narrated the original, Richard Ridings):
I'm sure there will be those who don't see the appeal of this concept. If you are one of those people, this game isn't for you. But if you loved Dungeon Keeper & Dungeon Keeper 2, you will love this game as well.

Burgers is a sidescroll shooter and an example of a terrible execution of an otherwise nice idea.
Sadly it has so many flaws that it is quite difficult to see any redeeming points about it. In fact the only one I can think about is the art style and animations.
It starts with the incredible unintuitive control scheme. A gamepad is highly recommended if you don't want to bother with fix key bindings as J to shoot. J! What could be a typical twin stick control was decided to be normal WASD/left stick movement with a button toggle to move backwards while shooting will always be in the direction you're facing.
You also shouldn't dare to pause or try to go into the main menu with Escape. It will crash your game every single time.
The story is a series of inexplicable events. You start as a Nazi Soldier shooting the French Resistance, then chasing after some sphere, shooting aliens, plant monsters and various other monsters coming seemingly out of nowhere before facing some SS troops.
Balancing is completely off. Your sidearm is more powerful than your primary weapon for some time. Until you are able to unlock "Sniper Rifles" which kill most things with one or two shots and penetrate the target. It is offset by a a smaller magazine size and less ammunition, but that is rarely an issue. Some missions grant you a special weapon like the flame thrower or electro gun, which again are vastly overpowered and hardly ever run dry. On the other hand bosses are unfathomable bullet sponges and trying to defeat them with your starting equipment is chore.
Replayability is limited at best. A story run will take 2 hours (excluding those damn crashes). While running the missions you will earn XP and Credits too unlock new weapons. Or rather lots of skins for slightly different weapons which often only differ slightly in magazine size, while damage output is dependent on the weapons class. Sadly you are stuck with your loadout once the session started. Thanks to the Escape-crash changing it means re-booting the game.
There are many, many more issues and sign of either not giving a♥♥♥♥♥♥or inability to fix them. Even though the game is only about 3 EUR I cannot recommend buying it.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Holy crap, this actually finally came out! Looks like I owe someone money.
I find it a lot more enjoyable and playable now that it's completed, but it still feels barely complete, a sentiment which even professional reviewers have noted.
The main Overgrowth campaign has its moments (i.e. the frustrating but very atmospheric foggy swamp level) but ends rather abruptly (just as the story hit a high note), and the built-in Lugaru redux campaign feels a bit like padding. Most lamentably, a recurring phrase in the main Overgrowth campaign is "You always have a choice" but there are no branching story paths or the like. Turner gets some funny lines, but it's kind of hard to otherwise see him as anything but a cliche anti-hero otherwise.
The core gameplay is flawed but enjoyable, but the level design rarely feels designed to make the most of the parkour's potential. And the bunny dropkick is somewhat rather overpowered.
I am in the middle of a playthrough of the Therium-2 mod (still in progress but highly excellent) and it feels more feature-complete and even adds new things. Might be worth the price of admission for some, I feel I got my money's worth although I am still encompassing only the core game here for the purposes of my review.
It's weird seeing this game finally come out. A commenter in a recent Rock Paper Scissors article about Overgrowth's release described it as a time capsule from an alternate universe where indie gaming never really took off like it has, which sounds about right.
I give this game a 7/10 (barely) and would recommend buying it, but only on sale. My feelings on the game are a bit complicated for a simplistic thumbs up or down.
ORIGINAL REVIEW BELOW FOR POSTERITY:
I can applaud Wolfire's ambition, and I appreciate that they bundle Receiver---which is a wonderful little bite-sized FPS---with Overgrowth, but that doesn't do much to offset two very key facts:
-Overgrowth is still in alpha, and a buggy alpha at that.
-It has been in alpha since 2008. SIX WHOLE YEARS.
I realize Wolfire is a very small studio, but thirty dollars for a buggy alpha is an extremely bad deal. They're at least transparent that it's an alpha, but I bought the game years ago before it was Greenlighted on Steam never even imagining that they would take this ridiculously long.
If you want to give Wolfire your money, go ahead. But keep in mind that this is nowhere NEAR a complete game---it's basically only a level editor/modkit and some assets at this point---and it's not clear when, if ever, a beta and/or a complete game will be forthcoming.
I recommend just buying Receiver instead. It's finished, it's cheap, it's interesting, and overall not only is it more bang for your buck but it still supports Wolfire.
If Wolfire learns some better time management skills and gets things moving, I may rewrite this review after sampling new features and content. Until then, this is a bad deal, and an example of the shortcomings of both Steam Greenlight and, to a greater extent, the whole concept of 'early access' in game sales.
EDIT: Before anyone gets snarky, I bought this game through Wolfire's website some time before it ever came to Steam. Also, I play games on a laptop, so sometimes I play games more than the time played record indicates. Now if you're going to make sarcastic comments at me, at least say something productive instead of trying to punch holes in my review, especially given that I at least tried to be fair.

Lugaru, at its time, was a very mechanically sound fighting-game for what  the developers had at the time, and Overgrowth is sure to deliver once it finishes development. For where Overgrowth is at now, it shows great potential of being a great third-person fighting game with anthropomorphic animals, but don't let the latter turn you off. The fighting mechanics are easy to learn, but difficult to master, with precise timing being the key to whether you defeat you opponent or you gettting pummeled to the ground. The game also shows off its beauty with a very gorgeous engine, with the models of each character being well-detailed and constructed, and the enviorments, although simple, showing off some very interesting architecture. The technology for the damage system is quite nice as well, with it being based off skeletal-like models, and recieving more or less damage in certain areas and how hard the impact is on the models. Weapon combat, just like in hand-to-hand combat, is very difficult to master, since the reaction time needed to block and parry attacks will determine whether you instantly get killed or come out unscathed. With the weapon combat comes the very nice blood decals, with every slice, stab, and thrown weapon leaving a nice, sharp cut or hole of blood on the body, probably the most realistic i've seen thus far in video games, though it only leaves blood marks and doesn't show signs of any physical degradation.
But probably one of the biggest strong points of Overgrowth is its editor, which leaves the user to creating their own maps, missions, and stories to their hearts content. With the devs leaving a fairly abundent assortment of props, enviorments, path-finding and other tools to the user's disposal, it leaves the user with their imagination on what they wish to create, or what they want to test. Though it will take time getting used to a rather bare-bones UI, the capabilities given supplies the user a tool that will keep the game alive from now until hopefully way long after release.
Although Overgrowth is still in development, it shows its technologic capabilities greatly, leaving only a few bugs and still incorporating mechanics like stealth into the mix. Although non-existant, it will be left to the users imagination what the story of Overgrowth will be about, and how our favorite ninja-rabbit Turner is doing after the events of Lugaru.

Since someone was "nice" enough to ask for it, Here is my full review.
Mass Effect 2
One of my favorite games of all time. I’ve played it from beginning to end, probably somewhere upwards of three to four times at least. I’ve owned it on both PC and PS3 before. In fact I still have some DLC from both versions through
There’s a lot to love here. It was an expansive sequel to Mass Effect that in your choices from the first game show up here, the gameplay was radically improved upon and the game just looks absolutely stunning!
Story
From a storytelling point of view this game is absolutely gaming fodder. In the tradition of the best RPGs you go out looking for your merry (well some of them are merry at least) group of followers. It’s got almost a Seven Samurai vibe going on here. You have to hunt down an assassin whom is forever cursed with the ability to relieve any of his memories perfectly forever. A loyal space marine haunted by the fate of what ever happened to his father. The loyal (or is she?) right hand woman to the corporation that has brought you back from brink of death itself. Old friends and some interesting new ones are met as well.
It feels like a good bottle of port.
Very smooth and relaxing to take it all in.
Without spoiling anything major story wise, I’ll just say it added to it in all the right ways. Really made the game shine giving you so much more immersion you really end up wanting to play through to find out how your choices unfold and where these characters might end up.

Sets a great stage for the last game.
Presentation
Well, it sure is pretty.
The difference here is akin to comparing Witcher 1 to Witcher 3. It holds up remarkably well with age. It looks like it could come out today on the PC. My only gripe would be it could with a small update give us a wee bit more access to under the hood settings wise but that may be a tad unrealitic of me of Bioware.
The game sizzles with amazing on screen effects, sound is really the main winner here though. Voice acting is the bar other games should set for itself. This game is pretty much one of the best voiced games I’ve ever heard to this day, easily in my top five. Witcher 3 and The Walking Dead season 1 edge it out just barely here in my book.
Gameplay
Oooo, it’s really fun this time around. It’s a cover shooter for sure, it has RPG underpinnings. Think small but powerful skill trees that equal up to either amazing combat abilties or skills to be used in game to help turn events or avoid combat all together, almost somewhere between Deus Ex and Call of Duty. It’s a lot of fun. It’s a squad based game so you almost always have a few allies in the thick of it with you which is really fun and makes combat managable but never impossible.
I would say if you like action games, with light tactical consideration this a great contender for you.

Lasting appeal.
Well it’s obviously a classic.
I don’t particular enjoy the 3rd game which this one builds up towards well. So that's not what hesitates me to recommend this edition of Mass Effect 2. That would be like hating on Empire for Return.  That being said I’ve owned it multiple times which is something I don’t do often. It is a blast to play. But once again, my primary hesitation here is the lack of DLC missing from the current editions. The DLC is amazing content but after so many years it’s still just missing from the game they currently sell via steam and also on consoles. They don't label this at all. Which to me is deceiving. It’s their choice to charge full price after all these years for something that actually fills in plot holes story wise. I really want to recommend this game to you but it kills me a little bit inside how much I and many others have already given them money wise that they won’t just give people this content for free or at least at a huge price cut after almost seven years. I want you to have it I just don't want you to spend almost 30 dollars plus the cost of the base game to get it!
I refuse to pay more than I paid for the game itself for all this content. A truly excellent game for its time, and still quite entertaining even today.  Lords of the Realm 2 is a game that revolves around attempting to take over a region, which is split into a number of counties.  Each county provides your effort with resources such as food, lumber, money, and men.
The computer AI is remarkably good considering the age of the game.  It can accomplish many intelligent context based tasks.  For example if the computer sees it does not have the manpower to hold an endangered county, it will wreck what it can and transport away all the resources so that they do not fall into enemy hands.  In combat (which is done RTS style) it can organize a cohesive attack when it has the advantage of numbers, or attempt to turtle behind cover when it is at a disadvantage.  The computer can organize small expendable raiding parties designed to burn your crop fields and cripple your economy, and knows to press the advantage if it spots a lightly defended territory.  Overall it cannot match a human player, but it greatly lowers the need for computer advantages still used today by many games to artificially inflate difficulty.
Computer controlled Lords have personalities and voice actors assigned to them for flavor, and although the voice acting is generally terrible, I must admit that it makes the game more enjoyable to have The Knight insult me in his exaggeratedly arrogant tone, or The Baron politely inform me of his intent to annex my territory.
The UI is easy to understand, and a marked step up from LotR 1.  There are tooltips and help topics; a brand new player will have no trouble diving right.  There are even auto saves, which was not a given at the time!  Very convenient!
LotR 2 is fast and fun, a truly great game for its time.  If you never played it, and are a fan of strategy, it's certainly worth a look!

In Blocks That Matter, little Tetrobot must solve platforming block puzzles by gathering matter and placing it in tetronimoes in order to save Alexey Pajitnov, the creator of Tetris, and Markus Persson, he of Minecraft fame.
Tetrobot’s adventure through Sweden (the land of indie games) is full of difficult challenges and brain-bending puzzles.  You’ll need to think out the entire level before making a move if you want to collect the Block That Matters, which contains an important historical video game where certain blocks… mattered.
The main adventure is a series of 40 levels where you must reach the exit portal.  Collecting blocks and using them smartly is your only option.  The Tetrobot can either drill into blocks from the side, or jump up and hit them from beneath to collect them.  But beware, he can’t drill while he is jumping in the air, nor can he drill blocks beneath him.  These simple limitations cause some seemingly simple situations to devolve into brain-frying problems.
The plinky-plunky soundtrack is cute and engaging, putting you into a puzzly mindset, though the over-reliance on deep bass meant I had to turn down my speakers whenever I started the game.
The cartoony graphics are great, and all the different blocks and terrains you will be exploring are interesting.  The pseudo-isometric viewpoint you are given is helpful, and it is usually easy to count how many blocks a certain jump will be.
The difficulty ramps fairly quickly, and sometimes a single mistake can mean having to redo minutes of work.  The sometimes open-ended nature of certain sections of puzzles can lead to later puzzles being unsolvable, though you never would have known that at the beginning of the level.  This situation will rarely prevent you from finishing a level, though it often means you can’t get the Block That Matters.
This was a fun game, though some of the platforming sections got on my nerves a bit, especially when I had to redo some other simple puzzles over and over again to retry the difficult section.  A bit more balancing or some sort of checkpoint system would have been really nice.  Overall I enjoyed seeking out the Blocks That Matter, and saving Alexey and Markus from their abduction.
There are 10 free bonus “chocolate” levels that were added as part of the Humble Voxatron Debut, so be sure to check those out!

Been looking for a TD to "scratch that itch" after recovering from GemCraft addiction. I've tried dozens and have been left flat... I was beginning to think that GemCraft ruined me for all other TD games. However, this one is doing the trick so far.
I've seen others try to deduce the formula as to what makes these games enjoyable/addicting, and have never really agreed with anyone so far. If I'm going to attempt the same, I would have to say it's the forced variation of defense (you really can't rely on one trap type) combined with the RPG like progression (runes unlock varied experiences on old maps, bringing you back for more and more). To some, this is considered "grindy", but you can only earn XP that surpasses your prior XP, preventing a stale sludging through old territory.
The metal soundtrack is a bit repetitive, yet fitting, and the narration of kill streak approval is a pleasing nostalgia harkening back to early 90s Mortal Combat binges in the arcade.... "Juicy"
All in all, this is the most satisfying TD I've played in nearly a year. Props to the devs.

Lugaru, at its time, was a very mechanically sound fighting-game for what  the developers had at the time, and Overgrowth is sure to deliver once it finishes development. For where Overgrowth is at now, it shows great potential of being a great third-person fighting game with anthropomorphic animals, but don't let the latter turn you off. The fighting mechanics are easy to learn, but difficult to master, with precise timing being the key to whether you defeat you opponent or you gettting pummeled to the ground. The game also shows off its beauty with a very gorgeous engine, with the models of each character being well-detailed and constructed, and the enviorments, although simple, showing off some very interesting architecture. The technology for the damage system is quite nice as well, with it being based off skeletal-like models, and recieving more or less damage in certain areas and how hard the impact is on the models. Weapon combat, just like in hand-to-hand combat, is very difficult to master, since the reaction time needed to block and parry attacks will determine whether you instantly get killed or come out unscathed. With the weapon combat comes the very nice blood decals, with every slice, stab, and thrown weapon leaving a nice, sharp cut or hole of blood on the body, probably the most realistic i've seen thus far in video games, though it only leaves blood marks and doesn't show signs of any physical degradation.
But probably one of the biggest strong points of Overgrowth is its editor, which leaves the user to creating their own maps, missions, and stories to their hearts content. With the devs leaving a fairly abundent assortment of props, enviorments, path-finding and other tools to the user's disposal, it leaves the user with their imagination on what they wish to create, or what they want to test. Though it will take time getting used to a rather bare-bones UI, the capabilities given supplies the user a tool that will keep the game alive from now until hopefully way long after release.
Although Overgrowth is still in development, it shows its technologic capabilities greatly, leaving only a few bugs and still incorporating mechanics like stealth into the mix. Although non-existant, it will be left to the users imagination what the story of Overgrowth will be about, and how our favorite ninja-rabbit Turner is doing after the events of Lugaru.

Blocks That Matter is a cute little puzzle platformer which is good fun, and has somewhat unique mechanics.  I'd played this game years ago and just recently replayed it to 100%, and definitely enjoyed it the second time around as well.
The game's not without its downsides.  As many others have mentioned, an 'undo' function would be greatly appreciated, though in general the levels aren't really long enough for that to be a terrible problem.  There's also three "Big Mama" levels which require you to race forward as a gigantic insta-death Slime chases you...  Those levels aren't too bad if you don't care about 100% completion (in fact, there's an option to skip them entirely from the pause menu), but if you ARE the sort of person to get hung up on 100%, they can be an excercise in frustration.  Especially the last one, which requires near-perfect gameplay to get a star on the level.  Many of the levels must be solved more than once to get 100%, as well.
Despite those drawbacks, though, I'd definitely recommend the game to anyone who does enjoy puzzle platformers.  There are some very nice "aha!" moments when a previously-unsolveable-seeming level clicks into place, and its charms far oughtweigh any problems it might have.
(I do feel compelled to mention that BTM's sequel "Tetrobot and Co" takes care of many of the issues which are found in this game - there's no even vaguely arcade-like sections like the Big Mama levels, an Undo function is available, and the levels can always be completed to 100% on the first time through.)

Just a first impressions here, but the game so far is so good I've got to get this out. I'm really impressed with this one overall. The controls are tight. The atmosphere is just ... amazing. Cyberpunk style isn't for anyone. You either love it or hate it I think. They nail it out of the park here, though. So if it is you're going to love the atmosphere. The story line is there. It makes sense, and it's a good one. It won't rock your socks off or anything, but it's definitely not over the top or crazy. It's just a good, solid story line. The shooter mechanics are a little different than what you see in other shooters. You have a ton of weapons that you pick up throughout the game. The game also forces you to pick up and use different weapons on the fly, and I like that. It also has a skill tree that is very robust, and it allows you to subtract skill points from other areas to boost up skill points in another. This is a great feature. You might realize there is a skill set that isn't suited to your play style. So you can go through the skill tree and delete those skills you find yourself not using or find not useful, and transfer those skillpoints elsewhere. It's a very refreshing feature. The graphics are great in themselves. The music is pretty good, too. It has an electronic/techno style of music feel that goes very well with the chaotic and fast paced nature of the game. There are sections where you have to take a knee and explore this town to talk with NPCs and get missions and side missions if you will. It's a nice way of breaking up the game I think, and it doesn't overstay its welcome in between stages. Overall, it is a very good game and a surprise game for sure. With all the other great stuff that has come out this year I hope like heck this one doesn't get overlooked. Check this one out!

Gemini Rue is, shall we say, an odd duck.  It's an indie sci-fi adventure title that's made the rounds as "the one to beat" in terms of independent adventure games.  Fortunately it falls in the "pretty good" range, while still suffering from a couple problems.
The voice acting is okay to passable, and serves it's purpose without being offensive.  The graphics are pixelated, and are a lot of fun for nerdy aging weirdo idiots (like myself) who cut their teeth playing old adventure games.  The story itself is very good, with a couple of neat twists and turns.  Finally we come to the gameplay, which is really the lowest point of the game.  The puzzles often have really obtuse and, in some cases, bizarre solutions (♥♥♥♥ the 'Kick' action for real, that thing still doesn't make any sense to me and I beat this thing), that make a guide pretty much a necessity at times.  Overall well worth what it costs, but not as great as you've been hearing.

Lords of the Realm II is a Medieval Turn based strategy game, and real-time strategy for the army battle phases. Lords of the Realm II was developed by Impressions Games, and published by Sierra Entertainment
and released in 1996.
"The year is 1268 A.D. The King is dead... ...There will be dark days ahead."
Lords of the Realm II is set in the lands of England and Wales, every petty warlord is scrambling to take the throne for their own purposes, you must conquer the usurpers and force them to recognize your superiority in battle, economics, and leadership.
There are two key characteristics to Lords of the Realm II: World/Map View, and Combat View. In World View, you govern your people, keep them happy, feed them, plant crops, allocate food and supplies between cities/states/provinces, direct where your peasants should work to maximize efficiency... really, just about everything takes place in the map view, and most of the strategy takes place here too.
As with most strategy games, there's a lot of details to cover, and in a review there isn't really that much time, the basic gist is: Get as many people as possible, make or buy weapons, build an army, "conquer thy neighbors".
The combat view is where you can implement rather creative tactics. If you're fighting on an open plane, you can try to formulate a strong defense using your natural surrounding, or just charge in and smash against the enemy line.
Can I have an achievement that says "I played this game as a little kid, and wasn't completely terrible at it"? As far as older video games goes, this game isn't nearly as brutal as a game like X-COM: UFO Defense, however it's just as much fun to play.
Without the nostalgia factor I don't know how much someone else might enjoy playing this game. But when I saw it was available on Steam, I tried to ignore it for a while, but ended up purchasing it within a week.
Lords of the Realm II, was definitely the best of the series. Lords II hours is priced at $2.99, I snagged the game, and then proceeded to played for 5 hours, 2 where I completely forgot I was supposed to be working on my next YouTube Video Review, and 3 hours spent streaming it on twitch boring my audience with my nostalgia gushing.
There is a "Lords of the Realm Complete" bundle for $12.99, I always wanted to know what the other games were like, so that's the bundle I purchased. Stay tuned to hear my reviews for those games as well!

It's clear that most maps have multiple ways to complete them - this is a huge plus IMO. Nonetheless you quickly find that your go-to strat on the last couple maps no longer works on the next map - I had to adapt constantly.
Can't say enough good stuff about this game, definitely a 9 or 9.5 out of 10. Only complaints would be that some of the traps seemed underpowered (and even here, I probably just didn't figure out the best way to leverage them), and one trap was given too late. Could've used a few more achievements that were map+rune specific, but that's more of a suggestion than a complaint.

TL-DR: If you like Tower Defense games, get this, it is one of the best out there. Way more towers than most games, lots of levels, good difficulty level, great game.
I think this might be the best Tower Defense game I've played. I played a lot starting with Warcraft 3 mods, and then Desktop Tower Defense the flash game. Since then I've played dozens of TD games, on iPhone, Android, and PC. They all have pros and cons, PVZ is unique and fun but not all that interesting or deep, Gemcraft is the same and also grindy, Defence Grid is great and has really nice graphics but the game maybe lacks a little of something, Bloonz is great but a bit repetitive, Creeper World is smart yet shallow and quite sedate, etc..etc.. I could easily list 20 more.
But there is something about this game that just ticks all the right boxes. It is challenging without being a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ you sometimes have to do a level a few times until you can finally nail it, but it is always doable without relying on luck or something. Also some games don't let you shape your path which annoys me, this game has plenty of path shaping so you get to pick different routes through the map. There are actually at least several ways to win each map, not just with the paths you make the creeps take, but with tower selection too. There are a LOT of towers in this game, unlike the lame TD games that only give you several, this one has something like 20 ish towers, each one with a unique effect, and each one upgradeable which sometimes gives an extra effect too. The maps are also made so that you use the environment a lot, there are bottomless pits, pools of lava, spikes on the wall, etc. You can sometimes ignore all of that and just win using towers, but sometimes you really need to use traps that fling enemies off the ledge into a pit or slam them into the spikes. There are also railroads running through many of the maps and you can again ignore these if you want, but it is a lot more efficient to make the creeps run along the path of the railway and get injured or killed by the mine carts that race along them.
The graphics are retro pixelly style but they look nice enough to be able to make out what everything is clearly, and everything has its own style and feel, each creep type works in a unique way and looks unique, the towers are easy to spot by looking at them etc. The game is also very satisfying when killing stuff. Creeps don't just die like some TD games, in this game they die violently based on what killed them, so if you throw them into a pit they shout AAAAAAAAAAHH!! If you smack them into spikes they will splat with a cloud of blood. If you electrocute them they ZAP! with a satisfying sizzle. In a game that is all about carnage, I think this is important, and the devs did a good job of it.
Also there is some longevity with the gameplay as well, each map has modifiers so you can play in normal mode which is fine for below average players. They might have to replay some missions while they are figuring the game out, but mostly I think they will win each map first time. But if you click the Blood modifier for example, it means you have only 1 life. I can win each map with that enabled and it gives more XP for each map. And there are many more that increase that further but make it much harder. And there are even ones that lower the health of the creeps to make it easier. So you can easily tweak the game to be a bit easier or harder depending on how good you are at the game. Overall I think this only changes the amount of grind in the game. If you are good and can win each map with the 1 life modifier like I do, it means there is no grind at all in the game. You don't need to re-play any levels, you can just keep going on to the next new map and you will already have enough gear to beat that. If you struggle with maps and are maybe getting less XP from not using any modifiers, and therefore getting fewer upgrades, you might need to re-play a few maps to level up. But in terms of grind this is nothing like some games. Overall this game just seems to be about giving you a fun time.
There are a decent number of levels, good for the price, and there are many more you can download on Steam Workshop.  Most TD games I just play to completion and then don't go back, there are only a few that I have completed multiple times, and this one of those games.
p.s. Ignore my play hours, I have completed this game multiple times on many devices, I have put a total of about 40 hours into it.
