Blocks that Matter -PC-
Blocks that Matter is a lighthearted pick up and play 2D side scroller that I had quite a bit of fun with. It’s is a tricky puzzle solving game with 50+ levels that will get more challenging as you go along. The gameplay and design follow closely to game like braid, limbo, and The Misadventures of P.B. Winterbottom. The art style is much more basic and cartoon like than the titles I mentioned too. I also don’t think Blocks that Matter is on the same level as braid and limbo, but it comes close.
In the past couple of month I’ve been playing every 2D side scroller that I can get my hands on. I’ve just been going nuts for these games. I’ve been using the site
to keep track of the 2D side scrollers so I can say that I’ve beat them all, but as of now I still have quite a few to go through. Here is a link  to the page I’m talking about. It’s a reader voted list of all the best 2D side scrollers of all time. I don’t necessarily agree with every choice, but It’s a pretty darn good list nonetheless. I don’t think you’re gonna see Blocks that Matters on that list anytime soon because it’s not very well known, but I think it deserves to be at least in the top 200.
So here is how you play: The object is to reach the exit portal, but to get there you’ll need to jump around over blocks, obstacles, and enemies. The only real ability you have is to place blocks on the map. But you can only place blocks 4 at a time, and this is what makes things tricky. Each block as different attributes, like wood blocks burn, sand blocks fall if the block under it is taken out, other blocks explode, and some blocks are permanent once placed.  Each level makes to solve a unique puzzle by placing your blocks in a certain fashion. Be prepared to have your brain teased over and over again. I said that the game is pick up and play, and by that I mean that for me I would get frustrated by a puzzle and just quit, only to have the answer to the puzzle come to me later and I’d hop back on. It’s really a cleaver game.
I picked it up on a steam indie bundle for pennies, and I feel like this game alone was worth the price of the 10 game bundle.  I put around 6-8 hours in the main story line to beat it, and there are more levels and challenges available to players for increased replay value.
There is a story to the game, but it’s not taken very seriously, and it can even be skipped ( I wish I had found out sooner). The story actually surrounds the developers of the game and how they get kidnapped or something. It was all good and what not, but to me, the way it was written, it was like the developers were honoring themselves. You’d have to play the game to understand, I felt like I was visiting some hipster indie developer loft where the developers tell each other how awesome they are. It really rubbed me the wrong way.
If the puzzles weren't so well thought out then this would be a pretty mediocre game, but the puzzles are brilliantly cleaver and make you really sit and think after you die repeatedly though trial and error. I’ve since suggested this game to several friends, and I would do the same to you loyal readers. Blocks that Matter is quite a bit of fun

I first played this on Xbox 360 several years ago and enjoyed it immensely, although I wasn't particularly bothered about the user generated levels. When I saw this was in the Steam sale (even though it's cheap already), I snapped it up and played it again, finding it just enjoyable as the first time round.
I felt I had to review this game, because many of the criticisms other reviewers have, are actually the aspects I *enjoy* because it makes it a bit more challenging, and gives the game a bit of longevity.
The lack of mid-level save points and undo ability means you actually have to sit down, look at the levels and really *think* about your next move rather than moving about at random knowing you've got a safety net to fall back on. The kind-of-sequel to this game (Tetrobot and Co) does have undo ability in it, but that suits the difficulty of that particular game. For this one though, being able to undo would have made it far too easy. Removing the requirement to put down exactly 4 blocks at the same time would also make it little more than a walkthrough.
If you're not scared of something which relies on you to think strategically, it's well worth the money - even at full price (currently £3.99). But if you want your hand held through the game, it's probably not something you'd enjoy (although you should probably try it anyway to give yourself an education).
I'll be fair; it's not perfect. The graphics are overly simple, sometimes jumping can be a bit 'take-a-guess', and the user-generated levels are an unnecessary addition, but none of these things detract from the gameplay in any way.
==================
TL;DR - if you're a wuss who can't handle a challenge, don't buy it. But if you like something which is a bit of an 'old school' challenge, go for it :)

I've had my eye on this game ever since the first trailer was released. However, I was reluctant to get it right away due to other, similarly advertised games that left me with huge disappointments (i.e. STRAFE).
Ruiner is, in essence, a twin-stick shooter. You control a nameless guy with a cybernetic arm and a weird screen-like mask that covers his entire head on his way to kill The Boss aka "Big Dog"; at least that's your main goal for the first ten to fifteen minutes of the game when - surprise! - a lot of excrement hits a spinning object.
Instead of talking, the protagonist communicates by displaying messages - often memes - on his mask. Don't expect any Shakespearian dialogue out of him - his "lines" are mostly limited to "KILL YOU", "HELLO DARKNESS" and "We were never friends". It may come as a surprise, but this game is NOT about dialogue or choice.
Your choices are mostly limited to how your enemies die (or you, if you're not careful). While there's a large arsenal of guns and some melee weapons as well, the choice mostly boils down to slashing things or putting holes in them (or burning/exploding/freezing them if you like). It should also be noted that all but your basic gun (the eponymous 'Ruiner') and melee weapon have limited ammo or durability, which means you usually have to pick up other weapons from the ground multiple times during a single fight in order to maximize your damage output. It's a mechanic I am generally not too fond of, but it does work well in this game. Combat in Ruiner is all about the flow, anyways.
The controls are absolutely critical in any game like Ruiner, and they are tight in this game. I personally played through this game using a gamepad (Dualshock 3 emulating a 360 Pad using SCP Toolkit if you're curious) and had no issues. The shooting could have been a little more precise in my opinion, but that's probably at least partly owed to using a gamepad instead of keyboard and mouse.
Ruiner knows what it is. The story is (mostly) straightforward, but the focus clearly was on fun, style and atmosphere in this game. The developers succeeded in creating a world that is dark, frightening and downright bizarre - but at the same time weirdly aesthetic. While Ruiner - much like many other games - is set in a cyberpunk world, the design is much closer to classic 80s cyberpunk Anime than any western cyberpunk setting. This serves to give the game a somewhat fresh and unique look compared to other contemporary cyberpunk games.
The action is fast-paced and, at times, combat can be challenging. That being said, I've often seen this game being criticized for its high level of difficulty, and while that may have been true in the past, the developers released some updates to game balance and (I think) a new easy mode along with it, which shouldn't be a problem for the average gamer - much less for experienced players well-accustomed to the twin-stick genre. I would classify myself as a maybe average action game player and had no trouble finishing the game on easy difficulty. I died 3, maybe 4 times overall, and all except one of my virtual deaths were due to me either running blindly into a trap (which is probably the only one in the entire game I could find that was that deadly) or being crushed by a landing dropship (twice in the same fight...). In order to get a better feel for the higher difficulty levels, I started a New Game+ afterwards (which, I think, is supposed to be the highest difficulty level) and managed to get through the entire Prologue (until you get to Rengkok for the first time) without dying once. It
challenging, but doable, though you do keep your skills from the previous playthrough so you start out slightly overpowered, which is why I reckon later levels will be much, much harder to beat.
On a sidenote, the 'hub' of Rengkok is very cool and looks great, but it's a shame there's not too much to explore. I'm seriously hoping for a sequel or expansion that includes more of the quirky and interesting characters found there.
So, do I like Ruiner? Hell yes! I like it very much. Do I love it? Kind of. The premise and realization of it is cool enough, and the game doesn't throw much in terms of pseudo-philosophical ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t at you (if at all) like some other games do. It knows what it is; it's a brutal, fast-paced action game set in a world full of bad and even worse people. Visually it's striking, though not without its flaws. Like another reviewer pointed out, the heavy use of colored light - mostly a glaring tone of red - sometimes makes it hard to see what's really going on. However, at the same time the high-contrast red/black look of the game (sometimes with a dash of bright cyan) together with the fantastic - if unusual - soundtrack help to make Ruiner a game that you won't forget easily. If not for its gameplay, then definitely for its style.

In this critic's own opinion: STAY AWAY FROM ALL FUTURE VI GAMES LLC productions, or their other sockpuppet account, "Vi Games." I have since ported my save files from the Steam version of this game to Origin (I bought Mass Effect 2 as a part of a humble bundle, so I had keys for both Steam and Origin versions of the game) both due to several crashing issues I ran into with the Steam version of the game, and due to the fact you don't get all of the DLC for the game through Steam. As it stands I will review the game based on my experiences with both platforms.
I first beat Mass Effect 2 on Steam all in one go, in the span of 12 hours. I could not put the game down for one second, I just had to keep playing. The characters I loved from the first game returned along with a large cast of new companions, all of which I have grown to love just as much as the original crew of the Normandy SR1. The story was improved as well, building up gradually to a climax that had me tense and crying on the edge of my seat. I've played this game to death, yet I still continue to return and relive every mission, every character arc, and of course, every romance. Goddamn Thane and Garrus still have my heart.
The gameplay was drastically improved from the first Mass Effect, though the RPG elements from the first game were stripped away completely, which disappointed me since I quite enjoyed customizing the armor and mods of my companions. (They brought back weapon modding in Mass Effect 3, however.) The Steam version of the game also had a lot of issues with freezing up on loading screens and crashed several times for me in my 120~ hours played, which was frustrating to deal with in the very least. However what inevitably broke the experience for me was the lack of DLC. Sure, yes there is free content available to download in the Digital Deluxe edition, though you cannot access the real meat of the DLC due to them only being available to purchase through Origin. I don't know why they weren’t packaged with the game, but I digress. Which takes us to;
This is mostly a review of the DLC, since the core game experience didn't change much between Steam and Origin (though the game crashes significantly less through Origin). I’ll keep the reviews for each DLC short and sweet, and I’ll only be reviewing the more substantial DLC, ie the ones with actual playable content in them.
Tense, atmospheric and carries a real sense of urgency throughout. Has a nice twist too. This DLC does have an impact in Mass Effect 3, though it’s no big loss if you don’t play it. Price is fair for what you get.
One of my favorite DLCs in any game, beaten only by the Leviathan DLC in Mass Effect 3. Has excellent buildup and plenty of content for its price. Has great action and awesome payoff, and it felt so good to have Liara back on my team again, if only briefly. Has a pretty big impact on Mass Effect 3, especially with your relationship with Liara.
Probably my least favorite DLC to play due to the Hammerhead sections (which is pretty much like… 50% of the playtime in the DLC) but the buildup is excellent and the climax horrifying and upsetting. (You’d have to be heartless to take the Renegade option at the end) Again, the Hammerhead sections will make you want to throw your computer across the room but if you’re interested in the premise, it’s worth to suffer through. Characters will make appearances in Mass Effect 3.
A fun DLC with a fun companion. Kasumi is seriously awesome, and the choice at the end of the DLC is a tough one. Definitely recommended. Kasumi appears in Mass Effect 3, and is integral to a certain quest on the Citadel.
This is one of the free DLC you will get upon installing the Cerberus Network addon on Origin, which is included in the Digital Deluxe Edition of Mass Effect 2. Zaeed is another awesome companion, and the quest included in the DLC is fun and tense, with some interesting morality choices at the end. Zaeed appears in Mass Effect 3.
This is another DLC you’ll get for free with ME2 Digi Deluxe. It’s not as much a quest as it is an optional side mission, where you return to the wreck of the Normandy SR1 and collect the dog tags of the fallen crew, and set up a memorial in their memory. Very somber and peaceful, compared to the rest of the game. Doesn’t have a huge impact on the story, but I still recommend it.
- the Paragon/Renegade points system takes a long time to stack up. I got so frustrated in my second playthrough of the game that I downloaded a save editor and manually added enough paragon points so I could win back a character's loyalty.
- There are some very strange bugs that show up occasionally on both Steam and Origin versions of the game during certain quests. Particularly the first two quests on Omega (the Archangel and the Professor dossiers). Both are fixed by save file reloads, but they can get annoying.
Overall, Mass Effect 2 is a fantastic step up from the first game, and is probably one of the best sequels I’ve played to date.Though the experience is much more fulfilling through Origin, the Steam Release is still fantastic, and I highly recommend it.

An improvement on ME1.
Better combat, better maps for sidequests, purpose to resource exploitation. There's some artificiality to your squad leveling-up with the almost Devil May Cry-like post mission briefings. Like the first game, the RPG element takes a backseat to the storytelling of this game, which I don't mind one bit. In ME2, your actions feel like they have even larger repercussions than in the first game.
The Mass Effect universe, a respectful and coherent pastiche of sf literature, is further expanded in the sequel. Reuniting with former crew mates and building new relationships remains the pulse at the heart of the game. I was a bit disappointed that your role holds less political importance than in the first game, but there is narrative logic in making Shepard into a black ops team leader instead of a political figure.
I have only a couple minor gameplay complaints. Since complaints help me choose a game in reviews, I'll spend most of my time on this:
First, there are fewer sidequests, and these sidequests don't carry the same narrative weight as in ME1 (even though the ME1 maps are copypasta). In ME1, you discovered unethical experiments, dealt with colony infestations, and the Spectre judgments you had to deal posed some nice character building moments.
Second complaint is the time sink of resource and credit hunting. You have to scan every room in every mission for possible income sources because otherwise you're broke and can't purchase upgrades. I completed every mission and still didn't have enough credits to purchase the last four upgrades. And some FREE upgrades are permanently missable during missions, which I luckily discovered early on, about four hours into the game. Resource management means something in this game, for which I'm grateful. However, scanning and probing planets also takes up about one third of my 38 hour game time--okay, I'm exaggerating, but it's such a drag that it really feels like you're spending half the game scanning for resources on planets because . Again, luckily I went nuts doing this, because apparently being overstocked helps with your ME3 file.
I want to be clear, despite these two things, I thoroughly enjoyed this game. Great story-telling, improved combat from the first game, improved maps--it's such good fun that I'm probably going to download the crappy EA platform to play the third game. That's saying a lot, isn't it?

Unlike most of the reviewers for this game, I am not a frothing Dungeon Keeper fan, so I have reviewed this one simply as fan of RTS games.  Because all I have at stake is the game's technical execution and replay value rather than a holdover chubby from 1999, I cannot recommend War for the Overworld unless you get a massive discount.
This isn't to say I didn't have some fun with it.  The game is a hodgepodge of things that have been lovingly crafted, mixed with bizarre design choices and bugs that make it hard to believe only one team worked on it.
The story mode is lengthy, and  I never finished the expansion because the game has an absolutely **itty ending that left a bad taste in my mouth.  You have to understand this game has basically zero chill and loves to throw you at the wolves as soon as possible, and for all that work the ending is garbage.  They could have addressed it in the Heart of Gold DLC, but instead they had you play a completely different (though thematically appopriate) underlord.
The UI was alright in a functional sense, though if it was possible to switch tabs using hotkeys, the game gave no indication of it.  However, I feel inclined to point out that it lags terribly as a result of some past "upgrade."
AI pathing is functional, at best.  Your minions have no problems roaming to different areas of your base to meet their needs, but they also have a wide aggro.  Frequently I found the odd minion engaging in battle in some other part of the map (not the roaming fliers) when they were supposed to be at home.  They also didn't seem to have problems walking through lava in later levels, damaging their own health in the process when there was a perfectly good bridge nearby.  Sloppy.
Workers deserve a special shoutout.  When not digging out areas you designate or mining gold deposits, there's an array of automated tasks they will engage.  The problem is this process is not bug free.  They typically claim every tile they can, including enemy tiles much to their own detriment, but sometimes they also get "hung up" on certain tasks.  I once found all my workers dancing back and forth over a single tile like a bunch of idiots because they couldn't figure out how to claim it.  Other times my crypts were full of dead bodies, and my workers got caught up in picking up dead enemies - and setting them back down again, repeating ad infinitum.  The worker rally flags also do NOTHING when they're stuck like this.  For a game that tried to automate a lot of basic tasks, there's a painful amount of babysitting these little ♥♥♥♥♥.
"Controlling" your units is done via rally flags.  There's a special peace flag to keep certain units from responding to the rally flag calls, and later on when you'll want somebody at home to keep torturing prisoners or making trap parts, you'll have to manually place them under this flag.  Certain other groups get their own flags, like Titans, beasts, or summoned undead.  You can make more warbands if you like with their own flags, but truthfully the game just doesn't need that much micromanagment.  While you can place the flag on specific enemies to prioritize targets, your troops will generally ignore all enemies on the way TO the flag, which means if you want to be smart you have to obsessively place and re-place the damned things for optimal combat.
Population control is a mystery.  No, really.  Building your base is essentially setting up work areas for specific types of units, who will show up using an algorithm that is never explained to you.  In theory, the capacity for each work area should determine how many of that unit you get, but it never works out that way.
One bug that really stood out to me was technically the last story mission.  The enemy sits inside a magical barrier, which you can do a ritual to remove for thirty seconds.  The enemy is supposed to send waves at you, but he can't pass through the barrier either.  I played for thirty or forty minutes, wiping out side objectives, wondering why everything was so quiet.  When I finally dropped the barrier to attack the main base, a flood of enemy troops ignored ALL of mine, who had been instructed to go into the base and were thus trapped inside when the barrier went back up, and they marched straight to my dungeon core and destroyed it.  I eventually solved the problem by overbuilding, but I really shouldn't have had to do that.
I found the banter of the units (and prisoners) entertaining.  The narrator, Richard Ridings, has a voice you never get tired of.  The units and environment had lots of visual details - though the whole game hogs resources so badly your computer will lag for a few minutes even after the game is closed.
I did have some fun - really.  But the broad and sweeping nature of the flag system for unit control, along with the bugs and various imbalances (I cleared the toughest map by throwing down disposable and temporary Frost Weavers and having my workers simply take all the enemy's stuff) really minimize the replay and strategic value, and those are two cardinal sins for an RTS game.  Unless you're a Dungeon Keeper fan, pay 15 dollars for the lot of it and not a penny more.
*** Special edit to respond to the developer ***
Hey Noontide (Lee),
The fact that it's an indie game surprised me, because I thought the quality was rather high for such a thing. :)
My comment about there seemingly being different teams was mostly about consistency.  Some things were so well-done, and some... were not.
The wandering minions thing happened frequently.  I think it had something to do with the layout of the base, and they were simply latching on to enemies far from the dungeon core.  I don't really have any other explanation for it.
I did know about the Impasse flags for the workers, and I didn't use them.  I might say it'd be simpler to not have workers claim every tile they can automatically, to make it a manual process instead, but really your solution was just as simple as mine, if not simpler.
The workers who were stuck on one tile were eventually dispersed by clearing an adjacent un-mined wall tile.  Them obsessively fussing over bodies when crypts or prisons were full however was only solved by creating more of one or the other, and that's a pretty serious bug.
The problem with obsessively placing and re-placing rally flags due to a lack of an "attack move" mostly is that it's a type of busywork.  Simple deletion of the flags does not make troops head back to base.  MANY times I found my minions whacking away at enemy doors and such instead of coming home, sometimes further engaging battles until their deaths.  Conceivably, to fix that, I would have to place a rally flag inside my base to get them to ignore everything.  Overall it's a little cumbersome.  Perhaps attack-move should be a separate flag?
The population tool-tips explain a lot.  Some of it sounds esoteric, but most of it sounds interesting.  However, being unable to determine the population or composition of the army makes implementing specific strategies unnecessarily difficult by a wide margin.  At this stage you simply have to hope you have enough units, and hope you have enough of the right type to counter the enemy.  Given that it's almost an RNG formula for your army, the relationships between armies are impossible to examine.  Things do seem to pan out anyway, and that's part of the problem.  You just sort of build and hope for the best, which isn't enough meat on the bone for any strategist, and ultimately resulted in the thumbs down.
Having said all that, I wish your team the best of luck, you have a decent little gem here and I hope you continue to improve it. :)

TL;DR: This mediocre shoot 'em up has potential but fails to impress.
Alright, I feel a bit bad bashing the first game by these developers but I hope they can use the feedback and I'll try to keep it as constructive as possible. I only finished the game once alone, so I can't review the co-op except for its technical aspects.
is a 2D shoot 'em up: as German soldiers during (I think) World War II you and your pals shoot soldiers and monsters and try to reach the end of the level, possibly fighting a boss at the end. There's a cheesy, dull story to go. Action games don't need great stories but it would surely help. The dialogue is lame and uninspired and still manages to host a few typos. Cutscenes have dialogue but no animations and during them the speech bubbles proceed without prompt, with just enough time (read: too little time) to eye them through.
Okay, so maybe the gameplay is better instead. First, I noted there is a high number of weapons, bought by the in-game money received for beating levels. Money can also be used on purchasing new characters. Roster is rather large for this kind of game, with seven characters. In addition to appearance the characters have slightly different health, speed and number of grenades.
While there are different weapon types, they all boil down to the same principle: shoot straight ahead, dealing damage to a single enemy at various doses. There are more powerful versions of the same weapons but the idea is the same. Perhaps different functions, like bullet penetration, crowd control, suppressive fire or similar could have made this more interesting. As enemies are fairly similar to each other, there's no need for high-powered weapons like sniper rifles either.
Found in levels there are a couple of special weapons , flamethrowers and electroguns, but they are simply overpowered as they mow down enemies like nothing. Fun, but takes away the point. They should have more limited ammunition instead.
There are many different kinds of enemies. However, they boil down to four types: a shooter, a melee brawler, a vehicle and boss.
Both humans and monsters can be shooters, but they are otherwise similar: shoot a bullet straight ahead, perhaps walk a bit in the process. Brawlers, either humans with knives or weird monster thingies with tentacles run straight at you and deal damage on touch. Perhaps some could be much faster or do some rushes or block bullets or something, but no, they are equally dull except for appearances.
Vehicles are actually fine and interesting but are seen in only a few levels and work more like mini bosses. Cars crush you (and even your unmounted enemies). APCs shoot and block the road (so you have to kill them) and tanks are similar, except they drop bombs as well.
The only qualm with vehicles (and perhaps with stronger creatures) is the lack of damage indication. Surely, some enemies spew blood and tissue and there's this yellow flash when shooting a tank but is it getting damaged? You wouldn't know until it break down and dies. By damage indication I mean like scratches or dents to their surface. I managed to mow down one tank by repeatedly slashing it from behind with a knife. It didn't seem to mind at all.
Three boss fights are all unique though a bit boring, as they are not particularly difficult even on hard difficulty. The reason is that they only have one attack pattern (one has actually two, the second one being a rarely used bomb). More pattern variety instead of heavy damage resistance would have made them more interesting.
Finally, the levels. Story mode levels are boring. There's a general lack of interesting features. Exploding barrels are everywhere but virtually nothing else gives the levels any character. Occasional box does nothing. The only level with character was one with haystacks and monsters coming out of them. In one of the levels I experienced a bunch of soldiers spawning right on top of myself, breaking the flow of the level.
Otherwise, only two of the ten levels caused any problems for me. The one difficult one had tanks, and those are incredibly hard to destroy, at least with regular weapons. The second one was a case of
but not because of enemies but because of friendly soldiers.
Normally, all enemies could be destroyed safely by shooting (or stabbing) and walking backwards. However, in this level the friendly soldiers also rush forward. The problem arises from the fact that they share collision with you. So, what happens when you are knee-deep in monsters, walking backwards, and a bunch of friendlies rush at from behind? What you'd expect: they push you right to the claws of the monsters. I died four times in that level, every time because of the griefing allies. The resulting rage could have been averted by making the friendlies collisionless with player characters.
The enemy and character sprites are pretty good. However, the lack of level features and cutscene animations render this fairly irrelevant. I'm sorry, I can't remember the music at all so it clearly wasn't action-packed enough for such game.
In addition to story mode there's an arena mode, where you get to try different scenarios: endless enemy waves, a fight against multiple bosses and fighting using mechs and a couple others. Arena games have indeed some co-op potential and it could be fun trying to beat them together with friends! Unfortunately, there is no local co-op (i.e. playing on the same computer). Internet gaming works only through direct IP connect and is called "local Wi-Fi" in-game (an erroneous remnant from the mobile game perhaps?).
The couple of single player only scenarios look interesting. However, the sniping game seems to give you only
bullet. This must be a bug, since there's a wave of enemies approaching and one is forced to look as the lone soldier is munched to death. Defense scenario is a tower defense with only upgradable walls and few defense abilities. Upgrading walls are controlled by mouse but the dropping bombs from the sky is
, instead being controlled by keyboard. As a result, both of the single player arena games are basically worthless, like unfinished experiments that should not have been included in the game.
It IS an easy 100% game achievement-wise. The campaign lasts less than 1 hour to play alone and grants enough money to get the needed guns.
The game should have been much longer, had more interesting features and story twists and more interesting combat mechanics (e.g. one should be able to aim with the guns). While costing only 3 bucks and having cards, the unpolished implementation unfortunately just isn't worth it.

Crusader Kings II is the best strategy game ever created. There's no way to reasonably dispute this.
Spanning almost 1000 years, the game allows you to employ nearly every strategy imaginable to propel your family to the top of the world. The journey is breathtaking. The initial learning curve is high, but once you figure out the basics everything else will make sense quickly. Read guides and expect to spend several days flailing around before you get the hang of things.
Remember chaos theory? Your starting position (geographic, physical, sexual, national, religious, political, economic, military, family, and other) and subsequent choices will result in a basically infinite number of scenarios. Your line could die out in a year or you could establish a unified empire. There is no end to the variety of gameplay. Add onto that the ability to start from many different positions (see above categories) and you can be a god.
Overall, probably you will spend around $100 to obtain the base game and most important content. Sometimes it is aggravating that Paradox has fragmented so much content into $1 (when on sale) minor DLCs. However, most of the minor DLCs only add flavor, such as portraits, clothes, shields, unit skins, etc., and are completely unnecessary for regular gameplay.
The most important content is in the $5-15 major DLCs, but each of them is worth the price. The major DLCs unlock the ability to play nearly every faction, religion, and culture, and change some mechanics to create a more enriched environment. Way of Life feels relatively overpowered vs vanilla, but mostly the major DLC are balanced. The ruler designer is fun, but because it doesn't work in Ironman you won't be able to get achievements if you use it. But don't expect many achievements at first; many of them require a variety of different starting points either by design or because it is very difficult to position yourself to secure them in the same game.
It would be unfair to not point out that Paradox releases free updates to the game with every major DLC release. These updates improve gameplay whether or not you purchase the DLC. Some major improvements include map expansion and mechanics changes. The DLC increases your ability to take advantage of the free changes.

Let's get this out of the way: I love Gemini Rue. The narrative was gripping, friendly characters were likable, and supporting characters all seemed like they belonged in the world and evoked the correct emotional response. The dark, rain drenched neo-noir setting is perfect for the story being told. Scenes were beautiful, the music fit superbly, the voice-acting was believable, and the sound effects were realistic. Is a person simply the sum of all experiences and outside input or is there more to a person? Gemini Rue explores identity, ethics, and even free will. Like all great pieces of fiction, which Gemini Rue definitely is, it'll leave you contemplating the questions it poses even if it doesn't offer a concrete answer. If you're an adventure game fan or simply like the themes, setting, and story presented, you owe it to yourself to look into Gemini Rue!

What can I say about the Elder Scrolls? It's been great since the very first game back in 1994. Morrowind was a treasure, and Oblivion was Morrowind, but with better graphics, a more solid story and improved NPC interaction. Oblivion goes on the list of games that will be installed on my PC the day I die. I will always go back to it.
The graphics are still very good, even five years later (released in 2006). The voice acting is on par with what you'd expect from a Blizzard product (real actors), and the story is simply epic. In my opinion, it outranks its standalone expansion Fallout 3 in every category except graphics. Exploration is less tedious, you feel less obliged to loot every goddamn thing (you don't need a steady income to pay for ammo), and the combat system (an update of the Morrowind system) is simply breathtaking.
Bethesda practically invented open-ended gameplay with The Elder Scrolls, and Oblivion is a handsome addition to any RPG collection.

Lords of the Realm II is like an old wine that only connoisseurs can appreciate...
I spent countless (not Countess!!!) hours of my youth playing this game.
So "let's get diggin'" into the game review:
The gameplay is not as complex as I remembered but, being the mechanics easier, then even a simpler strategic AI can play the game well: actually it's not a real threat, but it's just good enough to be a decent obstacle.
The AI is quite "idiot" in combat instead, especially when sieging, but the very basic old-style controls kinda compensate a bit... when groups of allied units with different speed get mixed, for instance, it's quite hard to control them. Just remember that this game is really old and that will make sense...
Lords of the Realm II features real time battles, an easy micromanagement, castle building/upgrading/repairing, resource gathering (wood, stone, iron), smithing, farming, turn based strategies (each turn is a season, and each season provides different challenges, like harvesting in autumn), very basic diplomacy, army provisioning, people's happiness and more. All in all it's a nice and winning mix: I can say there is no other game around like this, but many games copied from it.
I find it very satisfactory to station troops in enemy counties and let them feed on their crops; or to weaken enemies by sending small armies to their "capital" county, destroying all its fields and killing all the cattle! And enemy lords do that too... damnation to them!
The soundtracks are amazing, even if they're played continuously I never get tired of hearing them... they're very "medieval"!
The voice acting is nice too: low rank units (paesants, archers, macemen, pikemen, ...) sound rude and uneducated, like they really were; while high rank units (swordsmen and knights) are more polite. Very nice to hear!
I bought Lords of the Realm II without thinking twice out of nostalgia, but I really think it still has a lot of ludic value.

A very dull puzzle game, with an infuriating UI.
Even for me who isn't a puzzle game fan, the game is rather easy. The optional challenges provides actual challenge, but trying to play the game is an exercice in frustration. There is no way to rollback a move, so if you've made a bad move by mistake, you may have to replay the whole level entirely.
The "rewind time/rollback previous moves" is something that many modern puzzles games offer to avoid unnecessary frustration, but apparently, Block That Matters didn't get the memo. Worse, since the "run" button is the same as the main action button, theses mistakes will happen a lot.
Similarly, if you pause the game, you're supposed to use the "A" button of the Xbox 360 pad to go back to the game. But if, by mistake, you use the "B" button because most games use that, Block That Matters will happily throw you back to the level selection menu, erasing your progress in the current level, without a warning.

Be aware this is not a definitive review due to Overgrowth still being in alpha and not complete, these are just my thoughts on the game so far and what I have experienced with it. I had never even heard of Overgrowth until it came to steam only recently and it had been in development years before it even came to steam. I quickly became curious and watched videos on it online to see what the fuss was all about. This game has the potential for greatness. Overgrowth is a third person action game that has some of the most impressive physics combat I've seen. For an independently made game It is an absolute blast to get into a brawl with enemies and come out on top. However with the game being in production it isnt really a game... You see, when you log in to the menu it gives you a variety of premade maps to mess about in. There is no single player story to be had and there are some challenge modes that are very lack luster. However once you choose a map there is an ingame editor that lets you spawn objects, enemies and tweak with the games settings sort of like Little Big Planet. This is where things get interesting. You can create different senarios to the existing maps and can even share your creations online with other players and friends. It is a bit of an ordeal to do this as you have to sign up for the developers fourms and other time comsuming methods to get it working properly. However once it is done you never have to do it again and it is painless from there on out to share your work. I have to admit the price tag for an unfinished game is hard to justify, but this is purely a chance for the developers to show people their game and to promote it. I think Overgrowth has some great ideas to become an awesome game and It is worth to give it a shot. Not only will it help an independent game developer but give this game the attention it deserves.

This game's like a really beautiful woman with an imperfect personality; the surface was amazing but it didn't run bone-deep.  There are flaws that will be obvious after you've plunked down your money and have gotten engaged with this game.
But buy it anyhow.  It's not perfect, but it's far from terrible, and we need more teams of game developers from places like Poland trying to make something this cool, even if it wasn't a masterpiece.
So, thumbs up, despite...
..rocky writing and plot twists that aren't terrifically sensible (especially the end, which, without spoiling it, feels like it got reworked a half-dozen times but not by somebody with a good understanding of the story).
...gameplay that has a distinctly-inverted difficulty curve because certain level-up powers are very very important and greatly improve the overall feel of the difficulty of the game.
...not giving you said powers until you've grinded a bit more than is comfortable and have gotten through a few hard points.
...weapons design that, at best, felt bleak and badly-balanced and at best felt sublmely abusable because of how the Grinder mechanic effects player power over the course of play.
...enemies who come in about 4 real types other than bosses (and despite the "no bullet sponge" hype really are just stat-differences under the hood).
...some very choppy framerates on anything less than a pretty good PC, with only one major option that improved performance a lot (and said option, to lower the game's resolution, strongly suggests that maybe there are some pretty-serious optimization issues with shaders or setup for same).
...the linearity and, frankly, no replay value.  I think a major opportunity was wasted here, by not having a procedurally-generated area or five to use as side-quest battles.
...the side-quests are mainly just there for us twinkie completionists.
...the ridiculous difference in the hero's hitbox size on anything but Easy.
...some of the endgame weapons being way worse than the ones you could get commonly or the ones you inherently got throughout the game.  This game had me going through occasional moments of, "why was this balanced like THIS when it might've been a great moment if it had been stronger / did its main job better / wasn't so OP compared to all other choices on this level".  I feel like a game where we're going to have to memorize what drops and from what enemies really needs that to be interesting and worthwhile, and it largely felt like a wasted opportunity.
Despite all these caveats, I'm going to give it the thumbs-up that I feel it deserved in the end.
This game had, "we tried HARD" all over it.  The art oozed Cool, the level designs really tried to feel like more than tiny arenas to keep pathfinding costs reasonable, the Boss Fights were clearly labors of love.  The sound was adequate and the music was sometimes great (and sometimes pretty bad / mismatched for the scene, but hey, it certainly tried to deliver).
The game's weapons were pretty darn satisfying at times.
Kills felt solid.
Combo attacks felt like a great idea.
Powers felt useful and relevant (and the re-stat concept, where you could juggle your powers based on what you'd face, was great design).
In the end?  I think the game needed fresh eyes on it and about 90 days of further polish before it got released.  I think it needed a bigger budget to put in non-repeating, repeatable gameplay elements, so that it wasn't merely a linear slog with a grind-fest "time attack" mode tacked on.
I think that the whole concept of the "hub location" was largely wasted; it put a faux-RPG face on a game that basically plays like an updated Smash TV; there was tons of writing and dialog that looked meaningful, but utterly wasn't, and it felt like things the developers wanted to flesh out and ran out of time to do.
Graphically, I liked the neon look until it got old.  I really felt like sometimes the art director should've been reminded that Monochrome lighting looks fantastic when it's not the only lighting style (e.g., Blade Runner).  The change from the monochrome of the linear arenas and the color palette of the "hub" was especially jarring, because it was the only time it happened.
As you can tell, this game left me with a lot of different ways to go.  I'm pretty critical of the things that could have been better, but I think the developers did well enough and did something rare enough (it's not like the PC scene is swarming with this style of game) that I'd like them to keep making games.  So, there you have it; this game, like a bitter whiskey, might be an acquired taste, but I think it's worth the asking price for the connoisseur.

The year is 2091. Set in a cyberpunk world ruled by corporations, you play as a guy whose brain got hacked and he was sent on a mission to kill THE BOSS. The people who did that to you also kidnapped your brother and are holding him hostage, so when you finally regain your freedom, you move in to save him and get your revenge.
The cyberpunk setting is great to look at. It's dark and very detailed. Especially in the Rengkok city with all the neons lightning the place up. But also the levels, with all the industrial elements, they're just fantastic.
At first I tried playing with keyboard & mouse. The character movement, turning, aiming and shooting were ok, but using the special abilities was starting to over-complicate things (or maybe I'm just too old to keep up). So I tried the gamepad instead. And that just felt right.
All the menus and skill trees are smooth, no issues there.

one.

However, while the music was great, this game didn't have any voice-overs.

It's a top-down isometric twin-stick shooter. The left analog stick of your gamepad moves the character, while the right turns your around and aims your weapon. You are then attacked from all sides by various kinds of enemies and you have to kill them all. Sounds simple, right? Well it's not, but it is a lot of fun.
Ammo is very limited in each weapon, but luckily all enemies leave their guns behind so you can pick them up. You have to pick them up. Often.
After each fight a device gets dropped onto the field. It can "melt" all the weapons lying around into additional experience points. You just pick the one gun you want to keep, and get rid of the rest. Nothing goes to waste.
You can enable different skills to help you survive. The good thing about the skill tree is that you can distribute and re-distribute all the available points at all times. Picked a skill you didn't like? No problem, get all the skill points back and assign them somewhere else. And there's plenty to choose from. Energy shields, increased damage, hacking enemies to fight on your side, regenerate health, grenades, more ammo, improved pick-ups or slowing down time and more.
I've got exactly what I expected from this game - a lot of action-packed fun. With one unexpected surprise - a fantastic soundtrack.
- cyberpunk setting
- not too short, not too long
- SOUNDTRACK!
- no voice-overs in cutscenes
- keyboard and mouse controls could be simplified
- some boss fights not saving after completed stages - have to repeat the whole fight
Very good game, much fun, much time to invest in :)

I was thrilled to see this game on Steam, because it is one of my old favorite games from the late 90s.  I used to spend hours at night when I should have been sleeping playing this game, sending insults to The Baron while I was heavy-eyed and dozing off.  It was one of my introductions to games like Civilization, and I am not sure where to be thankful or angry at Impressions for that.
And I think comparing it to a small-scale Civilization is a good way to put it.  It's a lot simpler and more focused than Civ, and nowhere near the scope of Civ.
The concept of Lords 2 is that the king has died, and five pretenders to the throne are fighting it out with diplomacy and warfare going county-by-county.  Each player starts with a county, and can conquer thier neighbors while forming alliances and starting wars.  A second part of the game deals with commanding a battlefield in real time as you storm castles and conquer towns.
Part of what made this game special in its time is that the two  game modes combined two different strategy genres perfectly.  The main game was a turn-based strategy with a small amount of micromanaging of counties, while the skirmish mode was an RTS reminiscent of Warcraft without the building aspect.
The included "Siege pack" expanded on the RTS elements of the game, adding a Skirmish menu for custom battles and sieges.
The game is still a lot of fun, but doesn't quite hold up after nearly 2 decades.  The AI is not very competent in the skirmishes, and the controls during those battles is awkward.  Issuing orders in mid-fight can be a pain.  Fortunately there is an option to skip the battles and "autocalc" them, if they are frustrating.  This can be done at anytime, before the battle or during.
The micromanaging might be offputting to some people, but it is not particularly complicated.

So I previously mentioned that this has elements from both Stronghold and Total War games I'm going to give a few examples. The reason this is a bit like Stronghold outside the fact that it's the middle ages is because of the resource managment, you have a population that grows based upon health and happiness which is determined by how much your feeding them or if your feeding them at all and taxes, let it drop watch them die to illness and emmigrate to opposing towns. This is crucial that you make sure you keep them around as they are your workforce and your military when you recruit troops not only do you need to procure the weapons for the troop type you need the citizens to carry them so you have to find a balance of troops and workforce.
As for total war the campaign map is turnbased with the hybrid turns (everyone takes them at once) with towns slapped across the map. Also on the map you will see farm field which there are 3 types of and strategic resources being wood, stone, and iron. Here you will manage your peasantry and direct their work building castles, training troops, buying from the traveling merchants, and of course proving their can be only one king by slapping your neigbors silly.
There is abit more details I could throw in there but that's the core elements and if it sounds even slightly interesting to you definately buy it and then join me in moaning why these game mechanics haven't been replicated in a modern game engine.

Golf With Your Friends is an elaborate tale of a tragic loss, and phyrric victories. Every shape has a story. Every hole has a gap needed filled. I myself experienced such experiences, and have decided to record my memoirs here to share my experiences with the public from the Great Golf Race.
Myself and several others had gathered 'round the colorful and bountiful territory, known as Candyland. We prepped our colors; Green, Blue, White, more Blue, and Pink. We dashed off with ease, eventually landing at the terrifying chasm of the speedy gumdrops in a simple three swipes. Such irony, a tasty snack used against us as a weapon of mass destruction?
An ally had gunned his speed, luckily travelling through the narrow path, missing the plump drops by hairlengths. Another soon followed, only to be met with sugary death. It was my time to challenge them. I braced myself, groaning into my microphone before closing my eyes, opening them to see that my boldness had paid off. I finished the coarse with only five gentle, yet firm putts.
I turned back to watch the remaining two struggle to push through the gumdrops. Two, after at least eleven attempts, made it. We continued forth onto the next Course, accepting the lost of our eldest member.
Upon arrival to a watery stop, the floor made of Hyrdogen Oxide had stopped us from approaching our destination. We had to design rafts for our spherical embodiments. Upon cross, our initial organized group had fallen apart, leading to every man for himself. I was thrown off against the wall, before gasping for air, feeling for any land that I dreamt of. My wish was granted, I dragged myself onto the shore, rolling away to the end of the horrid waterland.
Several courses later, amidst the gurgling leaps of faiths and rummaging into each other's spherical forms, we encountered the final stage. The long anticipated finale was just ahead; we could see it's glimmering pole. There were two directions the group could of went in. Our initial ally, the common dim wit charged into one direction, only to reveal that he had no escape, that his final steps were already set in stone.
As for the rest of us, we left in the other direction. Expecting a challenging journey to and fro was no surprise to us, we lost an additional sphere, the opposite Blue. "At least there'll be no competition." The second blue golf ball claimed. We all chuckled at that, pushing onwards.
Seven putts in. My time was limited. Another ally, one who beared a street cone upon his head, had resorted to madness, coldly using his remaing putts to lash out anyone who attempted to gain entry and the end of the course. Myself and my fellow compatriot had to work with each other, as the clock ticked and the dreaded afterlife drew closer with every movement. We moved in sync in parellel with each other, confusing our former friend. Unfortunately, it had overtook him.
His last few breathes were spent wishing a horrible spell were upon us. "The Dark Lord is here!" No sentence was ever so chilling to me. He immedietly threw himself off the ledge, sealing his fate for endless centuries to come. With ten seconds left on the clock, myself and the final victor had quickly mourned his death, and dragged ourselves into the gaping hole, now satisfied that the remaining spheres were clear from the course.
What happened next was unbeknowest to me. I found myself on a new landscape, next to the very same balls that I had previously fought with and against before. Does this cruel world have an end, I thought?
10/10 would lose friends by contact again.

Well now that I've beaten all the maps and see the icon for a spike trap whenever I blink. I think I can give a proper summary.
Logos:
All the parts you'd expect in a rational td are here. Leveling towers, upgrade trees, gradual unlocking, ye olde basic dart tower that gets left on the side of the road as better towers are unlocked. Those of you familiar with Gemcraft will find a friendly skeuomorph in the wave bar. Difficulty is controled with a set of runes which will be familiar to those who've played Bastion. There's a novelty here though, as one of the runes makes the round easier in trade for lower XP gain. A brilliant use of the system.
Warfare stands out though by being significantly puzzle baised without being an actual puzzle (generally). Maps tease multiple optimal solutions with only a handful turning out be legitimate. After a few times I had thought I had found a general solution only to have a later map prove me wrong.
Pathos:
While other TD's relish in their direct damage traps Warfare gives significant love to the maligned physics traps. In Orcs Must Die the funnest traps were the ones that sent Orcs flying. Warfare's idea of crowd control is a spring trap into a bottomless pit and it
. Watching a harpoon trap drag heavy units into magma rarely gets old. While a delight the physics traps are no panacea, levels sometimes lack waste disposal chutes necessitating direct damage. The little blood explosions and pixel gibs help elevate the established spike and dart traps above their peers.
Ethos:
The lightning trap is crap, the slot machine is fun but when one of the result is self-destruct it's limited, the lich crypt while in theory fun takes up one of the 9 slots that could be better spent, calling a new wave always gives the same reward regardless of time left to it, lv4 lightning trap hits air lv3 does not what does and does not hit air is not delineated, dart towers have no utility or reason to use them later on, the lock on how far you can zoom out makes it hurt to look at for long periods on large screens.

Blocks that Matter will appeal to a very specific audience, and - sadly - that audience is not me.
There's nothing fundamentally broken about the game, it's a sweet little action/puzzler affair and it's not a purchase I regret.
However the mechanics do feel somewhat contrived; at it's heart you must place blocks to progress: you may only place four blocks contiguously and you may only destroy eight blocks in a row. Certain blocks fall when placed, others when touched. Some blocks will catch fire, others will not. Some can be drilled whilst others cannot. It's a puzzle game and as such needs rules but I found myself asking why they are so arbitrary a lot.
Possibly the biggest problem is that there are no save points during a level and there is no ability to rewind an action you didn't mean to make. Some (most) of the levels are too long and if you make a mistake jumping and running you'll find yourself redoing solved puzzle elements. Also if you make a mistake near the end of a puzzle you'll need to restart and redo all the jumping and running and blocking that went before. I found myself getting bored quite fast.
Blocks that matter is ultimately tedious rather than bad.

Disclaimer: the following text is totally unbiased and non sarcastic!
I have some gripes with the monetization of this game. It's clear that Larian hasn't enterend the realm of 2017 yet and DOS2 is really not up to par with todays standards:
1. DOS2 retails for 44.99US$ or your regional equivalent. A modern game with high production values, which DOS2 clearly has with its beautiful atmospheric graphics, its incredible well written story, an amazing voice acting performance, a grandiose orchestral soundtrack, dozens hours of content and deep tactical gameplay should retail for 59.99US$.
2. No pre order bonus. In the beginning of the game you meet a black cat with its own small storyline, but totally not essential to the grand story overall. DOS2 has tons of sidequests with their own story and those go further than the bland "go fetch me 10 wolf pelts" sidequests. Those sidequests make the game so much more engaging and rewarding to play. That black cat could be easily cut from the game and offered as a pre order bonus, which would be a good incentive for people to buy the game upfront without knowing if the game is any good. After launch you offer the black cat as a 9.99US$ DLC and make some more money out of it.
3. DOS2 comes with 6 origin stories, 6 unique characters, which greatly changes how you will experience your travels and adventures throughout Rivellon. This enhances the replayability of DOS2, but knowing this game is in one playthrough already al least 70 hours long this is perhaps a bit much to offer at a base price of 44.99US$, which really should be 59.99US$ (see point 1.). As you can take only 4 characters in your party, offering 4 origin stories in the base game is more than enough. You can easily cut two, say Beast (a Dwarven Pirate) and Fane (an Undead), and offer them in a Digital Deluxe Special Edition for an extra 20$:
- Divinity Original Sin 2: Pirate Edition for 79.99US$ with Beast origin story
- Divinity Original Sin 2: Undead Edition for 79.99US$ with Fane origin story
And of course you bundle this all together in:
- Divinity Original Sin 2: Gold Edition for 99.99US$ with all 6 origin stories
4. DOS2 doesn't have a season pass. Will Larian just patch and add extra content for free?
5. DOS2 makes you play and enjoy the game without cutting corners through microtransactions. If a character in your party dies, you must make sure you have a resurrection scroll to revive him/her or have enough gold to buy one from the NPC's in the game. There is no ingame store that let you buy ingame items or ingame gold for real money.
Despite these 5 points of criticism DOS2 is a fantastic game. It's one of the best cRPG's ever made and playing this game you feel you're playing something special. This truly is a classic: 10/10!

So after a handful and more hours in this game, here is my opinion!
Graphics: The graphics are fairly decent, offering some nice visuals and effects to keep your eye candy going for hours, if you are just chasing the graphical aspect.  They are not superb amazing but for this genre of game, they are fairly decent.. Overal an 8 out of 10 I would say!
Audio: The audio I found slighlty lacking in feeling.  The music of the game is really nice to listen too, but the sounds just seem boring and bland from my point of view.  Nothing much but hammers hitting walls, bots rambling and nothing really with the feeling off atmosphere to draw you in.. so Overal I would say a 6 out of 10 here.
Controls: The controls are pretty simple and easy to get used too if you like the WASD method, but there are a few bugs if you do not.  For myself I do not like the WASD method and prefer the original arrow keys method (Hence what they are designed for) and when setting the keys I want, the game often forgot them and went on to do it's on thing which was frustrating.
Gameplay with everything else: So the gameplay as we all know a survival game... You need to eat, drink, sleep etc in order to survival, all while building your base... Sounds like every other survival game out there!
The good thing about this game is the fact you can do coop with your friends ingame... Without buying or hosting a server, it can all be controlled through the ingame menu's which is an amazing feature, but there is one massive problem here... When doing this, you have a limit to distance how far you can go from the host... It is not that far at all, so bare in mind.  When doing it this way, you alone cannot go off to explore alone, you have to take the host with you because there is like a giant radious around you stopping you from going to far, like a child on a long leash..
So what else sets this game apart from every other game? Honestly.... Nothing! Ark has Dinosaurs.... Conan has basic mobs, some can only be killed by werewolves... You summon giant gods to destroy stuff, that is it. The thralls are NPCs in the game which is good, because most games like this do not have NPC's, so that is an added bonus and you can build with easy of the snapping tool.
Would I recommend this game? Really I want to say 60% yes and 40% no because to me, this offers nothing new and amazing that warrants the £26 asking price.... When the game is finished then it is worth maybe £26 but right now it is worth between £16..99 and £19.99 and the game offers nothing new to survival games, so proceed at caution.
Oh and one last thing, the updates for this game are pretty regular, which is really good work to see and I hope this continues... So right now as I write this review, updates are happening weekly if not daily to fix issues in the game.  So fingers crossed they keep this up to get it out of EA..

I ate this burger in under an hour.
It's a Harvey's type of burger-joint where you get a decently flame-broiled patty on a cheap bun awaiting your choice of toppings and condiments, and there are plenty of those to choose from.  But you'll most likely only pick three toppings and a couple of condiments, because, quite frankly, you won't give a sh-t. Overall, it was a solid eating, and it satisfied a hunger I never had.  I surprisingly ate the entire burger and earned five achievements for it, somehow "100%-ing" this under-achieved burger joint.  It definitely needs more achievements, and smarter ones too, because unlocking a cheap condiment is not really an achievement.  And, seriously, when I eat a whole burger and I'm ready to move on, don't keep me waiting for you to give me some cards, okay.  I got other joints to go to.  If you had done those achievements properly, I would have stayed longer, but you didn't, so, drop the cards before I bite into the burger, okay?  It's because of this I'll never return.
Anyways, its a cheap one-hit wonder burger joint that packs a decent punch.

Or hide into tar, tar + brimstone = steel fire, put that into a cauldron and take iron bars and steel fire and put it into a furnace to make steel, take steel & turn  it into Steel Reinforcement for the strongest structures. Building is more dynamic as you can build anywere by raising, turning or tilting the foundation or structure you want to place, no more looking for an only flat place to build which means there are no "only places to build."

Now the graphics, my my how nice they look it looks like directx12, Ark looks like crap as there is artifracing, light coming in through walls and requires a beast mode computer to run, all the meanwhile on teh same Unreal Engine 4. Well now that I've beaten all the maps and see the icon for a spike trap whenever I blink. I think I can give a proper summary.
Logos:
All the parts you'd expect in a rational td are here. Leveling towers, upgrade trees, gradual unlocking, ye olde basic dart tower that gets left on the side of the road as better towers are unlocked. Those of you familiar with Gemcraft will find a friendly skeuomorph in the wave bar. Difficulty is controled with a set of runes which will be familiar to those who've played Bastion. There's a novelty here though, as one of the runes makes the round easier in trade for lower XP gain. A brilliant use of the system.
Warfare stands out though by being significantly puzzle baised without being an actual puzzle (generally). Maps tease multiple optimal solutions with only a handful turning out be legitimate. After a few times I had thought I had found a general solution only to have a later map prove me wrong.
Pathos:
While other TD's relish in their direct damage traps Warfare gives significant love to the maligned physics traps. In Orcs Must Die the funnest traps were the ones that sent Orcs flying. Warfare's idea of crowd control is a spring trap into a bottomless pit and it
. Watching a harpoon trap drag heavy units into magma rarely gets old. While a delight the physics traps are no panacea, levels sometimes lack waste disposal chutes necessitating direct damage. The little blood explosions and pixel gibs help elevate the established spike and dart traps above their peers.
Ethos:
The lightning trap is crap, the slot machine is fun but when one of the result is self-destruct it's limited, the lich crypt while in theory fun takes up one of the 9 slots that could be better spent, calling a new wave always gives the same reward regardless of time left to it, lv4 lightning trap hits air lv3 does not what does and does not hit air is not delineated, dart towers have no utility or reason to use them later on, the lock on how far you can zoom out makes it hurt to look at for long periods on large screens.

For the longest time, Broforce was my most played PC indie, but I think it's safe to say Overgrowth has supplanted that as my go-to game.
Now Overgrowth isn't complete by a long shot. It's still lacking a real campaign or story and the available content consists of a few challenges, several maps ranging from parkour-friendly courses to open areas with enemies to an arena. There's a robust level editor and a growing library of user content.
But that's not what makes Overgrowth so fun, so addicting, and challenging. In my opinion, gameplay itself is paramount to making or breaking a game, and Overgrowth delivers in spades. The combat is up there with Arkham Asylum as my favorite fighting system in a game, simple to control yet complex in its execution and endlessly satisfying to watch. From agile evasion to smooth judo counters to tense knife fights or rolling under a swinging blade and digging a spear into an enemy's chest, the combat is just glorious fun
The movement alone offers some of the best 3D platforming I've played since Prince of Persia in 2003. You're fast and insanely maneuverable, able to jump huge distances, wall run with ease, bounce between walls and roll under obstacles. Speed running through the community parkour maps is so entertaining.
But Overgrowth isn't just great in its execution, but as a whole package inside and out. The anthropomorphic animal warriors and the semi-realistic atmosphere bring to mind classics like Redwall and Watership Down, and the brutality only cements those associations. A fight isn't just a simple exchange of blows; blades and hard hits leave bloody wounds across the body, blood that drips and stains in physics-accurate patterns. Fatal impacts against hard surfaces are accompanied by crunching bone. A stealthy neck slice sends arterial spray everywhere. A tough fight leaves you bloody and battered. Dodge at the wrong time and a kick will impact your head with a tangible sense of weight and momentum. It's these aspects that make the game such an enjoyable experience
But there's more to come, from the proper integration of species like dogs, rats, and cats, and a full story. The backstory of the world has already been fleshed out in Lugaru and this fascinating digital comic
and if the game's story is as engrossing as the stories in those pages, Overgrowth could truly be the Redwall of gaming.

This game is a tribute to Tetris and Minecraft. Blocks That Matter is a classic platform game. You control a little robot and have to reach the exit of each level. But to go to the next level, it is sometimes necessary to reach areas difficult to access. Logic, otherwise that would be not interesting.
This small robot thus needs to collect blocks of materials (wooden, stone, sand, steel, ruby...) to create tetrominoes and so move forward in the level. Thus yes, roughly, you have to dig as in Minecraft to get cubes, which you pile to make the various forms from Tetris to move forward. And yes, when you have 8 cubes side by side, you can blow up them, as in Tetris.
Other originality, cubes have various properties. If the blocks of stone or steel can hold normally in the air without problems, the blocks of sand or granite will fall inevitably on the ground if there is nothing to retain them; also, wooden blocks can be on fire, and ice blocks can slide on the ground.
This game is pretty long.
The main campaign contains about forty levels, and it will be needed between 6 to 8 hours to reach the end (according to your speed of reflection to solve the puzzles :p).
But reaching the last level does not mean that you ended the game.
Indeed, in every level, there are two objectives to achieve (besides the classic “reach the exit” one): there is a chest to pick up, and you also have to get a star by using the least possible your blocks to finish the level. Levels were built so that there are several puzzles in a single level. That is you will have a first puzzle to be made a success during your first passage in this level, but when you will have got back the improvements freed during the game, you can redo these levels by way of places which were until then surrounded by blocks which you could not break up to fetch the chest and/or have the star.
Note: Chests are trophies, easter eggs for other famous games, with in bulk: Boulder Dash, Portal, Bomberman, Tetris, Minecraft, VVVVVV, etc.
Besides the main campaign, there are 20 levels bonus, which free little by little according to the total number of stars acquired during the campaign. Another series of 10 levels bonus, on the theme of the chocolate, also comes to be added.
Finally, the game has a level editor (not obvious to use) allowing you to create and play your own levels, as well as to play and note the levels of other players.
Design is simple (they are only cubes!) but rather attractive. Musics are very nice. Scenario brings a small touch of humor, to perfect the whole.
Conclusion: a very nice platform / puzzle game, that you can play again and again.

There are many different games that RUINER borrows from (e.g., transistor, doom). However, Devolver somehow made the cacophony of ideas flow well. I wasn't expecting a great story going in, and when I finally came to the epilogue, I had mixed feelings. I'm still processing the conclusion my mind; some things fit, others don't.

The artwork is gritty and truly cyberesque. The soundtrack is one of the best I've heard--however, don't be fooled: it's not original content. To reiterate, the story and amount of content offered doesn't fully grant the asking price. However, the pure joy of combat makes these factors a bit irrelevant.
