Few experiences in gaming have ever left me absent of words, uncovering my identity in Knights of the Old Republic was one, trekking through the vastness of the Shoshone Forest in Firewatch, Delilah at my side, was another. With confidence I can now add another experience to this ever-growing list, exploring Ruiner’s downtrodden hub city, Heaven, half-functioning neon lights bathing the streets in an artificial violet glow. Devolver Digital is a studio which we’ve become rather familiar with as of late, through their publishing of the critically acclaimed Hotline Miami, as well The Talos Principle and both Shadow Warrior games. There’s a theme present in all three of the aforementioned games: each is a contender for game of the year in their respective time. That’s a running theme with games published by Devolver: they only publish the best of the best, and just the fact that a game has been published by them is akin to a seal of quality. Ruiner is a truly singular experience, with a heap of positive facets, and hardly a negative to be found. It clearly takes inspiration in its core gameplay concepts from Hotline Miami, with a heavy focus being on vicious melee fighting, where death comes almost instantly for both you and your foe. There’s a diverse armament to choose from, found all throughout the different levels, and while there may a handful of boring weapons, for every normal SMG you have weapons like the Xaar, firing a gargantuan beam which obliterates anything it comes into contact with. These weapons serve as potent, yet temporary upgrades, as their ammunition count rarely manages to last through even the shortest of fights, requiring you to often switch to melee combat. Creating such an ammo scarcity while providing no way to acquire more forces the player to switch weapons constantly, meaning that you’re going to end up using just about every weapon in the game at one point or another. This is an innovative way to ensure players experience your weaponry to its fullest extent, and that each implement of destruction amasses its time in the spotlight. Because of this the acquisition of new weapons flows naturally and you genuinely look forward to picking up some new hardware, as opposed to you feeling as if you’re being forced to.
Innovation saturates Ruiner, present in many of significant gameplay aspects, and especially so in one in particular: the skill system. As in most games, XP is required to level up, however XP  in Ruiner isn’t strictly called XP, that would be boring and normal, two things Ruiner absolutely isn’t, instead going by the name Karma. Karma is mainly acquired by taking out your enemies in the cleanest way possible and with the fewest mistakes, however it also litters the various levels in the form of destroyable, karma-filled crates. So not only does this encourage exploration, it also encourages you to make as few mistakes as possible as the better you do, the more karma you get at the end of the mission. Now that you know how to go about acquiring karma, you probably should know what you’re going to spend it on: skill points. Twelve skills are present for you to unlock, though most aren’t even available until certain points in the game, each one giving you something new to look forward to. Ruiner’s skills contain an extremely minimal amount of waste, with each upgrade having solid justification for being present, and none of them feeling out of place. The innovation I mentioned beforehand is that in Ruiner rebinding your skills is an integral part of gameplay, rather than just being a failsafe in case you accidentally screw up your build. To elaborate on that, many times throughout the game you’ll face what seems an insurmountable challenge, only to find out you can tear that challenge in half by simply switching your skills around and trying again. This may seem like the game forcing you to repeatedly smash your head into a wall until finally finding out what works, but I found instead I was actually enjoying the experimentation and all that I could create, not dreading it. My only gripe, really more of a nitpick, is that some bosses force the use of certain skills upon you, which kinda hampers the whole “build your character how you want” vibe that I was getting from the rest of the game. However, more than likely you’ll neither notice nor care about this because the bosses are going to give you a run for your money and then some. Bosses aren’t focused so much on being visually distinct, but more so on being distinct in their gameplay, each with significant differences in behaviors that need to be observed and countered. My favorite of the fights was M.O.T.H.E.R., an enormous automaton with a somehow even larger laser, which you have to either block with your shield or absorb with your skull, one of which more effective than the other. The fights entirety was pulse-pounding, which is no different from the rest of the game, every second was a race to see if I could deal enough damage to the bot to stop it from powering up its scarlet spear and ramming it straight through my torso. Thankfully, these boss encounters are not only extremely enjoyable but also extremely frequent, with at least one per level, often two or three, just going to show that Ruiner certainly doesn’t lack for content.
This is a game that stands out in so many ways I’ve been finding it hard to pick which one is most prominent, but I believe that would be the difficulty. Many games present the player with a challenge, but few are remembered specifically FOR that challenge, and because of that are forever immortalized as the best of the best.  In my eyes Ruiner has more than earned its place among these legends, with a difficulty so arduous, so unforgiving, that you’ll push for victory out of sheer spite for the game. Arenas in which you fight quickly turn into shrapnel-filled charnel houses, with enemies dashing across the screen, with a burning desire to kill you akin to your burning desire to kill them. When you load up and select hard in the difficulty menu, expect a hard difficulty, unlike many other games where hard may as well be renamed “for people who’ve played a game before”, Ruiner’s hard mode is absolutely not for the faint of heart. Battles are fierce and the levels turn you paranoid, fearing death is awaiting you around each and every corner, which it almost always is. Often times when I complete a game nowadays I feel like I just finished a job, yet when I finished Ruiner I felt a sense of accomplishment, like I had truly done something that was worthy of note. I think that’s emblematic of Ruiner as a whole, where other games make playing feel like a job, in Ruiner it’s a thrill, and it’s one that you won’t soon forget. Its beauty comes not in the form of absurdly photorealistic visuals that blur the line between virtual space and real life, but in the form of a more artistic approach to graphics. What surprises me the most is that Ruiner somehow managed to make a parking garage into a zone in which I wanted to explore every nook and cranny, just to make sure I grabbed everything I could find.
Every element of game design synergizes together to create an immaculate game worthy of only the highest praise. Well done Devolver, Ruiner is my 2017 Game of the Year.

I used to love this game, as evidenced by my hours, but once I played it for the umpteenth time and suffered through ME3, I started to think. And once that happened, everything fell apart in this game. Please note this has spoilers.
The game starts by killing off Shepard, an interesting kickstarter but then it falls on its face. You'd think that a near-death/resurrection would be life changing, but instead his/her death barely affects Shepard, and is only mentioned sparingly in a couple conversations. It seems to be a big missed opportunity NOT to explore how Shepard is affected by death, but Bioware prefers having Shepard automatically killing robots not 2 minutes after seeing the cinematic of his/her death. By the way, if you know your science, then there's no way Shepard's body would survive re-entry into that planet's atmosphere, let alone impact on the surface. For a game based off sci-fi, it's doing a poor job already.
Moving on, you discover that it was Cerberus who resurrected you, a super secret organization aiming to further human interests. But if you played the first game, you'd realize that Cerberus was basically Nazi ISIS on sterroids. From having a few minor bases that got utterly trashed in the first game, they now somehow are the equivalent of Section 31 from Star Trek. How the hell does that happen in
, and for being so advanced somehow they explain the events of ME1 as rogue cells? Given how OCD Illusive Man is about his assets, that's a poor explanation. And I haven't even reached the best part: No matter what character you play, you're forced to work with them. If you payed attention in the first game, you'd know only an ultra-evil human only Shepard would even think of working with these clowns. And even worse, there's absolutely no repercussions for it. Cerberus is an enemy of literally everybody, and now Shepard is in the exact same position as Saren: a Rogue Agent working with hostile forces, but instead every one is like "Oh you're working with the space nazis? Oh they are bad people, but we're not going to do anything because you have to further the plot!" Come on, you'd think they'd send a spectre to hunt you down. How cool would it be if you had to square off with the virmire survivor as the one who was tasked to take you down for joining Cerberus? Instead, the council just offers you spectre status again (if saved), even though that means nothing. *sigh*
Now here's where it really gets frustrating. The entire plot of ME2 can be summed up as Ocean's 11 in space minus the coolness of George Clooney and pals, and is about as relevant as a side quest. The shoddy final DLC, arrival, has more meaning to the main plot of the series than the overhyped suicide mission. The premise is that the Collectors, a creepy bug race, are stealing humans from colonies and are apparently going to target Earth (which you're supposed to care about now, not that you'd know from the first game), and Cerberus has brought you back to get a gang together to take them down. The Collectors come from one relay in the omega system, and the entire game pushes you to build up your squad to go through the relay and take them down. Wait, why go through the relay at all? Why not just mine the relay, camp and kill them, or even blow it up? Certainly Cerberus is morally capable of that, and the Collectors (stupidly) only have one ♥♥♥♥ing ship. And then their general, who is actually a reaper (seriously, who didn't see this coming) makes himself look like a total clown with his half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥taunts whenever he inhabits one of his bug bodies. Comedy at its finest.

Burgers is a side scrolling action game, developed and published by storm_sharks.  I am going to start out by saying, from the screenshots this game reminded me a lot of games like Castle Crashers, and Metal Slug, so was quite excited to try it out. Sadly what followed was quite possibly one of my worst gaming experiences of my entire life, and I’m talking Slaughtering Grounds levels of bad.
The game play idea is very simple, as with other side scrolling action games, you progress to the right hand side of your screen taking out enemies as you go, somehow this game doesn’t manage to even do that concept very well. Let’s start off with the controls, you obviously cannot miss them because as soon as you start the game, BAM there they are in your face very obnoxiously…at the start of every level too. There is a nice feature that I have not seen in games before, where you press a button and you can move backwards rather than moving the directional stick, I thought it was quite cool, only when I found out you couldn’t actually shoot whilst moving…so it turned out to be quite a pointless addition.  Most levels you will almost always run out of ammo for your weapons. This is infuriating when you are only about half way through the stage, and you have a trail of bad guys chasing you because you aren’t able to kill them, how do you get more ammo you ask? By killing bad guys…ironic huh.
The art style in Burgers is probably its only redeeming feature. The cartoon look to it really pleased the eye and most of the animations were done really well too. The background environments are almost just a copy and paste throughout the stage as you can see the copy point quite clearly.  Next, we have the sound effects, or a better wording would be, the lack of. The only sounds you will get out of this game are the sound of your automatic rifle and the sound of bullets landing on your foes. Nothing else. Seriously, nothing. The flamethrower gun makes no sound. Enemies charging at you, make no sound. No soundtrack, I thought maybe the game had bugged so reinstalled it, nope, nothing – it is seriously bad.
The game can be easy or hard, depending on how well you are at conserving your ammo and how quick you are at picking up the controls. I couldn’t get past the last level because of the poorly designed control system and, you guessed it, lack of ammo. I have been playing for just over an hour and have no intention to ever pick this game up again.
There aren’t any actual technical problems, what is there in the game does work, it just doesn’t make sense. I ran it on 1440p without any problems at 60 fps, but of course, it’s never going to be the most taxing of games on any modern day rig.
To sum up, Burgers, is 100% definitely the worst game I have played in the past 12 months, and it quite possibly the worst game I have ever played in my entire life. I am still shocked at how bad the sound department is of this game and the poorly produced gameplay. Do not give this game any time of day, even at £1,99 this game is not worth a single penny.

Crusader Kings II is the best strategy game ever created. There's no way to reasonably dispute this.
Spanning almost 1000 years, the game allows you to employ nearly every strategy imaginable to propel your family to the top of the world. The journey is breathtaking. The initial learning curve is high, but once you figure out the basics everything else will make sense quickly. Read guides and expect to spend several days flailing around before you get the hang of things.
Remember chaos theory? Your starting position (geographic, physical, sexual, national, religious, political, economic, military, family, and other) and subsequent choices will result in a basically infinite number of scenarios. Your line could die out in a year or you could establish a unified empire. There is no end to the variety of gameplay. Add onto that the ability to start from many different positions (see above categories) and you can be a god.
Overall, probably you will spend around $100 to obtain the base game and most important content. Sometimes it is aggravating that Paradox has fragmented so much content into $1 (when on sale) minor DLCs. However, most of the minor DLCs only add flavor, such as portraits, clothes, shields, unit skins, etc., and are completely unnecessary for regular gameplay.
The most important content is in the $5-15 major DLCs, but each of them is worth the price. The major DLCs unlock the ability to play nearly every faction, religion, and culture, and change some mechanics to create a more enriched environment. Way of Life feels relatively overpowered vs vanilla, but mostly the major DLC are balanced. The ruler designer is fun, but because it doesn't work in Ironman you won't be able to get achievements if you use it. But don't expect many achievements at first; many of them require a variety of different starting points either by design or because it is very difficult to position yourself to secure them in the same game.
It would be unfair to not point out that Paradox releases free updates to the game with every major DLC release. These updates improve gameplay whether or not you purchase the DLC. Some major improvements include map expansion and mechanics changes. The DLC increases your ability to take advantage of the free changes.

As the levels get progressively more open and the enemies faster and stronger, you're challenged to find the most efficient way of dispatching the advancing horde. Steam says I've got 20 hours in as of writing this review and there are still towers and enemies I've yet to encounter. Admittedly, I'm crap at the game, but having a ball just the same. If you're a wizard at such games, you also have the option of handicapping yourself with any number of debuffs through the rune system. I have a couple minor gripes. The art style is nice, but the soundtrack is limited - one song during battle, one for the map/leveling screen. These become quite repetitive. Futher, I'd like to be able to pull the camera out futher to be able to see the entire map, though that may be part of the management aspect. I just find it annoying as valuable time is wasted scrolling around. The variety of enemies is vast, and their unique characteristics require a mix of traps as you advance. Further, traps become progressively more expensive, so spamming (for example filling the room with floor spikes) will quickly drain your resources and leave you exposed. The numerous maps coupled with the replay options added through the rune system make it well worth the asking price for anyone who enjoys tower defense style games.

Do you like twin-stick shooters? Do you like depressing cyberpunk dystopias where life is cheap and you have no friends? Do you like brutally caving in peoples' skulls with a lead pipe and bullets? If you answered yes to some of these questions, you may have serious issues. You also might enjoy RUINER, which involves all of the above.
The time: 2091. The place: Rengkok, a wretched hive in southeast Asia. The job: KILL BOSS. As a man with a electronic billboard for a helmet, various cyberware and and an attitude towards violence one might call cavalier, dash, shoot and maim your way through crumbling parking garages, churning factories and nightmarish underground complexes in pursuit of your missing brother. Along the way you are aided from afar by a cheeky female hacker who constantly refers to you as "puppy". Make of that what you will. Between missions, you return to the safe hub of Rengkok South, where you can speak to various NPCs and get a glimpse of life on the edge.
While the fact that your movement is oriented to the map and not your camera initally threw me off, and the game's a bit short for its regular price, and it was really easy to overlook the hooligan to start the C.A.T.S. quests and lock myself out of an achivement for that run, thats about all the problems the game has. You've probably heard the game is hard, and in a way it is: It's very easy to die. But it's also pretty easy to win once you learn how. Its a bit precarious. And restarting is almost instantanious, so you don't lose much time at all. A bit of advice: If a boss is kicking your♥♥♥♥♥ try using the Supply Drop power to requisition the burst-fire railgun. It does insane single-target damage.
There's a ton of weapons, from simple pistols, smgs and shotguns to miniguns, flamethrowers and energy-spewing death machines that reduce your foes to meaty chunks 90s shooter style, and though you can only carry one gun and one melee weapon at a time, there's always more strewn about. And whenever your current pickup gun is depleted, you revert to the game's namesake gun: a machine pistol with unlimited reloads that can be upgraded through the skill tree. Cyber abilities are varied and all useful, as far as I can tell. The dash was a bit awkward to use, I think, but I really liked the Overload buff, which made some of the crazier fights a bit more managable, along with the Supply Drop, Reflex Booster (which acts to slow down time), and the essential passive bonuses to your weapons, health and energy. Also, being able to recover health from executions is pretty amazing. It feels like a bit like Doom 2016 or Wolfenstein: The New Order with its emphasis on moving fast and striking with overwhelming force. You cannot win this game by attrition. However, if an approach isn't working, you can redistribute your skill points freely at any time.
I didn't find the soundtrack great for listening by itself, but I have to admit it fits the game really well. The exception to the former is a 1994 track by Susumu Hirasawa used when in the Rengkok South hub: Island Door (Paranesian Circle), a beautiful song in its own right. The whole presentation is spot on, which seems to be a thing with Devolver-published games: Hotline Miami, STRAFE, Shadow Warrior. There's a heavy use of reds and oranges that stand out from the neon pink and teal used in retrowave-esque games, Good sound, asset design, character art and ambience. Some people might complain about how it layers on the particle effects, but that's the Unreal Engine for you. Still, if you have issues with that kind of thing, be aware that RUINER is very visually intense. Like, its one of those games that gives a seizure warning in the opening titles. Stay safe, kids.
RUINER is a polished and intense experience and a worthy addition to the twin-stick shooter genre.

I've waited a long while to review this game, and it's a good thing I did.  When I first purchased it something like a year ago, it was still quite buggy and otherwise rough around the edges.  However thanks to dedicated work by the developers (which continues to this day, I might add) this one has blossomed into a wonderful strategy title.
Fans of the old Dungeon Keeper games will absolutely love this one, as great care was taken to maintain the same style.  They even got the orignal voice actor who did the disembodied voice in the original games, Richard Ridings, to reprise a similar role for this one.  Added onto that is a number of helpful touches that the DK games lacked, such as more powerful tools to help direct your worker imps or restrict their movements in case of encroaching hostile territory.
It's superb as a nostaligia title, but also excellent as a strategy game in its own right.  Even if you've never heard of Dungeon Keeper, you'll want to check this one out for what will in your innocent eyes be a completely original style of game, unique with respect to most other strategy games.  It is something like an RTS mixed with small elements of city sim.  You will need to feed and pay your minions to keep them happy, requiring you to construct proper dungeon rooms to do these things.  They will also need beds for them to sleep in, and will benefit from various other dungeon rooms such as training facilities.  Knowing where and when to build which facilities is crucial to developing a powerful fighting force.  Added to this is the ability to construct various defenses to keep your dungeon secure from over zealous heroes and other threats.
Once you have built a powerful army, you can direct them into combat by placing rally flags.  You can also speed them along by grabbing them up with your "Hand of Evil" (aka, mouse cursor) and transporting them 10 at a time instantaneously across your dungeon toward the attack target.  Your minions each have unique abilities which they will employ in combat automatically, such as spinning attacks and hex magic.  You can also assist them directly by using your own dark magics to heal and buff your minions or damage and debuff the enemy.  Finally, should you desire a more personal touch, you can possess a minion's body to hack away at the enemy in first-person mode (which will dramatically boost the effectiveness of that minion when compared with computer control).
Fantastic Game, absolutely worth the modest price tag.  I highly recommend it.

When a game greets me with a splash screen that the game was "mostly made by one person, I tried to make it of good quality & interesting." I'm immediately put on edge.
Then the options screen was partially in russian, so I tried changing it to the english option, but nothing changed & so I changed it to russian & realised that the english settings in this admittedly Early Access title were just 'less russian' than the russian language settings.
Then an actually pretty cinematic opening cutscene with probably unintentionally hilarious 'english' voice acting & scripting, but it's unskippable & too long & basically, you are in a plane over a desert & you get shot & crash.
You then are dumped into a long hallway with no sprint, once you get to the end of the hallway you get in the plane from the cutscene & then you wake up in the desert were you crashed in the cutscene, I guess this is either out of order or was felt to be needed Prologue, otherwise we'd just assume we were born with that plane already in the air, how else could the events have played out thusly.
Anyway, so you're in the desert. You still can't sprint & there isn't context as to where you should be going, so you wander forwards, then more hilarious voice acting & suddently a marker off to the right, so you need to slowly walk over there while one of the 2 music tracks kicks in.
You can toggle between the music tracks the 2 key & disabled with the 3 key, the game even pops up cover art & band/track info in the corner of the screen, you don't often see that in games which makes me think this developer is in or knows people in the 2 bands (the songs weren't bad & I'd say they were the best part of the game, but I'm not likely to re-spend the $4.24 that I'll be being refunded on this, to buy them).
You walk all the way back to the marker & suddenly you are in a too dark cave & can sprint finally, out of nowhere we realise that now we are free from the confines of the plane which we weren't born & raised in, that we can run freely (also there are zombies in the cave, because of course there are zombies) & it seemed like you use RMB to aim & use the flashlight, couldn't seem to use a flashlight (which is too bright & crap when I wasn't aiming) & you didn't seem to be able to sprint while aiming & then I took 2 hits and died which sent me back to the main menu to consider watching the unskippable cutscene again before slowly wandering to the caves once more.
I didn't consider it worth it.
This could be good, eventually, although I'm mainly basing that on finding the voice acting amusing; if sprint gets patched in the opening sections in the next couple of days & the opening cutscene is skippable then I probably won't return it, that's possibly a stretch, I might play it again before returning it to see if it suddenly becomes good after that short zombie gameplay in which I died, but it just feels too sluggish to do over again with 2 hits of health to end up playing yet another janky zombie shooter on Steam.

I am [still] loving this game. I've played both solo and online, and both have their pros and cons. I'm [still] trying to get friends interested, so we can team up. The game is early access, and it has its issues. In addition, I have a wish list for quality of life improvements.
The things I like about the game:
1) The building system is some of the best in the genre. The only drawback is that folks can build wherever they want, which can fill the map with abandoned buildings. A current problem is building near thrall spawn points, which prevents respawning. Devs are experimenting with solutions. Private servers have rules and bans, but it's still tough to police.
2) The crafting system. The drawback is that it can get a little grindy. Some items are absurdly expensive with the required mats. A quiver of arrows takes 50 stone, but an entire sandstone wall takes 25. The recipes need further tweaking. But the currents assets are plentiful and pretty awesome.
3) The thrall system. Still a work in progress, with some animations still to come. Specialists still kneel at their benches, but Yog and Set priests raise their hands and dancers dance.
4) The world is gorgeous to look at and explore. The layout is well done. Mountains feel like mountains, waterfalls pour from high up. The moon needs a better texture, however.
5) Lots of survival elements, like hunger, thirst, item decay, spoilage, and corruption damage. There's deep water and swimming and possible drowning.
Negatives about the game:
1) AI is [still kind of] apallingly bad. Everything other than gazelles and rabbits wants to fight to the death, with no self-preservation in mind. It's like player versus a world filled with suicidal lunatics.
3) Map is mob-saturated. I like a lively world, but come on, now! I get that there should be danger to prevent the casual stroll, but a hyena every 30 feet is a bit too much. The predator-prey ratio is way out of balance. NPC placement is a bit sloppy.
4) Chat is underdeveloped and broken. Currently can't scroll through the dialogue. The page up and page down act as Home and End buttons.
Wishlist:
1) Need settlers, NPCs who can fill up your constructed villages. Like farmers and merchants and people walking to and fro. Not companions, per se, but non-hostile humans, other than ole Nunu. (Ran into Arcos the Wanderer. Better, but need more non-hostiles.)
2) Ladder/wall-climbing mechanics. Some games have them. Too many don't. It's 2017, folks! It's a neglected feature that is sorely missing from today's games.
3) Better NPC AI. A single hyena should run away, especially from a group of people. Have them travel in packs and gang up. That'll induce some adrenaline. Antelopes should definitely run away prior to being attacked. Not everything has to be hostile, except skeletons and werehyenas. But NPCs should warn the player "Don't come any closer!" etc.
4) I know it's a desert, but it does occasionally rain in the desert. (I love the sandstorm, though. That's a marvel to behold!)
Performance issues are as expected for EA: Some lag and rubber-banding, especially with higher population servers. I've got an older system, and I can play the game on medium graphics and such, and can play for hours without any issues. But they do pop up here and there. (Edit: Performance is getting better. Servers still occasionally crash, though.)
The devs put a lot of love into this game and it shows. They're passionate about their work, and are involved with the community. It's appreciated, and I hope more love for the game is coming. It's incomplete still, but there's defintely enough to make a playthrough worthwhile, so I definitely recommend it.

Dying of measles and surrounded by villainous factions, it seemed that her honored dynasty was about to end. Her father had united Christendom and ended the schism, but what could she do? Stressed by the pressure on all sides and mentally broken, she decended into lunacy... Who then would have guessed that madness might have such grand timing?
Many decades later she recalled the various laws she inacted to save the empire. She had pantsed her vassals into humiliation, outlawed turnips, banned bathing, and set up many heirless elders as stage kings within her empire.
Once she had her own heir, she made him king of all her realms. She used his vast armies to crush pethetic jihads and foolish dukes... but now she had the measles again...

The first impressions I had from this game were not the best at first but it quickly changed my mind once I gave a fair shot. Burgers is inspired by games like Castle Crashers where mindless co-op fun takes place. The idea is not original at all but I see this is coming from a new developer in the industry so consider that when providing useful feedback or even when playing the game.
The story is about a group of soldiers who were deployed for a mission that turned out to be more dangerous than expected and not with the enemies they had in mind. In order to save the world (cliché, I know) they have to ignore their main mission for a greater cause. At your disposal, you have several sorts of weapons that you can buy with some funny names with different designs as well. As you advance in the game you will level up and acquire money for said weapons which will become very useful in later levels. Speaking of the levels, there aren’t many of them and I guess that the small price reflects on the small content the game has to offer. Still, it can be a quick side distraction for those dead hours or if you just want a quick gaming session without having to worry about complex tutorials or something similar.
At this point there is no local co-op which can be a deal breaker for some, however I believe that this a feature that will planned for their next game. Still, it was a big missed opportunity. In the end, I believe this game can be worth your time, just don’t expect a quality story driven game or even a original concept, otherwise you will be disappointed.

Burgers is a horrible sidescrolling shooter flashgame with awful graphics and clunky controls. Firstly I thought it can be a good game anyways. It has a story, 9 levels and 3 challenging bosses. Very nice is the armory menu where you can unlock several different weapons and character upgrades with the in-game earned money. They are also partly XP locked - another decent detail in-game which is appreciated.
But if you finally start the story you fall into somekind of overwhelming cliche plot. Aliens, Nazis, World War are the very boring almost everywhere seen remix of stupidiness leading even into a lame final. Though each enemy looks unique, they seem pretty familiar to me and stolen from movies like "The 5th Element" or "Independence Day". The animations are poor like shrinking and expanding sprites. Most funny is just the reanimation nurse. But you don't want to remember any of this after playthrough once.
Another lack are the controls (Xbox controller supported) and their handling. P.e. you cannot run backwards and shoot simultaneously. Reload is manual and the hitboxes are unprecise. Gameplay turnsout mostly into run around and don't get hit by bullets or alien bodies. Because enemies spawn hidden behind haystacks and can suddenly rip you apart. The bullets don't have a lane, so they hit your entire body. Also annoying are street blocking tanks which you must destroy before you can proceed.
Somehow there's no possibility to exit to the main menu. Primarly the game is meant to play in coop but I haven't tested it. I don't wanna to know if the hosting works fine or not. Conclusion: I suggest to buy it cheap on sale, playthrough quickly and deinstall it again. The 5 achievements are quite easy to do.

If you played this when you were a kid then you must play it now. If you remember when CompUSA would demo computer games, and if you played computer games, you probably played this one. Highly reccomended for 2 reasons - Nostalgia & playing it again as the older, better version of yourself (just to see how much easier you crush this game). The music is still great, the unit vocals are still great and hilarious. The fighting was pretty good back in the day, even better than many current cell phone apps, but it does not compare to Total War. If anything, this is Total War before Total War was Total War.
Here's my strategy (you don't have to read this):
After playing every single Total War series, this game's economy and production is pretty easy to manage.
If you haven't noticed, the AI likes to garrison its' starting castle very quickly. This takes away from the labor force. They also like to take over counties very early, within about 10 turns or so. They are spreading themselves too thin. Within the first 10-15 turns, they have successfully sabotaged their production and increased their borders with armies of peasants, maybe a few archers and pikemen, and if the AI is The Countess, a little bit of macemen too.
The biggest thing to note is every AI has a seriously damaged economy and production. They've got hundreds of peasants in each army... empty towns... ruined fields... high taxes... unhappy populations.
I've found the -best way for me- to deal with this is to spend your first 10-25~ turns spending ALL OF YOUR MONEY on IRON and WOOD, leave your forestry, mining and quarrying OFF. You can make up to 100 weapons PER TURN this way. As you're doing this, make sure your garison is at maximum troop levels. Archers and pikemen will hold anything. I particularly like to have a garison of 50% archers, 25% crossbowmen and 25% pikemen.
So you're making tons of weapons, having a happy and healthy population of over 1700 people. Meanwhile, poor defenseless counties are being invaded one after another. No worries, your enemies are spreading themselves thin, crippling themselves with peasant armies and terrible economic management. ALL GAME you must keep spending your money on Iron and Wood. Unless a food shortage is imminent, spend some money on that, but by then, you'll have tens of thousands of coins to waste. On the England map, I made a Stone Castle in EVERY county, by buying most of my stone, and/or turning off any production that is not STONE in counties with quarries.
This is basically a HEAVY defensive strategy but when you're rolling around win tens of thousands of coin, with over 3000 weapons, NEVER using PEASANTS in your armies... it really doesn't matter how many counties the AI have. You will crush them.
Have no more than 4 wheat fields in a county with a large amount of total fields. 3 Wheat fields is pretty standard. Put tax at 7% when you're at 100 happiness. Put tax at 5% when you're around 80~. When you're below 60 happiness, have 0% tax, and buy some damn ale if you can.
It's pretty easy to be the greatest noble with the most coins, most troops, happiest people, most castles and most counties. The easiest way to get there FIRST, is to have the happiest people and the most coins... except you will be spending all of those coins on Iron and Wood during early game meaning, you will have the MOST and HAPPIEST people. Have a solid defensive garison and victory will be yours. The AI will try very hard with its peasant armies and crippled counties to take your castle. Be sure to keep an eye on SINGLE TROOP armies, which consist of 40~ peasants whom will raid your crops. You can easily ungarison your troops and auto-resolve these pests. 40 Peasant armies don't arrive until after you have smashed a greater army.
You can easily defend your castle against 2, 3, even 4 or 5 times the odds. Sometimes I just say, "Hell, I'm gonna let them in", and I lower the bridge. Prior to this, I make sure all of my men are at the last and final chokepoint inside the castle. For a Motte and Baily, It would be the tiny palisade surrounded by water. Pikes at the door, archers and crossbows off to the left or right so that they may shoot over the flag tower. Royal castles are particularly easy to defend, especially in combination with the 6 boiling oil pots. Just send all your men into the flag keep, pikes at the door, crossbows and archers behind, and just lower that damn draw bridge and let em' in. Have your oil pots at the front gates and just dump on them as they come in. Aim for their pikes and archers if you can. As for a Stone castle, that is an easy defense too. Just put all of your ranged ontop of the flag, and pikes at the only two stairways that lead up to the flag.
Have at least a Motte and Baily, because that second wall that they have to break through is where the money is, in any castle. Let them in through the first wall, don't allow them to use any other siege equipment by Letting Them In! Then just dump oil on them till their crippled force reaches your second gate, followed by a pike wall guarding your archers and crossbows.
There is no need to compete with how fast the AI takes counties. Don't be intimidated. Be a Prang Mantus, wait for your time to strike, preferably with over 600 men, including a majority of maces followed by swordsmen, then crossbows, then knights. Make sure to engage with your swordsmen first, with macemen following right behind your swords and/or with a hefty group of maces to hit the AI in the flank. ALWAYS use your knights to engage in the AI's flank AFTER they have initiated your melee units. Crossbows will sit right behind the melee lines and fire away. As for the AI's boiling oil pots, just send in 1 knight to tip them over before sending in your main force.
It's okay to train up a ton of army after you have made tons of weapons and garisoned your castle. If you've got 25 happiness, that's okay, either tax your people 0 or 1%. If you're gonna run out of money because you've been spending it on iron and wood to make weapons, just sell 10 or 15 swords, or knights here and there. It's okay to lose some more population due to unhappiness after raising an army. Because with an army at this size and professionalism, it can smash any AI army, because they all have peasants. Just make sure to front line with your armoured units, flank with your fast units, and dont let your ranged get touched.

First off I have to ask you if you've played the original. If you answered no to this question then I'd like to break it down for you; this game was a pioneer in it's time, and it's a relic from that past. When Jet Set Radio was initially released in 2000 it was an odd duckling, the closest comparison at the time was Tony Hawk's Pro Skater. At first glance it's a quirky skating game with shoddy camera control (limited by the technology at the time,) but it's much more than that; Jet Set Radio is an expression of freedom. Jet Set's story revolves around the idea of feelin' the soul of the street, feeling the funky vibes juiced out by Professor K. It was an artist's DIY dream, at least at the time. While you can collect the various 'souls of the street' (unlockable in-game graffiti) you also have the options to create your own graffiti. The graffiti interface isn't sophisticated, rather it feels like using MSPaint, but with some practice you can produce stunning graffiti. This game is about your personal involvement, your personal investment into that soul. Do you feel or, do you create, or do you just jive?
My earliest memories of this game will be one of the most cherished of my gaming experiences. I did not know what to expect, could not fathom what I was seeing in this old tale of Tokyo-to; it's about the direct rejection of commercialized culture, manufactured and souless creation. You do face rival gangs through-out the game, each one having their own style, their own call sign and graffiti, but the central focus is foiling the plot driven by the Rokkaku group, and it's owner Goji Rakkaku. The core concept of the game is to spray paint, or 'tag', enemy territories which gains you reputation in those areas. The controls can be a tad frustrating, requiring simple timing for Quick-Time-Event graffiti tagging, and at times the came can be really frustrating, limiting you to a front view and not allowing to properly survey the area which can cost you some life points. Thankfully Jet Set Radio is relatively forgiving, spacing out health packs through the level when you make up, or if you run into aforementioned control of camera struggles and lose a huge bar of health.
Case and point, one should not go in playing Jet Set Radio without first considering the era in which it was created. The music is undeniably 90's with several little sprinkles of Shibuya-kei tracks, electronica, it leaves a pleasant quirky japanese taste in your mouth. Were this game to be judged by todays standards it would reach a low rating, from about a 6.5 - 7.2. It's release is clearly aimed to fans of the series (JSR and JSRF,) who have been waiting to see an HD release or mention of a sequel. All considered, Jet Set Radio's real heart lies behind its charm, and if you can get over some of it's technical limitations then you will find yourself a true treat.

One of my favorite games of all time on the Dreamcast.  The visuals were jaw-dropping gorgeous, bright and detailed in their day and do not look at all dated or cheesy when rendered at 1080p with 4xAA.  The music is so unique and addictive that I played levels over and over again just to hear them.  Gameplay emphasizes movement, staying moving without hesitation, confidence as you progress in mastery of the controls to achieve heights in which a badly timed move will send you plumeting.  The PC version is essentially a perfect copy of the Dreamcast, though the framerate has a tendency to glitch (not present on the PS3 version), and also while the keyboard controls are well-thought out, I suggest playing this game with a good controller.  I bought this game on PC, PS3, iOS _and_ Android when it comes out because on Nexus 10 will be the best-looking platform for it, period, with the 2600x1600 screen and Sixaxis game controller.

Before you buy this game, realize it is very early in development and it is being developed by a single person.
Boundel is an old school mmo. Really gave me flashbacks to the Ever Quest days. It features an open world, classless progression, and "skill" based combat (No tab targeting).
- Cons -
- The dev is no graphical master, the textures are sub par for todays standards and the models are very low poly.
- The movement is questionable at times, getting stuck an what little clutter is on the ground. There is no jumping and the movement speed is very slow.
- Monsters are pretty unbalanced at this point. Level 22 mobs spawning with starting mobs. I once had a level 300 or so manticore spawn basically right beside town and kill me.
- On death you drop all your money and lose durability on gear. So far, there is no way to repair gear and it is destroyed uppon hitting 0 durability. As the game is heavly based on gear this can become really annoying with constant deaths.
- The server pop is usually under 10, which is very unfortunate.
- The ui is very limited and confusing at times. Lots of information on how stats work or what your total stats are is just not show.
- Pros -
- There is a lot of potential with the skill system. Unfortunately it's just really limited and bland at this point.
- There is a tonne of world to explore (albeit limited right now on what there is to find there and the diversity in locations)
This game has POTENTIAL, so much potential but unfortunately it's just not there yet. As of writing this review the game is on sale for about a buck. If you are at all interested I say pick it up to help support the dev but don't expect anything special right now.
- Things I would like to see in future updates -
- Better and clearer UI with more information available to the player.
- Item sorting in inventory.
- A way to repair gear. Items not being destroyed at 0 durability (Leave them as unusable).
- A better tutorial for new players.
- A way to obtain or fill out an ingame map.
- More races and character customization.
- Graphical improvements across the board (Models, textures, animations).
- Performance improvements.
- Standard attributes worked into the leveling system.
- More frequent quests.
- Party/grouping/guild systems.
- Combat balancing.
- Increased duration on buffs and summons (Longest as far as I can tell is 90s on a buff and most are almost half that)
- Hotkey on item pouch

I will always have fond memories of playing Archeage with my friends. Going to Mirage Isle and driving around the island with the cars nobody could afford and build, perusing the different house designs that we knew neither of us would be able to own and look at the awesome assortment of ships that were rare to see, due to their high cost.) Despite the one crippling flaw, the looming pay wall that cast a dark shadow on the whole game, our friendships and the adventures to be had kept us playing.
And so it was for hundreds and hundreds of hours (not reflected here since we played on the Glyph gaming service.) Sick of the limiting factors of having a default account, we invested in patron (the lowest tier of the subscription service) that allowed us to own a house. After being unable to find a home in our continent, we travelled to the other side and established our houses there. Of course like much of the rest of the roleplaying elements it was a pointless endeavour, since buying blueprints for and actually building, furniture was outrageously expensive and the house serving no real purpose than to exist. The only use of owning land was farming, which you could do by purchasing seeds and baby animals from the many stores throughout the world. Farming was on a timer, and required labour points to do (you regenerated labour points every few minutes. No points= no farming/building.)
So then we built our boats. After grinding the ridiculous Gildastar (To buy blueprints for houses, boats and vehicles you need to use a special currency called gildastars, because screw your gold!)  We purchased blueprints to the skimmer (the cheapest and only sailboat that any normal player can ever afford) and constructed them. We went sailing around the world, the crest of our small clan flying proudly on the sails.
In order to get more gildastars, to be able to buy the cool ships and houses, you need to go on traderuns. To do a traderun, you need to collect resources, craft a tradepack and take it to a location on the world, with a small number of these coins as a reward. Domestic traderuns are easy but pay terrible, due to the relative safety and protection of your continent. International traderuns nearly always descended into anarchy, as trade run routes were always set and as such preyed by high level players. Either way, we stopped traderuns when we realised that it was pointless.
So we invested more into the progression and combat in the game. There are hundreds of classes you can choose from, almost all of them useless. You can change your class ingame, which you will most likely do when you realise your selected class sucks. Quests consist primarily of fetch and kill objectives with no real depth or interesting content. Had it not been for my friends grinding alongside me, I would not have bothered at all. After nearly 400+ hours of ingame time, I still have no idea what most of the quests I did were about.
So then we decided to travel around the world. This is a strength of Archeage. The world is BEAUTIFULLY rendered and stunning. Much of the fun that we had was climbing up mountains, exploring the northern and eastern continents, meeting enemy players in peaceful zones and dancing with them. Thanks to the glider, you're able to glide through the air for a few minutes which is a cool feature. The different environments of the continents are also incredible and add to the depth of adventure. The large forests and European-esque architecture of Nuia, and the long grass and humid plains of Haranya are beautiful and fun to explore, but sadly quite shallow when you realise there's nothing much there.
So then we decided to make a clan. Through a special item you are able to import your own crest into the game and have it displayed on your cape and ship's sails. Clan politics was an aspect of the game we never really touched, since the mainstream clans were far out of our league. The in-game economy, an aspect that's well advertised about the game was crippled by gold traders, who spammed their ads in the chatbox and were never dealt with.
So when our Archeage adventure came to an end and we turned around, it became apparent to us just how flawed Archeage really is. The paywall that shut us out of much of the game's content, the repetitive quests and the boring player progression. Archeage will go down in history as being an MMORPG with such great potential that was ultimately squandered by a terrible money system and incompetent developers. It's a big shame really.

This game succeeds in replicating all of the fun we once had in the dungeon keeper titles.  Unfortunately that is where the problem with this title is as well.  I would not so much say that this game isn't recommended.  It just is not worth the price that it currently goes for.  When this goes on special (75% off at least)- take it.
It does have replayability in exactly the same sence as the old dungeon keeper games had - that is to say, doing exactly the same over and over again (because it was fun).  For me, this doesn't translate so much in modern gaming.
Further more, it was a massive surprise to learn that coop wasn't available for the campaign.   The campaign itself is rather easy and very short.  Skirmish and sandbox modes are pretty much just free for all bash - ups being made moderately fun by the swathe of different map designs out there.
Does this game succeed in what it sets out to do?  Absolutely.  It brings an old, nostalgic experience into modern times.  That in itself begs the question - do you buy this game or get Dungeon Keeper 2 to work on your current os?  The latter wont cost you any money and all you sacrefice is the graphics.
Technically this game is a disaster.  It chews up pc resources equal to something double its size and depth.  The graphics are pretty, particles are sweet and animations are "okay" - yet this beast eats up more resources on both my pc's than just about anything I have.  I'd go so far as to suspect that there may be some serious memory leakage going on or just not very clever design.
Again, this game isn't all that bad but I can find very few reasons to recommend it based on its current price.  As someone who played dungeon keeper for years, this game could hardly provide me with any reason to do so beyond 5 hours (that is how long it took me to complete the campaign).   Mind you, it appears the average playtime for the campaign varies between 6 to 12 hours, so do not use my time as the average.  Some of us grind harder than others :)
Coupled with the lack of any kind of intelligable innovation, the technical presentation of this title is atrocious.  Something "appearing" of this quality should at least be half way better designed.  I'm not sure if it is bad resource management or perhaps bias towards more mainstream hardware combinations.  What I can say is that between the group of friends I play with, all of us experience this kind of issue where the game is just hogging an inordinate amount of resources.  Things like this can be polished out with further tweaks from the developers whom appear to be quite active in community engagement (although, i would note in a very quetionable manner not befitting PR).
Multiplayer:
Coop campaigns are not existing yet.  It doesn't look like they will either.
Multiplayer is stock standard player vs player or player & player vs AI (this is what they deem coop - beware those steam tags).
The game devours resources so you can imagine what a horrible experience multiplayer becomes with 4 players on a large map.  That is, IF you can get the game to work on multiplayer.
Multiplayer requires you to download their little guide (or just go read the resources) so as to unblock the required ports and the likes.  Yes folks, we are talking peer to peer multiplayer.  Not only is this problematic for a whole swathe of players to set up, but (do i need to say this really?) it is NOT SECURE.  Not recommended (dont take my word for it - use google).
In closing,
The game is one of those "could have beens".  It could have been great, it could have been really fun.  And, hey, it still is for a few hours.  But not at that price.  You can buy 4 good indie games for the same price that would each provide you four to five times the play time.
Thus this is purely a title you'll invest in out of nostaliga and nothing else.  Guaranteed.
My recommendation:

The great thing about this is that it is very similar to Dungeon Keeper in its basic design, but with some graphical updates and new stuff to play with. There are some minor refinements, like that the campaign never requires you to use the first-person "possession" mode. It's fun, and could absolutely pass for a sequel to Dungeon Keeper, so it's reasonably worthwhile if you liked Dungeon Keeper. And it supports Linux, which is the reason I bought it.
However, it also has a small number of significantly annoying issues.
There isn't that much content! As you can see, it took me 33 hours to complete the game and DLC, and I play slowly and restarted several levels. Maybe the multiplayer is good, but I have not tried it.
Compared to Dungeon Keeper, the level design is a little bit rough with respect to discovering what you should do. In several levels I had to restart multiple times because there was some point on the map I was supposed to rush (because the scenario becomes unplayably hard past a certain number of minutes, so there is no time to  e.g. train minions) or NOT rush (because doing a certain thing causes every enemy in the level to pour down at once, or because it gets your minions wasted when the particular level provides no way to replace them), but no way to discover this without screwing up. This reduces the fun somewhat. The levels play significantly smoother in "Heart of Gold."
A Dungeon Keeper game doesn't need an amazing plot, but this still suffered from writing issues. The "plot" was so overbearing and lame that I'd rather have just played the scenarios without any plot, and I did not find the humor up to the Dungeon Keeper standard. To be clear, I enjoy dark humor. It made the game embarrassing to play in the room with other people and if I knew a sequel had the same writing, I probably wouldn't buy it.
There are also way, way too many confusing and irrelevant messages in-game, kickstarter in-jokes I guess; they feel almost constant and they are distracting and sometimes misleading. I really would have liked to be able to skip all that.
The cutscenes aren't really skippable and it would have been nice to be able to check the text from these like a "mission briefing" instead of being forced to sit through the really slow pan-arounds (which were more annoying for the performance issues). This would have been less of an issue except that the content of the cutscenes was so lame.
And there are some performance issues, nothing unplayable, but the game can get pretty choppy even on a fairly recent video card. I found myself avoiding the "reveal map" ability because it made the game unplayably slow.

Well. Where to begin.
To start off, i played dungeon keeper 2, never really dungeon keeper 1. I LOVED dk2. Absolutely played the hell out of it.
Obviously i cant play that anymore, so for ages i looked for a worthy successor to Bullfrog's games.
This game will do.
You can clearly see they've been inspired by the dungeon keeper series.
You start off with your hand, a dungeon heart that you need to protect, and some imps. With your hand, you can mark tiles for your imps to dig and claim for you. Then you can make rooms into the space you've dug out like a library, a lair where your minions rest, or a pig farm where your minions can feed on succulent pig flesh (They make such a satisfying splatter noise when you eat them), or a workshop where certain minions can build traps and doors to guard your dungeon.
As the game progresses, you get access to more rooms like the prison, torture chamber, graveyard or Sanctuary. You also unlock more defenses and spells, giving you more options during battle, planning your dungeon or keeping your gold up to level.
The campaign by itself is pretty decent, here and there are a few bugs the devs havent fixed yet, but nothing game-breaking as far as i could tell. I would also recommend the Heart of Gold DLC pack for another campaign, as that one was also nice to play, and adds a few extras.
Campaign however, is not the only thing you can play. You can skirmish against other Underlords, with AI that you can ramp up or reduce the difficulty of as you please, there are sandbox maps where you get a dungeon heart, lots and lots of space to build and dig and roomify as you please, with an inert hero portal and controls for it so you can choose when you want to have heroes banging on your doors.
There are a few things that require adjustment, but i wouldn't say they make the game unplayable, just a bit annoying sometimes.
Overall i'd say this game is a solid 7/10. Not as great as i had hoped, but it's not bad. Not bad at all.

Ok, let me get this out with: I have played it's prequel. Hated it. Don't ask me why. I just did. Good game, nice graphics, interesting combat. I hated it nonetheless.

I read up, tried a few different skill combinations, group options and skill synergies. And it worked. D:OS2 has many many fantastic elements - awesome exploration, a beautiful world, challenging combat with nuanced tactics. I'm just happy I decided to give it one final go. Now, who knows, maybe I'll try it's prequel again.

I got this for free and finally booted it up because it got achievements.  What is this, Wolfenstein?  Well.....no...
It's World War II (AGAIN) and you're a Nazi soldier fighting off some disgruntled citizens before fighting mutants and then your own troops.  (Because plot)   Contrary to the gameplay trailers and teasers, this is NOT a tower defense game.  You're simply trying to reach a target location while gunning down, burning, and zapping enemies that are in your way.  That said, you do not have to kill everything in your way, and sometimes you can just walk right through....sometimes.  (Don't always do this because you'll often get swarmed)   You'll run out of ammo often and will basically end up taking down tanks with a knife.....and it works.......
PROS:
Knife can blow up a tank...by stabbing it.
Not TOO buggy in terms of the controls.
Can be a little fun, but the fun is relatively short-lived.
Short, easy achievements.
Original monster designs.
Has a feeling similar to "The Culling of the Cows".
Not TERRIBLE for a first game project.
CONS:
Under normal circumstances, it costs $2.99
Death animations for burn and zap are the same, no matter the enemy.
VERY lackluster story.
ANOTHER Nazi Germany game based in World War II.
Pressing ESCAPE closes the game.
Pressing Shift-Tab closes the game.
Pressing Alt-Tab closes the game.
Cutscenes are not animated.  Some go by automatically leaving you a limited time to read it.
That's a lot of cons, yeah?  I will say I kinda' liked it.   But do I recommend it?   No.  If anything, this seems to be a free game with a price tag.  If it was free, I can see myself recommending this, despite the cons.  If you ever get it for free, try it out.  Aside from that, you should probably avoid this game unless you don't mind the price tag.
So....how do I rate this?   3/10? ....Too lenient.   2/10?  .....Too harsh.  Let's split the difference.
2.5/10   A free game with a price tag and has little imagination.

The music gets old fast and the game balance is all over the place.
You can't see all the waves at the start so you can't choose an appropriate loadout for half the maps without having played through most of it already and unavoidably lost.
The traps become available as you complete maps yet unlike any other tower defense the availability is almost directly proportional to how far you are through the game.  I got really tired of not having all the tools I wanted for any given map.
Also there's a lot of random chance involved in trap behavior and enemy movement.  Maybe your pusher trap will catch a whole lot of enemies, or maybe it will only push one!  Even if you set things up to clump up enemies the pusher will sometimes just fail to work properly or miss some of the clump.  There's serious reliability issues, which makes the fast-moving enemies that ignore demons (one of the best ways to control enemy movement) MAJOR problems, even if you plan for them.  You basically just have to hope that the setup you have is enough for whatever the level throws at you.
I don't like having to HOPE.  I want to be able to PLAN.
Edit: okay, now you can see what all the units in each wave are by scrolling the waves.  Yet that doesn't solve some of the most irritating problems with this game: MASS UNITS.  The game loves to throw like 50 of one type at you, and if your setup isn't specifically made to deal with that and actually WORKS to deal with that, you're screwed.  There are just too many enemy units that require specific traps to deal with, especially with runes enabled.

This game is a piece of art.
Developed by a pretty unknown studio the game has been being developed since 2006. It changed hands to Gamersfirst and the game has continued to be developed. (Gamersfirst might not be the best group to own the game but they keep it running)
The game is the culmination of a lot of different games that always got some things right but never went any further.
The game as a very robust crafting system with nearly 90% of the items found in game being craftable. (The other 10% is usually unique item drops or materials for crafting.)
The combat system while at times can be a bit wonky requires people to aim their shots and attacks (Something that a lot of people look for in an MMO today)
If you enjoy games like Fallout, Fallout 2, Fallout Tactics, Wasteland, or Wasteland 2 (This is in regards to the Genre and crafting/party system) Then this game is most likely going to fall into the Niche of games that you'll die for.
The game has a die-hard fan base that has kept it runing through the transitions and the bad times. The game has undergone a ton of updating and in the near future another sector will be added to the game. (Essentially another expansion.)
Many people discredit the game because of graphical glitches or a poorly designed tutorial. (Which graphics don't matter but the tutorial is credible.) Yet the game continues to find ways to bring people into the world.
The mythos of the game is incredible. The storylines are interesting and they dialogue is engaging. (Dialogue here meaning Text, you have to read =P ) I cannot find a lot to say about the game that is at fault.
PvP has consequences on the world and the Factions that battle it out are fun to engage with and make the game interesting to say the least with "Politics" in game. The economy is for the most part player driven and this engages people even more that like to play the market.
All in all this game is a solid 7/10 and hell it's free, so what are you waiting for? GET OUT THERE AND MAKE ME PROUD! I'll see you in the wastes.

The metagame of GemCraft, the upgrade system of Kingdom Rush, and the trap selection of Orcs Must Die. I mean that quite literally; elements of those games are shamelessly copy-pasted here, but rather than ending up like a round of "spot the stolen assets in this shovelware Unity game", they're put to excellent use to make one of the most impressive tower defense games yet seen.
It does have some pretty intense difficulty spikes, though. "Heroes Must Die" is where you'll really have to start putting on your thinking cap and abusing the level layouts as much as possible. It's kind of disappointing that the difficulty gradually mandates the pickiest minmaxing possible, and it also seems to drop mouse clicks on occasion which is frustrating when things get frantic. Still an addictive little package, and even comes with a level editor. I sprung for the mobile version too, and it's equally awesome minus the level editor.

Item durability/loss.

The core puzzle mechanic initially feels unnecessarily restrictive but once you've trained your brain to think in tetrominoes the game really starts to shine.
Most stages contain a 'Block That Matters', a treasure chest that is difficult to reach which contains a collectable block that references popular video games and ties in to the name of the level. These unlockables will bring a smile to the face of a lifelong gamer and provide instant replayability.
The music and art are similarly well done. However, the story and its characters are cheeseball and fall completely flat.
Nearly every puzzle rewards a strategic mind, but the few that rely on twitch reflexes quickly become infuriating as you battle sometimes sloppy controls (I can't tell you how many times I jumped up a narrow path and was SURE I avoided hitting my head on dripping lava, only to be killed. When I finally completed each passage, I didn't feel like I did anything different - just dumb luck).
All in all, Blocks That Matter was an enjoyable puzzle/platformer and I plan on returning to grind out a few more unlockables.

THIS IS A REVIEW POST GAME POST EVERYTHING (2016)
______________________________________________________________
NOTE: I have new OS and harddrives and transferred saves (ported saves from consoles), in total I have accumulated over 1,000 hours in this game as a rough estimate.
This game rocks.
Plain and simple this game is one of the best open world roleplaying experiences out there in the last 20 years of video game history. The character creation and flexible build your own character is simply bar none the best and easy experiences to use. I would put Skyrim up there but I truly believe Oblivion's class system downright outshines Skyrim everyday of the week.
The story is pretty straightforward, Sir Stewart (yes the emperor is voiced by none other than infamous J. Picard) urges you to take the Amulet of Kings to find his last son Sean Bean (Borimir's redemption) or "Martin" and close the Oblivion gates forever.
The game will hold your hand a tad in the beginning, but once you finish the opening quest it is all down hill from there. You can literally do anything and everything you ever wanted after. See a sick dungeon to crawl through? Go for it. Join the Mages Guild? Of course. Kill everyone and everything in sight as a mad sociopath? Cut loose.
Guilds and Sidequests feel fluid, but you can sometimes get caught in the infamous Bethesda game loop (Get quest > enter dungeon > kill baddies > get loot > get quest thing > return to sender). There are some amazing quests however that really make you appreciate the complexity of the game (Whodunit, The Collector, Taking care of lex, Kvatch, Knights of the White Stallion) and make you want to keep playing. Deadric quests are a good sense of fun, the level caps keeps you going long after some of the quests you've done are long completed and the hidden locations are awesome to discover.
The biggest replayability factor involved with this game currently is the slew of mods you could play. Some of the best quests ever to exist in video games are of mods in Oblivion (Tears of the Fiend, The Lost Spires, Malevolent) and other awesome add ons really add to the game in ways that the Devs couldn't.
This is and old game, and has a few issues with it (as always with any game) but there are some issues I want to make note of on my end that could help you and better your experience:
- The game sometimes will crash on a load, or won't entirely quit out (I run triple monitors only using 1 as my game screen)
- FOR WIN 10 USERS: Net Framework 3.5 is needed to run some older programs and mods if you go this route. Make sure you can still install 3.5 (most mods will not need this, just refer to the nexus community for help on that), I couldn't find any reasonable solution for it myself.
Other than that it is a solid game. A game that has outlasted its time and its outdated graphics to still be one of my favorite games of all time. I recommend this game to everyone even if they do not like RPGs. There is something for everyone to love.

The tactics involved in playing this game are layered endlessly. If NF has reason to believe you might be heading for straight for railgun heavies, you should respond with a light tank or APC rush early game (unless they are expecting you to, of course). Commanding actual players is extremely challenging but endlessly rewarding. Much like Age of Empires II, the gameplay does not reach any sort of nash-equilibria because the real bottleneck is your own ability to keep track of everything at once.
For the soldiers on the ground, the game is totally different. The tactical challenge lies is choosing your class, or the loadout of your tank, and in making sure that the decisions of the team as a whole make sense, and that nobody is missing some sneaky enemy tactic. The constant challenge otherwise is of course, to aim and respond, using cover to keep yourself alive while gaining ground on the enemy. All of the guns respond decently, but you'll find your preferences - I love the sniper and pistol, but many prefer the shotguns. Fortunately none of them are so overpowered that they become the only choice.
Unfortunately, although there are many players, most of the time none of them are playing at all. That's why you will see many people arguing over whether the game is "dead" or not. See for yourself with the

Golf With Your Friends by Blacklight Interactive based on the book "Golf With Your Friends" really lives up to it's hype. Although I prefer the book like a normie, I'll still give this game credit where it's due.
Golf With Your Friends is as graphically beautiful as any game of this perspective has ever been. Everything on the screen speaks of attention to loving detail and thoughtful placement, whether it's the arrangement of weeds on the grass or the animations of a golf ball rolling.
It's richly written, too, with everything from the descriptions of the settings in the menu to how aids you can make the game by putting on zero gravity with a pyramid shaped golf ball.
As with so many things in this world golf with your friends encourages you to experiment and hunt for the holes in the strangest places as they're only marked by a giant ♥♥♥♥ off pole. Sometimes you'll find a ghost who's magically floating around a haunted house that for some reason has a golf course in, and that ghost loves to mess up your entire life as he trys to hunt you down and kill you.
As one would imagine, the impact of agolf ball on the lives of the players family is immense and sprawling, so the reflections of players family reflectively vast: spanning from your Mum & Dad's professional ambitions, to the horrors of an undiagnosed infant, to uncle sSteve's bathing rituals, to his impact on the childhood of his older sister.
There is not only tragedy in this family’s story; it’s funny and moving and hopeful as well. But the tragedy doesn’t come from the player’s diagnosis, it comes from watching two loving parents attempting the impossible task of plugging into their child’s brain to know how he’s doing, and by extension, how they’re doing as parents. And watching them grapple with the dark thoughts and frustrations that arise out of that impossible task.
Despite all of these images and powerful performances, we never exactly solve the issue of why we're playing golf.
A format that tends to beg for a beginning, middle and end. But this game doesn't, it has no end and there is no end for golf is life.

I will try not to be too critical in this review. This game is great, but there are a lot of things that I absolutely cannot stand about it.
1. AI Drivers/Police
This topic is widely discussed by many players. To me, it feels like SCS was very lazy in creating the AI drivers, which is, in my opinion, one of the most important aspects of the game. The AI drivers are all over the place, and they will take turns when they want to, not when it is safe. I have found this very frustrating when I have lost thousands of dollars because an AI driver took a left turn right into my trailer or when merging onto the highway and that mustang comes and smashes right into the back of you. The police are another big problem in this game. They totally do not care about how fast they are going, but will give you a ticket for going 3 over the limit. I've seen a police car go whizzing by me at 65-70mph in a 55mph speed zone.
2. Barriers/Railroad Crossings
This is another topic that I feel SCS has not taken into account correctly and were very lazy when creating. When coming up on a railroad crossing, if the lights are flashing (but the barriers have not yet dropped down) an invisible barrier is placed where the barriers of the crossing that drop down would go. This makes it very frustrating when I'm going the speed limit of 55-80 mph along the road and the lights start flashing. I know that I don't have enough time to break, so my truck, trailer, and I are all screwed. I usually just pause the game and cancel the delivery because there's nothing I can do about it. Super frustrating driving hundreds of miles just to have it ruined because the creators of the game were lazy.
3. Speed Limits/Signs
For one, some of the speed limits are SUPER unrealistic, and wouldn't be considered safe in the real world. But the main thing is the speed limit signs. I try to play this game super realistically and not look at the GPS at all (even though I still have to every couple of minutes), but it just isn't possible. Some speed limit signs read "70mph" when the real speed limit is 55. I usually only go by these signs but I am starting to have to use the GPS more because I am getting unnecessary tickets for going "over the limit". Another problem I have is the change of speed limits. When pulling into a weight station, the speed limit is 15 mph, but you could be traveling on a 55mph highway. Going from 55 to 15 in the small amount of seconds it gives you to do so is nearly impossible, thus me receiving more unnecessary tickets. I find this ridiculous and really think that SCS was very lazy on, again, one of the most important aspects of the game.
4. Damage
The damage of the trailers is VERY unrealistic. I made a turn once and the very back tire of the trailer that I was hauling touched the dirt on the side of the road while making the turn. I was INSTANTLY hit with 5% damage on the trailer, all because Wal-Mart had to keep their precious tire all clean. Hitting signs by accident is the same story, except you get about 15% damage instead of 5%, which is super ridiculous. Side swiping a barrier or car will give you a whopping 20-35% damage on your truck and trailer, and don't even get me started about hitting barriers by accident at high speeds...
Like I said in the beginning, this is a great game. I just feel that SCS were very lazy with the development and did not take enough time (if any at all) to go over some of the key aspects of the game. I hope you found this review helpful.
