Burgers is a casual and very short, WW2 themed, side-scrolling twin-stick shooter made using Unity.  The only campaign can be played in singleplayer or coop mode.
For the most part the game is a let down with not enough levels of play, and those that are there are over too quickly.  The nice cartoony graphics and fast-moving gameplay make it hard to dislike.  The controls are rock-solid but the audio somewhat underwhelming.  Characters and weapons can be swapped in-game but only between playing sessions.  It seems that the developers may have been going for a free game with MT options for the weaponary and character selections but changed their minds during development.
There is a promising core of minimal features and gameplay in Burgers but at the moment it is far from being a product I could recommend.  Its lack of seriousness makes the game endearing but only worth a look if brought in a sale.  In short its a budget title that might be worth a dollar to someone.  Just because I dont recommend it, it doesnt mean you wont like it.
Casual, side-scrolling, twin-stick shooter
Alternative monster-ridden World War II theme
You play the role of a German soldier towards the end of the war (or other character) in an area that is about to become infested by alien looking monsters controlled by evil mind-controlling sphere.
There is only one campaign comprising of seven or so levels, which do not have to be played sequentially once unlocked.  It can be played in single-player and coop modes.
Only basic gameplay makes it into this game.  Basic movement, shooting direction, weapon changes and  ammo pick-ups are about all there is.  Enemies come in a few guises and some hide behind cover, while boss battles happen across most of the campaign levels.
There is a shop that uses credits earned for completing missions to buy new or upgraded weapons and change starting characters.  There are quite a few to choose from even if you can only carry three weapons (main rifle, pistol and knife.)  You also receive a handful of grenades which are best kept for bosses or vehicles/tanks.
Levelling is automatic with XP earned shown at the end of a mission, auto-upgrading character stats and unlocking the most powerful weapons.
While there is little wrong with the design I did find it somewhat minimal and inconsistent in terms of the game's overall vision.  Seems the devs may have started out making a game with MTs and then changed their minds.  Unless of course there is an iOS/tablet version which I would not have heard of.
As you would expect from a side-scroller enemies appear from the right of the screen and are fairly static therefore only providing a challenge in numbers or with higher protection.  There is a low to fair mix of enemies; humans in the guise of armed civilians or German soldiers together with a mashing of different aliens collectively form the mass of enemies you will face.  There are some bosses to defeat but only your inability to control your character will stop you from progressing.
In keeping with expectations game design is basic.  It works as a twin-stick shooter and my general feeling was that while it is devoid of alot of detail a good core was there to build upon.
Basic.  Unfortunately with most of the action appearing from the right of screen there are not many surprises and thus it doesnt need to be much more.
I used keyboard by default.  Optionally mouse can be used for shooting.  Overall they are solid and responsive.  Can also use controller but did not do so during my play sessions.
Very good.  Cartoony.  Depictions of soldiers and enemies are cute if nothing else.  Backdrops are limited to two or three locations with slight varations to give that extra dimension.  Perhaps the games best graphics are the representations of the weapons taken from WW2 and beyond.  Though the sprinkling of cutscenes that explain the story are apt.  Sadly though thats it.

As ludicrous as it might sound, I've grown to disregard puzzles in adventure games. I could love the script and adore the graphics but the gameplay itself rarely left on me any impression whatsoever. Then I played Gemini Rue.
What really strikes me about GR is how well its authors understood the concepts behind an adventure game. There are numerous games in which puzzles serve no more purpose than to slow the player down. This is not the case.
GR never ceases to be a coherent experience with its own logic and sense of freedom. Even when you're stuck, the game doesn't suddenly become a 2D background with several hotspots that you'll spend the next half an hour randomly combining with yourself and your junk. Puzzles never stand out but are an integral part of the story.
Gemini Rue is the game that I’d choose if asked to define adventure games. It’s not the pinnacle of the genre but it combines every last little thing that makes adventure games special.

Note: This game been tried out and reviewed in Steam offline mode or on Consoles.
Jet Set Radio is an original Dreamcast game came to the PSN, XBLA, and PC digital download.
Jet Set Radio takes place in an alternate Tokyo; Tokyo-to. Tokyo-to is a city where hip-hop/grafitti is the dominant culture and rollerskates are the transportation method of choice, at least amongst the gangs in town. You play as various characters from a local gang known as the GGs. Gameplay is simple. You skate around the city, grinding and jumping, and spray graffiti at marked locations, to assert GGs presence in the streets or wipe out rival gangs
Learning to skate in Jet Set Radio is kind of hard. Controlling your character isn't that intuitive, and accuracy in your movements is very important. There isn't that much lenience. If you screw up, you'll screw up. Sometimes it feels like your character has a mind of its own. Movement is definitely the weakest part of the game, However, the slightly awkward movement didn't stop it from being ridiculously fun. Gameplay is varied and level design is consistently well thought out. There isn't a dull level in the game.
Graphically and artistically, Tokyo-to is represented beautifully. It is clear that meticulous effort was taken in designing the city, which feels very familiar if you've been to Tokyo, but way cooler. This port looks great on the PC. At 1920x1080 it looks awesome thanks to cel-shaded characters and a highly developed cartoon style. Coupled with a very cool, slightly obscure upbeat hip-hop soundtrack, you can get lost in the world for quite some time.
The game has alot of replay value with the unlockables and I find myself playing it over and over even though I have everything unlocked on the Dreamcast.
Overall: Jet Grind Radio/Jet Set Radio remains simply one of the best games I have ever played, on the Dreamcast, if you have a Dreamcast you need to buy it right now. or on the PC but i still recommend it on the DC.
Note: I Love Dreamcast forever,ouh it is still right next to me here by the way

If this game was over $5 USD, this would be a negative review, that's how borderline the review is. The early gameplay is enjoyable enough, but later sections abandon the casual puzzle elements to push timed and precision platforming. By the end, Blocks really don't Matter, as they do nothing new in the later half. It's a mixed-up and clunky game, almost guaranteed to frustrate anyone by the end.
I was initially interested in the gameplay and story, both of which slowly fall apart. The game features seven core block types, and hides secrets behind special blocks you can't break at first. The character upgrade system feels decent, giving reason to replay older levels with new abilities. The number of upgrades is very small in fact, and the later blocks behave very similar to others. Gems are just a harder Stone, and Obsidian is an unbreakable Sponge. Puzzles become fairly stale towards the end of the game, with the extra Chocolate Castle levels adding some fresh changes.
The clunky controls and character that is literally a block makes things more difficult. Later levels rely heavily on guiding AI that will one-hit kill you, avoiding drops that will one-hit kill you, and traversing areas that allow no mistakes to slow you down. This is not a casual puzzler, and not a game about digging. It quickly expects precision and minimal mistakes.
It seems the game ran out of ideas near the end, and just turned up the difficulty in timing precise moves. There is an awkward level editor with very little information on how it works, and some extra levels that again rely on AI usage to solve puzzles. It's been some time since the game stumped me into an "Aha" moment. I feel the game makes references to other games to create conversations, as this game is not of the quality of its influences.
If you are looking for a relaxing game that will challenge your mind, I would look elsewhere. I've been enjoying Qbeh recently, it has nice puzzles with a great atmosphere and a push for exploration. Blocks That Matter fails to impress. Check videos or the demo, and know that the game pushes heavily into platforming in the later half. If you are still interested, it's not a regretable purchase at base price. I'd still recommend waiting for a sale, you aren't missing anything by waiting. Yes, this isn't a positive review, but the game is very mediocre.

Sure you can get decent gear from grinding out gold (which it what i did, I never put more than like $100 into this game aside from subscription) but you will NEVER catch up. It is literally impossible. By the time you grind to get gear where you can do %25 of someones health before dying, it will be time for the game to update, releasing better gear. The people who spend money will have that gear in days, where it would take the genuine players like 6+ months.
Also, the only people still playing this game are the ones who have put thousands of dollars into it, so unless you want someone to farm you for honor every day, don't even think about playing this. Hopefully the game will die like it deserves to and some other developer/publisher will make a game like this and do it right.

PROS:
- Tight mechanics
- Awesome audio/visual design, cyberpunk + 1000% edge.
- Great performance on mid-range hardware.
- Challenging and unforgiving, but not unfair and cheap.
CONS:
- No support for 5.1, output is locked to stereo. Best played with a Good pair of headphones.
- Occasional navigation issues due to lighting choices.
- Certain skill combinations feel a little overpowered near the end of the game, removing some of the tension which made the rest of the game so great. Could easily be balanced with a few tweaks.
- Could use some extra control options, such as a hold to activate skill over toggle and allocating extra keys for skills without having to use the radial menu.
- Switching skill sets mid battle needs streamlining, reallocating skill points so often breaks the flow of the game. Having the ability to make presets would be an easy fix for this.
CONCLUSION:
Ruiner is an absolute gem despite some rough edges. The whole experience feels cohesive in a way that most games don't even come close to, everything just works together so well.
The main complaint I hear about this game is that it can be a bit of a cluster♥♥♥♥ and deaths feel random and unfair at times. I didn't find this the case at all with my playthrough (Hard difficulty). Every death felt like my fault and usually was because I lost focus and started spamming inputs.
Using the hold and dodge mechanic to plan moves tactically and listening for audio cues is essential for survival, dashing around and mashing keys will get you killed every time.

It's still not fully optimized and still has a sticky U.I. in places, but I'm confident in saying this lives up to Dungeon Keeper now! It's definitely on par with the original two in terms of production quality and it's just going to get better from here. My favorite part is that you're basically playing an extra-dimensional demon in this one, with rival demons from other worlds and you're set on conquering a corrupt theocratic human empire. Pretty cool evolution on the DK story, even!  The singleplayer campaign is actually pretty well balanced/realized too.
It's a bit expensive for me to give it an easy recommendation, but put it on your radar if you want to experience Dungeon Keeper again.
Very interesting and engaging story. Makes me care a lot about all the characters.

Leaps and bounds better than the first game. The full voice acting is great. So many intricate details scattered throughout. This game is an ornate tapestry of rpg goodness. If you like Baldurs Gate,  Witcher, Deus Ex, X-Com and many more you will find something to enjoy here. The total freedom of being able to basically do anything you want within the games systems is so cool and rarely seen in any game. The music is amazing. Every fight and all the ambient music is a treat for the ears. The writing has much improved from the first game. I understand there is a lot of sarcasm and light heartedness but if you take it too far you undermine your own game. Thats my opinion anyway.
My only gripe is the balance. I have a 4 person party fully optimized with the best gear I can get and all skills I need and still im getting 1 shot by so many enemies. My tank is like a 2 shot. I know alot of it is picking your battles but unlike act 1 I have no more places to go to. Im stuck between 3 boss fights in act 2 and cant win any of them. Not sure how to proceed but I wont give up. This game is incredibly hard at most times.
